transcript: Simon & Schuster Audio presents Star Trek, First Contact by J.M. Dillard, read by Gates McFadden. Apethe, that was the greater evil. The card knew that an indifferent foe is more to be feared than one whose heart burns with honest hate. Apethe, it stretched out before him an infinite rose of face after flesh and metal face in a grey metal sea that knew no beauty, no appreciation of life, only the singular voice of the collective. He stood, the only living spot of color in a vast chamber, surrounded by thousands of cells, in each cell an upright Borg drone slept dreamlessly. This might be mindless, but not soulless. The Borg were both, and it was that fact which made him struggle when they pinned him down and slammed his head against the surgical table. As he stared up at his approaching fate, a silvery needle-sharp probe descending directly toward his eye, he thought, this is a foe I can never engage, for they will never care enough to return my hate. In the midst of his struggle an image came to him, a mouth, bloodless and Borg, and he heard not the thunderous voice of the collective but that of a woman. Hello, cuters. He shuddered at the sound of his own voice, the voice of the Borg. I am a low cuter, a Borg. Resistance is futile. At the very instant the probe pierced his eye, he screamed, not so much with pain as with pure rage of the enemy who did not care enough to hate. With a lurch to find himself, sitting on his couch in the ready room, he put a hand to his sweat dampened forehead, dismayed that he had dozed off while on duty and still alarmed by the intensity of the nightmare. He hastened to the small adjacent restroom and leaned low over the sink. Cold water on his face, again and again, washing away all traces of panic until his breathing slowed, and he had last dared rise to face his mirrored reflection. Low cuters. Abruptly he recalled the image of the ghost pale lips, a duct of luck utter in his Borg name. Try though he might, he could not remember the face attached to that mouth. As he stared into the mirror, a muscle just above his jaw spasmed, as though someone had plunged a needle from the inside of his mouth outwards through his cheek. It was accompanied by an odd sound that seemed to emanate from within Picard's own head. Impossible, of course, just tension brought on by the stress of the dream it would pass. But as he stood over the sink, the pain intensified and the muscle began to writhe continuously. When the last and sharpest burst of agony came, he gazed at his twitching cheek. The flesh trembled, then stretched out as if he were pressing hard from the inside with his tongue. At last the muscle tore and the skin burst. He stared in horrified fascination as darkly gleaming metal, slick with his own blood emerged from within him, a Borg servo. It rotated while Picard descended into mindless panic. Picard awoke, gasping on his own couch and abruptly sat up. He put a hand to his cheek to feel for the servo before realizing that he had awakened again from a nightmare, truly awakened. The couch and his arms beneath him were solid, real. The noise, too, was real. He rose from the couch and moved to the terminal and composed himself before tapping a control. A message coalesced on the screen. Incoming transmission. Starfleet Command to Captain J out the card, USS Enterprise NCC-1701-E, Command Authorization required. Authorization. The card. 4-7 Alpha Tango. The image on the screen faded at once, and was replaced by the image of Admiral Hayes at Starfleet headquarters. Catch you at a bad time, John Luke. No, of course not so. Hayes clearly did not believe the captain's reply, but the urgency of his message kept him from pursuing the matter. I've just received a disturbing report from Deep Space 5. Long-range sensors have picked up. The card interrupted. I know. The Borg. Surrounded by his senior crew, the card sat at the conference table in the observation lounge of the new Enterprise. The room was an elegant improvement over its predecessor. His most striking feature was a multitude of windows opening on to a star-littered indigo. A stunning sight. But the card could only think. All those sons, and orbiting them, how many habitable planets, and of those planets how many lifeforms are simulated by the Borg. How many cultures forever lost over the millennia, and how soon shall we join them? Six months earlier, he had sat in this room and stared up at the bulkhead, where models of all the Enterprise's previous incarnations A through D. Hung. He had already worked through his lingering sense of loss at his previous ship's destruction. The Enterprise D was irretrievably gone, but her spirit remained, permeating every atom, every cell of this vessel and her crew. Now Picard looked at his surroundings and dared not allow himself to feel attachment. This was merely another ship that might be lost. He drew his attention back to his staff. Data, riker, Troy, and Beverly. Their faces were the same, but they now wore the new uniforms, black, softened only by an inset at the shoulder and collarbone of dark gray. The effect was flattering, but a bit severe, and perhaps appropriate for the moment, given the devastating nature of the announcement he had just made. After his brief blunt statement that the Borg had reappeared, the expression grew somber, and five pairs of anxious eyes focused upon him. The fifth pair of eyes belonged to Jory LaForge, who, like the Enterprise E, seemed familiar yet changed. LaForge's visor had been replaced a short time before by electronic ocular implants, and Picard still felt mildly disconcerted every time he looked into his chief engineer's large eyes, with their dizzyingly intricate geometric designs, traced in black on starkly blue irises. Riker came to the point quickly. How many ships? One, and it's on a direct course for Earth. It will cross the Federation border in less than an hour. Admiral Hayes has begun mobilizing a fleet in the Taehfan sector. He hopes to stop the Borg before they reach Earth. Data, whose pale golden face reflected the concern he felt, courtesy of his activated emotion-ship, interjected. At maximum warp, it will take us three hours twenty-five minutes to reach. Picard swiveled in his chair to face the android. We're not going. Riker leaned forward, his dark eyebrows arching upward. What do you mean we're not going? Picard averted his gaze and stared out at the blurring stars. Our orders are to patrol the neutral zone in case the Romulans tried to take advantage of the situation. Deanna Troy was frankly disbelieving. The Romulans? Data spoke up immediately. Captain, there has been no unusual activity along the Romulan border for the past nine months. It seems highly unlikely that they would choose this moment to start a conflict. Beverly rested both elbows on the table. Maybe Starfleet feels we haven't had enough shakedown time. Perhaps she believed it, perhaps not. For Picard shot her a glance, and she had once lowered her gaze. As if in admission there might be another, deeper reason Starfleet had ordered the Enterprise E to stay away, but she was too loyal to utter it. LaForge dismissed Crusher's argument with the wave of his hand. We've been in space for six months. We're ready. The Enterprise E is the most advanced starship in the fleet. We should be in the front lines. If Jory suspected the same reason Beverly did, he did not show it, neither did Troy or Data. Riker's expression remained inscrutable. Picard worked to keep his own outrage from showing, and not particularly succeeding. I've voiced all these concerns to Starfleet Command. Their orders stand. Number one, set course for the neutral zone. Picard rose, then exited swiftly before the others saw his anger and shame. At the entrance to the ready room, Will Riker paused, pad in hand. He had performed the distasteful task assigned him as second in command. The Enterprise E now sailed a respectful distance from the neutral zone's border. The first scan had been completed, and it fell to Riker to present the results to the captain. Almost a full day had passed since Picard's stunning announcement that the Borg were headed toward Earth. The crew members, himself included, were undeniably frustrated, restless, even angry at Starfleet's refusal to let them be of real service. How much more offended and furious was Picard, who had once been captured by the Borg and used to kill his own people. Picard's greatest opportunity for expiation and the Enterprise crew's greatest opportunity to avenge their captain's suffering had arrived, and Starfleet denied him and them that chance. Will drew a breath and stepped forward. From the ready room, a blast of dark, thunderous music and anguished voices assaulted him. A half-full teacup on the captain's desk rattled in its saucer. Picard stood staring out at the stars, his back to the door. Rage seemed to emanate from his body into the air, riding upon each blaring, furious note. Picard turned to face his second in command. Without a word or a change in his taught expression, he tapped a control on his console. What do you have, number one? Riker handed him the pad. We finished our first sensor sweep of the neutral zone. As the captain scanned the readout, his lips thinned to a grim line. Fascinating. Twenty particles of space dust per cubic meter, fifty-two ultraviolet radiation spikes and a class two comet. He tossed the pad onto his desk. This is certainly worthy of our time. Captain, I know how you feel. The captain's hazel eyes narrowed and stared deep into Riker's with a fury and intensity that would have made any less loyal or determined friend and officer flinch and turn away in apology. Actually, I doubt very much that you know how I feel. Though Picard eyed him squarely, the focus of the captain's gaze seemed beyond him as if it were fixed fast upon ghosts from another time. The flaming hull of the starship Melbourne, the Saratoga, the gauge. Thirty-seven more starships and tens of thousands of lives aboard them were lost at Wolf 359 in the battle against the Borg. Thanks to the strategic knowledge of Locutus's human half, Captain Jean-Luc Picard. Riker took a step forward, his tone pointed. Captain, why are we out here chasing comets? Let's just say that Starfleet has every confidence in the Enterprise and her crew, but they're not so sure about her captain. They believe a man who was once captured by the Borg and assimilated should not be put in a situation where he would face them again. To do so would be to introduce an unstable element into a critical situation. That's crazy, Captain. Your experience with the Borg makes you the perfect man to lead this fight. Picard's expression darkened. Admiral Hayes disagrees. Bridge to Captain Picard. Go ahead, Councillor. We've just received word from Starfleet Command. They've engaged the Borg. Picard strode onto the bridge and noted that everything aboard the Enterprise E, including the situation that now confronted him in his crew, was strange, yet familiar. Strange, in that the captain's chair was now elevated above the rest to provide a better overview of the entire bridge. Familiar, in that once again the Enterprise crew anticipated a nightmarish battle with the Borg. Yet so unutterably strange, they should not be permitted to be part of it. Picard could not help but note the lines of tension etched on each officer's expression. The expression closest to conveying real calm belonged to Lieutenant Hawk at Khan, whose unflappable direct personality reminded the captain of Will Rikers, although Hawk was younger, clean-shaven and lean to the point of wireiness. Of course Hawk had not been aboard the Enterprise D when her captain had been captured by the Borg. He had never heard Locutus speak nor witnessed the fiery destruction of the 40 of Starfleet's finest warships. Impossible to understand the horror of the Borg unless one had met them in battle, or worse, in their own hide. Hawk's confidence sprang from ignorance and the captain did not look forward to seeing him lose either. Commander Data, foot Starfleet subspace frequency 1486 on audio. Wike ship to a demo, stand by to engage in grid 815, the client and Bozeman, fall back to mobile position 1. At the mention of the defiant, Troy, we concerned. All of them shared a single unspoken thought. Worfed. At Gollage flagship, we have it in visual range. We see it aboard Qubon course 0, part 215. Speed warp 9.8. We are aboard. Lower your shields and surrender your ships. We will add your biological and technological distinctiveness to our own. Your culture will adapt to service us. Resistance is futile. We are the Borg. Picard felt his flesh prickle. He stared out at the speechless stars on the main view screen and thought, how many planets. At the same time, an ominous realization came to him. He had known they were going to speak just then hadn't he? Even before they had uttered a sound, he had known the precise second they were going to speak. All units open fire. Remodulate shields. We're losing power. War core breach. All hands abandoned ship. This is the flagship. They've broken through the defense prison. They're heading toward our first ship course. Great ball to be attacked. The card caught Data's gaze and sliced a hand through the air. The transmission ceased at once. In any other situation, the card would have asked the senior bridge crew to accompany him to the ready room where he would have sought opinions and advice. After all, the wisest course was to consult cooler heads than his own. At the moment, he didn't give a damn. He leaned toward the card. Lieutenant Hawk, that course for Earth, maximum warp. The card shot a brief glance at an acruvent will wryker before turning to address his crew. I'm about to commit a direct violation of our order. Any of you who wish to object do so now and I'll note it in my log. Days are swivel to face the captain. I think I speak for everyone here, sir, when I say, to help with their orders. The card permitted himself a small bitter smile. Then read alerts, all hands to battle stations. As crew members scrambled to their stations, the card told himself, I'm probably taking all of these people to their deaths and myself to my own if all of us are lucky. And if we are not, I'm responsible here. But he would rather live with it for the time being than surrender without a fight to the evil of mindless apathy. So he settled back into his chair and ordered Hawk. Engage. But the warriors fury in his heart obliterated all pain, all fear and made him rise to his feet. To his relief, he did not hear the computer's urgent voice warning of an imminent warp-port breach. Kizzle-Bash moved toward the Khan, prepared to comply. But something she saw there made her glance up at her commander. Sir, there's another starship coming in. It's the Enterprise! The scarred, blackened surface of the Borg cube. The attack immediately drew the enemy's fire away from the crippled warship. The Borg in turn unleashed a retaliatory barrage that the new Enterprise absorbed with the faintest of shutters. Riker glanced up from his station. The Defiant is losing life support. The Borg had clearly not known he was about to destroy their ship. Or had they? Deanna Troi clearly sensed his turmoil. Her black eyes narrowed with concern, but before she could speak, the turbolift doors opened to reveal Dr. Crusher and behind her, Lieutenant Commander Worf. The Klingons' uniform was torn and bloodied. His deep brown face further darkened by soot. Picard did not smile at him. The situation was too grim for that. Welcome to the Enterprise E, Mr. Worf. Thank you, sir. The Defiant? Adrift? But salvageable? Riker smiled. That little ship? Worf snarled, revealing a glimpse of the dark, particularly fearsome-looking yellow teeth. Little? Riker rightly interpreted the display as good-humoured. Picard noted how much the bridge crew had missed the Klingon. We could use some help at Tactical Worf. In silence, the Enterprise E hurtled straight ahead into the blinding brilliance of the past. The air was close in the old crash and burn, stale and unpleasant, filled with a scent of sour sweat, moonshine and smoke. It was the smell, Lily decided, that it caused her headache. That and the two shots of brain numbing, vial tasting swill the past for the local liquor, and the fact that Zeph had had ten shots and was beginning to slur again. Whatever it was, she had grown suddenly furious, seized Zeph's arm and pulled him off his bar stool and out of the tattered olive-drab tent into the freezing April night. He filled her lungs with fresh air. The first breath was bracing, the second bitterly cold. Zeph pleaded. Lily, come on. He was in one of his manic modes tonight, a rather charming one, his cheeks flushed bright pink from liquor and cold. He looked like a boy instead of a worn fifty-year-old man. Lily knew it wasn't just the booze, it was the excitement, the anticipation of tomorrow. We're celebrating Lily, remember? We can celebrate when it's over. She made her way cautiously around the larger mud puddles, which were capped by a layer of frosted ice. Zeph followed alongside, arms out, pleading, come on Lily, one more round. You've had enough. I'm not riding that thing tomorrow with a drunken pilot. As she spoke, she wondered why she was so angry about the upcoming launch. Because it might not work. That's why. Because, for the first time in ten years, something had come along that made her dare hope. It was hard after ten years to remember much about life before the war, but she couldn't forget the university. All the math and physics classes that she secretly adored while complaining about them. They simply went away, ended in a moment of political insanity when she was twenty. No more dream of being an engineer. When it became clear that war was imminent, the university president sent them all home, and she stepped through the old doorway, luggage in hand, just in time to hear her dad's voice coming from the family room. That's it. It started. Lily's sister, Denise, had been living with her husband and kids in D.C., Ground Zero. Washington and three surrounding states had been blown off the map. Their house was left standing, but the growing radiation levels carried on the wind forced them to leave most everything behind. So they packed up the ground car and roamed like nomads, with dad's old camping gear looking for clean ground. What they took with them was stolen, of course, by road thieves with guns. She wound up stealing a gun in order to protect her parents. She'd even shot a total of five men and one woman in that first awful year. The car ran out of juice within a month's time. They'd had to abandon it and head out on foot, finally winding up at a horrifically crowded KOA campground. The first night at the KOA, Ma had laid down in a borrowed tent and said, Lily, I think I have cancer. She showed her the lung. Her Ma died of cancer, a disease you weren't supposed to have to fear anymore, but now you had to be afraid of everything again. Soon after, her dad took to drink. She let it go, until the night he used her pistol to kill himself. For a long time after, why she kept going, she couldn't say, except that maybe she was looking for something, and she found it the night she met Zeph. She had finally headed far north to Montana. It was one of the cleanest places around. She'd wandered into the local bar, the crash and burn, an old army tent really, set with a few tables, a rickety bar and an honest to God-duke box. And she'd sat right down beside Zeph Cochran. He was in one of his life of the party moods. To say he charmed the socks off her was putting it mildly. Within five minutes he'd learned her name and trade and history and propositioned her. He had a get-rich-quick scheme, he told her, and she could be part of it. Belly smiled. Yeah, right. Find another sucker, white boy. No, no, he said. He had come here to Montana because of the old missile silos. He was a physicist working on a project. Would she come to his place? There was something there he wanted to show her. And before she knew it, she was sitting cross-legged across from him on the cold dirt floor of his hut, listening to him explain that he needed certain mechanical parts to build a spaceship. She leapt up to leave. Zeph gently caught her hand. Damn it, Lily. Help me. I can't do this alone. Here. Let me show you. He'd named his ship the Phoenix. He grabbed a handful of blueprints off the cabinet, spread them out on the ground. He spoke swiftly, happily, of how the nuclear core contained in an old warhead could be harnessed for something he called a warp engine. She actually did understand much of what he told her, and it made frighteningly good sense. Warp drive. Back at the university they had called it hyperspace, and it was only an intangible dream. Light years reduced to a day's travel, the stars no longer impossibly distant. Lily, I have a deal with some Indonesians. They see the potential, and know it'll take some time, but they're willing to pay millions. She rubbed her freezing arms. Indonesia, huh? Is it warm there? So for the next few years, they played a little game with each other. He pretended to be nothing more than a hard-bitten entrepreneur desperate to strike at rich. While she pretended to be nothing more than a hard-bitten thief, the hungriever a piece of the action. Or so she reminded herself every time she dragged him from the crash and burn and tucked him into his own bed when he was too drunk to find his way home. Affection had nothing to do with it. She was merely taking care of her investment in the future. Beside her, Zeph grunted, bringing her back into the present to the frozen mud and biting air. Would it really happen? Would they be up there making history tomorrow as the first two people to travel using warp drive? And would the Indonesians really pay them all that money? What would it be like to have a solidly constructed house with real running water? Her gaze grew unfocused, but not enough to miss a fantastically swift-moving disk of light amid the stars. She touched Zeph's arm. What the hell is that? He glanced up, squinting hard to keep from seeing double. That, my dear, is the constellation Leo. No, that. Zeph lifted his face toward the sky and finally saw it. His faint, inebriated grin vanished. She saw two bright streaks emerging from the shining disk. For half a heartbeat's paws, both of them stood frozen with fearful puzzlement, trying to understand the distant thunder. Again, the alien ship detected the warp signature and is on its way to a rendezvous with history. Braced by members of Picard's senior crew, Lily stood beside Zephyrm, gripping his arm. Father away hidden by the darkness, Picard and Dr. Crusher stood apart, taking care that their mere presence did not alter the line of history. Lily gazed up at the sky, at the bright light that shone through the night clouds. The lights that had drawn every town's person to the silo. The lights of a descending spacecraft. A murmur passed through the crowd as the colossal ship at last emerged from the clouds. To Lily, it looked rather like a huge pterodactyl spreading its great wings as it lowered itself, feet first to the ground. As the alien ship's engines whined to a stop, she squeezed Zephyrm's arm, and he looked back at her, suddenly decades younger than the day they had met. The ones known as Will and Jordi stepped forward and took Zeph gently by the arm. Dr. Yaron, Zeph stared at them, perfectly sober, yet drunk with awe. My God, they're really from another world. Will smiled in his easy manner, and they're going to want to meet the man who flew that warp ship. A hatch in one of the landing claws began slowly to open, lights spilled out, illuminating the night air. Three hooded figures emerged, robed in elegant patterned brocades of charcoal, bronze, or bershine. One of the taller ones pulled back its hood, and at that instant, Lily ceased struggling against tears and permitted them to course down her cheeks. It was a man, a handsome man, with a strong jaw, strong cheekbones. If the stark lighting did not deceive, his complexion had a decidedly greenish cast. But it was the ears that made her realize, yes, this is a man, but it is most definitely not a human being. Slowly, regally, with remarkable and formal composure, the group's leader walked over to Cochrane and raised a hand, palm out. Zeph mimicked the gesture, adding an uncertain smile and a little wave. The alien indulged in neither, but spoke in flawless, unaccented English. Leave long and prosper. From the nearby shadows, Lily heard Picard's voice, I think it's time for us to make it a screech exit. Riker nodded. Riker to Enterprise, stand by to beam us up. He, Dr. Crusher and Leforge, moved deeper into the shadows. Picard stepped to the edge of the light and smiled at Lily. She walked up to him. I envy you, the world you're going to, an amused look came over his face. I envy you, taking these first steps into a new frontier. I'll miss you, Lily. She smiled as he clasped her hands, and then she forced herself to walk away into the blazing lights, but staying close enough to hear his voice. A God to Enterprise, energize. Lily knew she would never see any of them again. Even so, she could not resist, staring up into the night sky. Aboard the Enterprise E, now gratifyingly back to normal. The card looked upon his bridge in his senior crew. He felt appreciation for the future that awaited them, and all who had helped bring it to pass. Report, Mr. Wharf. The moon's gravitational field obscured our warp signature. The Vulcans did not detect us. Dordy looked up from his console. I've reconfigured our warp field to match the chronometric readings of the Borg Sphere. Recreate the Vortex Commander. Data half turned from his station. Most of his face still silver. Helm standing by. Lay in a course for the 24th century, Mr. Data. Something tells me our future will be there waiting for us. Course laid in, sir. Picard permitted himself the faintest of smiles. Make it so. And in the unseasonably warm Montana night, Lily Sloane stood just outside the crash and burn, staring up at the sky. There she saw what she'd been waiting for. A flash of rainbow light, and a tiny star sailing inside it, abruptly vanishing into the future. She smiled and took a step back to peer inside the tent, where Zeph was standing near the jukebox, waving his arms and talking a light-ear a minute. He was far too excited to touch the glass he poured for himself. Suddenly he reached out and, grinning broadly, hit a control on the jukebox. Each Vulcan lifted his or her right eyebrow. Then listened with perfectly detached scientific curiosity. Lily could not help but laugh delightedly along with the other sadness. The Phoenix had risen at last, and she was never coming down. Star Trek, first contact, was written by J.M. Dillard and read by Gates McFadden. It was abridged for audio by George Truett. The recording engineer was Jeff Thomas at Village Recorders, editing by Stephen Strassman. Music mix and post-production by Eric Foreman, sound designed by Gary Fink. Original music was composed by Carl Schurts, Dave Kursner, Eve McGlaryon, Carl Schurif, Richard Heyman, Sam McCallie, and Richard Emmett. description:
In this episode of Star Trek, J.M. Dillard shares his reading experience as he recounts a harrowing dream sequence involving resistance fighters against the Borg. The story details the protagonist's struggle with the Borg and their relentless pursuit despite being immune to hatred, leading to intense nightmares. In the dream sequence, the protagonist confronts an image of a woman who speaks cryptically before encountering a Borg drone named "Low Cutter," whose mouth he cannot remember from previous encounters due to his altered state.
The episode is narrated by Gates McFadden and explores themes of identity, resistance against tyranny, and the struggle between compassion and cold efficiency in the face of an unseen enemy.

transcript: Simon & Schuster Audio presents Star Trek, the Next Generation, Relics by Michael Jan Friedman, based on the television episode story and teleplay by Ronald D. Moore, read by James Doen, with an introduction and conclusion by Le Bar Burton. It's easy to idealize the past. Take sailing ships, for instance. Not the big hard-hulled vessels we use today to travel through subspace from one star system to another. No, I'm talking about the clumsy, little wooden canvas jobs men used in the old days to navigate their planet's oceans. When I was young, I liked to imagine myself at the helm of one of those ships, the wind singing in my ears, the taste of salt spray on my lips. I like to pretend that I was on some long, secret voyage sent off by a beautiful queen. There was always a beautiful queen it seemed, braving impossible dangers to explore lands no one had ever seen before. It was all stirring, very romantic. Of course, if my dreams had been a little more historically accurate, I probably wouldn't have come back alive from any of those voyages. In those days, sailors often didn't. If the scurvy didn't get them, there was a host of other diseases waiting in the wings, not to mention starvation, dehydration, and the occasional hurricane. Then I got older and my dreams came to revolve around more recent times. I imagined myself on board some early starship back in the days when everything was theoretical and experimental, and nobody was quite sure their shiny new machines would work the way they were supposed to. But I didn't dream that I was at the helm any longer, or even in charge. In those old or more mature dreams, I was the ship's engineer, the guy everyone turned to when things started to fall apart, the guy who could always figure out a way to do what needed to be done. Of course, it wasn't all romance and adventure in those days either, but the casualties were a lot fewer and the problems were a good deal more interesting. And so when I took the entrance exams for Starfleet Academy, I wasn't aspiring to be Jody LaForge Captain. All I wanted was to be Jody LaForge Chief Engineer. Then I could be one of those guys who put everything back together when it began to fall apart, just like in the good old days when they were still just feeling their way through the galaxy. Yeah, it's easy to idealize the past until you smack into it at warp 9.95. Captain Picard. Major John Luke Picard was in his ready room, studying a monograph on the formation of accretion bridges in binary star pairs. Yes, Mr. Data? Sir, there is something here that you should see. I'm on my way. Rising, the Captain rounded his desk and headed for the exit. Mr. Data would not have summoned him unless this were a matter of some urgency. As the ready room door slid aside, he noted that Will Riker, his first officer, was already hovering over Data's position at the aft science station. A moment later, he joined them. What is it, Data? A subspace radio wave, sir. I have identified the signal. The transmission appears to be a Starfleet code used between 50 and 80 years ago. Code 1, Alpha 0, ship in distress. Riker was intrigued. Computer, are there any Starfleet vessels reported missing in this sector? Negative. It was a Captain's turn to pose a question. Computer, expand parameters to include radiation sectors. A list of ships came up in one of the monitors. Transport ship SS Genolan, NC567, was reported missing on Stardate 7893.1 while en route to Norepin 5. Riker exchanged glances with a Captain. 75 years ago, sir. I'd say we've found the Genolan. But we're a long way from Norepin 5. They must have gone pretty far off course. Indeed, number one. Picard turned to Tina Rager, the petite black woman sitting at the con station. Ensign established coordinates for the source of the signal and plot a course for them. Warp factor 8. I, sir. Warp factor 8, Captain. Why the Haracer? The Captain frowned. His first officer had a point. If the Genolan had waited for 75 years, it could wait a little longer and yet call it intuition. Number one. Will Riker drum his fingers on the armrest of his seat in the command center? For four days, they'd been riding through subspace, heading for a rendezvous with what was left of the Genolan. Captain? It was Worf. Turning away from the science console, Picard answered him. Yes, Lieutenant? We are approaching the coordinates of the distress signal. The card turned to Ensign Rager. Bring us out of warp, Ensign. I, sir. Riker stood. He got antsy whenever the ship was about to close in on its objective, particularly one it had been pursuing as long as this one. Unfortunately, the main view screen showed nothing except an unfamiliar star field. They were still millions of kilometers short of the signal source, which they would now approach on impulse power. Suddenly, the Enterprise was rocked as if a giant hand had grasped it and was shaking it like a tambourine. Riker grasped at the back of Rager's chair to keep from being catapulted across the deck. Then, as abruptly as it started, the shaking stopped. But that was no guarantee that they wouldn't be treated to a repeat performance. Yellow alert. As Riker headed back to his place on the command center, Descartes and Data were barely a step behind him. The captain glanced at Worf. Report, Lieutenant? We have entered a massive gravitational field, sir. Descartes frowned, and he wasn't the only one. After all, there was nothing on the screen close enough to possess a gravitational field, much less one as powerful as the thing they'd run into. Riker turned to the Android second officer, hoping for more information. Data was bent over the op station, having replaced the crewmen who had been sitting there before. Mr. Data? Commander, there are no stellar bodies listed at these coordinates in our charts. However, sensor readings indicate the presence of an extremely strong gravitational source in this vicinity. It is directly ahead. It didn't make sense, Riker thought, unless the object creating the field was cloaked somehow. Picard must have had the same idea. Mr. Worf, can you localise the source of the gravity field? Yes, sir. On screen. The star field on the viewscreen changed, reflecting another view, and if one looked closely, there was a small, dark ball at its centre. The captain turned to Worf again. Magnify, Lieutenant? The image increased several orders of magnitude, until it could be seen more easily. It now appeared as round and smooth as a billiard ball. But because it was so dark, it was hard for Riker to discern anything else about it. Sensors? Data swiveled in his chair. I am having difficulty scanning the object. However, it would appear to be at least 200 million kilometres in diameter. Riker looked to Picard. The captain's surprise mirrored his own. Sir, that's almost the size of Earth's orbit around the Sun. Indeed, number one. Why didn't we detect it before now? Any idea, Data? Captain, the object's enormous mass is causing a great deal of gravimetric subspace interference. That interference might have prevented our sensors from detecting the object before we dropped out of warp. Picard's brow wrinkled as he gazed at the viewscreen. Mr. Data, could this be a Dyson Sphere? There is no comparative data, Captain. However, this object does fit the general parameters of Dyson's theory. Riker looked from one to the other. A Dyson Sphere? It's a very old theory, number one. I'm not surprised that you haven't heard of it. A 20th century physicist Freeman Dyson postulated that an enormous hollow sphere could be constructed around a star. This would have the advantage of harnessing all the radiant energy of the star, not just a fraction of it. A population living on the interior surface would therefore have a virtually inexhaustible source of power. Are you saying there might be people living in there? The answer was supplied by Data. Possibly a great number of people, Commander. The interior surface area of a sphere this size would be equivalent to that of more than two hundred fifty million class M planets. Woof. Looked up from this tactical console. Sir, I have located the distress signal. It is coming from a point on the northern hemisphere. Absorbing the information, Picard turned to Rager. Ensen, take us into synchronous orbit above that point. Hi, sir. They still had to answer the 75-year-old distress call Riker mused, but their interest in the Genolan had already paled beside their interest in the sphere. Gradually they pulled closer to it until they had last achieved the synchronous orbit that Picard desired. The monstrous object looked like a giant wall in space, stretching in every direction as far as the eye could see. Where before the sphere had appeared perfectly smooth, it was now possible to discern intricate patterns on the surface. We are holding position at thirty thousand kilometers above the surface, Captain. Thank you, Ensen. Sir, yes, Mr. Data. The distress signal is coming from a federation ship which has impacted on the surface of the sphere. It is the transport ship, Genolan. Riker nodded. Any life signs? Our sensors show none, sir. However, there are several small power emanations, and life support is still functioning at minimum levels. Out of the corner of his eye, Riker noticed Picard looking at him. Knowing exactly what the captain wanted, the first officer tapped his communicator. Bridge to engineering. Jordi, meet me in transporter room three. Then he turned to the Klingon security chief. Mr. Waugh. You're with me as well. As Jordi materialized on the Genolan with Riker and Wharf on either side of him, he scanned their surroundings. Huh. A bit cramped, isn't it? Riker took out his home. Come on. Let's have a look at it. The lights were dim. One or two of the consuls were damaged or burnt out. There were piles of ash on the floor, and in several spots the bulkhead was caved in. Jordi shook his head as he took it all in. This ship really went through the ringer even before it crashed. Wonder what happened to it. Sniffing the air, Riker turned to the Klingon. Pretty stale in here. See if you can increase the oxygen level lieutenant? Nodding, Wharf moved over to one of the consuls. Meanwhile, Jordi's tricorder led him to the transporter controls. Not that he expected to find anything of interest there, but he had to cover all the bases. A moment later, he was glad he had. Commander? What is it, Jordi? This transporter is still online. It's been fed power from the auxiliary systems. Riker bent over the transporter controls to do some checking of his own. How about that? The materialization subroutine has been disabled. And that's not all. The auxiliary phase and users have been connected to the emitter array. The override is completely gone, and the pattern buffer has been locked into a continuous diagnostic cycle. That doesn't make any sense. Locking the unit in a diagnostic mode just sends inert matter flowing through the pattern buffer. Suddenly, Jordi saw something on the console. Something he hadn't noticed before. Damn. Someone's pattern is still in the buffer. Riker's eyes narrowed as he followed Jordi's pointing finger. All right. It's completely intact. Less than .003 signaled degradation. But how is that possible? Jordi shrugged. I don't know. I've never seen a transporter system jury rigged like this. Riker frowned. Jordi, could someone survive in a transporter buffer for 75 years? The chief engineer bit his lip. It had never been attempted not to his knowledge anyway. But I know a way to find out, Commander. Ever so carefully, Jordi worked the controls of the transporter unit. Then taking a deep breath, he touched one final command area and looked to the tiny platform in front of him. In the next instant, he saw a figure taking shape. It wavered in the beam, acquiring a density at a snail's face. And then, with a last surge of energy, solidified. Riker shook his head in admiration. My God, Jordi, you did it. And so he had. For what stood before them was a living, breathing, denison of the 23rd century. And except for the arm he held in a sling, he was hardly the worst for wear. For a moment, Montgomery Scott was overcome by a wave of vertigo. He didn't know who he was, much less where he was. Then it all came flooding back to him. He was in the genolan, in the ops center. They crashed. Only he and Ensign Franklin had survived. And with a dearth of supplies staring them in the face, their only hope had been. He looked around. There were two men standing in front of the transporter platform, staring at him. One of them, the shorter of the two, wore a strange, high-tech band around his eyes. Both sported uniforms that he had never seen before, but they rescued him from the transporter loop, so they probably weren't hostile. The transporter loop, he thought. Franklin. Where was Franklin? Shaking off his wooziness, Scott came down off the platform and headed straight for the transporter console. Seemingly fascinated by him, the two men stepped aside to let him bustle by. No sooner had Scott reached the console than he began checking out its monitors, verifying his readings. Was Scott to get Franklin out of there? One of the men spoke up. Someone else's pattern is still in the buffer. I, Matt Franklin and I, went in together. Almost done, he told himself. Another couple of levels to examine. Here, and here, and then he'd, wait a minute. Scott stared at the last monitor, the one that covered the enducers. He didn't like this. Something's wrong. One of the enducers has failed. Turning to the man in the band, he bocked an order. Boost the gain on the matter stream. Moving to a nearby console, the man complied. Apparently, unhampered by the thing on his face. Come on, Franklin. Don't give up. I know you're in there. I can hear your electrons buzzing. Scott's mouth had gone dry. So dry, he could barely swallow. He worked furiously at his instruments, certain that he could perform just one more miracle. After all, he'd pulled Jim Kirk's bacon out of worse fires. And then he saw it. Franklin's signal profile. No, he thought. Oh Lord, no. When he finally tore his eyes away, they were moist with sorrow. Ah, it's no use. The signal patterns when degraded by 53% is gone. The last two words seemed to reverberate through the op center. The man in the band frowned and looked away. The taller man took a step forward. I'm sorry. So am I, lad. So am I. I'm Commander William Riker, first officer of the Starship Enterprise. At the name, Scott felt something rise within him. A gladness that, just for a second or two, made him forget his sorrow. The Enterprise, I should have known. And I bet it was Jim Kirk himself who hauled the old girl out of mouthwalls to come looking for me. He wondered just when Starfleet had started outfitting its officers in these skin-tight suits. There was barely enough room in them to hide a wart. The names, Captain Montgomery Scott. How long have I been missing? Riker looked at his companion. The man in the band just shrugged. This may seem as something of a shock, Captain Scott. But it's been a good, sir. The word had been spoken by someone with a deep voice, a very deep voice. Scott, like the others, turned in response and found himself staring at a savage, bony, browd cling on. The same sort of villain who tried to take his life time and again when he'd served under Kirk. And impossible as it seemed. The bloody heathen was wearing the same kind of uniform as Commander Riker. Did that mean? Could it possibly mean? Unperturbed. The Klingon addressed the first officer. I have restored life support, sir. The oxygen levels will return to normal shortly. Riker acknowledged the information with an odd. Then turned to the newcomer. Captain Scott? Scott saw Riker looking down at him. The man seemed sympathetic. I lad. This is Lieutenant Wolf. Scott sighed. He'd been hoping there was some other explanation. The first officer put a hand on his shoulder. Captain Scott, perhaps there are a few things we should talk about. Scott turned to him, feeling very much upstream without a paddle. I, and perhaps more than a few. It took a while for him to brief him on the truth, and a lot longer before he could even come close to accepting it. My God, thought Scott. 75 years. 75 years. The Jody and his fellow officers were halfway to the transporter room exit when they realized they'd left Captain Scott standing on the platform behind them. The man was gazing at the overhead transporter elements, muttering to no one in particular. I've changed the resonator array. Only three phase inverters. Jody saw the first officer turn to him. Mr. Leforsch, I think our guest is going to have a lot of questions. Don't worry, sir. I'll take care of him. Glancing at Scott, one last time. Riker gestured for a warth to accompany him. Together they left the transporter room. Meanwhile, Scott had moved off and was scrutinizing the optical data chips set into the bulkhead. Suddenly his features took on an almost horrified cast. Of all the... what have you done to the electronic enhancers? Jody smiled. Those were replaced with isolinear chips about 40 years ago. It's a lot more efficient now. I'm sure of that. Jody gestured to the exit. Shall we? Still a little dazed. Scott followed him out into the corridor. Here too, Scott's eyes scanned everything in sight. He was consumed by curiosity. You were saying that you were on your way to the northern colony when you had a warp engine failure? That's right. We had an overload in one of the plasma transfer conduits. The captain brought us out of warp. We hit some gravimetric interference and then there it was. A bigger slice. He pointed to a raised portion of the bulkhead. Is that a conduit interface? Yeah. There it was. The Dyson Sphere. Right? Hi. It was amazing. An actual Dyson Sphere. Can you imagine the engineering skills needed to even design such a structure? But his attention wasn't on his recollections of the sphere. It was on a wall panel a couple of meters up ahead. Suddenly he moved up to it and pulled the panel off its place in the bulkhead. Jody was uncertain that Scott knew what he was doing, but out of courtesy he didn't make a move to stop him. Liquid state energy transfer. No power lines at all. This looks like an optical data conduit. Be careful there, Captain Scott. That's no data conduit. It's an EPS power tap. Gently resting the panel from Scott. He replaced it on the wall. Tell me more about the Dyson Sphere. What happened when you first approached it? Scott shrugged. Up ahead a turbo lift station was coming into view. We began a standard survey of the surface, of course. We were just completing the initial orbital scan when our aft power coil suddenly exploded. We tried to compensate with the ventral relays, but there wasn't time enough. The ship got caught in the sphere's gravity well and down we went. Why? It's a miracle the ship's superstructure survived a crash like that. I nearly didn't. Franklin and I were the only ones that lived to tell the tale. Everyone else was killed by the impact. Jody tried to imagine the man's feelings when he realized he'd survived, but that so many others had perished. What made you think of using the transporter's pattern buffer to stay alive? Scott shook his head. We didn't have enough supplies to wait for our rescue, so I had to think of something. But locking it into a diagnostic cycle to keep the signal from degrading and cross connecting the phase enducers to provide a regenerative power source. It's brilliant. The older man was found. I'm afraid it's only 50% brilliant lad. Ensign Franklin deserved better. Noting the man's sadness, Jody changed the subject to something Scott could get excited about. I think you're going to like the 24th century Captain Scott. We've made some pretty amazing advances in the last 80 years. It worked. Scott seemed to perk up a bit as they entered the turbo lift. Looking around the compartment, he nodded approvingly. Hi. From what I can see, you've got a fine ship here, Mr. LaForge. It's a real beauty, in fact. I must admit to being a might overwhelmed. Jody grinned. Wait till you see the holodeck. Scott gave him a look of mingled surprise and curiosity. The... holodeck? So, what do you think, Lash? Beverly Crusher, Chief Medical Officer of the Starship Enterprise, looked down at her latest patient and shook her head. You're a treasure, Captain Scott. An absolute treasure. The only person ever to spend 75 years cycling around in a transporter and live to tell of it. Now, whole still, will you? Sitting on a bio-bed in sick bay, Scott winced as the doctor examined his injured limb. It's easy for you to say, Lash. Your arm has nave and broken for the last 75 years. Crusher glanced at Jody, who discarded Captain Scott to sick bay. Jody shrugged. Turning back to her tricorder readouts, Crusher considered the information there. You've got a hairline fracture of the humerus, Captain. It'll ache for a few days, but after that, it should be fine. Thank you, Lass. Scott turned to Jody. Well, I'll say this for your Enterprise. The doctors are a fair sight prettier than what I'm used to. Crusher couldn't help but smile. Flatterby will get you nowhere, Captain. Before Scott could reply, the sick bay doors opened to admit another visitor. This time, it was the man in charge of the Enterprise. Beautiful as ever, Jody made the introduction. Captain Scott, this is Captain Picard. Picard extended his hand. Jean-Luc Picard, Captain Scott. Welcome aboard. Scott clasped the Captain's hand as warmly as it was offered. Thank you, sir. Of all the ships that could have found me, I'm glad it was yours. But if you do not mind, call me Scotty. Very well. How are you feeling, Scotty? Good question. How am I feeling, Doctor? Crusher slipped a tri-gorder into her pocket. Well, other than a couple of bumps and bruises and a slightly battered arm, I'd say you feel fine for a man of 147. How about that, Captain? And I do not feel a day over 120. Picard smiled politely. I must say, I was surprised when Commander Riker told me you were aboard the Janolen. Our records didn't list you as one of their crew. Scott frowned ever so slightly. Ah, wasn't actually a member of the crew, Sir Truth to Tell. It was just a passenger. I was heading for Norpin Five, you see, to settle down and enjoy my retirement. If Picard had a reaction to that, he didn't show it. I see. Well, I would very much enjoy the opportunity to discuss your career at some point. History is one of my hobbies, and I'm sure you have some fascinating insights into the events of your time. Oh, Denny, no, if you'll cause them fascinating exactly, but I'd be happy to answer your questions. I look forward to it. Then he glanced at Jordi. Commander, we need to begin the full analysis of the Dyson Sphere. I'll get right on it, Sir. The Captain nodded approvingly, then returned his attention to their guest. Again, welcome aboard Captain Scott. And with that, Picard took his leave to him. Jordi turned to Scott. You heard the Captain. I have to get back to engineering to start that analysis. Scott's face lit up. Engineering that, I thought you'd never ask. And before Crusher could stop him, he'd moved down off the biobed to accompany Jordi. Just a minute, Captain. Exactly where do you think you're going? Scott looked at the doctor, puzzled. What is it, Lass? You finished your tests, have you not? True. But you've had quite a shock to your system. The first thing you're going to do is to get some rest. Scott seemed on the verge of protesting until Jordi intervened. We're pretty busy right now anyway, Captain Scott, but I'd be happy to give you a tour of engineering a little later when the doctor says it's okay. Scott looked from one of them to the other. Faced with the uniform resistance, he sighed. I, when the doctor says it's okay. Jordi smiled. Great. See you then. Here we are, Captain Scott. The ensign assigned to show Scott to his quarters, stopped in front of the door half way down the corridor from the turbo lift. After you, sir? Nodding. Scott took a step forward. The door opened to reveal the quarters that had been set aside for him. Good, Lord Man. Where have you put me? The ensign turned to stare at him. Well, these are standard guest quarters, sir. I can try to find something bigger if you wish. Scott's eyes widened. Bigger. You misunderstand me, lad. Why, in my day, even admirals didn't they have such quarters on a starship. And the only person who ever complained was the dolmen of Elas. You've never heard such whining from a grown woman in all your life. Uh, what, right, sir? You'll find the closet back there with a full wardrobe in your size. And this is the food replicator. And your computer terminal? But Scott wasn't paying very close attention. Again, he was dredging up memories. You know, these quarters remind me of a hotel room I once had on Argeleus. Oh, now there was a planet. Everything a man could want right at his fingertips. Of course, on our first visit, I ran into a wee bit of trouble there, but, uh, excuse me, sir, I, uh, I have to return the duty. Scott focused on his companion and frowned. What a fool he'd been. The ensign wasn't interested in the dolmen of Elas, or the accommodations on Argeleus, or any other stories he had to tell. He just wanted to get on with his business. Sorry, that's trouble, yeah, ensign. No trouble at all, sir. A moment later, the door closed behind the man, and Scott was alone. He sighed and sat down on the overstuffed couch they'd given him and looked around. Then he sighed again. Suddenly, he felt very, very lost. Down in engineering, a handful of men and women were working at consoles and checking displays. Jordi was all but oblivious to the activity, however. He was carrying out a task of his own. Commander N'forch. He looked up and saw Bartel, a tall, blonde woman, standing at the entrance to his office. Come on in, Bartel. I've got a job for you. The chief engineer swiveled his monitor around so Bartel could get a look at the graphic on it. The bridge wants a complete spectrographic scan of the sphere, and will need all the sensors to be synchronized. Of course, I can't recalibrate the after-ray with the warp engines in operation, so I need you to shut them down for the time, B'artel smiled. Consider it done, sir. As she headed for the engine core, Jordi went back to work on his terminal. Truth to tell, he was eager to perform this spectrographic analysis. He was as curious about the sphere as anyone else. In fact, he was so intent on setting up the scan that he barely heard the sudden outbreak of conversation outside.
