I just had the clean up detail pile every last one of these wee beasties onto the transporter platform. And he looks at me, sort of horrified. Sort of the way you're looking now, Lan. And says, but, Scottie, you didn't need to just transport them out into space, did you? So, I put on an offended expression, and I say, I'm a kind-hearted dancer. I give them a good home. And the captain says, where's Scottie? Spit it out now? When I tell him that I gave the beasties to the Klingons. Just before they went into warp, I transported the whole kitten kaboodle into their engine room as a wee parting gift. The younger man shook his head. You didn't. May I be struck by lightning if I changed a single word of it? The turbolift doors opened and Geordie ushered him out. Alright, now I've got one for you. As they started down the corridor, he related in broad strokes, of course. The most preposterous story he could think of. It felt good to be telling Scottie a tall tale, instead of the other way around. Oh, come on, now, Lan. You're pulling an old man's leg. No, really. This alien space, baby, which was about the size of a four-story building, really thought the Enterprise was its mother. It was suckling power directly from the ship's fusion reactors. So, what did you do? Didn't he tell me? You changed the power frequency and soured the milk. That's right. How did you know? Scottie shrugged. Great mind-sink alike. They laughed at that. But just seconds later, Scott's smile seemed to feed a bit. Enjoy these times, Jory. You're the chief engineer of a starship. It's a time of your life that'll never come again. And once it's gone, it's gone for good. Not that retirement is so bad, mind you. I hear the norpen colony is very, uh, quiet this time of year. Jory stopped in front of the shuttle bay doors. Scottie stopped, too, a little surprised. I thought you were going to buy me a drink and ten-forward? Didn't you tell me you're withdrawing your offer? Baby, but only in favor of a better one. As the door slid aside, Jory led the way into the shuttle bay. Consumed with curiosity, Scott followed. He wasn't disappointed either. Not a single bit. Picard, Riker, Wharf, Dr. Crusher, Troy and Data were all standing beside a large gleaming shuttle craft. The vehicle's space door was open. Stunned, Scott looked it over. Then glanced back at his friends. Does this mean what I think it means? You're going to give me one of your shuttles? Picard smiled warmly. Call it an extended loan. Since you lost your ship while saving ours, it seemed that only fair to supply you with another one. Jory leaned closer to his fellow engineer. It's a bit slow, but it'll get you to the norpen colony if that's where you really want to go. Scott considered the ship. And very slowly a change came over his features. He seemed different. Rejuvenated, Jory thought. Lad, the norpen colony is where old men go to retire. Maybe I'll end up there someday, but nay just yet. There's still a lot I want to see. In fact, well, perhaps I'd best be off. You know, before I get a chance to think twice about it. Crusher looked at him, obviously disappointed. So soon? I'll ask. And didn't he be telling me I need to stay and rest up? Any more of this sort of rest and they'll be carrying me out on a stretcher? Though you're still the prettiest physician I ever saw. A flurry of goodbyes followed. When it was all over, Scotty took La Forza's arm and escorted him out of the earshot. There are good crew Jory, and she's a fine ship this enterprise. A credit to her name. But I've always found that a ship is only as good as the engineer who takes care of her. And from what I can see, you could not be in better hands. Jory clapped Scott on the shoulder. Better get a move on. Scottie nodded. Eyeland. Right, Jory. It seemed like Eons had passed since I kicked the man out of my engineering section. And even longer than that since I stopped him from tampering with that EPS power tap. Scottie had come a long way since we brought him aboard the Enterprise. If I'd been dumped into the next century without warning or preparation, I doubt if I would have adjusted half as well. Getting into the shuttle, my friend Scotty shut the space door behind him. I watched with mixed emotions as he started the engine and gave us all a thumbs up sign. Then, as Captain Picard himself worked the bay door controls, Scotty nudged the shuttle to the brink of space where an invisible force field separated the air in the shuttle bay from the cold and airless void. I could almost see the look in Scotty's eyes. It was all out there. Everything he could ever want. New worlds, new civilizations, new adventures. And someday, I was sure he'd find some of those old friends he'd lost track of. The ones with whom he'd served so long and so well on Jim Kirk's Enterprise. Of course, there was danger and uncertainty and disappointment out there too, but that came with the territory, didn't it? And who knew that territory better than Captain Montgomery Scott? Moments later, the shuttle took off into the star-pricked expanse of space. It got smaller and smaller as it gradually pulled away from us, finally banking and setting a course for only its pilot new wear. But I was happy. Very happy for my friend Scotty. Captain Picard was right, I thought. Men need a sense of purpose in their lives, a sense of going somewhere, a sense of moving forward. And once again, Scotty had that sense of purpose. He'd been through his share of tribulations since we pulled him out of that transporter loop on the genolan. He'd had to make some pretty big adjustments. But in the long run, I had a feeling Scotty was going to like the 24th century.
description: In this episode of Star Trek, Michael Jan Friedman reads from Ronald D. Moore's story for "Relics," a key scene where the first officer and chief engineer discuss engineering issues aboard the Enterprise. As the captain studies an accretion bridge formation chart, Data reports receiving a subspace radio message, suggesting tension in their relationship between command and technical expertise.

title: Warped
file_path: media/StarTrek DS9/Warped.mp4
transcript: Simon & Schuster Audio presents Star Trek, Deep Space Nine, Warped by KW Jeter, read by Renéal Bérz-Zhén-Wau. A hand, darted into the water, through the ribbons of green weeds, streaming in the current into the darkness between the stones, smooth as black pearls. A fist came back up, with flashes of silver wriggling from either side, a clear rivulet dripping from the elbow. Jake Sisko regarded the fish in the other boy's grasp. He was filled with both admiration and a stomach-notting unease at the other's lightning quickness. Too fast, he thought. That's not right. The two boys hunkered, knees to chest on the largest rock in the middle of the creek. The other boy thrust the captured fish in front of Jake's face. Look! Look at it! The creature's round eyes were emblems of unreasoning panic. The pink rimmed gills fluttering wide in the strangling air. Its mouth made an idiot ole, as the boys thumb traced the seam of its belly. Jake wanted to tell the other boy to let the fish go, to throw it back into the water, but he was afraid to. He didn't even know the other boy's name, but then he didn't need to. All we've done of fish before, they're nothing special. The other boy weighed the creature's fate and tossed it away. He leaned over the side of the rock, shading his eyes to hunt for something better. Jake felt the squeeze around his heart relax. In the distance, on the creek's other side, the grass's feathery tops parted and settled together again, as a hidden shape moved below them. He knew it was the big orange tabby with battered ears that lived on the mice from the barn beyond the hill. Or the barn that used to be over there, it had gradually faded away as though pushed from existence by this little world's new commanding presence. Everything here had changed, or was about to. Jake's companion leaned closer to the water. I saw something down there. The boy's hand brushed through the green weeds. He stretched out, chest against the rock, so he could reach all the way down. Then sitting back on his haunches, the boy held up the prize. For a moment, Jake thought the wetly shining thing was just a rock. Then he saw the stubby clawed legs poking out from the corners. It was a turtle. The boy reached into the pocket of his jeans and fetched out the little folding knife. This'll be fun, Jake. You know it will. Jake squeezed his eyes shut. It didn't do any good to keep whispering to himself that nothing here was real. The boy poked at the side of the shell with the knife point, as though trying to find a hidden latch. He held the knife out to Jake. You want to? Jake shook his head. I'll just watch this time. While the boy focused his attention back on the struggling turtle, Jake was remembering when he had first become aware of the other boy's presence here. He hadn't even seen him, but had found his handy work. In the woods farther down the creek, in the damp smelling shadows, he had found a space of bare earth, scraped out of the tangled roots and dead leaves, empty except for something that lay beneath a swarm of flies. A cat. Or what had been one. He had stepped back from it in disgust and had almost tripped over one of the cords that looped around the trunks of the nearest trees and pulled the dead thing into a spread eagled X on the ground. Since then he had seen more things and never without feeling sick in his gut afterwards. He closed his eyes when he heard a tiny sound. The whisper the knife made when it cut through something soft and yielding. Not for the first time he wished everything around him was a dream, a real dream, the kind from which he could wake when it got too scary. A section of bulkhead, the curved wall between the gridded floor and the overhead light panels, rippled like flowing water for a moment, then peeled away and recoelessed into the form of deep space nines, chief of security. Odo looked around the angle of the nearest corner. There was no sign of the individual he had been tracking, Armont Wyus, an itinerant freight handler who had been catching occasional pick-up work in the station's main docking pylon. Odo turned and retrieved a small plastoid box with a pair of dangling probe wires. He had hidden it there before flowing into his own molecule thick concealment over the bulkhead segment. The device extracted access codes and corresponding names from the databanks of the station's hollow suites. Wyus had spent an inordinate amount of time here immersed in the artificial worlds of the hollow suites that had been installed along this remote passageway several levels away from the main action of the promenade. This habit alone served as an identifying quirk for Wyus. Why this need for privacy? A thug like Armont Wyus wouldn't care what other people thought of his recreational activities. But Wyus also had enough rudimentary intelligence left to elude a tracker made Odo feel uneasy. Armont Wyus was somewhere else aboard the station. The sooner the suspect was located, the better. There were three corpses lying in the station's morgue. Each of them had been ripped open from throat to bipedal lower extremities by a honed pry blade. The pry blade was a folding tool that the freight handlers on the loading docks used to slice through heavy cables and lever apart stuck container seals. Two of the corpses had been the frenzied product of one of Wyus's co-workers who had slit his own throat before Odo could apprehend him. The third and latest murder had been committed more discreetly with no clue left behind. No clue other than the rousing of Odo's sharper instincts every time he had seen Wyus skulking through the station's corridors. Something in the eyes or rather behind them like a worm uncoiling around the pit of a small fruit that plus the rather more concrete datum of Wyus's pry blade being missing from his locker. At the moment, the hollow suite closest to Odo was occupied. Odo inserted the probe wires beneath the edge of the door's control panel to obtain the exact credit access code. On the device's small readout panel, the numbers shifted, held for a moment, then changed to letters. One by one, they spelled out the name Cisco. Followed by the initial J, the access code for the station commander's son, Jake. Odo switched off the device and stowed it in his uniform pocket. A wordless concern magged at him, but there was no time to puzzle over it now. He turned and strode quickly toward the corridor's hub. When he reached the crowded promenade, Odo spotted Armant Wyus. Odo pulled himself back into the shadow of a structural pillar to keep from being cited in turn by his target. Across the promenade, the sweating, heavy jawed face of Armant Wyus was still visible. Even from this far away, Odo could pick up the murderous rage given off by the man. When Wyus's simmering gaze swung away, Odo moved in closer. Only the flash of the metal pry blade stabbed Odo's vision. The crowd surged back from Wyus, away from the naked blade. Odo wedged himself through the humanoid wall. The turbolift doors had opened a few meters away from Wyus. Odo realized that was what Wyus was waiting for. Two people had emerged from the turbolift. Major Kira and Commander Cisco, they were talking to each other, not perceiving the outbreak of chaos their entrance had caused until it was too late. Odo launched himself over the last ring of bodies as Commander Cisco spotted the arc of descending metal and raised his forearm to ward off the blurring stroke aimed at him. Major Kira dropped into a crouch and propelled both herself and Commander Cisco out of the blade's path. Before Odo could do anything to assist, it was over. Cisco rolled against Wyus's legs with enough force to stagger him against the wall. The pry blade flew out of Wyus's grasp and skittered across the promenade deck. So hit Wyus with an elbow check to the abdomen and Wyus dropped to his knees. Odo pulled Wyus's arm back and snapped a pair of restraints onto his wrists. I've got him. Are you alright, Commander? Cisco brushed down the front of his uniform and nodded. A little adrenaline overdose constable, but nothing serious. How about you, Major? Don't worry about me. Who the hell is this creep anyway, Odo? The suspect's identity has already been established. His motives remain the subject of an ongoing investigation. Cisco peered into Wyus's slack-jawed face. Constable, is this connected to the... incidents you spoke to me about previously? I'm afraid that's likely to be the case, Commander. I see. We'll need to discuss this matter further. Have a complete report ready for me by the end of the shift. Odo gave a quick nod in acknowledgment and barked at the circle of gawking faces. There's nothing to see here. Move along. A path opened through the crowd and Odo shoved the suspect toward the security station at the other end of the promenade. Cisco and Kira continued to their destination. Quarks, establishment. Kira had just returned from her home planet, Bejor, and Cisco wanted a full briefing about the political developments there. Pork brought two mugs of synthail to their booth, compliments of the house. Cisco activated the booth's privacy shield, and the murmur of voices from outside was cut to a dead silence. Kira took a careful sip, then pushed the mug away. Commander, the situation on Bejor is much worse than we had thought it would be. Cisco nodded slowly. The severity front? Who else? It looks like we severely underestimated the strength of anti-federation sentiment on Bejor. The commander set down his half-empty mug. So what do you think, Major? What would you estimate the chances for the severity front? Kira shook her head. I don't know. Perhaps the Kai's absence from Bejor, the splinter groups and factions opposed to membership in the Federation have managed to unite their efforts behind the front single banner. The front's chances are good. Real good. How any of your people can oppose a process that will bring their world such benefits? Commander, we've gone over this before. The simple truth is that those supposed benefits just haven't shown up yet, have they? So far the Federation hasn't delivered. These things take time, Major, but there will be a tremendous expenditure of financial and technical resources upon this sector. For God's sake, Commander, the Cardassians told us as much while they were stripping every leaf and speck of minerals from the planet. We don't have time for patience. We've suffered enough. Cisco drew himself up to full height. If that's the case, then, despite our earlier assessment, your world may be a long way from readiness for Federation membership and its benefits. The Federation Council has concerns other than the welfare of Bejor and its people. Kira had heard the lecture from him before. Commander, if Bejor is so far down the list of the Federation's priorities, then you'd better be prepared for Bejor to take a good hard look at what it gets out of dealing with the Federation. And is that what you want, Major, for Bejor to go its own way? She again felt the tug, the division between the oldest loyalty of her heart and the new one she had assumed. She shook her head. No. I wouldn't be here at Deep Space Nine if that was what I wanted. Cisco pushed back his chair and rose to leave. Very well. I'll need your complete report on the political situation on Bejor, and I mean absolutely complete names, alliances, antagonisms, influences that we can bring to bear on different factions. Everything, Major. Kira watched as the Commander threaded his way among the crowded tables, heading for the bar's exit. She lifted the mug and took a sip. The tastes sharply bitter on her tongue. Oh, doh entered Cisco's office and the Commander waved into a chair. Cisco turned toward the computer panel on the desk. The last screen full of Odo's report still showed. Let's get down to business Constable. This is a very distressing situation that's developed. Odo's eyes were two hotly glaring coals. It's more than that, Commander. It's intolerable. Constable, this Armant-Wyos individual you have in custody. I take it he would have been our third perpetrator. That is if he had managed to land the blow he had aimed at myself and Major Kira. Yes, Commander. Cisco began scrolling through the text of Odo's report. Since the other two perpetrators ended their rampages by committing suicide that would make our Wyos an important subject of investigation. He is the only one we've managed to apprehend alive. Are there any traceable connections between him and the others? Odo shrugged. Nothing definitive. I'm still sifting through the details. Wyos is not an unknown quantity. We can track his employment history through nearly two decades. He's just a run of the mill itinerant laborer of marginal intelligence and skills. There are millions of them wandering between planets. And you believe you can connect this extremely ordinary individual with our little group of dead murderers? Commander, he did take a swing at your head with an open pryblade. And some of Wyos's bizarre ramblings are similar to recordings made by the murderers and expost facto accounts of their crimes. In all cases there are common elements of an absorbing fantasy construct in which the individuals seem to be trapped in a not particularly pleasant world. Well constable as long as we have this material from the murderers and presumably more material forthcoming from our attempted murderer, we should put it through as much analysis as possible. I quite agree, Commander. That's why I've asked Lieutenant Dax to begin a separate investigation. Dr. Bashir will assist her. I've turned copies of all my records pertaining to this case over to her and given her complete access to the prisoner, Armant Wyos. She indicated that she understood the urgency attached to this matter and has already started work on it. Constable, give this matter your highest priority. Notify me at once of any new developments. Of course, Commander. As soon as Odo had left the office, Cisco sent the report back to the computer's confidential archives. For once, Odo's dark musings seemed accurate. His report on the murders had gone into distressing levels of detail. Science officer Jadzi Adax already was deep into her research. Not all the things she had begun monitoring were taking place inside Armant Wyos' skull. There were others. Commander from the various sensors arrayed in the empty starlet space between DS9. Deviations in readings that were so small as to be almost imperceptible. Just enough to form, not a pattern, but the barest suggestion of one, the outline of a shape not yet visible to her. Until she knew what they meant, it was best to keep the observations to herself. She turned her attention to the computer screen. There, the smaller universe of Armant Wyos was being carefully pried apart. Rose of numbers bounced between a narrow range of values, giving her a real-time monitoring of his physiological processes. Something was going on inside the subject's visual information process. Dax thought, he's seeing things. But what? Near dreams, even nightmares, didn't produce such neuroanatomical storms. She scanned past the other numbers, hormone levels whipsawed between states of panic and anger. With another command, she switched the screen to a view from the overhead camera in the subject's secured isolation chamber. Dax observed the clenching of the jaw, the straining neck tendons, the feverish sweat upon the brow. Computer, give me audible on this subject. No, I can't stop! I can't stop! The voice was scarcely human, a howl of anguish from the darkest unexplored caverns of the mind. No, no, no! Please, please! Alright computer, that's enough. Computer I want all material from this subject indexed against the recordings logged on by the Chief Security, Reference Tag, Epidemic. Give me a breakdown on all distinctive word patterns and imagery that crosslink between the recordings. Dax knew there was nothing to do now but wait. Odo continued his own investigations. He cornered Chief O'Brien on the engineering deck and dragged Goond him along on a search of one of DS9's remoter and less frequented corridors. It held a row of new hollow-suites that had recently been shipped on board the station. These were the hollow-suites why us had favored. Odo hadn't been able to conjecture why anyone would travel all this way to use them when there were better maintained ones on the promenade. O'Brien knew that the hollow-suites had been checked out prior to activation, but after he had examined the internal components of one of the hollow-suites, O'Brien had emerged with a rectangular black box in his hands, proof that someone had tampered with the mechanism. Odo and O'Brien immediately took the black box to Dax for analysis, shortly after she summoned Cisco to her laboratory. As he rubbed his thumb across the enameled surface of the box's casing, Dax filled him in on her investigation. She pointed to the workbench along the laboratory's other side. The unit's interior components are over there. You've completed your analysis on them. For the most part, I'm afraid Benjamin that we'll have a difficult time determining the source of these devices. Whoever built them didn't leave a lot of clues inside. Cisco picked up one of the pieces, a mute crystalline cylinder. What about its function? Its effect on these altered hollow-suites. It's not good news, Benjamin. There are some very serious consequences to what I've found here. Related to the epidemic of murders, she nodded. Basically the situation with the hollow-suites in the indicated sector is as Odo suspected. They've all been tampered with. An operations crew is currently removing the other modules identical to this one. The technology that's employed in these modules is a very powerful and illicit sensory input technology that's usually referred to as CI. Cortical induction. It's not anything new, but CI technology was suppressed by the Federation authorities. Her hand moved slowly above the bench as though her fingertips could read the message encoded in the carefully separated pieces. You know how an unmodified hollow-suite works, Benjamin. Essentially, it creates an illusory experience by presenting sensory data to the user's normal percept system, including tactile sensations by means of low-level tractor beams or by replicating objects that can actually be touched and held. What makes the CI technology so powerful is that it bypasses the sense organs entirely. It operates by inducing the desired current flow and synaptic discharges in the neurofibers of the user's brain. The resulting experience is much more commanding in the intensity of the illusion created. If undergone often enough, it can begin to override the user's perception of reality itself. The consequences, as we've seen, can be severe. Dax, are you quite sure that there's a definite connection between these CI modules and the outbreak of murders on board DS9? My investigation into the matter is still at a preliminary stage, Benjamin. A great deal will be determined by the correlation I find between the CI programming and the analysis of what I've been recording from the subject Armant-Wios. Very well, Dax. Keep me apprised immediately of any new developments. His gaze moved again across the sparkling and mute pieces laid out on the bench's surface. Then he turned away and strode out the laboratory door. Major Kira caught up with Cisco as he headed for the ops deck. Commander, I've received some transmissions from our contacts on Bajor updating the political situation. There's been some developments just in the time that I've been back here at the station. Oh, Major, and what are they? Unfortunately, Commander, it's all in line with what I've previously reported. The severity front has made some significant advances. They've acquired a highly effective spokesman, a general hour. Cisco's brow furrowed in concentration. Who is he? Kira shrugged. A hero of the Bajoran resistance? That's where the military title comes from, at least. Since the Cardassian occupation ended, though, he's been a constant thorn in the side of the provisional government. My own assessment would be that he can shift his positions to whatever will bring him the most power so he can be pretty dangerous. Major, I have yet to meet a Bajoran that I wouldn't consider dangerous. Yourself included, of course. Cisco rubbed the corner of his brow as if pushing back his accumulating concerns. Keep me posted, Major. If anything happens with this general hour, we'll make containing the effects a top priority. He walked away from her, knowing full well that there was more that she had wanted to tell him and more that needed taking care of. There was always more. Odo was waiting in Cisco's office. How's the investigation going, Constable? We've made considerable progress, Commander. I've been able to extract a record from each of the Hollow Suites that has been tampered with, establishing all of the recent users. My initial suspicions were borne out. All of the murderers and Armant-Wires were frequent users of the altered Hollow Suites. Fine, Constable. Keep up the good work, and get back to me if you uncover anything new. Cisco switched on his computer panel. He looked up a few seconds later, realizing that Odo was still sitting across the desk from him. He asked, is there something else constable? Yes, there was something else I wanted to bring to your attention. It's a personal matter, I think, to do with you. Then I'm afraid I don't have time for it. Right now I don't have a personal life. I believe it's important, Commander. Is it really that urgent? I think it is. It's about your son, Jake. As I've said, I've extracted the list of frequent users of the altered Hollow Suites, and Jake is one of them. Are you sure? Odo nodded. I had O'Brien check out the device he constructed for me that reads out the access codes. The data I've obtained is reliable. Your son's use of the altered Hollow Suites appears to still be in a preliminary stage. The pattern we've seen of increasingly frequent visits has only just started to accelerate in his case. There's time. Constable were all of those CI modules removed from the Hollow Suites in question. Actually, they weren't, Commander. We left one module online, with a security monitor attached in case we needed to investigate its effects in situ, as it were. Thank you, Constable. That's all. As Commander of the Station, Cisco had no problem in entering the restricted sector with a simple computer override and finding the one Hollow Suite that had been left functional. He peeled away Odo's security seal and dropped it on the floor beside him. He set the Hollow Suites programming for what he knew was one of his son's favorites. With the press of his finger, the door slid open and he stepped inside to a sunlit world. The doorway closed behind him, completing the Hollow Suites' illusion. A warm summer wind moved across a field of yellow grasses. The barely perceptible scent of cool running water came from beyond the dense stand of trees some distance away. He had been here before with Jake. In the woods' darkness, he found the first wrong thing. The whitening bones of a cat, the dry fragments spread obscenely apart by coarse twine looped around the nearest tree trunks. The cat's skull bared its teeth in a silent howl. He walked on back into the sunlight to the creek's edge, water purled against the rocks. Less than a meter away, he found more death. The body of a man sprawled face down, fingertips clawing into the muddy bank. Kneeling down, Cisco turned the body over and found himself gazing at his own face. Citeless eyes fixed upon the sun. Somebody was watching him. He could feel it. He looked up and saw a man with arms folded across his chest, eyes dark as holes into night. A mocking smile twisted one side of his narrow face. Cisco let the corpse with his face slip from his grasp. Who are you? Don't you know? I'm a cog. I live here. Cisco's rage burst like a red flower in his vision, blinding him as he leaped forward, hands outstretched for the throat of the image that vanished. His fingers scraped hard into the wet earth and rounded stones at the creek's edge. Cisco drew back onto his haunches. The illusion of water mingled with his own blood fell into the stream and was born from his sight. From an arched open window of the Temple of Kyo Paka, Kira could see the runabout that had brought her home once more. The rough stone of the wall set into place centuries ago and ornamented with the carved tracery of a long dead artisan contrasted with the smoothly functional lines of the craft. One of the Temple's acolytes moved up beside Kira. We did not expect to see you again so soon after your last visit. The station did not notify us of your coming. They don't know I'm here. I didn't tell anyone at Deep Space Nine where I was going. I didn't submit a flight plan. I just went and came here. I'm not sure why. The sun's edge had risen over the horizon enough to bring a smoke-like mist from the damp fields. The acolyte waited in silence until Kira spoke again. There's some crisis going on aboard the station. Right now, Commander Sisko's attention is entirely taken up with that. And frankly, if he were burnt out on dealing with every little twist and turn in bajorin politics, I wouldn't blame him. So you decided to take care of this latest problem with the severity front all by yourself. I suppose it's too important to let it slide and then just hope that we can pick up the pieces later. There might not be a later, if our and the other front leaders get their way as far as bajorin involvement with the Federation. The acolyte raised an eyebrow. And you feel that by yourself you can change all that? There was one person who kept it from happening before. Yes, but you're not Kai Obaka. Kira sighed. I don't think I'm not painfully aware of that. A smile from the acolyte. Perhaps if you persist in this endeavor you will learn much. I doubt if even the Kai was born with all the virtues she possessed before she answered the call of the prophets. Kira stepped back from the arched window. As much as the temple's quiet had returned a measure of strength to her soul, she knew that the time to leave had come. There were people in the capital whom she needed to see, words to be spoken, and with any luck, and negotiations to be made. As she made her way toward the twisting stone steps the other woman called to her. You go with our hopes and the blessing of one that is no longer with us. Commander Sisko faced Dr. Bashir in one of the infirmary's small consulting rooms. Sisko knew that the doctor would err on the side of kindness. That was why he ordered the station's chief medical officer to tell the truth no matter what pain and guilt was involved. The doctor smiled. It actually looks pretty good. I ran a complete battery of tests on Jake. Everything from real-time neural pathway charting and catacloming receptor indices to old fashioned raw shocking plots, and I found a healthy young boy, physically and mentally. There's no sign of either the synaptic degeneration or obsessive thought patterning that we've seen with Armant Wiles and the others. Sisko heard his own voice as though it were coming from someone else. You've forgotten something, Doctor. I've seen evidence of my son's condition that doesn't show up in all your scannings and tests. In that hollow suite. I saw my own death. I saw my murdered corpse lying on the ground. An illusion, Commander. Anger flared inside Sisko. An illusion that couldn't exist at all unless it reflected something true. Something in Jake. The CI module found something inside my son. And with Major Norese returned to active duty, Odo could concentrate on his duties aboard Deep Space Nine. I should be returning to the security office commander. Yes, of course, Constable, I didn't mean to detain you. The door slid shut after Odo, and Sisko went to his living quarters to lie down. When he opened the door, he saw Jake idly tossing a baseball and catching it. His son looked up at him. You look kind of tired, Dad. Sisko managed to smile. A little more than usual, I suppose. But tell you what, after I get some rest, I could use a little baseball practice. Jake regarded him with a mixture of hope and skepticism. You sure? I mean, you've been busy a lot. Sisko sat and closed his eyes, rolling his head back against the sofa cushion. Only busy with things that don't even exist, Jake. And they can wait. Jake watched his father for a moment longer, then slid off his fielder's glove and set it down on the sofa cushion between them. He stood up, glancing back over his shoulder as he headed to his room. leaving his father to his long, delayed rest. Post-production supervisor was Linda Wollman. The recording engineer was Sam Aronson. Tape editors were Dave Levan and Pete Pentelis of Norwood production, with sound design by Gary Fink. Original music was composed by Sam McCallay, Carl Schuritz, Eve Biglarian, and Richard Emmett. The associate producer was Florence Burrow Adams. Star Trek, Deep Space Nine, Warped, was directed by Jill Dembe Guest. This has been a presentation of Simon & Schuster Audio.
description: In this episode titled "Warped", Renéal Bérz-Zhén-Wau narrates the story of Jake Sisko and his companion as they explore a creek in Star Trek: Deep Space Nine. The boys encounter a fish that is not normal, and Jake feels a strange sensation when he sees a turtle for the first time. As they continue their adventure, Jake realizes that everything here seems to be different from what he's accustomed to.

transcript: Side Five, Objective Beijor by John Peel. Continuing on page 163. Shakaar nodded. That, as you humans say, is the good news. I can tell from your expression that there is also bad, and that it probably outweighs the good. Yes, Cisco admitted. Even if Torque is on our side, I am not sure that his fellow-hivemasters will agree with him that Beijor should be spared. They seem pretty set on making you their next target. Shakaar sighed. "'How can any race be so indifferent to the suffering they cause?' he exclaimed. They aren't indifferent," Cisco corrected him. They do feel badly about the whole thing, but they're working on some great design and feel that the needs of the hive take precedence over the wishes of aliens. "'Wonderful,' Shakaar shook his head. "'So we're going to be attacked by a race that doesn't wish us any harm, but will kill us anyway.' "'That's about it,' agreed Cisco. "'Naturally my people and I will do everything in our power to stop them,' Shakaar. "'I know that, Captain, and we are truly grateful. We also will do everything in our power to stop the hive. Let us both pray that our combined efforts will be successful.' He terminated the conversation. So sighed and settled back. It had gone better than he'd feared. Shakaar at least was a very rational man and didn't waste time or words on recriminations or foolish posturing. But there was no denying that this was a dire situation, and their only hope at the moment was one sympathetic alien who might turn out to be completely powerless in the end. Sauna was both elated and terrified. When Torque had broken the good news to her that they would not be separated after all, she had at first been thrilled. Her confidence in him had not been misplaced. He had salvaged their relationship without compromising his integrity. Now, however, as she stood prepared to accompany him to the alien vessel, she was having twinges of fear. She had never been off the hive before. None of her people had, as far back as the first hive, to leave the comfort and friendship of her people, to risk her life with aliens. That was quite frankly scaring her. She did not know what to expect. The only thing that prevented her from panicking and backing out of this trip was Torque's confidence. He had to be as scared as she was, but he trusted and liked these aliens. They had saved his life and the lives of others. That spoke well for them. They lived in a space station of their own which showed their intellectual evolution. But they terrified her. Aliens! Sauna wished she could behave more like a scientist, to simply accept facts and not burden herself with emotional issues. But she could not. The idea of being out among the stars she loved was appealing, and she would be going where none of her race had gone before. She and Torque were pioneers. She wished it were someone else, but it was not. Torque gave her an encouraging smile. Courage, he whispered to her, stroking her shell affectionately. I will not shame you, she promised. I know that, he answered. Ah, here is Odo now. Sauna looked around the vestibule as the alien, the first she had ever seen, arrived. She couldn't suppress a shudder and a gasp as she saw him. Forgive me, she said, attempting to excuse her lack of respect. I did not mean to be rude, but you are so. Ugly, asked Odo. He bent his head to one side and studied her. I am not offended. Others have thought me so before, and doubtless others will in the future. I am sure I must look as ugly to you, Sauna stammered. Not quite, Odo replied. But I have the advantage over you. I have met thousands of alien intelligences, and am beyond such reactions. Considering I am your first alien, I think you are doing rather well. Please, by his understanding, Odo, Sauna inclined her head. You are very kind. Well, Odo said brush-clay, as if embarrassed by the compliment. I think it is time that we left. He looked at Sauna and then talked. Are you both prepared for this? Sauna swallowed nervously. Will it hurt? She asked. Not at all. There will be a momentary sense of dislocation, and then you will be on board the defiant. It is a safe and not unpleasant experience. Odo tapped the badge on his clothing. Three to beam over. Trying hard not to panic, Sauna steal her nerves for whatever was about to happen. For an instant there was nothing at all. Then she felt a tingle throughout her body, and her vision seemed to shimmer. When this cleared, her surroundings were utterly different. She stood within a different chamber on a slightly raised platform. Facing her were three beings that were clearly non-hive. In rough shape and appearance they resembled Odo, but she realized that there were minor and possibly significant differences. Welcome to the defiant. The one who had spoken and stepped forward was tall and dark in coloring. This must be the Cisco of whom Torqu had spoken. Her guest was confirmed when Torqu stepped down and greeted the man. Thank you, Captain Sisco. May I present Sauna, she is my assistant and my one to be. I am pleased to meet you, Sauna. Sisco smiled at her, and gestured for her to leave the platform. Please join us. Thank you, Captain. Sauna followed Torqu staying close to him. These aliens were strange-looking and puzzling to her, and at the same time exhilarating, an alien species. No, several if what Torqu had said was accurate. Cisco finished the introductions. This is Major Kira, and this is Chief O'Brien. Sauna bowed her head to each in turn. Kira was also tall, but her nose structure was odd. She also wore some form of ornamentation in one ear, perhaps for some ritual reason. She was judged by the shape of her unshelled body, a female. O'Brien was stockier, and she guessed probably male. It was difficult to be certain with alien races. Could she judge them by the standards of the hive? Let's go to the bridge, Sisco suggested. Then we can get underway for Deep Space Nine. Sauna followed along as a part of the group, trying to absorb as many details of the craft through which she passed as she could. The alien named Kira fell in beside her. So, Kira said, your Torqu's one to be. Does that mean you two have a relationship, then? Sauna bowed her head. Yes. As soon as is possible, we are to become one. She wrinkled her snout. Do you have similar ritual arrangements? Yes, answered Kira, laughing. We call them marriages. Ah, Sauna nodded. Interesting. Here we are. Kira gestured for Sauna to proceed her through an open doorway. Unlike the hive, these doorways slid aside instead of irising open. Moving on the bridge of the ship, Sauna stared about in amazement. It looked very complex and busy. It was also very cramped and dark compared to her workspace on the hive. She realized that space on this small craft was at a premium, but did it really have to be so small? She realized she was judging the aliens again and clamped down on those thoughts. There were several work stations, most of them staffed by the same kind of humans as she had already met. The far end of the room was taken up by a large screen, which was at the moment completely blank. I'm afraid we don't have chairs to fit you, Cisco commented as he led them across the bridge. I'm having some fabricated for the quarters you'll be assigned on Deep Space Nine, though. Meanwhile, I hope you won't be too uncomfortable here. This will be fine, Captain, Torque, said politely. Sauna could tell that he felt rather confined in the room also, but he was being polite. The aliens were trying their best, after all. Good. Cisco moved to what was obviously a chair designed for his body and sat down. It was weird seeing an intelligent being bend like that without snapping a limb. Helm set course back to DS-9, Warp Five. Acknowledged, the Helm's woman answered. There was the briefest flair of sound from whatever powered this ship, and then it settled back down to the background hum again. Are we moving, Captain? asked Sauna. Yes, Cisco replied. The inertial dampers keep you from realizing it, though. Fascinating, she commented. Your technology is truly amazing. Cisco laughed. I had bought the same of yours. In climbing her head, Sauna agreed. We both have some unique aspects to our lives, I suspect. She glanced up from the screen, hungrally. Is it possible for me to view the stars? I am excited to be out here among them, Captain. I have never been in space before. Cisco glanced at Torque. I have kept the screen blanked out in case of problems, he said carefully and politely. And I appreciate the thought, Captain, Torque answered, but I must get used to the sight of the stars. He looked toward the screen. This is only a representation, is it not? Perhaps then it will not affect me as strongly. Proud of her mail, Sauna said. And I am with you, my love. I will try and give you strength. How many other mails would dare so much as he? Very well, Cisco agreed. But if it does prove to be too much for you, I am switching it off. He moved to one of the panels and tapped in a series of commands. Get ready, he warned them. Screen is coming online, now. The blankness vanished slowly, and gradually images started to form. The background was dark, and then thousands of points of light came into view. The stars, and she was among them. Beside her, Torque gave a strangled gasp of shock and terror. She whirled to him in concern. He was rigid with fear, but he had not curled into a ball. Sauna could see the tension in every line of his face and body, and his hands were clutched into claws. He was shaking and sweating, but he was fighting off the worst of it. I am so proud of you, she whispered in his ear. Torque managed a very strained nod of his head, but he was spending almost all of his powers of concentration on fighting the terror that was ripping at his soul. This was a fight she could offer only emotional support for. He would have to wage this war alone. Glancing around, Sauna saw that Sisko was watching with concern. He is all right, Sauna informed the captain. It will get better for him soon. This representation of the stars does not seem to be as hard on him as the real thing. I am glad to hear it, Sisko replied, removing his hand from the screen's controls. As long as you are sure. I am. She stared greedily back at the screen again, drinking in the view. It was magnificent. Is it possible to change the angle of view, she asked? I should like to see what the hive looks like from the outside. Of course. Sisko manipulated the controls again. Slowly the picture shifted. He was doing this out of concern for Torque. She was certain, and she felt grateful for this. Torque was still rigid, but he seemed less tense now. He really was getting acclimatized to the view. On the screen the stars shifted, and then the hive moved into the image. When it was centered, the picture stopped. They were receding from the hive quite quickly, and the beautiful shape was getting smaller and smaller as she watched rapidly. Her home, and the home of her people for thousands of generations, no hive dweller had ever been this far away in all of history. She felt a pang of sickness wishing to be back, but that was swallowed up in her sense of wonder. What further marvels lay ahead of her. She was on the adventure of a lifetime. The only cloud over it was the possibility that it might end with the destruction of an inhabited planet, if the hive masters had their way. Chapter 19. Rom, Rom, where are you, you lazy good for nothing? Quark scanned his stockroom angrily. Here I am, brother. Rom popped out from behind a stack of crates carrying a barrel of Romulan ale. I was just, well, don't, snapped Quark. This is no time for such frivolities. Put that thing down and listen to me. With a grunt of relief, Rom did as he was asked. What is it, brother? He asked anxiously. You look worried. Of course I look worried, you idiot. Anyone with half a brain would be worried. He glared at Rom. That's why you're not worried, of course. He handed across a pad. Here go and take inventory in storage room nine. Room nine? Rom looked confused, but you told me never to go in there. Quark sighed, then growled. And now I'm telling you to go in there. Can't you do anything I tell you without argument? Of course I can, brother. Rom said quickly. Uh, isn't room nine where you store your armaments? Special orders, Quark yelled angrily. Special orders, remember that. I've put the access code on the pad so you can get in. Rom wisely didn't mention that he already knew it. Of course I get it, he exclaimed happily. You're going to be selling arms to the Bajorans for their upcoming war. How perceptive. Quark's voice dripped sarcasm. Of course I am. Then we're getting out of here fast. Rom frowned. But why, brother? Rule of acquisition number thirty-five states don't start quoting the rules to me, snapped Quark. I knew them backwards before you'd learned to stop drooling. War is good for business. Rom, think for a minute. Assuming it won't overload your wiring, why is war good for business? After considering the question, Rom's face lit up with a smile. Because we can sell weapons to both sides and medical supplies to the survivors at vastly inflated prices. Right, Quark replied through gritted teeth. Now, when the hive reaches Bajor, they aim to take the planet apart for its minerals. And whatever else they need. What can we sell them that they can't just take? Uhh. Nothing? Rom guessed. Right. And the Bajoran race will be wiped out, won't they? So they won't be buying anything. There's no profit to be made in genocide. And once Bajor is gone, the odds are that these aliens will swallow the station next. That's why I'm getting out of here. You can stay if you like. Rom thought about this for a moment. No, I think I'll come with you. Lucky me, Quark snapped. Now go and check the inventory. I'm expecting some important customers for everything there later today. Nodding over and over again, Rom scurried away. Quark watched him go with a sigh. Then he straightened his jacket and headed back to his office to place a call. It was time to reserve seats on the first shuttle out of here after his business was concluded. Sixteen calls later, he wound up calling ops. The face of Lieutenant Soika stared back at him. Quark, the officer said. Is there something I can do for you? Yes. The Ferengi could barely control his temper. You can tell me why nobody wants to sell me a seat on any ship leaving this station. Ah. Soika tried to look sympathetic but failed miserably. That would be because Captain Sisko left strict orders that you were not to leave the station. What? Quark was almost apoplectic. How dare he! He has no right to restrict my movement. I'm not a Federation citizen. I want to speak to him immediately. Soika shook his head. Sorry, Quark. He's not on station right now. But I'll tell him you called and ask him to get back to you, okay? No, it is not okay. Quark yelled. He felt like breaking something, but the only objects close at hand were much too expensive to destroy. Did he say why he won't let me leave? Something about rats and sinking ships, I think, Soika answered. Again, you'd have to ask him. He paused. Have a nice day. The screen went blank. Quark squealed in frustration. We have to be ready for war, Jero insisted. He gave Shekar a placating look. I understand how much you loathe the idea, but it is being forced upon us by these aliens. Shekar muttered something under his breath and then moved across his room to join Jero and Kai-win. She was seated at the conference table with a regal expression on her face. I understand necessity, Shekar replied, and I've ordered all Bajoran forces mobilized. If the Hive starts to move in our direction, then we'll be prepared to launch an all-out strike to try and stop it, though the profits know we very little firepower, even with all of our forces combined. You're still thinking defensively, objected Jero. We have the forces now. We could strike while the Hive is still fissioning. Hit it while it is weak. We stand a better chance of destroying it now than we would if it were in orbit above our planet. I don't believe so, Shekar said once again. Besides, Captain Sisko thinks that he may be able to persuade these aliens not to attack. He thinks, scoffed Jero. And you are willing to risk the fate of Bajor on what some outworlder thinks. I'm more Bajoran than you are, snapped Shekar. I don't recall ever hearing of any of your exploits against the Cardassians during the occupation. Jero shook his head slightly. I am a man of thought and not of crude violence. Really, Shekar noted, for a man of thought you seem to have amassed quite an array of weaponry, photon cannons, short-range strike craft. He glared at his opponent. And the fate of Bajor does not rest on an outsider. After all, Captain Sisko is the emissary of whom the profits speak. Isn't he, Kai-win? Without missing a beat, Win replied, So many think, Shekar. I myself am open-minded. I'm sure you are, Shekar thought. Well, to try and foil the emissary's plans would run counter to the profits' will, in that case. And none of us would wish to do that, would we? He glared from one to the other. No, Win finally replied. We would not. She gave Jero a mildly reproving stare. Perhaps our colleague has been a trifle hasty in his urgings, but it was done with the best interests of Bajor at heart, I am sure. Of course, agreed Shekar. But for the moment, I think that the best thing we can do for the safety of Bajor is to pray that Captain Sisko's plan succeeds. A noble sentiment, agreed Kai-win. Jero simply scowled and turned away. Sana couldn't take her eyes away from the screen as the defiant prepared to dock with Deep Space Nine. The station looked so small, but she had to keep reminding herself that these people didn't have the same needs or philosophy as hers. To them, she supposed, the hive must look huge and wasteful. Torque stood beside her, his eyes fixed on the screen also. Only the tension in his body and the haunted expression in his eyes told her that he was still under a great deal of strain. Otherwise he was covering up his fears quite well. Secure docking clamps, Sisko ordered, and then stand down. The crew began to power down their systems, and Sisko rose from his command chair to join Sana and Torque. I trust this experience was not too traumatic, he said politely. It was tolerable, Torque managed to say. I was not as stressed as I had feared. Perhaps it is possible, after all, to overcome this agaraphobia. With sufficient incentive, I believe it is, agreed Sisko. Turning to Sana, he asked, and how did you find the trip? Exhilarating, she confessed, to be able to move so swiftly through space, to journey from star to star in so short at time. Captain, this freedom of yours is quite intoxicating. Sisko smiled. I've often thought the same, he admitted. Sometimes I just long for an excuse to get away from DS9 and out into space again. Come, let me show you to your quarters. You can relax a while there before we travel down to Beijou, and you meet with their representatives. Thank you, said Torque. That would be greatly appreciated. I am a little fatigued. Following their host, Sana once again stared all around as they left the defiant. Many of the corotters they traversed were quite deserted. Aside from the ugliness of the decor, she could almost imagine that she was back within the hive again. From time to time though they passed other beings. Most of them were either human or bajorin. Thanks to major Kira's conversations on the way here, Sana had learned that the nose ridges were quite distinctive for the bajorins. She felt rather proud of herself for being able to distinguish between the two, given such a small distinction. Then she saw one being who was clearly neither. He was a tall, hefty looking individual, a dull gray in color, with a bare head and a large skull on his face. Like the humans he wore clothing. When he was past them, Sana asked curiously, what kind of being was that? That? Sisko smiled. That was Morn. He's most likely on his way to Quarks. He spends most of his life there. What is a Morn? Sana asked. To be honest, I'm not entirely sure, replied the captain. He's the only one of his kind I've ever seen. Oh! Sana was astonished that there might be species on the station that Sisko knew so little about. How many different alien races are there on Deep Space Nine? It varies a lot, Sisko answered. At least thirty, I'd say. Sometimes as many as a hundred. Sana looked shocked. I'm sure you'll get used to it. Sisko laughed. The first hundred aliens are the hardest to spot. After that it gets really easy. They reached the rooms set aside for Sana and Torque. They adjoined one another, and Sisko showed them how to open the doors and to order food and drink on the replicators. It seemed to be straightforward enough. I have to go to Ops now. Sisko informed them. We'll be going on to Bajor in a few hours if you feel up to it. Thank you, Captain, Torque replied. I am certain we will be fine with a little rest. Good. Sisko paused in the doorway. I've had the shutters over your windows closed, he added. You can open them if you desire by ordering the room computer to perform the task. I thought it better that way. Torque inclined his head. Your thoughtfulness is most appreciated, Captain. He watched as Sisko left and the door closed. Then he turned to Sana. What do you think? He asked her. Think. She wrinkled her nose in amusement. It is hard to know what to think. There has been so much that is new. But I think that you are right about these aliens, Torque. They are a considerate and intelligent species. In fact, I like them. Good. Torque eased himself into one of the chairs that Sisko had fabricated for them. So do I. They are fascinating, are they not? Yes. Sana stroked his shell in concern. Now, how do you feel? I know how difficult this has all been for you. I am as well as can be expected, Torque answered. He could not lie to her. I do feel uncomfortable, but I know that what I do is for the best. We must correctly evaluate this planet, Bejou. I could not live with myself if the world were destroyed needlessly. Sana was glad to hear this. Perhaps we will be able to convince them to move, she said gently. They do seem to be intelligent. At least as intelligent as our ancestors were when they made the move into space. Surely they will listen to reason. Torque smiled at her. They have brought us here, hoping to convince us that their way is best, he reminded her. But they are bright, she objected, so we may be able to win them over to our side. Torque snout wrinkled. I do not feel that this Sisko is a person who changes his way so simply, he replied. He is a decisive person and a very strong one. I wish I possessed one tenth of his conviction and courage. Do not speak like that, exclaimed Sana. She took his hand in hers. What you have already done took more courage than I ever hoped to see in one lifetime. Torque smiled gently and glanced over at the shuttered window. Perhaps you should open the portal. I know how much you hunger for the sight of space again. She hesitated. Are you sure? Yes, he answered. I must get used to it if I am to function on Beijou. I would rather not, of course, but it is my duty. He took a deep breath and steeled himself. Open the shutter. Very well. Sana crossed to the computer and tapped the command key that Sisko had shown her. Computer, she ordered. Open the shutter. Affirmative, the computer replied. With the faintest of hisses, the steel shutter slid aside to reveal a view of the stars. From where she stood, Sana could see a faint glow off to one edge of the window. She glanced back at Torque who stood stiffly, his face a mask. I can manage, he gasped. It was clearly a struggle, but there was nothing that she could do at the moment to aid him. Sana nodded and then moved forward, drawn irresistibly to the glow. As she neared the window, a new object resolved itself. She stared out across space at the globe she could see. It was small, but quite distinct. She could make out vague whiteness across the blue disc. It had to be the planet Beijor that she was observing. It was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen in her life. Hanging in the blackness of space, the tiny globe seemed so small and fragile. Yet it was a planet that bore all the comforts of life, rivers and seas, flowers and animals, and people and cities. Sana did not care what decision the Hive Masters made about this world. She knew only one thing. To destroy such a work of beauty would be the gravest crime that anyone could ever commit. Whatever the Masters decided, whatever even Torque decided, she was absolutely clear in her own hearts. Beijor must not be harmed. Chapter 20. So what do you think of our visitors, Major? Cisco steepled his hands and stared across his desk at Kira. She was standing at attention and looking even more uncomfortable in that pose than usual. Personally? She shrugged. I liked them. Sana seems like a nice person and Torque is clearly trying to control fears that are almost tearing him apart. As a species though, how can I have anything but disgust for them? They destroyed it to rain for. I had friends there, people I grew up with. They're dead because of these murderers. Cisco nodded, empathizing with the struggle inside her. And how do you resolve this? How can I? She asked. All I can tell you, Captain, is that I know my duty. If the Hive does come for Beijor and going back to my world to fight for it, I don't care what you or Starfleet think. I understand, Major. Cisco replied. But I can't allow that. Nor I suspect will your government. You're their liaison on this station and you can't simply desert your post when you feel like it. It's not simply feeling, argued Kira. I have to be where I can do my people the most good. Your place, Cisco said carefully, is where your people say it is, and they want you here, Major. He stood up and walked around his desk to join her. Noris, believe me. I understand how you feel. When my wife was murdered by the Borg, I wanted to go out and hunt down every last Borg in existence. But I came to my senses. I've even been able to deal with my grief and my loss. But you cannot abandon your post simply because of personal feelings. You lost a wife and friends to the Borg. Kira agreed with sympathy. I may lose my world to these invaders. It's not really the same thing. It's exactly the same thing. Cisco insisted. The scale is different. I'll grant you, but the principle is the same. Noris, we're both officers. When we put on our uniforms, we assumed duties that go beyond our personal desires. We have responsibilities. Yours is here and now to deep space nine, as is mine. I promise you, I will do all that is in my power to safeguard Beijou. But I need to know that you'll be covering my back. I'm pretty certain that Beijou needs you here, but I'm absolutely certain that I need you here. He could see her struggling between her logic and her heart. There was nothing more he could say to persuade her, and he simply waited. Finally, she nodded. You're right, Captain, she said tightly. I should be here, not on Beijou. Whatever you need of me, I'll do. She sighed. But I can't help wanting to be there. Good. Cisco touched her shoulder. I appreciate the difficult decision you've made. Now, he broke off as his desk communicator beat. Yes, he growled, irritated at being interrupted. What is it? Sorry to disturb you, Captain. Came Dax's voice. But there's someone here to see you. He claims it's urgent. Cisco sighed. Who is it? Vedek Yaka, sir. Cisco winced. He'd had dealings with Yaka, but he was a very good friend. Before, the Vedek was a deeply religious man with his own agenda to pursue. He was absolutely convinced that Cisco was the emissary promised in the writings of the prophets and the Savior of Beijou. His first inclination was to ask the man to go away. On the other hand, Cisco couldn't afford to alienate any of the Vedics, especially at a time like this. Send him in. He decided reluctantly. That sounds like my cue to leave, Kira said. My sympathies. She had little time for most of the members of the religious orders outside of the late Vedek Burial. She nodded to Vedek Yaka as he entered Cisco's office and the door closed behind her. Vedek, Cisco said in greeking, emissary replied the monk. He bowed his head and then smiled slightly. His gray beard looked even more grizzled than usual, and his eyes showed lines of stress. It was good of you to see me. I know how important your time is, especially now. Well, what can I do for you? Cisco asked, getting directly to the point. The upcoming crisis, I imagine. Naturally, agreed Yaka in his deep sonorous tones. Kai win has been to see Shaka and has adduced a quotation from the third prophecy of Andakai as her reason. I believe she has seriously misinterpreted the text. Cisco spread his hands. Forgive me, but I'm not an expert on your holy writings, Vedek. I doubt I can be of help in any dispute the two of you may have. I understand that. Yaka agreed. However, the text she used is one of the emissary prophecies and should be correctly applied to you. I was afraid of that, mumbled Cisco. Listen and see if you do not agree that it is most opposite to this time of testing we are undergoing. Yaka held up his head in hands and recited. The land will be torn asunder as great wings hover. Death will be on all who witness and mourning on the lips of the few who survive. Weep for the lost, the children, the land. Weep for it and they are no more. In that terrible day shall all my people be one. Stand firm, for one shall protect you, and two shall convert. In their faith, Vajor will be made whole." He looked sharply at Cisco. You see the significance, of course. Cisco wasn't sure how to reply. He knew that many of the writings of the prophets had been truly inspired in some strange way. I knew it because the records said so, but the records have been altered. He shook his head. I had simply accepted the histories on faith without using my intelligence to study them. We all do that. Cisco told him. We accept things without question because we believe them to be correct. Perhaps agreed Torques. But in this case the deceit was deadly. The runabout exited the wormhole in a final blaze of light. The passage constricted behind them and then vanished. Cisco glanced at Torque. Where to? He asked. Deep Space Nine, Torque replied. I must contact the hive. Captain, could you also recall sauna and dax from Beijo? I know we are going to need their aid for what we must now do. Of course. Cisco patched into the bajaran net. A moment later he was looking at Kira's face. Major returned to DS9 with dax and sauna. I don't care if you have to kidnap her to get her to come along. Just do it. Kira managed to smile. There's no need to be that extreme, she answered. Kira is dying to get back anyway. She and dax have discovered something very significant, Captain. Save it for later, Cisco replied. I want you moving now. Understood. The screen went blank. What could they have found out? Cisco mused. I have a suspicion that they have discovered much the same information that I have, Torque replied. Sauna had the data that Hossier gave me before I departed the hive. He's in a strange code, but I suspect it is the real information that the first hive wished to pass on to future generations. Let's save this until everyone is together, suggested Cisco. Am I right in thinking that this might be a way to stop the hive and save Bajor? Torque nodded. Yes, Captain. We may be able to restore the original programming to the hive, but I do not think that it will be accomplished peacefully. There are too many powerful forces on the enemy side. The enemy side, Cisco echoed. Yes, Captain. Torque smiled. For what it is worth, we are definitely allies in your quest to stop the hive. I pledge to do my utmost to see that Bajor survives. Well, Cisco muttered to himself. It looks like the profits came through again. Bree sighed and then straightened up from her workstation. "'That is it,' she announced to her colleagues. I have completed the text of our message, and it is ready to be transmitted to the hive at large. Then do so,' a voice called. "'It is not that simple,' Bree replied. Access to the comps has been denied by a security override. Our act of rebellion has alerted Dron and his fellows to our knowledge. He is working to ensure that we are isolated and that we do not cause dissent before Bajor is absorbed. "'Then we must stop him,' another said. Again it is not that simple,' Bree shook her head. These were intelligent people, but they simply didn't understand the nature of the political beast. Dron, through Master Raldar, controls the security forces. They in turn control what messages reach the hive. We cannot take on the security forces. We would be an open rebellion. And likely to lose,' she added realistically, "'We are not fighters.' "'Then you are saying we can do nothing? The Dron will succeed? "'No,' Bree answered. I am saying that we need a different approach to the problem. We are scientists. There must be a way for us to see around this problem and to overcome it.'" One of the younger members of her staff approached. "'I have some comp skills,' she said hesitantly. If access to the comps is coded, I may be able to deduce the coding. If I may try, of course,' Bree moved aside to let the other work. That is an indication of what I mean. Dron is being sneaky, and we had better learn how to be sneakier. She looked at them all with affection. After all, we are a lot smarter than they are. Are we not? Before anyone could respond there came a heavy blow on the door. Security, a voice called, open up. "'No,' one of the astronomers exclaimed, panicking. We cannot allow them in. We cannot keep them out.' Bree contradicted him. They could burn down the door, which will only delay them. "'What do you propose?' he demanded. That we surrender? No one is suggesting surrender.' Bree hobbled across to the door and hit the entry plate. It iris opened to reveal a half dozen males beyond. Each carried a tingler weapon. "'Ah! Come to harass us, have you?' The leader moved inside and glared at her. Mr. Raldar has asked us to keep you confined and isolated,' he replied. "'You are acting in a treasonous fashion, and that cannot be allowed to continue.' "'Really?' Bree appeared at him intently. "'I know you. Are you not dimness?' "'Yes,' the officer replied, scowling at her. "'I thought so. I was one of your tutors.' He snorted. "'I always believed that you were an intelligent pupil. A shame that I was so wrong.' "'I am not the one who is wrong,' dimness replied with dignity. I listened to the voices of the Hive Masters, which you do not." "'Well, then,' Bree told him, "'did they tell you why we object to their voices?' "'We do not need to know that,' dimness replied. "'Only that you do not listen.' Bree snorted again. "'Oh, well, spoken,' she mocked. I can see that you are using your brains only to keep your ears apart. Next thing, you will be telling me that you are only obeying orders, and it does not matter what those orders are.' I began dimness, and then he caught himself. You are attempting to bait me to prevent me from doing my job. "'Yes,' Bree agreed, surprising him. "'But I ask you also to hear what I have to say. You know me. Am I a dangerous or vicious person?' "'No,' dimness said reluctantly. "'And if you were ordered to kill us all, would you obey without thinking?' The Hive Masters would never order that, protested dimness. It is unthinkable. They have already killed,' Bree informed him. "'The blood of thousands of innocents is upon our hands, and if we do nothing, the blood of more will join it.' She could see the struggle that was going on within dimness. He had been trained by Raldar to obey orders without question, but she had instilled in all of her pupils the need to question everything. Which would win out here? "'What do you mean?' dimness asked finally. The planet that was absorbed had intelligent beings upon it,' Bree explained. Even now the Hive is in progress toward another inhabited world. These people will not leave it, so Dron aims to kill them and absorb their world anyway. "'Kill,' echoed dimness. He looked stunned. "'Do you have proof for what you say?' "'Plenty of proof,' Bree informed him. She gestured to where the young female worked on the computer. "'We are attempting to make it known to the Hive at large. Everyone must know that Dron is making all of us guilty of murder, but we cannot override the security codes.' Dimness strode to the computer and gestured for the woman there to step aside. "'I must review this data,' he told her. "'If what you say is true, then I can override the lockout and disseminate the information for you.' Smiling, Bree turned to her scared companion. "'You see?' she asked. "'I knew that there had to be a way. Dron has seriously underestimated the Hive if he believes he can force us to become killers.' "'Dron slammed his fist down on the conference table with fury. "'Rout-ar!' he growled. "'You idiot! Can nothing you do be trusted?' "'Nervously the security master wrung his hands together. "'I do not understand,' he protested. "'What have I done now?' "'The security force that you sent to arrest Bree and the other astronomers,' Dron snapped. "'It has not done so. "'Worse, it appears that they have gone over to her side. "'Someone is systematically removing the security blocks from her computer "'and allowing her access to the comp networks.' "'Well, D'Arshuk, as he studied the information screen, "'I do not understand,' he moaned. "'That has become abundantly clear,' Dron informed him. "'This is your last chance. "'Go to the Astronomy section, please.' "'Go to the Astronomy section. "'Take with you only security men you trust implicitly. "'Stop these traitors now! "'Kill them if you must. "'But stop them.' Chapter 26. Gavron watched his screens with deep satisfaction. Hammer and anvil wings were continuing to engage the enemy craft. Both were suffering heavy losses, but inflicting the same. On the main screen he caught the tail end of a fight with one Cardassian cruiser raking a hive's ship with concentrated phaser fire. The alien ship attempted to pull free, but the Cardassian pilot was, of course, superb. End of side six.
description: In "Objective Beijor," John Peel continues a podcast episode discussing the challenges faced by humans on their mission. Despite having already survived Beijor's attack, Shakaar and Cisco must still contend with the threat of another hive-destroying alien race. The episode explores the characters' inner turmoil as they grapple with the unknowns ahead, including Sauna, whose fear is palpable but her faith in Torque remains unwavering. Their only hope lies in an unlikely ally who seems to have little power over their fate, adding a sense of urgency and drama to the narrative.
