Stop at that point to hear the beginning of the book. Library of Congress Annotation. The Hive, a huge starship housing billions of insect-like aliens, is heading for the planet Bejour for fuel and raw material. Within a week, the Bajorans will face annihilation, unless Captain Sisko and the crew of Deep Space Nine find a way to stop the powerful invaders. A Star Trek Deep Space Nine novel, 1996. From the book Jacket, Captain Sisko must protect a planet from total destruction. The Hive came from another galaxy. Variants of alien beings living inside a vast biological starship. They have already destroyed one planet, converting it into raw material and fuel for their endless voyage through the cosmos. Now the Hive is heading for Bejour, and they have given the planet's inhabitants an ominous warning, evacuate in three days or die along with their world. The Bajorans would rather die than abandon their sacred home, but their hastily assembled military fleet does not stand a chance against the awesome power of the Hive, unless Captain Sisko can penetrate the Hive's defenses and discover their most closely guarded secret, all of Bejour faces extinction. This book is in memory of Harold F. Taylor, now on the greatest trek of all. Chapter 1. Target coming in range now, Captain. Captain Benjamin Sisko nodded. Thank you, Major. He leaned forward in the command chair of the USS Defiant and stared intently at the viewscreen. All weapons to full power, raise shields. All weapons powered. Here in her race glanced up from her panel to Sisko's left. There was a gleam of excitement in her eyes, and the more than fleeting suggestion of a smile on her lips. Ready on your command. Sisko could understand her feelings perfectly. It had been more than a month since any of them had been off Deep Space Nine at all, and it felt really good to be back in space and back in action. Though commanding DS-9 was hardly a simple desk job, it was good to spread one's wings and head out among the stars again. Hold steady. Shields at full, Captain. Chief O'Brien reported from his panel. Thank you, Chief. Sisko could feel the thrill of the hunt now. He watched the forward image intently, waiting for the first glimpse of the... There she is, Captain, Jeddzia Dax said. She was seated at navigation between Sisko and the screen. Her superior eyesight had caught the briefest flicker of movement that he now belatedly noticed. It's a caldery sea raider, all right, added Odo from his station. Classic configuration, and they've powered up their weapons, too. The shapeshifter was the only one who didn't look eager for this confrontation. It was mostly because he still hadn't mastered the art of shaping his somewhat rudimentary features into semblances of human emotions. They can outrun most ships in this quadrant, Sisko murmured. But they can't beat this one. Open a hailing frequency, he called out. Open, Dax responded. This is Captain Benjamin Sisko of the Federation starship Defiant, to caldery sea raider, he said slowly and clearly. You are ordered to stand down your weapons and prepare to be boarded. We have reason to believe that you are running illicit weapons to the Marquis. He gestured to Dax for her to terminate the transmission. Now, he said, let's see what their reply is, shall we? He hunched forward in his command chair, feeling the tension building within him. They've changed course, Odo announced grimly. They are now heading directly for us. He shook his head, foolish, and typically humanoid. They are also opening fire. The screen dimmed automatically as twin phaser bolts lanced out from the dark-shaped ship that skimmed toward them. The Defiant trembled slightly as the bolts impacted on the ship's deflectors. I think we can take that as a no, Kira commented. No damage to shields, O'Brien called. Still raised in eyebrow. He hadn't really expected the caldery sea to surrender. They were a volatile species at the best of times, and he had been certain that they were indeed the gunrunners he was after. Still, he hadn't expected them to do anything as foolish as trying to attack the Defiant. Even so I think we had better defend ourselves, Chief. He spun to face Major Kira. Fire a warning shot across their bow. Across? Kira sounded disappointed. Across? He repeated with a slight smile. For the first one at any rate. And fire! Kira obeyed. The Defiant shuddered slightly as the phasers lanced out across the void at the twisting raider. Open a channel, Cisco ordered Dax, and stay as close to them as you can manage. When Dax nodded he called aloud. Go to Caldery Sea Raider. I repeat, stand down or we shall be forced to disable you. I cannot be certain that this will not result in some loss of life to you. Another twin blast of phasers shot from the raider, again dissipating harmlessly against the shields. Grim Cisco turned to his bajorin first officer. All right, Major. Target their engine to cells and tick them out. Aye, sir. Kira replied with a great deal of satisfaction. Her hands flew over the phaser controls. Captain, O'Brien called out suddenly. I'm registering a drop in shield strength. He sounded harried and puzzled. They're down to 95% and dropping. What? Cisco spun to face him. What's causing it, Chief? O'Brien glared down at the panels. Outside interference, he said. There's some kind of jamming signal coming from the raider. It's causing interference in the generator wave somehow. I've never seen anything like it. Shields are now down to 80%. Cisco turned back to Kira. Now would be a good time to fire, he said gently. I'd agree with you, Captain. Kira agreed, frustration evident in her voice. But whatever's affecting the shields is affecting the targeting sensors, too. I just can't get a lock on a confirmed target. Plus, she added angrily. Power levels on the phasers are dropping. We soon won't be able to fire them at all. Best guess then, he ordered scowling. Any damage you can do to stop this attack. He spun back to O'Brien. Any idea yet what's causing this, Chief? None. The engineer answered, irritated with the reply. As Major Kira says, all our sensors are being affected, too, so I can't get a straight reading on this thing. Off the top of my head I'd say it was some sort of modified delta emitter array. But how they could power one from a craft that small beats me. I could do with a bit of time to study it, say a couple of weeks. He gave a mild grin. Not funny, Chief. Cisco objected. Status? Embarrassed, O'Brien checked his panel. Shields down to sixty percent in falling. They're coming about, O'Dow announced. I'd guess they aim to attack us now. It's difficult to read my instruments, but it looks like they're preparing to fire again. As Cisco watched the viewscreen, he saw the dart-shaped radar heading for them. Twin phaser beams lanced out, slashing into the defiant. The ship shuddered as the inertial dampers have struggled to keep her steady. The lights in the cabin dimmed, flicked, and then settled down to about half their former level. That's it, O'Brien announced. The shields are down completely. The power interference is spiraling around inside the systems now. We've lost the phasers, Kira reported grimly. I'm firing a photon torpedo. She glanced up and managed a tight smile. I'd guessed guess, so you'd better hope I'm feeling lucky today. Cisco nodded. There were very few options left to them. Whatever weapon the Cowderisi were using, it was wreaking havoc with his ship. Another run like the last one would destroy them. He watched as the ship on the screen began to turn. Then the picture started to break up as the power levels continued to fall. Damn, he muttered. If he was going to die, he would prefer to stare his fate in the face as he did so. There was the flash of a photon torpedo ejection, and the ship shook with the strain. A strain that they wouldn't normally have even felt thanks to the dampers. Now it seemed as if the defiant was falling apart about their ears. Then there was a bright flash on what was left of the picture screen, the torpedo detonation. But had Kira hit the target? After several seconds, everyone on the bridge stared at the screen, holding their breath. Nothing came into sight. Finally, Odo called out, I'm registering to bury ahead. The raider was completely destroyed. Well done, Cisco said, sighing with relief. Very nice shooting. Thank you, Kira said with a smile. And where he'd been sitting, watching the others, Julian Bashir spoke up. Remind me not to play dots with you today, Major. Even blindfolded, I think you'd beat me. The only one of the crew not smiling was O'Brien. With a scowl, he said, I just wish we hadn't been forced to destroy their ship. He shook his head. I'd have loved to get a good long look at that weapon of theirs. We all would, Chief. We all agreed. But under the circumstances, I think we did well just to survive. How are the systems now that the raider is gone? Recovering slightly, O'Brien answered, but not by much. We're going to be limping back to DS9, Captain. Cisco nodded. I'm in no hurry right now. How long will it take to get the defiant back up to par when we do reach home? O'Brien shook his head. It depends on how many systems were damaged, and by how much, he replied, I can't get consistent readings here. It could be days or even weeks, if we've got the spares, and if there aren't too many repairs on the station to keep my crew busy. I understand. Cisco turned back to Dax. Set course for home, best speed. He managed a small smile. You could manage a rough estimate of how long it'll take us, I'd appreciate it. As soon as I can, Benjamin. Dax bent to her task. Cisco saw that her hands, instead of flying across her board as they normally did, lingered and repeated tasks several times. Finally she looked up. Course-lady and executed. She shook her head. It's really slow, I'm afraid. It's going to take us at least six hours to get back. Understood. Can you patch through a channel back to DS9? We'd better let them know we'll be late for dinner. I'll try my best. She bent back to her board again. A moment or two later she said, I've got a weak audio link, Benjamin. It's all I can raise. I'm glad for even that, Cisco told her. Cisco to Ops, can you read me? Ops here came a faint crackling voice. Your signal is very faint, Captain. Are you all right? Not exactly, Mr. Soika, Cisco replied. We've destroyed the Kaldorissi Raider, but sustained damage. We should be home in about six hours. Understood. Lieutenant Soika's weak voice came back. Do you need assistance? I could have a run-about out to you pretty quickly. Thank you, no, Cisco said ruefully. We'll just head back under our own steam, licking our wounds. Cisco out. He cut the link. Gazing at the screen, he sighed. The picture was still rather fuzzy. Cinematic of the ship's damage. Still, at least they had survived and stopped the weaponry shipment. Whatever new weapon the Kaldorissi had, it would be up to Starfleet now to try and track it down and neutralize it. He'd have O'Brien transmit a full report when they reached home. Then the chief was going to be very busy getting the defiant back into order. Cisco could only hope that until it was fixed, there wouldn't be a need for it. And he knew how weak his chances were that this would be so. On DS9, crises were the order of the day. The picture too. You have betrayed us all and everything that we believe in. Even though he had been more than half expecting this accusation, Tork winced at the words that Harle spat out. There was a pain in his thorax as he faced his oldest and once dearest friend. Harle, it is not like that. Believe me, I have no intention. It does not matter what you mean now. Harle retorted, his anger and disappointment clear on his face. They have sucked you in. In a short while you will be just like them. And I thought you believed in what we talked about. He gave us note of disgust. I should have known better. Harle. Enough. As always, Sana's voice was quiet and yet piercing. Despite his mood, Harle subsided. As Sana one had something she inevitably got her way and without undue effort. You are not being fair to Tork, and in your hearts you must know this. You have not given him a chance to explain. Her lips twitched mischievously. And isn't that your main complaint against the Hive Masters, that they will not listen? She gestured toward Tork. Now, here is an apprentice Hive Master, and you will not allow him to speak. Is that fair? He is not an apprentice Hive Master. Harle replied so collab, but somewhat chastened. He is our ex-friend who has gone over to the side of the enemy. Please, beg to Tork, listen to me. Harle, I have not betrayed you. You know very well that my determination was what led me to become a Hive Master. I did not seek the position. It was thrust upon me. Of course it was. Sneared Harle, his nostril dilating rapidly, showing his disgust. But why? Was it because such elevated positions are hereditary in your lineage? He snorted again. Or because the other Hive Masters are trying to buy your silence by offering you the post and expecting you to silence the rest of the student critics' payment. Have they asked that of you yet? Are they waiting until you discover that you can no longer live without all the privileges of the exalted position of Hive Master? Tork knew that it was mostly Harle's anger speaking, but he couldn't help being hurt and irritated by his old friend. Harle, he said, trying to stay reasonable, you know me. You know my commitment to the truth. Surely, you must see that I am not going to abandon all that I believe in, simply because I have been appointed a Hive Master. All I see, Harle snapped back, is that badge on your carapace? He gestured at the symbol of the Hive that Tork now wore. The badge that we all agreed stands for repression of thought and maintenance of the status quill. How could you? Tork's patience was wearing thin now. Because I believe that there are some Hive Masters who are not against us, he replied, because I think that it is not the office that is wrong, but some who hold the position. Because I think that working from within I can affect changes, because if the public sees even just one Hive Master who will listen instead of simply giving orders, then change is possible. Because I think that in this thing I am right, and you are being a thick-scold idiot. Harle stabbed out one long bony finger, quivering with anger. Perhaps, just perhaps, you believe that now, he snarled, but it will not last. Remember your precious texts. Power is its own reward and curse. He grimaced. Or have you already forgotten all of your studies? I have forgotten nothing, Tork answered, striving to keep his temper, but you it appears have forgotten one thing, our friendship. Harle deliberately turned his carapace on Tork. You have already murdered our friendship. The Tork I once thought I knew and respected is dead. All that is left is a Hive Master. He spat the last word and then stormed from the meeting-room. The door hissed shut behind him. Sanna placed a hand on Tork's shoulder. Well, she said gently. That went better than I expected it to. His hearts lifted slightly at her touch, as they always did, but it could not ease the pain he felt. He would not listen, Tork said bitterly. He did not try and understand. Laughing, Sanna shook her head. Norle, Tork, now who is having unreasonable expectations, you know what he is like. Anger consumes him too often. She shook her shapely head. But it will not last. The flame that burns brightest dies fastest, she quoted. His anger will be gone shortly, and he will begin to think again. I hope so. Tork gave a long sigh. I know it was foolish of me to expect otherwise, but I had hoped. Yes, Sanna said gently. And that is where you are so different from harm. You hope. You work hard and strive for reason and change. Harle simply wants to sweep away the old and bring in the new. And this is not possible. Your way is the better way. It warned his thorax to hear us speak so well of him. Then you approve of my acceptance? He asked eagerly. Sanna smiled at him. I have always approved of you, Tork, she replied. You are a calm, reasoning and caring individual. She touched his carapace again, and Tork felt a thrill of mingled love and lust pass through him. You are my hope. It took a great deal of self-control for Tork to quash the burning feelings within him. Though he had undergone his determination, and was now officially an adult, Sanna had not. If he made his feelings for her known, it would not only be immoral, but illegal. Perhaps as a high of master, Tork would be immune to such charges as immorality, but he simply could not chance it. It wasn't just the fear of being caught. He knew that Sanna would say nothing, even if he were to make unwelcome dendy-licid advances to her, but that he could not use his office as a shield for his crimes. After all, wasn't that one of the things that had always most disgusted him about the Hive Masters, one rule for the Hive and one for the Masters? He had to be better than that, not only for the sake of his own soul, but also as an example to everyone, especially Sanna. She looked at him with her wise eyes, and he was pierced by an arrow of certainty. She knew what he had been thinking. I am sorry, Tork. She told him, removing her hand. I should not have done that. It was wrong of me to test you in that way. He started to say, to tell her she had done nothing wrong. She didn't allow him to finish. I was deliberately tempting you, she said, smiling slightly. I should have known that you would not succumb. I wanted to, he replied. As an adult, he was morally bound never to approach a single female child. Like the fact that she was from the same hatching-year as himself, Sanna had not undergone determination herself, and was thus still technically a child. "'But you did not,' she said fondly. "'Whatever howl thinks you have proven that your sense of honor remains untouched. And as a child,' she added ironically, "'I am allowed to say what you cannot at present.' I love you, Tork, and want to be one with you.' She held up her hand. Do not say anything, yet." Tork understood once again how much wisdom she possessed. Sanna always knew exactly how far to go. She had effectively promised herself to him, without compromising his morals. With her love and his new position, he had almost everything he had ever desired from life. "'Do you have any idea when your determination will be?' he asked her. Of course it was supposed to be a surprise. His certainly had been. But there were always ways that the news could get around. Within the next few cycles, she replied, and I also suspect what the outcome will be. Seeing his amazement, she laughed. "'Do not be so naive, Tork. Some determinations are quite obvious, most in fact.' Mine was not,' he answered. "'Perhaps,' Sanna's lips twitched again. "'But it is not exactly unexpected. I believe you will make an exemplary hive master. Perhaps the first such in several centuries.' Her support and love made his thorax warm again. Tork fought down his emotions, striving to be what she expected of him. "'And what do you believe your determination will make you?' he asked. An astronomer. If she had told him that she was expecting to become a sex provider, she couldn't have shocked him more. An astronomer,' he gasped weakly. "'You can't be serious. Why not?' Sanna cocked her head to one side and regarded him evenly. It's an unpleasant job, agreed, but a necessary one, especially now. But you,' Tork struggled weakly with his prejudices. "'Sanna, how could you?' "'It is because I can that I expect to become one,' Sanna answered. "'If this disgusts and repels you, I am truly sorry.' She smiled ruefully. "'That is one reason, beyond the impropriety, that I did not wish you to declare your love for me. If you no longer wish to associate with me, I will understand. It might be poor for your public image.' "'My image be damned,' he snapped back, still struggling to accept the idea. "'And my feelings for you have not changed.' "'Of course they have,' Sanna said simply. "'I understand.' "'Well, I do not,' Tork told her bluntly and with candor. "'I do not understand how you could wish to be an astronomer,' he almost choked on the word. "'But,' he took a deep breath. "'If that is what you wish to be, then I will do all I can to support your decision. "'I may not understand it, but I do not care about that. "'I will try to understand.' "'He drew on every ounce of courage he had and tried to reinforce his hearts. "'Show me.' Sanna stared at him in something like a alarm. "'Tork, there is no need. There is a need,' he said almost roughly. "'If this is to be your chosen pathway, then I will be forced to share it with you. I must understand it. Show me.' She bowed her head slightly. "'It is not wise,' she replied. "'Love is not always wise,' he told her. "'So be it,' Sanna raised her head and he could see the love in her eyes. "'If not for the boundary that separated them, what passions they could share this night?' "'Very well,' she agreed. "'Come with me.' She led him through the web of the student quarter. Tork followed trying to steal himself for the ordeal that was ahead. He was scared. There was no point in denying that, either to himself or to Sanna. But he had to do this, for both of their sakes. They left the more traveled byways and talked new. They were coming close to the wall of the hive. Their destination was an almost empty room. The walls, as always, were metal. But these had no decorations or furniture. The only thing in the room with them was a small control panel. She locked the door behind them to prevent accidental intrusion of the unprepared. Sanna turned to Tork. "'I love you,' she told him. "'You do not need to do this for me. I will understand and respect you without this. I know that you will,' he agreed. "'But I do this for us, and I will not respect myself if I do not share it with you. Sanna sighed and bowed her head in acceptance. "'Very well,' she agreed. She crossed to the control panel, her hands hovering uncertainly above it. "'Try hard to endure this, my love.' He didn't dare speak. Instead he simply gave a single curtain odd. Her fingers danced over the controls. The wall in front of them both began to iris open. Panels slid back into their recesses with a hiss. As they moved, the lights within the room died down. And the stars became visible. Thousands, perhaps millions of stars, littered across the whole vast space in front of Tork. Stars that burned with beautiful entrancing intensity. As it went on without end to the openness of space. Tork felt the vast emptiness beyond the fragile transparent shielding reaching out from the stars and into the core of his being. The openness pierced his soul. The immensity of it all overwhelmed him. Striving to escape the vast nothingness he shrieked then curled reflexively into a fetal ball. description: The episode "Star Trek DS9 Objective Bajor Part 1" by John Peel is a novel set in Star Trek's Deep Space Nine universe, detailing Captain Sisko and his crew facing off against an advanced alien threat called the Hive on the planet Bejour. The book explores themes of survival, sacrifice, and duty as they try to protect their home from destruction and discover the Hive's ultimate goal.

"'That means he works for you. "'Aud that you did not know this. "'I was reassigned,' stammered Took, "'but the damage had been done. "'The other masters in the room stared alternately at him "'and at Raalda. "'Really?' asked Hoseer. "'And who changed your determination for you? "'Only a hive master could do that.' "'He stared at his fellows one at a time. "'Any one wished to confess to having changed Took's status for him? "'There was dead silence. "'I thought not.' "'Happily, Torc said, "'I moved that this matter be investigated more thoroughly, "'and that Took be taken to restraining cells for the time being, "'and that Harle be set free. "'And,' he finished glaring at Raalda, "'that security master Raalda give a full and sufficient explanation "'for this to the assembled masters. "'There was a surge of agreement with his motions, "'which drawn cut short. "'What you say,' he commented smoothly, "'is clearly only reasonable and just.' "'He gestured to the guards who struck the manacles from Harle "'and transferred them to the protesting Took. "'Take him away. "'And you, Raalda, had better go as well. "'I shall want a full accounting of this from you at our next meeting.' "'Raalda was scowling deeply and glaring at Torc, "'Odo and Hoseer in turn. "'Finally,' he nodded. "'I obey,' he growled in low tones, "'and then stalked from the room. "'Drawnd turned to survey Torc in the Nodo. "'It appears that this matter is more complicated than it first appeared,' "'he said slowly. "'I thank you for your help. "'I suspect it will take some time for the truth to emerge. "'I'm sure it will,' Odo agreed cynically. "'That's often the case in such matters.' "'Torque turned to Odo in Cisco with a smile. "'Once again I am in your debt,' he said. "'You have saved the reputation and life of a friend.' "'It seems to be becoming a habit,' Cisco replied. "'If there is anything that I can do in return,' "'Torque said simply, please name it.' "'There is one thing,' Cisco answered. "'You have kindly shown us some of the hive "'and answered many of our questions. "'I feel that I am beginning to understand your people. "'Now perhaps you will let me return the favor "'so that you may start to understand mine.' "'Torque snout wrinkled. "'I do not understand you. "'A company may back to Bajor,' Cisco asked. "'See how they live. "'Try and understand why they will not leave their homes.' "'There was a collective gasp at this suggestion, "'and Torque was clearly shaken by the suggestion.' "'I'm sorry,' Cisco said, feigning puzzlement. "'Have I offended in some way?' "'He already had a good idea what the answer would be.' "'Drawing moved forward. "'What you ask is absolutely impossible,' he explained. "'Surely you must realize this.' "'I'm sorry,' Cisco replied, determined to make him spell it out. "'But I don't. "'Why is it impossible?' "'When Dron didn't seem inclined to reply, "'Macon stepped forward. "'It is because we are too well adapted to our lives "'here inside the hive. "'Everything that is outside is nonessential "'and counter to our well-being.' "'His earlier insight, Cisco realized, had been correct. "'He had guessed the reason for the non-transparent barrier, "'the lack of help, the reaction of the non-injured hive members "'to no apparent threat. "'You can't stand space,' he murmured. "'You can't be outside or look outside.' "'Odo frowned. "'You mean this entire species is agoraphobic? "'He demanded.' "'Yes,' Cisco said. "'They are. "'That's why they view planet dwellers as insane. "'They can't cope with the concept themselves "'and declare the idea madness instead of their response. "'That is not true,' Dron blustered. "'Our approach is rational. "'There is nothing wrong with any of us.' "'Then prove it,' Cisco said. "'Open a window into space. "'Look on the stars.' "'Dron couldn't disguise his shudder of revotion. "'That's disgusting.' "'That's what I thought,' Cisco glared around the room. "'It isn't the planet dwellers who are insane,' he said gently. "'Has it occurred to you that you're the ones not facing up to reality? "'You can't say things like that about us,' "'Pecat yelled. "'We are not deviant in any way. "'Our way is the only true evolved way to live.' "'Odo sneered.' "'Really.' "'How evolved. "'How true a life can you have hiding behind walls "'built from flimsy logic and half-truths. "'None of you has the courage to face the facts.' "'I do,' Torque swallowed inside. "'I will go with you to see Beijou.' "'What?' "'Pecat stared at his colleague in revotion. "'You will allow yourself to be deluded by these aliens?' "'No,' Torque answered gently. "'This is my decision. "'The captain is correct. "'How can we understand the bajorans "'if we are not willing to experience what they experience?' "'The rain will burn.' "'We'll see her later kindly hand on Torque's shell.' "'But you are badly affected by the sight of the stars,' he said. "'We all know that. "'You tried the experience once already and failed.' "'Then I will try again,' Torque replied. "'He was obviously unhappy but determined. "'I cannot stand by and do nothing.' "'Captain Sisko and his friends have proven their good intentions. "'Can we do any less?' Sisko cleared his throat. "'It's a brave decision,' he said with genuine sympathy. "'But is it a wise one? "'If you retreat into your shell again when you reach Beijou, then you will learn nothing. "'I may have underestimated how difficult it is for all of your people. "'Perhaps this is not a wise idea.' Oseir smiled slightly and gave Torque a significant look. "'It is not so for all of our people, Captain,' he replied without turning. "'A small percentage of us can stare into space without ill effect. "'They are our astronomers.' "'Clearly his words meant something very significant to Torque. "'The alien's face lit up with delight and hope.' "'Yes,' he breathed. "'He turned to Dron. "'Grandmaster, I formally request your permission to accompany the Captain back to the world of Beijou, to study it and report back to the Hive Masters in assembly.' Dron had obviously been trying to understand what had been happening and to turn it to his best advantage. He scowled at the request but clearly needed to reply. "'Are you sure that this is wise?' he asked, playing for time. "'It may affect you very adversely. "'I know the risks,' Torque answered with confidence. "'I am willing to undertake them.' Dron glanced around the room, taking in the feelings of his fellow council members. "'Then I have little option but to grant your request,' he decided. "'You will accompany the aliens and report back to us as soon as possible.' "'If you are able,' he added significantly. "'Thank you,' Torque said. "'I shall endeavour to serve the Hive to the best of my limited abilities.' "'His snout twitched. "'There is one further matter. "'The possibility is that I may indeed become incapacitated by shock. "'Therefore I request a companion to aid me who will not be so affected.' "'Do you have anyone in mind?' asked Hoseer before Dron could say anything. "'Yes,' Torque said. "'An astronomer named Sana. "'I know she is unaffected by agoraphobia.' "'Macon looked shocked. "'But she has only just passed her determination,' he objected. "'She has been assigned to Team Two as an astronomer. "'The determination cannot be wrong.' "'But it could of course be changed at the request of a Hive master. "'For personal reasons,' Dron said slyly. "'Sisco wasn't following this exchange, but there was obviously some kind of power play going on here. Dron and Torque were clearly battling over something. "'This is not a personal request,' Torque answered smoothly. "'Such a request for change of determination for selfish reasons would go against everything our society holds dear.' "'As Macon said, the determination is infallible, but it is not omniscient.' "'He smiled at Hoseer. "'What is that supposed to mean?' demanded Macon, frowning. "'Simply that the determination is made on the best possible data available,' Torque replied, "'at the time of determination.' "'He looked around the room. "'But the task of assistant to an ambassador to Beijo was not available at the time that Sana took her determination. "'So she could not have been appointed to the post. "'I believe that Sana is the person best suited to the task, "'and am willing to have her undergo a second determination in order to prove it.' "'There was another round of shocked muttering in the room. "'There has never been a second determination,' Premon protested. "'It is without precedent. So is this situation,' argued Hoseer. "'I, for one, move that we simply accept our colleagues' recommendation. "'He is bravely risking his life in sanity to try and help in a difficult situation, "'one that none of us would volunteer to undertake,' he added significantly. "'His choice of assistance seems wise to me.' Drawn didn't appear to be happy with the direction in which the discussion was going, but he was obviously not intending to lose control. "'We do seem to be moving quickly in new directions,' he commented. "'But as matters are very pressing, I, for one, will agree to forego a second determination for this "'Sana. Unless anyone has any serious objections, therefore, "'I am inclined to agree with our young colleagues' request. "'Is there any dissent?' "'Though Macon looked as if he might challenge the ruling, "'he subsided under one of Drawn's withering glares. There was no other comment. "'Then it is agreed,' Drawn commented. "'He turned to face Cisco. "'You will accept full responsibility for the safety of our observers,' he demanded. "'I will,' Cisco agreed. "'I promise you all that I shall do everything in my power to keep both talk and Sana safe.' "'So be it,' Drawn turned to the Hive Masters. "'I believe that is quite sufficient for one meeting. We all have our duties to attend to.' "'They all got the point of that message and began filing out of the room in clumps of two or three, "'all talking in low tones. After a moment only Hoseer, Torque and Drawn were left with Cisco and Odo.' "'Hoseer clapped Torque cheerily on the shell. "'I admire your courage, youngster,' he commented. "'Before you leave, stop by and see me. And when you return, I look forward to hearing "'what you have to say.' "'He inclined his head at Drawn and then turned to Cisco. "'Captain, it has been very interesting. I hope that we show me again under less tense circumstances.' "'Cisco liked the old alien. He was craftier than he seemed and was clearly playing some "'political games of his own. Likewise,' he commented. "'Hoseer nodded and then left the room. "'Torque bowed to Drawn. Thank you for your wise decisions, Grandmaster,' he murmured. "'I will endeavour to fulfil the trust you have placed in me.' "'Drawn nodded. Remember always that we serve the greater good of the Hive,' he said. "'Do not be swayed by emotion or appearances. "'Judge Wisely and return in safety.' "'Torque nodded and then led Cisco and Odo outside. "'I must inform Sana of the Hive Master's decision,' he said. "'We should be ready to go with you in less than one of your hours, if that is acceptable.' "'That's fine, Torque,' Cisco answered. "'I'd better get back to my ship. "'Constable, would you be kind enough to wait here and then escort our guests to the Defiant?' "'Of course,' Cisco slapped his communicator. "'Cisco to Defiant, one to beam back.' "'In the council chamber, Drawn crossed to the other door and Irested open. "'Raldar stepped in, looking duly chagrind. "'I would hardly call that a clever scheme,' Drawn snapped. "'Not only did you not succeed in placing the blame on Harle, "'but you even managed to implicate yourself in the business. "'What do you have to say for yourself?' "'It was the fault of that alien, Odo,' complained Raldar. "'If he had not interfered, then Hossir or one of the others would have,' "'explained Drawn. "'At least take the blame for your mistakes, honestly. "'Harle is cleared and you yourself are seen in a poor light.' "'He considered for a moment. "'It might be better if that idiot, too, were not around to create further problems.' "'Raldar nodded. "'I fear that he might just take his own life out of guilt and remorse for what he has done.' "'That sounds more than plausible,' agreed Drawn. "'The Hive Master slumped onto his seat. "'Perhaps we can then allow the matter to fade in memory, "'especially with the formation of the second Hive. "'There are more important matters to consider than one foolish worker with a grudge.' "'He started tapping out commands on his comp. "'The division will go according to plan. "'The masters will be split between the two hives. "'You will remain with me on Hive 1. "'Pecat will be Grandmaster of Hive 2.' "'That was to have been my Hive,' exclaimed Raldar angrily. "'You had agreed. "'That was before this fiasco,' Drawn snapped. "'You have shown yourself lacking in good judgment. "'If you redeem yourself, and I say again, if, "'then you will become my successor. "'Otherwise you will become nothing. "'Do you understand me?' "'Fighting to control his anger in disappointment,' "'Raldar managed to curt nod.' "'Good.' "'And what of torque?' asked Raldar, more subdued. "'He has escaped both traps you laid for him. "'You have been listening at doors again, I see,' "'Drawn's snout wrinkled in irritation. "'True, torque has proven to be more flexible than I had expected. "'Obviously, Oseir favors the youth.' "'Raldar sneered. "'Out of anger over losing the Grandmaster post to you,' he suggested. "'He never desired it,' Drawn snorted. "'Hosir is bright and cunning, but he lacks ambition and drive. "'Until recently he has never gone against me in any decision. "'I think his shell has finally started to firm up. "'Hosir sees torque as his protege, "'and wishes to groom him to be everything that he never had the nerve to become. "'There was a thoughtful look on Drawn's face. "'Even if I do wish you to be my successor, "'you may face a challenge from torque. "'He is barely more than a child,' protested Raldar. "'But an intelligent one,' thunder drawn, "'and unless you show yourself to be cleverer than you have today, "'he will become the next Grandmaster. You have to apply yourself.'" Raldar bowed again. "'As you say,' he agreed, trying to sound submissive. "'May I ask why you allowed him to accompany the aliens? "'Surely you cannot be thinking of allowing him to change your objectives.' "'Do not even think such thoughts,' drawn snarled. "'The great design will go forward, "'even if we have to wipe out a dozen worlds.'" "'No,' he continued in a more calm vein. "'I allowed torque to go for one simple reason. "'When the aliens cannot dissuade us from our course, "'they will obviously hold torque hostage "'to try and force us to change our plans. "'They will threaten to kill him if we proceed. "'We will never allow such perfidious behavior "'to affect our destiny, and we will refuse. "'They will kill him. "'When they do that, torque will become a martyr to our people, "'and he will cease to be a problem to you and me. "'Better a dead martyr than a live problem.'" Raldar nodded. "'You have thought it all out clearly,' he said in admiration. "'The great design will succeed.'" "'Of course,' drawn stood up. "'Now I must rest. "'This has all been fatigued. "'See to tuke and wait for my call. "'The time for action has come.'" Chapter 18 It felt good to be back on the defiant. The hive had been fascinating and even more than a trifle enviable if only DS9 had some of the facilities that were available on that ship. Cisco smiled ruefully. Sometimes the Spartan nature of Deep Space 9 made him wish that he were assigned to either a starship or a star base. Then came a challenge such as this, and he knew he was where he was meant to be. Still he had several calls to make, none of which were likely to be pleasant. When he reached his ready room, the first one he placed was to Admiral Noguchi. The old man managed a thin smile. "'I hope you have good news to report, Captain.'" "'I wish I had, sir,' Cisco replied. The hivemasters are still intent on making Bajor their next target, and nothing I've managed to do so far has convinced them to change their minds. However, one of the masters, Torque, is accompanying me back to Bajor to study the situation for himself. I believe he is sympathetic, and I hope that I can win him over to our side." Noguchi nodded. "'But will one lone voice for us affect them?" "'Frankly, I'm not sure,' Cisco admitted, but there's very little hope otherwise." "'I understand, Captain.'" Noguchi drew himself up straight. Then Starfleet's orders are clear. If you cannot persuade the hive to change its plans, you must do all within your power to stop them. We cannot allow these intruders to devastate another planet, particularly not Bajor. Is that clear, Captain? Perfectly. Even though he had been expecting the command, it still disturbed Cisco. They are not a bad people, Admiral. I hope we can negotiate a peaceful settlement. So do I, Captain," Noguchi said fervently. Starfleet wants nothing more than peace, but we cannot allow a planet-wracking society to remain at large in this galaxy. He glanced at his pad. "'Relief will not be with you any faster,' he apologized. "'This one is on your shoulders, Benjamin. I'm sorry.'" "'So am I, Admiral,' Cisco admitted, but it's part of my job.' He signed off, feeling weary. That communication had been bad enough, but he was dreading the next one. A few moments later, Gol de Cott's suprasilius smile greeted him. "'Captain, allow me to congratulate you on your recent promotion. It couldn't have happened to a better human.'" "'Thank you, Du Cott,' Cisco answered, but this is not a social call. I assume you have been briefed on the situation in the Derein system by your ship that's sitting here watching. Du Cott inclined his head slightly. You mean the tragic destruction of Derein IV and the appalling loss of life with it? Sadly, yes." He spread his hands. "'I wish I could help, but complications have arisen, and there is little we can do but offer condolences.'" "'You'd better save them for your own people,' Cisco told him, and was slightly pleased to see the smug expression wiped off the Cardassian's face. "'What do you mean, Captain?' Cisco hedged for a moment. Do you know what is happening to the hive at this moment? "'Decot glanced away for a few seconds and then back. It appears to be suffering some kind of splitting process,' he replied. "'My observers think it may be fissioning into two separate craft. Your observers are quite correct,' Cisco confirmed. In two days there will be two identical hives, each with the capacity and appetite of the first hive. "'That is unfortunate,' Ducot answered. Then the point sank home and he scowled into the screen. "'Apertite, you mean that the two hives will be seeking further worlds to plunder?' "'Precisely. One of the hives is targeting Bajour. Ducot clucked his tongue. That's a shame. I assume that the Federation will be protecting their ally. "'We will be doing everything that we can,' Cisco extemporised. "'What should interest you more is that the second hive will be heading for Cardassia Prime.' "'That completely wiped the last vestiges of his smugness away. "'What?' "'If it was possible for a Cardassian to look paler, "'Ducot managed that astounding feat. "'Cardassia Prime?' "'Your hearing is excellent.' "'Sisco leaned forward. "'I wish we could offer you assistance but under the circumstances.' "'He spread his arms. "'Given their level of technology, Ducot, "'I'd strongly advise you to try and talk to these people to avoid a war.' "'Thank you for your concern, Captain,' Ducot managed to say, looking very pained. "'But we know best how to look after our own interests. "'Thank you for this information. "'Now, I believe I had better discuss this matter with my colleagues.' "'The screen went blank.' "'At least I managed to shake him up a bit,' Cisco thought. "'But the Cardassians were in a much better position to meet this threat head on than Bajor was. "'Cardassia had three fleets stationed within two days of the homeworld at all times. "'Maybe they would stand a chance if it came down to a war with the Hive. "'Bajor had no such forces. "'The only things that stood between it and the Hive were the Defiant and Deep Space Nine, "'and there wasn't a great deal of firepower concentrated between the two of them. "'He could put off his next call no longer. "'A moment later he was looking into the troubled eyes of Shakha, "'the first minister grimaced slightly. "'It's too much to hope for good news, I imagine,' he said. "'I'm afraid so,' agreed Cisco. "'The Hive Masters remain firm in their intentions. "'However, I will be bringing one of their number with me back to DS9 and then on to Bajor. "'He is willing to listen to whatever you have to say. "'I think he is sympathetic to our point of view. "'And we may be able to win him over. "'End of side four.
description: Objective Bejor Part 2 is a podcast episode featuring John Peel discussing the dramatic story of Marrel and Cisco's desperate attempt to stop a rogue ship that is rapidly approaching Bajor in an effort to avenge past losses. Despite their conflicting goals, they must work together to save the lives of those aboard the intruding vessel while ensuring their own survival. The tension builds as the crew faces impossible odds and crucial choices that could determine the fate of both Bajor and their mission on DS9.

Thirty seconds later, docking clamps were released and the Defiant was pulling away from its birth. As the Defiant grew near of the scene, Cisco saw in the main viewer three vessels, a forangi marauder and two bajorn transports. O'Brien reported from his operations console. The bajorn ships don't seem to be affected by the phaser hits. They're continuing onward. The bajorin choice to bombard the section of the pharingi vessel that housed the plasma weapon was a wise tactical maneuver. But it should not have worked. Slowly, Julian made his way over to Kira's console and leaned in and examined the readout. Captain, with this type of radiation in such concentrated amounts, I think it's possible that we might be missing something. Once the defiant returned to deep space nine, Cisco contacted Brackdore aboard the creek to inform him of the battle and his result. Brackdore appeared on the compound. The Nagas agrees to let Bejor receive medicine and food, in spite of our blockade and this is how he's repaid? Then you know about the encounter with the transports. Of course we know about the Nimes. But the decor class Marauder would not require any assistance to defeat two of those new Bejor and vessels. What sensor records? Those from the Nimes, of course. You recovered the ship then? A handful of survivors did. They brought the Nimes back to the blockade. We read no life signs after the battle. Is that why the survivors reported an attempt to board their ship? Damon, we were searching for survivors. I thought you said your scans showed no signs of life aboard the Nimes. If a full review of the logs shows that the Defiant was directly involved in the annihilation of more than 250 Ferengi, there will be grave consequences. The Damon gestured to somebody off-screen and the communication abruptly ended. For a couple of minutes, Cisco stood and stared at the Ferengi emblem on the compound. Cisco took a man to war. I want you to find out all you can about the Ferengi Marauder, Nimes. There was no one in the hole to see the cargo container melt. The cube, like several others about it, was apparently headed for Johnson City on Gamma Hydra IV, carrying a shipment of handmade bajorin Merniary dolls. The container lost its solid form liquefying into humanoid form. Odo did not hesitate, but raced to a computer station. Odo worked the controls with his 14 digits and looked at the manifests with the other holes, at the crew roster, at the depressurization instructions for certain cargos. Abruptly, Odo's many fingers stopped their frenzied movements across the console of the computer station. He rapidly evaluated the path he would have to take to reach what he wanted to inspect. The Karama, you say? The notion that the Karama provided ships to the bajorins, or even the aridians. Kira shook her head. It doesn't fit. As far as we know, the Karama had no trade agreements with the aridians. War fatted. Nor do the Karama manufacture star ships. Cisco's head had begun to pound. Cisco thought, is there something here, or are we just looking for light in the black hole? He turned to face his crew. So why would the Ferengi want us to think the transports had beaten the Marauder and killed its crew? Cisco moved over to the table and leaned over it. The Ferengi staged this battle to make it appear as though the Bajorans were instigating the fighting. Dax agreed. This is the one way the Ferengi believe they could be absolutely sure that the Federation wouldn't defend Bajor. If the Bajorans themselves were the aggressors, the chief took a step toward the table and held a pad he was carrying out to Cisco. Well, that might explain this then. This arrived from Starfleet just before it came down here. It's their report, Mr. Warf requested on the Ferengi Marauder Nimus. It says that the Starship Nimus is one of Grandnake's ex-personal honor guard. Romm lay on the hard surface of his bunk, shivering. Snows had buried the brittle land, and daylight hours had grown short, but it was not the cold that shook Romm so violently right now. It was Fere. White had said that he was taking Quark to see Colonel Mitra. Quark had been gone for a while, and as his time away from the barracks increased, so too did Romm's conviction that he would never return. Or because you wanted to see me fail? Maybe even get into trouble with the Ferengi Commerce Authority. That's the problem with always making deals, Quark. You can be certain of your enemies' identities, but do you know who your friends are? Quark found Odo's question cryptic. What did he mean? Surely he was not claiming to be Quark's friend, was he? They arrived at Quark's quarters. In the small star cabin stood Rom. Quark left Odo and went inside. Brother, I need to tell you something. I think we were set up by Quark. Are you out of your mind, Rom? Quark saved us, you idiot. But he didn't make a homing device. When we got in the shuttle, I found the device he supposedly put together near the back of the cabin. It was just a mass of parts from a medical scanner and a phaser. They have been connected together, but they didn't make anything that functioned. But then how did he call the shuttle? I don't know. But don't you think it's a pretty big coincidence that right after we escape from Bejor, we were picked up by the Defiant? Are you suggesting that Quark is working with somebody from the station? Somebody on the Defiant? I don't know, brother. Maybe somebody from the station. Who? Sisko, maybe? If Quark had voluntarily stayed in the camp on Bejor when he had the capability of calling his shuttle and escaping at any time, then Quark was sure that he would have to have been paid extremely well. And Sisko would not have been able to do that. There was somebody who obviously could pay well. Well, ran Nagazek. But why would the Nagaz want them to escape and be picked up by the crew of the Defiant? Where was the Prophet Fazek? No, it made no sense for it to be the Nagaz. But who? Using the cloaking device, the Defiant flew at maximum war. On the bridge's main viewer, the tactical display showed the Ferengi Armada scores and scores of ships. Cisco turned to Dax. Can you punch us through undetected? Dax looked up from the con. I think so. We should be able to sneak through. Do it. And head us towards Ferengi Arm. Soon, Dax announced from the con. We are approaching Ferengi Arm. Worf interrupted. Captain, I am picking up readings of two marauders already in orbit. Quark walked to the center of the bridge. Quark pointed at the marauder on the main viewer. First, there'll be some legal requirements that want you to stipulate to. It could take some time. Mr. Worf, open hailing frequencies. Let's do what we have to do. This is Captain Benjamin Cisco of the Federation Starship Defiant. We have a board of Ferengi Citizen who requests an immediate audience with the Grand Nagaz. Do you then agree to release the Ferengi Alliance from all claims of liability to your vessel and its crew arising from your stay within Ferengi space? Cisco sighed. But Quark whispered, standard language, Captain. Cisco nodded to Lettek. Yes. Quark, you have a house on Ferenginar? Yes. My mother lives there. And all of your required insurance policies and riders are current? Yes. And all of your premiums have been paid? Yes. Through the end of the year as required. Then, Captain Cisco, if you'll lower your deflectors, we will transport Quark to Grand Nagazex Estate. Cisco was surprised at the ease with which they had reached this juncture. Cisco looked over once more at Quark. Good luck, Quark. And thank you. Worse. Through. After Quark was gone, Lettek looked at Cisco. We'll inform you when the Nagaz is done with Quark. And so, unable to do anything else, Cisco and his crew settled in to wait. Worse. Through. When Quark materialized, there were two men in the transporter room. One approached Quark. Welcome to the home of Grand Nagex at Quark. His house is his house. Quark responded in the traditional way, as are its contents. My name is Corlin. I am one of the Grand Nagaz's personal friends. Grand Nagaz's personal assistants. The Grand Nagaz has left orders to bring you to the chamber of the sun. It's one of his favorite rooms. Corlin led Quark into an extremely tall, enormously long hall. As they traveled down the hall, Quark appeared at the tapestries. They depicted renowned moments in Ferengi history, the opening of the sacred marketplace, the founding of the first bank of Ferenginar. Quark found the display inspiring. Approximately two-thirds of the way down the corridor, Quarlin proceeded to a set of doors on the right side of the hall. As the door swung open, Quarlin announced, Grand Nagasek will be with you shortly. Quark moved forward into the chamber, which was as tall as the hall was, and it was at least big enough to comfortily contain the defiant within it, the brilliant rays of the sun shone in great angled beams into the chamber. Quark strode across the length of the chamber to the great window. He had so rarely seen such lovely weather on his home world. He brought his face right up to the transparent surface. From behind him came Zex's voice. It's a holographic pedestrian, but on night they've outside, this wall actually can be made transparent. Quark was disappointed. The weather is bad. It's prondushing out there right now. There were 178 different words for rain in the Ferengi language. Perdushing referred to long, slim drops falling constantly at a slight angle. Almost as an afterthought, Zex slid his hands from the knob of his cane that had been fashioned in his own image from gold-pressed latinum. Quark dropped to one knee and kissed the top of the cane. This way, Quark? The Nagase shuffled his ancient body along one side of the room until he reached a large, ornamented chair where he sat down. He motioned for Quark to sit across from him. Quark, you have fine business in things. And since that is the case, I have to ask myself, what's in it for you? I'm a fugitive from the Bajorans right now, and I've lost my bar. For talking to you about these manners, Captain Sisko has promised me political asylum if I want it. If you change your mind and sell the Orb to the Bajorans, he promised me amnesty and the possibility of getting my bar back. Oh, it is Captain Thysko who is driving this talk. Yes, although the business reasoning is mine. There's also the rule of acquisition that every once in a while declare peace. Oh, like Quark, I'll provide you with a response shortly. Suddenly, Corlin appeared. Least way, Quark. I'll escort you back to the transporter room. Quark followed Corlin out of the chamber of the Sun and back to the transporter room. This is my final order, Captain. If it is not immediately accepted, then the war with Bajor will proceed. I understand, Negas. I'll get you that agreement right away. Mr. Worf, open the channel to First Minister Shakar on Bajor. Captain, I cannot raise Bajor. It appears that someone is jamming transmissions either near or within the system. Of course, Sisko thought. There was a war about to be fought. Or already being fought. And both sides would be attempting to block the other's communications. Dax, set a course for Bajor, maximum possible speed. Sisko reached up and touched the door chime to Quark and Romb's quarters. Romb stood just inside. Quark's asleep? You seem tired too, Romb. He didn't provide many details. Do you want to talk about it? Come on. We'll go to my quarters where we can talk privately. Romb followed Sisko to his cabin. There, quietly and visibly anguished. Romb told Sisko about Galatep and Sergeant White and Colonel Mitra and the very worst days of his life. As the Defiant reached the field of battle, Sisko left war from charge of the ship and took the shuttle Da Vinci to the planet. Sisko was thrown into the port bulkhead. A powerful phaser blast had hit the Da Vinci. It was unclear from the readings who had fired on the Da Vinci, but Sisko hoped that it had been the Ferengi. More than likely, though, it had been the Bajorans, shooting from the surface of the small ship attempting to penetrate their defenses. Sisko tried to open communications with Chikar or anybody else on Bejord, and was again unsuccessful. As the next blast narrowly missed the shuttle, Sisko knew what was going to happen. The Da Vinci was going to be shot down. Still, he did not want the debris of the shuttle's wreckage to rain down on the Bajoran capital and its inhabitants. He entered the new course along with automatic landing instructions, then staggered through the shuttering cabin to the emergency transporter. Computer, energized transporter. Sisko materialized on the floor in Chikar's office. He was alone. He made his way to the First Minister's Companel and activated it. First Minister Chikar, this is Captain Sisko. I must speak with you immediately. I'm in your office. I'm Bejord. Sisko materialized on a platform in an operation center. A woman, dressed in the uniform of the Bajoran militia, stepped up to the platform and greeted him. Captain Sisko, the First Minister is waiting for you. Sisko found the First Minister studying a console with two other militia officers. Chikar, I have an offer from Grand Nega's Zek to end the fighting. Zek is willing to do away with the auction completely. If you'll rescind your edict and meet his price for the orb, which is Bejord's last bid plus the 35 new transports you acquired from the Iridians. Chikar regarded Sisko for what seemed like a very long time. Bejord accepts the terms. A Two things bothered Quark. One was Union. The more Quark considered Rome's conviction, that Quark somehow set them up, the more he became involved in the fight. had somehow set them up. The more he became inclined to believe it. Quark glanced down at the status monitor on the screen and saw that his latest series of queries were still pending. It had been like that since his return a week ago to Deep Space 9. His tedious searches for information about court consuming great chunks of time. Unfortunately, his quest for information about court had so far proved fruitless. Quark got up and walked across his quarters to the replicator. Archurian slug wine. He took the glass and sipped. Not as good as the real thing from Archer 4 of course. Not as thick or as pulpit, but considering the past few months, it would do. Quark strode over to the comp panel and eyed the brief message displayed there. Search subject not found. Computer, when the search is complete, don't notify me audibly. Oral notification cancelled. Quark headed for his bedroom. He would check the results in the morning. Colonel Mitra slipped silently into the room and waited a moment for his eyes to adjust to the dimness. His eyes were still cold. Perhaps they had survived the raw days and nights of Gallatep Winter because of their coldness. His skin was more than Ashenian was translucent. Gouches in his sunken cheeks marked the places where flesh had died and fallen away. In three strides Mitra was at the bedroom door. He walked to the bed and looked down at his brain. He adjusted his grip on his knife using what remained of his hands. The cold had killed the tips of his fingers. Dead tissue falling away to expose the bone beneath. He bent down and eased the blade below the wide circular spans of Quark's left ear. Prisoner Ape's quark's eyes began to thutter open. Griss. Dress me as Gull. Gull Mitra. Yes. Commander of Gallatep. The butcher of Gallatep. He jerked his arm backward, dragging the edge of the knife up and through the cartilage of Quark's ear. Quark bolted up in bed, his hands rushing to the gaping hole on the side of his head. Instead, what he felt was the mass of his ear, hole and uninjured. Ah, only a dream. Mitra is dead. It was only a dream. Knowing that sleep had deserted him for the night, he went back to the main room and his search for sense in an irrational universe. Later, as Quark worked at the companel, there it was. The results of his latest search had come back positive. It turned out to be a three-year-old announcement of new appointees in several areas of the Ferengi government. Court's duty was as a personal assistant to the Grand Nagas. And that brought Quark four-square to the other thing that had been troubling him. Zeck himself. Maybe the Nagas had blundered in his handling of the auction of the orb. Zeck pays Court to get arrested and remain interned on Bejor until the specific time when Court calls his shuttle and helps the prisoners escape. He then steers them almost directly to the defiant, where he fakes an accident both to cover his actions and to gain Cisco's attention. Could the Nagas have known that Cisco would bring Quark to Ferenginar? Quark looked back at the companel. He would have to seek additional clues because there were two things Quark was sure of. When all of this had started, the Nagas had failed to sell the orb to the Bejorans. And when it had ended, he had sold the orb to the Bejorans. That indicated to Quark that Grand Nagas Zeck was losing his touch. Disgusted and sad, Quark switched off the companel. I don't really want to know what happened. In his office on Deep Space Nine, Cisco picked up a pad from his desk and read through the first minister's letter a second time. Shakar had elected to do all the right things, and he had done those things quickly. Although the edict, Barringi from Bajorans space had been rescinded immediately upon the delivery of the Ninth Orb to Bejor, Shakar also stated that the Bajorans were trying to determine how Colonel Mitra had managed to reopen and resupply Gallatin. Finally, the letter confirmed a rumor Cisco had considered too good to be true. The death toll during the war had been zero. Come in. Quark entered the office and approached Cisco's desk. You asked to see me, Captain? Yes, I did, Quark. Thank you for what you did. The fact that you were able to change Zeck's mind. Well, you probably saved tens of thousands of lives. You're welcome, I guess. Quark turned and headed for the doors. Quark, is everything all right? Quark hesitated for a moment. I think the Nagus may be losing his business skills. I think that's an understatement, Quark. The Nagus miscalculated. By ejecting the Bajorans from the auction, it forced the Bajorans to cut the Ferengi off from the wormhole, which resulted in the Ferengi blockade, and in the eventual arming of Bejor by the Iridians. Oh, did Captain, I thought before you told me that the Bajorans got those new star ships from the Karama. I think you asked about the origin of those ships. We believe that they were first owned by the Karama. Anyway, the star ships were actually sold to the Bajorans by the Iridians, and now they belong to the Ferengi. Quark appeared stunned and then ill. Captain, I was the one who negotiated the sale of those star ships to the Iridians. You arranged the transaction between the Karama and the Iridians? No, I sold those star ships to the Iridians from the Ferengi. Quark paused, putting it all together. It all makes sense now. It was all for greater profits. Zex, together, Cisco and Quark traced their way through the maze of the Nagus's great scheme. Zex had intentionally expelled the Bajorans from the auction, expecting that they would react by closing the wormhole to the Ferengi. That action had given the Nagus sufficient cause to blockade Bejor. Cisco shook his head. It's so easy to see now that the blockade was a roost. I couldn't figure out why the Nagus would execute a blockade and then allow food and medicine through. It was because the Nagus had no real interest in hurting the Bajorans people. Cisco then explained to Quark how Chacar had purchased the 35 star ships from the Iridians. The Nagus had doubtless made sure that when he allowed Quark to sell the ships to the Iridians, that they knew the Bajorans would shortly be looking to arm themselves. And he would have played upon the Iridians thirst for saleable information by suggesting this means of gaining access to DS9's gamma quadrant data. Cisco then told Quark about the staged encounter between the Bajorans ships and the Marauder, and how Zex had used that as the cause to the Claire war. What I don't understand, Quark, is why did the Nagus do all of this? Thirty-five brand new star ships, Captain. Well, thirty-five slightly used star ships. The Nagus sold those same ships to the Iridians for a huge profit. And now he's going to sell those same thirty-five star ships to the Karama. Cisco felt his jaw drop. That's who they were built for in the first place. Yep, Zex is a genius. So all of this Quark, everything, was simply so the Nagus could make greater profits. Quark nodded. And the Iridians now have an information pipeline into Deep Space Nine in the gamma quadrant. With his ties to the Iridians, I'm sure the Nagus will also be able to take advantage of that arrangement. The Nagus ended up with everything he wanted. The thirty-fourth rule of acquisition really applies here. War is good for business. Cisco reached across the desk and handed Quark a pad. Maybe not everything he wanted. This is the contract between the Iridians and the Bajorns, permitting the Iridians access to the data from our communications relay in the gamma quadrant. I want to find some way of allowing the Bajorns to fulfill the letter of this contract without our having to compromise our data. I thought you might be able to help. Quark read the document. Simplicity itself, Captain. This contract states that the Bajorns must allow the Iridians to monitor all transmissions from the gamma quadrant relay to the station. But it does not demand that the Iridians understand those transmissions. Cisco understood immediately. Encryption. Exactly, Captain. You're quite a businessman, Quark. Quark tipped his head in acknowledgment and left. In Quark's bar, the Bolean placed his thumb on Quark's banking device, completing the transaction. I'm sure you'll be very satisfied with this Betazoid gift box. It better work. Of course it'll work. Quark walked back down to the other end of the bar. More never seemed to tire of asking him questions about his experiences. So, where was I? I was telling you about the Nagas's palace. As Quark recounted his arrival at Zex's state, he privately marveled at the shrewdness and cunning of the Nagas. Zex was brilliant. Quark had not told Cisco about court, about his being employed by the Nagas and about how he had made sure that Quark had been delivered into Cisco's hands at just the right time. Zex is a master. As Quark finished telling his story, he noticed Major Kira enter the bar. Major, what can I do for you? You can listen, Quark. I'm all ears. To Quark's astonishment. Kira smiled. I just wanted to tell you that I'm sorry. I heard about what happened to you on Bejor. And I also heard about you talking with the Nagas. To get him to sell us the orb. I wanted to thank you for what you did. I still don't understand you. Or the forangi way of life. But I guess that's not really a reason to hate you. No, Major. And if it's any consolation, I don't understand you either. Kira seemed uncomfortable. She turned on her heel and strode out of the bar. Later that night, when he was closing the bar, Quark smiled again when he thought back to the Major's visit and to her apology. Perhaps it was a starting point for better understanding between the two of them. Quark finished locking up. And after he had counted and secured the day's receipts, he went to his old familiar place behind the bar and switched on the bar. And switched on the comp panel. There was a deal out there waiting for him. Just had to find it. The Nagas had inspired him. One day Quark knew he would own his own moon. It took patience and experience. But if you looked in the right places with the right perspective, it was just possible that the universe actually could make sense. It makes sense. description: In the final episode of "The 34th Rule," Captain Cisco leads his crew in a daring assault on the powerful forangi marauder and two bajorn transports, using disruptor blasts to weaken their shields before launching photon torpedoes that obliterate them. Despite this impressive tactical maneuver, radiation from the destroyed vessel threatens the lives of those aboard. The episode ends with a dramatic conclusion as Captain Cisco falls unconscious in his chair, leaving Kira to lead the crew back to safety.

transcript: The The universe was about to make sense. Quark stood behind the bar and anxiously studied the display screen above the replicator. Every few seconds one complicated set of matrices replaced another causing the display to emit a soft, electronic hum and Quark's mind hummed along with it. It's going to happen. Every values would slide the way he had foreseen. He would arrange the final transactions in this elaborate financial dance, and it would be done. Soon he would be one step closer, one significant step closer to being able to purchase the moon he had long dreamed of owning. Quark's mind devoured the ever-changing numbers until the heavy, shuffling of feet directly behind him, prompted him to blank the data. It was only more. The lumbering figure dropped onto a seat on the other side of the bar and set down a tall, cobalt blue glass. Quark nodded toward the glass. You need a refill? He reached for the glass, but mourn pulled it away and pointed a finger inside. Quark peered over the rim and saw a small amount of bright yellow liquid. Oh, you don't want that? There's no flavor left in that. You're really going through this stuff. I'm going to have to order another case of Trania from my supplier. While mourn picked up his glass, Quark took the time to scan the rest of the bar. Lieutenant Commander Dax was down from ops to provide her amusing, sometimes biting, commentary of the weekly dart match between Chief O'Brien and Dr. Rashear. And somewhere Quark was fairly sure, Odo alert. Earlier, Quark had heard the shapeshifter come in and heard the strange liquid rushing sound Odo made whenever he moved quickly, no matter his form. The sound, though nearly sub-audible, was unmistakable to Ferengi years. He looked back over at mourn. Now what I should do is just close the entire place down. If the deal I'm working on right now proceeds the way I designed it to, I should have enough assets to make a successful transition to a new business. What do I need this place for anymore? It's always been more trouble than profit. I'm not just a bartender, you know. I'm not even just a bar owner. I'm a businessman. There's a difference. One continued to regard him without saying anything. Fine. Just keep staring at me like that. Quark stepped over to the screen and touched a finger to the control section. The alarm ceased. Morn, enjoy your tronya. I've got work to do. Quark returned to the display and brought the arrays of data back up on the screen. He scanned the read-outs, symbols representing dozens of different currencies. Ferengi, Bajoran, Bolian, Eurydian, and others decorated the screen. A slight tingling began in his earlopes. He reread the file while his hand hovered above the transmit button. Quark hesitated. Once he approved the transactions, there would be no turning back. This is your best chance, the best deal you've ever put together. It will work. He repeated the 62nd rule of acquisition in his head. To riskier the road, to greater the profit. He jabbed the button and waited. Failure now would destroy him. My moon, cousin Gail owns his own moon. He recalled the luxurious estate from which Gail had ruled his natural satellite, whereas sophisticated communications console permitted monitoring of three different financial exchanges. For years Quark had privately aspired to Gail as standard of achievement. Over time Quark's brother, Rahm, had come to share in his vision, frequently in treating Quark to describe the moon and his home he intended to have constructed on its surface. Rahm would even offer his own details of life there, talking about his room and about what he would do there. Mentioning such activities as raising small animals, like cotton, tails, you braid, and tranny cats, and the like, and planting a garden. The tranquil picture Rahm painted of life on the moon bespoke his view that Quark would retire there. But Quark had no intention of dwelling in retirement. Business was not only his livelihood. It was his recreation as well. Had Zek attained the office of Grand-Nagus for the sake of the office itself? No, of course not. Money begets money. And power begets money. And the Nagus, while serving in his official role, also used the influence and resources of his position to continue engaging with great success in his own business ventures. On his moon Quark would do the same. Two words began to flash on the display. Incoming transmission. Quark felt exhilarated and terrified at the same time. Contracts had been written and agreed to. Money's had been spent and received. Inventories had been purchased and sold. All as a result of his foresight and maneuvering. Like the proverbial wise man, Quark could hear profit in the wind. And it sounded sweet. Barely able to curb his excitement. He manipulated the display controls to gain access to his primary account on Bejour. His gaze traveled to the bottom line of the report. A long string of digits representing his net worth was displayed there in red. Quark gasped. Right now he was deeper in debt than any individual in the quadrant. The 97 minutes following Quark's financial ruin were among the most difficult to live through in his life. It will work out. Everything is happening just the way you planned it. His debts not only surpassed his assets, they dwarfed them. The great sums Quark owed had gone to fund a single purchase. The commodity was one not typically available to individuals, but Quark had been in the right place at the right time. Quark saw the words incoming transmission flashing on the display. His earlobes grew cold from fear, heat slipping from them like water spilling down a drain. He punched the receive button and the message printed on the screen. Quark read it twice then a third time just to be sure he did not misread any details. To check the chronometer, he had another 23 minutes yet to make good on his debt. He smiled. It had not even been dramatic. Quark worked quickly at the display and gained access to his account on Bejor. His net worth came up in black. The deal had been very profitable. He had done it. Now finally Quark had seed money. From here, he could really start to deal, really begin to build up his finances to the point where he could afford the moon and its accoutrements. He turned to face the rest of the bar. Everybody drinks are on sale. Drinks are half price for the next quarter hour. He had been about to say drinks are on the house, but he was interrupted by the financial planner in his head who wanted to know why, just because he had successfully concluded a deal. He was about to behave so foolishly. I really should give up this place. Leaving this place and these people would be nice, and Quark eventually would, but not yet. Being here at the mouth of the wormhole had permitted him to make this first-sizeable deal. Turning once more to the display, Quark reexamined the number, spelling out his net worth. This makes sense. This is how the universe is supposed to work. In a corner of the octagonal room, Grand-Negas-Zec stood, leaning on his cane. The Nagas regarded an old wooden box. A pair of hinged doors closed at the moment were set into one side. Fielded up as it was, the box hardly seemed impressive, but Zec smiled as he contemplated how much profit he estimated its contents would bring him. The Nagas gazed around, verifying that arrangements were complete. The Antaroom had been configured for the imminent arrival of a delegation from Bejor, led by their minister for religious artifacts. The Bajorans were vigorously seeking to obtain the object that now sat in his room, in the box, sitting on the pedestal table, an orb of the prophets. The orb was one of only nine such objects known to exist. At one time, every known orb had been kept on Bejor, but when the decades-long Cardassian occupation of Bejor had entered several years ago, all but one of the objects had been seized by the departing conquerors. Zec had come into possession of this orb, the ninth orb, the so-called orb of wisdom, through a contact on Cardassian III. The orbs were curious artifacts. Our glass shaped in a vibrant green color, they glowed from within, and had been known to defy gravity. Other more spiritual powers had long been rumored. The orb was the type of commodity that the Nagas loved to peddle, because many factions were compelled by different reasons to possess it. As Zec had anticipated, no group desired to possess it more than the Bajorans. They asked, Kajol demanded. Zec put them off, maintaining that there was other business he needed to conduct before he could even concern himself with the sale of the orb. Eventually, the Nagas had received an impassioned letter signed by both the Bajorans' highest governmental officer and their religious leader. In the letter, the first minister and the Kai argued that because the orb had originally been found in their star system, it truly belonged to the Bajoran people. They pledged to pay a reasonable price for it. The subtext suggested that they might even be willing to pay an unreasonable price. They had to have the orb. Zec had expected the letter, and he used it as the impetus to begin the process, an auction that would lead to the eventual sale of the orb, and the Bajorans had entered the bidding. Zec looked over at the box in which the orb sat and wondered what the Bajorans would bid for it today. There seemed little question that the amount would be sizable. Whatever amount the Bajorans bid, he knew it would not be enough. Major Kiran Aris strode into Quark's near closing time. Because of the lateness of the hour, Quark had already sent all of his employees home, but for one of the doppelgirls, Lita, and Broick.
