transcript: Jim, I have been and will be your friend. I plunged into fire. The fire died before brutal cold, and I experienced a terrible numbing much worse than the flames. Death ripped the spirit from my body. This I remember. My spirit in the care of Dr. McCoy felt his terror and confusion and fear of madness. This I remember. The Vulcan elder Tilar created the refusion that joined my body and my spirit again. I felt both joy and peace. This too I remember. But I have so much else to learn before I am myself again. The Vulcan scholars studying me and helping me regain my memory say that pain and terror and joy have no place in the Vulcan way. Those feelings, any feelings, will only interfere. All this I must forget. The Traveler sang. It sent its songs into space. In return it received new songs from other beings. Oblivious to distance and time, it drove a network of communication across the galaxy. When it discovered a newly evolved intelligence to add to its delicate fabric, it rejoiced. On much rarer occasions, it reaved. When the song of one of its entities changed from delight and discovery to distress and confusion, the Traveler listened and thought. When the song transmuted into pain and fear, the Traveler made its decision, changed its course toward the song's small blue world and accelerated to a tremendous speed. During its journey toward the blue world's ordinary yellow sun, the troubled music ripped apart into incoherence. Though the Traveler sang reassurance, the songs faded. Finally, they died. The Traveler hurtled toward the silence, transmuting its music into the dirge. Admiral James T. Kirk had stolen and destroyed the Starship Enterprise. He had sabotaged a Starfleet vessel. He had incited mutiny. More important, he had disobeyed direct orders. His defenders claimed he had good reason for his actions, but so far he had refused to appear in his own defense. At the headquarters of the United Federation of Planets, his court-martial progressed. Emeritus ambassador, Sarak of Vulcan, arrived only moments before he was scheduled to testify on Admiral Kirk's behalf. He paused at the entrance of the Dark Council Hall. A harsh glare flashed over the stepped ranks of seats. A counselor's murdered. On a screen above the chamber, a violent explosion roiled and rumbled. A thunderous voice filled the room. Commander Kruge's heroic crew died by this devious Federation land. Commander Kruge himself was abandoned to perish on the surface of an exploding planet. A second explosion filled the screen with the actinic light, a warp engine's gone critical. The Enterprise struggled against its death, but another explosion ragged. It fell from space into atmosphere. It glowed with the friction of its speed. It burned. It disappeared in ashes and inflames. The Klingon's mission recorder focused on the face of James Kirk. Ah, Kamarag shouted. Hold the image! Hold! The image froze. James Kirk gazed at his dying ship. Observe! Kamarag's brow ridge pulsed with anger. The quintessential devil, James, T. Kirk, renegade and terrorist. He is responsible for the murder of the Klingon crew and the theft of their vessel. But his true aims were more sinister. Behold, the real plot and intentions. One image of James Kirk dissolved into a second. The new image, uniformed, calm, well-groomed, gazed out at the audience. A complex diagram glowed into being. Genesis, Kirk said. As a procedure by which the molecular structure of matter is broken down and reformed, a diagram became a torpedo. The Genesis device ought toward a lifeless world, a tidal wave of fire raced across the rocky surface. Stone and dust became water and air and fertile soil. In this simulation, James Kirk said, a barren rock becomes a world with water, atmosphere and a functioning ecosystem capable of sustaining most known forms of carbon-based life. Kamarag banished the image with an abrupt gesture. Admiral Kirk himself just detonated this dreadful weapon. The chamber's lights rose. This Genesis planet was no more and no less than a secret base from which to annihilate the Klingon people. Kamarag let us outrage build. We demand the extra-tition of Kirk. We demand justice! description: The podcast episode "009 - Star Trek Audiobook The Voyage Home Part 1" features a conversation between Jim and Admiral James T. Kirk discussing their journey back to the past. They recall several significant events, including the refusion surgery that reunites their spirit with body and the painful lessons of forgotten emotions. As they continue on this odyssey, they must confront the restrictions placed upon them by the Vulcan scholars who study them. Their encounter with Admiral Kamarag from Klingon Space leads to an explosive revelation about the destruction of the Starship Enterprise due to Kirk's disobedience. The episode explores themes of identity, self-discovery, and the consequences of actions in a manner reminiscent of Star Trek conventions while delving into personal and historical truths through Kirk’s eyes.

transcript: Chapter 1. Memory. We left Vulcan on the fifth of Tazmin. Since then, it has been a day of remembrance on all the great ships that survive. Before embracing exile, Karatek had been a physicist at the Vulcan Space Institute in a chikar he would never see again. Now that Vulcan was receding fast, both in fact and in memory, the fifth of Tazmin had become a day of meditation and reflection. Lost, it was Karatek's duty to ask, was it the fleet that needed the fifth of Tazmin or Karatek himself? He glanced out into the long night. Here were a few stars, no planets, therefore no new home. Beside the view screen were hangings woven in traditional designs. His consort had hung them in his meditation chamber to soften the severity of the bulkheads. They fluttered constantly as air circulated through the ship like blood through a heart. The air was cold. It smelled of chemicals, not the wild sweetness of the desert as the sun erupted up from the horizon, turning the cold into blazing heat and dazzling light, shimmering off the crimson sand. Karatek focused on the gleaming crystals and blood-metal circuits of his coronet. Of all the tasks he performed as one of Shavok's leaders, Karatek thought the duty of remembrance was probably the most valuable. Certainly it was the one for which he was best suited. The thought, as it always did, brought some reassurance. He had reluctantly inherited the task of command, and it still came hard to him. Most of the people he would have preferred to follow were long dead. He adjusted the coronet. His hair was brittle from the air, even more arid than that of Vulcan. It had begun to grey earlier than it would have done on the homeworld, assuming he had managed to survive the battles that had been the motherworld's daily lot. From years of making this record, he knew that the great green gems that were the coronet's memory, created in an art banned by the adepts both of Gaul and Montsileur, pulsed in time with the beat of the blood in his temples. Wrapped around the glowing crystals were fine drawn, unbreakable metal wires. And with blood metal, the wires formed intricate lavices that simultaneously ornamented the memory device and linked into his cerebral cortex through filaments almost too delicate to be felt. The tiny wounds those wires inflicted every time he set the coronet on his head stung for a moment longer as they healed. They would reopen when he removed the crown. But the pain didn't matter. As Sorok said, there was no pain. There was not pain enough to interrupt the thoughts, memories, sensations, and even the emotions. For even after years of study of Sorok's disciplines, Carotax emotional control remained imperfect. That the memory device would capture and record for all the years of exile and afterward when they finally found a new homeworld. If that day ever came in the long night of their exile. It was Carotax's habit to combine meditation and memory. But the task that Sorok had personally entrusted to him turned bitter every fifth of Tazmin when he recalled the events from the past year and sealed them in the coronet's memory. I could make the calculation if I chose of today's date on the mother world. At our current speed, well 3.9 years have passed on board this ship and its consorts, 25.86 years have passed on Vulcan. Obviously today is not the fifth of Tazmin back on Vulcan. Although some who follow Sorok deem hope to be illogical, I cannot agree. Sorok may have been ruthless, but he was never cruel. Therefore I believe it is not illogical to hope that the homeworld has survived, and that finally, after all the bloodshed, it may live long and prosper as Lady Metrani wished us. She may still be alive. I hope she is well. On all the ships that have survived thus far, other memories occupy us today. It is with grief that I must record the loss of seven ships. Carotax took a deep breath. He organized his thoughts, then marshaled all his courage before he made himself pour the memories of that loss into the coronet's glowing green gems. He recalled faces that from now on he would see only in memory, and knew the crown would preserve them for all times. Tears blurred his vision before the veils flicked across his eyes, preventing precious moisture from evaporating in the dry air of this chamber, or art from home fluttered in a ceaseless artificial breeze. Those ships that died had acted in error. They had paid for their error with their lives, and Carotax had failed to dissuade them. Their blood was on his hands. In the last council among all the ships that traveled like a caravan across the forge through this greater desert of stars, Carotax had heard a propulsion model advocated by an unlikely, possibly unholy alliance of technocrat party functionaries with two of the adepts from goal. Much to the council's not well concealed astonishment. They had even been joined by some of the Tivikram, who had found themselves trapped on board the great ships. When they left at the start of what had to be, it just had to be the last civil war on Vulcan. The new propulsion model admittedly had at first been intriguing. It fused technology with the arts of the mind in a way that gall adepts had once condemned as blasphemy. Those same as scruples, Carotax recalled, had caused the priestess at the shrine atop Mount Salaya to hand over to Surak the crown of memory that Carotax now held. But ultimately the new system was bad politics and worse science. Carotax had decided. He had refused to consider it for Shavok. And he had argued against his implementation on any of the ships, with all the authority of this training as a physicist and his experience as a propulsion engineer. What had become of the logic of the adepts who advocated its use? For them to abandon their former scruples, Carotax shut it. Seven ships went against the council's vote and installed the new propulsion system. How triumphantly they must have raced ahead, Carotax imagined. You see, the augmented drive works. When we return to the fleet, we shall tell Carotax how wrong he was, and then we shall bring the ships home. Those ships had raced off like boys who dashed ahead of their friends on a dare, looking back to laugh or jeer, only to find that their mad dash forward had taken them to the Lematias dam or to the edge of a precipice with no time to stop, no rock or root to grab to save themselves. They had left themselves no margin for error and therefore no escape. Carotax shook his head. How illogical it was of him to seek to deny his memory and the evidence of his own ships' sensors. But in strict honesty, let the coronet record his denial too. Something hot trickled down his temple. He had jarred loose one of the filaments that bound him to the coronet. In the most ancient rites, blood had been used as a sacrifice to appease the catras of travelers lost in the desert, spirits blowing on the wind until they dissolved. You alone of all on board this ship traveled with Surak. Though your journey now is greater, there is still no reason to lose control, he chagged himself. The coronet would capture his self-recrimination as well as his mourning. His memories would be preserved, but one of the thoughts and emotions, in the cotras of the people on board those lost ships. For the initial acceleration trial, the gall-adettes had been linked to brother and sister-adettes on other ships. Some of those adepts had burned themselves out. Some had died as hearts and blood vessels burst from the strain. Others survived, if one wished to call it life. Of the survivors, some howled, while others sacked or lay soiled, mindless and silent. A burden on family and healers who would tend them gently until their lives ends. For there was no desert into which they could walk, had they been able to move. And it was thought blasphemy to assist them out into the long night. As for the seven lost ships, Carrotak hoped that gravitic strains would have made their engines explode. There had always been that possibility. The minute structural weaknesses he had distrusted would, at least, have given the people within the quick, merciful, insane death, before the black hole that had opened before them sucked them into a night to avoid even of stars. Perhaps if Carrotak had argued more forcefully, if he had explained more clearly to Commissioner to Partha how risky that drive was, the ships now lost to the exile's fleet would still be traveling alongside Shavok, across this trackless forge of stars. The catastrophe had caused some of the scientists who followed Surak to theorize that a chance, perhaps 1.3%, perhaps even less, existed that at least one of the ships might have survived to transit through the madness of space, light and gravity into which they had plunged. Perhaps if an exit were possible, such a ship might emerge in some other place, near some other star, that might possess even one Minshara-class world, and in this second exile, finally find itself a home. The mathematics of that theory would dubious, cold comfort, if logic could be considered comfort. What was, was. Carrotak's eyes scolded. This much of his own disgrace he could spare future generations he told himself. He pulled the coronet off. A brief warmth almost as hot as the tears he fought to suppress spread at his temples as the filaments withdrew. His bio-control healed the tiny wounds almost instantly. The pain of memory lingered. The coronet glowed in his hands. The flicker and the crystals almost as subtle as the whisper of micrometeorites and dust as they brushed against the ship's hull. Useful finds of Tretanium and Derenium had enabled the surviving engineers to strengthen the ship's hulls in case they had to last well beyond the initial estimates of 100 years. For all the emphasis on safety, the obsessive care the exiles took to strengthen their ships in case the journey lasted past even the most pessimistic estimates. They had made no advance that wasn't accompanied by accidents. A barrage of delta rays two years ago had taken out half of one ship's population and exposed the remainder to radiation that would, to no doubt, shorten their lives, make their deaths more painful and reap a deadly harvest among any children they dared to have. Among the survivors had been a cadre of the fiercely independent Tivikram, whose priest kings had plunged Vulcan into at least three wars and constant borders skirmishes in the past hundred years. A raid on the shuttles that carried the exiles to their ships had resulted in Tivikram coming on board. They had never wanted to be there. The surviving Tivikram had seized the opportunity of catastrophic crew loss to stage a mutiny. Its control of the ship from its surviving crew and turned back. Karatek had watched that ship explode as its engineers loyal to the fleet staged a desperate final rebellion. He himself had trained at least two of them. In physics, not in logic. Karatek remembered the explosion as well as the pain of recalling it. The gems that were his colonnets eternal memory flickered. The rainbows buried in their depth shimmering. He realized that his tears had fallen on them. Where is your control? Karatek tightened his hand on the artifact. Even though crystals and metal pressed into his skin, the coronet felt agreeably warm in his hands. At the last council have voted been taken to decrease some elements of life support. Vulcan's air had been thin. It was no sacrifice to reduce oxygen content. And a slightly lower gravity actually made them feel stronger than they were and gave them greater ease in manipulating heavy engine components or hull plating. But Karatek had never quite accustomed himself to the cold. They could drape the bulkheads with weavings created here on the loom's built for the workshops. Psychologists had deemed necessary to help ease the bleakness of the ship's environment. They could fill compartments with art. A geode found on a mining expedition. A ceramic representation made by his adopted son Solor of the Shavok for which this ship was named. They could wear warmer tunics and cloaks over their ship suits, but the ship was still cold. An incentive of course to find a new homeworld and find it soon. Illogical to have mixed feelings about that idea. Illogical to admit to feelings at all. If I forget the old Vulcan, Karatek murmured. He squeezed his eyes shut, trying to form a mantra of control before resuming the coronet and the torment of memory. Sunlight on the sands outside Shekar, where the flanged gate had stood for millennia, for he had watched for pilgrims and caravans ever since he was a boy. For he had seen Surak and two of his disciples emerge from the desert, take his life into their hands and weave it like a thread of blood metal into the tapestry of their hopes and dreams for their people. A soft chime sounded. His lips softened in what would have been in the days before he met Surak, a smile, as his consort to Visas slipped into his study. On this fifth of Tasmaine, she wore the dulled blood green a morning. The color didn't suit her, but she was always beautiful to him. Karatek rose as to Visas entered the room. She pressed one hand to the small of her back. She was pregnant now with what would be the fourth child of her body. With the door open he could hear shouting in the corridor outside the quarters. You're part in my husband, she said, with the impeccable manners that had been hers since childhood, the formal training of a well-born Vulcan. Their eldest daughter, Dad these many years, had had similar manners, as did Sarissa, their adopted child, who combined them with the control she too had learned from Surak. By now their grandson, stranded back on Vulcan with his parents in the last dreadful moments of violence before the final shuttles lifted off the mother world, might well have children of his own. Children I shall never see, descendants of my house. There was some satisfaction in knowing that his house, if nothing else, would continue, assuming that Vulcan itself survived. As if sensing his thoughts through their bond, to Visas stepped close to him. Karatek held out joint fingers to touch her free hand, then used their hand clasp to ease her into his chair. This child to be, however, this child of their exile would have everything that Karatek could provide, despite the healer's concerns about the health of a child born in a long radiation filled transit between Star and Star. Healers like physicists, adepts and warriors had been wrong before. They could be wrong again. With Tavisa present, her fingers brushing his, the tiny chamber held all the warmth of home. The as-word, he asked, gazing into her eyes. The shuttle awaits. Its pilot begs pardon if my meditations were interrupted, but he asks that he comes swiftly, to avoid further controversy. Karatek raised a brow at his wife's choice of words. Tavisa was a mistress of understatement. The decision taken at the last council to limit travel between ships and postpone transfers of people or families from one ship to another had been unpopular. But limit and postpone were words that the exiles, like the Vulcans left so far behind them, had grown to distrust. As a result, any time a shuttle took off from any of the ships, Karatek heard protests and charges of favoritism. If Shavok was cold, the shuttles would be colder. Karatek had helped modify their design, diverting most of their energy to propulsion, lest they fall behind the fleet and, lacking the power to catch up, be marooned alone in the night. Another reason that councils were infrequent now. But there was another reason still, one that was barely whispered. After Tavikram rebels had commandeered one ship, the council had calculated a 47.1% chance that two easy transfers could allow factions to concentrate themselves in individual ships and gain power again. "'One figure, faster than the others, was caught by the blast and sent flying. "'The landing field had been created to be a killing ground that gave their betrayers the opportunity to take out any ships before the mining colonists could get them into the air. "'Satask was ill, aged before his time. In delegating function, he had ceded some authority and lost valuable information. Karatek would not believe that the fleet's commander could betray them.' With communications so sharply restricted, this colony had no chance of appealing to satask or more reasonable members of the exile living on their brother world. In addition to betraying Karatek and his family, Avarak had made victims out of some exiles and accomplices out of others. In the years to come of this second exile from what should have been his home, Karatek would remember. Memory had always been his duty. And until reparations were made, he would not forgive. The ice overhead shuttered. A shock quake, followed by aftershocks. Overhead raged the storm. The first of many they must survive until they took back what was theirs. Static hissed, disrupting communications again. Then as reception improved, Avarak's face came back into focus. And Karatek heard his voice assured, arrogant, and enjoying himself far too much. description: In this episode, we delve into the second book of "Star Trek" - The Vulcan's Soul Trilogy. Karatek, a leader in charge of commanding after his homeworld's exile, grapples with remembrance as he seeks closure on the past and prepares for an uncertain future in exile.

transcript: The Romulan Star Empire comes under attack by a mysterious and alarmingly powerful enemy because the Federation is unwilling to become embroiled in a sustained conflict Ambassador Spock and others must defy their government and meet the new threat head on. And now, Star Trek, Vulcan's soul, book one, Exodus. Chapter 1. 2364. History is the intellectual form in which a culture decides for itself the meaning of its past, Johann Hoisinga. None of the Vulcan, Romulan, human, Cardassian, and Klingon diplomats assembled had notified their governments officially of this meeting in the center of the Romulan neutral zone. Easier by far, thought Ambassador Spock to get forgiveness than permission. His might have invented that saying, but its applications were universal. The only problem was that Spock was not totally certain that forgiveness in this case would be all that easy to attain, not for this meeting. He suspected that various presidents, pre-tours, legates, chancellors, and a host of other titles would disapprove even more strenuously of where he and his colleagues had chosen to meet. Scans indicated that the echoing, circular chamber located approximately 300.58 meters beneath the jagged surface of an airless asteroid had begun its existence as a bubble in molten rock approximately 3.2 billion earth years ago. Those same scans had also proved that the desolate chunk of rock had once been part of a planet, shattered by some catastrophe and flung free. The symbolism was explicit. Those who didn't learn from history were destined to repeat it. That was a maxim Spock had found both in Surak's, Analects, and in human philosophy. Would old enemies prove apt students of history not their own? Spock found it difficult to assess that probability. For now at least the assembled diplomats, aides, warriors, and covert operatives eyed one another with a sensible caution, but no rage, at least not yet. To some extent, wariness was only to be expected. For Vulcan's rage was illogical. For Romulans it was counterproductive. For Klingons, Cardassians, and humans, however, well, Spock not only assumed that the weapons scanners each side had insisted on bringing in with the best available and working effectively, he had checked their effectiveness himself. But even the efficacy of the weapons scanners installed on this chunk of rock didn't matter. What need had the participants in this conference of physical weapons when they had thoughts and words, the deadliest weapons of all? Gathered around a black stone table that had been ancient before their ancestors had ever walked upright, let alone fought each other. The members of this shadow council all seemed willing to tolerate their enemy's presence. At least for now they were willing to listen. Spock's eyes met those of his own long-time personal antagonist. His father, Surak, might have chosen never to meld minds with him, but Spock thought that for once they were in perfect understanding. It was logical to exploit the willingness of these participants in a most secret conference to talk and to listen, but that willingness was fragile. One wrong word, one false step, even a misunderstood glance could destroy it. Surak raised his eyebrow minutely at his son. Now it begins. Rising from his black stone chair, Vulcan's senior ambassador held up his hand with its fingers parted in formal Vulcan greeting. Instantly he gained the attention of every diplomat and every guard in the room. Even more than his son, Surak was legendary for the just, wily, and occasionally ruthless methods he had employed lifelong to win his diplomatic battles. Even the Romulans, knowing he was no friend of theirs, had conceded that Surak, as eldest of the participants, was the logical representative to make the opening statement. We come to serve. Surak began, pitching his voice to carry throughout the echoing stone bubble. Instantly attentive, wary eyes targeted the august old Vulcan. At the sight of our meeting serve as a warning and an inspiration to us, Surak told the men and women assembled around the stone table, reinforcing the symbolism, Spock thought. Well done, Father. Spock had seen the geologic assays of this asteroid. They showed minute traces of types of radiation indicating that the cataclysm that had destroyed the planet had been deliberate. Thus far, however, no one had been able to learn whether it had been destroyed by its enemies or its own inhabitants. Even now some radiation remained in the desolate rock. It wouldn't prove harmful, Spock knew, if this clandestine meeting with Romulan negotiators was kept brief. That knowledge was shared by every one of the diplomats, officers, and scientists present. And even if concerned about radiation levels hadn't been a considerable incentive for concluding these talks quickly, the destruction of bases on both sides of the neutral zone made speed and necessity. I am not here. Surak continued to make resounding speeches about historic moments. We are not here for that. Instead, I urge the representatives assembled today to choose the logical path. We must reason together to prevent our own home worlds from being shattered on the fords which were this planet's culture perished. Surak's reflection on the gleaming black walls was only slightly distorted by the ancient inscriptions that no one had ever been able to decipher. His heavy white robes of office gleaming with iridescent cobblish and gems of white, the red of Vulcan soil and the green of its children's blood seemed simultaneously to weigh him down and sustain him. For an instant the image in the shining stones seemed to waver. Spock tensed in case Surak needed assistance. His father was barely two hundred. When had his shoulders become so thin? Using the car in it felt a little different from the trance he entered when he meditated. Ticarit caratex to the command center came over the speakers. I come, he told them, and hastened past the men standing guard. They feared sabotage. Surak message is coming through from the surface. Not the mother world, not even the name of the planet. A long pause told Caratex that Torin's gift had been accepted. I grieve with thee, he said. Around him the crew bowed their heads and nodded sympathy. Together, he and Ruinek stepped onto the transporter days. Energize, Spock commanded. Though a try apparently wasted no funds on ship decor, or perhaps had no spare funds at all, Spock thoughtfully stored that possible bit of data away for future analysis. The years of practicing martial arts clearly had kept his Romulan warrior skills honed. Moving with a professional soldier's speed, he leaped, bringing down the two Watry with two blows, swiftly, silently and efficiently. A third Watry, who had been hidden from them by the bulk of the first two, turned sharply to see what had just happened to the others. Spock heard him draw in a breath for a shout. But before the Watry could sound an alarm, Spock gestured. Ruenak caught the Watry, pulling him off balance and dragging him helplessly backward. Spock calmly brought the Watry down, with the quick grip that humans had once dubbed the Vulcan nerve pinch. As the Watry went limp, Ruenak lowered him soundlessly to the floor, then gave Spock an approving nod. Unfortunately, though, the walls of the corridor were smooth. Gambling that we can get the device and be gone before they and we are found. He gestured to Ruenak, onward. Together they moved forward and utter silence, since the schematics told Spock that the amplification of the Watry was not able to be found. Spock that the amplification device would be in the anti-chamber to the main power drive, just ahead. Spock stopped short. Ah, there were complications. Of course there would be complications, he told himself sternly. For which laxity of course, Charvane could pay dearly, but that didn't mean that the Watry would be so conveniently careless as well. The amplification device itself seemed to be quite unremarkable, a featureless rectangular box of some matte black material. Judging from its small size, no larger than that long ago cloaking device, it looked fortunately reasonably portable. And even more fortunately, it clearly wasn't welded into the rest of the power drive. Spock didn't doubt that he could detach it from its connections, hopefully without damaging it or himself in the process, if only he had the time in which to do it. Unfortunately though, a double circle of fifteen Watry surrounded the device. He gestured to Ruenak, can you? Ruenak gave him a raised eyebrow. You must be joking, look back. There is little time for logical conclusions. In brief, all I need to do is get near enough to the device to detach it. But how am I going to? Then inspiration struck. Spock backed off from the chamber full of Watry just enough to let him send a whispered message to Sonic without being overheard. Ready to transport a room personnel. Have them beam up and hold and the pattern buffers everyone in this chamber save Ruenak and me. Hold but do not materialize them. She must truly have been wondering what her husband could possibly be thinking, but Sonic merely said, understood. In only a few moments, a shimmering filled the room. There was only a finite amount of time before someone came to check on the guards, and another finite amount of time that so many could be held in stasis. With Ruenak's standing watch, Spock studied the housings. No, he definitely could not simply detance them at random. As he suspected, a security system had been at work here too, creating a specific pattern of color and shape that had to be followed as each housing was released. What would happen if the pattern was broken? An explosion, a lethal gas, an equally lethal shock. The illogical to consider what might or might not happen, logical to assume that it would be suitably unpleasant. Closing his mind of the fact that precious seconds were passing, Spock carefully studied the pattern, swiftly analyzing possibilities and mathematical progressions. Then working with deliberate care, he began to delicately detach the housings. Yes, he did have the correct pattern. But he was not sure what even the smallest slip, the slightest stray spark might trigger. One more connection. There. No, one last connection remains. Here they come. Ruenak snapped. Finished. Good timing. Wait here, let me. The device was definitely heavier than it looked. With a grunt of effort, Ruenak hoisted it into his arms. And Spock told Savic, return the what try, and be prepared to beam us up precisely after that. It was perfectly timed. The startled guards found themselves suddenly back in reality. Not sure what had just happened to them. Even as the new guards came rushing in, and Spock, Ruenak, and the amplification device vanished into sparkling air. And then they were back in reality. As the transporter room of the Alliance formed about them again, Ruenak stepped down from the dais, staggering a little, and gladly handed his heavy burden to the waiting engineers, who had an anti-grav pallet waiting for it. We have it, sir. They quickly began shielding the device, to keep it from attempting an interface with Savic's ship and a possible lethal explosion. While the engineers continued their work, Spock and Ruenak hurried back to the bridge. Sir, Ruenak said riley. He was uncertain of what rank you held. Commander of the Romulan Star Empire, last time I was actually in service. Not exactly useful here. With an odd to Savic, who nodded approval back at him, Spock opened hailing frequencies between the Watrai, the Federation ships, and the Romulans. Without preamble, Spock began. We have aboard our ship a certain vital weapons device formally belonging to the Watrai. I am certain that they will be willing to verify this fact. There was heavy silence from the Watrai. Embarrassed silence, presumably, Spock thought. He didn't wait. Instead, he then told Sharvanak, I would find it quite a rearable to use the device to save the Romulans, but only if you are willing to order your fleet to drop their shields as well. What are you suggesting? Instead of answering, Spock said to the Watrai, I would be willing to return your property to you, but again, only if you are willing to order your fleet to drop their shields. What madness is this? Sharvanak snapped. No madness, merely logic. You dare to call it logic? I call it cunning. And word anyone other than you, I would take myself betrayed. You know that this matter cannot be resolved. If we open fire, the murderer race retaliates, and neither side can know which side a thief and trickster will fade her. Now, which of the two of us are wonderies the thief and which one is the trickster? Romulanak commented, Riley. Not that it matters. The only ones left with functioning shields after all this maneuvering are our nice friendly federationships. Exactly so, said Sonic. In what ruinak at once ironically dubbed full Starfleet bluffing mode, she swore to all listening. I will open fire on whoever shoots first. The Romulans and the Watrai really did have no choice but to accept the reality of the stalemate, Spock thought. They would have to agree. Did they though? No matter what she might be thinking, Charvadek was too honorable for anything like trickery. But this was still all suddenly a little too easy to be logically credible. Why was there no more resistance from the Watrai than a few harsh words? To the transporter room, Spock snapped. Ruinak hurried after him and so did Chekhov. Admiral, Sonic shouted. No, I'm not being left behind this time. Closely followed by both Ruinak and Chekhov, who was moving with a younger man's speed and determination, Spock reached the transporter room just as someone dark clad and masked, beamed aboard from the Watrai ship. The Watrai leaped straight at the device, wrestling with it, trying to tear off its shielding. Chekhov, who was nearest to the intruder, threw himself at the alien, not trying anything as foolish as fighting, since a younger warrior was bound to be stronger, but just hanging on with all his might, trying to drag the Watrai away from the device. Chekhov, get back. Spock shouted. No, damn it. Just help me hold him. Pavel, now a transporter beam is activating. Get back. But the Watrai and Chekhov were now tangled up in the Watrai's flowing robes. Chekhov's struggling couldn't pull free in time. The Watrai transporter beam caught him as well as the Watrai intruder, and they both faded out in a shower of sparks. Spock raced to the transporter controls, struggling to recover Chekhov, refusing to let himself feel anything but calm determination, logic. The Watrai program was similar to that used by the Federation, since there were only so many ways to use a scientific principle, but it wasn't identical. The frequencies weren't quite the same, and there was no time to puzzle out the differences. For a moment, he thought he'd succeeded. Chekhov and the Watrai are rematerialized on the transporter platform, struggling fiercely, but then the image wavered, distorting, breaking up. Spock heard a horse scream of agony. Then the figures were...gone. Spock's hands tightened on the console so fiercely that the composite cracked. Ruenek, after a stunned moment of silence, began to murmur a prayer in Romulan. It seemed the only thing that could be done. Spock could only logically deduce that Chekhov and his enemy had both died in a transporter malfunction, possibly the result of incompatible energies between the Starfleet and the Watrai ships. What had seemed to have victory had just been turned into a stunning personal loss. He chose this. Spock told himself. There is no blame. His voice sternly under control. Spock reported what he had witnessed to the bridge, speaking formally to Sonic, saying the words he had never thought to speak. Admiral Pavel Chekhov is dead. transcript: Dr. Mordro should not have killed the captain. I'm well aware of that. Dr. Mordro has taken his controversial theories on temporal displacement and put them into practice. Temporal displacement. Motion through time. You mean time travel? I have just said so. So you intend to use his theories to go back to yesterday and save Jim's life? I don't see why your plan is any different or any more ethical than the one I suggested. It is very little different in effect, only in means and motive. Your motive was to save the captain's life. Mine is to stop Dr. Mordro. Forgive me, Spock. If I failed to appreciate such subtle shades of ethics, no subtlety is involved. However, I have not provided you with sufficient information to understand my logic. McCoy said himself unwillingly for a long discourse. But as Spock related what he had learned in the past few hours, the doctor grew interested despite himself. Finally, he realized where the explanation was heading. Spock, you're telling me that Jim wasn't killed by the George Mordro we have in custody on the Enterprise at all, that it was some other George Mordro, one from the future, precisely. I don't believe it. Why not? It's too complicated, it's too my theory possesses one unique factor which may persuade you to help me. Why, if this hypothesis is correct, then these events are a serious perturbation in the time stream. They must be put right. Captain Kirk need not die. He must not die. McCoy rubbed his eyes, sorting through Spock's reasoning, and made a certain amount of absurd sense. Alright, Spock, what do you want me to do? I'll help you if I can. Did a flicker of relief even of gratitude pass over the Vulcan's face? McCoy chose to believe so. He must take charge while Dr. Mordro and I build the hardware to take me back to yesterday. This will require time. It would be better if we were not disturbed. You don't need to be in a rush, McCoy grinned. After all, we have plenty of time. But we do not. The effort required to change an event is proportional to the square of its distance in the past. You mean the longer you wait, the harder it will be? I sleep. Unfortunately, I have no choice. Dr. Mordro was convicted of causing people to disappear. I do not doubt that Mr. Brathwaite believes the professor killed them and disposed of their bodies. As time-changing became known, it would be used as indeed Dr. Mordro has already used it. The result would be as chaotic as space-time in the region of the naked singularity. If Dr. McCoy and I are detected, we will undoubtedly find ourselves court-martialed and on our way to the same rehabilitation colony that awaits Dr. Mordro. It would be unfair to expose anyone else to this risk. I explained to Dr. McCoy that what we are attempting is not without its peril, and that being sent to a rehabilitation colony is not the greatest of the possible dangers. Mr. Brathwaite, the rumor is the prisoner couldn't have escaped without help, so there must be a conspiracy. A conspiracy? What tribe? Get Mr. Brathwaite up here, on the double. Spock, has turned over command to you? For the moment. The formal hierarchy calls for Montgomery Scott to assume command. Scott is working on the engines. He hasn't got time to be in command. He's too important, right where he is. Brathwaite turned to leave. Ian, McCoy used his softest southern draw. Brathwaite stopped. Ian, whether you like it or not, I'm in command. If you keep harassing the crew, I'll confine you to quarters. Brathwaite swung around as fist clenched. Do you think you can do that, do you? McCoy smiled as kindly as old country doctor smiled. Try me. McCoy joined Spock in the transport room. The Vulcan bent over the open console, attaching a peculiarly organic looking device to the controls. Spock, what happens to us? If you go back in time and change things around, we won't exist anymore. Of course we will, Dr. McCoy. Not here, not now, not doing what we're doing. What happens to this probability version of all of us? Nothing. McCoy snorted with frustration. If I succeed, this version of us will never have occurred. We will not fade out of existence because we never will have existed in the first place. It is quite simple and logical. McCoy gave up his pulse accelerated with nervousness and fear. Let's do it and be done. Very well. Spock picked up a second equally organic looking device and slung it over his shoulder. Shall I wait for you here? Will you come back immediately after you go? Or McCoy could not resist? Or before? Spock replied with perfect seriousness. I will endeavor not to be turned before I leave, though it would be an intriguing experiment. However, as you so astutely pointed out, if I succeed, I will not need to come back. If I fail, I will endeavor to be gone less than one hour. If I do not return, he hesitated, then pointed out a switch on the unit attached to the transporter. The auxiliary changer will pull me back, but it is unlikely that I would survive if you were forced to use it. Then I won't. You must. Otherwise, the conflict between where I am and where I should be could create a damaging paradox. If I am gone more than one day, you must bring me back. Alright, Mr. Spock. Spock stepped onto the transporter platform. Goodbye, Mr. Spock. Good luck. Spock touched a control on this unit of the time changing. A tremendous flash of rainbow lightning in government. A nice and clear light. But this bird that I should see is the sea. The ship lay in a moment of darkness and silence so complete that McCoy thought the explosion had deafened and blinded him. The Enterprise had lost all power. Spock materialized on the transporter platform in a blaze of rainbow light. He had not known how the transition would affect him. Every muscle in this body felt wrenched. Mr. Spock? Spock turned slowly, entirely drained of energy. Mr. Scott stood in the doorway, looking at him with a concerned expression. Mr. Scott, I should have expected you. Did you have had me? I are right. There is something wrong with the transporter. I simply noticed some minor power fluctuations. They could become reasons for complete. I can come back and help you as soon as I've reported to Captain Kirk about the engines. That is unnecessary. The work is almost complete. I assure you are right. Spock did not reply. Scott remained in the doorway a moment longer, then turned and left Spock alone. Spock concealed himself near the lift in shadows, waiting until he thought he could enter the lift unobserved. When Dr. Mordro's future self appeared, Spock would confront him. Ah, Spock. I thought you came searching for me. The Vulcan spun around and found himself face to face with Dr. Mordro. I should have known better than to involve you at all, but I had to get you away from that damn singularity. He caused me more trouble than Bratwaite and Kirk and the whole Federation together. Throwing himself sideways, Spock drew his face. Dr. Mordro's gun went off, as Spider-Whipped will it slam Spock against the bulkhead. He slumped to the deck, knowing he had faith. Spock opened his eyes. He knew his clouded vision to be a symptom of Spider-Whipped. He tried to ignore the prospect of his own death. He tried to do something, anything. Perhaps he still had time to stop Professor Mordro, to save Jim's life. He saw and felt the temple reaching toward him. He joked away, rolling to escape it. He wiped the blood from his eyes, his vision cleared. After grazing his temple, the bullet had embedded itself in the bulkhead. The Spider-Whipped began to grow downward, seeking warmth and nerve cells. The mass of fibers reached toward him, shivering like a skeet of silver thread. description: In this episode of the Audiobook Star Trek series featuring Vonda N. McIntyre's "Entropy Effect," audiobook reader George DeCay delivers an in-depth read of the novel, with Leonard Neatmoy voicing Spock. The story explores a new phenomenon discovered in space called singularity and its potential danger to inhabited worlds. Despite the challenges presented by the unknown phenomena, Captain James T. Kirk leads his crew on an expedition to gather data and understand this cosmic event before it has too much impact on our understanding of time itself. The conclusion is uncertain, leaving readers and listeners with both awe and worry about the future of scientific discovery in space.

Leslie took out his tricorder and scanned the area in a full circle. Sweating profusely, he wiped his forehead on his sleeve. They're not here, sir. That could be good news or bad. The tricorder only responded to living beings. If the scientists were dead already, Kirk whipped out his communicator. Mr. Sulu, I want a sensor scan of this place, a radius of two kilometers from my position. There's a group of humans just west of the installation, and one Vulcan. Do you need more detailed data? No, thank you, Lieutenant. Kirk out. Leslie smiled. They got out. Apparently. Come on, Mr. Leslie. Let's see if there's anything around here we can salvage. The group began to move down the hillside. They had the look of a people that was going home. There was hope in their eyes, David thought. Not bitterness. Relief. Not anger. Even Dr. Budrow had calmed down considerably since Spock retrieved the G7 unit from its hiding place in the hills. The colony administrator had been cradling the device like a baby ever since. But as he took his mother's hand and descended the slope, David felt strangely detached from the spirit of relief and hopefulness. He felt as if the colony's destruction was a nightmare that could have been avoided. Sure, the Enterprise had sent the Klingons packing, but at what cost? If the Klingons had just been left alone, if they hadn't been confronted and provoked by Starfleet, would they have trained their disruptors on the domes? The boy's horror grew worse as he descended the slope and approached the domes. It was like walking through a bad dream. His mother was expressionless, but her hand gave her away. It was trembling ever so slightly in David's grasp. Unburnt tatters of domed material reared and flapped at them. They reminded the boy of huge beasts, writhing in agony. The smell of smoke made his eyes start to water. Setting his teeth, David pushed on. Why had it been necessary for the military to show up? Why? Then he and his mother came inside of the place where her garden used to stand. One of the gold-shirted men from the Enterprise knelt in the scorched tangle that was once a patch of living things. David recognized him too. It was Captain Kirk, the one who had confronted the Klingons. The man looked up at the boy and his mother. He was holding something. It was so desiccated, so black and twisted that it took David a moment to figure out what it was. Finally, he recognized it. It was one of the Klingon specimens, one of the fire blossoms. Where did the Captain get off touching his mother's plants? He was the one who destroyed her garden in the first place, just as clearly as if he'd pressed the trigger on the disruptor and septor. Suddenly, David's anger surged and spilled over, and the world melted, caught in the heat of his righteous fury. Kirk was surprised when he looked up and saw Carol, but he was even more surprised to see her holding the hand of the blonde boy. He'd seen the boy around the colony, but until now he'd had no idea they were related. Still, as he compared their faces, the conclusion was inescapable. It was Carol's child. But why hadn't she told him? Why had she... And then he took another look at the boy, and he had his answer. My God. He felt a smile take over. I've got a son. That's when Carol and the boy turned their heads and saw him standing there, looking at them. Gaping at them was more like it. The Captain started toward them, not sure of what he would say when he got there, not sure of anything except the inexorable pull of his own flesh and blood. The youngster's expression slowly began to change, but not to one of joy. Instead, his mouth twisted and hardened as if he'd just eaten something he didn't like. Even then, Kirk didn't quite catch on. Not until the boy barked something at him, something about Klingons and destruction, and the Captain realized what had contorted those young features. It was hatred, pure seething hatred, that it was all directed at him. He did this, Mom. It's his fault. David, what are you saying? For a moment, the youngsters seemed on the verge of telling her. Then he just turned and walked away. Kirk looked at Carol. She seemed miserable. Yes, he is who you think he is. We'll talk later. Later, he said numbly. He watched Carol disappear around the curve of a ruined dome. In the wind that whistled through the installation, the Captain could still hear the boy's bizarre and discomfiting accusation. His fault. His fault. The air in the water bologna was clean and fragrant. It was impossible to tell that there had been a disastrous fire somewhere nearby. Jim turned to Carol. What did you tell him about his father, I mean? The truth to an extent that I met his father a long time ago, and that his father went away before he was born. It must have been hard, raising him by yourself all these years. Not as hard as you might think. He's a good boy. Spock told me what happened out there in the hills. He's more than just a good boy. He's something... I don't know. Something special. I wish I could take some credit for that. I wish I had had some part in him, Carol. Why? Why let me go on all this time, not knowing. Wait, what's better for everyone? If you've known what could you have given him? A couple of days here and there. You'd only have felt guilty for not spending more time with him. Carol took his hands and hers and squeezed. In my kind of work, there's a place for a family, for a child. I'm not saying you're a terrible person for wanting to be a starship captain, but you've got to admit David couldn't have toddled around your bridge while you were out there fighting Klingons. And now he hates me. Oh, that'll pass. I'll explain that you weren't delaying for any of this. But for all we know, you saved our lives as much as Spock did. I appreciate that. But I'd appreciate it more if you went a step further. Tell him he has a father, someone who cares about him, even if he's not around. If I were a boy, especially a boy David's age, that would be important to me. Hell, it'd make all the difference in the world. Promise you'll tell him about me, Carol. Not now, but when he's over, what happened today, when you feel the time is right? She sighed. Maybe Jim was right. And then again, maybe she'd be opening Pandora's box. Knowing his father was a starship captain, David might someday want to be like him, to go flitting around the galaxy, giving up all promise of a home and a family. And she desperately didn't want that. I promise to think about it. But you've got to promise me something in return. Don't suddenly show up on the next planet we're working on, or the one after that. Let him grow up making his own decision. Then, if he wants to seek you out, I won't have any objections. Deal? Deal. Take us out of orbit, Mr. Sulu. Half impulse. I, sir. The captain watched the viewscreen as the red sphere of Beta-Kensandia III began to vanish into the recesses of space. He had departed from hundreds of worlds, but he had never left quite so much behind. Spock and McCoy stood on either side of him. It shouldn't take too long for them to rebuild. True, their new domes should arrive in a matter of weeks. And with Dr. Boudreau's G7 unit intact, they'll be back in business inside a month. Of course, some star fleets going to have to pay a little more attention to this sector in the future. The Klingons may be back. I do not believe they will return in the near future, Captain. Given the actions of the Klingon who rescued us, I would speculate that Beta-Kensandia III was more of a political pawn than an actual strategic objective. And since one of you become an expert on Klingon nature. Doctor, all scientific theory is based on observation and extrapolation. I am merely applying the same procedures to social theory. People aren't energy emissions, Spock. They're unpredictable. Yes, Doctor, predictably so. The captain swiveled in his seat. You know, I've heard the two of you go head to head before, but I don't think I've ever heard quite as specious an argument as this one. If I didn't know better, I'd think you were trying to distract me from something. You have any idea what he's talking about, Spock? I am at a loss, Doctor. Turning back to the view screen, Kirk allowed himself a smile that neither Spock nor McCoy could see. And also a reflection. He was leaving much behind. But he was also taking much with him. After all, there were families. And there were families. Faces of Fire was written and adapted for audio by Michael Jan Friedman and read by Vibi Dash. The recording engineer was Vince Lubinsky, editing, post-production and sound design by Gary Pink. Original music was composed by Richard Emmett, Sam McCally, Carl Schurts and Eve Biglarian. Theme music from the Star Trek television series was composed by Alexander Courage and Gene Roddenberry and used courtesy of ruined music. The associate producer was Ilyssa Shokoff. Faces of Fire was produced and directed by Carol Shapiro.
description: In "Faces of Fire," episode 45, Captain Kirk and his team face a challenge in convincing a herd of Kubaya beasts to leave the area. Despite initial doubts about the effectiveness of their plan, they finally succeed with the help of medical officer McCoy's efforts. This victory is celebrated by Minister Omalas of the Federation, who awards them credit for their work. The episode highlights the importance of perseverance and teamwork in achieving a seemingly impossible goal.
