transcript: Trafford's face was twitching as McCoy had never seen it twitch before. I cannot say how much I regret what happened. I should have anticipated such a turn of events. I should have sent more guards to escort you. Once again there were eight of them in the Hall of Government. McCoy, Jim, Scotty, the ambassador and the four menteele ministers. The tension in the air was almost palpable. You acted as you saw fit first minister. There is no need for self-recrimination. Even with a derma-plast patch over one eye, Farquar was as insufferably diplomatic as ever. And with all due respect, even a dozen guards wouldn't have been able to keep the Oberat in line, not after what happened to those two young men. It appears the Oberat have gotten their hands on the supply of phasor pistols. We will have to find their source and cut it off. In the meanwhile we have waited long enough. It is time to sit down and work out a solution. We can begin this afternoon. I agree. The sooner the better. First Minister, I'd like to make a recommendation. I know how closely you embrace your religious beliefs, but wouldn't it serve everyone's interests, the Cubayas included? If you were to keep the animals away from the sacred precinct, if only for a little while? Captain, I believe we are overstepping our bounds. We didn't come here to remold the cultural values of... Despite the ambassador's protest, Kirk plunged on. Consider the safety of the beast's first minister. Imagine if the Oberat had chosen to attack the Cubaya that came through in the first wave, instead of waiting and hoping for a solution. They could have slaughtered the animals wholesale. Maybe next time they will. As you point out, Captain Kirk, there is much at stake. However, there will be no discussion of curbing the rangeings of the Cubaya. Not for a day, not even for a minute. If necessary, we will increase our security in the precinct, but we will not compromise our beliefs. McCoy cursed inwardly. In other words, he thought, thanks for the help, but next time keep it to yourself. Traffic looked to the ambassador. This afternoon, then. This afternoon, first minister. The room they occupied was almost as large as the Hall of Government, and with its tall stained glass windows just as impressive too. How could you have said such a thing, Captain? How could you have even considered it? Kirk shrugged, concentrating on the stained glass images, and not on the ambassador's voice. That way, there was at least a chance he'd get through this without blowing up. Seems like a good idea at the time. It could hardly have been a worse idea. That's the problem with having ships personnel participate in diplomatic endeavors. The captain wasn't going to take the bait. He wasn't. He was going to memorize every detail of these fine stained glass works of art right down to the number of kubaya in them, which was considerable. Fine. Ignore me. See how far that gets you. And with that, he strutted out of the chamber, leaving a razor-edged silence in his wake. Scotty was the one who finally broke it. How bold a self-important, narrow-minded stubborn fops! You can say that again, Mr. Scott. I had him pegged from the moment I laid eyes on him. So you did, Bones. And I was foolish enough to try to talk you out of it. Obviously, he's forgotten you saved his worthless hide not so long ago. Worthless hide indeed. I just wish there were some way to defuse the situation before the death toll starts to mount. If we could get in touch with those two O'Brock ministers, Nenikki and Omolos. See the matter from their angle. Maybe we could get some fresh ideas. Bones looked it and thoughtfully. Worthless hide. Maybe there is a way. What are you saying, Doctor? You two stay here. I'll be right back. There's something I want you to try on. Shading his eyes from this world's blinding white sun, Lutek wiped his eyes on his sleeve. How many hours of this could a Klingon take? As he approached the top of the slope, he made out a deep basin of a valley up ahead. Like everything else here, it was reddish brown. More importantly, one of the walls was pocked with a series of openings, caves, natural hiding places, and shelter from the biting winds which a pack of children would need in order to survive up here. Smiling to himself, taking out his disruptor, Lutek made his way down into the basin. With his hunters' strides, it didn't take long at all to close the gap. Finally, he reached his destination, a small ledge directly above the first cave. Gathering himself, he dropped and twisted, training his weapon on the darkness within. The children might be in the cave's recesses, he thought, but he couldn't be sure. After the blinding light of the sun, the interior of the place looked pitch black to him. Careful to stay alert, Lutek advanced into the darkness. He made out vague shapes. Training his disruptor on them, he advanced a little further. The shapes still didn't move, not even with the gentle rise and fall of the chest area that usually denoted sleep. Coming closer, he saw why. They weren't children, they were just rocks. Lutek nudged one with his foot, it rolled away. Suddenly a red ball of agony exploded in the Klingons temple, dropping him to one knee. Lutek flung up his hands to protect himself angry and confused. Something big and heavy hit his right hand, the one that held the disruptor, but he managed to hang onto it. Squinting through the blood that was running into his eyes, he made out a number of small forms swarming like carrion creatures around a carcass. Pointing his weapon at the nearest of him, he started to depress the trigger. That's when he felt something on his shoulder and whirled to look up at a larger form than any of the others. He barely made out the features of a full-grown Vulcan before a thicker darkness engulfed him. The Klingon went limp and Spock's grasp. Letting go, he watched the inert body slumped to the ground. Then he took stock of the children who stood around him. Three boys and two girls, each armed with a rather substantial-looking rock. This was a trap? A boy with black hair and narrow features nodded eagerly. Yes, sir. We spotted the Klingon a long way off, so we were ready for him. And when he went into the cave, we came in after him with our rocks and, you need not explain, I believe I understand your strategy. The boy stopped, disappointed. The Vulcan was sorry for that, but there were more important matters to be dealt with right now. Squatting, Spock took the disruptor from the Klingon's fingers and tucked it into his sample pouch. Then slipping his hands beneath the Klingon's armpits, he dragged him into the back of the cave. Finally, he checked the Klingons' belt for food and found a number of heavy brown-grain pellets, not very appealing, but they would have to do. The youngsters looked at the Klingon fair hungrily. Without a thought for himself, Spock gave out the pellets and watched the children wolf them down. But one of the boys, peering at him from beneath tangled blonde curls, handed half his allotment back. You have to eat too. Spock shook his head. My needs are different. The child had no reason not to believe him. Shrugging, he gobbled down the remainder of his pellets. Some of the youngsters were better at concealing their fears than others. The blonde boy seemed to be the best of all. There was something about him that Spock found familiar. The Vulcan just couldn't put his finger on it. The boy spoke up. What are the Klingons after anyway? This world is not all that distant from the Klingon Empire. They may simply be asserting their right to it. However, it is also possible. They have received intelligence about the colony's work and wish to seize whatever new technologies have been developed. The youngster grunted. Well, that makes sense. What does not make sense is your assault on the Klingon. The children looked at him as if he just admitted he was a Klingon himself. Perhaps he had been too abrupt in changing topics. But we got him. With my help. In any case, I cannot allow a repeat of a maneuver. It is too dangerous. They looked at him with hard eyes and hard faces. We've got to help our parents. I am certain your parents will prefer you to be safe, to retreat into the hills as far as you can and to stay there until help arrives. The blonde boy looked at him shrewdly. And what about you? What are you going to do? I do not know yet. You're going to try to help the people back in the colony. If circumstances allow, I will no doubt make an attempt. And what your chances be better if you get some help? It was quite logical. The Vulcan gave the blonde boy credit. My chances of helping your parents will be greater. Yes. But my chances of losing you will also be greater. It will be a trade off. The boy shook his head. We're not just going to run away and hide. We're going to help. With you or without you. Spock cocked an eyebrow. Apparently he had little choice in the matter. If the children could not be convinced to retreat to a safer place, he would have to protect them. And the only way to do that was to join forces with them. Very well. We will work together. However, you must follow my directions. If we are to lay traps for our pursuers, they must be more efficient than the one that caught him. He tilted his head to indicate the Klingon. The blonde boy nodded. You got a deal. I will need to know your names. Mine is Spock. For the first time the blonde child seemed reticent. David. I'm Fepper. Garcia. Medford. One. Spock couldn't help but notice that they all used their last names. All except for David. He was the only one who'd given the Vulcan his first name. And reluctantly at that. There was more to the blonde boy than met the eye, Spock decided. This time when they visited the sacred precinct of the Obarat, no one even glanced in the direction. It felt more than a little strange after the hostility they'd encountered the day before. Kirk made a mental note to describe the experienced bones. After all, it was the doctor who had equipped them with facial prosthetics, subdermal dyes and optical overlays all designed to make them look like allureans. Before long they came to the open-air market they'd glimpsed during their official visit. The crowd was thin now. Some of the merchants were even starting to pack up their wares for the evening. Looks like it's good a place to start as any mister scott. After you, sir. As they approached the square, the captains scanned the stalls. Some offered fresh vegetables. Others displayed long ornate robes of vaguely religious-looking nature and still others showed metal or ceramic cookware. Midway across the far side of the marketplace, there was an open doorway with a number of Obarat standing just inside it. They all appeared to have mugs in their hands. I may not know much, sir, but I can spot a tavern a mile away. And information flows fast and loose where there's liquor to loosen the tongue. Crossing the plaza, they walked up to the open doorway as if they belonged there. Some of the Obarat stopped their conversations and glanced curiously at the newcomers, but no one challenged them. Inside they found what they had expected. Neger lighting, shadowy corners full of tables and a vaguely conspiratorial drone of voices. Moving to the bar, Kirk procured two mugs and laid down a number of Malorian coins. From the way the bartender's eyes lit up, he gathered that he'd handed over more than he had to. Then, mugs in hand, he and Scotty found an unoccupied table in the darkest of the places four corners. Onceing at the next table, he tried to think of the best way to start a dialogue with some Obarat. Finally, he opted for the direct approach, raising his mug to one of the patrons. Good day. Hm, they've been worse, they've been better. You knew here, aren't you? Yes, we are. A hell of a time to visit. What with all the trouble that's going on? Actually, it's the trouble that's prompted the visit. Oh, got family here, are you worried about? In a sense, I mean, aren't we all brothers when you come down to it? It's the way I feel. He indicated the other two seated at his table. In fact, that's how we all feel. Kirk turned to Scotty. You see, I told you we'd find good reception in this place. If you cannot find solidarity here in these try-in times, where can you find it? Times are trying, alright. But yesterday, the Dan Mantiel marched to procession of off-worlders and armed guards through the precinct. It was a slap in the face, a reminder of how little they respect us. Second, Obarat spoke up. True, but we taught them they couldn't do that kind of thing. A couple of our boys took one of their guards down. The first Obarat made a gesture of dismissal. Now that was nothing to be proud of. We lost two to their one, and they weren't much more than babies. Well, at least we showed them. At least we didn't let it go unnoticed like we'd done in the past. But first, Obarat dismissed that idea as well. So what? It's not going to make them stop abusing the sacred ground. The third man at the table, who had been silent up until now, finally spoke. They'll never stop that, not unless we make them. There's time enough for that, and no need to lose young lives in the process. The first Obarat turned to the captain in Scotty again. Sorry, you didn't come here to listen to us argue, did you? With all due respect, no. One can hear the same arguments wherever they are Obarat. He looked around as if leery of spies. Though there are some in the precinct I'd give much to listen to. All three of his listeners nodded gravely. Hmm, I believe I know what you mean. Do you know where we might find him? It seemed to Kirk, the men knew, but were reluctant to say. In the end, however, their caution gave way. Well, if you like, we can take it to them. We'd like that very much. Reaching an unspoken consensus, the Obarat raised their mugs and drained them. Kirk and Scotty did the same. Come. The first Obarat made his way toward the door. The disguised humans followed, and the other two Obarat brought up the rear. Outside it was full sunset. They crossed the plaza with its tables and booths now empty of merchants, retracing some of the steps Kirk and Scotty had taken minutes earlier. However, instead of heading for the broad thoroughfare, the Obarat led them another way into the narrowest street they'd seen yet. As they entered the cool deep shadowed space between the buildings, the captain could see that the passage eventually ended in a cul-de-sac. About halfway there, one of the Obarat turned to Scotty. Where'd you say you were from again? We didn't say, but we're from Torrel. Never been there myself. Nice place? Oh, the nicest. The man had no chance to inquire further, because one of his comrades stopped and knocked sharply on a door. It opened. A pair of silvery eyes caught the light flickering as they glanced from one caller to the next. That's all right, they're friends. The sentinel grunted, turned to others deeper within and barked something the captain couldn't quite make out, then he gestured for them to come inside. They entered, moving slowly because it was difficult to see. Even more so after the door closed behind the last of them. Reaching out instinctively, Kirk felt a wall and followed it. They went on that way for a while. Then a small flare of blue light erupted off to their right. A moment later, a second flare ignited on their left. Even before his eyes adjusted to the illumination, the captain could see that they were at the threshold of a large room, and it was full of Obarat, perhaps a dozen of them. One of his escorts stepped forward and indicated the humans with the gesture. A couple of visitors from Torl come to confer with our leaders. One of the men in the room eyed them. Interesting. I'm from Torl, and I've never seen them before in my life. Suddenly, Scotty took a crushing blow to the back of his head. As the engineer crumpled, Kirk whirled, expecting more of the same. He barely eluded a meaty fist that would have laid him out alongside Scotty. Then gripping his attacker's wrist with both hands, he flung the man over his shoulder. Screening with pain, the Obarat hurtled into two of his comrades. At the same time, Kirk went for Scotty, aiming to scoop him up and make for the exit. Unfortunately, it didn't work out that way. He barely lifted Scotty off the ground before something hit him hard outside of the head. His last thought before he lost consciousness was that all McCoy's harm would have been for nothing. Farquark glared at McCoy from the other side of the doctor's desk. They did what? McCoy scowled. They went back to the precinct. By themselves? What in blazes were they thinking? Probably that they'd be able to end this conflict sooner with some input from the Obarat. They just went to meet with the Obarat just like that? No, not just like that. They took some precautions. Like some minor facial surgery to make them look like Malloryans. Ambassador looked at him, amazed. You performed surgery on them? Damn it, it was the only way to give them a shot at finding Menicki and Omaloss. I figured... So it was your idea? Yes, it was my blasted idea. They needed to get close to the missing ministers. This was a way to do that. But they were supposed to have been backed by now. Something's happened to them. I can feel it in my bones. And what would you have me do about it? Tell the council? That's exactly right. The council may be the only hope they've got now. Farquark looked at him as if he were crazy. I meant that as a joke. If the council sent a squad into the precinct right now, it might destroy what little chance for peace still exists. And if they don't, the captain and Scotty may be goners. We can't risk the lives of thousands, maybe millions to save a couple of foolhardy star-fleet adventurers. Those foolhardy adventurers saved your bacon not so long ago. How dare you write them off like that? I wasn't the one who told them to go back to the precinct. I wasn't the one who suggested they risked their lives. Oh, that stung. Even more so because McCoy knew that the ambassador was right. Alright, dammit, you win. We won't go to the council. We'll just keep our fingers crossed and hope that Jim and Scotty come out of this alive. Jim, you call your captain by his first name? Is there anything wrong with that? You know, ambassador, there's more to life and diplomacy than protocol. For the first time since they met, McCoy had the feeling that Farquar was listening to him, really listening to him. Then the old stiffness came back into the man's spine and he tugged down on his tunic. I'm going to beam down alone. If the ministers ask, I'll say that the captain and his people were required to, uh, address some technical problem. Fine. Tell them whatever you want. But doctor didn't give a damn what excuse the ambassador gave the council. He was too preoccupied with the fate of his friends. Halfway to the door, Farquar stopped and turned back. Dr. McCoy, I just want you to know that I'm concerned about them as well. Even if I don't show it. Phones glanced at him, more than a little surprised. Thanks. Mm, you're welcome. Then he turned again and exited the doctor's office. Under Spock's painstaking guidance, the disruptors Blue Bean cut a large chunk of fullyated rock out of the hillside. Finally, the chunk of rock fell free. Now came the part that required something else. Spock would have to separate the various laminate leaves of which the rock was constructed. Nealing, he sighted the disruptor along the fault line of the top layer. Then depressed the firing pad again. The Bean sliced the leaves apart, starting with the left hand edge and working its way to the right. A few seconds later, the top laminate was free. The Vulcan stepped back to judge his handiwork. By that time, the children had begun to gather around for a closer look. Pfeffer looked up at Spock. Can we touch it? Is it hot? You may indeed touch it. You may even lift it up. The boy's eyes lit up. Taking the edge of the laminate in his hands, he pulled at it experimentally. It moved easily. Careful, it is brittle. Ms. Medford, would you help Mr. Pfeffer? Eagerly, Medford picked up the other end of the leaf. Together, she and the red-haired boy carried it down to the strip of level ground below. Can I help carry the next one? I see no reason why not. Again, the Vulcan applied with the disruptor bean. A moment later, Juan and Garcia were carrying another leaf down the hill. Only one more laminate was required, with great care Spock went to work again, and this cut was the cleanest of all. Allowing the beam to lapse, he placed the disruptor back in his sample pouch. And done too soon. The sun was dropping quickly in the west. Soon it would be too dark to use the weapon without drawing attention to themselves. David looked up at him. Everyone else was at the bottom of the hill. Wanna hand? Please. Together they lifted the sheet of rock and brought it down to where the others were waiting for them. As the children watched, still hardly believing one could take apart a rock as if it were a sandwich, they set the laminate down near the others. The Vulcan scanned the terrain to make sure there were no Klingons approaching. Then he turned his attention to the pit. It was a man's height in diameter and twice as deep. Excavated only minutes earlier by the force of the borrowed disruptor. Spock took the Klingon weapon out again and cut a slot in the hole. What's that for? The idea, Mr. Garcia, is to take one of these leaves we've carried here and place the bottom edge of it in the slot. Then to lean the other edge up against the side of the pit. The second leaf will rest on the first at a more or less perpendicular angle. And the third will rest on the second. Ooh, like a house of cards. Yes, we will cover the topmost sheet with loose dirt and packet. With a little care, it will look like part of the path. Oh, I get it. When someone steps on it, he falls in. That is correct. The brittle top sheet of rock will give way followed by the one below it and the one below that until our passerby finds himself at the bottom of the hole. Now we must hurry. It is necessary to cover this hole while we still have the light. Captain, wake up! Even before he threw off the last heavy tatters of his stupor, Kirk recognized the voice as Scotty's. As he opened his eyes, he had already begun to put together the features that went with the voice, the round face, the brown eyes full of intelligence and good cheer. He wasn't prepared for the deep-set silver orbs that peered at him out of a leathery visage. If he'd been able to, he would have jumped to his feet. Unfortunately, that wasn't an option. Not with the thick, coarse ropes binding his hands and feet. Sir, are you all right? For a minute, I thought they'd brained ya. The captain managed to smile. No, Scotty. I've still got my wits or most of them anyway. They've taken our communicators, sir. Kirk nodded. Their captors had been thorough. He turned from Scotty to survey their surroundings. They were in a small chamber with a single window. A door was set into the far wall. Kirk was certain it was locked and well guarded. Not that escape was their top priority. They'd come here to establish a dialogue with the Oberat. And that was the first time I was able to get to the ship. And that was what they were going to do. Three Oberat entered the room. Two of them armed with phasers. They're awake. Get them on their feet. The phaser bearers did as they were told. Each of them took an arm and hauled a prisoner up off the floor. Kirk offered no resistance. Damned Mantile spies. Who sent you? And for what purpose? Before we get into all that, I should tell you we're not what we seem. We're aliens. Members of the Federation diplomatic team assigned here. This is all the product of prosthetics and subdermal dies. Underneath we're human. And I suppose there's a way to prove what you say. You could open my shirt. The disguise only covers our faces and hands. Do as he says, Zobbit. The one called Zobbit tucked his phaser into his belt behind him so that the prisoner couldn't grab it and began unfastening the front of Kirk's tunic. After a moment he gasped. Oh, they really are the off-worlders. Yes, and we didn't come here to spy on you. We came to find the Oberat ministers, Manicki and Omalas. We wanted to hear their side of the story. Sorry to disappoint you, but Manicki and Omalas are not here. And even if they were, they would not waste time speaking with you. There's no possibility of reconciliation with the Mantile. They are too obsessed with their damn kubaya. Perhaps we should let Manicki and Omalas make that decision. After all. Enough. I do not need an off-worlder to tell me what is best for my people. There was something about the way he said it that gave Kirk pause. Suddenly he realized why. You're one of the ministers, aren't you? Yes, I am Manicki. So you see, what I say, I do not believe your intervention will accomplish anything. I know where have I speak. You've nave and tried it. If you'd only come back to the negotiation table, you'd see. See what? That our sacred places are meaningless? Less important than a herd of dirty beasts? All right then. Stay here and do what you have to. But give us a better idea of what your needs are so we can try to formulate a solution. The minister shook his head. He looked incredulous. Do you truly believe we will let you go after you've seen our hiding place? The captain's mouth went dry. This was definitely not a positive development. That wouldn't be very intelligent, Minister. You may have taken our communicators, but my people know we're in the precinct. If we're gone too long, they'll tell traffic. We do not fear traffic. Manicki turned to his fellow Oberot. Dispose of them. His comrades raised their phasers, and Kirk had no doubt about the level of destruction the weapons were set for. Excuse me. But I would like to try a different approach. A hunched and elderly figure came through the doorway. Release them, Manicki. You are too trusting, Omalos. Omalos. Kirk eyed the older man in a new light. Maybe you are not trusting enough, Manicki. This off-worlder offers a way to settle our dispute without further bloodshed. Is that not worth taking a few chances? I say it again. Release them. The younger man thought about it. His captives' lives hanging in the balance. Finally, he reached a decision, if a reluctant one. Do as Omalos says. Omalos led them to a windowless room. As Kirk and Scotty watched, he crossed to the Chester drawers that stood against the wall. You say you wish to understand the Oberot? Opening one of the drawers, Omalos extracted three ancient-looking leather-bound books. With unmistakable reverence, he placed them on the table. All you need to know of us, you will find in these. Kirk reached out and touched the nearest of the tomes. As he'd guessed, the leather was oily to the touch. Obviously well cared for. Sitting down, the minister drew one of the books to him and opened it to the first delicate yellow page. Tiltting his head, he indicated his wish that the humans followed suit. Carefully, they did just that. And so began their education in the ways of the Oberot. Vellid seethed with anger. Say that again, Krug. The first officer seems to have vanished, Captain. Also those with him. Only Dyrat and Rogue are left, and they've been unable to find the children. How difficult can it be to find a pack of human brats? If you wish, I will take a second squad and investigate. No, stay here, Krug, until I return you are in charge of the mission. Until you return Excellency? Yes, I'm going out there myself to finish the job that Gidra started. You may find yourself first officer of the Kadunra sooner than any of us expected, Krug. I'm pleased to serve you in whatever capacity you deem appropriate. I'll bet you are. Now, round up some men for me and good ones. Choral, Engath, Norg, Zorok, and the Niknash, Grail. We've already wasted more than a day on this foolishness. McCoy was in sickbay lost in thought when he sensed someone else's presence. Whirling, he saw two Malorians standing behind him. Then he realized that they weren't Malorians at all. Jim, Scotty, in the Flash Doctor, they have not exactly how wrong. I was starting to wonder what happened to you two. At one point, in fact, I even wondered out loud to the Ambassador. The captain looked at him and frowned. At least McCoy thought it was a frown. It was hard to tell with Kirk's prosthesis getting in the way. Sorry, Jim, I was worried. It's all right, Bones, I understand. Now, if you're not too busy, could you get this thing off my face? Actually, it was Mr. Scott who had his prosthesis applied first. In all fairness, his should be the first to come off. While he was waiting, Kirk activated an intercom unit. How's it going up there, Mr. Zulu? The helmsmen had been sitting in for the captain up on the bridge. Couldn't be better, sir. Welcome back. Thank you, Lieutenant. How's my fireblossom doing? Fine, sir. Why? Can't you smell it from there? Haha, carry on, Lieutenant. By then, the doctor had excise the bulk of the prosthesis from Scotty's face. The engineer's skin was still black and his eyes were still silver, but at least his features had been restored. Oh, but it feels good to get that off. So, did you two get what you went down there for? Hard to say, Doctor. We managed to speak with Omaloss and Menakee. We even got a chance to read the Oberot's holy scriptures, but we're still not within sniffing distance of... Damn it, Bones. That's it. Blaze is Jim. I'm trying to conduct surgery here. What the devil are you shouting about? I've got the solution, Doctor. The answer to the Malurian's problem. And wait till you hear what it is. He could get used to being in charge, Krug told himself. He placed his feet up on the desk in front of him. Yes, he could get used to it very easily. Second officer, I have news from the Cotton Rock from the security chief. There's been an accident. What? Leaping to his feet, Krug growled and snapped his communicator off his belt. Security, what's going on up there? We've had an explosion in the cargo hold next to the warp engines. Any idea who did it? None. The damage is extensive. We're limited to impulse power. I want those engines ready again in a matter of hours and see to it that the culprits found. The captain won't want to hear that there's a saboteur in our ranks. Aye, sir. Krug put away his communicator and glared at the messenger. Well, what are you waiting for? Get back to what you were doing. The man didn't need to be told twice. Alone again, Krug pounded his fist on the desk in front of him. A saboteur. It was an outrage. And if security didn't find him soon, suddenly Krug didn't feel quite so comfortable being in charge. There was a feeling of hostility in the Hall of Government that had not been there before. Krug couldn't help but notice it as he, McCoy and Scotty followed Farquar into the chamber. Traffic and the other Mantile ministers stood grim-faced around their conference table. A monitor stood before one of the windows, dark for now, but soon to be illuminated with the images of only one of the people. The windows are dark for now, but soon to be illuminated with the images of Omaloss and Menicki. Stopping before traffic, Farquar put his fingers to his temples. We are grateful for your indulgence, First Minister. If you can stop the bloodshed, Ambassador, it is we who will be grateful. Though I must remind you, our dedication to the Kubaya has not diminished. Nor will we yield on the subject of their rights and well-being. We understand, First Minister. Then let us proceed. At a sign from traffic, a guard moved to activate the monitor. A moment later, the screen came alive. It showed Omaloss and Menicki in a bare, windowless room, one that gave no hint of where they might be. After all, there was no guarantee that the Federation's plan would work, and if it didn't, the Oberite didn't want to give away their whereabouts. Omaloss looked at Trafford. Good day, First Minister. And to you, colleague. Perhaps it will be a good day for all of us. All eyes fell on Kirk, taking a deep breath. He launched into the speech he'd prepared the night before. As you all know, I had a chance to visit with the Oberite in their sacred precinct. Minister Omaloss was kind enough to show us his people's holy book. That was McCoy's cue to hand the Captain an electronic slate. Kirk glanced at it. He wanted to get the quote exactly right. Correct me if I'm wrong, Minister Omaloss. But your objection to the Kubaya is based on the following passage. No beast of forest or field shall set itself down on the sacred soil. That is indeed the basis for our protest, Captain. Alright then. Now some time ago we suggested to the council that a predator, a get-trex, for instance, might be domesticated and left in the vicinity of your sacred ground. That would be an outrage. They get tricks and are even less welcome than the Kubaya. So we were informed, Minister Amanake. We then amended our suggestion, replacing an actual predator with a scent of water. That too was deemed inappropriate. As was a chemical compound that simulates such a scent. We even offered to supply a compound that copies the scent of a beast never seen on this planet, and that was rejected as well. As it should have been, Captain, none of those strategies would satisfy our scriptures. Fine. No beast smells. But what about the scent of a flower? Again, Kirk consulted the electronic slate. You shall adorn the sacred stones with all manner of flowers and growing things. Isn't that what your scripture says, Minister Omalas? So it is. We have never objected to flowers in the sacred precinct. But I do not think a plant will accomplish your purpose, Captain. I have never heard of one that would keep a Kubaya away with its scent. In fact, the beasts are notoriously attractive to most strong smelling flowers. That's correct. As long as you limit the discussion to Malurian flowers. Kirk whipped out his communicator. Mr. Kyle, you can send down the specimen now. It took only a second or two for a flowering plant with long dark blue petals to materialize at the captain's feet. Kirk held it out to the monitor. A cling on fire, Blossom Gentlemen. It emits a scent that the Kubaya are sure to find unpleasant. I don't smell a thing. Well, of course not. You're not a Kubaya. And that's the beauty of it. No Malurian will be bothered by the scent, but it'll keep the beasts at a considerable distance. Oma lost regard at the doctor. You know this for a fact. I've had an opportunity to gather plenty of sensor data on the Kubaya, so I know how their all-factory systems work. Seems they're a lot like a cling on beast called a porous, and a porous avoid fire blossoms like the plague. Do you think we will call off our revolt on your word alone? There is a way to prove I know what I'm talking about. I've already begun synthesizing compounds that copy the fire blossom scent. We can place them in the Kubaya's path, and if they turn away, we know we've got something. And if not, believe me, there won't be any, if not. For us to believe we must be present, doctor. Suit yourself. Menicki turned to his fellow Oberot. You mean come out of hiding? That is impossible. There is another saying in the scriptures, Menicki, for the overly cautious everything is impossible.
description: In episode 032, "Faces Of Fire," James T. Kirk faces a tense situation as representatives from different species gather to discuss cultural values and animal management. The conversation becomes heated when someone suggests keeping animals away from their sacred precincts temporarily, leading to unforeseen consequences that threaten the security of those present. Despite initial attempts by the ambassador to prevent such an action, Kirk decides it's time to address the underlying issues rather than reprimanding them for their misstep.

Star Date, 3998.6 The abandoned observation post loomed up out of the grey hills like a swamp spider. A single window showed a faint orange light. As Kira approached it, the mystery surrounding this meeting forced him to anticipate a trap. After all, he had no lack of enemies. And yet the Klingon hadn't dared ignore the invitation. If he was right about the identity of the one who called him here, it would have been more dangerous not to come. Fifty meters from the outermost structure, he saw Klingons among the shadows. Holding his arms up, he showed them he was weaponless. They swarmed around him, disruptors at the ready. At the entrance, Kira found more warriors. Opening the door, they ushered him through. The place was as stark inside as out. Just a few pieces of furniture were caught in the light of a single standing fixture. But Kira's gaze didn't linger on the furnishings. It was drawn to the massive form by the window that turned and fixed him with its gaze. Leave us. The warriors filed out, the last one closing the door behind him. With a casual sweep of his arm, the figure indicated a chair. Sit. Kira did as he was told. The figure took another chair one closer to the light. As he left the shadows, his features were thrown into stark relief. Even though Kira had suspected his host's identity all along, the sight of the man still came as a shock to him. Carefully told himself, it was important not to show weakness. You know who I am? I do. You're kopronic, emperor of the Klingons. Very good. No doubt you're wondering why I called you here. Well, I won't keep you in suspense. What have you heard about the loyal opposition, Kira, or to use their proper name, the Gevashray. Ah, so that is what this was about, Kira thought. The rise of the Gevashray, the clans of the homeworld's southern continent. I have heard they are gaining ground in the council emperor, increasing their influence. That's a polite way of putting it. The Gevashray are sending my counselors to early retirements by whatever means seems most expedient, not excluding murder. The emperors lip curled in noble disdain. The mighty Gomordog, my people and yours, are sinking like a herd of purists in a salt marsh. I will not see my people trampled, Kira, and I most definitely will not give up my throne without a fight. Emperor Collis, the most famous Gomordog of all, warned us of times like these when our room would be challenged. You are familiar with his teachings? I am. Do you recall his advice? In his ramen ah? Darkness will fall, enemies will circle us round and round, but we will not yield, we will wear faces of fire. And what does this mean to you? This phrase faces of fire. According to the commentaries, it has two meanings. One pertains to the quality of determination. If one's determination is great enough, he can surmount any obstacle. And the second meaning, a reference to one's skill at deception, a warning to remain circumspect in all one's dealings, particularly with one's enemies. Very good. I've chosen well, it seems. Kira's heart was beating hard. How may I serve you, Emperor? How, indeed. As Captain James T. Kirk entered sick bay, he saw Chief Medical Officer Leonard McCoy standing in front of one of the new bio monitors. The doctor was shaking his head. What's on your mind, Jim? A new assignment. We're picking up an ambassador at Starbase 12 and taking him to the Alpha Maluria system. Huh? An ambassador, eh? I hope that wasn't meant to cheer me up. He comes highly recommended bones. From what I understand, he worked wonders at Gamma Falluvia. Oh, sure. They're all highly recommended. Then they get under your skin like MacLavian Mountain Ants. Doctor, you can't judge the man before he sets foot on the ship. He could be the exception to the rule. He could be helpful. Oh, right, Jim. And Mugatu have wings. Bones. He'll be be beaming up in 45 minutes. I'd like you to be in the briefing room when he arrives. But I want your word. You'll be civil. No pokes at the diplomatic corps. No comments about their success rate. I'm not making any promises, Jim. It isn't a proposal, Doctor. It's an order. By the time McCoy reached the briefing room, Spock was already seated at the table that dominated the place. A moment later, the briefing room doors opened and the captain ushered in their guest. Gentlemen, this is Ambassador Marlon Farquhar. He's been assigned by the Federation to mediate a civil conflict on Alpha Maluria VI. Ambassador, First Officer Spock, and Chief Medical Officer Leonard McCoy. Farquhar was nearly a head taller than the captain, though he stooped a little at the shoulders. His age was difficult to ascertain, somewhere between 40 and 60. The man's blue eyes darted like frightened fish. Farquhar turned to the captain. I suppose we should get started now. Absolutely. Gesturing for the ambassador to take an empty chair, the captain pulled out another one for himself. Before we go any further, gentlemen, I should tell you there's been a change of plans. We received new orders just a few minutes ago. I'm afraid I don't understand, captain. We're still going to Alpha Maluria, Ambassador, but we're going to make a stop on the way. Reaching for the monitor in the middle of the table, he pressed a button and the screen displayed a star map. Beta Kinsandia, on the fringe of Federation Space, and home to a research colony headed by Dr. Eve Budrow. Budrow? The Terraforma? The same. What's more, Bones, you'll get a chance to meet him. You'll be conducting routine medical check-ups for the entire colony. Spock, you'll be busy as well, assimilating data for a report on the Terraforma's scientific progress. All in all, it needn't be a long stopover. We can still be at Alpha Maluria inside of two weeks. This is an outrage, captain. A political cauldron like Alpha Maluria 6 must take precedence over everything, especially a routine visit to an insignificant research colony. Ambassador, I'm merely following orders just as you are. There's a difference. I may not diverge from my orders. As captain of this ship, you have the latitude to rearrange your itinerary. Starfleet has no idea of what the Malorians are like, or of the lengths to which they will go and their devotion to their religious ideals. It's up to you, Captain, to turn your ship around and hold on a second, Ambassador. You may think routine colony visits are a waste of time, but I don't. I can't tell you how many lives have been saved by such visits. Maybe that's hard to accept when you're focused on one planet and one set of circumstances, but it's the code I've got to live by. I see. And that's your final word? My final word. The Ambassador got up and walked out. As the doors closed behind him, the captain looked at his officers. Well, gentlemen, that could have gone better. The boy named David shaded his eyes from the frosty glare of Beta Canzandia and considered the fissure at his feet. It had to be a good six feet from one side to the other, and it was so deep the bottom was lost in shadow. What's the matter, Marcus? Don't think you can handle it? The challenge came from Timmy Rodden, a boy with a broad nose and wide set pale green eyes. Rodden was the oldest of them. He'd had more practice in finding a person's soft spots. David looked at the four other children who surrounded him. Pfeffer, with his red hair and his freckled cheeks, won with her black ponytail and her delicate features. Medford, with her chocolate brown eyes and complexion to match, and Garcia, whose narrow face looked painfully sharp between his wind-bitten jug handle ears. Well, Marcus, are you going to jump it? Or is it too dangerous for you? Oh, it was too dangerous. David knew that, but he couldn't look like a coward. What are you waiting for? This is stupid. We ought to go home before someone gets hurt. Rodden dismissed Medford with a roll of his eyes. You're a girl. What do you know? I know we're not supposed to be here. The only way anybody's going to know is if one of us says something and nobody's going to do that. So, what's the big deal? David took another look at the fissure. Maybe Medford was right. Maybe this was stupid. I've changed my mind. I'm not going to do it. Rodden's expression changed from one of challenge to one of derision. Not doing it. What are you, chicken? David could feel his cheeks turning as red as peppers. He shrugged, bunching the shoulders of his park up around his ears. That's all right. I guess it's hard when you don't have a father. The taunt hit David like a blow to the chest. Suddenly, he no longer had a choice in the matter. He had to prove he was a man. He had to prove he had become one without a father. On second thought, I guess I'll do it after all. Taking a last look into the fissure, David backed away a good 20 paces. He knew he needed a running star to him. He'd fall short. For a fleeting moment, he had a vision of the eerie cold darkness flying up at him and the sound of crunching bones and the sickening knowledge that the bones being crunched were his. Then the vision passed and David crouched. He could hear his heartbeat big and loud in his chest. Lowering his head, he began to sprint. After a second or two, he raised his head and saw the fissure looming before him like the open jaws of some beast too big to comprehend. Putting a little extra into his last two strides, he leaped high and far. And his heels hit the ground and he was past the fissure, skidding and rolling and finally coming to a breathless halt on all fours. He stayed that way for a moment, trying to make his heart stop beating so fast. When he got up, Royden was laughing. What's so funny? You are. I can't believe you did it. What a skeez it. David flinched at the word. Royden had told him it was a Klingon curse and it meant the lowest, most disgusting thing in the whole galaxy. You dared me. So, you do everything everybody dares you do? Royden laughed again and finally understanding Pfeffer joined him. Garcia ventured a chuckle as well. But David wasn't buying it. The older boy had changed the rules in the middle of the game. No way. You dared me and I did it. Now you do it. Or are you too scared? Royden reddened. For a second or two, he seemed ready to accept the challenge. He shrugged it off. First you jump back the other way. Why, so you can make fun of me again? Suit yourself. Come on everybody. Let's get back. Chicken here can take the long way around. Yeah, the long way around. David wanted to punch Pfeffer's face in. If the crack in the ground hadn't separated them, he might have. As Royden started back in the direction of the colony, the other four children fell into line behind him. Over come with anger. David's lower lips started to tremble. He thought about telling their parents what had happened here, but he couldn't. He wasn't a snitch. Suddenly, maybe half a dozen meters from the crevice. Medford did an about-face and started back. Royden stopped for a moment to stare at her. Like puppets, the others stopped and stared too. Forget something, Medford? Nope. I'm just going to wait for Marcus. He might be a while. That's okay. I'm not in a hurry. The older boy shrugged and left, and the others followed. When Royden and his companions had dropped out of sight, Medford looked at David. They had surprised she was smiling. You know, Royden wasn't wrong. You should never have jumped this crack, no matter who dared you. I know it was stupid. You don't really have to wait for me. Well, I sure as heck don't want to go back with them. David scanned the length of the fissure. To the east, the crack seemed to get narrower as it went. In another hundred meters or so, it wouldn't take much of an effort to get across. What shouldn't be any problem to jump back down there? Nothing doing. We'll walk, Marcus. You on that side and me on this. And we'll keep walking till we find the end of this thing. Carad's estate was in the fog-shrouded foothills outside the Imperial City. It was a typical, comor dawg residence constructed of dark, polished woods that reflected the dying light. Carad was greeted at the door by Carad's house mistress, an elderly woman named Wistor, who led him into the reception hall. You will wait here. Lord Carad will be with you presently. After a moment or two, the old war horse appeared, filling a doorway with his bulk. But for the graying of his whiskers, Carad seemed no older than when he'd been master of security for the second fleet. Welcome. It's been a long time, Carad. Too long, friend of my father. Carad took Carad by the arm and led him into the water garden. I opened a keg of ale only yesterday, Carad. I think you will enjoy it. Your garden is quite pleasing, Carad. I've had a great deal of time to cultivate it since my retirement. He showed Carad to a table made of flat stones and poured the ale. Carad was right. The stuff attacked the taste buds like a warrior. Now Carad tell me what I can do for you. At one time, friend of my father, you were privy to a great deal of information. Some say even more than the emperor himself. It was my duty to keep a breast of things. What sort of information were you looking for? Carad told him, though he was careful to avoid any mention of Copronic. Oh, the Gevashray. I too have been concerned about them. I'm glad to see I'm not alone. I need a way to penetrate their defenses, to disrupt their movement. Well then. There's a Gevashray named Graeil of the Niknash clan. Some time ago, he laid a trap for his own kinsmen, a play for power. The trap was never sprung, nor was it discovered. However, one who knows of this indiscretion might find Graeil willing to do his bidding. After all, if others in the Niknash clan got wind of his treachery. Hmm, Graeil of the Niknash. I'll remember the name. And what about you, friend of my father? Is there nothing I can offer in return for your assistance? The downfall of the Gevashray will be reward enough. Kirk sat back in McCoy's overstuffed, easy chair and relaxed. Sometimes he felt more at ease in the doctor's quarters than in his own. Here, where there was no temptation to work, he could escape. And these days, he needed an escape. He'd had about all he could take from Ambassador Marlon Farquar. Suddenly, McCoy appeared with a bottle of sorry and brandy. I knew I had this stashed away somewhere. Sorry to keep you waiting. No trouble at all bones. The doctor headed for his bar selected two glasses from a hidden compartment and plunked them down on the counter in front of him. The brandy caught the light as he poured. Here you go, Jim, two old friends. I'll drink to that. And while we're on the subject, I came across an interesting name on the beta-Kensandia roster. Mentioned it earlier, in fact, except Farquar has been keeping you so busy with his infernal litany about Alpha Malluria. I didn't have a chance. Lord saved me from little minds. Bones, the name? An old friend you said? Hmm? Oh, right. Sorry. It's Carol Marcus. Kirk grinned. Carol Marcus, he thought. On beta-Kensandia III. Small galaxy wasn't it? What's that grin about, Jim? Thinking of fanning the embers? Kirk smiled at the metaphor, leaning against the bulkhead he thought about it. After all, it had been a long time for both of them. People could change a great deal in all that time. Or they could change not at all. David tried not to show how tired he was as he tripped into the dome. Hearing him come in, his mother smiled. There you are. The tone of her voice sent a bolt of fear up his spine. Had she found out where he'd been? Had someone squealed? What do you mean, Mom? She pointed to the chronometer that hung from a gently curving wall. It's nearly dinner time. You're cutting it pretty close these days, young man. So what did you do after school today? Anything interesting? Uh, you know, hung out with the other kids. How's that Timmy, Roydon treating you? Oh fine, Mom. Just fine. Pulling down on the zipper of his parka, he took it off and hung it up. You're sure, Lamb? Come on, Mom. Give a guy a break. You said you wouldn't call me that anymore. All right, I'll give a guy a break. But first, the guy's got to wash up for dinner. Dad started to do that, grateful that she hadn't pressed him any harder about the day's activities, or for that matter about Timmy Roydon. Then something weird happened. He stopped halfway to the washroom as if he couldn't make himself move any further. Hey, Mom. Shut up, he told himself. What are you doing? You had it made in the shade. Yes, David? Mom, do I need a father? Why do you ask? I need a friend. Why couldn't he have kept his mouth shut? I heard somebody talking about it today. That's all, you know, saying that fathers were important things to have. I knew something was wrong. The kids were giving you a hard time, weren't they? Sort of. She came to him, put her arms around him. I know it's not easy being different, David, but you've got to make the best of it. You've got to remember that you're as good as you think you are. Not as good as they think you are. He didn't want to be different. He wanted a father, if not his real one, then someone else. You understand what I'm saying, right? Father or no father, you're still the best kid around. Sure, Mom, I understand. But more than he'd ever wanted anything in his life, David Marcus yearned for a man he could look up to. The The Dark and Unpopulated, the bridge of the Kadenra seemed more spotan than ever as Velod entered and took his place in the captain's chair. On the forward view screen, there was an image of Alal Pecuk, the world where he and his crew had laid over. Stretching his long arms and legs, the Klingon could still feel the dull pain of his half-heeled wounds, acquired in the course of a bloody brawl in one of Alal Pecuk's drinking houses. He grinned at the memory of it. But now it was time to pursue more weighty matters. Bringing his fist down on one of the metal studs on his armrest, he altered the picture on the screen. Instead of the cloud-strewn horizon of Alal Pecuk, it showed the familiar countenance of Dumeric, his maternal uncle, and the newest member of the High Council. Ah, right on time, nephew. Dumeric's smile was thin-lipped, his gaze intense, a nearby torch cast a red glow over one side of his craggy face. I am your servant, Uncle. Good. You have heard of the world called Farana? In the nineteenth ring, the sector disputed by the Federation? The same. The humans and their allies call it Beta-Kanzandia III. According to our spies, they've established a research colony there. Incredible, as it may sound, they're developing a technology to remake barren planets in the world of the human homeworld. Copronic is curious about this technology. He wants it seized while it's still within easy reach of the Empire. Originally, he wished to entrust its acquisition to one of his kinsmen. I argued, however, that no one's better suited to the task than my nephew. It was true, valid thought. He was not only a better captain than the Emperor's kin, he was more familiar with the sector in question. And of course, if his mission were successful, it could only enhance the standing of the Gevashray in the Great Hall. The advised nephew, the Kamur Dog will not exactly cheer you on. After all, as much as your triumph will strengthen our position in the Empire, a failure would knock us down twice as far. That is why I have chosen you. Suppose you will prevail, no matter what the Federation and the Kamur Dog throw against you. Vellid acknowledged the praise with a nod of his shaggy head. He didn't like being a pawn in Dumeric's council games, but these were political times. Besides, it was a chance to rub Copronic's Gamur Dog nose in the dirt. Vellid pounded his chest with his closed fist. It is my duty to serve my Emperor's pleasure. See to it that you don't please him too much, nephew. Cal? She looked up at the sound of her name and saw Dr. Budro standing at the entrance to the garden enclosure. Everything alright? It's the fire blossoms. Oh, the Klingon specimens? I thought they were doing so well. They're doing fine. The problem is they're turning out to be lousy neighbors. Everything around them is dying. Oh, lousy neighbors. Like the Klingons themselves? Just remember, adaptability and oxygen production are of no use if the damn things won't coexist with our Terran plants when the time comes. Our ultimate goal, remember, is to terraform the fire blossom or whatever else we come up with is just a natural means of speeding up the process. And that's my speech for the day. So, what brings you out here so early in the morning? I thought you hated the cold. Oh, I do. But I just got some news and I wanted to tell you before someone else does. We're expecting visitors. Medical exams? Is it time for those already? Which ship is it anyway? It's the Enterprise. Oh, is there a problem? Of course not. It's just that I know the captain of that ship, Jim Kirk. Well, really? I've never heard you mention him. I knew him a long time ago. A very long time ago. The The room was circular, made of dark red vein stone with a great sand glass dome of a ceiling. As Kiruk entered, he saw an Orion dancer only half concealed by the scarlet veils it swirled around her. The dancers' movements were supple, suggestive as she undulated to the rhythm of a hidden drummer. On the devans that lined the walls, scores of Klingons glared at her but lost in their eyes. There were shouts of approval and hoots of laughter. Kiruk smiled. It had been some time since he'd visited this pleasure compound. He was almost tempted to relive the coarser pleasures of his youth. My lord? Kiruk turned to the Mitochrosian who had appeared before him. Her pale slender figure draped in long blue robes, her hair of purplish silver. It seemed she was in charge here. How may I serve you, Lord? I am meeting someone. He may already be here. The Mitochrosian smelled faintly of fire blossoms. Yes, a young man. You writhed just a few moments ago and said you would be able to do that. Follow me. She let Kiruk down one of the corridors that projected from the main chamber. There were booths on either side of the walkway. The Mitochrosian stopped at one and knocked on an upright. The blood-red curtain that concealed the booth was drawn aside. A pair of eyes took them in, a head knotted, shaking a mane of long braided hair. The braids marked the man as a gevish ray. He had a goblet in front of him. Leave us. The Mitochrosian nodded and vanished discreetly. Sliding into the booth, Kiruk noted the yellow eyes that gloured at him. You are Kiruk. Yes. And you are grail of the knicknash. You called me here for a reason? What is it? His bravado sounded hollow and no wonder. Kiruk had ended his message with but two words. I know. They had been enough to put grail on notice. I have worked for you to do and make no mistake. You will do it. Or I will put you in a position of wise man fears to be hunted by his own clan. What could possibly make my clan want to hunt me? You already know or you wouldn't have risked your reputation responding to a comor dog's invitation. But I understand. You wish to test the weight of my threat. Somewhat more than a year ago, you arranged the assassination of your older cousin, a man named Teshrin. If he died, you would have succeeded him as head of the knicknash. You lie. Kiruk showed his teeth, though he kept his voice down. Don't interrupt me again, get a stray or you'll regret it. Scowling grail subdued his anger, his eyes smoldered, but he kept silent. As I was saying, you arranged your cousin's murder. He was traveling to Zlarat for a secret meeting of clan elders. Hired men to kill him. However, your assassins began embroiled in a fight along the way, one which proved fatal to all but one of them. So Teshrin was never accosted at all, and he never knew about your plan to replace him. The muscles in grail's jaw worked. How did you discover this? The assassin who survived, of course. All right. How much do you want? How much? As in money? It was only then that grail began to comprehend what this was really about. If it's not money, then what did you come here for? Why, your cooperation, of course. Only a small thing, grail of the neatnash, compared to what you dared before. The younger man had turned a shade paler as Kiruk spoke. All right. What is it you want me to do? Kiruk told him, taking a deep breath, the younger man nodded. It will be done. Right, sir. Pushing the curtain aside, Kiruk left the booth and walked away down the corridor. As he passed other booths, each with its own mystery, its own secrets, he pondered the seeds he had planted. Would grail do as he'd been instructed? Kiruk believed he would. After all, the man's life depended on it. When Kiruk materialized in the colony's main dome, alongside Spock and McCoy, there were two people waiting to greet them. One was Eve Budrow, whose gray goatee and deep-set eyes he recognized from the Enterprise's files. The other was Carol Marcus. It was all that Captain could do to focus on the colony administrator first. I'm Jim Kiruk, pleased to meet you, Doctor. And I, you, Captain. I understand you and Doctor Marcus have met before. That's true. We have. Good to see you again, Captain. Likewise. Carol was exactly as Kiruk remembered her. And what did she think of him? He looked into her eyes, but he couldn't tell. Before he knew what bones was shaking hands with the colony administrator. Let her be coy. I'll be conducting the medical exams. And this is my science officer, Mr. Spock. He'll be reporting on your progress here. Budrow evidently knew enough not to try to shake the Vulcan's hand. Mr. Spock? He inclined his head slightly. The Vulcan responded in kind. I am looking forward to our working together, Doctor. I have followed your work closely over the years. Budrow smiled. In that case, I'm certain we'll get along quite well indeed. Actually, I would like to get started as soon as possible. Ooh, of course, Mr. Spock. I'll accompany you myself. Budrow turned back to McCoy. We have cleared out an unused storage dome for your use, Doctor. I trust it will be suitable as an examination area, just as long as it's clean. It is that. Carol, why don't you show the Doctor to his accommodations? And then after they're taken care of, perhaps Captain Kiruk would like to explore the Boulonia. Boulonia, Doctor? As in the park on the outskirts of Paris. I miss the city of my birth, Captain. Of course, our Boulonia is rather humble compared to the original. But on this world, sick or and as forest of all. In that case, I look forward to it. Then it's settled. And after all your endeavors are underway, we'll meet for dinner. Agreed? We'll be honored, Doctor. Good morning. Budrow's laboratory was housed in the colony's central dome. As Spock followed the doctor inside, he took in the entire facility at a glance. Along the curve of the wall, there was a continuous rank of some thirty workstations, about two-thirds of which were currently occupied. The Vulcan directed his attention toward a cylindrical structure suspended halfway between floor and ceiling by a lattice of long, narrow tubes. Is this the G7 unit? Budrow considered the cylinder and smiled. Yes, it is. Together they approached the unit and inspected it more closely. About a meter long, with a diameter about half its length, G7 reflected their visages. In its smooth, shiny surface. You have been pleased with the results? I have missed your spot, yes. But then I am principally concerned with the reproduction rates. If you ask Dr. Marcus about our results, she'll tell you that the specimen's oxygen production is not what it might be. However, if our specimens are reproducing like mad, what difference does it make if each produces a little less oxygen than it should? In the end, we'll still get what we want, an atmosphere breathable by most species in the Federation. What about the beam itself? I understood you were working on increasing its effective range. Quite quite, Mr. Spock. In fact, we've made great strides in that regard. When we began, we were only able to affect specimens within a tenth of a kilometer radius. Now we have a grouping as distant as three kilometers. I'll show you how we did it, if you like. I would like that very much. The Valed was in his quarters, sharpening his favorite knife when he heard the rap on his door. Rising, he took the knife into the space between his belt and the small of his back. Enter. The heavy door to his quarters slid aside, revealing the lean form of his gunnery officer. The young man took two steps into the cabin and the door closed behind him. No threat here, Valed told himself. Removing the knife from its hiding place, he flipped it, point first into the throwing board on his wall. What is it? There is to be an assassination, Excellency. First Officer Gidris is the intended victim. And the assassin? The second officer? You have evidence? Or has the second officer confided in you? No, my lord. No evidence. But it is obvious, nonetheless. I see. Under normal circumstances, the captain would have allowed the assassination to proceed. After all, it was part of the process by which Klingons remained strong. However, these were not normal circumstances. Valed wished his crew to be as stable as possible when they arrived at Farana. You've made your report, gunnery officer. You may leave. As you wish, Excellency. The Klingons turned and exited the cabin. Valed watched him go and not without a certain amount of satisfaction. After all, his current security officer was getting old, Gunnery Officer Grahle would make a fine replacement. The Buddha was right, Captain Kirk observed. This world's Boir de Boulogne was somewhat humble compared to the original. Actually, it was a cluster of perhaps 50 gold and needle conifers, none of which was more than a dozen feet tall. As Captain Kirk walked among them with Carol at his side, the foliage was barely thick enough to block out his view of the white colony domes. You say these are hybrids? Half Aldebaran Aerostoy, half Marikite, Castlana. We planted four of them to start out. None were more than a foot high. As you can see, they responded well to the G7 beam, at least in terms of growth. But they don't produce as much oxygen as I'd like, and oxygen production is the key. I believe there's a glitch in the G7 technology, which is altering the plant's DNA somehow, though I'm nowhere near proving it. For a moment, silence hung in the frosty air. It seemed more personal than any of the talk that had passed between them, more lush with feeling. Anyway, we're about to test a different kind of vegetation. Ever see a Klingon fire blossom? Where did you get hold of a Klingon plant? Not just one, a number of them. Remember the Klingon ship found a few months ago by the Potemkin? Or should I say the wreckage of a ship? Sure, the one whose impulse engines blew? It had every admiral in the fleet buzzing for weeks, but a couple of compartments survived intact. One was the captain's quarters, and his hobby must have been cultivating fire blossoms. I see. How convenient. A funny thing is that the fire blossom is outperforming everything else in the garden. And I didn't have to splice any genes to make it. It occurs as naturally as you are I. Right now, it can't seem to get along with its neighbors, but I'm hoping we can find neighbors it alike. Kirk looked around at the tops of the golden conifers, emblazoned against the crisp blue sky. Let's say you find a way to tame your fire blossom, or you come up with a hybrid that does what you want, or you isolate the glitch in the G7 beam and correct it. Then what? Provided we can continue to make the Federation believe in us, we find another planet, one of those marginal places where there's barely enough warmth and oxygen to support life, and we make it into a garden. Beyond the branches, the sun was sinking, turning the colony domes pink with its dying light. Carol's cheeks were turning ruddy with cold. He remembered that about her, how red her face used to get, and how beautiful it made her eyes look by contrast. You sound happy, Doctor. I am. The happiest I've been in a long time. I mean, I complained about oxygen production and such, but we're making real strides here. I can see the day when we'll be able to terraform any planet at all, and I've got a chance to be a part of it. And what about you, Jim? Are you happy? Most of the time? It isn't all glory and adventure, of course. People die, people who depend on you to keep them safe and secure, and too often you have to compromise your ideals for the sake of policy. But you get a chance to see something new every day, maybe something no one has ever seen before, and every now and then you strike a blow for something you believe in. Would you trade it for something else? The Captain hesitated, understanding the significance of the question. After all, he'd heard it before, but the answer hadn't changed. No, I wouldn't. Or rather, I couldn't. It might not have been what he wanted to tell her or what she wanted to hear, but it was the truth. No less today than eleven years ago. I had a feeling you'd say that. Instantly Kirk regretted making the conversation personal. He should have left things as they were. He should have left the past. Be the past. I'm sorry, Carol. I didn't mean for this to happen. It's all right, Jim. If you hadn't brought it up, I probably would have done it myself. I guess neither of us has changed very much. We're still two people going in different directions, though we may wish it were otherwise. Honey, our life gives you just what you really want.
description: The podcast episode "030 - Star Trek Audiobook Faces of Fire 1 of 4" features an audio adaptation of Michael Jan Friedman's "Star Trek: Faces of Fire." It begins with the opening scenes of a Klingon observation post, where Kira encounters a figure who turns out to be Emperor Collis of the Gomordog Empire. Embracing fierce determination, Emperor Collis calls for unity in the face of threats from the Gevashray, an opposition faction seeking power over his kingdom and the homeworld's southern continent.
