transcript: It had been a lonely night and a restless one. Kirk sat up in bed and surveyed his quarters. They had that uncertain, not quite real look, the predictable result of not enough sleep. It was his own fault. If he hadn't resurrected the past the night before, if he hadn't stirred it up. Kirk tapped the stud that activated his personal monitor, and Lieutenant Duhura's image came up on the screen. Sorry to bother you so early, sir, but it's Mr. Spock. He's calling from the Colonies Communication Center. Put in through, Lieutenant. Duhura's salt-review was replaced by the Vulcan's poker-faced calm. Good morning, Captain. Is it Spock? It's difficult to tell. The Vulcan arched in highbrow. I wish to make a request, sir. Dr. Marcus believes that there is a flaw in the G7 unit's operation, one which is leading to decreased oxygen production. I would like an opportunity to find the flaw, and perhaps to correct it. The Enterprise can pick me up on its return trip through the sector. The captain thought about it. You think you can make a different Spock? I think it is possible. Alright then, you've got my blessing. Thank you, Captain. Spock out. An instant later, the screen went blank, and the captain was alone again with his thoughts. McCoy was washing his hands at the sink when the doors whispered open, and his next patient walked into the room. Glancing over his shoulder, he was surprised to find a boy looking back at him. Howdy. The boy had curly blond hair and soft brown eyes. Are you the doctor? Yep. My name's Leonard. What's yours? David. Though he couldn't have been more than ten or eleven, the boy didn't exhibit any of the childish qualities the Phefer and Garcia kids had. There was no weariness in him, just a lot of healthy curiosity. Are you here all alone, David? Usually kids see me with their parents. I was supposed to meet my mom here, but I was a little early, so... So you decided to come see what this medical exam business is all about? Well, there's not much to see, just this, really. It's called a tricorder. Dr. Marcus, this is a surprise. Can I help you? The woman was a little out of breath, as if she'd been rushing. Frowning, she glanced at the boy. Hi, David. The boy looked up at her. Hi, Mom. McCoy cursed himself for a fool. Now that he saw them together, there was no mistaking their relationship. They had the same coloring, the same proud cheekbones and graceful bearing. I see my son beat me here, doctor. I hope he hasn't been any trouble. None at all. So Carol Marcus had a son. Clearly, the captain had a surprise in store. Well then, as long as you're both here, why don't we get started? I'll just call up the colony roster and... Hmm... That's strange. David's not listed. David, would you excuse us a moment? I have something to discuss with Dr. McCoy. The boy shot her the kind of withering look children give their parents when they're excluded from conversations, but he didn't argue. As the doors closed behind him, Carol turned to look at the doctor. There was an almost defiant cast to her features. Dr. McCoy, David is on the colony personnel roster. He's just not on the one you have. And the reason he doesn't appear there is because Dr. Boudreau was doing me a favor. I don't get it. What were you trying to do? Keep me from examining him? No, I'm not that foolish. You see, a long time ago, I knew Jim Kirk quite well. I'm old at Captain's mentioned you once or twice. He spoke well of you too, but that doesn't explain. He doesn't know. I have a child, Dr. McCoy, and I want it to stay that way. Bones began to ask why, but before he could get the words out, all the pieces fell into place. Kirk's relationship with Carol Marcus had ended about ten years ago, and there was something about the boy's eyes that seemed rather familiar now that he thought about it. The boy is Jim's son. Yes, but as I'm sure you know, your captain has no inkling David exists. I wish they'd sent some other ship, but they sent the Enterprise. And once you knew they were coming, you convinced Dr. Boudreau to give me a personal computer separate from the colony's main processor. And to delete David's name from my roster so Jim wouldn't suspect anything. But why go to all this trouble? Why don't you want Jim to know? That's none of your business. Dr. Marcus, it's his flesh and blood. He has a right. No, it's up to me what he knows and what he doesn't. Blaze's put yourself in Jim's place. Imagine someone keeping that kind of thing from you. I don't have to justify my actions, Dr. McCoy, not to anybody. I'll go get David. As she turned away from him, he called after her. Damn it, woman. At least give it some thought. So McCoy wanted you to reconsider. Uh-huh. But my decision was the same as before. David is my business. Jim's not to know about him. Carol and Dr. Boudreau were in the lab dome, working at adjacent terminals, speaking in low tones so no one else could hear. Why, don't you approve? Now that I've met the man, I can't help but feel for him. He strikes me as a kind I wouldn't mind having for a friend. You wouldn't be disappointed either. He's a very good friend. That's part of the problem, isn't it? If you hated him, you wouldn't feel so guilty. It was part of the problem, all right? The night before when they were walking in the woods, she'd almost weakened. She'd almost said she wanted him back, no matter what. That doesn't change anything. I've still got to look after my son's best interest, and that means sticking to my guns. Did I hear something about guns? In a long, dizzy moment, Carol whirled and saw Jim standing behind her. She felt her cheeks grow hot. Kirk smiled. Something wrong? No, you just startled me, that's all. Sorry, I came to say goodbye. Dr. McCoy tells me he's finished his checkups. And as you know, Spock's staying on a while, so there's no excuse for us to linger. Well then, I guess we'll see you on your way back. For just a fraction of a second, his smile faltered. And she knew that you wouldn't see him on the way back. The Enterprise would come for Spock, but the Captain wouldn't be him down. It was good seeing you again, Carol. He turned to Boudreau. Doctor? Thank you for your help, Captain. And then he was leaving. But Carol felt an ache in her throat before she knew what she was doing. She called out, Jim, wait! He stopped, turned and looked at her expectantly. Why had she cried out? She asked herself. What had she meant to tell him? Suddenly something occurred to her, something that seemed fitting somehow, and more importantly, something that would postpone his leaving by a minute or two. Come on, where are we going? You'll see. Holding onto his arm, she guided him to their destination at the far end of the garden. What are these? The Klingon flowers I was telling you about, the fire blossoms. She got down on her knees and dug one out with her bare hands, brushing aside a strand of hair that had gotten in her eyes. Carol handed it to him. Water it occasionally, outside of that, you don't have to worry. They're tough to kill. A parting gift? Something like that? You know, it was always hard to say goodbye to you. You always managed. Jim nodded. He was a genius. One more time. He took out his communicator. One to beam up. In the next couple of instances, he began to shimmer and then to fade. Finally, he was gone altogether. Valed turned to see his second officer enter the weapons room. Big shoulder and strapping, his large, protuberant eyes sought the captains. Is something a miss, sir? Valed made a sweeping gesture with his left hand. A moment later, the room was empty of all personnel except the two of them. Valed himself and second officer Krug. I understand you plan to assassinate first officer Gidris. Krug stiffened, but he didn't ask how Valed knew. That is correct. Normally, I do not interfere, but this time I will stand in your way. Is it permitted to ask why? Valed told him what he wanted to know. By the time he was done, Krug knew almost as much about their mission as Valed himself did. So you see, second officer, there is no room for personal ambition on this ship, at least until we complete our mission. I have one request, my lord, that you refrain from informing Gidris of my intention to kill him. It would, after all, make my job that much more difficult when the time comes. Done. I will keep your intention a secret. Krug granted. When I am first officer, Excellency, I will make you wonder how you ever tolerated a porous like Gidris. See that you do, Krug. See that you do. Once again, there were four of them in the briefing room. However, with Spock back at Beta Kensendia, Scotty had been brought in to round out the diplomatic team. As you know, we will be arriving shortly at Alpha Maloria 6, the side of a certain amount of civil unrest. As you also know, Ambassador Farquhar has been assigned the task of settling this unrest. Ambassador? The situation is not simply one of unrest, Captain. It borders on civil war. You see, the planet has two main religious groups, the Mantile and the Oberot. In recent months they have come into conflict over a herd of docile beasts in the region. Beasts which, according to the Mantile, carry the souls of long dead holy men. As a result, they insist on allowing the beasts access to anywhere and everywhere, including an ancient city which happens to contain the holy places of the Oberot. Ah, and the Oberot take offense of the idea. Very astute, Mr. Scott. Ironically, the Mantile sacred beasts were dying off some years ago until the Federation provided them with certain medicines. Thanks to us, the animals are now more plentiful than ever. Which is why they have begun to broaden the path of their seasonal migrations to include the Oberot sacred precinct. When the first beasts passed through some days ago, there were heated protests. But the main part of the herd is still on its way, and when it passes through. He let his words hang in the air. They had the desired effect, eliciting visions of religion-inspired chaos and carnage. Let me get this straight. These people are ready to go to war over whether or not animals have the right to walk in the streets? To put it succinctly, Doctor. Yes. And as Federation citizens, the Mallorians have the right to ask for a sis- Kirk reached out to the monitor in the center of the table. Yes, Ahura. There's a response to our hail, sir. On screen, please, Lieutenant. A moment later, the monitors showed the image of the Mallorian's highest official, First Minister, Trafford. Like all Mallorians, his skin was as black as ebony with web-like patterns around the mouth and chin area. The silvery pale eyes looked out at the captain from cavernous sockets. Greetings. I'm James T. Kirk, captain of the Enterprise. I believe you were expecting us, First Minister. Blessed be your every incarnation, Captain. We haven't even been expecting you. The skin around Trafford's mouth seemed to be twitching. Kirk was no expert on Mallorian facial expressions, but he couldn't escape the feeling that something was amiss. Oh, no. We're too late. Ignoring Farquhar, though that was no easy task under the circumstances, the captain concentrated on Trafford. You seem discomfited, First Minister. Am I to understand that the discord has intensified? It has, indeed. If you beam down to our government hall, I will elaborate. As you wish, Kirk out. As Trafford's image faded, the captain noticed Farquhar glaring at him. I told you there was no time to waste, Captain. Now the conflict has escalated, and who knows to what extent? As annoying as the man's manner was, he wasn't entirely wrong. The conflict had escalated, and a good deal more quickly than Starfleet had anticipated. Ambassador, I suggest we wait to see exactly what has transpired among the Mallorians before we formulate any opinions. Sure. Let's wait, as if waiting wasn't what got us into this mess. The Mallorian Hall of Government was a hexagonal room with six long windows. As Kirk and his party materialized, they saw Trafford and three other robed figures waiting for them. The ambassador took the initiative, touching his index and middle finger to his temples. First Minister? Trafford returned the gesture. You must be Ambassador Farquhar. I am, and these are my colleagues from Starfleet, Captain Kirk, whom you've met, Dr. McCoy and Lieutenant Commander Scott. They have been dispatched to assist me in my mission. McCoy leaned close to Kirk. Compare his assistance. In a nutshell, Bones. Yes. Trafford looked to his own colleagues. Allow me to introduce my fellow ministers, Antrath, Ilemon and Daser. Regrettably, Menicki and Omelos have absented themselves from these premises indefinitely. They have resigned as ministers. The ambassador nodded. Glancing at the captain, he expanded on Trafford's explanation. Menicki and Omelos were Oberot. I see. And the reason for their departure, First Minister? Finding no satisfaction in this chamber. Menicki and Omelos took their arguments to the streets. There was violence. They went into hiding. We suspect they are still here in the Mother City, but it is only a suspicion. That is unfortunate. It will complicate matters considerably. Indeed. You know, it might not be a bad idea for us to visit the Oberot's holy places. And I'd like to get a look at your sacred places. There is no need for that, Captain. I'd like to see the holy places as well, but I don't think the First Minister would want us to disturb the sacred beasts. On the contrary, Ambassador, if you are to help us, you must get a feeling for the things we hold dear. I will make arrangements for you to see both. The holy places of the Oberot and the Sacred Herd. Only a slight readiness in his cheeks betray the Ambassador's peak. He touched his fingers to his temples again. As you wish, First Minister. From the playground, the domed colony buildings in the distance looked like pearls half buried in the ochre-colored ground. And the lab-dome, David noted, looked like the biggest pearl of all. That's where Mr. Spock was bound to be, talking with Dr. Budro about the G7 unit, which was about all he'd done since he got here. His mother had made it clear he was supposed to avoid Mr. Spock as best he could, though she hadn't said why. Hey, Marcus. He turned at the sound of his name. Then was sitting on the top rung of the playground's white plastic monkey bars. Pfeffer and Juan were twisting themselves around a lower rung while Medford and Garcia tossed a football. Daydreaming again, Marcus. How come you're always a million miles away? David didn't answer. He just walked over to the white plastic swing set and sat down on one of the swings. My dad says daydreamers never get anywhere. He says they dream their whole lives away. Planting his feet and launching himself backward, David began to swing. Immediately the air felt even cooler against his face. And as he kicked higher and higher, he lost himself in the hard blue sky. He found it easier and easier to forget Royden and Pfeffer and their little cruelties. Hey, Marcus. It was Royden again, no doubt he'd seen another opportunity to call David a daydreamer. This time, though, Royden could shout himself purple. Hey, Marcus. Marcus. That was Pfeffer, joining in on the fun. Ignore it, David told himself. Don't give in. Marcus. It was Medford. David opened his eyes. The other children were clustered around the swing set. Their eyes drawn to the colony buildings. He looked that way also and saw a swarm of dark figures making its way from dome to dome. And they weren't colonists, not by a long shot. As David leaped from the swing and landed on the sandy ground, he saw a flash of light among the domes. Pfeffer moaned a single word. Calling ons. David took another look at the dark, scurrying figures and knew that Pfeffer was right. They were clings. The worst killers in the galaxy. Their parents, his mother, they were all in terrible danger. One began to cry. It got David's brain working again. Listen, everybody. They're going to come for us next. They're going to check the colony roster and realize we're missing and come after us. But we're just kids. No, we're humans. I don't know what they're doing here, but you can be sure they don't want witnesses. I say we go back into the hills. We'll be safe there. As always, all eyes fell on Roydon. He shook his head. You're talking like little kids. They'll find us no matter where we hide. And when they do, they'll torture us to death. To death? It was just like back at the Fisher. Roydon was too good at making the others think what he wanted them to think. He could make courage seem like stupidity and common sense seem like cowardice. I'm not going to just stand here and wait for them to find us. I'm going. Who's with me? Nobody's going with you, Marcus. They're staying here with me. Nobody moved. Not even Medford. David didn't want to leave his friends at the mercy of the Klingons, but he had no choice. Turning his back on them, he started up the hill. Before he'd gone half a dozen steps, however, he heard a terrible high-pitched scream from down among the colony buildings. Glancing back over his shoulders, he saw yet another flash. Suddenly, Medford started after him. He could see she had tears in her eyes, but she was coming along. Even more unexpectedly, Juan followed and Garcia as well. And finally, Pfeffer. That left Roydon standing all alone in the shadow of the monkey bars. The older boy glared at David and his companions. You're crazy. You're just going to make it worse for everybody. But his words seemed strangely flat and lifeless. David wasn't sure how, but Roydon's hold on them had been broken. Lane brains. Skisits. You're making a big mistake. Still amazed at the way things had turned out, David resumed his trek up the hillside. The others fell in behind him. Roydon's voice cracked like a whip in the chill air. You'll see I was right. You'll see. Carol saw it out of the corner of her eye. A flash of blue-white light outside her garden enclosure. But when she turned, there was nothing there. She was about to chalk it up to imagination when she saw a whole series of flashes, one right after the other. And then, as she sat back on her haunches and tried to figure out what was going on, a screen pierced the stillness. Her blood froze. Dropping the vegan fern she held in her hands, she scrambled for the entrance, and would have gone tearing out of the place altogether where it not for the sight that stopped her like a doranium wall. Clingons. A lot of them. Maybe as many as 20, swaggering about in their heavy, dark body armor. They were hurting the colonists out of the laboratory dome, waving their weapons as if they were only too eager to use them. Carol knew now what the flashes had been. Disruptor fire. Had they actually killed anyone? Her stomach clenched painfully at the thought. Suddenly she remembered. David. Where was he? In the hills, she thought, with the other children. Safe, at least for now. But they wouldn't be safe for long. Once the invaders accessed the computer's personnel files, they'd know that the children were missing. They were all on the colony roster, not the one that had gone up to the enterprise with David's name purposely left out, but the master list in the central computer. Her heart began to race. She did nothing else. She had to purge the children from the files. Counting to 200, she poked her head out of the enclosure again. There was no one around. Neither Clingons nor colonists. Praying no one spotted her, she made her way across the flat open space between the garden and the lab dome entrance. It seemed like an eternity before the lab door slid aside, revealing the interior of the lab. Keeping inside, she headed for the nearest workstation, unable to keep from noticing how many of the monitors had been smashed. At the G7 unit, it was gone. The lattice work of energy transfer tubes that dominated the center of the lab had a gap in it a meter long. No doubt the Clingons were dismantling it at this very moment, and in the process undoing all that Dr. Boudreau had accomplished. After all, there was only one G7 unit in the entire galaxy. If it were destroyed, it would take years to build another. Turning her attention to the terminal in front of her, Carol called up the colony personnel directory. Her fingers danced over the keyboard, deleting the names of the children one at a time. Finally, she was done. And not a moment too soon, because in the next instant, the door slid open and a grinning Clingon filled the aperture with his bulk. Carol clenched her teeth as he aimed his disruptor at her. For a long moment, she thought she was a goner. But her luck held. The Clingon didn't press the trigger. He just gestured for her to come outside. Thank God she thought. Suddenly, sharing the fate of her colleagues didn't seem so terrible compared to the alternative. Are you certain, Gidris? Quite certain, Captain Vellard. Mallet has only had a day to examine the human's research data. But it is already fairly obvious. The central unit, the device that accelerates plant growth, is missing. Then one of the colonists must be missing as well. Actually, Captain, we have one colonists too many. The captain of the cotton rod leaned forward, planting his elbows on the desk before him. The desk that had so recently belonged to one of the colonists. Too many? How is that possible? I can't say for sure, Excellency, but I suspect his age is a factor. He is twelve years old. Too young, perhaps, to be listed as an official member of the colony? Vellard thought about it, then shook his head. The Federation maintains lists of all its equipment components. Why not an individual, no matter how young he is? There must be another explanation. Bring me the boy. Maybe he can tell us himself. Damn, I've never seen such a herd. You can say that again, sir. A huge blue-green valley spread out the fourth. In the valley was a broad river sparkling in the bronze light of Alpha Malluria. And in the river, crowding it from bank to bank, stood the Cubaya. The beasts that stood at the center of this world's religious conflict. From Kirk's vantage point, they looked like walruses with short, muscular legs instead of flippers. Not a very attractive animal, but then it wasn't the beast's beauty that commended them to the mantile. Their guide looked back at them over his shoulder. Oh, do not worry about getting too close. They are used to seeing riders around. We have them patrolling for predators along the river, though the predators themselves are not the biggest danger. It is the wind which carries the predators scent. The Cubaya may look lethargic now, but if they should catch the smell of a get-trex, you will find them most active. If we did not provide protection for the herd, more Cubaya would die in stampedes than in the jaws of the get-trexin. Scotty turned to the captain. Big in your pardon, sir, but isn't that the solution to our problem? Kirk started to ask the engineer what he meant. Then he stopped himself. I see what you mean, Scotty. Ambassador, Mr. Scott here may have come up with an answer, a way to satisfy both the mantile and the oborat. And that is... Scotty told him. The ambassador nodded sagely. It just might work. I'll send word to the council to expect us. Your name? Timothy... Roydon. There are two Roydons listed in the personnel file. Excellency? Neither is called Timothy. How is it that you are not listed with the others, boy? Timothy Roydon, if that was truly his name, shook his head. I don't know. The truth, or I'll personally see to it that you suffer. The boys eyes grew red and wet as they looked up at the Klingon. His nose started to run. It was amazing how easily human children could be broken. Vell had heard it from the other captains who'd had dealings with Federation colonies, but until now he hadn't believed it. I told him to come back. Vell had leaned forward until his elbows rested on his knees and his face was mere inches from the humans. Who? You told who to come back? Marcus and the others. I told them, but they wouldn't listen. The one you call Marcus and these others, who are they? They're kids like me. And they took the G7 unit? Suddenly the boy looked confused. No, the unit's in the lab dome. Do you mean to tell me you don't know what happened to it? I don't know anything about the G7. I swear it. Please don't hurt me. Please. The captain was caught between anger and revulsion. Enough, Gidris. More than enough. Take him away. Obediently, Gidris dragged the boy out of his chair and flung him in the direction of the door. Timothy Royden stumbled, recovering only long enough to shoot Vell at a miserable frightened glance. Then Gidris shoved him out of the dome altogether. Vell had shook his head. If one of his sons had turned out like the human child, he would have died long ago and at his father's hands. Pushing his revulsion to one side, he asked himself what his next step should be. There was only one answer. Despite Timothy Royden's protestations, the other human children who had also failed to show up in the computer files apparently must have taken the G7 device. And if that were so, they had to be found. As before, traffic and his colleagues were waiting for the Federation people. But this time the first minister seemed more impatient. Matters have taken a turn for the worse, haven't they, first minister? You are perceptive, Captain. As the Kubaya approached the Mother City, the rioting is spreading to other cities across our world. We restore order in one place, only to find the Oberot have created chaos in two others. I'm sorry to hear that first minister, but we may have found a way to resolve your dispute. So I understand, Ambassador, please present your solution, but remember we will tolerate nothing that may displace the Kubaya against their wishes. Understood. We've heard that the Kubaya have a strong negative reaction to predator sense. In short, they run from them. If this is the case, why not domesticate one or two of these predators and leave them in the vicinity of the sacred monuments? The Kubaya will not be harmed, but rather encouraged to stay away. The ministers conferred in subdued tones. Then they regarded the ambassador again. It is unacceptable. The Oberot will reject the intrusion of the get-trexin in their sacred areas as strongly as they reject the Kubaya. One form of beast is like another to them. The ambassador's mouth was open. He closed it, then darted a side-long glance at Scotty as if to say, sorry, but it really wasn't a very good idea to begin with. But McCoy wasn't as willing as Farquhar to throw in the towel. Wait a minute. Let's think about this. If we can't use real animals, how about just their sense? We can extract them without causing the get-trexin any discomfort. Traffic held up his hand. That would be just as unacceptable to the Oberot. Any evidence of a get-trex even just its scent constitutes a desecration of their sacred ground. What then? How about a chemical compound? One which smells like the get-trexin, but is created in a laboratory. It would have the same effect in the Kubaya as the real thing but being artificial. It shouldn't put the Oberot's noses out of joint. Real our artificial doctor, it would smell like a get-trex and the Oberot would reject the idea. McCoy scowled. Alright, what if the compound emulates a beast this world has never heard of? Say a Terran Wolverine or an Aldebaran Kyrgyz. They probably have the same effect on the Kubaya. Traffic shook his head. I am afraid not. You must understand, Doctor. The Oberot are simply not a reasonable people. Seems to me there's an answer out there somewhere if we can only dig it out. First Minister, I apologize on behalf of all of us. Next time we won't waste your time with flimsy suggestions. Flimsy of all the- a look from the captain stopped the chief engineer. Ambassador, you need not worry about making demands on our time. We do not expect you to solve this problem on your own after all. Farquar placed his index and middle fingers against his temples. As you wish, first Minister. You see, Captain? Krug was standing in the human's garden enclosure. He watched Velad stroke the long dark petals of one of the fire blossoms. And where did the human say these came from? The wreck of the Ullud. The Ullud, under Captain Amag, an a-feet-com or dog-culturator of flowers. Do you understand what they were doing, Krug? They were removing the dying specimens from around the fire blossoms so they could plant these others in their place. These lesser organisms could not stand up to the presence of a Klingon life form. Just as the colonists cannot stand up to us. The Federation is so weak as to make even the comor dogs seem strong by comparison. Suddenly Gidris appeared in the entranceway. There were two others with him, Lutek and Oros. The first officer didn't seem pleased to see Velad and Krug together. You have something for me, Gidris? Indeed, Captain. Tarik's completed his sensor scan. It seems Timothy Rodden was not the only human the computer failed to mention. The sensors have detected five others huddled together in the hills north of this place. And sir, all of them are children. Then the Rodden, who helped with speaking the truth. These children must have the G7 unit or at least know where it is. Krug had a thought. Excellency, the humans have gone to great lengths to see that we do not gain access to this device. Perhaps this technology, what do they call it, terraforming, is not as benign as it seems. Gidris brow writhed with curiosity. What does that mean? What it means, Gidris, is that the G7 mechanism may be a weapon despite appearances to the contrary. And if that's so, we're fortunate it's only in the hands of younglings. If we can bring it back to the whole world, the possibilities are most intriguing. Velad turned to Gidris. Take a half dozen men, including Lutek and Oros out there and track down the missing children. When you find them, you will find the device. Gidris beat his fist against his body armor. I hear and obey Excellency. To Captain Kirk's eye, the sacred precinct of the Oberach looked as old as civilization itself. Two and three story buildings leaned together like drunken conspirators. Underfoot, the cobblestones were worn and cracked. It was the kind of place he might have liked to linger in if not for the deadly stairs and muttered curses that dogged his group's every step. Feeling a little unwanted? More than little bones. Then again we should have expected a few funny looks. They must wonder what we're up to. Especially since we've got a couple of armed man teal watching over us. Nothing like seeing the enemy parade and through your streets to make you feel a wee bit insecure. I don't see the point in commenting on it, gentlemen. The first minister made it clear he wouldn't allow us to tour the area without an escort and I, for one, am glad he insisted. Kirk glanced at their pair of man teal security guards and frowned. As they emerged from the street into a somewhat wider thoroughfare, he noticed a squirt. A square full of people a block away. It was the first open area they'd seen. What's that? The nearer of the guards shrugged. The market is where they all brought by their food and clothing. Can we see it? It's not advisable. In such a crowd, it would be nearly impossible to... Without thinking, the captain took hold of the ambassador and drove him into the ground behind a wooden push cart. A moment later, he was glad his reflexes had been so sharp. As he looked back, he saw a couple of Oberot youths spraying phaser fire. Their man teal guards returned the fire. One of them paid the price for it, taking a lethal hit in the center of his chest. The others stood his ground, however. Without flinching, he aimed, fired, and took down one of their assailants. The other Oberot started to back away, squeezing off a couple of glasses to cover his retreat. They didn't help. Cooley, the surviving man teal, skewered him from a bloody stain on the cobblestones. He still had his phaser in his hand, though he had the presence of mind not to make it obvious. Captain, are you all right, sir? Fine, Scotty. Let's see if we can keep it that way. Kirk to Enterprise. This is the Enterprise. Something wrong, Captain? The crowd was starting to pursue them. Affirmative, Sulu. Have Chief Kyle lock onto my coordinates and beam up five, including two Malurians, one dead and one alive. It was a pause on the other end. Captain, Kyle says there are great many Malurians within close proximity. It may take some time to isolate the ones who are with you. Tell Kyle to move at Lieutenant. We may not have that much time. Kirk out. The crowd behind them was growing. Out of the corner of his eye, the captain saw something thrown at him. He ducked. As it passed by, he saw what it was. A piece of ancient masonry. Another chunk came, whizzing its gaudy. Even able to avoid it entirely, he took a glancing blow off his shoulder. God help us, the captain thought. Before long, it'll be a blast of gauntlet. Yet another projectile fell among them. The ambassador clutched the side of his head. Blood trickled from between his fingers. And that was going to run. Kirk could see it in his face. Don't do it, ambassador. Don't even think about it. Thrusting his chin out, Farquhar struggled to do as he was told. But his lower lip was trembling, barely able to contain his outrage. They weren't going to last much longer. Suddenly, the Oberot in the intersection charged. Their leader headed for Kirk with a chunk of rock in his hand, prepared to bludgeon him with it. As the captain braced for the impact, nothing happened. And then he realized why that should be. He was no longer standing in a narrow street in the Oberot Sacred Precinct. He was on a platform in the Enterprise's transporter room.
description: The episode features Star Trek audiobook "Faces Of Fire" where Captain Kirk discovers a flaw in the G7 unit's operation and seeks assistance from Lieutenant Duhura on a return trip through the sector. McCoy meets with David, the son of Dr. Marcus, and learns that Carol, one of the character's patients, has a son named David who is not listed on any colony roster. They proceed to have an in-depth discussion about medical exams and establish a bond between them as parents/doctor-child relationships.

transcript: 6 hours later Spock had analyzed the information so many ways that even he was losing track of the permutations. The results were discouraging. As if to underscore his lack of success, the bridge door is whisked open and McCoy strolled over to the science council. Well, Spock, how much longer are you going to twiddle your thumbs before you bothered a locator Jim and the rest of the crew who disappeared in that window? Spock continued studying the data on the screen in front of him. I am not twiddling my thumbs, as you so picturesquely put it, Doctor. A race as ancient as this one probably did operate according to principles that we do not understand. This device appears to have been designed by creatures nearly as irrational as you. McCoy rolled his eyes toward the ceiling and started toward the door. Sorry I asked. Spock turned back to his computer and realized that the artifact's shields might randomly shift frequencies. While such protection methods were completely logical, a society which used them on their public transportation devices was not. He wondered if the aliens were protecting themselves from outside invaders or if their security precautions had been directed against their own people. Sulu swiveled his chair to face Spock. Mr. Spock, we think there are six alien creatures near the artifact, but half of them are within the areas of maximum sensor distortion. Another creature has gone to ground in an area of extremely broken terrain and we are having trouble pinpointing its location. Spock read the notations on the screen. The possible life form readings were scattered over an area with a 30 kilometer radius centered around the second artifact. Spock leaned back in his chair, his hand steepled in front of him. It could hardly be an accident that the Enterprise was missing six people and that their best estimate showed six aliens on the planet. Lieutenant Ohura notified Dr. Call that we will be transporting down to site N4 at first light in that area. Spock resumed the study of the site. Which of the aliens should he contact? Here's Sunset, Kirk's host drifted to sleep, exhausted by the day's exertions. Kirk became aware of random images drifting through his mind. Strange crab-like beings with translucent shells floated and tumbled past the rock's fire where he was sitting. The creatures called themselves the K'lith. At first he was content observed as they performed their aerial ballet for his benefit. It was only after many minutes in dream time that he perceived that the inky-black splotches on each dancer's carapace were tiny anti-gravity units. The devices stood out in stark contrast to the rainbow hues of the K'lith's shells. As he watched the colors flicker over their carapaces, he began to see patterns that repeated themselves over and over. The longer he watched, the more he became convinced that the K'lith were singing. The color patterns and the timing of the changes formed the basis of the K'lith language. In the language of movement and color, the history of the K'lith civilization unfolded around him. From the first proto-k'lith that emerged to conquer the land up to the mighty builders who had ruled the known universe. As the history of the K'lith civilization unfolded, the dance became more complicated and the dancers' colors became brighter. To maintain the unity of their civilization, cast rules, language, and specialized motor skills were permanently imprinted on the lower brains of the young when they reached a certain size. Shaped by that defining event, the unique elements of each K'lith personality emerged and were stored in the higher brain. Kirk realized that stepping into the artifact had transformed his body into that of a K'lith, the only intelligent race imaginable to the device's programmers. At the height of their civilization, the K'lith had lived on over a hundred worlds. Some planets had been similar to the K'lith-ton world, warm and lush, filled with abundant food animals and ripe for serving K'lith needs. Other planets had needed much work, exterminating indigenous life forms, reforming ecosystems, or altering climates. The dance became a flashing, swirling, twisting maelstrom recounting the glorious conquests of the K'lith people. Sorting through the flood of information, Kirk realized that he owed his survival as an individual to the K'lith's unique bicameral brain. His human memories and knowledge were stored, separate and isolated, in the higher brain, while the lower brain contained the knowledge for functioning in a kilik body and using kilik technology. Under the force of his excitement, his dreamscape fractured into a kaleidoscope of images that world and gyrated around him. In the morning, everything seemed clearer or sharply defined. Kirk let his mind swim through the remnants of his dreams, sifting and culling the chaotic images for the truths beneath them. If he couldn't master the linkage between the kilik brains and find a way to cross the mental barriers at will, he could control his host body. The separation of instinct and intellect suggested that Kirk's extended flight across Karata IV's grasslands was a response to something pre-programmed into his host's lower brain. That thought brought images of the kilik's justice system into Kirk's consciousness. With a start, Kirk realized that his host, the kilik to his body he presently inhabited, was fearful of punishment and apparently on the run, and he began to understand why this host had been selected for him. When he went through the window, the artifact could not find a template for a dominant male and had apparently settled on the closest available model, a convicted felon. It was an unsettling thought, but it at least explained his circumstances. His next step, Kirk decided, was to test his new insights by convincing his host to return to the transit frame. Getting water would be the first test of whether he could order the kilik's body to do his sailing. With the image of a refreshing drink of water firmly in mind, Kirk tried to move from his hiding hole. At first there was no response. Remembering what it felt like when his arm fell asleep, Kirk shuddered at the idea of having pins and needles in eight legs at the same time. He returned to his experiment at the previous afternoon, concentrating on bringing his pincers together and slowly lifting an appendage to eye level. This time, he got a response. Kirk threw himself into mastering his kilik body, imposing his will on nerves and muscles paralyzed by the long inactivity. After fifteen minutes he could still move only one set of pincers or bend one joint, and he was beginning to fear that he was trapped. He kept trying, knowing it was the only way he could escape and finally his perseverance was rewarded. Apparently, his muscles needed to reach a critical internal temperature before they would work. With relief, Kirk dragged his kilik body from beneath the slab of rock and struggled to stand. By the time he reached the mouth of the narrow canyon, Kirk felt reasonably confident of his ability to manage the kilik body. His stream was muddy and unappealing, but Kirk decided he didn't have much choice for available drinking water. Before he could act on the thought, his lower brain took over bending his knees until his jaws were resting below the water. The water was tepid and bitter from dissolved minerals, but his sediment filters removed most of the suspended grit and clay. He allowed his body to drink until it could hold no more water. Next, he needed to get back to the artifact. Kirk looked around, assessing the canyon for routes to the uplands above. Reluctantly, he started downstream away from his goal. Somewhere the canyon walls would flatten out, and he could climb up onto the surrounding hills. A sharp wind was blowing out of the east as the Enterprise's landing party materialized on a hill at site and fore. Signaling to a security guard to accompany him, Spock started downhill along a band of flattened grass. He had decided to contact the individual closest to the artifact to learn if he could communicate with the aliens. After that, he would attempt to contact the being who was hiding in the canyon lands to the northwest of the artifact in hopes that it was Kirk. Although the justification for this decision, that the captain would react differently than the rest of the crew, was weak, he had not found a better reason for choosing which alien to contact. One of the aliens was over the first hill, moving in slow, random zigzags that had kept it in the vicinity of the artifact. Spock and the guard with him approached the alien cautiously, giving it plenty of time to see them coming. At first it gave no indication that it saw them. Instead, it continued to amble along as though it were the only living thing on the planet. Fascinating. It appears to be looking past us as though we are not here. Ensign, cover me while I move in closer. The guard trained his phaser on the alien while Spock moved beside it. Even this failed to produce a response until he stepped directly into the creature's path. Then inexplicably it froze, its limbs locking beneath it. Spock to Enterprise. Lock onto the alien who is at these coordinates and beam it aboard. He stepped back from the alien and the transporter effect coalesced around it, dissolving the creature into golden sparkles. Spock waited for the ship to request additional instructions. Finally, the instrument chirped to life with Scott's voice. Mr. Spock, we have a weak problem with this beast that you had us transport up. Yet when preserved the moment the transporter released it, and it caught up Mr. Kyle Fair bad before he could stun it with our phasers. The critter didn't take too kindly to our phasers. It died. Mr. Scott, your phasers should have been on stun setting. The weapons were on stun setting, Mr. Spock. Unfortunately we failed to communicate what that meant to our guest. Spock knew that the stun setting should not have been lethal to any being the size of the one they had been to the Enterprise. Why was the alien dead? Mr. Sulu, status report about the other aliens. Of the remaining aliens on the planet, four are approximately where they have been all along. The alien that was hiding in the canyon lands is moving, but we don't know why. Continue monitoring the aliens. I shall continue my analysis of tricorder and sensor readings. Mr. Scott, beam me up. Three hours and countless dead ends later, Spock wondered what they had missed. The sensor logs contain more information than he needed, but he could not reduce the data to anything useful. The effort he had put into unraveling the secrets of the alien machinery implied that they had used extremely sophisticated security measures. Suddenly, Sulu interrupted his train of thought. Mr. Spock, look at this. The main view screen showed the wavering shape of a crab-like creature attempting to scale the 10-meter scarp at the top of a landslide. The crab-like body was not suited for climbing, yet the creature chose its hand holes with a caution that spoke of much practice. Spock wondered if it could be Captain Kirk. He remembered how many times the captain had asked him to go rock climbing. Watching the crab-like being attempt to scale a cliff that it was in no way equipped to climb, convince Spock that Kirk was trapped inside the body of that alien. Mr. Sulu, I will need a squad of security men in 15 minutes. We are beaming down to contact that alien at our earliest opportunity. Spock ordered his team to beam down out of sight of the creature. He was taking no chances. Even if Kirk was inside the creature's body, he would not expect the group from the Enterprise to greet him as he crawled the last centimeters over the lip of the canyon. By the time the landing party was assembled, the crab-like being had almost reached the top of the cliff. Spock found the first sight of the alien unsettling, like a dull toothache that did not seem to belong to any one tooth. Except for its size, the alien resembled a king crab with an outsized body perched on top of long, stout, segmented legs. The carapace was translucent, but blotched with purples and blues that shifted from moment to moment. The eyes were similar to human eyes, with central pupils surrounded by magenta irises, but they were mounted on stalks that allowed them to swivel independently. The creature pulled itself over the edge of the cliff and staggered to its feet. For a moment it just looked around. Its color shifting to a deeper, more uniform blue. It did not notice the Enterprise's landing party. It turned away from the humans and started uphill, moving at a deliberate pace. Spock extrapolated its heading. Unless he completely misjudged the alien's intentions, it was headed toward the artifact. Spock to Enterprise, 12 to beam up, with the first contingent returning to the planet immediately. We wished to materialize 100 meters uphill of the alien, in a location where he cannot miss us. Kirk dragged his kalik body over the top of the cliff. He gave himself a moment to collect his wits after the climb. The kalik lower brain, he sensed, was almost incapacitated from terror at what he had forced his body to do. The best thing for this internal warfare, Kirk decided, was to keep his body moving. He checked the area for signs that the enforcers had been there. After a moment's confusion, Kirk realized the kalik had originated that thought. His host was still convinced that his society's equivalent of the Gestapo was after him. After a few minutes, as his host's brain decided that no enforcers or any other kalik were in the area, it began to relax and to move his legs with greater coordination. When the bipedal creatures appeared directly before him, the kalik brain seized with terror. His limbs froze in mid-stride and momentum carried his body forward, pitching him ignominiously to the ground at Spock's feet. Mortified at this betrayal, Kirk struggled to reassert control over his body. It was like trying to unravel a pile of wet spaghetti. Kirk studied his tricorder readings with a familiar cocked eyebrow. Fascinating, this creature's physiology shows it to be totally unrelated to any known species in the galaxy. Kirk struggled to regain his feet but discovered that his kalik brain had retreated from the reality facing it. Struggling to remain calm, Kirk tried to tap into his kalik awareness to discover the cause of this sudden catatonia. At first, random images and chaotic swirls of colors surged through his mind. He realized that the bright abstract images filling his mind represented the kalik language. He relaxed and let the patterns flow through his mind, trying to follow the emotions that accompanied them. As the thoughts repeated themselves, Kirk deciphered the gist of how the crab-like aliens viewed the world. They considered themselves the pinnacle of life, the goal toward which the universe had been striving since its hatching. As they developed spaceflight and moved outward from their homeworld, their discoveries confirmed their belief in their superiority and uniqueness. Many beings that interfered with their expansion or contradicted their world view were thoroughly and ruthlessly exterminated. The kalik firmly came to believe that they were the only intelligent race that had ever evolved or would ever evolve and that belief became the foundation of their collective view of the universe. His host had been thrown into panic by the appearance of a lower life form that controlled technological devices. The kalik mindset was so fiercely xenophobic that Kirk could barely comprehend the intensity of its faith to deny that other intelligent beings could exist, even when staring one in the face, went beyond the most outrageous limits ever conjectured by anyone in the Federation. That knowledge, however, did nothing to solve Kirk's current problem. How could he catch Spock's attention? Kirk felt inspiration strike. Fighting to contain his growing sense of urgency, he concentrated on the thought that Spock was a kalik. Hot angry zigzags of red and black, powerful symbols of rejection and denial surged through his brain. The kalik lower brain would not yield its prejudices so quickly. Kirk's eyebrow raised even higher. Fascinating. The colors and patterns on the carapace are changing. With a rapidity that suggests this is a normal function of these creatures. He ran his tricorder over Kirk's shell with his sensors only a few millimeters above the surface. Kirk wondered if Spock could mine mill with him to read his thoughts, but he was not sure if the physiology of the kalik brain permitted telepathic transmission. He had to establish communications quickly. He concentrated on talking to Spock and explaining to him who and what the kalik were. A soothing pattern of interwoven blues and greens washed across his vision. But he knew that adapting the kalik language so he could contact Spock was impossible. The kalik system of projecting shapes and colors on their translucent shells and the deep seated imprinting of their language on their lower brains defeated his desire to write English letters on his shell for Spock to read. He needed a different approach. Suddenly he knew what to do. description: In this episode, Simon & Schuster Audio Works presents "Star Trek: Windows on a Lost World" by V. E. Mitchell performed by Walter Kaney. The episode details Captain James T. Kirk's arrival at the Karata system in the Deltzifer Cluster with a team of researchers from New Exquale on Paranine. Despite the low odds of finding artifacts, the crew embarks on a mission to explore the remote systems and gather valuable information about the Mistorian culture. The star system is gradually fading, making it difficult to detect signs of intelligent life, but Kirk's determination drives him forward. The survey will take 7.25 days, with Spock promising thorough coverage in the asteroid belt, which could provide crucial insights into this previously unexplored quadrant.

As best he could tell, the creature had four pairs of legs, which were coordinated by a complex series of rules that Kirk needed to learn so he could control the alien's body. He told himself not to force it, although everything in him screamed for immediate and decisive action. He concentrated on the body in which he was imprisoned. At first he had little luck. It was almost as if his mind had been encased in an alien android with none of the sensory inputs connected. That meant that the alien's mind probably did not recognize his presence either. With a measure of control established over his host size, Kirk tried to manipulate other parts of the alien's body. Wedged into the tiny space beneath the slab of rock, Kirk could not afford any energetic experiments, but he needed to know how this strange crab-like body operated. Concentrating on a mental image of his hand, Kirk visualized closing his thumb against his forefinger and lifting his arm until the hand was in front of his face. Nothing happened, and he realized that he was at his host's mercy until he learned how to connect with the alien's nervous system, how to control the strange crab-like body. Spock to Enterprise It took all of his Vulcan control to keep his voice pitched to an absolute flat tone. Around him he heard a ripple of dismay pass through the landing party. He could almost hear what the humans were thinking as clearly as if one of them had spoken the words aloud. The captain had disappeared into the artifact without anything registering on their tricorders, and Spock was acting as if Kirk had stepped out for a morning stroll. Enterprise has Captain Kirk come through the other side of the window yet? At last this communicator crackled to life. This is Sulu, Mr. Spock. We don't know if the captain and his party came through the artifact. At the precise moment when the captain entered the window, something zapped the probes we had positioned around the second artifact. description: In this episode titled "Windows on a Lost World," host Thaligas explores an artifact from the 1950s, which has been sealed for centuries and is now surrounded by spider work and broken slabs of basalt. As he ventures inside, he encounters strange fields around the surface, causing him to question whether the object's location will be safe once he attempts to explore it further. Thaligas eventually finds a window-like panel that appears to allow something or someone to pass through, which could make all the difference in accessing its secrets and potentially saving lives.

description: In this episode of "Lost Enterprise," Captain Johnson leads a Starfleet vessel in attempting to evacuate refugees from Bajor during a border conflict with Cardassian forces. Despite the Admiral's initial reluctance, they successfully save 40 people and proceed to Starbase 94. The captain is then tasked with setting up an asylum for the Bedorians who were previously left behind and ensures that the cargo bay space is not compromised by taking on a second job at a shipyard while still ensuring safety. The episode concludes with the crew's engagement in another mission, where they must navigate through a challenging environment and face off against Cardassian forces.

description: In this episode of "Lost Enterprise," a former captain from the USS Enterprise finds himself captured by Dominion forces after unknowingly joining their invasion force. Despite being warned about them earlier, he decides to fight back against what he believes is an unjust attack. The ship's warp engines fail, and they're forced into a desperate situation as they try to find a way off their planet before it's too late.

description: In this episode of Lost Enterprise, Captain Johnson embarks on an exploration mission far beyond Starfleet's expectations, unaware of the mysterious Admiral's Shadow who has been sent there to uncover their true purpose and ensure they don't interfere with ongoing operations. description: The podcast episode discusses the struggles faced by Spock during his journey through "Star Trek" audiobook series, particularly focusing on the characters of Tsai and Tsakkul, as well as their methods for mind control. The conversation touches upon the power dynamics between humans and the ancient High Masters, specifically highlighting the Romulans' need to gain control over powerful mental powers for war-loving races. Spock's inability to address this situation is further explored in the episode, leading to a discussion on how Tsai intends to guard against Tsakkul's telepathic powers and shield herself from their influence.

description: In episode 005 of Star Trek Audiobook "The Lost Years," James Duan narrates the story of a seasoned traveler who has been forced to reevaluate their path in life following the tragic loss of someone close. The setting is ancient Gaul, where they come upon a mystical phenomenon—the ghost rain—mirroring an event from two millennia ago and highlighting themes of impermanence and spiritual awakening.
