As Caridwen glanced up at him sharply, he replied, sorry, Dr. Lewellen, but almost the entire galaxy is familiar with the fact that the Enterprise's mission was recently completed. Surely, you know, Spock served as first officer of order. But she was unshaken. I admit that freely, but I didn't pick the card. Mr. Spock did. Caridwen looked down at the next card. Strangely, the next card doesn't reflect the first one at all. Far from it. The Five of Cups indicates you actually felt regret and betrayal after this successful journey. She glanced up at Spock. The Vulcan's expression revealed nothing but Kirk shifted uncomfortably in his chair. Caridwen turned the next two cards face up. Now, into the present. The Six of Cups means that you still feel nostalgic right now, wishing things would go back to the way they were. She dimpled her suddenly. This second one is rather interesting. The Queen of Cups. Interesting. You will meet a mysterious woman with a great depth of feeling. Spock lifted a brow. Would this be a tall, dark stranger? Maybe. It could be a Terran woman who will come along and read your tarot. Let's try the future, shall we? Then, her red hand flipped the last card over. As she did, McCoy felt her tense. An odd light came into her eyes. Fear, McCoy thought, though by the time she looked up at Spock again it had vanished. If this were Dwayne's idea of a joke, McCoy didn't find it very funny. Finally, Dwayne spoke. Her expression controlled. Bear in mind, the cards need not be interpreted, literally. They only reflect trends, which can always be changed by appropriate action. The future we see reflected here may not come to pass. Spark frowned. Then how shall I judge the accuracy of your prediction, Dr. Lewell? But Caridwen didn't answer. She seemed to mesmerize by the cards. The coy looked at the picture on the next card. A black robed and hooded figure carrying a sigh. He drew in his breath. If Caridwen were going to play a joke on Spark, this would not be consistent with her sense of humor. When she finally spoke, her tone was detached. All right. Death. The card is usually not interpreted, literally. It signifies a drastic change. One type of loss, Spark interrupted. I am somewhat familiar with the tarot archetypes. It could also mean physical death, could it not? Duan answered reluctantly. Yes. Or the death of someone close to you. This next one is the magician ill dignified. That is upside down. It means... Forgive me, Mr. Spark. I'm not quite sure what it means here. It has something to do with the Death card, a power. She didn't finish the thought, but stared down at the cards as if too stricken to make sense of them. After a moment, she spoke again. The last card is the Four of Swords. It indicates a need for reflection and solitude. The need to find a place where the mind can seek peace after the great loss. That's it. That's all there is. Carid Duan picked up her glass and took a very long drink. Kirk's skepticism had faded. He was frowning at Spock with concern, but the Vulcan seemed unruffled by everyone else's distress. It's interesting, Dr. Llewellyn. I shall wait to see whether your predictions come true. McCoy shifted in his chair. If things had been tense before, they were even worse now. Duan sat back, looking distracted and nursing her drink. Kirk stared at the cards and said nothing. Uncomfortable with the silence, McCoy tried to make light of the reading. Now that last prediction must have been for me, Spock. That's exactly what I need, solitude and reflection. You know of a nice quiet place where I could get away? This was the end of my lecture tonight, and I have some free time. Now, if there's a quiet, restable place in the galaxy, I figure it would have to be here on Vulcan. Spock pondered something before finally answering. There is such a place, Doctor. It is not one that many outworlders visit. The mountain retreat of Gaul. McCoy tilted his head confused. Well, I thought only monks or whatever you call them were allowed there. Not exclusively, Doctor. There is an area reserved for visitors. The Colenaru, the monks, as you call them, attend to the needs of the visitors. You would be free to relax, to meditate, to be alone. I would be honored if you would accompany me as my guest. Naturally, you would have your own quarters and complete privacy. To end interrupted suddenly her expression once more animated. Mr. Spock, would it be too rude of me to ask to go along? I would dearly love to interview some of the Colenaru. I was quite serious when I said that this could be my next research project. Spock hesitated. You are welcome to come, Doctor Llewellyn. But I can't promise that the Colenaru would agree to discuss their beliefs with you. In fact, I strongly doubt they will. But Dwayne was insistent. It's more than worth the risk. To McCoy's surprise, Spock did not extend the invitation to Kirk. After appointed silence, the Admiral rose. I enjoyed meeting you, Doctor Llewellyn. It's been very interesting. But I'm afraid I've got to be leaving. I've got a subtle catch. Oh, where are you headed, Jim? To the planet, Johnna. They needed some help negotiating a treaty. Take care, Bones. Spock? He gave each of them a quick nod before he turned and strode from the bar. Later, after Spock was gone, McCoy sat in the bar with Dwayne, who was unusually quiet. Cara, Dwayne, I've got this funny feeling that you really did believe what you were telling Spock. If I didn't know you better, I'd say these, uh, those, uh, those silly cards upset you. He expected a sharp, humorous retort. But Dwayne turned to him with a somber expression. Would you like to know something, Leonard? Right now, I wish I didn't believe in those silly cards. Something about the way she said it. Made a chill travel down McCoy's spine. Two days later, Cara, Dwayne, Spock, and McCoy arrived at Goll just after sunrise, before the desert had a chance to heat. Cara, Dwayne insisted on taking them in her scout. The vessel was small enough for intra-planet trips. Besides, the idea that she could leave again at any minute calmed her. Now it was midday, hot, and intensely bright. Inside her small, dark cell, Cara, Dwayne sat cross-legged on the stone floor and stared into a candle's flame. He had lied to Spock about the card. She'd known it meant death the moment she saw it, and that it was somehow tied to the upside-down image of the magician. It was a disturbing talent she had, one that she had never been able to talk about to anyone. It happened first with her grandparents when she was twelve. She'd known three weeks before they died, but at first she thought it was some sort of waking nightmare. She told no one. But after the two of them were killed, she still kept it to herself. After all, no one would have believed her. They would have called it hindsight coincidence. When she felt the same terror for her aunt, and then years later for her father, she kept silent. Each time she would tell herself she was wrong, until time proved her right. Michael had been the hardest. She'd had a crush on him less than a week when she felt compelled to read his card for him. He was very impressed at the accuracy with which she'd painted his past and present. She turned over the future, hoping to find herself there, and instead saw death. She told him the same thing she told Spock, and tried to believe it herself. But she hadn't just seen it. She'd felt it. The same cold heaviness, just as she had had for her grandparents, her aunt, her father. Stupidly, she had refused to believe it, and let herself fall in love with him. Three weeks later, the cards proved right, and now to feel the same ugly chill, to see death grinning up at her from a stranger's cards. And impulse, she'd volunteer to go with Spock and McCoy to Gall, suddenly afraid to leave them. Perhaps on Gall, she could learn what to do to keep the cards from coming true. Instinct told her that the solution lay with the colonaro. The heavy stone door to herself slid open a crack. McCoy's voice called. To when? She turned toward the door. Come in, Leonard. McCoy stepped inside, gasping with effort. Those heavy doors are sure going to give me a hernia. To when? Do you realize you're sitting in the middle of the floor staring at a candle? These naval watchers must be getting to you. Did you come here for a particular reason, Leonard, or just to irritate me? McCoy ran a hand over his perspiring forehead. I was bored. It's too hot to walk outside, but if you go down to the base of the mountain there, hot springs, we could go for a swim. Besides, it's cooler down there. Cara Dwayne stared back at the candle. Maybe later. What's with you, Dwayne? I thought you were all excited about talking to these colonaro guys. And all the months I've known you, I've never seen you like this. Do you really that worried about something happening to Spock? She shrugged without looking at him. Spock's a stranger. Why would I be concerned about him? But McCoy persisted. Dwayne, Spock and I are very good friends. I don't believe in those infernal cards of yours. But the way you're acting is beginning to make me nervous. Relenting, she faced him. I'm sorry, Leonard. I don't mean to scare you. If Spock doesn't want the future I read for him, all he has to do is act. McCoy frowned and puzzled. And who? What? I don't know. Spock must figure it out for himself. Dwayne, if it's not Spock that's bothering you, then what is it? Ever since you've read these cards, you've been acting strangely. She turned away again. It's personal. I need some time alone. That's all. It was a lie. More than anything else, she wanted to unburden herself to McCoy to have him reassure her that everything was all right. She knew his reassurances would all be lies. McCoy answered softly. All right, Dwayne. But that's what you really want. She didn't turn around to watch him go. In the white robes of a colonar student, Spock walked through the stone archway into the desert outside. His return to Gaul had brought a sense of familiarity and peace. He had made the correct decision. He felt, for the first time in his life, a Vulcan among Vulcans. There was even a measure of satisfaction in participating in the time honored custom of taking leave of a friend. Spock walked to the edge of the community garden where Seykhar knelt, harvesting vegetables for the evening meal. His sleeves were rolled above his elbows and the muscles of a thick forearm rippled as he lifted the vegetables from the sun-parch soil. The scene was an ancient one. For fifty thousand seasons, postulants had harvested food in the same manner in the same hostile stretch of sand. Seykhar, I have come to take my leave. Seykhar stopped and peered up at Spock. Spock's words were the first step in the ritual. They obliged Seykhar to answer and step forward from the garden. The briefest surrender of mental shields, a simple mind touch, a shared memory, and any obligation the two had ever had to each other would be negated. But Seykhar did not move. I am required to finish several tasks today, Spock. I do not have time now, but tonight I will take my leave of you. I would not have been more shocked, had Seykhar laughed aloud. For Seykhar, to refuse to complete the ritual at the moment of asking, was contrary to custom and courtesy. Even if Seykhar were busy, it did not excuse him from taking leave of a friend. Yet Seykhar's face was placid, as if he were totally unaware that he had just behaved in a most unvulcan mannered old friend. Come back two hours after Sunset Spock. Spock gathered his composure and answered, very well, Seykhar. He left puzzled. Seykhar went back to his gardening and did not look up again. Dad, blast it! McCoy sat tangled in a bedsheet and rubbed his right elbow, which had just made contact with the hard-stone floor. He had just fallen off the narrow ledge that doubled as his table and bed. His tiny cell was warm during the day, and McCoy assumed that since the desert cooled off at night, his room would too. That was before he learned how efficient the black rock was at holding the heat. The cooler had got outside, the hotter it got in McCoy's room. Some retreat this was turning out to be. If he could just make it through the night, he'd get Dwayne to take him back to the city in the morning. He laid back down on the warmth-generating stone and closed his eyes. It was simply too damn early to be trying to sleep. He was doing it out of sheer boredom. True, he had wanted to get away, but he wanted to go someplace where he could do something. He sighed. The source of his unrest was Dwayne, of course. And this damn thing was Spock. Although Cara Dwayne's dire prediction didn't seem to bother the Vulcan at all. But ever since that night, something seemed to be eating at Dwayne. As for McCoy, he refused to be afraid of Spock dying on sheer principle. A beat of sweat trickled down his forehead and stung his eye. That did it. McCoy jumped up and pulled on his clothes. Maybe he'd take a nice stroll out in the chilly air. He slipped through the doorway and tiptoeed down the hall, mindful of all the Vulcan ears behind the other half-open doors. He paused at Cara Dwayne's door, which was open just a crack. Inside the yellow orange candle-like, flickered, Dwayne, you still awake? No answer. With a grunt, McCoy pushed against the door's formidable stone-mass. Cara Dwayne was sitting inside, still staring into the flame of the now-melted-down candle. She came too with a jerk and put a hand to her heart. Her eyes were wild. McCoy hung back awkwardly. I, uh, didn't mean to start it yet, Dwayne. I was going to cool off in the scout and wondered if you wanted to join me. She stared at him with her hand still over her heart and whispered, No, no, I-I don't think so, Leonard. When she said nothing else, just sat staring at him with that oddly disturbing expression, McCoy added, Well, if it's locked, I'll need the override combination. If it's all right. It's quite all right, Leonard. It's unlocked. This is-this is what-she faltered, her eyes filling with tears. Alarmed, McCoy crouched beside her and put a hand on her shoulder. Dwayne, are you really that upset about Spock? There's nothing you or I can do, Leonard. It's more than just the cards. They only reaffirmed what I felt. You'll think I'm crazy, but I just know. She said it was such utter conviction that McCoy caught his breath. You mean you know when people are going to die? She nodded and hung her head. McCoy was scarcely able to believe what she was saying. She looked up at him. When I read Spock's cards, it seemed to hover over all of us, even me, and then it moved around the table. It settled over the two of you. McCoy stared at her, not wanting to understand what she was saying. Spock? In me? Caridwen was looking at him as if he were already dead. Silently she nodded. For one brief instant McCoy allowed himself to believe and felt a thrill of honest fear. And then, common sense kicked in, he rose angrily to his feet. Enough! This is ridiculous! Caridwen reached after him. Please! Don't go out into the desert tonight, Leonard. Stay here where it's safe. Go on, it's safe, I can feel it. Dwayne, I realize you're upset and worried about me and I'm flattered. But I'm not going to die anytime soon and that's a promise. And Spock? Well, I've seen him in a lot of tight situations and he's always been able to take care of himself. He rose, her face taught with worry. In a gesture of concern that touched McCoy, she reached a hand to his cheek. I wish. I could believe it, Leonard. Please, promise me you won't go out into the desert. I'm going to the scout and that's that. I'm not going to stay in this infernal heat. Only what you foresaw was my being roasted to death on a bed of hot stones. She didn't smile. Then please be careful, Leonard. Why, always am. He touched her cheek. Outside in the corridor, McCoy forced himself to forget Dwayne's dire prediction. Death indeed. The only dangers here at Gall were heat and boredom. Though both, McCoy reflected with grim humor were rapidly escalating to lethal levels. McCoy made it to the vessel without incident and stepped inside. The air in the ship was hot and stale, but he switched on the controls. In no time the environment of the cabin reached earth's normal conditions. Caridwen had a small servitor on the ship. McCoy chose a gin and tonic since it was the only liquor available on the program. The tumbler that appeared was ice cold, sweating, and admirably tall. McCoy settled back into a thickly cushioned seat, sipped his drink, and gave a blissful sigh. He'd sleep here, then return to the retreat early the next morning. In his enthusiasm, he drank up the gin and tonic a little too quickly. Then programmed up two more before he crawled onto the bunk and fell into a deep, contented sleep. Seikar stood in the dark hallway and was afraid. While he believed with his mind that there was no shame in feeling so, his years of exposure to Vulcan training made the acceptance of emotion difficult. Some time ago he realized that even if he succeeded in freeing others from Surak's influence, he himself would never be completely free. Now that the time for action had come, he had to search deep within himself to find that other Seikar. Seikar the free Seikar, the Romulan sympathizer. He had been so long among the Kolinaru that he had come close to forgetting his original purpose. The feeling of being drugged finally wore off and McCoy sat propped up on the bunk, contemplating a means of escape. Even if he managed to catch the Vulcan off guard and knock him out, there was the matter of navigating the ship and McCoy couldn't pilot himself out of a wet paper bag. With a sigh, McCoy gave up the notion of escape and tried to figure out what was wrong with Zakl, the odd symptoms, the facial grimaces, the erratic behavior, the gruesome decidedly unvulcan smile could be caused by a medical problem, such as a brain tumor, triggering psychosis. At least it sounded more plausible than Zakl's claim that he was some sort of a dead Vulcan ruler. Quietly, McCoy rose and tittoed over to the storage compartment across from the bunk, then raised the lid. Inside he found a small metascanner. McCoy removed it, closed the lid, then strolled, nonchalantly, up behind the seated Zakl. The doctor waved the scanner quickly over the Vulcan. It bleeped softly before McCoy could hide it behind his back. Zakl glanced at it and raised a brow. Then returned to his controls. He was behaving like a normal Vulcan again. Perhaps the madness had only been temporary. Encouraged, McCoy struck up a casual conversation. How much are longer before we get to where we're going? Approximately 3.4 hours. We are stopping at Arc Turis to obtain a cloaking device. One is necessary in order to safely enter the neutral zone. McCoy hesitated, then directed his warmest smile at the Vulcan. You know, if you'd just let me off on Arc Turis, it would be easier on both of us. calmly, the Vulcan shook his head. Impossible, it would allow you to inform the authorities before I have a chance to escape to the neutral zone. I can't risk that, Dr. McCoy. Come on, Zakl. You could leave me someplace deserted to give you enough time. The Vulcan glanced sharply at him. My name is Sekar. Who told you about Zakl? Has he spoken with you? McCoy drew in a breath and took a step backwards. Ah, well, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. I must have gotten confused on the name. Sekar, you say, well, I'd certainly appreciate it if you'd consider what I said, Sekar. The doctors scurried to the safety of the bunk and peeked at the scanner readout. Then sighed and dropped the scanner on the bunk. Nothing. Not a single reading beyond the norm. The Vulcan was perfectly healthy. Except that he was certifiably insane. And there wasn't anything McCoy could do about it except pray for a chance to escape. And consider the possibility that Carrod went's prediction had been right after all. Spock acquired a sleek, Vulcan shuttle equipped with warp drive and transporter. By then McCoy and his kidnapper had been gone for hours. After the passage of so much time, Carrod went feared that tracking the stolen scout's course was impossible. Spock and Sai failed to share her despair. They busied themselves with preparing the craft for takeoff. Carrod went sat in the pilot seat as Spock called out the system's check-off. All the while she fought a growing sense of futility that threatened to spill over into tears. When she could stand it no more, she interrupted Spock. How can we possibly find Leonard? They could have gone in any direction. Tracing a small craft like that will be impossible. Spock glanced enigmatically at her, then returned his attention to his control panel. All systems function all doubt to Leuen, ready for takeoff. But which heading, Spock? Behind her, a voice entoned. Mark 414. Carrod went turned. Sai sat in the passenger seat, her eyes closed. Her hands were steepled in an attitude of meditation. Spock entered the heading into the navigational computer, then glanced over at Carrod went and said, I mastered Sai will be directing us. Missedified, Carrod went turned back to her own control panel. The Vulcan's calmness brought a strange comfort. Carrod went, waited until the craft sailed out of Vulcan's orbit and the Airy-B system, and reached warp drive before she returned her gaze to Sai. The master was still in a trance. Carrod went, realized she was concentrating on the Vulcan inside the scout. Curious, Carrod went faced Spock. Mr. Spock, I swore I'd never reveal anything, and I don't see how I can help you without knowing what we're up against. What is this katra that say castowel? Is it a weapon? Eyes averted, Spock answered reluctantly. It is a spirit. The spirit of a Vulcan, Zacle, he died some two thousand years ago. Carrod went, drew in a soft breath. The anthropologist in her half smiled in wonder. My god, but how? Zacle's katra was preserved, as are all those of Kolinar High Masters. His mental powers were great, but his scruples were non-existent. He was a great enemy of Surax. His own students turned against him and imprisoned him. Carrod went frowned. I still don't understand, Spock. Why is Tsai worried about Zacle's knowledge getting to the Romulans? Surely they have their own methods for mind control? Spock interrupted with an intensity she had never seen in him. The humans of today cannot conceive of the type of power wielded by the ancient High Masters. These were the most powerful of all magicians. It is recorded that Zacle killed his enemies simply by willing it. The methods he used were quite gruesome. When the Romulans separated from the Vulcans, none of the old High Masters went with them. Those on Vulcan chose to align themselves with Surax. The discipline underwent a radical change in philosophy. The path of Kolinar still harnesses great mental powers, but applies them inward. To the individuals mind any motions rather than using them to control others. For the Romulans to gain control of these powers for any war-loving race to gain control of them, Spock broke off and shook his head. I can discuss this no more. Tsai is attempting to guard us from Zacle's telepathic powers. I can try to shield my own thoughts, but it increases our chances of being detected. She went and turned away to stare blindly at the view screen. My God! With a thrill of fear, she recalled the card that touched death. The magician ill- dignified. The ship was no longer moving. McCoy woke and pushed himself to a sitting position, then stood up and peered at the pilot's chair. It was empty. Seikar must have landed the scout on Arc Turus. McCoy called out as he rose unsteadily to his feet. Seikar? Uh... Zacle? No reply. McCoy crowed with as much energy as he could muster. Hell, Eluya! I've been abandoned! He dashed to the front of the ship and settled into the pilot's chair. It took him a minute to find the subspace radio control. This is a Class I distress call! A little burst of static made him grimace and cover his offended ears with his hands. McCoy tried again. This time the noise was even louder. Discouraged, he switched the radio off, then headed for the hatch. Eagerly, confidently, he strode face first into the hatch and landed sprawled on his backside, rubbing his nose. The Vulcan had locked him in the ship with no chance of escape. McCoy returned to the console and slumped in the pilot's chair. So this was what Dwen foresaw. McCoy cut down in the prime of life by a crazed Vulcan. Spock would have deemed it poetic justice. McCoy leaned forward and rested as far as against the console. A sound at the hatch distracted him from his misery. The doctor raised his head just as the hatch opened. He expected to see Zakko, and therefore saw nothing. Nothing that is, until he adjusted his vision downward to where the stocky figure of the tellerite stood. To McCoy's human eyes, the tellerite squat, hair-covered body, and decidedly poor-seen features were repugnant, though its thick fur was a strikingly lovely shade of copper. The diminuative alien raised a phaser and growled at McCoy in a language that was definitely not standard. Under normal conditions, the doctor would have been terrified. Now he grinned hugely at his attacker. You want to steal the scout, don't you? The tellerite admitted a nasty snarl and gestured with the phaser. Cheerfully, McCoy raised his hands and retreated from the pilot's chair. You're more than welcome to it, friend. He took a step backwards toward the hatch as the thief crossed over to the controls. The hatch moved open behind the doctor who was babbling with relief. Thank you, thank you, thank you, and bless you. He stepped outside and sank into damp, marshy ground as the hatch closed. He was free, free and alone in the October night. McCoy turned and ran before his accidental benefactor could change his mind. It was night and the ground was thick, ankle-deep mud that was littered with garbage. McCoy ran as fast as he could in the treacherous slime in front of him, shown the bright glow of a city. He'd find his way to a public comm station, fly down the nearest Federation vessel and see when and spark again. As the time-worn saying goes, Arturis is the place where everyone goes to make deals. Nestled in the center of a major pirate corridor, Arturis has stubbornly resisted all over chores from the Romulans, the Klingons, and even the Federation. The planet is infamous, one of the few bona fide anarchy in the galaxy. There is no Arturian government, therefore there is no bureaucracy, no red tape, and certainly no laws. If any part of the planet can be said to be ruled by anyone to any degree, it is related to who owns the deadliest weapon at any given moment. While Arturis is the one place in the galaxy, where Klingons, Romulans, and Terans are free to enjoy the lucrative aspect of illegal trade between their empires, the reality is scarcely utopian. Swift and bloody fights are commonplace in the bars, and the natives are un-pregidist as to the Alka. They regard their Terran Klingon and Romulan visitors with equal contempt. It was into this unhealthy milieu that McCoy stumbled. Before him stood the city, a collection of sleek and shining edifices that contrasted shockingly with a squalor outside. Each building was veiled by its own force field. As McCoy neared, he saw that the nearest building was also guarded by two armed, surly, Arturis. The doctor approached them with an ingratiating smile. Excuse me, sirs, but my name is Dr. Leonard McCoy, and I need to get to a public calm. I was kidnapped, you see, and I— One guard curled his upper lip, revealing black toothless gums, and snarled at McCoy with a conviction of a trained doberman. The other raised his phaser, and picked out a spot in the middle of McCoy's forehead. McCoy raised his hands and backed away. The guards cackled derisively as the doctor darted back into the dark street, discouraged. McCoy was preparing to approach a different building. When he heard the sound of feminine laughter behind him, he turned and saw a tall shadowy figure. It stepped forward into the city's glow. Like all arturans, she was humanoid, and the ghostly pale skin of her forehead was creased with folds of excess skin, reminding McCoy of a certain Asian breed of dog. Her ear lobes were pangulous and crested with dozens of sparkling earrings, and she was quite bald, save for an ornament of exotic feathers on the crown of her head. At the sight of McCoy, her thick lips stretched into a smile. You hear our new? McCoy answered eagerly. Yes, yes, is this Arturus? She nodded. I need very badly to get to a public comm station. I need to get in touch with Federation authorities. The Arturans threw back her head and laughed. Her feather spray fluttered in the humid breeze. On Octurus you will find public comms not private comms, yes. Money. Much more. While the money doesn't matter, if you can just get me to a comm, I'll pay you. Name your price. She lowered her eyelids and studied him.
description: In this episode of "Star Trek Audiobook The Lost Years", Dr. Caridwen presents a demonstration of her divination skills using Habreini stones and old-earth tarot cards, challenging Starfleet scientists to prove their theories on telepathy or alternative methods of divination. Spock, intrigued by the experiment, reluctantly agrees to participate, while Kirk remains skeptical. Dwen's peculiar ability to read minds leads to an unexpected communication with a Vulcan, revealing that her condition is akin to congenital speech loss in humans. This demonstration challenges their theories and highlights the complexity of human perception and understanding beyond conventional science.

transcript: Simon & Schuster Audio Works presents Star Trek, Pro, performed by James Duhan. In its 500 millennia of existence, the entity had been given many names. Some had called it Pro, some wanderer. Its creators had not named it, for they did not name machines. Instead, they described it, seeker, communicator, protector, nurturer, and recorder. For those were its functions. But most often they had described it as seeker. But that was its ultimate purpose. To find somewhere in the galaxy erased the equal of their own, with which it could speak in the true language. When that day came, the entity would return, bringing with it the message that the creators were no longer alone in a universe that seemed to favor only the scurrying might that had, before the winnering, dominated the waterless areas of their own planet. But in its half-million years, in the waters of hundreds of worlds, it had found only primitives that in another million years might be able to speak, might be capable of learning the true language. For millennia, the blue world the entity had recently departed had held such primitives. Time and again it had returned, listening to their evolving story, prompting them in the direction of speech, but then they had fallen silent. No amount of calling had brought forth a response until finally the creator's instructions had said, prepare the world for new life, whatever the cause of the primitives' extinction, remove it. But the instructions had barely begun to be implemented when the primitives had reappeared and raised their planet-bound voices in joy. The entity had stopped, considering the puzzle. Had the primitives made a sudden evolutionary leap? Had they developed abilities even the creators had not possessed? Or had another race transported them to some other world and then returned them? There were no answers. In the end, the creators' instructions, incomplete as they were proving to be, had left no choice for the entity but to move on to continue its search. But it would return soon to the blue world because of the unanswered questions there, the possibilities that circled soundlessly, endlessly, in the entities ever evolving crystalline pathways. Jim Kirk was glad he'd come home. He'd been halfway across the galaxy and back, seen more different cities in a year than most Starfleet officers saw in a lifetime, and still, there was no place like San Francisco. He'd decided to adopt it as his hometown, his first day at the academy. When he and Gary Mitchell went running up and down the rolling hills of the old city, there were few places he could walk that didn't bring to mind some memory. Which is why the site of Golden Gate Park on this, his last morning on Earth, came as such a surprise. Everything was so lush, so overgrown, all residual effects of the monsoon-like rains brought on by the probe just a few short months ago. Well, if the repercussions were all like this, Kirk didn't think that would be such a bad thing. Even the air smelled fresher, almost as if the rains had somehow washed clean the entire planet. He was glad for the chance to spend time on his homeworld these last few days, but he could feel the restlessness building up inside him. All I ask is a tall ship and a star to steer her by. That was still all he wanted. He'd gotten the word from Starfleet Command yesterday afternoon. description: In "Star Trek Audiobook Probe 1 of 4," Simon & Schuster Audio Works presents James Duhan's performance of an audiobook featuring Star Trek's entity, also known as Pro or Wanderer. The probe seeks to find another being capable of speaking in its true language, having found none on hundreds of worlds since millennia ago. It returns to Earth just before the end of Captain Kirk's year-long mission, where it encounters lush Golden Gate Park and reimagines life on a blue planet that once had primitives without speech. The entity finds hope for communication and decides to return soon to continue its search, as the unresolved questions from an incomplete directive remain unanswered.

All that's left is to see how our friends on the Galtis feel about joining our landing party. By the time they reached the bridge, it was apparent that the Romulans were not waiting around. In a few moments, Iran was on screen. His usual smile replaced by flinty grimness. Captain Kirk, Ambassador T.M. requests that all Romulans aboard the Enterprise be transported to the Galtis without delay. And where is Ambassador T.M. is he one of the ones who just transported down to the Cavern? You know about the Cavern then? Yes Commander, and the Crystal within. Do you notify T.M. and his colleagues that personnel from the Enterprise will be beaming down? Of course Captain. With a faint flicker of a smile, Iran broke the connection. Okoyes stepped onto the transporter platform with Kirk, Spock, Dr. Benar, and Dejan pushed back the hood of his fur-lined field jacket and wiped the first traces of sweat from his forehead. The transporter energies gripped him, and the transporter room flickered out of existence, he placed the frozen moment later by darkness. My koyes cursed to himself. I didn't make it! That blasted machine finally did me in. Let me hanging and whatever no man's landed sends things through. But then he felt the pressure of his own weight on the soles of his boots and the icy shock of his perspiration evaporating from his face. Out of the corner of his eye, a small bubble of light that a moment later seemed to explode. Dr. Benar had turned on her halogen lamp. Kirk and Spock were on either side of him, and Dejan was next to Dr. Benar. Underfoot was translucent glass-smooth ice. Overhead was only darkness. The roof of the Cavern was beyond the reach of Benar's lamp. Fifty meters away in the direction of the original bubble of light, he saw the whitish-green dome that was the crystal, or as much of it as poked up through the ice. Next to it, wearing even bulkier jackets than his own were the Romulans. Two were working with a pair of antenna-like devices while the third turned and faced the group from the Enterprise. Spock looked up from his dry-quarter. The one facing us is armed, Captain. Kirk turned to the Romulan archeologist. Dejan, under the circumstances, if you would prefer to be beamed back aboard the Enterprise, I will stay. I will not let that pompous-ass tea-arm determine my movements. Kirk began to lead the way across the ice. Their boots clicked on the ice as if on steel. After a dozen meters of light from Benar's lamp penetrated the shadows and revealed the watchers face. Kirk nodded. Ambassador Tejan? Tejan's eyes surveyed the group and rested on Dejan. Kadejan? Have you come to join your countrymen? I have not. Tejan almost smiled. That is good. The Empire was served far better by your defection. Roughly Tejan turned us back on Dejan and the others and resumed watching the two Romulans as they worked. Kirk turned and continued toward the crystal. Thousands of geometrically perfect facets became visible in what from a distance had seemed like a simple dome. Spock's gloved hands turned his dry-quarter toward the crystal facets and moved the input grid slowly along. For a few seconds he lowered the tricorder. There is no magnetic field associated with this crystal, as was the case on tomorrow's. But there is a detectable structural distortion which suggests that perhaps another form of energy might be keeping the data stored in the crystal. In all likelihood, it is the same form of energy the probe employs. Stopped abruptly as a faint glow pulsed somewhere deep within the crystal far below the surface of the ice. The flow still pale, flooded to the surface of the crystal and cast an eerie light throughout the cavern. The cavern's true dimensions became apparent. A kilometer above their heads was the ceiling, as smooth and glass-like as they ice beneath their boots. At least three kilometers in all directions the walls were also smooth and unbroken, except for half way up one wall where there was a tunnel, which must have been an entrance when the cavern was all or mostly underwater. The glow flowed out of the crystal like a luminous fog. McCoy saw that his fingers seemed to glow, his arms fuzzy and indistinct. He grabbed his communicator to hail the transporter room when Kirk ripped his arm. The big bones look up. McCoy looked up and gasped. Where moments before there had been only the distant, smooth roof of the cavern, there was a kilometer of rippling crystal clear water. And swimming serenely through it, no more than a hundred meters over his head, was a flipper with a flipper. The other would have dwarfed anything that ever swam the seas of earth. McCoy watched as at least a hundred of the lavuyathans swarmed overhead. While they danced, Spock, you were right, except they looked more like super dolphins and super whales. The cavern hadn't suddenly filled with water. A hologram. Spock, is this crystal a source? Unknown, Captain, whatever the source, it is not any known form of holographic projector. As in the case of the probe's emissions, there is no direct evidence of any form of energy transfer. Spock broke off as the crystal vanished. Followed a moment later by the ice floor beneath their feet. But it was not gone. McCoy could still feel the pressure on the bottom of his boots. Soon the glow that enveloped them vanished, and more of the gigantic, dolphin-like creatures appeared below them, swimming serenely through what must have been solid ice. Overhead, something glittered like the surface of the ocean. Suddenly there were sounds coming at them from all sides, a total cacophony like the emissions of the probe. Dr. Bernard abandoned her tricorder and began working with one of her own tools, a sonic probe. Then she breathed a sonic hologram. These images reflect sound. Kirk excitedly turned to McCoy. Of course, bones! You said it yourself! Not super whales, but super dolphins. And dolphins see more with their sonar than with their eyes. So any images would have the ability to be seen by their sonar. For a long moment they all stood silently, listening and watching the images of the massive creatures flow through the image of water. Finally, Spock said, I believe, Captain, you and Dr. Bernard may have given me the key to the probe's emissions. Kirk reached for his communicator. Let's get back to the Enterprise and see if you're right. Deep within the entity, one of the crystal pathways had shunned a bit of data in a different direction. And the entity had remembered the crystal wisdom. The entity had reached out for the memories and wisdom of the creators and had spoken softly to the crystal wisdom, gently awakening it, and the information had begun to flow. The entity turned its attention to the two space-going bubbles it had brought with it. It loosened its grip, but did not release them. Commander Hiran had decided that Sub-Sensurian Kital bore watching and had so instructed his trusted crew members, and now he had proof of Kital's treachery and had summoned him to his quarters. When Sub-Sensurian Kital entered, he stood at attention before Hiran, who remained seated behind his desk. Sub-Sensurian Kital, do you have plans of your own for the Galtis? For just an instant, a flicker of surprise widened the AIDS eyes. I do not understand, Commander. What precisely are you referring to? A conversation that took place a few minutes ago in your quarters between yourself and another of Tiam's AIDS. The questions you were asking Sub-Sensurian about our maneuverability and firepower might have been more appropriately asked of me, the ship's commander. Kital's face remained impassive, but finally he nodded. I was making preparations for the possibility that Ambassador Tiam will fail to gain useful information from the crystal. May I ask Commander Hiran if Ambassador Tiam ordered you to fire on that object called the probe, would you obey? I would not. Such an attack would be suicidal. What if I told you there was a chance that the Galtis would not be destroyed? I believe we may be inside the object's defensive perimeter and we could damage it severely if we were to launch a sudden attack. An intriguing possibility, but Tiam seems extremely anxious to find a way of communicating with this thing. As we all are, however, we must consider the possibility that the Enterprise will succeed, and we must destroy it rather than take the chance the Federation will learn how to control that thing and turn it into a weapon against the Empire. Sub-Sensurian, Kital, I do not believe the Federation would act that way, particularly now that there is a chance of a real peace between our peoples. Kital, that loose, a harsh, bitter laugh. Huda, you are a fool, Hiran. Hiran reached for his intercom to call his guards and have Kital confined to quarters, but before he could activate it, Kital had reached across the desk and slapped Hiran's hand away. A moment later, the door to the corridor burst open and two of Tiam's aides stepped inside, Phaser's train on Commander Hiran. Tiam knew something was wrong, Lamomatigal T's transporter room formed around him, and he saw a genuine, not Kital, was waiting for him. Rest now in a somber Commander's uniform, Genu had jettisoned all traces of Sub-Sensurian Kital. Almost before the transporter energies released Tiam, Genu turned to his aid. Place Ambassador Tiam with Commander Hiran. It is time to end this charade. We will destroy the object, and if we do not succeed and it destroys us, in all likelihood, the object will destroy the Enterprise as well. Genu left to go to the bridge and his aid motion to Tiam with his phaser and led him to Hiran's quarters, where he shot Tiam inside. Gen's log started 8496.4. Spock says the key to the probe's emissions came to him from what Dr. Benar and I said about the images and sounds in the Crystal Cavern, that the images were sonic holograms. He explained that Earth dolphins used the clicks of their sonar to look at an object while simultaneously using whistling sounds to communicate with other dolphins. That would be the equivalent of a human speaking in two different pitches and carrying on two different conversations simultaneously. Spock's hypothesis is that the probe could be saying many things at once at many different frequencies. Currently, Spock has instructed the computer to isolate each band of frequencies that contains a pattern and to treat each as a possible separate language. It will be a while before the computer completes its analysis. Meanwhile, I'm worried about Riley. He still is not awakened from his coma, even though Dr. McCoy expected him to wake up three days ago, we can only wait and hope. The entity had resolved one paradox, only to have another replacing. The chances these mites were responsible for the disappearance and reappearance of the primitives on the Blue World were increasing, as were the chances that they were somehow connected to the mites that had driven the creators from the homeworld. The entity would wait and observe. And if the mites proved to be the same, if they proved to make use of the same killing rays, their mimicking of the true language would not save them. While Tiam talked with Hiran and realized that indeed he had been a pawn in Genyu's hands and that Genyu would destroy them all. Genyu was informing the bridge crew of his plan. The Galtis would lure the Enterprise closer to the object and then attack the object, ensuring the destruction of the Enterprise. The Galtis would possibly escape harm by being within the perimeter of the object's defenses. Sub-Santurian Usal had stood by with the others while Genyu had accused Hiran of treason and announced what Usal could only call madness. Surely they would all die. Suddenly, he knew what he had to at least try to do. He made his way to Hiran's quarters. Once there, he used his phaser to stun the guards and drag them inside. Hiran immediately took charge and determined they must reach the bridge and confront Genyu. Hiran, Tiam and Usal went to the lift. Hiran cursed and revealed it had been disabled. Genyu would have also sealed off all other entrances to the bridge. Tiam swallowed. His lips dry as parchment. It is another possibility. My quarters, there is a subspace transceiver. We could contact the interim committee. Hiran spun to face the ambassador. Halfway across the galaxy don't be a fool, Tiam. Even as Tiam slumped, Hiran brightened. He turned to Usal. Go, try to cut the power to the weapons or the bridge. Without another word, the Sub-Santurian sprinted for the nearest entrance to the service stairs. Then Hiran gripped Tiam's arm and dragged him toward the stairs. Come, Tiam. Take me to this transmitter of yours. The glittering blackness of the probe filled the Enterprise View screen. The bridge crew had watched while the Gautis engaged impulse power and headed toward the probe's orbit. Uhera turned to Kirk. Still no response to our hail, Captain. Sulu volunteered from the helm. And it looks like they're heading for that crystal appendage. The Gautis is now at minimum impulse and barely moving. Kirk shook his head because it didn't make sense. Suddenly, Uhera announced that the Gautis was responding. On screen, the probe and the minuscule Gautis vanished to be replaced by a badly out-of-focus image of the Romulan bridge with an equally out-of-focus commander Hiran, whose voice was oddly distorted. Captain Kirk, I must reluctantly request your assistance. We have decided to investigate the object's crystal appendage more closely. Now that we have approached it, we find we are unable to maneuver. If you could approach to within-tractor beam range in an attempt to free us. And get caught ourselves, Kirk interrupted. No, Captain. The effect appears to have a very short range. You will be able to get within-tractor beam range without exposing yourself to danger. Kirk was puzzled by the bluer'd images and distorted sound. Commander Hiran, is the probe affecting your transmissions? My yours are blurred as well, Captain Kirk. Perhaps it is a result of whatever field is preventing us from moving. Kirk turned the saloon at the helm. Take us in, Mr. saloon. Reverse course, the moment you detect any loss of efficiency in our impulse engines. Kirk started to look back at the screen when the audio channel was cut. Uhura glanced up. Captain, there is a subspace hail from the Galtis. Audio only. This is Commander Hiran. Captain Kirk, I must warn you. Kirk vaulted from the con and was at Uhura's side in a second. Commander Hiran was just speaking to me from the Galtis bridge. A poor image? Out of focus? Yes, but... It is Genu, the one you knew as Kital. He has taken over the bridge and is using the computer to alter his image. What is your warning, Commander Hiran? Genu plans to fire every weapon we have into the cavity beneath that thing's appendage and hopes to damage the massive crystal structure just below it. He expects the thing to return fire and vaporize both the Kaltis and the Enterprise. Kirk let out a deep breath. So that's why he wanted us close in. But if you can't stop him, how do you expect us to? Fire on him first, Kirk. If you cannot limit your fire to his weapons, you must destroy the Daltis. But Hiran, why is Genu doing this? He is afraid you will learn to control that thing and you will use it to destroy the Empire. Where is Tiam? He is here and agrees with this decision, but he wants to be beamed over before you act. Spock broke in. Captain, the Galtis phaser banks are being overcharged, presumably to maximize their initial discharge. Sulu turned to Kirk. Galtis shields raised Captain. Kirk ignored the knot in his stomach. The transporters were gone. And Spock said with urgency. Captain, the computer is producing a translation of the probe's emissions. Kirk turned to face his senior officer. What? Timing? Can we talk to it? If you can, Spock, tell it to get the hell out of here now. Spock's fingers jabbed at half a dozen controls. He said with no emotion in his voice, you are in danger. Remove yourself immediately from this area. Yet another paradox assaulted the entity. The might that had first mimicked the true language were doing it again. And yet they were not. It was something totally new. A warning of danger. It was not carried by the true language in its entirety, but by only one primitive aspect of it. And the might chose to use more aspects. They would have communicated a thousand times more information. But perhaps it was all they were capable of. The entity searched for the danger. But there was none. Even if these might possess the killing rays, the might's space going bubbles would be reduced to atoms if they used those rays. The entity communicated, there is no danger. On the Enterprise, Kirk was already at the Science Station next to Spock when they received the message from the probe. There is no danger. Spock spoke to the probe. There is a weapon about to be fired at you. We cannot stop it. If you can stop it, there will be time to explain. Time to talk. Sulu turned to the captain. Gautis Phaserbanks leveling off. They could fire any second. Kirk knew he couldn't take the chance. Fire, Mr. Sulu. Time to talk. The entity seized on that fragment of the might's message. They wanted to communicate. The entity reached out and gripped the space going bubbles and the might's within them. And everywhere in the Enterprise and Gautis, all motion stopped. Genyoo's order to fire all phasers was frozen in his throat. In the sick bay of the Enterprise, Kevin Riley could not breathe. And it ripped him free of the nightmares that had held him captive for so long. Gently, swiftly. The entity placed the might's and their space going bubbles beyond the point at which their killing rays, if indeed they possessed them, could trigger a response. Then it released them and communicated. We will talk. Captain's Log, Stardate, 8501.2. According to Mr. Sulu's looking out the window calculations, the probe made equally good time on the return leg of what must have been one of the longest towing jobs in either Federation or the return leg. It's departure moments after releasing the Enterprise and the Gautis at the edge of the Tamara system was equally speedy. Not surprisingly, the Tamara's Peace Conference has not been resumed. The one surprise is that the Reformed-minded interim government is still in power, albeit precariously. They are reportedly getting a boost from Hiran's accusations of sabotage against Ambassador Tiam and Commander Genu. We learned a lot from the probe in the last three days, and the probe has picked up a little from us mites. Spock became the only mite to be allowed direct access to the probe's innards, as McCoy calls them, and he was able to resolve the various paradoxes. With the help of the Enterprise computer, Spock expanded on the creator's rather rigid definition of intelligence so that it now includes most technologically advanced mites. Similarly, he modified its goals so that it would search for the survivors of the creators who may be the A regions. Captain Kirk watched Commander Hiran materialize on the transporter platform with the barest trace of what struck Kirk as a wistful smile. With both the Enterprise and the Gautis awaiting final orders, Hiran had asked that Kirk allow him to complete his tour of the Enterprise. Instead of completing the tour, Kirk found himself repeating part of it, escorting Commander Hiran to the botanical gardens. If you would care to walk on the grass again, Commander Hiran, I suppose it could be tolerated for a time? Hiran laughed and said, taking a walk through a garden with a Federation captain is not something easily forgotten. Hiran stopped on the bank of the stream that meandered through one corner of the garden. You suspect, Captain, that I want more than a few minutes in your decadent Federation garden. Correct? Well, the thought had crossed my mind, Commander. I know that Tiam and Genu would welcome my defection. Otherwise, they would not have stood by so calmly when I announced my intention to transport over. They would doubtless do better in the Citadel with only their version of the mission, which is one of the reasons I cannot stay. Kirk nodded. And the other reasons? Our victory this time was tiny. There will not be a shooting-warm. Perhaps someday our victories will be larger. I know that someday your admiral Cartwright might be replaced by someone perhaps like yourself, and that replacement will need a source of information he can trust. A tingle rushed at Kirk's scalp. He certainly will, Commander. Together, they made their way to the lift. The Probe by Margaret Wonder Bonano was adapted for audio by George Truitz and performed by James Duan. The recording engineer was Steven Strassman with post-production and sound design by Steven Erickson. Original music was composed by Sam McCally, Carl Schuritz, Richard Heyman, Richard Emmett, and Eve Begglarian. Theme music from the Star Trek television series was composed by Alexander Courage and Jean Rothenberry, used courtesy of Bruin Music. The associate producer was Elisa Shokoff. Probe was directed and produced by Karen Frillman.
description: In this final episode of "Star Trek Audiobook Probe," the crystal sensor probe finally lands on Earth 120 degrees from the galactic disk, after three days in space. The crew's first contact with the planet results in a chilling discovery: no life forms exist and the surface temperature has cooled to record low temperatures due to an asteroid impact millions of years ago. The episode explores the profound implications of this encounter and concludes with Kirk speculating on how such technology could be used for interstellar travel, highlighting its potential far beyond the confines of Star Trek's universe.
