transcript: The entity paused and extended its crystal sensor, neither knowing nor caring, that it was at the very edge of Federation Space. The defining the shape and content of the space surrounding it raced along the microscopically glittering pathways that honeycomb its vast interior. The entity modified its course as it had done millions of times since its journey began, unaware that it was entering a domain called the neutral zoom. It knew nothing of the great war that had ravaged both civilizations, nor of the buffer that had allowed an uneasy peace to be maintained for more than a human century. It was, after all, a machine. It could only continue to observe, to search, to learn, to protect, as it had been designed to do. Already at the very limit of the crystal sensor's range, another world was entering its awareness. Another world whose primitives, like those on the Blue World it had recently departed held promise, with a special alertness, it sought the voice of that distant world. It was still too distant to pick out individual voices or songs of the primitives. Normally, the full focus of the crystal sensor would have produced a soft but joyous symphony, but there was a change. In emotion its creators had called sadness, perhaps despair. A single cry said the sensor dancing, a cry that rose simultaneously from all the primitives that still survived on that distant world. Save us. Captain's Logs, Stardate 848.7. I have reviewed with Commander Riley the procedures to be followed once in orbit around tomorrow's four. The first face-to-face meetings will be on the planet's surface, no weapons. All personnel who beam down are to have their communicators, and transporter chiefs will keep a fix on each of us at all times. Meetings will continue, alternating between the ships, until some kind of agreement is reached or both sides have had enough. On the first evening, Federation musicians will perform on the Enterprise, followed the next evening by Romulan musicians performing on the Galtish. Both Riley and I are worried that Dr. Benard, having seen several of her closest friends tortured and killed by Romulans, might not be able to handle working cheek-to-jowl with a batch of Romulans. So I have asked Mr. Sulu to be an archeological sitter and stick close to Dr. Benard. I am worried that the Romulans' insistence on Dr. Benard's being in charge could be less an attempt to make up for their earlier offenses than to exploit them in some way to sabotage the conference. A short while ago I received word from Spock that the probe had crossed the neutral zone and re-entered Romulan space, doubling its velocity. Starfleet passed on this information to the Romulan Interim Committee, which currently denied the probe's existence. Meanwhile, Spock has made no real progress with the probe recordings. On a rise overlooking the desert-like remains of what had once been a terrorist-fertile valley, Kirk stood with Spock, Sulu, Riley and Benard. They faced four stiffly formal Romulans. Beyond them in the valley proper, the ruins of Tamara's four stretched almost to the sandy horizon. The conspicuous absence of fanfare reinforced Kirk's opinion that the Romulans wanted to imply that the conference was unimportant to them. When the introductions were over, Dejan and Dr. Benard, escorted by an enthusiastic Sulu, escaped to survey a few square meters of the ruins. Centurion Tion stood watching, silent and tense, next to a seemingly relaxed Riley. The one remaining Romulan, a sub-centurion, introduced as Kital, stood solemnly to one side, his eyes tracking Sulu and the two archaeologists as if his life depended on it. I ran, turned to Kirk, as if on a sudden impulse. It appears there will be precious little to occupy you and me on this mission, Captain Kirk. I would be honored to conduct you on a tour of my ship if you will do the same for me. Centurion Tion remained silent, watching and listening, a cold smile shaped the corners of his mouth. Kirk looked high-ran straight in the eye and hoped he was not making a mistake. I'll personally escort you, Commander Highran. Kirk surveyed the mixture of colorful costumes and regulation Starfleet issue, all swimming in an unintelligible hub of voices. On the surface, this first reception in the most spacious rektak the Enterprise had to offer was a genuine miracle after a hundred years of cold and sometimes not so cold war. Even Dr. Bernard, though she had yet to join in with anything so unvulcan as laughter, appeared comfortable. Kirk's only moment of fright had come not from Bernard but from a stout silver-haired cotalan female who had been repeatedly poking a lanky Romulan male in the chest to emphasize her point. Just when Kirk expected the Romulan to draw back an anger, he exploded in laughter instead. On the other hand, there was Tion, like an iceberg in the shipping lanes. Even Riley had given up after uncounted attempts at Small Talk. After Highran and his observation post immediately to Kirk's right, let go aside. My pet diplomat seems to be behaving in an decidedly undiplomatic manner. You will excuse me, Kirk, while I have a word with him. By all means, Commander, no one likes a party pooper. Kirk wondered what Romulan equivalent the translator in Highran's ear would supply. Whenever it was, it seemed to delight him because he laughed. That is priceless, Kirk. I shall remember it at my next staff meeting. So sane, Highran navigated the throng and spoke quietly in Tion's ear. The centurion stiffened, his eyes flashing, but finally, witting his teeth, he nodded. Finally it was time for the music. A solo piano recital by Maestro Andrew Penal. Acknowledging the polite applause, Penal seated himself, signaled for the computerized orchestral accompaniment he had arranged for, and began to play thunderously, spectacularly, all sparkling and dazzling, flying fingers. When he finished, he stood with a flourish and bowed to the applause. Kirk turned to Ahura, at least he stood, didn't he? Ahura grinned at the captain. He has to be pretty good to do all that flailing around and still hit most of the right notes. As the applause died down, Kirk noticed with alarm that Tion was heading for the platform. Penal looked equally alarmed as the Romulan bored down on him. Valatedly, Kirk tried to intercept Tion, who strode onto the platform, his hand extended, not as a threat, but as an invitation to the human ritual of a handshake. A brilliant performance, Maestro Penal. Ha, thank you, Ambassador Tion. Come from you, that's quite a compliment, I understand your wife is a musician as well. She is, in fact, she is the reason I have taken the liberty of approaching you. You see, the piano is one of her favorite instruments. Your playing has so inspired her that she was wondering if she might indulge herself with this one. Wow, of course, Ambassador! And Penal strode quickly to where Jandra stood and took her on. For a moment, she nervously resisted, casting a dark look at her husband. But then the scattered applause from the Federation musicians began. She smiled, took Penal's arm, and allowed herself to be escorted to the piano. She sat motionless for a moment. Then brushed her fingers soundlessly across the keys. For several seconds, she sat with her eyes closed, giving Kirk for just a moment, the unreal impression that she was somehow mind-melding with the instrument. Then she looked up at Penal. The piece you concluded with. Now, would your computer have the accompaniment for the second movement? Penal, not it. The program is designed to follow the lead of the player. A moment later, the computer accompaniment began. The genre played with other simple, full start or misstep. Where Penal had thrown his entire body into the playing, Jandra remained almost eerily motionless as her fingers coaxed the sound from the keys. She let the sound drift out and envelop her listeners. And then she drew them in. When she lifted her fingers from the keys at the conclusion, there was total silence. Then the applause broke out, and Sulu next to Kirk laughed as he joined the others. She's as good as Penal thinks he is. Kirk looked around to locate Penal. If he had looked a second later, he would have seen only the maestro's broad smile. But in that first second, he saw the mixture of fury and humiliation that had not yet been completely obscured. His smile now firmly in place. Penal bounded back onto the platform. He took Jandra's hand as she stood up from the piano. That was stunning, my lady. Absoluteness stunning. Ambassador T.M. Your wife's performance has given you urgency to your mission. You and your college must succeed if only so that her gifts may be shared with the worlds of the Federation. I would be honored to be her sponsor and advisor. Even T.M. seemed taken aback by Penal's infusiveness. Jandra and I thank you, my stropenalt. And we will do our best in the coming days not to disappoint the Federation. From a far corner of the room, a pair of Romulans in the uniform of sub-centurions watched with well-disguised pleasure the exchange on the platform. The older one spoke softly to the younger. We could not have asked for better. If their late brothers' activities did not provide sufficient motive for Federation revenge, its public humiliation of one of their own will leave no doubt whatsoever. Back on the Galtige, Jandra realized that her decision had been made, without knowing precisely when. Certainly not when that buffoon Penal had made his offer. Perhaps it had been the crowd afterward, not as they told her how much they had been moved by her performance, but as they lingered to talk of other things, to inquire about her life, her own happiness. Her decision had been made. But it still had to be carried out, and the first step, perhaps the hardest of all, would be to talk to Dejan. She dared not simply make her move, leaving him to face the consequences. About Teon, she was not worried. Whatever became of him, it would be his due. Bracing herself, she moved down the corridor to her brother's quarters. She was startled by the suddenness with which the door snapped open. Little sister, come in! I was right, you see. They wished to flaunt you, to prove Romulan's superiority even in such lesser activities as music. Jandra was afraid that her momentary burst of courage that had allowed her to wrap at her brother's door would desert her, and she would never get it back. I must speak with you, brother. I have decided to defect to the Federation. For a long moment there was only silence. Her brother's face was frozen. His mouth still opened with unspoken words. Suddenly, he laughed and snatched her off her feet, hugging her and whirling her about the tiny room. You have remarkable timing, just like a musician. I have been pacing the floor for hours, it seems, trying to work up the courage to tell you. Precisely, the same thing. The next morning Dr. Benard and the Romulan archaeologist Dejan stood next to the prefab headquarters at the mouth of the valley as their team spread out and began threading their way as rapidly as practical through the ruins. The evening before, the reception shop talk had led quickly to an agreement to pair off Romulan and Federation so that during the initial survey each pair would have the use of a tricorder, which the Romulan archaeologists readily admitted were superior to their own devices. Everyone had leapt into action virtually the moment they were being down. First, they made a fast survey of the entire valley with all tricorder readings transferred to both enterprise and galtige computers at the end of each day. Then they set out to concentrate on the most promising areas. To Benard's eyes, this decaying grey world with a feeble sun, dim and forbidding, was stunningly beautiful. Yet she was finding that if she closed her eyes, it was all too easy to imagine that she stood amid the ruins of Colus III with a different Romulan at her side. Like most Romulans, Dejan was shorter and slighter a build than the average Vulcan. His coloring was lighter. Pale curling hair framed a face set with dark green eyes, Outrear decided that he had to be the fraternal twin of the musician Jandra. He was handsome by either human or Romulan standards, although that obviously meant nothing. The Romulan in charge on Colus III had been even more handsome, and his clinical torture and butchery of her friends and colleagues and brother had literally stolen her sanity. Only the Vulcans had been able to help her reclaim her mind, and more. They had taught her the mind rules. She had achieved a halting mastery over her emotions and had dealt with her rage, her hatred. She had attained a measure of peace. But now with the Romulan actually standing beside her, close enough to reach out and touch, his features echoing those of that other. She felt it all coming back. The fear, the hatred, the loathing that had built up in her during that year on Colus. The fear, she could control. It was an animal reaction, a function of the lower brain and easily dealt with. The hatred was more difficult. In that year her mantra had been, I will survive to see you dead. And it had worked. But this was a different world at different time, and that hatred, if uncontrolled, could steal from her the opportunity of a lifetime. First of all, it was illogical. Dejan was not responsible for the events on Colus 3. He was, after all, an archaeologist like herself, not a military tyrant and torturer like the creature on Colus 3. She turned and began striding toward the beginnings of the hills that flanked and protected the valley. Come Dejan, there is a structure I would find before all others. The Exodus Hall. Together they made their way higher. The powder-fine sands squeaking softly under their boots. Some time later, they were more than a mile from the mouth of the valley, looking down from one of the highest points in the westward hills. The dozen pairs of Federation and Romulan archaeologists in the ruins below looked like insects scurrying through an unending maze. Benar pointed toward a segment of the ruins near the far side of the valley. This is one of the nodes. Dejan followed her finger with his eyes, searching the ruins. Yes, I see it now. Remarkable, Dr. Benar. I would never in a thousand years have recognized that for what it is. In minutes she had located another principal node and a feeling of triumph was coursing through her, almost drowning out the ever distant cries of Colus 3 and the Exodus Hall. It was there, double the size of any she had seen before and the most intact structure in the valley. Before getting to inform her partner, she began to make her way down the slope. Remarkable, Captain! Iron Smile indicated a soft-edged envy of the trees and grass that lined the winding paths of the Enterprise Botanical Garden. The guided tour had, at Hyran's request, gotten underway early before the first working diplomatic meeting which was set to begin on the Galtisj at 0900. Hyran did not want his so far-friendly relationship with Kirk to be complicated by Tiam's opening solvos on the diplomatic front. Hyran shook his head in wonder. Truly remarkable! But tell me, Captain Kirk, do you hold any hopes for this? Fairy boat ride we are both on? Hopes? Yes! Expectations? No. The Romulan-eyed Kirk as if debating whether to go on. I will tell you, honestly, Federation Captain. My hopes were higher at the start of the Blide before I became familiar with St. Shirley and Tiam. Does that surprise you? Kirk smiled. Only that you admit it. Then I will admit something else, and this just may surprise you. It is my secret hope that the archeologists determine that the Ariesians were the ancestors of you humans. And my government would be obliged by its own terms to give the Federation access to this world. We will be responsible for carving the first path through the forest of the neutral zone. I hope my own government would see it in the same light if the Ariesians proved to be your ancestors. As do I. But tell me, Kirk, now that we are exchanging confidences, how real is this so-called? It is called probe. My government denies. Very real, Hiran, and very dangerous. Indeed? You have seen it personally? I have. And I have heard it. I have seen what it can do. I could show you the records as we have offered to show your government. And I would be glad to look, but I fear it would not change anything. Tion will know more listen to me than to you, nor would those whose orders he follows. Whoever forced the selection of St. Jurian Tion was no friend to reform, I tell you. Startled at such openness, Kirk wondered that this Hiran were genuine. He looked up to see Hiran tentatively touch a booted toe to the grass at the edge of the path. Is it permitted to depart from the paths? It's not encouraged, but it's certainly permitted, particularly for a distinguished guest such as yourself. In the way, Kirk moved off the path onto the grass. Commander Riley entered the Galtige conference room at 0900. He had not, truth be told, slept all that well last night. On the other hand, St. Jurian Tion and his four aides looked thoroughly alert and rested. Riley took his place at the conference table, a small tricorder before him. He had spent the last few days filling his head with Romulan psychology, attitudes, beliefs. But little of it, he suspected, would prove useful in dealing with Tion. As always, Riley found himself preparing to rely on something which, in their own disparate ways, both Captain Kirk and Ambassador Sarak had advised him to rely upon a long time ago, his instincts. And this time, instinct told Kevin Riley, start with a reality check. He and TM could spout polite or not so polite platitudes at each other all day, but none of it would mean a thing unless both sides were operating in the same universe. And the Romulan interim government's initial response to the data concerning the probe's movement toward Romulan territory was prima facie evidence that someone in the interim government was not operating in the real universe. The government had denied twice that the probe existed. Ambassador TM, we have received only hours ago new data regarding the location and course of the object we have unofficially designated the probe. Are you familiar with that object? Tion's face displayed a moderate skull. I am, of course, familiar as the fiction the Federation is attempting to perpetrate. What I fear I am not familiar with is the reason the Federation persists in its attempts. Ah, we persist, Ambassador TM. For the same reason, Oi persist in sitting in this chair rather than falling through it to the floor. The chair exists. The probe exists. It has done major damage to Earth. It has now passed through the neutral zone and has entered, possibly re-entered Romulan space. Re-entered, Commander Riley. Are you now claiming this fiction of yours originated in the Empire? Just a tall Ambassador TM, if we thought it had, I doubt that we would be sitting here today. Very well then, Commander Riley. If you are not accusing the Romulan Empire of anything, I see no point in discussing it further. Riley slid a paper across the table toward the Romulans. These are the most recent coordinates. The probe will soon be beyond the range of Federation ships, so any further tracking will be up to the Empire. So, Commander Riley, you have turned this fiction over to us. Is that what you're saying? Riley paused. This was going nowhere. What I am saying, Ambassador TM, is that the probe is not a fiction. I fail to see any point in trying to discuss any of the other countless other issues about which there is ample room for legitimate differences of opinion. We would simply be wasting our time. And with that, Riley stood up from the table and strode from the room. Though it was a little more than three kilometers from their hilltop vantage point to the structure identified as the Exodus Hall, it took Benar and Daejan more than an hour to reach it, partly because there was no such thing as a direct route. Walking the streets, they could sense that patterns existed, could come around a curve and see some aspect of the ruins the patterns had told them to expect. Then the Exodus Hall appeared before them. After a single survey around the squat, low-dome de-building, Benar took from her kit a small short-range phaser-like device. Its normal use was in extracting fossils from the rock strata in which they were found. Ten careful minutes with this device could replace dozens of hours with tiny picks, tweezers, and brushes. Setting it to full power, she brought it within an inch of what the tricorder told her was the weakest section of the walls. She pressed the activator and heard the faint wine as the first layer of the wall surface disappeared in the greenish glow. She heard the sandy shuffle of feet behind her and, out of the way, Benar clamped down on a screen as visions of another time crashed down on her. Visions she had hoped that the years on Vulcan had forever banished. She was inside a structure, not outside, and the footsteps were echoing in the corridor outside her room herself, and she knew that Delhar was coming for her once again. She touched her shoulder and she spun and saw Delhar's hated face above her, and she lurched to her feet, raising the excavating tool and thrusting it at him, screaming her fury and confused terror. When Sulu looked up from his studies on the Arasianness Agency, he realized he should have instructed the computer to interrupt him when the archaeological teams beamed down. They had already been on the surface for half an hour. He darted from his quarters and headed for the transporter room at a run. You have a bead on Dr. Benar? The ensign at the controls did some checking. Yes, she's down in the middle of the row, sir. Ensign don't put me down right on top of her. Give me some distance. Sulu didn't want to start a Benar, or make her think he was keeping an eye on her, although that was exactly what he was doing. When the transporter field released him, Benar and Dejan were in clear view. They're back to him. Benar was using an excavating tool of some kind. As Sulu approached, Benar kneeled down and held the tool close to the wall. The Romulan took a step closer, leaning down to watch more closely, as he did his kit brushed against her shoulder. Sulu was only yards away, getting ready to call out a casual greeting when Benar stiffened and screamed an animal like lipstick of screech and growl. She swung about, swinging the still glowing tool toward the Romulan's face. Sulu lunged forward as best he could in the sand. The Romulan was backing away while Benar lurched forward, jabbing the excavating tool at his face. She shouted. Sulu grabbed her from behind, pinning her arms at her side. For an instant, her body writhed and struggled bruisingly. Then in a split second, she stopped. Held herself totally motionless. She went limp. The weapon fell to the sand. Sulu maintains his grip on Benar while he looked at the Romulan. Dejan! What the hell's going on here? Dejan's face was as if he were going into shock. Dr. Benar shuddered. Commanded, Sulu. You can now release me. I have recovered. Tentatively he let her go and looked from one to the other. So, one of you won a clue, me in? The Romulan looked at Sulu. He called me Delar. Sulu looked at Benar who gave us light nod. On Calus 3, for a moment, she looked at Dejan. I will be more careful in the future. Dejan had gone even paler. You were on Calus 3? For a long moment, the Romulan was silent. He closed his eyes to bring his labored breathing and pounding heart under control. Finally, he looked at Benar, lowering his eyes as he spoke. Dejan was the commander of the forces on Calus 3. He was also my brother. From a vantage point 100 meters from the Exodus Hall. Two Romulans, their sub-centurion uniforms replaced by the nondescript garb, favored by the archeologists quietly retreated. If not for the intervention of the Enterprise Commander, one major part of their mission would have been complete. Had she been allowed to kill or seriously injure Delar's brother, it would have been relatively simple to dispose of her and arrange it to look as if they had killed each other. But now, knowing what Benar with her Vulcan logic was capable of, she would almost certainly take precautions. The older one said, we will find another means of ending this charade. Once out of sight and sound of the Exodus Hall, they signaled to be transported back to the Gautij. The Lulu paced in the sand as Benar worked to breach the wall of the Exodus Hall. Everyone had been counting on the conference and consequently the debut, to last at least several days. But now, some faction among the Romulans was deliberately trying to sabotage it. Despite Dr. Benar's flashback to her time on Calus 3, she had insisted on continuing to work with Dejan, and he had agreed. Both were aware that this unique opportunity could vanish at any moment. Sulu turned to Dejan. I was giving myself a crash course on Erision's this morning, but I hadn't got to the part about the Exodus Hall yet. Dejan seemed relieved to speak, to take his mind off waiting. The theory, Commander, is that the contents of the hall may tell us where the Erision's went. The hall appeared to have been domed as this is, and the dome fragments appear to contain segments of a star map, with certain of the stars highlighted. Like a planetarium. Benar looked over her shoulder from where she still used the excavating tool on a thinning surface of the wall. The corsion was not mosaic of stars, unless their science was even further beyond ours. The coordinates of the highlighted stars may be held in a crystalline memory device. A number have been found in other Exodus halls, but little information has been recovered from them. The fields used to encode the data have been so weakened that the bulk of the data was lost. It seemed hours later to Sulu when he stood with Dr. Benar and Dejan inside the Exodus hall looking up at its domed ceiling. In the light of the halogen lamp, thousands of tiny points of light and hundreds of brighter ones glittered above them. In the exact center on a pedestal was a miniature duplicate of the dome, with only the highlighted stars visible. Benar went directly to the pedestal, her tricorder out. In tact, the crystalline lattice structure is stable, the magnetic field is faint but not erratic. We may have little time. Coudogen, it is my opinion that the instruments aboard the Enterprise would have a better chance of retrieving the data than those aboard the Romulanship. Do you agree? Dejan gestured at the Romulan instrument in his hand, a primitive version of a tricorder. I have no objection though Tiam and the others might. We will not tell them until it is done. Commander Sulu, it will be safest to transport the crystalline device in a shuttle. Sulu flipped open his communicator to start making the arrangements.
description: In this episode of Star Trek Audiobook Probe 2 of 4, Captain James Kirk leads a meeting aboard the Enterprise to discuss procedures for potential future meetings between Federation and Romulan representatives. The probe has crossed into Romulan space, doubling its velocity. Spock continues his work on the probe recordings while Kirk prepares for upcoming discussions with the Romulans.

In any event, barring a miracle, the best we will be able to do by the time the probe arrives in the vicinity of Tamaras is to use Spock's modified tractor beam to, in effect, send the probe's own words back to it. Dr. McCoy is worried about Ambassador Riley because he has suddenly fallen into a coma. It is our hope that he will awaken soon. Nothing Hyran could say could convince Tiam that he was little more than a dupe. They could have found any number of paranoid would-be diplomats in the capital without bringing you in from the provinces. But there is only one dejan, brother to Delar, and you are married to his sister. You certainly can't believe its sheer coincidence. Believe what you will, Commander, the fact remains that I am the Empire's official representative, and as such I am the final authority on all dealings with the Federation in the current situation. Tiam made the situation clear to everyone in the crew. All communications had to be cleared and monitored by him to emphasize his words. His aid, sub-centurion Kital, stood at Tiam's side, phaser plainly in view. Later, those who had recommended him as Ambassador spoke to him through the secret sub-space transceiver in his quarters. They told him that as the result of this timely evidence of Federation treachery, the reformers were in full retreat. It was shortly after that Tiam was notified the Enterprise had taken itself out of orbit around Tamaaras. A self-satisfied Tiam scowled at Hyran. So, Commander, the conference is at an end. The hostages were not returned. That constitutes unacceptable behavior. Hyran could only shake his head. As you well know, they have gone to attempt to communicate with that thing and have repeatedly suggested that we accompany them. Doesn't the truth mean anything to you? Tiam ignored Hyran's remark. I prefer that we observe from a distance. Considering what that thing did to an unarmed cargo ship millions of kilometers distant, I would not care to get within range whether it's under the control of the Federation or not. Sulu had taken the helm for the rendezvous with the probe. Chekhov was at the navigator station, Ughura at the Khan station, Scott at the engineering station, Spock at the science station. McCoy watched the viewscreen at Kirk's left. They had already traveled through three centuries of time in a refurbished Klingon rust bucket to stop this thing. Whatever it was. And now, in the Enterprise, they would face it again. Together. The only non-crew member on the bridge was Jandra, whose uncanny ability had first detected a pattern in the midst of the probe's chaotic emissions. Ughura turned to the captain. One furious reports, the probe is maintaining its course through the neutral zone and should be entering our own sensor range at any moment. Kirk kept his eyes on the viewscreen. Ready, Mr. Spock? Ready, Captain. Mr. Scott, I, Captain. Back up battery power fully charged and fully shielded. And if we lose primary and secondary power, we'll still have life support and impulse power. And tractor beams. It would not do to lose our voice. So Mr. Spock, start the conversation. Ughura looked around sharply from the Khan station. Captain, when furious reports an alteration in the probe's course. Kirk suppressed a curse. It already knows we're here. Sensors are obviously longer rains than ours. Mr. Sulu, put us in front of it again. Warp factor of your choice. I-I, Captain. The star-bao of warp entry filled the viewscreen for a moment as Sulu engaged the drive. When the Enterprise was once more in the path of the probe, Spock reported from the science station. It is now within direct sensor range, Captain. But it is again changing course to avoid us. Kirk muttered and ordered Sulu to get in front of it again. Once again, the entity altered its path to avoid the object. But this time, altered its path to such a degree that the object could not intercept it. Suddenly, the crystal sensor touched the still distant object. And billions of crystal pathways that had lain dormant for hundreds of millennia sprang to life in recognition, silencing the entity's voice. The true language the calculation said. The knights are speaking in the true language. Kirk was considering their inability to intercept the probe when Spock interrupted his thoughts. Captain, the probe has ceased its emissions and is slowing rapidly. I'll stop, Mr. Sulu. Mr. Spock reduced tractor beam output by 50%. Now that we have its attention, we don't want a shout. It might shout back and knock out Commander Scott's super shielded backup power systems. Commander Ahura, hail the Galtij again. Not responding, sir. Spock kept checking the readout at his science station. Captain, the object appears to be emitting again, but at a reduced level. So, it knows how to whisper as well as shout. Now if we could just figure out what the hell it's whispering about, Mr. Spock. Are its emissions now the same as the ones in your recordings? Unknown as yet, Captain. The computer has not yet established any matches. Ohura interrupted. Captain, the Galtij is responding to the probe. The paradox emerged into the crystalline paths within milliseconds. The mites were speaking in the true language, but the mites did not possess the power of true speech. The mites' speech was a crude imitation, where true speech would have reached out to the crystal sensor. The imitation did not. The crystal sensor had to reach out and retrieve the vibrations of the true language. Yet its creator's instructions had been clear. Return with the news the moment the existence of others capable of speaking the true language is confirmed. But then the content of what the mites were speaking became clear to the entity. It was the same message that the entity itself had spoken to every passing world, a greeting, and a history, and an invitation. And now the reply had come, but it was not true speech. It was mimicking the true language. The paradox was beyond its power to resolve. So there was only one course of action open, returned to its creators, and lay the paradox before them. The entity reached out and drew metallic bubbles to itself. Engineers logged start out 8, 4, 9, 4, 0.6. The enterprise and the galtige are now being held in some kind of field by the probe and dragged along at more than warp 12. Even at that speed the enterprise is proving equal to the stress. We appear to be moving toward an unexplored quadrant of the Orion arm. The captain has tried to reach Starfleet, but communications outside the probe's field appear to be blocked. Of course, it's a relief to know that the thing is not heading straight for Earth. Mr. Spock has been analyzing the probe and finds it has a crystalline core that is identical in structure to the crystal found in the Exodus Hall on Tamaras 4. But it's too far a jump to say that the probe may have been built by the Ariesians. I, myself, am interested in what kind of power makes that behemoth fly so fast, and the captain has asked me to work on that puzzle with Mr. Spock. The life support systems on the galtige were not shielded and had gone off and on several times. Tiam had passed out several times struggling to breeze. Finally he came to and heard sub-centurion Kital say, All systems check out as fully functional commander, but there is no response from any empire facility. Tiam started toward Hyran to demand to know what was happening when the muzzle of a phaser pressed to his side, stopped him. It was Kital. He spoke softly so no one but Tiam could hear him. Come with me, Tiam. It is past time you understood the situation aboard the galtige. Stoned, Tiam didn't resist as Kital led him from the bridge. A minute later they were in Kital's Spartan quarters. Kital gestured for Tiam to sit on the bench like bunk. My apologies, ambassador, for the crudeness of my approach, but it is necessary for you to be told and imperative that Hyran not suspect. What gives you the right to talk to me this way? Kital broke in impatiently. Do not waste your time with foolish questions. Simply listen. I have been authorized by those responsible for your presence here to assume control whenever I felt the circumstances warranted. Such action. Tiam scowled uneasily. Who are you talking about? I know I've no such. I refer to those you so often consult using the subspace transceiver hidden in your quarters. Later, once communications are restored with the Empire, you will be allowed to verify my authority. I wouldn't prefer your cooperation, but I will settle for your obedience. And if I refuse, then you will die Tiam. And believe me, disposing of you will be far easier for me than what I was forced to do to my friend, Yutak. Kital paused. A faint smile, touching the corners of his mouth. Perhaps you are too proud to subordinate yourself to a lowly sub-centurion. If it will make it easier for you, I will introduce myself. I am Commander Genu, most recently of the Shalyar. Except for the obstinacy of certain members of the interim committee, I would still be its commander. Tiam swallowed away some of his throat tightening anger. So Hiran was right after all. I have not been the player, but a pawn. But now that I know the truth, we will see who is player and who is pawn. Tiam stood. If it is for the good of the Empire, you will of course have my full cooperation. Kirk watched as a scowling Commander Hiran fill the Enterprise view screen. Commander Hiran, it's good to hear from you. A flicker of a smile momentarily softened the edges of the scow. It's good to be allowed to contact you. I thank you for the information that you have been sending regarding your activities. I would have communicated in return, but obviously Ambassador Tiam felt differently. But he will be here shortly to tell you that he now feels we should cooperate in the face of a common enemy. A moment later, Tiam moved into the image. Captain Kirk, in view of the external threat we both face, I would urge a complete pooling of our resources and information. Tow that end, I am prepared to acknowledge I have in my possession a recording of the alien object's emissions made during its earlier pass through the Empire. I am also prepared to acknowledge that my wife Jandra and her brother Adejan were not kidnapped, but transported to the Enterprise of their own free will. Kirk's eyes widen slightly at this evidence of a reformed Tiam who continued. Captain Kirk, I will transmit the recording of the object's emissions for your use. I will also, as you so desire, suggest to our musicians that they join yours in this effort to communicate with that thing out there. Kirk turned questioningly to Spock, who nodded in agreement. We accept your offer, Ambassador Tiam.
description: In this episode of Star Trek Audiobook Probe 3 of 4, we explore an entity that encounters a world with "grey and sharp-edged structures" built by mites who have inhabited space-going metallic bubbles. The entity learns about the atrocities committed by these creatures but is unable to prevent them from continuing their destructive ways due to its limited capabilities. As the episode progresses, we learn of the horrors faced by primitives on that planet as well as the destruction caused by a previous encounter with space-going mites.

Yes, as you suspect our world has something of value after all, something neither empire knew of. Why does a planet blessed with people like you need someone like me? A small smile flicked across her face. Experience, James. After today, I can attest to its value. Then Kurt recognized the sound of the attacker's anti-grav car taking off. Teilani held onto his arm, watching with him as the car banked over the barn and sped off toward the north. There must have been three of them. Kurt stared after the car. Then why didn't the third one come after us too? Teilani's voice shook with a burst of anger, with hatred. Why do they want to destroy my world? She pressed her head against Kurt's chest. He held her close. There were no more questions in his mind. No more uncertainties. Time was slipping too quickly through his fingers. He would not let this chance slip through as well. He was a civilian. James T. Kirk was a civilian. And he was moving forward again. With a likeness of being he had not felt in a long time, he headed toward the central hall of the San Francisco Travel Court. Teilani was waiting for him there, and her face lit up as she saw him emerge from the crowd. He didn't know what would happen next in his life. But here at the crossroads of the galaxy, he was no longer without direction. Teilani had a private yacht, standing by already, cleared for launch. Near it was the pilot, one of Teilani's hybrid race furrowed brow pointed ears. It was a great honor to meet you, sir. Full of hope, rejecting doubt, Kirk held Teilani's hand tightly as they boarded the yacht. Soon the yacht shot up through the night, heading toward Teilani's ship. Stars became crisp and unwavering. He was back in space. With satisfaction, he watched the western seaboard of North America recede on a flight viewscreen. He turned to Teilani. Is your ship in free orbit or dot? He took the dock james. He patiently folded his hands together, no doubt her ship had required servicing for the boyage head. But judging from their continued ascent, the pilot was taking them past the orbital plane of most commercial space dogs. Finally, the pilot announced their own docking approach. Kirk stared dead ahead, but saw nothing. Then the earth's thin layer of air flashed red, flared blue, white, and the sun was before them. In the sudden wash of that brilliant dawn, Kirk saw his destination. Teilani's ship was the Enterprise. Teilani, how? Teilani left her seat in Nelt by Kirk's. My planet negotiated for her james. But she was going to be used in more games. Teilani lightly kissed Kirk's cheek. A goodwill gesture on the Federation's part. She's to become the first ship in Charles' planetary defense group. The Enterprise called out to Kirk beyond the clouds, among the stars. One last time. The artificial gravity felt right. The air smelled a bit too much like chemical cleansers, but the temperature was set precisely where he preferred it. Overall though, Teilani was right. The Enterprise was different. Most noticeably, her warp generators were offline. The bridge environment was quieter too. The crew replaced by the slow flickering of the status lights on her new automated control stations. The greatest change of all though was not in the hardware of the vessel. It was in the crew. They were all Teilani's people, young Klingon Romulans in such robust, dynamic health that Kirk felt another year older for each one he saw. There wasn't a Starfleet uniform in sight. He smiled and studied his crew again. The oldest child he had seen was no more than twenty-five standard years. Captain, just so you know, the Enterprise served the best parts of her. Starfleet's taken those back. After a kind of depleted condition, if you know what I mean. You may give the word anytime, James. Kirk faced forward. The Earth filled the viewscreen, clouds wide, oceans sparkling. A place he no longer belonged. Navigator lay in a course for child, best possible speed, and take us out of orbit ahead in boss power. The Enterprise hummed to life around. After docking that same day, Czechovuhura and Sulu found themselves rushed to Admiral Androva Drake's house in San Francisco's Presidio District. Consider also the ramifications of an investigation into the use of the weapon. In the confusion that would follow, the individual worlds of the Federation would have to choose sides. The Council would be in chaos. Drake wrapped up the analysis with the ultimate conclusion. Ariadne walked over to an armchair, sat down, hooking one leg over the arm, letting it swing. How'd anyone as predictable as Kirk ever last so long in the service let alone command a starship? Drake grinned the smile of a predator. Years have not been kind to Kirk. I've done my best to keep it that way. The Excelsior was Sulu's ship, but at this moment everyone looked Spock. First, it may be that events are exactly as Admiral Drake has described them to us, Captain Kirk, for personal reasons, has become an unwitting pawn in an attempt to discover the secret of a powerful Klingon doomsday weapon. However, second possibility is that Telani's people themselves may be responsible for involving the captain. Oh, who were interrupted? And the third possibility, Mr. Spock. That nothing Admiral Drake said to us is correct. McCoy was the only one at the table who did not appear to be reassured by Spock's analysis. description: In this episode, James T. Kirk and his companion Alani visit a Romulan museum disguised as an armory where they find out it's actually a secret supply base for the Klingons, including a Romulan bird of prey with weapons stored on display cases. The museum is part of a larger secret operation by the Federation to prepare for potential war between Klingon and Romulan nations.

description: In this episode of "Star Trek Audiobook: The Ashes of Eden," Captain Sulu of the Excelsior follows up on an old acquaintance from his past adventures in the Federation's fleet. After learning that Kirk had looped back three times to muddy the subspace waters, they discover four possible trails leading away from the obvious choice. However, their pursuit is foiled by three Klingon battle cruisers dropping out of warp ahead of them, prompting Sulu to order a full power shield activation and phasers on standby in response to threats against Chancellor Azepur. The journey back to the Enterprise feels like déjà vu, but now they face an unexpected confrontation with armed forces rather than their old nemesis Kirk.

By now, Chekov realized they were under the Tellerite fore-shuttled in the cargo bay, and its crew was on board. Why has Jay done this to us? She said it herself, Pablo. No witnesses. But it's clear she needs bodies. What I still can't think of. What I still can't figure out is what Chau-Che Kameh is. Probably a coat-name of some kind. Maybe a type of experimental Klingon weapon system. Then it makes no sense Jay has done this to us. That's exactly what you're supposed to be buying. Not exactly, Pavel. Otherwise we wouldn't be here. The cargo bay was being depressurized. Warm, suffocation, and well in sceneration. Chekov strained every muscle against his bonds. Nothing gave. I'll miss you, Pavel. He fought once more against his bonds. He heard Uura do the same. His lungs ached. Black stars flared at the edges of his vision. Then there was no more air debris. The outer doors in cargo bay 12 opened before the straining pumps had removed all of the atmosphere. A sudden storm of ice crystals pruned from the growing gap between the moving doors. The tellerite ore shuttled in the cargo bay brought its maneuvering systems online. Pavel Jekyll had clenched his eyes shut to prevent the moisture coating them from sublimating in the vacuum. He had gassed desperately for a last one full of oxygen. But now, air flooded his lungs so easily he was shocked at opening one eye. Captain Hikaru Sulu, written down at his friends who were on the transporter platform. Uura's face tightened in confusion as she looked around. The Excellio, Sulu's laugh was deep and genuine. Oh, oh, oh, I'm sorry. I know I shouldn't. What the expression on your face, Pavel? Chekov didn't share Sulu's good humor. He was still shivering with the cold of space. How long have you been tracking us? Sulu's smile melted in the force of Chekov's withering stare. Pavel, calm down. You're safe now. We've tracked you since the beginning of your mission. I had my orders only to interfere if I thought you were in immediate danger of being killed. And someone did try to kill you, so let's do something about it. Uura held Chekov back and said, Sulu, it was jade. Sulu looked stunned. But this was her operation. She's supposed to be one of the top agents at Starfleet Intelligence. Uura told Sulu about the enigmatic exchange between court and jade in the cargo bay. Sulu walked around the transporter console and hit a control. Computer, identify a Klingon organization designated Imperial Forecasters, and in that context, Level Crimson. The Imperial Forecasters were a division of the Klingon Strategic Operations Bureau. The Crimson Level corresponds to Starfleet's security classification, Ultra Secret. It was responsible for planning doomsday scenarios. Uura cleared a throat. Computer, translate the Klingon phrase, Chump Chach-kim-ay. The phrase occurs in the context of the death poem of Molar. It translates as the children of heaven, referring to those who would inherit the lands destroyed by Molar during his final war against callers and his followers. Sulu shook his hand. Court was once involved in planning doomsday scenarios for the Empire, and offers to share something to what he believes is an illegal arms dealer? Chekov stated the obvious. It must be a weapon, Sulu nodded. A weapon so terrible, it would only be used in the event the Empire was defeated. And whatever kind of weapon the children of heaven is, it was enough to make a top Starfleet intelligent agent willing to kill two other agents so she could get the secret for herself. We're going to have to take this to Admiral Drake himself. Chekov looked puzzled. Admiral And-lo-Wadre by him. He was just appointed Commander-in-Chief Starfleet. You want us to report the in-person? I think we have to assume that a Starfleet intelligence agent like Jade has full access to current subspace codes. Sulu toggled another control of the Council. Captain to the bridge. Lay in a course for Earth. The instant Kirk coalesced from the transporter beam, he knew he had failed. He shifted his boots in the Sun-Baked Dust. He smelled the heat of the place and thought the impulse to grab his communicator and request an immediate beam out. His Starfleet duties were a little more than routine, filling his days with detail that in the end amounted to nothing. So he'd come here to the final port in a fruitless mission. He was in Iowa. On the farm. Where he had been born. Where so long ago his father had held his hand on summer nights and first shone him the stars, where he would find his first best destiny. He opened the front flap on his uniform jacket and a futile gesture against the heat. He walked toward the farmhouse. As his boots thudded on the worn wood of the porch steps, he tried not to remember how he had once raced up them. He put his hand on the quartz screen of the lock plate by the front door. The scanning mechanism was a century old like most of the fixtures in the house, but it still worked. The door lock clicked. Kirk stepped into the front hall. The house was empty. All the furniture long since gone to cousins. He looked around the two quiet house thinking about the fate of his work, his job. If he left Starfleet, he wouldn't even have that anymore. He went upstairs. His room was much smaller than he remembered. The doorframe still bore the marks his older brother, Sam, had made to measure Kirk's growth. The wood creaked downstairs. Kirk stopped breathing. There was someone else here. Kirk came alive. His hand reached instinctively for his belt and his phaser. But of course there was no weapon there. Weapons were no longer needed on this perfect earth. Kirk moved swiftly silently to the stairway. The hallway was empty. He glided down the stairs as silent as a Vulcan. He saw a shadow move across the hallway floor just for an instant blocking the sun. The intruder was in the kitchen. Like smoke, he moved through the hallway of his home and into the kitchen doorway. He was prepared for anything. Except for what he saw. The young woman, from the reception, of the Klingon brow, the Romulan ears. She wore a black form-fitting jumpsuit, a woman superbly muscled, an athlete by any standard. She exploded into a census. Dimly he thought he should say, something. Who are you? Her smile was instant. She moved toward him until she was so close he could feel the heat of her. I am Tae Lanie. The breath carried flowers and soft wheels. Erasing the staleness of the empty house. Her touch was incredible. Both soft and bitingly electric at the same time. He was aware of nothing but the weight of her body against his, the taste of her. The scent of her. He kissed her with an urgency he hadn't known in years, but suddenly he pushed her away and he felt her surprise. Her dark eyes seemed to glow. But James, at the reception I saw this in your eyes. What are you doing in my parents' home? How do you know me? The whole galaxy knows you. She moved a hand to the neck of her jumpsuit to the tiny control switch of the fabric sealer. She pressed a finger to the control. The fabric of her jumpsuit parted down her neck. There's time enough for talk later. Kirk willed himself to keep his eyes locked on hers. There won't be a later unless you answer me now. Suddenly, Tae Lanie's smile was one that encouraged friendship, not desire. Ask me, whatever you wish to know, James. I have no secrets from you. Why were you at the reception? To celebrate the selection of Starfleet's new commander-in-chief? That's not what I meant. Invitations went out to Starfleet personnel, diplomats, industry leaders from the Federation. Yes, James, and to the Klingon Empire, the Romulan Star Empire, the first Federation, the Unaligned Worlds. And which are you? She looked down for a moment as if the questions were difficult. Unaligned? For now. That made no sense to Kirk. The heritage of her brow and ears clearly said she was one of either the Klingon or Romulan empires. But your parents? Tae Lanie traced a finger along the sweep of one delicately pointed ear. Once, my home was a colony world. We opted for independence many years ago. Kirk's instincts instantly told him her statement was the beginning of the story. Her initial mind dazzling approached him and had been some sort of smoke scream. She had something to tell him. Something she wanted from him. The afternoon was shaping up to be far more rewarding than he had first thought when he had arrived. It was then the attack began. The kitchen window behind Tae Lanie erupted in a starburst of glittering glassite shards. A spray of green blood blossomed over her shoulder, expanding like a galaxy in space. Her scream was low, drawn out, distorted. She hit the floor, hair-flying, she slid, moaned, blood smearing from the angry green gas atop her shoulder, the black jumpsuit torn. The far wall shuttered with a spray of plaster. He scooped her into his arms and holding her securely. He burst through the kitchen doorway, heading for the stairway. He knew there was at least two attackers. The angled the two projectile blasts had told him that. The projectile weapons also gave Kirk a clue to the attacker's motives. If they had wanted a kidney, either Tae Lanie or him, they'd be using phasers to stun them. Their use of projectile weapons indicated they wanted to kill someone and have a body left to show for it, to prove that the job had been done or to teach others a lesson. Kirk could imagine there would be a few old guard clean rods who would want a phaser amount of existence, but he was certain even Spock would conclude that whoever was charging up the port stairs of his family farmhouse, they weren't after James G. Kirk. They were after Tae Lanie. He heard them fumbled with the lock plate. His glance swept upwards of stairs. The academy taught that high ground was always preferable, but that meant it was always expected. Kirk pushed his boot against a section of the wood paddling that ran up the side of the stairway. A hidden half-sized door popped open. The damn smell of the cellar had felled. It had been his playground as a child. He ducked down, forcing his way through the small door as he heard a projectile blast the front door's ancient lock plate. He sat down heavily on the top step, still holding Tae Lanie. She stirred and looked up at him. The instant after the cellar door clicked shut, Kirk heard two harsh voices. Their speech was clipped. He couldn't make out the language. Kirk eased Tae Lanie to the step below him. He placed a hand on her shoulder to guide her down the wooden stairs into the darkness. And the footsteps above resumed, became fainter. The attackers moved upward to the higher ground. Kirk smiled. This was going to be easy. He reached for his belt, brought out his communicator. He moved closer to Tae Lanie and put her arm around his waist. He tapped the silent emergency recall button on the communicator. In seconds, the Starfleet transporter grid would beam him and Tae Lanie to an orbital station. He brazed for the cool wash of the transporter beam. It didn't come. Whoever the attackers were, they had a subspace jammer operating nearby. The transporter wasn't going to save the day. But that suited Kirk. The two intruders remained upstairs, but eventually, they'd think about the cellar. In the darkness, Kirk guided Tae Lanie toward where he knew the far wall would be. He reached out blindly and touched the subtle wall. He slid his fingers along the rough polycrete until he found the edge of the tunnel door to the old bomb shelter. He found the small handle, twisted it. In the tunnel he found the light switch. Kirk motioned for Tae Lanie to go first. Kirk listened one last time for footsteps. They were coming downstairs fast. He entered the tunnel, pulled the door shut, threw the sliding lock. Run! They scrambled along the tunnel. It turned sharply at 30 meters where the entrance to the bomb shelter was. Tae Lanie's slow as she saw the bomb shelter's entrance, but it was not Kirk's destination. It would only be a trap. He urged her to keep running. The door to the barn entrance was dead ahead. He shoved open the door, pulled Tae Lanie through, then closed it behind them. They stood in a sunken stairwell, opened to the bar. Sunlight filtered him through the old doors. He sprinted up the polycrete stairs. He found some old hay bales by the empty horse stalls. Together he and Tae Lanie tossed five bales into the forest. The attackers would have to dig their way out once they realized they couldn't open the door. Tae Lanie whispered to him. I don't hear them. Kirk heard the thought of a vehicle door outside. He crept to a narrow gap between two boards in the barn's high wall. An anti-grav car was parked in the yard halfway between the barn and the farmhouse. The attackers wore nondescript civilian clothes that would not attract attention on any world. His attackers' foreheads were furrowed like a Klingons, but their ears were pointed. Tae Lanie, do you know them? Tae Lanie shook her head, but they're your people. Her dark eyes burned into him. They don't want me, James. They want you. Kirk didn't believe her. He watched the two Klingon Romulans in a heated conversation. The one in the vehicle slammed shut the cover of the subspace jammer on his lap. They would have to know it was functioning properly. They'd know that he and Tae Lanie were still somewhere near. Kirk stared at the anti-grav car and suddenly realized what he had missed. Tae Lanie, how did you get here? A car. I parked it down by the gate. Kirk calculated the odds and knew the car was too far away. The youth in the car got out. Both of them stood in the yard. Dark eyes sweeping the area. Weapons held ready. They're going to find us. If we're going to take control of the situation, we have to make them find us under our terms, not theirs. Tae Lanie raised an eyebrow in appreciation. Tell me what to do. Kirk looked around the barn. It was all so familiar. As kids, he and Sam had saved the Federation a thousand times here. He decided the enemy would never chance. It took less than a minute to set the trap. The Klingon Romulans were already beginning to move toward the barn. Kirk watched them from his vantage point high in the halot. Tae Lanie now crouched by the empty horse stalls. Kirk tossed a small piece of chip polycrete so it hit the barn door. Instantly both Klingon Romulans fired at the door, splintering its ancient wood. Then one of the youths ran forward, kicked away the remains of the two barn boards. He eased through, slowly, gleaming weapon leading the way. There's no escape. Except your fate. Diorably. Kirk held his position, knowing you could not be seen. The youth said something over his shoulder, his partner edged warily through the splintered door. Kirk waited till the two Klingon Romulans stood shoulder to shoulder than he tossed his second chip of polycrete. It landed far back in the barn's depths. It was Kirk's signal to Tae Lanie. She made her move. Like a molten shadow, she flew from a stall, summers holding over the half-height door, flipping over, landing precisely on her feet and continuing on. The barn rang with the sounds of explosions as the attacker's shots traced Tae Lanie's path, always a heartbeat behind. Kirk leapt from the halot, rocketing down on the rope looped around the old hay pulley, pulling up his legs just so to hit each attacker squarely in the back of each boot. The wrenching impact sent shocks of fire along Kirk's legs and up his back. He released the rope and landed running. One youth lay face down on the barn's polycrete floor, but his partner was on his knees. The kneeling youth brought his weapon up. Tae Lanie charged. Her blood curdling Klingon death cry filled the barn. The youth's weapon wavered. That moment's distraction was all Kirk needed. He leapt forward and hit the youth's shoulder to chest. It was the final indignity to Kirk's challenged muscles. Something tore in his shoulder. Kirk's teeth ground together. He tasted blood from the cuts on his face. He still grabbed the bare-armed youth by the front of his vest and drove in hard with a solid headbutt. Stars flashed before Kirk's eyes with a sharp crack of his forehead against the youth's heavy brow ridges. But green blood flooded from the attacker's nose. His dark eyes lost focus. Kirk sat back on the floor, taking inventory of his aching joints and limbs. Tae Lanie knelt beside him. She held both attacker's weapons. You heard James. Kirk laughed at the understatement. Tae Lanie frowned. You think this is amusing? No, I was just thinking that I haven't felt this good in years. When Kirk felt he could breathe without setting fire to his shoulder, he knelt beside one of the felt attacker's. He held his hand to the youth's chest and put his fingers to the youth's neck. The attacker was dead. I didn't hit him that hard. He went to the second youth, still faced down on the floor. The second youth was also dead and made no sense. They weren't meant to die from a blow to the jaw or a kick to the back. Tae Lanie tried to comfort him. But they were trying to kill you, James. He held Tae Lanie by the shoulders. Why were they trying to kill me? You owe me answers. But she touched his face again, held out a single finger, stained with red blood. His blood. There's a med kid in my car. He nodded wierly and started from the barn door. Tae Lanie quickly took hold of his hand as if to steady him.
description: In this episode of Star Trek audiobook "The Ashes of Eden," William Shatler reads the story of Captain James T. Kirk's reappearance on Arridian III, where he continues his journey as a hero's funeral. The audiobook explores the final adventure and reveals key details from the last days spent with William Riker and other Starfleet officers preparing for their return to Earth.

transcript: The Ugenix Wars, Volume 1. By Greg Cox, read by Anthony Stewart-Head. Captain's Logs, Tardate, 7004.1. Under top secret orders and Starfleet command, the Enterprise is enrude to the Paragon Colony on the planet's Sicker Axe. To evaluate that colony's recent request to join the United Federation of Planets, that issue is one of the Federation's fundamental principles. The center is old taboo, perhaps second only, to the prime directive in its scope and sanctity. Genetic engineering? Unhumans? Dr. Leonard McCoy was utterly aghast. He stared across the conference table at his friend and captain, James T. Kirk. Have the brass that Starfleet lost their paper pushing little minds? Human genetic engineering has been banned throughout the Federation since its very founding, and for good reason. Kirk smiled at his friend's predictably cantankerous response. Calm down bones. Nobody's talking about lifting the ban right away, just rethinking it a bit. After all, it's been 300 years since the Ugenix War. Good Lord James, you're a good man. You met, Khan. Don't you remember what sort of a monster you was? Kirk nodded. Only four years had passed since the captain had made the mistake of reviving the genetically enhanced crew of the SS Botany Bay, all of whom had been trapped in suspended animation since fleeing the Earth in the 1990s, following their disastrous defeat in the infamous Ugenix War. Their charismatic leader, Khan Nune and Singh, had briefly captured the Enterprise and nearly killed Kirk, before the captain had managed to turn the tables on Khan and his fellow supermen, stranding them on a primitive planet somewhere near the Muhtarra sector. Your point is well taken, Doctor. In fact, it's our first-hand experience with Khan and his followers at Persuaded Commodore Mendez to assign this fact-finding mission to us. Our recommendations will carry a lot of weight with the Federation Council when they meet to decide the future of the Paragon Colony on Sicker Axe. McCoy seems somewhat mollified. So what's the story with this so-called Paragon Colony anyway? How in blue blazes do we end up with a community of genetically engineered humans here in the 23rd century? Kirk led Mr. Spock, the only other person in the conference room, Phil McCoy in on the background of the colony. The Paragon Colony was founded over a century ago outside the Federation's sphere of influence by individuals who sought to create a genetically engineered society. The colony has had little or no contact with outsiders until very recently when they discreetly appealed for membership in the Federation. In exchange for a said membership, they offer the Federation generations of expertise in human genetic engineering. McCoy rode his eyes heavenward. God help us. Kirk leaned toward McCoy. To be honest, Bones, a few of our top strategies have called Starfleet's attention to the fact that humanity is threatened by species such as the Romulans and Klingons, who are physically superior to ordinary humans in many ways. They argue that we need to close the genetic gap by breeding enhanced humans who can stand toe-to-toe with whatever alien species we encounter. McCoy looked positively appalled. Jim, the Klingons are rushing over an evolutionary cliff, so we have to hurry up and join them? Good, Lord, we're talking about the very stuff that makes us human in the first place. Spock took a more objective perspective. Despite humanity's own unfortunate experiences, a number of other sentient species have indulged in eugenics without suffering the adverse consequences recorded in your history. I should have known you'd be in favor of this lunatic proposition. What else could one expect from someone whose people have done their damnedest to breed honest emotion out of their own blood and bones? Spock corrected McCoy. The Vulcan repudiation of emotion is a result of over two millennia of intellectual and philosophical discipline and not a matter of mere biology. Furthermore, I did not say that I supported the power gong-cullen is petitioned to join the Federation. At present, there is insufficient data on which to make that decision. McCoy sank back into his chair. Why do I even try to talk sense to you, you pointy-eared walking tricorder? What about you, Jim? What do you think about all this? Kirk's initial response to the Commodore's classified communication had echoed McCoy's. Why risk creating another calm? On further reflection, though, perhaps it was time to take another, less emotional look at the potential pros and cons of human genetic engineering. Doctor, I believe it was Samuel Hopkins of the first Continental Congress who said he had never encountered an issue so dangerous that it couldn't be talked about. With that in mind, gentlemen, I intend to keep an open mind until we arrive at Sicker Axe and hear what the colonists have to say. McCoy headed for the exit, but Spock lingered behind. A word of advice, Captain. While I do not share the good doctors' excessively visceral reaction to the matter at hand, his suggestion that you look to the history of your own world is not without merit. As we have learned through our own experiences in the past, the latter part of the 20th century was an extremely volatile period in Earth's history. Besides Kahn and his fellow genetic tyrants, a number of crucial variables were at work, including, for example, the covert activities of Gary Sevene and his associates. The future of the human race remains to be charted, Captain, but a fuller knowledge of the past can only inform your decisions in the days to come. Kirk recalled that Gary Sevene, an undercover operative for an unknown alien civilization, and his human partner, a young woman named Roberta Lincoln, had played key roles in the cataclysmic drive. And the cataclysmic drama of the Eugenics Wars. An excellent suggestion, Mr. Spock. How long until we reach Sicker Axe? At our current rate of speed, Captain, approximately 72 hours, 34 minutes. Please take the bridge, Mr. Spock. I believe I'll remain here for a while more. After Spock left, Kirk found himself alone within the slipping blue walls of the conference room. Computer, access Earth's historical records for the late 20th century. Begin with the first citation relevant to the topic designated Eugenics Wars. Processing request for data. Beginning historical display now. East Berlin, German Democratic Republic, March 14, 1974. Roberta Lincoln paced nervously outside the Russian Embassy, hugging herself against the chill of the cold night air. The young blonde woman peered at her wristwatch. It was ten past two in the morning. What's keeping Sävenen at Darncat? They should be back by now. The last thing she wanted to do was to attract the attention of the local cops, or worse yet, one of the innumerable informants working for the Stasi, the dreaded East German secret police. You think I'd be used to this sort of thing by now? Roberta had been working with Gary Severn, alias Supervisor 1994, for nearly six years now, ever since that unforgettable afternoon in 1968, when she'd shown up for what she thought was an ordinary secretarial job, only to find herself caught up in a bizarre happening involving nuclear missiles, talking computers, and a starship from the future. Roberta cast a wistful glance southward toward the lights of the Brandenburg Gate, only a block and a half away. The imposing marble arches, along with their attendant armed border guards and vigilant watchdogs, marked the frontier between East and West Berlin, making the safety of the Allied sectors seem tantalizingly close. Pacing nervously as she looked upward, a man in a business suit was repelling down the front of the embassy. The bottom end of a black nylon cable struck the sidewalk only seconds before the man himself touched down on the pavement. A tall, slender individual in a conservative grey suit, he looked to be in his late 30s. A sleek black cat was draped over his shoulders. A white collar studied with sparkling transparent gems glitted against the feline's glossy fur. The cat sprang from seven shoulders onto the pavement. Seven looked to the cat, quiet Isis. An enormous searchlight mounted atop a sentry tower just before the Brandenburg Gate swung in their direction, exposing Roberta, seven men Isis, to a blinding glare that lit up the entire block. Seven scooped up Isis and began running up the boulevard, away from the onrushing soldiers. This way Roberta. Roberta stared vailfully at the retreating back of her employer. I definitely had to talk to seven about hazard pain. Soldiers and dogs pursued the fleeing trio around a corner where dark and storefronts faced each other across an unremarkable strip of asphalt. Of the suspects, there was no trace at all. Only an odd blue mist that seemed to glow with its own faint luminosity. The swirling blue fog completely filled the empty vault-sized chamber. Seconds later, a breathless young woman stepped out of the vault, followed by a somewhat older man carrying a cat. Overhead lights came on automatically, revealing a tidy office decorated with contemporary furniture. Roberta was still winded from their headlong flight from the East German troopers. Gary Seven had managed to transport them back to New York City just in time. As the vault's heavy iron door swung closed, wooden panels slid out to conceal the door behind three shelves of cocktail grasses. Gary Seven's private office now looked entirely ordinary. Isis leapt from Seven's arms, landing nimblier on the plush orange carpet, where she promptly set to work licking the smell of East Berlin from her fur. Seven sat down at his desk and removed a thin sheaf of paper from the Manila envelope he had just borrowed from the Russian Embassy. Judging from the skull on his face, he didn't like what he was reading. According to these classified reports, the Russians have misplaced several of their top geneticists and biochemists. Unfortunately, many of the world's top scientists, particularly those specializing in applied genetic engineering, have seemingly dropped off the face of the Earth. Seven paused to let Roberta assimilate what she had just heard. Genetic engineering? She was familiar with the basic idea, but she thought that modern science was still years away from actually being able to tamper with anybody's DNA. Then again, most people didn't know about extraterrestrial social workers or instantaneous matter transmission. Seven looked up at her. This could have very disturbing consequences, Ms. Lincoln. Your people are nowhere near ready for that sort of control of your own genetic makeup. Roberta shook her head, wondering, how come whenever the human race grows up there suddenly my people? She couldn't resist the temptation to tweak Seven a little. Correct me if I'm wrong, but aren't you the product of generations of selective breeding and fancy genetic tinkering? South out was not numbered among Gary Seven's personal failings. My sponsors know what they're doing. The problem and the danger, Ms. Lincoln, is genocide of one form or another, and the very real possibility of genetic warfare. Galactic history teaches us that once a species succeeds in creating a superior version of themselves, it's then one very short step to viewing the rest of the species as unworthy, obsolete, and ultimately disposable. Roberta eyed him quizzically from across the room. How do I know that you don't make up half of this stuff? Well, that, Ms. Lincoln, you'll just have to trust me. Bye! Pouched on the back of the plush chair nearby, Isis mewed in agreement. Even after six years of working with Seven and Isis, Roberta knew frustratingly little about the mysterious aliens behind this little operation. Just that they had snatched up Seven's great, great, great ancestors some six thousand years ago, trained their offspring for Upteen Generations, then sent good old supervisor 194 back to Earth to keep his fellow humans from starting World War III. Whenever she asked Seven about his superiors up there, he told her that she didn't need to know anything more, that greater knowledge of the Aegis, as he sometimes called them, would not assist her in her work and might actually compromise the alien's grand design should the information fall into the wrong way. One of these days she vowed she would pry the full scoop out of Seven. Now, however, did not seem like the right time to press the issue. The boss had more pressing matters on his mind, like these inexplicably AWOL chromosome counters. Seven leaned back into his chair. With any luck, we can nip this dangerous experiment in the bud before it goes too far. The Sterile Air-conditioned Laboratory at the Secret Base for the Chrysalis Project resembled a gleaming, high-tech kitchen. Dr. Sarina Ka'ur was pruning yet another collection of human embryos. The 30-ish scientist felt an undeniable sense of accomplishment. Each of the two dozen embryos arrayed upon the counter was suspended in a sterile dish containing an artificial growth medium of her own invention. Each was the result of a long and meticulous process of elimination and experimentation, expressly designed to engineer human embryos genetically superior to those created through the random genetic shuffling of ordinary reproduction. The Chrysalis Project aspired to create a new breed of man and woman. Of these two dozen eggs, only those she judged suitable would be implanted in the surrogate mothers who had agreed to carry the babies to term. She patted her abdomen, already bulging slightly beneath her voluminous white lab coat. She, along with nearly every other female member of Chrysalis, was glad to volunteer her own body as a biological petri dish in which the future of humanity was growing day by day. Studying an embryo beneath a powerful electron microscope, she couldn't help marvelling at the exquisite machinery tucked away in the nucleus of every cell in the fetus. Nearly two meters of stringy nucleic acids capable of producing an individual who might someday change the world, just like their older brothers and sisters. Her imagination pictured the struggling chaotic world outside this pristine laboratory, an endangered planet filled with flawed imperfect men and women. If only they knew what tomorrow brings. The man at the hotel palestros front desk smiled at Roberta. Welcome to Rome, Dr. Niri. May I see some identification? Roberta nodded, pushing around in her handbag for her phony ID. She knew from experience that Gary Seven's advanced Beta 5 computer manufactured the best forgeries on the planet. She blithely handed over Verona Caniri's passport and driver's license. Isis squawked impatiently from within the plastic carrying case at Roberta's feet. Roberta sighed inwardly. It was my idea to bring the damn cattle on. The clerk handed back her documents along with a set of room keys. Roberta nodded gratefully, then hefted both her suitcase and Isis' carrier off the floor. She yawned, pretending to be jet lagged from the long flight from America. In fact, she and Isis had taken the Blue Smoke Express to a deserted back alley two blocks away. As far as any curious onlookers might be concerned, she was just another newly arrived delegate to the International Conference on Genetic Research and Experimentation. Two months of pursuing assorted useless leads had not brought her and Gary Seven any closer to solving the mystery of the missing scientists. Her mission in Rome was twofold. Keep a sharp eye out for any of the absent geneticists who might be tempted to attend the conference, while simultaneously presenting a likely target to whomever was responsible for the scientists' disappearances. Just call me Bade. No time for sightseeing while the fate of the world hangs in the balance. When Roberta reached her room, she liberated Isis from the confines of the plastic carrier. Without so much as a meow of thanks, the jet black feline scurried away to check out the bathroom. A few seconds later, the door to the bathroom closed behind the cat. Don't take all day in there Isis. You're not the only one who wants to freshen up. Eventually the bathroom door swung open and the cat patted out onto the carpeted floor. In fewer than twenty years after the agreement was signed, Nimbus 3 was a desert, and the starving homesteaders fashioned homemade weapons and began to fight each other for the dwindling gathering gathered on the desert horizon. The alien homesteader John paused in his work of drilling for water and stared beyond the shimmering bands of heat at the growing cloud of dust.
