Fearlessly the stranger approached him and gently removed the weapon from John's trembling hands. Your pain runs deep. John turned away, overwhelmed by guilt and grief. His touch spoke of great physical strength. Let us explore it together. The stranger collected himself and began to concentrate deeply. John immediately became transfixed, tears flooded his dirty cheeks. Then the stranger spoke. Each of us hides a secret pain which must be reckoned with. Join my quest as a stranger helped him to his field to unask. What is it you seek? What all have sought since time began, the ultimate knowledge. To find it will need a starship. John from, puzzled. There are no starships on Nimbus 3. John could not see the stranger's shadowed face, but he heard the amusement in his toe. Perhaps I have a way to bring one here. description: In this episode of Star Trek audiobook "Star Trek V, The Final Frontier," Simon & Chuster's audio works presents an adaptation of William Schatner and Harv Bennett's story. Featuring J.M. Dillard as the narrator, George DeKade reads the personal log from Commander Spock on Nimbus 3 after a successful mission but with significant loss due to its recent turbulent history and the challenges faced by the crew in adapting to the new ship. The episode explores the consequences of neglecting peace efforts for the betterment of the galaxy and the harsh realities that can follow when unchecked greed and ambition lead to destruction.

transcript: Simon and Schuster audio presents Star Trek, Vulcan's Heart by Joseph Sherman and Susan Schwartz, read by Tim Russ. At Ambassador to Serix Estate on Vulcan, Lieutenant Jean-Luc Picard of Starfleet, 24 Earth years old, was feeling painfully aware of his youth amid this distinguished gathering. He was trying at the same time not to sweat. Triox injections might help a human deal with Vulcan's thinner atmosphere, but the climate was still unbelievably warm. Already hotter than good old Taren Hell, isn't it? Picard turned sharply and found himself staring into a weather-worn, aged face. Doctor Admiral McCoy. At ease, son, you're not going to tell me you read about me in school, are you, Lieutenant, whoever? Picard, sir. Jean-Luc Picard. A pleasure, Lieutenant Jean-Luc Picard. McCoy murmured in his ear. Nice turnout, but then Spock's earned it. Picard tried to picture himself sitting in a chair in relatively cool shade, but the fantasy wasn't working. He turned to McCoy. About the betrothal, I understood that it was normal Vulcan practice for to take place between 70-year-old children. That's right, but today it's two adults getting betroved. Two people who've been colleagues and friends for decades now. There are exceptions to every rule. Picard rather suspected that this late betrothal was more a matter of convenience, or maybe politics, when someone as cunning as the father of the groom ambassador, Serik, was involved. He suddenly realized that a high-ranking officer had moved to McCoy's side, Captain Truman House of the Armstrong, Commander Savic's ship. McCoy smiled at Captain House. Worried about your first officer? Hardly, Commander Savic can take care of herself. This blast furnace of a world to see this. He'd better be good to her, or ambassador or not, he'll hear from my crew and me. The dawn wind rustled. The star fleet officers straightened to attention. Serik, in the dark blue-gray robes of a Vulcan ambassador, stepped from behind one of the reddish polished stones. Then ambassador Spock stepped forward, just as impressive as his father. Captain House whispered to McCoy, There! Will you just look at her? Commander Savic glided forward from between two pillars, her dark hair spilling down her back. She stopped beside Spock, and he murmured a few words to her. Into the amphitheater came a tendons bearing a sedan chair, whose occupant was female and very old. McCoy stood at attention. My God, it's Tapao! Picard drew a startled breath. Tapao of Vulcan had been one of the most important political forces on the planet for at least two centuries. Spock dropped to one knee before Tapao, who leaned forward to touch the ambassador's temple. Tapao beckoned to Savic. She sank down in a reverence as graceful as a dance, and they both sank into trance at the old woman's touch. At Tapao's nod, the betrothed pair began to speak. First Spock, my mind to your mind. Then Savic, my thoughts to your thoughts, parted from me and never parted. Never and always touching, and touched. At those words, Tapao extended her ancient hands to cover Spock's and Savic's fingers, as if sealing their vows. Now thee are one. At the appointed time thee shall be drawn together. Spock rose and held out his hand. Two fingers extended for the public contact permitted to bonded pairs. Savic brushed Spock's fingers formally with her own. And that was very much that. McCoy turned to Picard. Come on, Lieutenant! Show us over. Let's get the rest of the formalities over with. The Starfleet officers formed into a long line, and one by one, they paid their respects. When it was Picard's turn, he bowed and raised his hand in the split-fingered Vulcan salute he had been practicing for days. Spock nodded. Welcome to Vulcan. Savic added, your presence honors us. Captain Howes approached Savic. Savic, may I ask you a question? She raised an eyebrow. As you wish, sir. Will you require more time here on Vulcan? You and the Ambassador? After Garrett explained what she knew to Keel, the admiral gave the bad news to her straight. The protection of the male vocalony must be top priority if we do have any hope of avoiding all out war. Under the circumstances, Captain Garrett, you're on your own. I don't need to tell you to govern yourself accordingly. As for Savic, Sarek of Vulcan has contacted me. Commander Savic must be returned to Vulcan for debriefing. As the Honor Blade sped out and away from Romulus, it cut across the neutral zone, unploped for greater speed. If the Fates were with them, they would outrace the fleet to Narendra Three. As the universe blurred and blazed about them, Charvanik leaned forward slightly and thought, We are coming, Voskyar, my old Tholoft. We will overtake you and your arrogantly named Victorious, and that so dishonorably launched fleet. Charvanik had nothing but pride in her crew. Then Navigator Akenda announced, coming out of warp speed in 20 seconds. Charvanik realized that the fleet must emerge from the warp drive some distance from Narendra Three. There would not be much time to wait. In the Narendra system, Seven ships as one flashed out of warp speed, drawing the suddenly curving light of space around them like a cloak of blazing colors. Charvanik allowed herself one quick flash of exultation at the glory of the site. Her communications officer sub-commander Selta turned to her. Commander, I think I can tap into fleet communications without being detected. The bridge's main viewscreen blurred from a view of a viewable colony ahead, to General Voskyar, who was finishing the speech to his troops. We go to smash the Klingon base, the military base of Narendra Three, and we go now, and we shall return victorious. Voskyar! Selta, his face pale, looked up at Charvanik. Commander, communication is coming in for us from the victorious. From General Voskyar. Pinamon Selta. Voskyar shouted at her. Honor blade, you are in a system without orders. You will stand down, lower shields, and prepare to be boarded. All engines stop sub-commander Selta. Open fleet-wide hailing frequencies. Straightening in her chair, Charvanik broadcast to Voskyar's fleet. This is Charvanik, Commander and Nobleborn of the Honor Blade. Know this warriors. Narendra Three is no military base. They are unarmed civilians. Frequencies being jammed, Commander. Voskyar's fierce image formed on the screen, laughing. Now is this not tragic? She is still the Federation's pet, but worry not, warriors of the Empire. When we return in victory, she will no longer inflict madness or imperial connections on us. Voskyar's image vanished, replaced by a vista of space and the Seven Romulan ships. So, this is what our death looks like, Charvanik thought. Then, suppressing emotions as ruthlessly as any Vulcan, she gave the order. Attack! The Honor Blade quickly sent three warbirds on the fiery path to Erebus. But the element of surprise was gone now, and Voskyar was shouting orders at the fleet. Close ranks. Close ranks, damn you. At Charvanik's signal, the Honor Blade zoomed in a daring rush between two closing ships, firing at them while they dared not fire lest they hit each other. But now the Honor Blade's flank was exposed. Charvanik shouted, deflectors up! Too late. The Honor Blade lurched wildly, then lurched again. But they weren't dead. Damage report. Weapons down three-quarters commander, deflectors at minimum, life support holding at 78%. As reports came in, Charvanik learned there were twenty dead, forty-seven more injured. She wondered why Voskyar did not finish them off. Leave the traitor there. We will take the ship in tow on our way back to the homeworld after our glorious victory. Charvanik realized that Voskyar would rather run the risk of leaving her alive, so that there would be more glory for him. She watched the surviving ships of his fleet streak on toward their prey. The Honor Blade helpless to stop them. And then Charvanik began firing off orders to the crew. Engineering, I want those engines back online as quickly as possible, Tarkvi. Medic, see to the wounded. Give the worst off the final honor. Your hand is mine. She paused, seeing the tension in all the bridge crew. All of you hear me. We may not see our homes again. You knew that. We may well die reviled as traitors. But by all the powers that may be, if we must die, it shall be as warriors. We shall die with Honor. With Honor! We shall die with Honor. We shall die with Honor. We shall die with Honor. We shall die with Honor. We shall die with Honor.
description: In this podcast episode, Lieutenant Jean-Luc Picard of Starfleet is introduced as a member of the high-ranking officers at the Ambassador's estate on Vulcan, where he has encountered several notable individuals including Spock. The conversation highlights the age disparity between them due to their respective ages and introduces an unusual betrothal occurring between two adults on this alien world.

transcript: Spock was hard put not to tremble as Karak's body was carried off, but the violence of the knife-fight still echoed within him, striking ancient cords Spock most firmly refused to hear. Control, he told himself. Control. As calmly as though Karak's and Ruinex duel to the death had never happened, Narviat glanced at Spock and those he trusted. It did not include Ruinex. Very deliberately Spock moved to Ruinex's side. Let me see your injuries. Ruinex shrugged. Miracuts. I've endured worse. Ignoring Ruinex protests, Spock staunch the blood with a wad of torn off tunic. Narviat glanced at Ruinex. You do realize, of course, that after what has occurred, you can't possibly return to your patron and your old wife. Ruinex nodded stiffly. No need to tell me, sir. I had no future there. So be it, Ruinex. Come. Narviat led them through a maze of the tunnels to a cave furnished with a makeshift table and chairs. He held up a cautioning hand. Remember where we are at this time. Namely we are practically under our noble praetor's feet. One of the rebels snickered. Next time he'll be under ours. All the Romulans laughed at that, save for a stocky man in the dark robes of a scholar. Narviat frowned slightly. Thericott is something wrong. I merely think it less than wise to celebrate before the battle has begun. Ruinex studied him a moment longer, then shrugged. But Spock continued to watch the scholar. Were it not a breach of courtesy, he would already have a hand on Thericott's temples to know his thoughts. Spock turned his attention to the table and the unrolled charts. He tried to focus on what seemed the same plans, the same useless debates. There was no logic to his anger. Then the realization struck Spock with a force of a savage blow. But bothered him was not from him alone, but from all around him and he shouted out. A trap. We have been betrayed. Members of the praetor's guards roughed forward as he shouted the warning, storming in from both entrances with the eruptor rifles ready and knives drawn, blocking escape. Spock fought with bare hands and ferocity at the heart of him. A cold, utterly rational core reminded him. They cannot fire their disruptors in such close quarters, not without killing their fellows. But I have not killed. I will not kill. The Romulans fought with the sheer ferocity of those who know that death and combat is far preferable to death by slow, humiliating pain. Ruinek hesitated for a moment. Then he hurled himself into the battle. Knives flashed. All at once, there were no more foes to fight. As Spock stood pending, Narviat's allies moved from fallen body to fallen body, hunting remaining signs of life. The wounded guards received no mercy. One foe remained, backing away. Thericott. Spock lunged at the scholar. Caught him. Why Thericott? Despair blazed from Thericott's eyes. Drolith has my family. Had my family. He has betrayed me. Once he had all the information I could give him, he murdered my sweet wife, Katara. I know this. You see that dead guard? The monster who lies there? He wears my wife's marriage bracelet on his belt, which he could not have removed while Katara lived. Narviat put a hand on Thericott's shoulder. I must ask you this. How much have you revealed? Thericott blinked fiercely. Not that much. Drolith knows me, meh. But I did not betray you by Nick. Thericott's different, proudly. I shall not be a burden. A knife flashed in his hand. Triumph, Narviat. Slay Drolith for me. Send him to burn forever. Then with quick academic precision, Thericott slashed open his own throat. Narviat caught his sagging body, heedless of the spouting blood. With the smallest of shutters, Narviat let the body go slack. Then fumbled in his belt pouch till he had found two crystals and placed them on Thericott's eyes. Then he murmured a prayer. Covered with Thericott's blood, Narviat got to his feet. We cannot linger. Some guards might have escaped. All of you leave. Wait for my signal. We shall meet again. Without another word, Narviat began climbing the nearest stairway. When he was at the surface, Spock heard a crisp voice say, Admiral Narviat, you are under arrest. He had effectively blocked the entrance to the stairway, hiding Spock and Ruenek. Spock motioned to Ruenek. Back! They stood in utter silence as Narviat was marched away. Spock, testing, found his mind remaining mercifully clear. The fight with the Romulan guards temporarily banked the fires of Pawn Far. Logic told him that Narviat would not be executed immediately. The Admiral was too important in rank and bloodline and was too popular with the people. He turned to Ruenek. Gather the others. They cannot have gone far. Soon the other rebels hurried forward, eyes wild with shock and fury. Silence. Hear me out. Some of you, I know, work in the government bureaucracy. You have access to a great many offices. Here is what we shall need. And Spock told his plan. After they had gone to do what he had asked, he and Ruenek cautiously climbed the stairway. The alley was empty. As they left the alley and entered a busy street, Ruenek turned to Spock. We have a new problem. You can hardly go back to Commander Charvanick's empty house and you can certainly not go on to Admiral Narviat's estate. And I can't bring you to my former quarters either. Indeed. However, I have a better sight in mind. The Imperial Palace. Ruenek's stomachs. What better place to hide? Come to Ruenek. Let's see if the Emperor will receive us. Drawloth's guards were still patrolling outside the Imperial Palace. Ruenek, playing the role of Spock's bodyguard, told them. This is the Akademician's Simicos of Bardet, honored by his Imperial Majesty. The guards were wary. Akademician. Spock acted his pedantic role. Precisely. Now kindly step aside. You would not wish the Emperor to learn that I had been detained. As the massive gates swung open, Spock and Ruenek entered the gardens and found a network of streams and ponds, too regular in shape to be natural. The water sparkled in the sunlight and fish glinted here and there below the surface like so many living green and yellow jewels. Ruenek pointed to a tall, lean figure. That is the Emperor himself. Fisher said to be the Emperor's special study. Spock noted that Emperor Sharkhek was clearly no young man, but there seemed to be nothing of the decrepit figurehead who had collapsed during the meeting of the Senate. Spock realized the Emperor had been playing a role, fighting for survival. As they approached, the Emperor looked at Spock's medallion. So interesting. I have never given a medallion to you. Who are you? Ruenek with a gasp fell to one knee. Ah! Stan! You make me uncomfortable. Then the Emperor frowned at Ruenek. But you are injured. Spock spoke for Ruenek. Subcommanded Ruenek has been in a jewel of honor and won. Sharkhek nodded at Spock. I see. Quite admirable. And you are... Ruenek interceded. Your Majesty, this is academician Simecos, a distant kinsman of Commander Charvanek and Admiral Naviatt. The ancient eyes studied Spock shrewdly. And thus, kin to myself, eh? Very distant perhaps? Ah! What the sub-command there is weary from his wounds. A casual wave of the Emperor's hand brought several servants running. Some in my position. Make this officer comfortable. Go with them, Ruenek. Gazing after Ruenek, the Emperor murmured to Spock. Now, walk with me, Simecos. Or, whoever you truly are. Spock spoke cleanly. I am a Vulcan. Are you? How fascinating. Now, knowing of the Vulcan reputation for reasonable honesty, are you here as a vanguard to Federation attack? Spock met the Emperor's gaze directly. No, I am not. My word on my honor and the honor of Vulcan, I am not. And why, then, are you here? There is one who imperils us both, the Empire and the Federation. You mean, Drolith? I do not fear the truth. I brow-raised Spock countered. Then I will ask this. Do you know of the attack in motion against Narentra III? The wise, fierce eyes glanced away. Oh, yes, I know. But I can do nothing. A fool so seduced by my scholarly research, I forgot what I was. Never do that. Never forget. But you are Naviad's associate, and our Naviad is ambitious, even ruthless. But he is, underneath it all, a worthy son of this house. If Naviad dies, I see no way to replace Drolith. And now, Naviad has been arrested. Yes, I have my sources of information. Do what you must do, only for the sake of the people. Drolith sat at his work desk in his office, studying the computer stream, not bothering to glance at the guard who was reporting to him. And there is nothing else, my traitor. Yes, the academicians, Simicos, did visit with the Emperor, but they stayed out near the fish ponds where there is no place for spy eyes or ears. And Simicos' aid. That might have been one sub-commander runic, but none of our people could get a clear image. Academician Simicos and his aid left the palace long before nightfall and took lodgings near the Imperial University of Kiberitan. There, he filed for permission to use an office in the Bureau of Statistics and Information. The file was on Drolith's screen, together with the research proposal, a comparison of grain consumption by military versus civilians on the Romulan colony worlds. Drolith glanced up at the guard. I wish a close watch kept on the research. See to it. Seric! The little aid scurried inside. My traitor? The Emperor is about to be ill. Empmanship for medical treatment. Of course. See to it. Drolith turned back to the console, keyed in certain security codes and the image on the screen sharpened from text to visual. A spy eye staring into a prison cell. The man who sat on the cell's cot wore prison garb. His hair hanging loose about his face, looked as though he had combed it with his fingers. Drolith's smile thinned. Naviatt was entirely too secure in the knowledge that the praider dared not torture him in any way that would leave physical marks. The drugs were too risky with so important a prisoner. Drolith flipped open a secure channel to give an order. Add variable frequency subsonics. But carefully. If he is reduced to lunacy, you will join him. Drolith knew that eventually Naviatt would break and surrender the details of his treasonous plot. And then of course, during the forthcoming victory celebrations over Narenza III, he would die a traitor's death. Promiliating, protracted and agonizing. As the Enterprise sped towards the Narendra system, the chronometers all told Captain Garrett the same cold fact. Three hours had come and gone and they were still a ship's hour from Narendra III. Lieutenant Commander Verani looked up from his communication station on the bridge. Captain, long-range scans picking up something. Two, three, no four, four, down from seven. That's progress. Hamelsman Castillo registered sudden alarm. They're declocking. Though Tholov's voice was very soft, his body and antenna became rigid without rage as he stared at his data. Bad news. The Romulans had begun to fire under Andrew III. Garrett ordered that tactical display be put on screen. The display enlarged, just in time to reveal three Klingon scout craft exploding into white hot fireballs. Disruptors engulfed another Klingon ship into a blinding blaze. Captain, I'm picking up a Klingon message. To all ships in this sector, now hear this. Our Empire's civilian outpost on Narendra III has been attacked in overpowering numbers without his devoid of all honor. A small flotilla of one man's ships struggled up from the planet's gravity well. A warbird that seemed to be hovering. A predator with outstretched wings picked Klingon ships off almost lazily one by one. The image on the view screen reformed. An elderly Klingon propped himself up against his console. Flames surged in background. Garrett called. Narendra Station, this is the Federation starship Enterprise. We're on our way. To her astonishment, the Klingon gave her an almost gallant salute. Well met, Enterprise. Hunt with us. Fight at our side. We've been such glory that warriors will howl to honor our memory. The image suddenly flared, broke up, and reassembled. Through the static, Garrett shouted. Narendra Station, we are coming. Hold on. The Klingon laughed. Ha ha ha. Before I jettison station records, have you a word for our poets to remember, Enterprise? Garrett matched the Klingon's determined green. Tell your bards and those pointed Romulans that before we're through the Romulan language will be spoken only in hell. The Klingon roared with laughter. Ha ha! Well said, Enterprise. Welcome to our war. The Klingons around him took up the ritual battle cry. Hetikwomek Hakashotam! It is a good day to die. The station shuttered. The old Klingon screamed in pain and rage as a piece of debris struck him. Castillo warned. Captain, the station's going to blow. The explosion was blinding. Behind her, Garrett heard Tholoff's sharp intake of breath. Captain, we are getting some gravimetric anomalies. Some manner of rift is opening up. Garrett waved Tholoff to silence. Steady, bring phasers online. Marani called out. Captain, one of the war birds is headed toward us. Garrett rattled off a series of orders. Load photon torpedoes, shields on full. Lock on target, fire at will. The war bird's disruptors blazed with sudden poisonous green light. The Enterprise shuttered, then rocked from side to side. Garrett gave another order. Lay down a trail of photon torpedoes. We're going to dodge that war bird. On my mark. Now! The Enterprise's sudden change of direction caught the war bird by surprise. Science officer Tholoff interrupted. Fluctuation's increasing, Captain. As the anomaly grew, space tore, revealing churning lights in all the colors of heaven. Disruptor fire blazed from the pursuing war bird. The Enterprise convulsed. A deadly light bloomed on Garrett's board. Fluctuation's in the structural integrity field. Two war birds bracketed the ship, firing with efficient viciousness. The Enterprise bucked again, rocking almost out of control. The ship held together. One by one, ship's communications brought Garrett news of the loss of irreplaceable people as the ship failed. When the ship took another hit from one of the three surviving war birds, a console came crashing down across her legs. Her gaze was on the war birds, preparing to fire what she knew would be a fatal salvo. A flash of memory. Her self, as a tall, gawky young girl, who had looked up at the stars from the fields of home and staked her claim to them. She straightened as best she could. If ace of action, Mr. Castillo, where there's life, there's hope. Warp engines are offline, Captain. With a blaze of green, disruptor fire engulf the ship. Shield down, Captain. Debris raked the bridge. Garrett heard Verani screaming. They were trapped. The shields down, they could not stand. They ordered. Release the log buoy. Then she opened the hailing frequency to the broadest possible van. This is Captain Garrett. She struggled for enough breath to finish her distress call, then stiffened with horror as she stared at the screens. The anomaly was moving. The enterprise was being sucked into it. The rift twisted as it opened, taking on aspects of a wormhole. White light erupted, shading up to purple. Then the raving of the Romulans' destructor fire paled by comparison. Then everything went black. On the honor blade, Charvanek impatiently hit a communications button. Lock V, her engineer replied. Ready, Commander. It's as good as it's going to get. We finally got the engines functioning well enough to get the battered lady back under the security of her cloak. Charvanek glanced about the wreckage of the bridge and opened ship-wide communications. Hear me, all of you. Contact the first officer if you choose not to continue the fight. You can go in the shuttles. There is to be no shame attached to any who do so. She waited but no one on the crew took her up on her offer. Charvanek's voice showed her pride. My eaglits, you will snatch honor from the halls of Erebus itself. She drew her honor blade, blooded it against a thumb in ritual sacrifice, as her ship crept toward Narendra Three. Suddenly, over the communications channel came a human voice. This is Captain Rachel Garrett of the USS Enterprise. Charvanek ordered that the honor blade de-cloped. Weapons taught thee. Do we have weapons? Powering up, Commander, but it's going to take time. All space suddenly seemed to blaze with a blinding blue-white light. A blaze into which the Enterprise vanished. Charvanek blinked her eyes, dazzled. A crew member called out. An anomaly, Commander. A rift in space. Charvanek ordered. A pervasive action. The overworked engines groaned into life and suddenly died. Her bridge crew reported. Commander, ship's instruments just reversed themselves. But in the next instant, Commander instruments are returning to normal. The ferocious rainbow patterns of the rift subsided, then abruptly quickened again. The Enterprise was visible again and fighting more fiercely than before. After fire raved out, followed by a salvo of photon torpedoes. Family Enterprise's shields wavered and fell. Tuck-fi interrupted from engineering. Weapons powered up. Charvanek gave the order to attack the Warbirds. The honor blade leapt forward, disruptors firing even as its engines faltered. Charvanek leaned forward in her chair. False Guiar's Warbird, the victorious, laid dead ahead. Charvanek shouted at the viewscreen. Now we die together, False Guiar. Ramming speed. The victorious, at the last possible moment, more energy blazed from the honor blade, but the hit was only a glancing blow. The victorious was turning. It would be False Guiar's kill. The first onslaught took out the honor blade's shields and center bridge crew hurtling across the deck. The second broadside disabled its warp engines. The honor blade and its crew waited for the third salvo, which would surely send it to the last review. They waited while their life support faltered. Charvanek uncapped a switch, marked with the emblem of the Warbird. Initiate final honor sequence on my mark. Now, for one breathless moment, the sequence began. But then circuits exploded, fused, and fell still. My children, I offer you my profound apology. She held up her own honor blade, kissed the gleaming ancient steel, and set it down on the blood-stained, battered deck. She drew her sidearm and vaporized the blade. It at least would not be stained by captivity. She had time for one last glance about the honor blade's ruined smoky deck. She touched the amulet that was on a chain around her neck. It contained a data storage device to which she had transferred the record of the battle. Then the transporter beam caught her. In the victorious brig, Charvanek knelt by Tarkvi, her engineer. Why, she wondered, couldn't the fates have given him the mercy of a swift death. Tarkvi, I can still grant you the final honor. Do you consent? Relief filled his voice. Yes, nobleborn. She ordered the rest of her crew to keep watch. She traded her grip on Tarkvi's hand, for one on his shoulder, then rested her other hand against his face. She whispered as intimately as if they had been lovers. Thank you for these many years, Tarkvi. Tell them an Arabis of the honor blade. And when they ask whom you serve, tell them, I am heralded for Charvanek, for Liviana. As Tarkvi's eyes widened in amazement that she confided her secret name, she snapped his neck. A commotion in the corridor behind the brig's force field brought her to stark alertness. The field snapped off as a man wearing a commander's insignia stepped in. Molskyar's fleet second. When he removed his helmet, Charvanek was almost speechless. It was Tau. He had not changed in all the years since he stood at the right hand. You look well, Tau. Careerism agrees with you. What else was I to do? What do you think would be left to a sub-commander whose commander had disappeared? I secured a position at the Academy on Bardet. It was the best I could do. Then in the last purge, the Praider ordered me back to ship duty, assigned me to General Volskyar. He hesitated, then continued. I have heard that you asked for aid for your crew. He had pawned a small, carefully wrapped ricotta trace of a familiar pungent odor. Too wrath. Quick, painless suicide. Reluctantly she shook her head. There is not enough here for all my crew. Tau glanced at the dead engineer. I shall send guards for the body and perform the rites myself. But then he paused. Is there truly nothing else I can do? Charvanek broke the chain holding her amulet, the trinket that held the true record of Nerenger III. She pressed the amulet into Tau's reluctant hand, and offering for the dead. I would like a kinsman to have it if possible. Tau knew she met Navi at. She gave her the briefest of hand-to-chest salutes. Then left. In a faceless government building in Kibera, Tann, Spock and Ruaneck found the office where the rebels had the false research project underway. Room 235 was as grey and bland as everything else. A small chamber, crowded with antiquated files, old-fashioned tape storage, and somewhat more modern consoles. Spock inquired if there had been visitors, and a thin-faced young man named Jaren answered. Two times so far, attendants have stopped by to see how we were managing. Ridda, a sturdy woman of no certain age, snorted. And they checked our materials too thoroughly for mere attendants. Spock gave her a sharp-warning glare. With meticulous pedantry that made the Romulans mutter under their breath, he paged through every bit of the gathered material until he had found a security device. He said in the calm voice of an academician, what is this? Surely, some manner of security device. What carelessness. Someone must be wondering even now where he lost it. We shall keep it safe. Spock wrapped up the tiny spy eye with fussy care so securely that no signal could be received by anyone watching or listening. And two of the rebels lifted a massive file cabinet to one side to reveal a ragged opening in one wall. With a wary glance back at Spock, Ruenet crept through the opening. The computer consoles that had been set down in a hastily cleared area seemed almost jarringly modern amidst the dust. Jaren grinned. We asked for corridor B because I remembered that it was slated for renovation. That room 235 should happen to adjoin this thing. Look, he's not logical. Let me remind you that Drolith is not a fool. He is certain to have already puzzled out that Semicos, Commander Charmnack, and Admiral Narviat are connected. Narviat's release must be our first priority. Then Spock asked if anyone could hack into Drolith's own security cameras and an earnest young Romulan barely more than a boy sat at a console. Soon the young Romulan stabbed at a volume control. I have it. I've found slightly than adjusted the game. Sorry, that's as good as it's going to get. Spock bruskely waved into silence and concentrated on the screen. Drolith and with him General Volskiar. The room felt quiet. Everyone paid close attention. In the Prater's private study, General Volskiar stood at full military attention. Drolith was almost dark olive with rage. You lost how many ships? Four warbirds out of seven? But my Prater, we did fully achieve our objective. One was lost to the Enterprise and the others were lost not to an honorable, honest enemy, but to the darkest, foulest treason. My Prater, I hold as prisoner the woman who was once known as Commander Charvanek. She who has set an ambush and has murdered our own. Drolith struggled for composure. I take it that no one has seen her being brought back to Key Baritan. True my Prater, only my crew. Drolith nodded with some satisfaction, but he wondered why Charvanek would have taken such a wild chance. The name shot into his mind without warning. Narviet, who together with Charvanek was linked by blood to the Emperor. Drolith returned his attention to the General. All rumbulous shall celebrate General Volskiar. There will be a grand public festival to honor our glorious victory over the aggressor Klingons and the treacherous Federation. And the traitor? A woman shall of course be questioned, but discreetly. We do not wish a martyr. Drolith broke off with a muttered oath as a warning light on his desk console began to flash. Someone was spying on him. With the rebels Spock listened about the massacre of Narendra Thre. He thought of his betrothed. Savic. Savic. Had she gotten through with her message or died en route. But now something was very wrong with what they were hearing. Spock shouted. Take contact, now. When the startled young Romulan failed to act to shove him out of the way and disconnected the system himself. But Ruhinek nodded in understanding. He's right. Didn't you hear what Volskiar was saying? Vague ramblings about the ship's supplies? Spock cut in. Exactly. Drolith knew someone was spying on him and was trying to trace us. Spock took Ruhinek aside. How adept are you at breaking into systems and coaxing out records? Ruhinek shook his head. No one trains a warrior for that. But carrot can. Ruhinek snagged a scrawny teenage girl by the arm and pulled her over to them. Carrot here can work wonders. Cracked just about any electronic system. Can't you, Carrot? Spock pointed at a console and she sat down as he explained his plan. Before we may reveal, Drolith is the enemy of the people. We must have evidence. Carrot, see if you can access some death records. Senators who met with fatal accidents within the last five years. Oh, easy. They don't guard those. Is this what you want? Spock and Ruhinek studied the data together. Fascinating. Your ronulin senators seem to be a singularly unfortunate lot. And there are many transfers of estates into the praetor's personal accounts. So Carrot, one more search if you would. Let's see if you can cross-reference how many of the deceased were known to be activist. Preferably those actually on record as speaking out against the praetor. When Spock scanned the new list of names and matched them with the list of the deceased, he raised an eyebrow. To speak out against Drolith too openly does seem to increase a senator's risk of meeting with a fatal accident. Ruhinek snorted. All this is conclusive evidence against Drolith showing he's corrupt but it's not going to help Admiral Narviet and we can't give up on Commander Charvinek either. At the thought of Charvinek, Spock felt the fire surge up and nearly blind him. He fought for control. What we need is an undeniable link between Drolith and the massacre of Narendr III. Irrefutable evidence that Drolith, not Charvinek or Narviet is the traitor. Carrot, can you locate Narviet? Carrot's fingers flew over the keyboard. Lots of rooms. Secret ones. See? No clear way in or out. Cells bet you. Cells Drolith doesn't want anyone to know are there but can't get any closer. Lots of spiders around there. All around. Just that one little room. Ambassador, Starfleet's sector Admiral Lin is on a secured line and wishes to speak with you. Admiral Lin sat in the position Spock had identified for Serik long ago as, at attention, an indication of great respect. How is Commander Savik, Ambassador? Very ill. Do you think she'd be up to answering a few questions vital to our investigation? Commander Savik cannot answer questions now, Admiral. I see. Ambassador, I'm afraid I'm going to have to ask you to take on a task. One of my most reliable captains has pulled two Romulans out of a wrecked scout. They, the one of them who's conscious, call themselves part of their underground. The elder Romulan is comatose, apparently injured in a shipboard accident. The younger wants asylum on Vulcan for himself and his brother. Serik raised an eyebrow. Underneath his logic, the smallest flame of hope would not be denied. Oh, my son. My son may it be you. Without breaking eye contact with Admiral Lin, Serik coded messages for security to meet him at the medical center. Admiral Lin, I will assume responsibility for these Romulan refugees. That's fine, Ambassador. The ship will approach Vulcan, beam them down, and leave. Security Chief Osmanski, a tall, sturdy human from Vulcan's Starfleet base, glanced at Serik. Passengers are ready for transport, shall I? Serik nodded. If you would. Two figures materialized on the small platform. A tall Romulan in a very battered, stained military tunic, braced a lean figure against his shoulder. One arm flung about him, protectively, to keep him upright. Subcommander Ruinek, I am... but Ruinek had already identified him. My Lord Ambassador, I have brought your son home. As the guards moved in, the refugee staggered down from the transporter platform, bearing the ship's hand. The ship's hand was a very beautiful platform, bearing his unconscious companion with him. We've had a rough flight, sir. A defective ship nearly took us with it. Your son saved us, but he is very ill. He met Serik's eyes fully, for an instant, and Serik knew that Ruinek suspected the truth about Spock. Serik hastily knelt beside Spock and put out his hands to touch his son's temples. He had a very limited temperature and arranged metabolism, characteristic of the last stages of Plaktau. Spock suddenly tensed, and Serik slapped him. Slapped him again. Ruinek reached out to stop him. Sir, what are you doing? Serik explained. Pain helped him enter the trance. It will help him focus now that he struggles to wake. Serik gestured at a guard to signal healer to sell us to attend him. The security guard nearest to Ruinek gestured with his side arm. The Romulan turned to Serik, sudden despair in his eyes. There is no need for alarm. I will debrief our guest myself later, after he is rested and refreshed. Serik opened his personal communicator and pressed the proper code. Our M. Corel returned to my estate if you would. You will be receiving company there shortly. One distant cousin. My guest will be accompanied by Starfleet guards. See that they are treated with proper courtesy too, and that they do not intrude upon my guest's privacy unless it becomes necessary. The footsteps of the healer to sell us caused a commotion among the security guards. In the confusion no one was looking at Serik. He took this second of privacy to shut his eyes and let out his breath in a silent sigh of unbearable relief. My son, my daughter are both here now. Let them live. They must live. It is illogical after having come so far that my children would not have a chance at life. Charvanek found Narviad in what had been Dralith's private study. He glanced up at her, eyes brightening. Charvanek glanced about the room. You've gotten rid of all the mirrors. Narviad snorted. I had to get rid of them. It was like living in a room full of clones. Charvanek, live on a. Please be seated. Taken aback by the use of her private name, she sat. Without a word, Narviad pushed a bracelet across the desk to her. Her heart gave a great start. The bracelet had his and her personal insignias entwined, hastily carved into what had been a plain silver band. Narviad clearly took her silence for reluctance. Dralith left affairs in an unbelievable mess. It is going to take years just to get everything straightened out. I desperately need someone I can trust at my side. Not very romantic, Charvanek thought dryly, but then he can't allow himself the liability of romance. For that matter, can I? Without a word, Charvanek took the bracelet and slid it on to her wrist. It would be properly adjusted at the ceremony. Glancing up, she saw just for an unguarded moment, honest love shining in Narviad's eyes. She always had felt a warmth towards Narviad. That just might turn into something stronger, and they needed each other. Farewell, Spock. May you live long and prosper with your Savic. At Sarak's estate, Ruenek didn't even know who or what he was anymore. He glanced down at the clothes he'd been given. A flowing tunic, cinched in by a woven belt, fitted trousers, a great deal more comfortable than uniform. Ambassador Sarak actually cared how he looked. But agreeable though the outfit might be, it made him a stranger to himself. The honor blade had his belt no longer seemed a natural extension of what he was. Ruenek hurled open the room's shutters, sure he was going to find bars or armed guards ready to shoot. Instead, oh, fates, it was a desert. The open, peaceful sweep of space. The breeze was shifting, blowing in off the cooling desert, and Ruenek took a deep breath of dry, fragrant air. Without any warning, the scene suddenly changed in his mind, and was all at once alien, all at once far too alien. Ruenek quickly closed the shutters, hands trembling. There was one very familiar item, his honor blade. With a sharply in drawn breath, very much like a psalm. Ruenek drew the weapon from its sheath, studying its unmarred beauty. His vow to rescue Spock was fulfilled. When one came right down to the hard facts of it, there was absolutely no more point to his life. Nothing else to hold him here. But Ambassador Sarak had given him hospitality. It would be the height of dishonorable behavior to stain that hospitality with even and honorable suicide. For what seemed in eternity, Ruenek sat shivering, unable to grasp the knife. He put it down on the desk, and desperate to stop himself from doing anything else, switched on the computer console. The screen came instantly to life. Studying the cryptic Vulcan menus revealed, Ruenek felt the faintest stirring of curiosity. What programs had been left for him to access? Sirak's palm print opened the door to the guest suite. There was the Romulan, awake and unhurt, staring intently at the computer screen. When Ruenek realized who had entered, he nearly lost his balance jumping to his feet. My Lord Ambassador, forgive me Aya. The hunger for knowledge, Ruenek, is no reason for embarrassment. But Spock, sir, how is it likely my son will survive? But it is possible that my daughter will not. Let us speak of other matters. Sarak glanced at the screen. Ruenek, but how is it that you speak and read Vulcan? Federation Standard II, more or less. There was a long, boring winter one year, and you can only do so many military exercises, so I can only find the Federation Standard Book, though. No tape, so my accent is terrible. Obviously you learn languages swiftly. I should think that such a skill would be an asset. An asset? Knowing Vulcan and Federation Standard could have gotten me executed as a spy. Do you speak any less perilous languages? Smattering of Barolian and some Zarak? Sarak paused and spoke. Unromulus, why did you risk your life to learn? Ruenek glanced down. I... I don't know how to say this, sir, but I couldn't endure not learning, even if it meant running risks. You're pardoned, sir, but what happens to me now? You are my guest, Ruenek. I will, assuming that you wish it, provide tutors and whatever educational tapes we both think logical. Perhaps linguistics should be the main subject of your study. And one thing more, Ruenek, I shall also provide a healer for you. Sarak pointed to the unsheathed honor blades still lying on the desk. In the days ahead you may find the burden of your life's total change too heavy to bear alone. But why? Why should you care about what happens to me? You saved my son's life, even knowing what it would cost you. And I am always in need of aides who have both a gift for languages and a first-hand understanding of emotions. Sir, are you offering me your patronage? I am offering you the chance to make your own choice. Sarak permitted himself the slightest of satisfied smiles and left. Even before the transporter effect faded, Vulcan's sunlight hit Dr. Leonard McCoy, retired Federation Starfleet admiral. He strode forward boldly, refusing to trudge as if his knees were hurting, toward the somber figure who stood waiting for him. Behind the figure rose the quietly elegant white walls of the Vulcan Science Academy's medical center. The hood was pushed slightly back to reveal a strong, absolutely unreadable face. Sarak of Vulcan raised his hand. Live long and prosper. McCoy held up his hand. I come to serve. Peace and long life. I'm glad I was already en route to Vulcan when I got your message. Sarak gave a slight nod of his head in a gesture of courtesy. It is good for Spock to have his friends with him at such a time. They started toward the medical center together. Once inside, Sarak pointed McCoy toward a blank white door and stepped back. You're a part in Dr. I have some final arrangements to make. McCoy tentatively pressed the door chime and the door slid open. He saw Spock in robes of a red so dark it was almost black. Spock, are you all right? McCoy. He stepped back enough to allow McCoy a glimpse inside. A massive bed, looking heavy enough to have given a cling on pause, lay on its side. Bedding and cushions shredded and strewn about the room. Everything that could be overturned or smashed had been. McCoy knew how savage Vulcans could be on the rare occasions that they let their feelings come out. He turned and saw Savic, seated at a mirror of some presumably shatterproof material. McCoy's breath caught in his throat. She looked radiant. Magnificent. McCoy saw Spock and Savic glance at each other. New fire sparking in their eyes. What was that old saying? You have your marriage for yourself, you have your wedding for your relatives. Once again McCoy stood on a Vulcan plateau, seemingly in the middle of nowhere. He easily picked out Mount Salaya, a jagged silhouette in the light of Vulcan's afternoon. It was Spock's family ancient place of Kunit Kalafiy. Nothing much had changed. He looked about at the other wedding guests. Ughura, even after all these years, she was still beautiful. She was wearing not dress uniform but a flowing robe of kintikloth. McCoy edged past three silent Vulcans to her side. Madam, you look even more beautiful than I remember. Ughura smiled out shown the light glinting on her necklace and earrings. Leonard, you flatter her. I promised to dance at Savic's wedding, and I certainly can't dance and address uniform. McCoy retorted. At least you can dance. I should have got my knees upgraded five years ago. Directly in front of him loomed a tall figure and a hooded cloak. The figure turned. McCoy frowned, studying a teasingly familiar face. Ruinek, you're that Romulan refugee, aren't you? The one I heard brought Spock home. Clearly embarrassed. Ruinek looked away, staring out over the wide vista of desert and mountain. Does what you see look familiar? In a strange way, the air is so much hotter, yet it is all so very beautiful. And it somehow feels right. And no one needs to watch one's back. Spock entered through the archway alone, straight-backed and noble in his flowing ambassadorial robes. A second litter was carried into the circle. A shrouded figure was helped out. The figure threw off the dark cloak, revealing blazing red robes, a fine-boned, fierce ancient face. McCoy was astounded. T'Laur, the high priestess. Damn. I wish I felt as good as she looks. The ancient eyes studied first Ruinek, then recognized McCoy. She gave him the barest nod of her head. Next came Ambassador Serk, his robes of state, darkest blue. Finally there was Savic, eyes properly downcast, her flowing silver robes gleaming like a river in a wasteland. Spock and Savic, not quite touching, knelt before T'Laur. Very gently, with never a quiver in her thin hand. She touched their temples. And with spectacularly right timing, lightning flashed over Mount Salaya. McCoy heard the couple murmur, parted and never parted. Never and always touching and touched. T'Laur gestured to the couple to rise. V'R'Wed. Spock, son of Sarik, son of Solkar, and Savic, Vulcan's daughter. Spock touched his wife's fingers with his own and led her away. Serik stopped them only long enough to say, I am pleased that your wedding has gone so well. Then Spock and Savic went down from the plateau together, out into the desert. The day was already fading, and long blue shadows lay across the sands. Side by side, touching each other's minds, they recited their vows together. Alone. Parted and never parted. Never and always touching and touched. Then, since they were alone, they held hands like any other lovers, and together watched the sunset. Soon enough, they must be parted. But for now, this time was their own. Star Trek. Vulcan's Heart. Was written by Joseph Ashurman and Susan Schwartz. And read by Tim Russ. It was A Bridge For Audio by George Truett. It was recorded at the Village Recorder in Los Angeles, California, by Timothy Tam. Editing by Stephen Strassman. Sound Design and Post-production by Gary Fink. Original music was composed by Carl Schurts, Eve Beglarian, Carl Sareeth, Sam McCally, and Richard Emmett. The production coordinator was Sally Hearst. Star Trek. Vulcan's Heart was produced and directed by Linda Wollman. This has been a presentation of Simon and Schuster Audio. Also available from Simon and Schuster Audio. Star Trek. Vulcan's Forge. Star Trek. Borg. And Star Trek. Klingon. Star Trek. Vulcan's Heart is available in book form from Pocket Books.
