transcript: Siamen & Schuster Audio presents Star Trek Prime Directive Written and Adapted for Audio by Judith and Garfield Reeves-Stevins This program is read by James Doohan. The following is a memory-alpha-audio data transcript. Code, Starfleet Command, Subcode, Five Year Missions Title, Historical Analysis, Extract Follows. By this time of the original 12 Starships that had embarked on Starfleet's visionary program of five year missions, five Constitution class vessels had already been lost in the service of the Federation. The USS constellation was the last casualty of an ancient war, sacrificed by her commander to destroy a weapon capable of annihilating whole planets. The Intrepid was consumed by an alien life-form in the Gamma-7A system, her entire crew of Vulcans wiped out in one hideous instant. The Excalibur was destroyed in war game maneuvers during the testing of a flawed, multatronic-controlled computer. The defiant disappeared into interface space in the Tholian Annex, trapped forever in a dimension beyond our own. And the Enterprise, as far as anyone knew, was hopelessly crippled during the tragic incident at Talon IV. Yet, despite such high cost, the returns to the Federation from the five-year mission's epic exploration and expansion were always greater. Thus, new Starships could always be commissioned. And for new crews, there was never any shortage of those beings who were driven by the Federation's greatest dream, to no more, to explore to the farthest limits, and then to go beyond. At the Federation Starfleet Academy, they called this dream, L'Oreve Deitwale, the Dream of Stars. And it was at the Academy that planners created the system that would guide a select few of those extraordinary beings who were driven by the dream of Stars to the only role that could fulfill their fire and purpose. Starship Captain. Starfleet and its Academy ensured that the Federation's planners could boldly set their course for the future, creating new missions and building new ships. They knew that there would be no end to those who would volunteer to take part because the dream of Stars, once acknowledged, could never be denied. But what the planners did not yet know by this time was that once the dream had been experienced, neither could it ever be willingly surrendered. It was a lesson the planners were eventually due to learn, and their system had already created the man who would teach it to them, once and for all. Memory Alpha transcript ends. Part 1, Aftermath. The Enterprise had been butchered, and Chief Engineer Montgomery Scott found himself thinking that it might have been better if she had died all at once and he withered. In the silence of the aft observation lounge, deserted in the ship's early-morning cycle, Scott leaned his head against the cool smoothness of the large viewport. He closed his eyes, thinking of another time when he might have touched any part of the ship and felt within her the hum of her generators, powered by the wedding song of matter and anti-matter. But there were no vibrations now. That life had fled. Scott opened his eyes again. His breath had fogged the viewport, and the haze it made suddenly flared silver-white as the Enterprise's orbit took her over Talon's moon into the full-reflected sunlight of Talon's sun. It cruelly showed how the blue-white gleam of the ship's hull metal was streaked with black from the energy arcs that had penetrated her overloaded shields just before the end. Scott's trained eye scanned the upper surface of the engineering hull, evaluating the inelegant arrangement of roughly bonded pressure plates and repair bands. He cringed at the imperfection of the work. It was Star-based mechanics who worked on her and her eyes. Scott and only a handful of others were all that remained on board of the Enterprise's original crew. At least, Scott thought again for the thousands time, at least, if I had been on the bridge when it happened, then this would be over for me too. And I'd be with the captain, wherever the poor lad is. Behind him, the observation lounge door puffed open and Scott cringed, knowing it could only be one person. Good morning, Mr. Scott. The work is proceeding nicely, wouldn't you say? Scott took a breath to calm himself. In the viewport's reflection, he saw the glowing lights of that ridiculous swagger stick spin through the air as lieutenant-styles flipped it under his arm. It was a damned annoying affectation on a starship, but then Stiles was a damned annoying man. I suppose it is. You don't sound too pleased, Mr. Scott. Scott hated the smug smile that split the man's sharp features. There's only one way to treat this ship, Mr. Stiles. You don't feel my chaps are treating the right way? Then Stiles turned to Scott, and the chief engineer stared in shock, as he saw that Stiles no longer wore the stylized comet insignia of the USS monitor on his gold command shirt. He wore the insignia of the Enterprise. Like it? Starfleet has reassigned me. I'm commanding the Enterprise now. No, Scott thought. Never. A ship needs a captain, lieutenant. An operational ship needs a captain, Mr. Scott. And the Enterprise is anything but. The experts have made up their minds then. In a manner of speaking, the decision has been made to detach what's remaining of the portness out. Of course, the Tugs will take the ship out of the system first, just in case. Scott had to look away. They were gambling with all that was left of the Enterprise. In case she slingshots into warp, what do they think is going to happen to her then that hasn't happened already? If the ship does slingshot, then it's apt to be an unfocused focus transition. The experts from the Cochrane Institute have calculated that the star bow effect could be quite spectacular. And the officials from the first contact office feel that every step should be taken to ensure that the event is not observable from the surface of Talon IV. The prime directives taken enough of a beating down there as it is, wouldn't you say? And if the ship doesn't slingshot, then there happened to be two constitution-rated warp nacelles at Earth's space-lock. But they're intended for the entrepid, too. Come now, Mr. Scott. It would take more time than a year to finish a new ship from scratch. But with new nacelles and a full wiring team of construction drones, the Enterprise could be back in service in a tenth that time. Scott stared at the man, suddenly seeing the real reason for his good spirits. And then, of course, she'd be needing a new Captain, wouldn't she? Well, thank you for your vote of confidence, Mr. Scott, though I'm afraid I'd just be first officer to begin with. But in time, she would be mine. Oh, yes. And then we'd see how the Enterprise could perform with a real Captain at her helm. Scott had a difficult decision to make, and in the end, he decided not to deck styles. There were more honorable ways to attempt to leave the service than by striking another officer. Though for the moment, he couldn't think of one more satisfying. Lieutenant Stiles are... Yes? When the time comes for the Porteness L to be detached, go on. With all respect, sir, I hope she slingshots you all the way to hell. As Stiles sputtered, Scott squared his shoulders and marched unhurriedly from the observation lounge. There was nothing more that Starfleet could do to him that hadn't already been done to his ship. Later, in the privacy of his quarters, Scott stared at his personal view screen. Screen on! The view screen came to life. Still displaying the final transmission feed he had requested last night. The source was sensor satellite two. One of eight the Enterprise had placed into orbit around Talon 4, half a million kilometers distant from its moon. The satellite was in a fixed geostationary position above the planet's main ocean. And almost four months earlier, Scott had seen the images it had obtained of Talon 4's surface and the vessels. The satellite could also pick up the heat trails of submersible vehicles deep beneath the ocean's surface and even identify the nation-states to which they belonged and the weaponry each carried. But now the oceans of Talon 4 had no vessels, submersible or otherwise, and the stockpiled weaponry had all been expended, creating dense, globe-insurcling clouds. Where the planet's sun could still shine through, the once-blue ocean was stained deep purple by an unknown algae-like organism. It had blossomed through all of Talon's seas and had swiftly overwhelmed the planet's radiation-devastated ecosystem. Undoubtedly, there were other ecological outrages unfolding just as dramatically throughout the rest of Talon 4's biosphere. Suddenly, Scott noticed the words printed out on the screen to identify the feed. Sensors satellite too. Kirk's world. He slapped his hand against the base of the machine, hitting its manual switch to off hard enough to make the screen shake. Yes, slimy, sons of... His voice choked off in anger. Kirk's world. He had heard the replacement crew using that hateful name for Talon 4, and now they had gone so far as to program it into the automated logs. While he'd program a worm to go through the computer and delete all such references, he'd take Stiles' name out of the duty roster as well and transfer him to kitchen operations. I'll turn the ship upside down before I'll... Ahh, what's that use? He'd been about to say before I let them win. But the truth was, they already had. Computer. Working. Prepare a hard copy message to Vice Admiral Hammersmith Starbase 29. From Scott, etc. Message goes effective immediately. I wish to tender my resignation from Star... Clarification. Aye, what is it? Starfully Command Regulation 106, paragraph 1, specifically identifies the role of the chief engineer as subject to preeminent exception to term of service procedures as detailed in Starfully Command. Computer, could you digest that gobbledygook for me? The chief engineer cannot resign while the enterprise is undergoing a class 2 refit. Scott put his elbow on the desk and rested his head on his hand. Even Starfleet equipment seemed out to get him. But he had picked up a few tricks in his years with Kirk, especially when it came to Kirk's way with computers. Computer, if I resign effective immediately, then I will no longer be the chief engineer when Hammersmith received my message. Therefore, he will not be empowered to prevent my resignation, but the computer didn't hesitate for a microsecond. That is a circular argument. Well, then, let me put it to you this way. If you don't transmit my message to the Vice Admiral... then I shall rewire you into a food processor. This time, the computer remains silent. Well, computer, what are you doing? Scanning personal records of Montgomery Scott to determine level of technical proficiency in the reconstruction of organic materials synthesizers from computer circuitry. And... the computer reset its audio circuits. Message has dictated reads, effective immediately. I wish to tender my resignation from Star. Please proceed. Thank you, computer. Scott turned back to the patient view screen that had displayed the words he had dictated. Though it was difficult for the engineer to admit it, for the first time, machinery wasn't enough. He no longer belonged, on board the Enterprise. What had made this ship so special, so alive, was her crew and her captain. The spirit of her would live just as well somewhere else as long as they could be together again. And they would be together, Scott suddenly realized they had to be. Scott smiled. The first time he had felt like it in months. Then he spoke the rest of the words that would separate him from Starfleet. So, like Spock and Kirk and McCoy and all the rest, he would be free to do what duty demanded of him. Find the answer. James Kirk remembered the pharragant, the first real ship he had served on. A Constitution-class starship, much like the Enterprise. He had been a Green Lieutenant and had spent his first six months managing supply crates in the ship's cargo bay. He found it somehow fitting that he had returned there now, in spirit, if not in a place. Surprised that he had retained so much of an almost fifteen-year-old skill, Kirk deftly managed the controls of a Mark IV tractor beamweb to receive, sort, and secure the rapid stream of cargo crates being loaded onto the freighter. SS Ian Shelton. From a commercial space dock orbiting the colony world of Intrater II, as Kirk worked the controls, the voice of the orbital transfer controller, came over the communicator link on the Mark IV's console. How are you doing in there Shelton? All conditions are not... everything's okay so far. Kirk still had to concentrate to keep from falling into the old patterns of speech. Okay, hot chat. The last load's coming through now. Looks like you set a new record. As he manipulated the final crates into position, Kirk heard the cargo bay control room door slide over the door. It was Anne Gavro, the ship's captain, and his employer of the day. She was a few years older than Kirk, with just a few telltale strands of white, in otherwise sandy and curly short hair. And she wore a beat-up flight jacket with an impressive number of colorful patches from all the different systems she had traveled to. From the corner of his eye, Kirk saw Gavro standing by the cargo bay viewport to watch him stack the last of the crates with the tractor beams. Woooo! Nice arrangement of crates, Leonard. Perfectly balanced distribution of mass. Gavro seemed to study Kirk for a moment, then said, if you're interested, the shelter needs a cargo master. Why? This ship's fully automated. You only need a cargo master when you're in port. And there's lots around to hire. Kirk knew that from experience. He had spent five days waiting for employment in the dock worker's pool at the Colony World Space Dock, suffering the indignity of pain for food, water, and oxygen. Well, that's a new one. Usually I'm in the position of telling people like you why I don't want to sign them on board. Look, the Shelton's next stop is Hanover. At War Four, we can be there in just under fifteen days. Kirk saw it for a moment. Hanover would put him about a light year closer to Starbase 29 without having to pay for passage. I'll take the job. Good decision, Gavro had a mysterious look and ary. It's the same one I would have made. The The One day out from the Colony World of Intrader II, cruising steadily under automatic pilot at War Four, the SS-Ein Shelton was deep in interstellar space. Gavro's freighter was little more than an unadorned cylindrical hull with a central bridge tower, stuck in mid-chips, as if it had been no more than an afterthought. But still, Kirk preferred being on the freighter's cramped bridge, where he could see the stars move past the viewscreen. Even if he did have to put up with the three black and orange cats that had free run of the ship, Kirk heard footsteps behind him on the ladder leading up to the bridge. It had to be Gavro. She was the only other person on board. Hi, Leonard. Thought you might be interested in a game of chess? We're coming up to a course correction soon. Thought I'd monitor it and then? Certainly. Gavro crouched down by a chair at the impulse station to scratch the ears of the two cats sleeping there. One of the cats shifted its position to place a second ear beneath Gavro's fingers, but neither cat opened its eyes to acknowledge their benefactor. Give me a dog any day, Kirk thought. One of the cats wrapped its paws around Gavro's hand and gave it an experimental chew. Are they any particular breed or clone branch? Kirk asked. No, Gavro said. That's the nice part. There are no old-fashioned natural mix from Earth. Fairly hard to get these days. What are their names? This is Comac. This is Fitzpatrick and Nagura is below deck sleeping on the mass converter. Comac, Fitzpatrick and Nagura? Kirk repeated. Gavro smiled because one of her secrets had just been revealed, and Kirk realized he'd revealed one of his own by his immediate reaction to the names. The cats were each named after a Starfleet admiral. How long were you in Starfleet? 21 years. That's a long time. Took me that long to figure out I wasn't going to get what I wanted. She tapped her fist against the impulse control council. One of these? A ship of my own? But there are hundreds of ships in Starfleet. True. But at the time I left there were only thirteen that mattered. Ah, Kirk said. No wonder he liked her. She was just like him. I exact on the Yorktown for Decker, Gavro explained. That gave me a taste for it. Then one Decker made Commodore and transferred to the constellation. I was certain I'd get his chair. I knew the ship and had the experience. But they offered me the Hawking instead. Kirk nodded in understanding. The Hawking was a science vessel with a crew of just over 100. Its mission was restricted to worlds without intelligent life, a witch had already been exposed to the Federation. For a scientist or technical specialist, it was a near perfect posting. But for an explorer, it was the equivalent to being condemned to perpetual second place. I protested. I sent subspace memos to command demanding a review. And after due consideration, blah, blah, blah, nothing changed. Decker said he'd take me with him to the constellation, but I knew I couldn't be second. Not again. And as things turned out, maybe I did the right thing by not going with him. Decker was a good officer, a good man. The entire crew of the constellation had been killed by an ancient and alien war machine. Decker had sacrificed the ship and his life to avenge their deaths. I know. And then to cover his slip, Kirk added. I was in Starfleet too. Gavro stared at Kirk as if coming to a decision. I know you were. Captain Kirk. Kirk felt the hair on the back of his neck bristle. How long have you known who I am? Since I saw you in the dock workers pool? But don't worry. I know you, Kirk. At least I know your type. You're like me. The kind of officer that gives the admiralty their grey hairs. You've got to be resourceful and inventive enough to run the show when you're weeks away from getting advice and orders from Starfleet Command. But when you get those orders, you have to be the kind of person who'll follow them even if you don't agree. It's an almost impossible mix. Like matter and antimatter. What's your point, Captain? My point is, whatever else you might be, Maverick, Impetuous, Stubborn, and all those other things starship captains have to be, you're not a world killer. I know what you had to go through to get the Enterprise. I know what I went through to get even this close to a starship of my own. She held up two fingers, a centimeter apart. And I know the system doesn't let maniacs get that close, or go so far. For all that I have my reservations about Starfleet, even I have to admit the system works. Well, if the system works as well as you say, then why don't you accept what Starfleet's hearing on Talon concluded? I accept most of the hearing's conclusions. Talon 4 was an inhabited, technologically advanced world. A few decades at most from first contact. The Enterprise went to the Talon system, and within five days, Talon 4 was a graveyard for an entire civilization. But you don't accept that it was my fault. Do you? No. The word hung in the silence of the small bridge. Then why be surprised that I think the same thing? Because the Admiralty thinks otherwise. I said, I thought the Starfleet system works. The Admiralty is another matter. Come on Kirk, don't be so defensive. I'm on your side. That's why I brought you on board. Alright? I figured, if you were already out so far in this sector, then you would probably appreciate getting another parsec or two closer to Talon. Because that's where you're going, isn't it? That's where I'd be going. Kirk watched the stars on the viewscreen. He asked himself, what he would have done if Starfleet had reassigned him to another patrol ship years ago instead of giving him the Enterprise? Would he have stuck it out in a second place command, hoping for another chance? Or would he have done what Gavroa had done, resigned and taken command some other way? He decided he would have ended up here on the Eon Sheldon, or a ship just like her, a winner by the only rules that counted his own. I do appreciate it, thank you. But, Gavroa could sense the question building in Kirk. How can you be so sure about me? You don't have the slightest idea about what really happened on Talon 4. But I will, won't I? If I were you, I'd want someone else to know the whole story. And I tell you, Kirk, 14 days in space on an automated ship, is a long, long time. Not as long as my five days at Talon 4, Kirk thought. But Gavroa was right. It was time for Kirk to tell his story. Part 2, the last mission. Part 2, the last mission. It had all begun, three and a half months earlier, when the Enterprise had first been ordered into the Talon system, under a complete communications blackout. Captain's Log supplemental. In six hours, Mr. Spock, Dr. McCoy and I will travel by shuttle to Outpost 47, a Starfleet first contact office base, hidden on the moon of Talon 4. From that base, more than 100 FCO researchers have spent eight years studying Talon 4 civilization, which is a collection of cultures and nation states with many similarities to late 20th century Earth, including the fact that the planets two major political powers are poised on the brink of a thermal nuclear war, which could wipe out all life and their world. As we approach Talon 4, I can feel an unusual excitement building in the crew. For some reason, they have taken an extremely personal interest in this mission, and the turnout at the background briefing sessions run by Lieutenant Carolyn Palamas has been most impressive. I am planning to attend her next presentation myself. Lieutenant Carolyn Palamas had been the ship's anthropology and archaeology officer from the start of the five-year mission. In that time, Kirk could remember her accompanying him on a handful of landing parties, most notably the mission to Pollux 4, when the Enterprise had encountered an alien who might well have been known to ancient humans as the Greek God Apollo. Palamas was also an attractive, blonde-haired and blue-eyed human and well-liked by her staff and crew. But still, Kirk knew there had to be more than just her popularity to account for the crew's unprecedented interest in the lieutenant's lectures about Talon 4. When Kirk entered the Enterprise's theater, he had to silently refuse a dozen crew members who immediately offered to give them their seats. He preferred to lean back against one of the back walls. At least there, he could sneak out again if the presentation weren't interesting. He noticed Spock sitting off to the side in the second row, close to the podium. Surprisingly, Dr. McCoy was sitting beside the science officer. At the podium, Lieutenant Palamas was just coming to the end of her briefing. And finally, coming up on the screen now, is a computer composite of a typical set of Talon 4's dominant intelligent species. On the large view screen behind Palamas, an image appeared of two reddish-skinned Talon adults and one green-skinned child. Lying beside them was what appeared to be an incompletely formed larval version of a Talon. However, according to the scale grid, the softly rounded pale white form was the same size as the two adults on the screen, about two and a half meters high. Each adult's reptilian face was the shape of a smoothly curving forward-sloping egg sliced by a wide, lipless mouth which opened and shut, revealing an upper and lower row of small sharp teeth. The face was dominated by a pair of large yellow eyes, twice the size of a human and dotted by small black central pupils. The child's face had less slope, no teeth and much larger eyes. Palamas read from her screenpad notes. As you can see, the Talon are sorry and bipeds, sharing some of the characteristics of Terran lizards and birds, notably in the loose folds of pebble-textured skin and the thin delicate skeletal structure. Also, as is typical on more than 90% of Class M planets, there are two sexes on Talon IV, and the female parent carries the live young to term. An ensign wearing a red support services shirt raised her hand and Palamas nodded at her. Then what's that fourth figure on the screen, the one that looks like a large egg casing? What we're looking at here is an adult hibernation cocoon. Many of the life forms on Talon IV can release a substance which hardens into a shell that protects them during the seasons when water virtually disappears from the planet's equatorial deserts. The Talon themselves still retain this capability. However, because of their relatively advanced technology, such as extensive irrigation projects and climate controlled housing, a hibernation cocoon like this one is rarely seen among the Talon except in cases of extreme trauma or illness. There also seem to be some cultural taboos about the nature of the cocoon of which we can't be sure, because the Talon themselves are reluctant to discuss them in their own broadcast transmissions. Unfortunately, those public sources offer the only data that FCO has been able to study in detail so far. Someone called out from the audience without bothering to raise his hand. Wow, that's only because the Enterprise hasn't gotten there yet. Kirk smiled at his cruise enthusiasm. One of the Enterprise's functions on this mission would be to place sensor satellites in orbit around Talon IV to gather more detailed information than the FCO had been able to obtain through their monitoring station on Talon's moon. We're out of time for now, so I'd like to thank you all for your attendance today. Tomorrow, I'll continue with an overview of the planet's rating on the Richter scale of culture. Kirk moved against the flow of people leaving the auditorium so he could join Spock and McCoy. Both officers were now in a private discussion with Palamas at the podium as she gathered up her screen pad and microtakes. As Kirk approached, he heard them discuss the Talon's chances of surviving the war they faced. Tell me, Lieutenant, is the situation on Talon actually that precarious? We've seen dozens of worlds successfully pass through tense political situations and the Talon cultures do appear to be stable. Palamas frowned as she straightened her pile of microtapes. Captain, we have also seen dozens of worlds fail to survive situations similar to the one Talon is experiencing. I think that's why the crew has become so caught up in our mission to Talon IV. We're all hoping that the Talon will survive their present difficulties the way Earth did. And, well, go on, please. Kirk smiled to encourage her to continue. I think some of the crew are hoping that this might turn into a first contact mission, sir. Why would anyone think we're on a first contact mission? The Talon people have barely left the orbit of their own planet. They're still under the jurisdiction of the first contact office. I know, Captain, but there is also a better than 50% chance that the opposing sides on Talon will become involved in an all-out fusion war. We've been able to pull out fusion war within the next six months. And since membership in the Federation has been shown to have a calming influence on a planet's regional disputes, some of the crew feel that perhaps to save the Talon, we'd reveal ourselves? Well, yes. Something like that. Kirk turned to Spock, a concerned look on his face. Spock, according to the FCO projections, one might the Talon be expected to be able to learn that there are space-faring cultures in their vicinity. At the minimum estimation, Captain, the Talon are at least 20 to 30 standard years from achieving the required technological breakthroughs. Kirk turned to Lieutenant Palamas, still serious. Twenty to thirty years, Lieutenant. I'm surprised the crew isn't more aware of General Order No. 1. Ooh, they're aware, Captain Kirk. A lot of them just can't see the point of non-interference, if it means an entire race might die. Given the severity of the situation, they think that Starfleet and the Federation Council might make an exception to the Prime Directive. Spock placed his hands behind his back. Everyone turned to him, knowing he was about to speak. As soon as an exception is made, Lieutenant, it is no longer the Prime Directive. As a historian, you should be aware of the tragedies that inevitably result when a more powerful culture attempts to set standards for those that cannot stand against it. The Federation cannot presume to have either the moral or ethical right to proclaim what other cultures should do until those cultures have achieved a level of development sufficient enough to consider what we have to offer. Then they must be free to turn us down without feeling forced to capitulate in order to gain our advanced technology and knowledge. For those reasons, among many others, the Prime Directive is a most logical and necessary position. Kirk could see the fire building in the Lieutenant's eyes as she responded to Spock's lecture. But as a historian, I am also aware that it was an uncrewed Vulcan robot probe that prevented a cometary fragment from wiping out half of Central Europe in the early 1900s. The diverted fragments struck an uninhabited region of Siberia, and that changed the future history of the entire Earth. But Spock was not swayed. That incident was a preventable natural disaster, not in any way caused by the humans of the time. And the Prime Directive explicitly directs us to protect emerging cultures from similar disasters, provided we do not reveal ourselves. Indeed, the Enterprise herself has done so many times in the past. Upset now, but trying not to let it show, the Lieutenant conceded the argument. All I meant is that I shall be very sad if we are forced to do nothing as we witness an entire race commit suicide. As shall I, Lieutenant Spock said. And Kirk knew it was a rare admission for the science officer to make to someone he did not know well. As Palamas left them, Kirk fell silent, thinking about what she had said. The Lieutenant wouldn't be the only crew member who would be upset if the Enterprise were forced to do nothing but watch, as a world destroyed itself. But it won't come to that, Kirk told himself. It can't come to that. He was a starship captain. He would not allow it. Chief Engineers, Personal Log Supplemental. We are now in orbit around the Moon of Talon IV, and while Captain Kirk, Mr. Spock, and their landing party are at the first contact office outpost here, I am in temporary command of the Enterprise. While the ship remains in excellent working order and the cruise morale is high, I am beginning to have some misgivings about this mission. Which I believe the Captain and Mr. Spock share. In the almost five years I have served under Captain Kirk, this ship has never been forced to operate under such severe blackout conditions. In addition to shutting down all equipment that might generate electromagnetic signals, the Talon could detect, we are also prevented from using most of our sensors, our broad beam subspace communicators, and our threat. Our transporters, which is why the landing party is now underway to the outpost by shuttle. What none of us can understand, including Mr. Spock, I might add, is why the first contact office is concerned that the Talon people might be able to detect the subspace radiation produced by our devices. All reports indicate that their technology could not possibly be that advanced. However, there is always the possibility they have obtained advanced technology from elsewhere.
description: In this episode of Star Trek audiobook Prime Directive, we follow the journey of a young engineer named Montgomery Scott as he experiences the legacy of the Enterprise's tragic demise. The story explores how his experiences lead him to become the one who will teach the Federation's planners about the enduring nature of their dream: the "Dream of Stars." Scott's story is a testament to the incredible impact the Starfleet Academy had on shaping future generations, and it highlights the importance of the Prime Directive in ensuring that new stars are always set.

transcript: Scott's footsteps echoed in the empty corridors of FCO Outpost 47. The 120 personnel who had once worked there had been recalled to Earth five days after the devastation of Talon 4 and the facility had been deserted ever since. Scott came to the doors marked Mission Planning Center and they reluctantly slid open before him, sticking from disuse. The people working in the vast room looked up from their tables and desks piled high with microtapes and hard copies. Each worker was a member of the Federation's Emergency Investigation Team sent to analyze exactly what had happened on Talon 4 during the Enterprise's last mission. Lieutenant Carolyn Palamas came up to Scott to take the boxes of data disks he carried. Already more than half the Enterprise's crew had been transferred back to the Talon system. Many of them helped the investigators while they waited for their ship to be repaired. Then a familiar voice called out to Scott. It was the investigation team leader. Mr. Scott, I require your assistance. Scott felt he had been suddenly transported back four months in time. He had missed that voice more than he had known and he was glad that Vice Admiral Hammer Smith had refused to accept his resignation. I, Mr. Spock, am coming. Scott went to the desk where Spock was working with Mario Cardinale, the outpost former manager of communications. How do you do in Mr. Spock? Spock looked up from the large desk where he worked. The terminal screen before him displayed row after row of the multicolored paint splatters that Scott now recognized as Talon's script. How am I doing what, Mr. Scott? I, Scott thought, have missed the voice, if not necessarily what it says from time to time. I mean, are the modified terminals working out for you? Yes, Mr. Scott. However, I shall require full computer access to the main monitoring lab. Mr. Cardinale can provide you with details. The begging you pardon Mr. Spock, but there's not much of any communications to be monitoring in the vicinity these days. True. Though there are eight standard years worth of previously captured data to analyze, the monitoring room would make the process more efficient. I'll get on it right away, Mr. Spock. Scott saw the clouded look that came to Spock's face. Oh, well, you know what I mean. When Scott left the workroom with Cardinale, Vice Admiral Hammersmith appeared in the doorway. He was an imposing man, tall, muscular, with space black skin. Ah, engineer, I'm glad I found you. Lieutenant Stiles reports that the construction drones have finished replacing the master translator nodes and that the warp generators in the new nacelles are locked in and ready to power up. Scott hesitated. So then, what you're saying, sir, is that the, uh, enterprise is ready to be taken out? The Vice Admiral nodded. For trials first, of course. The warp engines have to be tuned over the next few weeks before she can be classified operational again. But Stiles says she'll be ready to break orbit in six hours. I see, sir. Scott glanced back into the controlled excitement of the workroom. Spock must be onto something, he thought. Have you found any evidence to back your claim, engineer? No, sir, but with Mr. Spock here and Hammersmith shook his head. I'm afraid Mr. Spock is here on a completely different matter. He is no longer associated with Starfleet. The only reason he was allowed through the blockade at all is because the Federation appointed him head of the official investigation team. Until the council debate over the status of Talon is concluded one way or another, there is nothing more that can be done here. The Federation is more than just one planet in this one system, and Starfleet has too many ships and personnel here already. We need the enterprise out doing her job, and we need you on her doing yours. Oh, please Admiral, I know that was just a few more days I could... Lieutenant Commander Scott. I have given you all the latitude that my orders allow. Now you, sir, are ordered to report to Lieutenant Styles aboard the Enterprise in six hours. Do you understand, Mr. Scott? Scott's shoulders slumped. He had come so close only to lose again. I, Admiral, I shall report aboard the Enterprise in six hours. Thank you for your patience, sir. Good man, engineer. Amherst Smith nodded in dismissal. Then entered the workroom. Scott and Cardenale headed out to the main monitor lab to prepare it for Mr. Spock. One hour before Scott was to report back to the Enterprise, Spock entered the monitoring lab. He looked approvingly around it. All displays were now functional. The viewscreen flickered with a hundred focus patterns awaiting input. Scott and Cardenale looked up as Spock approached the center command console. Ah, Mr. Spock. We're ready for you anytime. Good work, Mr. Scott. I shall begin transferring my files here as soon as the others arrive. The others? Scott didn't understand. Yes, Mr. Scott. If my calculations are correct, then they should be arriving at any moment. Who? Spock turned the chief engineer. But before he could answer, a transporter chime filled the lab. Scott blinked as two figures took form. Spock greeted them when the beam had faded. Welcome, Mr. Wilforth and Ms. Mallet. The outpost's former director and his manager of sampling operations came forward to the command console. Wilforth slowly gazed around the room as if he had never expected to see it again. Scott checked the time readout on the console chronometer. In forty minutes, he'd be beaming back up to the Enterprise. His cardinality greeted Wilforth and Mallet. Scott drew Spock aside. You see, I've been ordered back to the Enterprise, Mrs. Spock. And I'm afraid that this might be the last time I get a chance to talk with you in the next few weeks. What do you wish to say? Have you been working on anything that would make sense of what happened here, man? Certainly, Mr. Scott? Well, did you find anything? I believe I said I am working on it, Mr. Scott. Any chance of coming up with something in the next 30 minutes? Unquestionably. Spock's answer took Scott by surprise. What? You mean that? Well, you'll have the answer that quickly. Part of the answer, at any rate, Mr. Scott. From the center of the lab, another transporter charm sounded. It was louder than before. Multiple beams coming in. As I said earlier, Spock continued, I have been waiting for the others to arrive. Scott followed Spock's gaze to the lab center, where five golden shafts of light and matter swirled into beam. Scott suddenly blinked in surprise. Captain Kirk! Hoorah! Kekkof! Shulu! Dr. McCoy! The Enterprise Five were at last to reunite. Scott was duly impressed by the stories each of his friends and fellow officers told. Yet one important question had not been answered. But how did you manage to run Starfleet's blockade of the Talon system? Mr. Scott, running a Starfleet blockade would be a criminal act. Well, exactly, Mr. Spock. That's why I'm wondering how they all managed to get through it? Kirk stood by Spock's side. We were let through, Scotty. As of now, we've all been hired by Mr. Spock to help him in his investigation. The reunion was abruptly interrupted by the chirp of Scott's communicator. Scott flipped the device open. Scott here? Lieutenant Styles, temporary commander of the USS Enterprise here, Mr. Scott. I believe your time is up. Prepare to be beam to board. Scott knew it was time to make a stand. I can't be beamed up right now, Lieutenant. And why not? We had a wee bit of an emergency down here. Good lord, Mr. Scott. You've got half of Starfleet orbiting over you right now. How can you have an emergency in an FCO base? Why, the communications are out! Scott dropped the communicator to the floor and stepped on it. Kirk went to Scott and put a hand on his shoulder. Scottie, Styles is an officious knit, I know. But he's your commanding officer. Scott was past caring. I, Captain, I know. But I've spent three months taking apart the Enterprise, trying to find out what happened to her. And it's only now that Mr. Spock's come that we have a chance of finding out. And if we can prove that we were attacked, then the Vice Admiral will let me stay here until we find out who did it and why? I'm sure of it. Kirk turned to Spock. What do you say, Spock? Can you prove it? Spock had the former FCO officials and the former Enterprise crew face the Master Viewscreen. He called for the first data channel he had prepared and the image of a Federation shuttle appeared in a large section of the Viewscreen. Spock asked Cardenale to open the next data channel and a flood of images began to move across the screen. Spock provided a commentary for his audience. These are pictures of other so-called extra-planetary space vehicles which were reported in the public update media on Talon. That thought it was one of the oddest disoritments of flying vehicles he had ever seen. Willforth stepped closer to the screen. But our computers were able to scan through every image, Spock. We found nothing. No Mr. Willforth. The FCO did not scan through every image, only every image available to the FCO. Spock looked at Cardenale. Data channel 200, if you please. The new series of pictures came on screen. Twelve of them, each a clear and detailed image of what could only be a Federation shuttle traveling through the atmosphere. The FCO never had a chance to analyze these images because they were obtained from Talon's military computer networks by the Enterprise's sensor satellites. This outpost was shut down before you could evaluate any of these images. We analyzed them today and as they clearly show without a doubt, the Talon were aware of the FCO's operations on their world. To Carol Mallet, who had been in charge of the outpost shuttle operations, Spock's words were an insult. Look here. I only conducted 20 sampling runs to Talon. It's inconceivable that they could have been sophisticated enough to record my operations 13 out of 20 times. Suddenly, Vice Admiral Hammersmith strode into the room, accompanied by Lieutenant's styles and three red-shirted security guards. I disagree, Miss Mallet. The evidence is right up there on the screen. And it appears that Starfleet is going to have to open a board of inquiry so it can spread the blame around. Now, where's Lieutenant Commander Scott hiding? Spock adjusted a control on the console. What is on the screen is only a portion of the evidence, as you call it. A second series of images of flying craft came on the screen. They were wingless, long, and streamlined, with pinched in middle sections. Scott tried to count them, but there were too many. They didn't fill the entire screen, so he knew there were fewer than one hundred. But still, there were more than five times as many as the images of the shuttles. The only problem was, Scott couldn't tell what the craft were. Neither could Hammersmith. What are those supposed to be, Mr. Spock? For want of a precise term, I choose to call them sampling shuttles. The two of them were too forth protested, but the FCO doesn't use anything that looks like that. They are not FCO shuttles, Spock explained. Neither are they from any known world within the Federation. Or without Scott's eyes filled with excitement. Yes, Spock. That's it. But Hammersmith didn't share that excitement. He was icy when he spoke. Just what are you trying to tell us, Spock? Spock asked for data channel 210. Scott brought it online. A geopolitical map of Talon IV appeared. Moments later, a flurry of hundreds of dots and triangles flashed on and off across it. Spock pointed at the screen. Look at the frequency of sightings. I submit that these are alien craft engaged in a systematic series of provocative sorties designed for one reason only. To heighten the fear of war on Talon and to make the military and political leaders of the planet arm themselves to the point where stability could no longer be possible. Hammersmith was amazed. Are you saying that aliens were attempting to start a war with Talon? Spock corrected the Vice Admiral's assumption. Not with Talon, but on Talon. Hammersmith shook his head. This can't be right, Mr. Spock. It's impossible to Kirk step between Spock and Hammersmith. No wrong, Admiral. Whatever you think about the existence of any unidentified aliens, Spock is right in his conclusions. The data came from the Talon themselves. The data cannot be ignored. Someone was trying to get the Talon to destroy their own world. McCoy joined Spock and Kirk. Well, then the Prime Directive wasn't broken. The three of them faced Hammersmith together. But Kirk was on the attack now that Spock had given him the ammunition he needed and McCoy had given him the support. Dr. McCoy is right. The Prime Directive does not apply here. Talon IV's normal development had already been altered by these aliens' attempts to increase political and military tensions. It was right for the Enterprise to step in. Hammersmith backed off, obviously shaken. What possible reason could there be to destroy all life on a planet? Spock reached for another switch on the console. But not all life on Talon has been destroyed, Admiral. A new satellite image of Talon IV came up on the viewscreen. The choking clouds of dust and radioactive poison which had swept the planet were almost gone now. The land masses were still streaked black and brown. The once white polar ice caps were grey with soot from the worldwide firestorm that had raged for weeks after the disaster. The only sign of life remaining on the planet was in the oceans. Now choked with the deep purple algae-like organism that had mutated and bloomed in the days after the planet's death. What could possibly live down there? Hammersmith's expression was one of sorrow and anger. Spock gestured to Cardinali. Mr. Cardinali, have the computer show what lies beneath the clouds. Cardinali typed in the commands. Slowly the computer created a master picture of the planet's surface as it had been two days after the disaster. Walls of fire followed the coastlines where the cities had been clustered, forests and farmlands blazed. Then, Scott thought the computer made an error as the oceans were reconstructed. The first section cleared, showed that a mutated bloom of purple algae had already appeared. More of the oceans cleared. Scott saw another bloom. And another. Scott felt his flesh creep as the rest of the planet appeared as it had been that day. The algae blooms were studded across the ocean in a regular geometric pattern. A koi's eyes widened. God Lord! Hammersmith was stunned. No! Spock's expression remained unchanged. The algae-like organism which now dominates Talon's oceans is not a mutation brought on by radiation. Nor is it native to Talon. It is an artificial life form which was ceded on that planet quite deliberately. Just as the nuclear holocaust was deliberately induced to ensure that the world would be made for time for it. Scott was horrified. Who would do such a thing, Spock? Spock calmly brought back the pictures of the streamlined alien shuttles. They would, he said. Kirk's face was grim and set. But who are they, Spock? Where are they? The lunar dust of Talon's moon drifted up in a small eddy, disturbed by the vortex of the water. The dust of that moon was marked by Kirk's footsteps. Kirk peered through the faceplate of his environmental suit at what waited for him on the brightly lit lunar landscape. Three more columns of sparkling light appeared. Spock, McCoy, and Ughura. Kirk heard Ughura gasp in astonishment. Spock immediately held up a vacuum armored tricorder. Fascinating. McCoy checked his own scanners in disbelief. Then his voice crackled over the helmet speaker. Well, forget fascinating, Spock. How about downright impossible? From the barren rocks and soil of Talon's moon, beneath the blazing radiation of unfiltered sunlight and completely exposed to the hard vacuum of space, there was life. Kirk moved forward with long, low gravity strides to meet it. What he approached was obviously a base of sorts. About twenty of the sleek, pinch-wasted shuttles were hidden in the shallows of a rocky overhang. The shuttles were stacked on top of each other like a pile of kindling. The overhang had protected them from direct overhead observation by the Talon and the FCO. Though Kirk couldn't understand why the rest of the base had not been detected by the FCO's long-range scans nor had any scan detected the aliens, and there were hundreds of them. The aliens' black and silver-segmented bodies reminded Kirk of meter-long wasps, but they moved across the lunar soil like spiders on eight spindly silver legs. Cautiously, Kirk and the rest of the landing-party edged closer to the creatures as they swarmed around their shuttles and masked near several large silver and black domes that were scattered on the rocky surface. Uhura motioned toward the aliens. Are they machines? Kirk saw the communications specialist working with a large, flat computer board with controls enlarged for use by personnel in protective gear. That's the incredible part! McCoy checked his medical scanners. They've got organic parts inside them and free water. A high metabolism rate too. I wouldn't be surprised if they're somehow eating the radiation from the sun. Kirk was fascinated by the aliens' thin legs. They seem to be made of solid metal. Are they some kind of artificial construct spock? Organics built into a mechanical shell? I see no indication of anything artificial in their structure, Captain. I believe that these are living creatures, either genetically engineered or independently evolved to consume radiation and live in hard vacuum. Sir, it was Uuhura. I am picking up a great deal of low-level radio static, and it seems to be coming from these things. Uuhura? Uuhura? Is there any chance that the creatures are communicating by radio transmissions? I... Why not? I'll try to link up with one. Uuhura approached two of the creatures who were stroking a small, silverish bubble that appeared to have sprouted from the ground. Kirk leaned down to get a better look at the creatures. Spock, any idea what those bubbles are or what they're made from? The domes are composed of the same substances as the alien creatures and their shuttles. Spock glanced down at his tricorder. Captain, I believe that we must be looking at different versions of the same life form, or at the very least, different species who share the same evolutionary past. Are you saying the shuttles and the domes are also alive? Pointed his tricorder in the direction of one of the large black and silver bubble domes, it was nearly five meters across. Essentially? Yes. Odd. Spock continued to read from his tricorder. There also appears to be a pressurized atmosphere inside this dome, well insulated and with the quantity of liquid. Water. And? Plants? Plant life? Kirk was surprised. You're sure there's nothing higher? Most certain captain. Kirk pulled his phaser from the side of his suit, twisted the intensity setting on it and fired at the bubble before either Spock or McCoy could say anything to change his mind. A long stream of white vapor sprayed up some small hole that faded the mud. The vapor instantly changed to solid crystals and for a few moments it appeared to snow around the bubble. As the crystals rapidly sublimated in the vacuum, the area around the bubble cleared again. The only difference now was that a thick sludge oozed from the hole freezing as it fell to the ground in fist-sized chunks. Glittered with a white gloss of fine frost, but the color of the sludge was apparent. Purple. Kirk replaced his phaser. That's the algae, isn't it? The same organism that's taken over the oceans of Talon 4. Spock scanned the mass of thick, freezing material that pushed through the bubble skin. Correct, Captain. But how did you decide this? It's not an obvious deduction. McCoy didn't agree. Why not, Spock? The creatures are probably growing the algae to eat. Dr. McCoy, as both our readings show, these creatures do not require food. They thrive on hard radiation. The algae cannot sustain them. Captain, it was a who we were calling. You were right, sir. They are talking over radio frequencies. Uhura had found a large boulder on which to place her computer panel. Nearby, one alien methodically ripped apart a second. A small pile of other disassembled creatures was nearby. I'm patching through its main channel to our helmet speaker, sir. It seems to be able to generate low-frequency radio waves. Not much range, but the ability is definitely there. McCoy stepped over to examine the creature, casting his shadow across it. Suddenly, Kirk's helmet speaker crackled with a confused, blurry aesthetic. McCoy was puzzled. That's their language? That's just a raw signal, Doctor. Uhura changed the settings on her board. I'll run it through the universal translator. Strange life, block food. It was the clipped mechanical voice of the universal translator circuitry. Strange life, block food, over here, over here, strange life. Captain Kirk, the aliens are speaking in one of the primary languages of Talon. Suddenly McCoy sputtered in surprise as four of the aliens grabbed his legs and began to drag him away, sending up a cloud of billion-year-old dust. Before Kirk could act, the aliens released the Doctor. You all right, Bones? Well, just fine. McCoy pushed himself up from the ground. His suit was streaked with black lunar soil. And thank you for your help, Mr. Spock. From where you were standing, you must have seen them coming. I did, Doctor. Then why didn't you do something about it? The creatures were simply responding to their fellow beings' call for help. Doctor McCoy was casting a shadow over the creature we were observing, thus cutting off the sun's radiation, which is the creature's supply of food. As you will notice, the creature's transmission has now ceased. Spock, have you completed your analysis? Captain, if my preliminary conclusions are correct, then what we see here are not intelligent life forms. They are little more than worker insects, a group hive mentality, which has worked to make Talon for a suitable environment for growing the algae-like organism. It seems likely that they have absorbed the Talon language simply by listening to the planet's radio transmissions over the years. McCoy was skeptical. Years, Spock. In the time that this system has been under FCO jurisdiction, no alien vessels have been sighted entering it. Therefore the creatures were here long before the FCO arrived. Kirk gazed out at the hundreds of aliens moving in the distance, sharing the same moon and no one ever detected them. Since the aliens are composed of the rock and soil which covered this moon, the FCO's general scans would not have been able to distinguish the drones from their surroundings. Kirk watched as the busy alien near Ahura finished ripping apart its victim. He wondered what was going on in the creature's mind. According to Ahura, there was a way to find out. He moved closer to the alien, who had been disturbed by McCoy's shadow. Ahura? Can you link my helmet communicator to this one right here? Ahura brought her board over. Hi sir. Setting the frequencies now. Go ahead. Kirk moved to cast his shadow on the creature. The translator's circuits came to life instantly. Strange life blocked food over here, over here. Strange life blocked food. Kirk spoke. Would you like the food to continue? Yes. Food. Eat. Ahura's link worked both ways. Kirk stepped aside. Then after a few moments, he blocked the sun once more. The creature went into its recitation. Kirk repeated his question. Would you like the food to continue? Yes. Food. Eat. Then tell me who you are. The creature didn't protest or try to negotiate. We are the many. Do you know what I am? You are strange life. Give back food now. As if it were running low on energy, the alien paused in the midst of dismantling another of its kind. Kirk stepped aside and let the alien have a few more seconds of light. Kirk began to move again. Do you know where you are? Here. Was the creature's answer. It apparently did not need the threat of light starvation to answer questions. What do you do here? Work. It twisted a leg off the immobile creature before it. Why do you work? The alien did not respond. Spocked it. Captain, if you are indeed conversing with a mind that functions at little more than an instinctual level, it will not be able to understand higher concepts such as motivation. It would be like asking a paramecium why it absorbs food. It is not a conscious decision. But Spark, there has to be some conscious intelligence at work here. Kirk turned to his former first officer. Think of what they accomplished on Talon. They were able to manipulate the entire planetary defense system. They realigned warhead circuitry, blocked our sensors and deflectors, launched Talon missiles at us. How could they do all that without conscious thought? Captain, everything these creatures did was achieved by merely manipulating the data that passed through electronic and trans-stater-based equipment. Just as birds can fly without conscious knowledge of aerodynamics and a virus can reprogram the complex chemistry of a living host without any awareness, these creatures can apparently provoke nuclear exchanges on a planet without any conscious knowledge of the cultures they are manipulating. McCoy was appalled by the analogy. There is a huge gap between flapping some wings and blowing up a planet, Mr. Spock. Only into greed, Doctor, as we have all seen in our voyages, given enough time, virtually any characteristic can be evolved. Given enough time, virtually any behavior can be learned. Kirk stared at the continuing dismemberment ritual. They've done this before, haven't they? Undoubtedly, Captain, perhaps millions of times to achieve this level of sophistication. Kirk's mind reeled at the destruction that these creatures might have caused throughout the galaxy to grow food they couldn't use themselves. He wouldn't accept that it was arbitrary action. No matter how they had evolved, no matter how their behavior had been learned, somehow, somewhere there had to be a reason for it. He stood in the sun and blocked the creature's food again. Why do the many work? The creature still did not respond. Spock moved toward Kirk. Captain, it cannot answer. But Kirk persisted. Did you hear me? Why do the many work? He kicked a cloud of slowly falling lunar dust at the creature, but it continued its task without pause. Jim, let it go. Spock's right. It's like questioning a child. Child, Kirk thought. That was the answer. It had to be. He changed his approach. What is your work? The creature stopped moving its legs, running out of energy in Kirk's shadow. Again he asked, what is your work? The translator came online. Do so the seeds of life. Why? To grow food. But they don't eat the food, Kirk thought. They don't need the food. Why? To the many grow food. What purpose does the food serve? The creature's foot pads scrabbled weakly in the loose soil as it tried to call out from beneath Kirk's shadow. Kirk moved with it, keeping it blocked, knowing his conversation with it was preventing it from calling for help over the same frequency. I said, why do the many grow the food? The creature finally answered. The many grow the food for the one. Kirk stopped. The one. What is the one? The one is that which consumes the food. Obviously, the drones were not the one. Because what could a hive mentality know about individuality, Kirk thought. He began to feel a cold chill of apprehension. When will the one consume the food? When the one is here. Where is the one now? A burst of unintelligible static rushed from the helmet speaker. Ughura, what did the creature say? What language was that? Ughura studied the readouts on her computer board. Sir, that wasn't a language. It was... she put the board down and turned to Kirk. Sir, the creature transmitted. Co-ordinates. Kirk and Stiles glared at each other across the conference table in the ready room of Outpost 47. Neither had forgotten their first and last tour together on the pharragant. Stiles did not bother to disguise his sarcasm. Let me get this straight. You and the Enterprise aren't guilty of any wrongdoing because of a colony of vacuum-breathing rock-eating insects which even though they have no intelligence were somehow able to trick the Talon into blowing themselves up. You've beamed up once too often, Kirk. I always knew it would happen. But Vice Admiral Hammersmith was interested in other matters. Stow a lieutenant, you two, Kirk. He glanced down at Wilfoth's desk and again read the printout sheet of the coordinates of the one. Do you accept this as reliable data, Mr. Spock? The drones have no reason to lie to us. Assuming that they have the capabilities there. However, I cannot vouch for what might actually occupy those coordinates. There's only one way to find out, Kirk said. We have to go there and see for ourselves. Well, those coordinates are only a half-light-year away, McCoy said. At warp six, a ship could reach that location in less than one day, Spock added. Hammersmith held up his hands to quiet everyone. No one's going anywhere. Is that clear? Yes, sir. Stiles spoke smartly. I've got more than four hundred private vessels already stationed keeping at the edge of this system. Hammersmith went on. Half the galaxy is geared up to send aid to Talon for, and I don't have enough personnel or ships to keep them out as it is. By my estimation, Spock offered, the console debate on aid to Talon should have ended by now. Even if it has ended Spock, it's still going to take two days for the subspace relay to reach us. Hammersmith almost sounded apologetic. I wish I had some way out, but until the question of the prime directive is resolved, I'll have to keep every warp-capable ship bouncing around the system to turn back blockade runners. The answer hit Kirk like a phasor bolt. Every warp-capable ship, Admiral? Then you don't mean the Enterprise. Tails looked from Kirk to the Vice Admiral in alarm. What do you mean? He doesn't mean the Enterprise. I spent three months getting her warp-capable again. She's got new warp-nessels and hammer-smith-ignored styles. Brand new, unrated warp-nessels, which have to be tuned into balance well away from the gravity well of a star. So the ship won't risk hitting a wormhole. Kirk concluded his argument. That means the Enterprise is not warp-capable within the Talon system. She's no use to you here. He grinned. You said you wished you had a way out of this, Admiral. Hammer-smith nodded his head in agreement. A look of peace coming to his face at last. Kirk had found his compromise. And I'll ask Mr. Scott if he'd mind taking along some civilian observers on his operational trials. Thank you, Kirk. Styles exploded. You can't do that. You said she was mine. Hammer-smith turned slowly to Styles' eyes wide. I beg your pardon, Lieutenant. Styles stammered incoherently. Did you just tell an admiral what he could or couldn't do? Hammer-smith began to rise from his chair. Styles was hull-metal-white. He glared at Kirk. Oh, someday, Kirk. Someday I'm going to catch up to you and... Kirk laughed easily. Maybe someday, Styles. But the important thing is... That's not today.
description: Lieutenant Spock is joining Scott on a mission to Talon 4, where he and his team are analyzing the aftermath of an event that occurred during the Enterprise's last mission. Despite the pressing nature of the task, Spock has been delayed due to concerns about computer access and efficiency in monitoring the system. The episode explores themes of communication and adaptation in a new environment.
