transcript: High above the Talon Moon, on a course that would take them through the long shadows of a lunar mountain range to screen them from any astronomers on Talon 4, Kirk piloted the shuttle John Burke. He was accompanied by Spock and McCoy, precisely two kilometers of stern and holding to the same course, Sunu piloted the shuttle Galileo with Uhura, Chekhov and Carolyn Palamas. Outpost 47 was concealed deep within a nondescript mountain on the moon of Talon 4. The only access to it was through a large opening leading directly to a shuttle landing bay, but that opening was camouflaged by a holographic projection of a mountain wall, successfully hiding the base from Talon lunar probes. Inside the Outposts main monitoring lab, FCO researchers and their computers listened in on virtually all public communication transmissions from Talon 4, including 300 television channels, more than 5,000 radio channels and several hundred thousand personal channels. To Kirk, the main monitoring lab resembled a Starship's bridge enlarged ten times. It had a circular layout, ringed by at least 50 subsystem stations with a central command desk instead of a con. Five technicians, outfitted with audio inputs, sat at the command desk constantly adjusting controls while observing a master view screen twice as tall and four times as wide as the bridge screen on the enterprise. But instead of showing a single screen, the master screen divided into over 100 identical small rectangular displays and 10 expanded ones. The overall effect was overwhelming. Kirk couldn't make out what was being shown on most of them, but on one he recognized the sorry and face of a Talon, and among the background drone of noise in the monitoring lab, he heard a whispery and unfamiliar alien language that appeared to be in sync with the movements of the Talon's mouth. Next to Kirk, Carol Mallet smiled at the effect the lab was having on him. Mallet was an attractive red-haired woman who wore a shuttle pilot's uniform. She was the outpost's flight director and had already conducted more than 20 research flights to Talon IV to obtain samples of the planet's soil, plant and animal life. At the moment, she was earnestly discussing the outpost's extensive communications network with Uhula. Kirk became aware of Spock at his side. Captain, I believe you should look at the third large display from the right on the main screen. Kirk and Mallet turned to the screen, along with the others from the landing party. Kirk was stunned by what he saw. Is that a pick-up from a security sensor in the outpost landing bay? Kirk did not want to believe what the alternative was. No, Mallet said. That's what's called a news broadcast. It's like an on-interactive update channel. It was then that Kirk understood the reason for the tension in his dealings with this outpost and the reason for the unprecedented communications blackout. There on the screen from a Talonews transmission was a blurry but all too recognizable image of what was unquestionably a Federation shuttle in flight. It could only mean that the FCO itself was on the brink of compromising the prime directive, however unintentionally. Kirk turned abruptly from the screen. I think we've done enough sightseeing for now. It's time we met the director of this base. The director of FCO Outpost 47 was Zalen Wilforth. He was slight in build, pale skinned, and appeared nervous. As Kirk rose from his seat at the conference table in the Outpost's ready room, he guessed that from the director's name Wilforth was of combined earth and centaurin heritage. The centaurin part was confirmed when they shook hands and Kirk felt the extra joint in the director's little finger. Wilforth was accompanied by his two senior managers, Carol Mallet and Mario Cardenale, the Outpost's communication manager. Cardenale was a large, powerfully built human, probably from some high-gravity colony world. Wilforth sat down at one end of the table with his managers on either side. Kirk joined his landing party at the table's opposite end and immediately took charge of the meeting. We've seen the news broadcast in the main monitoring lab. As far as the Talon are concerned, they have an image of an alien spacecraft, don't they? Wilforth squirmed uncomfortably in his chair as he answered. Some think so. Many Talon are forward thinking, and their successes in orbital and lunar missions have awakened Loreb De Twil, the dream of stars. As on most space-faring pre-contact worlds, there is considerable public debate about the likelihood that other civilizations might exist around other stars. Sometimes there have been violent altercations between supporters of both groups, those who believe and those who do not. And the Talon are not particularly violent race. Spock joined the conversation. Yet they are poised on the brink of global war. Well that's quite true, Mr. Spock. And that's the main problem we face. There is nothing in Talon cultural history to suggest that they would ever be capable of reaching such a position. The FCO has never seen a culture progress so rapidly towards self-destruction. We are at a loss to explain it. How long ago was the sampling shuttle detected? Kirk asked. We believe six months ago I admit there's a chance that one of the two nations, we call them the Browns and the Greens, that are near war on Talon, have attained other images of our research shuttles. If so, whichever side those images hasn't released them, probably to prevent its opponent from gaining information about the state of its advanced imaging technology. Spock spoke again. Director Wilforth, I do not understand why you ordered a complete communications blackout, including matter transmissions. If you are convinced that Talon sensors are limited to the ordinary visual and energy spectrums, they do not have our advanced Trans-Stater technology. Director Wilforth looked even more agitated than before. Well true, Mr. Spock. The Talon do not have Trans-Stater capability. However, the planet does have large deposits of rubindium. How extraordinary. From Spock's response, Kirk knew that his science officer was thoroughly astounded. Rubindium crystals were crucial to the development of subspace communications technology. They were so sensitive to the faster-than-light energy spectrum that if the Talon were conducted collecting any experiments with the crystals, there was a chance they could detect subspace radiation emissions from the Enterprise. Spock drew the obvious conclusion. Then if the Talon are at present conducting rubindium experiments, any strong subspace activity in their system could lead them to conclude that they had detected an interstellar communications network, even though they would not have developed the technology to intercept, generate, or receive messages of their own. Truly a unique set of circumstances. Kirk leaned toward Wilforth. Has the FCO made a ruling on how this might affect the application of the Prime Directive? Kirk asked Wilforth. No, Captain. As you well know, the Prime Directive is one of the most rigorously enforced regulations in the Federation and one of the most complex. Any special ruling would have to be made solely on the basis of precise, unquestionable data. We don't have enough of that right now. What data do you have? Well, basically, it comes down to this. First, our monitoring leads us to believe that the Talon are aware that they are under our covert observation, though we do not know precisely how that is possible. Well, second, the majority of Talon, especially their leaders, do not accept that this observation would be the activity of non-Talon aliens. Instead, each of the opposing forces on Talon IV believes the other is responsible. Kirk looked over at Spock before speaking again. They both understood the nightmarish situation the FCO was in. Are you saying that there is a chance that FCO operations have intensified the feelings of distrust between the two sides and that the increased potential for war which now exists on Talon is the result of interference? Exactly. Wilfirth was relieved that Kirk seemed to follow his reasoning. And that's where the enterprise comes in. Obviously, we need access to information that is not being released publicly. We need to know all the details of the shuttle sighting. We have to know what phenomena spurred the two sides to upgrade their sensor systems so that the shuttle could be recorded. The sensor satellites you are placing in orbit for us will give us that data. But Kirk disagreed. Director, given the state of the military alert on Talon IV and the fact that the Talon suspect that they are already under observation, it's too risky to deploy close orbiting satellites around that world. He stood up to end the meeting. I'm sure you understand that in a situation like this, I have to report back to Starfleet Command for specific orders. To take the enterprise into a mission that might compromise the prime directive is beyond my authority as a Starship Commander. Captain Kirk, you don't have time to report back to Starfleet. Because of the subspace blackout conditions, it will take you 14 days to hear back from Starfleet after you transmit your report. I'm quite aware of the time frame, Director Wilforth. No, Captain, you're not. The director looked down at the tabletop afraid to meet Kirk's eyes. You see, the situation on Talon is impossible. It cannot hold for another 14 days. There's a very good chance it won't last even three more days. No matter what your orders say, you don't have time to contact Starfleet. Kirk was shocked. The situation was far worse than the reports had stated. I'm sorry to do this to you, Captain Kirk, but I do know that when a Starship Commander must act within a time period which prevents communication with a higher authority, that Starship Commander is empowered to act independently in a manner which he or she believes is in keeping with the best interests of Starfleet and the Federation. Kirk sat back down. The director was right. There is no more time, Captain Kirk, and under the circumstances as a Starship Commander, you are the highest authority in charge of what happens next. Wilforth looked up and finally met Kirk's eyes. The fate of an entire civilized world and the lives of more than two billion beings now rests in your hands, sir. What will you do? Chief Engineer's Log Supplemental. The Enterprise is now in orbit around Talon 4, using all her deflectors to avoid being detected by the Talon's ground-based radar units. Captain Kirk has decided to help Director Wilforth obtain the classified information needed to determine why the Talon seemed to be aware of the FCO. To collect this data, we have now deployed eight sensor satellites that can monitor even the most secure military communications network. On Talon 4 itself, the situation remains tense, with the latest threat to peace being an incident, involving an unidentified intrusion into the Green Nation's polar airspace. Talon negotiators from both the Green and the Brown Nations are working hard to diffuse the situation peacefully. And for all the power of the Enterprise, the only action we can take is to pray that they are successful. Three hours later, the Enterprise once again filled with the sound of cheers. Her mission had ended in a way even her captain had not expected. Talon 4 was at peace. McCoy stood with Spock by Kirk's chair on the bridge. It has been a most fascinating sequence of events, Spock said. McCoy's grin was blinding. Fascinating. That's not the word for it, Mr. Spock. They went from the brink of destruction to a secure future and less than a day of intense negotiations. That's what I'd call a miracle. Kirk stood up from his chair and stretched wierly. Gentlemen, I have no doubt that a few decades from now when the Talon historians study the recordings we've made today, they'll agree with you both. For the first time since his initial meeting with Director Wilforth, Kirk felt himself begin to relax. The mission was over and the prime directive had not been broken. Of all the hundreds of rooms in the Enterprise, Kirk's favorite was the Urbarium, especially during ship's night when the lighting was subdued and the night blooming flowers filled the air with their elusive fragrance. It always reminded him of home. The farm in Iowa, his mother's garden, the summer nights when the skies shimmered with uncountable stars. Kirk closed his eyes and drew in another deep breath. Fifty thousand kilometers beyond the viewport, Talon IV also rested in peace. Such undisturbed moments were rare on the Enterprise, so he was not surprised when the paging whistle sounded. But the red alert was like a knife. Chekhov's voice, under the thunder-com. Bridge to captain, bridge to captain, we have missile launchers on Talon IV, we have detonations. Kirk pushed his way through the turbo-lift doors and arrived on the bridge out of breath. The view screen showed the terrible truth in full magnification. The day side of Talon glittered with the brilliant pin-prick flares of fusion fireballs. Dozens, hundreds, more sparkling into hellish life with each second. Why, Kirk whirled to a Hurrah. What happened? A Hurrah, a desperate unknown captain. There has been no mention of any war preparations on any of the comm channels we've been monitoring. Tulu, take us in there, full impulse. Even as the helmsman acknowledged the order, the image of Talon swelled on the screen. The ship was in fixed orbit in seconds, poised over Talon IV. Chekhov, evaluation. The Ensign's hands trembled over his controls. Great, you seen same captain. All weapons have been launched. All weapons. There is no strategy. No plan. Just they are firing everything. Kirk saw his straw and grasped at it. Are you saying malfunction, mister? Is that it? Is that a malfunction down there? Chekhov grimaced. They can't want to do this. Not like that. It must be something else that caused it. The turbo-lift doors burst open again. Spock burst onto the bridge, still adjusting his uniform. His mouth opened as he saw what was on the screen, but he said nothing. Everything's been launched, Spock. No plan, no strategy. That is senseless. Exactly, Spock. Senseless. Something to do with disarming the automated alert systems. That's the only explanation. Perhaps captain. Even Spock was shaken by the destruction spreading on the screen. The Talon are not capable of such insanity. But without more information, we can't be sure what triggered it. We can't be certain what to do. Kirk turned to his crew. Bring those missiles down. No, Captain. Spock stepped away from his station to confront Kirk. Without data, without communication logs, you cannot. I know, Spock. I know. Kirk thrust out his arm to point at the screen. But look what they're doing to themselves down there. He made his decision. Everyone, I cannot order you to act against the Prime Directive. But I believe that something else beyond the Talon's control has caused this, and I believe we are justified in stopping it. Kirk looked at each of his bridge crew in turn. After a moment's hesitation, Spock was at his station. Processing targeting data. Chekhov spoke next. So I volunteered to bring down the missiles. Transmitting self-destruct and callback codes. Uhura said. Sulu brought the ship about. Moving in on main missile flights. McCoy ran from the turbo lift then stopped in horror at what he saw. My God, those ignorance fools! It's not their fault bones. It has to be a massive equipment malfunction. They trusted too much to their computers, or maybe Captain Kirk. All radio frequencies are jam-sir over a jab at her controls and frustration. Nothing can get through, not even the Talon's own messages. Can you broadcast on subspace and phase down to radio frequencies once you've passed the jamming boundary? Ahura looked at Spock. Mr. Spock, I'll need your help to... I will begin the proper sensor alignment. Kirk stared at the screen, willing the miniature sons that grew silently on it to disappear. On the planet's night side, the arc of atmosphere already clowed red from the firestorms that had erupted. Where are those phasers, Mr. Chekhov? Sir, targeting modes are not working. I can't lock on anything all signals are being jammed. What? That's impossible. The Talon don't have the technology, could it be in effect of all the fusion explosions? Kirk saw more fireballs blossom on the rabbit's surface of Talon. The planet looked as if its core had exploded and was bursting through its shell. Perhaps, Captain, but our sensors are useless. What if we went in closer, boosted power to all subspace systems and punched through the interference? That... could work, Spock confirmed. Salu, take us in past the jamming layer. Salu hesitated for an instant. Sir, that will take us through the ionosphere and into the atmosphere proper. Won't be the first time, Kirk said, his fists were clenched. Take us in. The Enterprise fell toward Talon for... Within seconds, a rough buffeting of atmospheric flight shook the bridge. Kirk knew Mr. Scott would be complaining for days to come. Check off. Try those phasers again. The familiar wine of the phaser capacitors echoed through the bridge. They're working. Kirk off slapped the side of his console in triumph. Limited range, but they're working. Buhura, try the self-destruct signals again. Yes, sir. Getting some response, sir. The ship bucked wildly. Wild winds screamed against her hull. Shockways from multiple explosions. Salu's hands moved feverishly over the controls. This is like flying through water, sir. Buhura cashed and pulled her earpiece from her ear. That is subspace feedback on all calm channels, Spock said. This is not a natural phenomenon. This is a deliberate attempt to... Salu broke in urgently. Incoming missiles. Impossible, Kirk answered. We have been targeted. Spock confirmed. Missiles are locked. What the talent can't do this, Spock? They don't have the capability. The communication page sounded. Scott's voice came over the intercom. Scott to bridge. If you don't mind me asking, what the hell's going on up there? Five seconds to missile impact Spock. Full power to shield, Scotty. Now! Now! Salu! Get us out of... The Fuse Green flare brilliant white until the visual compensators cut in. The ship shutted as if it had smashed into solid rock. Buhura fell from her chair. Spock slammed over the railing and all Kirk could hear was every bridge alarm screaming at him in betrayal. Salu's cry cut through the alarms. Captain, the impulse is gone. We're in freefall. Impact on planet surface in one minute. The rush of air outside the home. Lows in a frantic wail. Kirk felt his heart stop. With the impulse engines gone, there was only one way up. But it was madness. Madness. Warp us out, Salu! Warp us out! Scott shouted over the intercom. Captain, we're too deep into the planet's gravity well. We won't survive the transition to warp. Now Salu, there is no other... The whole metal crepe and the ship twisted as another barrage of missiles detonated against her shields. Spock pulled himself back to his feet. Green blood flooded his eyes from a cache on his forehead. Thirty seconds to impact, Salu announced. Going to warp... now! It was like death. The view screen went black. The lights cut out. He failed. And there was only a long endless fall into utter darkness. Then the emergency lights flickered back on and Kirk saw everything before him blur in a high speed vibration. Spock said, the emergency system's on-line. Partial gravity returned. Flour trails flickered from every object as local time slowed down. Scott's voice was planed to slow and warbling over the calm link. Warp generators are runaway. Link to singularity on runaway. Jefferson missiles! Kirk felt trapped in thick liquid. The Enterprise had to cut her warp space link to Talon IV's gravity well, or the ship would become trapped in an endless moment of time. Spock struggled to respond. Crew evacuation complete. Starboard Nacelle away. Kirk felt stretched like rubber. The view screen flickered to show the infinite fractal nightmare of the gravitational wormhole that loomed hungrily before them. He felt a part of him wrenched away as a long white graceful form of the starboard warped Nacelle flew down the maw of the beast, distorted, dizzying eddies of higher dimensional realities. Gravity failed, and they fell again. Kirk's hands gripped the sides of his tear. His foot hooked under the seat to hold him in place. Someone flew through the air beside him. Equipment consoles flared and sparked. No, Kirk thought. I won't let you go. I won't let you go alone. Spock continued to report. Fort Nacelle locked in position. Cannot Jefferson. Only one more chance Kirk thought. Worse than the last. He ordered Spock to eject all matter and anti-matter into the wormhole. Spock didn't argue. If the singularity won, they would not even know death. Only the torment of being forever trapped in the agonizing instant just before the end. Kirk saw the twin ionized jets of matter and anti-matter stream down the wormhole with agonizing slowness. Then at last they met and interacted. The screen went blank. Time stopped. Kirk fell into oblivion. Kirk awoke to the sound of a spray hypo. McCoy stared down at him. The doctor's face was haggard and blood smeared. Kirk was all McCoy said and he moved on to the others. Kirk pushed himself from the floor of the bridge. He did it on a lean because the gravity field was out of alignment, placing the floor on a relative five degree angle. Spock filled the air. He heard moans. Half the station displays were out. The other half flickered with gibberish. And only a few battery lights were working, making the whole area dark and murky. Spock staggered to Kirk's side, a green-soaked bandage covering the gas on his forehead. It worked. The matter-anti-matter explosion pushed us out of the gravity well into normal space. But what else did it do? Kirk normally surveyed the shattered bridge. His ship was dying around him. How long have I been out? Three minutes, eighteen seconds. Spock seemed weak and distracted. Every trans-stater circuit on the ship appears to be fused. The subspace energy pulse directed at us was incredible. But from where? Unknown, Captain. Unknown. Kirk saw a shape move onto the viewscreen. It was Talon. The planet was on fire. The entire planet. It drifted slowly across the screen, then disappeared. The Enterprise spun slowly, adrift in space. We are quite powerless. Spock said before Kirk could ask. Kirk heard a dull, thudding noise. And then one of the kicking panels by the turbo-lift popped out of position. Scott appeared holding a hand light that sent a solid shaft of light through the smoke. He was followed by two medical technicians. Oh, thank heavens, you're all right, Captain. The column systems out, the turbo-lifts. Scott saw Talon move across the viewscreen. Oh, no. How did it happen? And what happened to the ship? We were attacked by Talon missiles. Spock's tone betrayed no emotion. Kirk watched Scott's reaction. The fact that the Enterprise had been attacked meant that without a doubt, the Talon had known the ship was in orbit around their planet, indirect and flagrant violation of the prime directive. Scott was a good officer. He'd know what he would have to do next under such circumstances. Mr. Spock, are you sure that the Talon missiles were directed at the Enterprise herself? Kirk put his hand on Scott's shoulder. They were Scotty. The Talon knew we were here. They came after us. Scott looked at the screen. description: In this podcast episode, Captain Kirk and his crew face an unexpected challenge when they find themselves at a remote outpost on the moon of Talon 4, cut off from communication with Earth. The main monitoring lab is so advanced that it resembles a Starship's bridge enlarged ten times. While trying to decipher communications, they witness a news broadcast that includes a blurry image of what appears to be an alien species, raising questions about their interactions and potentially altering the nature of the outpost itself.

description: In this podcast episode "003 - Vulcans Forge Audiobook side 1", Simon & Schuster Audio presents Star Trek with Alkins Forge by Josepha Sherman and Susan Schwartz, read by Leonard Nimoy. Captain Spock of the science vessel trepid two meets veteran crew member David Rabine, who is now assigned to planetary duty on Obsidian. The pair discuss the challenges faced by the planet's inhabitants due to a malfunctioning solar system causing crop failure and other issues.

description: The podcast episode "004 - Vulcans Forge Audiobook side 2" discusses the ancient words spoken by Spock regarding the desire for peace and the rejection of conflict between humans and Vulcans. It also mentions that Spock was offered a nomination but declined, stating that he is not suitable for such an offer as he committed murder. The episode then shifts to discuss a fictional situation involving a nomad prince who suggests trying readjusting power cells to get more energy from solar power for survival in the desert.

description: In this episode of Star Trek Audiobook "The Return" (Part 2), Captain Jean-Luc Picard and Beverly Crusher face a harrowing confrontation with an advanced Borg structure, reminiscent of the events at Starbase 804. Despite initial signs that they might be captured by the Borg, it becomes clear that the cube is awaiting their retrieval rather than being in sleep mode as initially suspected. The episode explores themes of survival and resilience against formidable adversaries, showcasing the complex operations within the Federation's efforts to counteract an unexpected threat from the Borg.

Below them, on a lower plaza, 10 stories deep, a sunken dome stretched away kilometers wide, its surface pulsing with flashing traces of cold blue light. Picard folded his tricorder shut. That's the central note. Kirk turned to the captain. Now, why don't you come back? Now that we found it, I can deal with it. But can you deal with them, Captain Kirk? Kirk turned to look in the direction Picard looked, along the wide deck that ran from the passageway in a sweeping circle around the glowing dome and sunken plaza. He saw what Picard saw. Org. Closets of it, marching closer. Kirk and Picard ducked behind a power conduit more than five meters thick. Picard pointed to a switching lever on the side of the stained and mineral encrusted metal that formed the pipe. This lever will do it. It will cut the power to the central note's core and trigger feedback surge that will burn out all its circuits. Picard, how can you know all this? I don't. But look, cutest us. The massive approaching board was coming closer. Then we should cut the power now. No, Captain Kirk. We have to time it for the Enterprise's return. That way, there's still a chance for us to get out. How do we hold them back till then? Picard smiled. You don't. I do. Picard opened a black carry-all pouch. Kirk glanced inside. Saw the Borg interface. To destroy the Borg homeworld, Picard must become luchutus again. Picard attached the neural plate to his face. The power cell in the subspace transmitter were already strapped to his chest. He jabbed the jack hole. A faint blue crackle of energy leapt along the input cable to the power cell of Picard's shoulder. Picard's eyes rolled back in his head until a link white remained. Beyond the conduit, the Borg horde advanced. And then Picard rose to his feet beside Kirk, facing the enemy as it approached. Kirk stood as well. Picard, isn't working. Picard stared at Kirk as if he were nothing more than the metallic debris that littered this world. We are luchutus. We are Borg. Kirk grabbed Picard by the shoulder, shook him. Fight in the card. The card's eyes cleared. Jim, it wasn't supposed to be like this. It's too strong. Kirk twisted Picard around to face the advancing Borg. Tell him to stop or I'll cut the power off now. Picard screamed and swung at Kirk. Resistance! Resistance is futile. Kirk grabbed his arm. Held him. You are Jean-Luc Picard. You are a starship captain. Act like one. And Kirk slapped him. And slapped him again until Picard brought up his hand and caught Kirk's arm in mid-swing. I think you've convinced me. Picard faced the Borg, now no more than a handful of meters away. We are Borg. The collective is safe. Return. Return to your functions. Kirk tensed as he watched the Borg hesitate. Picard's eyes fluttered. This power cut off Picard. How long do we have after we throw it? Picard held his hands to his head. Feedback is immediate. The instant we throw the lever, the note is... Whoever pulls that lever will die. Kirk had heard enough. He grabbed the interface cable and pulled it free. Kirk checked his tricorder. We've got 60 seconds until the Enterprise does our fly by. Picard nodded. I can take it from here. In case you don't remember Jean-Luc, whoever pulls that lever and destroys the node gets trapped in the power search. And I'm already dying. Spock's voice crackled out of Kirk's combat. Enterprise to a way team. We are at 30 seconds to emergency beam out. What is your status? Kirk slugged Picard in the jaw as hard as he could. Picard dropped like a dead weight. Kirk dragged him away by his collar until he was well away from the power conduit. Kirk to Enterprise. Spock here. Keep the ship out of danger Mr. Spock and lock onto my signal. One to beam out. Then he tossed his comb badge onto Picard's chest and stepped back. Picard reacted to the impact of the badge. His eyes opened. He started to speak. Then dissolved in the transporter as the Enterprise once more claimed her all. Kirk turned back to the power conduit. Grab the lever in both hands. Felt it move easily. Then he closed his eyes. Squeeze his hands tight. Pulled. Heard a sudden deafening roar of thunder coming from the dome. Then he heard a scrape as quiet as a footstep behind him. Kirk turned. Opened his eyes. Solve him. On the bridge of the Enterprise to which he had been directly beamed. Picard shielded his eyes against the sudden glare from the viewscreen. On it a blinding column of light shot up from the Borg home world directly from the location of what had been the central node. Ripples of explosions began to spread out across the home world surface following the strict lines and angles of circuitry. Beside him, Beverly Crusher took his hand. Riker stood beside her. Data and LaFords sat together at the helm. At his station, Worf made no effort to hide his eyes from the light. And Picard saw tears roll down Troy's cheeks. He knew the counselor was overwhelmed by the emotions of all who surrounded her, their joy and their grief. The explosions spread out in a web of fire encompassing a third of the home world as a thousand other cube ships broke from its surface and jumped to transwarp fleeing the death of whatever this planet had been. There would still be Borg somewhere, Picard knew. But the Federation had been preserved because of one man. Riker spoke their thoughts. A great man has died today. Spock turned to look at Riker. His expression was disturbing, both unfathomable and familiar. Finally he spoke. Captain Picard, now I believe the bridge is yours. Picard watched in silence as Spock slowly left the bridge. When he was gone, Riker turned to his captain. Did you see the look on Spock's face? I've seen it before. At the salvage camp, Spock still doesn't believe that Kirk's dead. Picard looked at the combag in his hand. He remembered fleeting images of what he had seen in Kirk's mind. What Spock had shown him there. There are always possibilities. The Borg homeworld was a blazing pyre, bringing light to a system that had been dark for a time too long to be measured. Triumphant, victorious in the new dawn's light, the starship Enterprise set course for home. One voyage at an end. The ongoing mission far from over. Star Trek, the Return, was written by William Shatner with Judith and Garfield Reeve Stevens and read by William Shatner. It was adapted for audio by George Truett. The recording engineer was Mike Hanley. The tape editor was Stephen Strassman with post-production and sound design by Gary Fink. Additional post-production by Stephen Strassman. Original music was composed by Sam McCallay, Carl Shurps, Eve Viglarian and Richard M. The associate producer was Florence Barrow Adams. Star Trek, the Return, was produced and directed by Linda Wollman.

transcript: Simon & Chuster Audio presents Star Trek, The Return, by William Shatner, with Judith and Garfield Reeve-Stevins, read by William Shatner. He fell, alone, twisting through the air of Viridian 3, the shriek of the metal bridge echoing in his ears, spinning, the sun flashing into his eyes, the shadows of golfing, light shadow, like the beating of wings, like all the days of his life intersecting. In an Iowa cornfield, he sees the stars, a boy of five in his father's arms, in Starfleet headquarters, Admiral Nagura reaching out to shake his hand. Congratulations, Captain, the Enterprise is yours. Then one shadow blocked the light, broke his fall. He turned his head, looked up, saw a face he recognized from the future. Did we do it? Did we make a difference? The other in his odd uniform, but with the familiar touchstone of Starfleet on his chest, now by his side. Oh yes, we made a difference, thank you. This stranger, this Picard, had offered his friendship. In another lifetime, perhaps, it might have been so. At least I could do for the Captain of the Enterprise. Voices called him from the darkness. Through the lattice work of the twisted metal above him, he glimpsed the edge of something moving, something coming closer. It cut through sky, through light and shadows. The final wisps of existence lifted from him in a feathered haze of light, revealing all that lay beyond still to come. Oh my. And then he fell again. Alone. James T. Kirk was dead. As Commander William Riker resolved from the transporter beam, beside the grave of that Starfleet legend, he was surprised by the sudden thought that had come to him. Of all that had happened on this desolate world of Rodeon three only a month ago, the fate of James T. Kirk weighed most heavily on his mind. Half a planet away, the shattered hulk of the USS Enterprise lay on ruins, slowly being carved into transporter loads of recyclable scrap by a team of Starfleet engineers. Though the ship was beyond salvage, in accordance with the prime directive, no trace of it could remain on this world. In the days that had passed since the Enterprise had blazed through the atmosphere of Rodeon three to her first and final landing, Riker's thought still kept turning to the fate of the captain of an earlier Enterprise, the first Enterprise. On a distant outcropping, Riker saw a lone sentinel, a dried desert wind shifting the elegant black robes he wore. He had come from Romulus against all logic, Spock. Riker knew the Vulcan ambassador had worked with Kirk as a living breathing individual, yet Spock was also as much a legend. What could it be like Riker wondered to lose a friend, then 78 years later, to lose him again? A few days after the crew of Riker's Enterprise had been rescued, Starfleet intelligence had mounted an emergency extraction mission to bring Spock from the home world of the Romulan Star Empire to Verdean III, so he might accompany his friend on his final voyage. The extraction was not an operation to be undertaken lightly. Relations between the Romulans and the Federation had been strained for centuries. Spock was instrumental in the efforts to reduce those tensions by decades of secret negotiations and intended to reconcile the Romulans with the Vulcans. Though the Romulans were an offshoot of the Vulcan race, they had rejected the logic which had saved their Vulcan ancestors from succumbing to their primitive passionate blood-drenched beginnings. So who better than Spock, a child of emotional humans and logical Vulcans, to understand both sides and work for unification? On the horizon the last radiance spike of the dying sun flared then vanished behind a distant peak. Overhead, stars emerged from the deepening twilight. Far away, Riker saw Spock bow his head as if lost in memory. Riker, go ahead. Commander Riker, this is Killborn with... Her heartbeat the static cleared and Killborn's distraught voice cut through the vertia night. Can't tell where they're coming from, two shuttles gone, we need... Riker tapped his badge again. Riker, to Ambassador Spock. A moment passed, then the deep familiar voice answered... Spock here. Ambassador, there appears to be some trouble at the salvage site. I'm going to have to ask you to remain here while I beam back to check the situation. Of course, Commander. What is the nature of the trouble? I'm not sure. It almost sounds as if they're under attack. Spock said nothing more. Logically, there was nothing more to be said. Riker to transport a control beam me to the salvage site. In the cool tingle of the transporter effect, the grave site shimmered. And then will Riker beamed into hell? Driving rain sprayed through the ragged hole of the canopy of the portable transporter platform, drenching Riker the instant the transporter's exclusion field shut down. Riker shouted over the storm to the officers near him. Move! Move! He shoved ahead toward the steps that led to the dueroplased walkways, linking the buildings of the salvage camp spread out before him. The bombarded camp had become a collection of looming shadows, except when the sky blazed with alien fire. Riker caught up with a lieutenant balloon. She leaned over the walkway railing, staring to the east, where a sputtering ball of plasma flared against the doranium skin of the Enterprise's lifeless saucer. A wave of heat blasted him from the side as a barracks building detonated and a rocketing fountain of blinding plasma fire. Flaming debris arked downward. Riker grabbed Baru's arm, yanking her off the walkway into the mud. And an armless thunderclap reached out and scooped the mud from behind Tossum the middle of the rain. Baru's arm flew away from his grasp. Riker twisted as he fell through the hiss of crisscrossing shrapnel and hit cold mud. He rolled through and struggled to his feet. Lieutenant Baru! You could see no trace of Baru or other officers who had been close by. Commander Riker! Riker wheeled to see Baru struggling toward him. She was layered in mud. She limped. One hand wrapped tightly over her shoulder, the other arm hung uselessly. Who's doing this, sir? Riker had no idea, not even suspicions. We have to get to a shuttle, Lieutenant. Baru's gaze swept the camp. There won't be any shutters. Riker took hold of her good arm. You won't know till we look. This way. More explosions shook the saucer hull. Riker's jaw tightened as he heard screams blend with the roar of the unseen craft, the hum of their weapons, the roar of the flames. They skirted the burning mound of wreckage that had been a storage warehouse. Beyond it, Riker could see the smoking pits that were all that remained with shuttle pads. Two Tesla-class shuttles lay in pieces nearby, split open like used packing crates. Killborn was there. More engineers worked with him. Riker called to Killborn. Who are they? Killborn looked up at him with shadowed eyes. I don't know. They took out the firegate. Riker felt acid, coarse through his stomach. The only other Starfleet vessels in the Viridian system were a handful of transport traitors and engineering support cruisers. Without the firegate, the survivors of the salvage camp were at the mercy of its attackers. And what are they after? Killborn shook his head. I don't know. There's nothing important left in the Enterprise. All the tactical computer cores were pulled on the first day. Phasers, shields, everything classified has already been taken out. Killborn held out a strike order. Whoever they are, they're flooding us with sensor scans. They know where each one of us is. We've got to retreat Commander into the forest. Riker looked at the engineering shuttle. It couldn't fly. That wasn't all it was good for. Does this shuttle still have demolition charges? Killborn thought Riker must be crazy. You can't be serious, sir. Riker grabbed the Haggard chief engineer by a short front. Starfleet doesn't run. I want both torpedoes prepped for atmospheric detonation. Killborn's high voice shook. Commander, the second you turn on the shuttle's targeting system, whatever's attacking us, is going to incinerate us. Riker smiled grimly. It took less than two minutes to prepare the torpedoes for simultaneous activation, target lock and launch. Riker turned to Killborn. Get your people out of here. Riker felt Buru's hand on his arm. Sir, you can't do this alone. Don't worry, Lieutenant. I plan to live forever. Riker punched a command sequence into the tricorder. Then he hefted the tricorder in his hand and threw it into the storm. It landed 50 meters away, disappearing into the mud. After 30 seconds, Lieutenant, that tricorder is going to put out a signal that makes it look like a phaser bank coming online. Buru smiled. A distraction. Riker jerked his head to the side. Go with Killborn. Head into the forest. Then Riker pulled himself through the off-angle door of the shuttle out of the rain. Inside the flight deck was at a 20-degree slope. Riker braced himself on the co-pilot's chair as his mud-coated boots slipped on the traction carpet. He activated the shuttle's torpedo substation. Quickly, he set the torpedoes to target any moving object 100 meters in altitude or above. As soon as the panel confirmed his input, he hurried back through the shuttle's cargo hold to the airlock door. The instant he appeared in the doorway, a green bolt of energy hit the mud 50 meters in front of it, vaporizing the tricorder in a spray of steam. Riker felt a rush of earth. The distraction had worked. But the beam did not shut off. It pushed on through the mud, rending it like water before the prowl of a ship, closing on the second weapon signal, the shuttle. Riker gripped the sides of the door and pushed a loop free. His boots slipped. He fell, chest slamming into the raised ridge of the airlock seal. He felt a rib crack and looked up to see the inexorable green bolt crackling toward him 10 meters away. The beam reached out for him. A hat grabbed his wrist. Commander. Baru hadn't left him. She hauled him out of the shuttle with desperate strength. All in that one terrible moment as she hurled him away from her to safety, he heard her cry. Heard the hiss of vaporized flesh. Heard the hum of torpedoes launching. The shuttle sliced into. He rolled onto his back in time to see two ionized streaks of plasma exhaust bank into the storm clouds as the torpedoes sought their targets. The clouds lit up like dawn. Riker carefully, painfully drew himself up into a sitting position. He saw Baru's hand. Outstretched, reaching for him. Out of the mud, he gripped it, pulled. And the hand in the forearm and nothing else of the young lieutenant slipped from the mud. Riker dropped the hand in horror. Hellish fires from the camp and the saucers still lived the low, roiling clouds, but there were no more explosions. No more screams of low-flying craft. Warm rain bathed his eyes. Gentle as tears, the attack was over. And Riker knew he couldn't rest until he had found those responsible and answered the question. Why? Alone in the darkness by the grave site, Spock had found a rock to sit on. He was 143 standard years old, advanced middle age for a Vulcan in good health. For almost half an hour he maintained his position, observing moving points of light against the stars and the streaks of multi-colored light that were exchanged between them. Starships in orbital battle. The night air thrummed. In large was approaching through the sky. Spock rose slowly to his feet. He could see nothing, but his robes began to swirl around him, blown about by some kind of backwash. Directly above him the stars wavered and then disappeared, blacked out by a silhouette of something he couldn't identify. A sudden light danced at the edge of his vision. Spock looked down the slope point Kirk sprayed. Amber rays spiked out from between the rocks of the simple care. The light emanating from Kirk's grave, brightened, limiting and a fade. Spock clearly heard the sounds of rocks falling against themselves. Among the stars the signs of the space battle ended. Above Spock the watching stars returned and the thrumming backwash ceased as suddenly as if a ship had gone to warp. Spock drew an emergency light from his belt and made his way down the slope to Kirk's grave. He played the light against the karen. The rocks had fallen in. The grave was empty. Spock looked at the stars. It was not at all logical, but for a moment a most improbable thought came to him. Perhaps some journeys were never meant to end. There were always possibilities. High above Aridian 3 flashing in sunlight, a 30 meter wide slab of curved uranium home metal slowly spun in the silence of space. The black letters etched into its surface red USS Farragut NCC60597. It was the largest piece of debris that remained at the starship. The rest was a cloud of dazzling shards, slowly dispersing. On board the avatar of Tomet, the Romulan commander-salator El watch the whole metal impassibly on the main view screen of her bridge. The sider she could send sub-commander translation. A great victory commander. Salatrel turned into command-share. This was no victory. They had no reason to expect us. They had no warning. It was an operational procedure. Nothing more. What of Kirk? Her science officer answered from the engineering console where transported displays flashed. DNA analysis confirms identity of the remains commander. When the attack craft docks, the remains will be beamed directly into the stasis unit. For the first time since this mission had begun, Salatrel permitted herself a small smile. She sat back in triumph. Decloak and prepared to receive incoming craft. She glanced up at sub-commander Tran, who remained standing beside her. We'll have our war soon enough. Tran's eyes narrowed with predatory anticipation. War and victory. Over the centuries, the Dante field had been mapped, explored and abandoned by every space-going culture in the sector. Whatever its origin, each of the thousands of asteroids in the field was worthless and without interest. The avatar of Tomed decloped as she dropped from warp on the outskirts of the Dante field. Moving with deceptive grace near the field center, the warbird closed on one large asteroid without slowing until its impact was inevitable. But then one small part of the asteroid's surface rippled with holographic distortion as the warbird made contact and passed safely through. Inside the hollow body beyond the holographic camouflage, the rough interior was set and was studded with directional grids of docking lights. Eight other warbirds were docked within the main cavern, with 27 Romulan birds of prey, more than a hundred scout ships and uncounted other smaller vessels. Without a doubt, Dante base was on a war footing. The Tomed followed the line of pulsing lights that guided it to its bay. Soon, Salatrel was deep within the hollowed-out asteroid. She ignored the tunnels that led to her private quarters. She headed through two sets of blast doors to arrive at the Alpha Secura secondary docking cavern where the other ship waited. Its method of docking had been unorthodox. Instead of the clean seal between adaptable docking rings, the other ship appeared to have grown into the metal and rock of Dante. Tenderls of cable and connecting conduits spread out of the portal-like connective tissue, securing the ship to the asteroid, not in one place, but hundreds. Once she was within the ship, Salatrel followed the Romulan markings that led her to the security doors. As the doors unfolded, Salatrel smelled the slightly fetid holdred with the liquid that pulsed through the twisted pipes that lined the chamber, an overlay of technology above alien and Romulan. The myriad light channels snaked along the curved walls, angling in through the empty air to converge like a web on the immense machine at the heart of the chamber. Under company, Salatrel approached the arc. That was the name her scientists had given to the alien machine's central component. An elongated container three meters along its widest axis made from bulging asymmetrical panels of a transparent mineral bound by gilded struts of gold wire. She glanced into the shadows of the control pit facing the arc in the center of the chamber. Among the Romulan computers, the technicians worked in the darkness. A scientist's voice echoed from hidden speakers. Transporter systems are online. Then someone called to her from that darkness. The technician, now called Vaux the warrior, who had once been her lover. A matter, it is time. She released her breath, proceed, responding instantly the alien machine began to vibrate. A rhythmic thudding shook the scarred metal neck. Mist spilled out of the control pit where the Romulan computer consoles had been installed to operate the device. The broadcast voices of the scientists and the technicians rattle through the rest of the systems check. A slow wave of light within the liquid filled arc quickened rhythmically with an orange gleam that fractured into stabbing golden flickers. An energy discharge crackled off a resonating coil a hundred meters away, lighting the vast chamber with the uncontained fury of storm. Then the light in the arc began to fade. Shadowy mass now began visible in the dense murky liquid. Desiccated, corrupted. The monstrous remnants of the heated past, floating before a solitrell. She heard a technician's voice. Now confirming nanite transmission. Some flash and explosion from the machine's flank sent sparks cascading through the chamber. Vaux calmly announced. Medical team to the arc. Sallotrell reached the scaffold first. The arc was two meters above her. She stared up into its darkened heart, saw the shape within, saw that shape move. She leapt for the ladder, two of her scientists close behind her. The shape within the arc struggled, arms flailing. She grabbed a tool from the startled scientist's hands, spun it around and smashed its handle on the transparent panel. A gout of liquid sprayed into her face. She clotted the edges of the shattered panel and tugged at the metal band between the broken panel and the next. Her face was smeared with the arc's nutrient fluid. It tasted bitter, salty, like an ocean choked with life. Get him out, get him. She gasped as a hand shot up from the arc, grabbed her arm and drew her into the suffocating depths of the arc. But die now here with him. Was not why she had risked her life, her name, her world. Sallotrell pulled back in the awful darkness of the arc until the terrible hand slipped off her arm and she stumbled back and out free. Except. The dark shape settled in the fluid, no longer moving. No! Live! The dark liquid erupted from the arc, like the impact of a gathering Russian wave. The scaffolding gave way in one corner, sending the two scientists tumbling to the deck below. But Sallotrell did not fall. She felt the hand return, this time grabbing her neck. Sallotell gripped the muscled forearm with her own torn hands. She looked up and saw. Kirk! I is alive with a madness she could not comprehend. The flesh of his shoulders and neck twisted and shimmered as its contours changed, reformed and realigned by the microscopic nanite devices that still work within him, restoring him, rebuilding him. His mouth gaped open as a heap with deep desperate guests for air. Sallotrell poured at her own throat, felt the acid pain of air rushing into a ravaged throat. A different hand joined hers in the struggle. Vox saved her. He stood before her, holding Kirk in place without effort. For a moment she was confused. Her beloved was before her standing in profile. His noble Romulan brow high and defiant. Then he turned to her and the nightmare returned. Half his face was gone. Up seenly replaced by black circuitry patches, laser sights, tubes and coils of binauronic implants. The inescapable hallmarks of assimilation. His old name was no longer a part of him, along with everything else he had been. He was Vox now. Romulan's speaker of the Borg Collective. The alien machine stirred, rumbling ominously. Vox turned to her. We must leave the chamber. Sallotrell nodded, unable to speak. Kirk's body was frozen in contorted posture. His strength no match for the implanted manipulator that had replaced Vox's right arm. We will take him to the medical facilities in Dante vase. Sallotrell backed away as the Borg Romulans took Kirk from Vox. Kirk's ancient uniform hung in tatters destroyed by the energies that had coursed through him once his body had been transported into the Ark. He walked stiffly. Like an orotum, the living dead of Romulan myth, Sallotrell found that fitting. Amazing. In ten days that creature will cause the Federation itself to fall before they. You're wrong. We have made an agreement. The Federation will fall before us. Sallotrell nodded relieved that Vox had met nothing more than what she had already accepted. Romulans and Borg working together. It was the price she had paid to restore the hated James T. Kirk to life. In ten days she would know if it had been worth the bargain. Starfleet vessels were doranium white, but some starfleet vessels were as dark as the void between the stars, intentionally coated and micro-defracted carbon to absorb all visible radiation that fell upon them. The USS monitor was one such vessel, the latest in the defined class, space black on silent running, closing in on a dying ancient world deep in the core frontier. Its destination, new titan. Overpowered, densely shielded, excessively armed, carrying more weaponry than three galaxy-class starships. She was the result of Starfleet's feathered preparations to fight a war against the Borg, a war that had yet to come to pass. But there were always possibilities. The monitor eased into a non-standard polar orbit over new titan. The only sign of its presence was the winking out, then the reappearance of the stars it passed. Its double-sealed hangar door opened. A small personnel shuttle emerged, propelled by low-gain tractor beams, undetectable past ten kilometers. It moved away from the monitor, dropping for new titan like a falling lance. The pilot, tightly strapped into her seat, maintained her calm expression and kept her hand steady on the controls. Behind her, her five passengers clung to the bench seats running along both sides of the shuttle's hold. Their expressions were unknown. For each war a carbon-black combat helmet with an opaque blast shield in place capable of deflecting a full force beam from a Type 3 phaser. The rest of their black uniforms were as heavily armored. Three of the passengers braced themselves with phaser rifles. The only identifying insignia they wore was the Starfleet Delta slashed by a bolt of red lightning. The crest of Starfleet's newest specialist division. That and their name tags. Wineline, Bayer, Krewl. Instead of weapons the other two passengers carried sealed equipment pods. They also wore name tags. Crusher, Picard. John Luke Picard felt himself shift as the shuttle slowly banged. He opened his helmet. Across from him, Wineline lifted her own blast shield and yanked open her helmet's visor. She was mostly human, though there was a hint of alien heritage in the assured gaze of her dark eyes. With a black-gloved fist, Wineline tapped the helmet of Bayer beside her. He opened his helmet as well, full of human. Bayer tapped the helmet of the third team member. Krewl lifted his shield, opened his visor, and grunted, sweat gleaming from the ridges of his crested forehead. John, Wineline looked at Krewl. You still complaining? Krewl bared his teeth at her. Human battle gear, too much protection. Not enough weaponry. Wineline unfastened her seatweb and leaned over to tap Beverly's helmet. We'll be over the drop zone in 300 seconds. Picard and Beverly looked at each other past the confines of their battle helmets, and Beverly whispered, This isn't a side of Starfleet we see very often. Picard forced himself to smile. It's a big galaxy, Doctor. He caught sight of the equipment pod strapped to her waist. He knew it carried the interface. Beverly followed his gaze to see what he looked at. She reached out to put her hand on his. It will be all right, Jean-Luc. We won't have to use it. Wineline stood up, then moved to the rear of the shuttle, and pulled down three times on a side mounted manual release cleaver. Thirty seconds. The rear decking of the cargo hold dropped open onto darkness. Exactly as they had trained, Picard and Beverly sealed the helmets and got to their feet. Wineline watched the readout on her tricorder. She raised her finger, paused, brought it down, pointed to Krewl. Without hesitation, the Klingon stepped over the open deck and dropped through it. And Wineline pointed at Picard, and as he had done a dozen times in the monitor's hall of suite, he stepped out into nothingness. He flipped over, dangling feet first, with still no sensation of falling, though he knew from the training simulations that the surface of new Titan was rushing up at them at 50 km per hour. He looked up and saw the densely packed stars of the galactic core. A dark object moved against them, then slowed. Beverly decided, or Wineline. He rocked in his harness as the anti-gravs on his back began to work harder. The harness dug into Picard with a sudden, sharp snap. His holodeck training paid off as he reflexively swung his legs together and bent his knees, then he slammed into dirt and rolled as he'd been trained. A moment later, Beverly hit and rolled an arm's length away. Before Picard could speak, he felt cruel and bare behind him, soundlessly detaching his anti-grav units from the back of his harness. There was the first to break the silence. They tracked us. He pointed ahead where a Starfleet blue phaser beam cut through the night from the horizon and found an unseen target that flared in a silent explosion. Picard recognized the glimmer of an antimatter reaction. Beverly looked shocked. Was that our shuttle? Wineline nodded. The pilot had to activate the engines to climb out of the atmosphere, which means the sense of feels they're using are more sensitive than we thought. Give me a reading crew. A complete phaser cannon? Crew growled in acknowledgement. Wineline glanced at Picard. That's a good sign. It means whoever's there is making due with the equipment at hand, they haven't brought in anything new. Picard was troubled by Wineline's apparent complacency. A pilot just died. How can that be a good sign? We all knew the risks, Captain. Wineline pointed ahead. Two kilometers double time, crew on point. The shuttle again by her directness. Picard began running, keeping cruel sensor shadows centered in his visor. He could hear Beverly's matchy pace just behind him. Wineline and Bear ran behind Beverly. The terrain of this region of new Titan was rough, strung with boulders. It reminded Picard of the nature preserves on Mars. Fifteen minutes and two kilometers later, crew waved them to a stop at the base of a low hill. Wineline stood before them, commanding their attention. This is it, all systems powered out and stay low. Her hands hit the controls of her forearm pad. The green glow of her night vision display faded from her helmet. Picard did the same and blinked as his eyes adjusted to the star glow. Then they looked over the rise and Picard's throat suddenly felt as dry as the rocks he lay across. In a baron of royal, or half a kilometer away, a plasteal perimeter barrier glowed in the clear, effusion-powered spotlights lay their first objective. Starbase 804 By the manuals, what lay before them was a Type 7 forward reconnaissance starbase standard issue on Class M planets where atmospheric domes were not required. But this starbase was no longer a standard issue. Wineline pointed straight ahead. Captain, do you confirm what I see? Picard swallowed painfully. The headlights sprayed up the sides of Starbase 804, bringing every centimeter of chaotic detail into hideous relief. Pipes and conduits, doranium sheets, prefab housing sections, even parts of the shuttles that should be on the pad. There were traces of everything used in the construction of the Starbase, now taken apart and reassembled into one of the most basic shapes of technology. A cube. Picard slowly nodded. I confer. Wineline brought her forearm up to her helmet and tapped a single control, then transmitted in a theoretically undetectable microburst to the monitor, far above the bipolar orbit. Archangel, this is Red Leader, we have positive confirmation. Repeat, positive confirmation. Starbase 804 has been assimilated by the Borg. Within their armored gloves, Picard squeezed his hands into fists, preparing himself for what he knew must come. He was running out of possibilities. And ignored the distant whisper deep within his mind and walked among the Borg alone. All around Picard, they went about their task of assimilating Starbase 804. Teams of them worked as little more than ants or termites. Using their biomechanical implants and augmentations to carve up the prefab buildings, remove the Starfleet equipment and process everything for the greater good of the collective. After Viridian 3 and his encounter with the Nexus, Picard had been sure he would draw at least a year behind a desk. A galaxy-class starship had been lost on his watch. The boards of inquiry alone would take months. But Starfleet was nothing if not responsive and realistic. Picard's testimony had taken less than half a day. He was still reeling from the speed of the inquiry and its conclusion as he and Will Riker had left the hearing room. And only when Picard saw Commander Elizabeth Shelby waiting for him did he understand that Starfleet had its own reasons for dealing with the Enterprise hearing so quickly. She waved Picard into an empty office and bluntly stated the facts. Starfleet intelligence had reason to believe that a series of distant outposts on the core frontier were being raided by the Borg. Picard protested. But the Borg are defeated. He had seen it himself. After the once mindless creatures had been awakened to their own individuality, the threat of the collective had been removed. Captain, it is Starfleet's belief that what you contacted, what you and your crew defeated, was only one branch of the collective. A single tentacle, if you will, of a monster that's spreading through the galaxy. Do you honestly think you have changed anything by changing just the handful of Borg with which you have had personal contact? We're not saying we believe that facing the Borg is a hopeless proposition. You were able to neutralize one branch, to us that clearly implies the other yet to be engaged branches can also be defeated. At that Picard had disagreed vehemently. But whatever strategy we use on one branch, the next branch instantly knows how to defend itself. Shelby had smiled at his passion. We're not just going after the branches, Captain. We're going after the head. Somewhere out there is the central point from which all the branches emanate. We shall find that source, and we shall destroy it. Then she had given him his new orders. Picard was to join the tactical team to be based at Starbase 804. Once there, when suspected Borg activity was detected, Picard was to be deployed with Starfleet its new anti-Borg specialists, the mission objective, capture, and return of a Borg vessel. Four years ago Picard himself had been assimilated, made part of the Borg Collective, and its irresistible group mind. As low cutis of Borg, he had actually led the collective against Starfleet in the devastating battle of Wolf 359, giving the Borg full access to every Starfleet secret locked in his mind. And though every trace of Borg technology had been surgically removed from his body, in his mind the tendrils of the collective remained, and Starfleet knew that. Shelby had put the pieces of the interface on the table then, the latest from Starfleet R&D. The interface filled him with inexpressible dread. One part was simply an insulated cable, containing a microprocessor on one input jack and a slender transformer on the other. The other was a sleek power cell coupled with a short range subspace transmitter, small enough to be carried unseen in a hand. But the third piece was an asymmetrical plate of silicon, curved to fit the contours of the human face and skull. In this case, Picard's face and skull. Together, they formed a Borg-derived neural interface, just like the one that had been implanted in Picard's flesh and in his mind. Then Commander Shelby had informed Picard, you will be accompanied by Dr. Beverly Crusher. She's already been briefed. Except for Beverly, Picard had had no contact with his crew since that day. We require the protective device in casing your sensory stump. The flat, emotionless voice startled Picard from his reverie, a Borg barred his path. Since it had been human, female, Starfleet. Beneath the cybernetic augmentations fused to its chest and ribcage, he could see the remnants of a Starfleet duty uniform. Its communicator was still in position. Borg wires extended from it and entered that abused skin in the seemingly random series of small puckers. A thicker, red cable ran up from the communicator and into its temple. Whatever it had been. It was a Borg now. Manipulator Arm extended, a cutting blade, worrying. Are you defective? I will give you my protective device. Picard knew if he did not remove his helmet now, the mission would be over before it had begun. The Borg held out its living hand. Picard gave her the helmet, keeping his head downcast. Eyes averted. The Borg did not step away. You will direct your visual sensors upward. Picard took a deep breath and looked up. Locutus? The Borg who stood before Picard looked troubled because the collective was troubled. Locutus is physically here, but not present among their joint thoughts. The Borg trained its manipulator arm on Picard. The thin blue rod of an X-ray welding and glowed along the mechanical arm. The collective had long evolved the behavior to treat anomalous phenomena as threatening and therefore subject to immediate destruction. At this moment Picard was a threat, but he also knew how the Borg functioned. Picard looked at the Borg. Are you defective? Whatever the Borg had been about to do, its primary behavior was now circumvented by a diagnostic subroutine. A verbal order from Locutus had been enough to trigger it. Once on no sign of the rest of the Y-line's team, each had planned to enter the base separately to avoid attracting the collective's attention. They were to rendezvous in two more hours. Finally, the Borg responded. No defects detected? The Borg angled its head. Communing. Locutus is missing. You are defective. The X-ray welding began to glow, began to whine as its quantum capacitor built its charge. Picard stumbled back as the female Borg suddenly shimmered in a blaze of phased energy then vanished. Picard looked around, saw Sue Windline three meters away. Have you been following me? Captain, my job is to get you to that cube ship? Keep walking. Windline tossed him his helmet. Picard pulled the helmet on, closed the visor, and marched forward. He wished he were somehow locking Locutus back into his deep and hidden cell somewhere in his core, but he knew it was too late. All around him, he heard the whisper of the collective. Though whether it sprang from the Borg or his own subconscious, he could not be sure. Come back, Trump. Come back. Spock. Kirk ran calling for help, something chasing him, into the bowels of the ship, running, always running, changing the rules, nothing made sense. Horses, Antonio, the stars in space, the man in the strange uniform, Starfleet uniform. Picard. He went through space through time, following Yosemite. Spock. He hadn't been alone at Yosemite, climbing the mountain, but this time he was, until he felt the pressure of a cold cloth on his forehead. He reached for it, needed to take it away. Shhh. He moved the cloth and saw he didn't know her. She spoke softly. Do you know where you are? The Enterprise? The woman shook her head. Do you know who you are? Of course he did. He smiled, opened his mouth. Nothing came out. Panic. It's alright. I know who did this to you. You were very brave. Kirk felt relief. People counted on him, all 430 aboard the Enterprise. The Enterprise. What is it? Where am I? You were injured in battle. Kirk was aware of a cool breeze across his chest. He looked down expecting to see a uniform of some sort, but what kind of uniform? He saw nothing. Who was he? You said I was injured? In battle? Against the enemy. She picked up a small pad and pressed to control a far corner of the stark room faded away. This is the enemy. The viewpoint in space shifted. A vessel came into view. Kirk felt it tugging in his heart. The vessel was magnificent. The woman pointed to the ship. The Enterprise. The enemy. Kirk was surprised. The ship didn't feel like the enemy. The woman looked at him. Say it. The Enterprise. The enemy. The woman adjusted another control on her past. Kirk gasped with sudden pain. Say it. Kirk gasped. Enterprise. The enemy. The woman smiled at us. Instantly Kirk felt the pain and a wave of pleasure swept through him. She caressed his face. The monsters who did this to you will not survive. He looked into her dark eyes. Are we? Yes. I thought I had lost you. They will not go unpunished. Who? The enemy. Kirk looked past her at the Enterprise. It was a holographic model he finally realized. A wave of fear swept through him as he gazed upon it. Utter Revulsion. He glared at her. A federation. She nodded. Star Fleet. Instantly Kirk felt a stab of pain sliced through his bowels. Star Fleet. The image of the heated ship faded away replaced by another dynamic bird-like with a double home and raptor proud bridge. The Enterprise streaked at it. Weapons blazing. The raptor ship erupted in plasma. In death, the woman continued. A colony vessel. Women and children farming supplies. And this. A planet spun through space. The holographic viewpoints spiraled in like a reentering spacecraft. Hello, Kirk stretched farming fields in checkerboard perfection. Over a rise a city appeared. Fresh, bold, new. Then the tractor beam struck, scooping up the city like a handful of dirt. Within the immense tractor beam, the delicate spires of the city's temples crumbled. He could hear the distant cries of hundreds, thousands. Kirk held Salatrell's hand. He reached out to her face, tore ears, traced their tips, then touched his own. Am I? She smiled. No, you are human, a patriot. Dedicated to peace, non-interference. Dedicated to the destruction of the enemy. Kirk nodded. The Enterprise. The Federation. Starfleet. Salatrell touched the patch he held at her side. What do you want to do? Kirk's pain increased. Destroy them. The pain did not just fade. It was replaced by pleasure. Are you glad you're back? Kirk nuzzled his face against her neck, lightly kissed the fine hairs that covered her name. Yes, I'm glad. Who is the enemy? Kirk found it hard to concentrate. He needed her. Show me again. She aimed her pad at the holographically blurred corner pressed to control. An image appeared their life size, a humanoid, Salatrell whispered. The enemy. He must be destroyed. He must be killed. The figure reached for him from the holographic haze, gloating, fueled by the pain and the hate of the thousands of atrocities committed by the Federation and Starfleet against the Romulan race. Kirk spoke the name of the enemy. Jean-Luc Picard. Jean-Luc Picard must die.
description: In this episode, William Shatner reads "The Return" audiobook by Judith and Garfield Reeve-Stevins from Simon & Chuster Audio Presents Star Trek. It delves into the life-changing moment when James T. Kirk's death is revealed to Spock as they are separated on a distant planet. This event prompts both characters to reflect on their past connections and the impact of their friendship on each other’s lives, leading to significant emotional revelations for both.
