transcript: Throughout the known galaxy from Deep Space Nine to the new frontier, from a delta quadrant to the bridge of a starship enterprise, the sudden reactivation of the Iconian Gateways as destabilized interstellar relations between planets and cultures, previously separated by countless light-years. And honor all of valiant commanders has leaped through separate gateways to face the unknown, and now it is up to Captain Jean-Luc Picard to find the ageless Iconians themselves and reveal the mystery of where the Iconians disappeared to many long eons ago, and what they want now. The answers lie on the other side, and that is where Picard is gone. Star Trek, the next generation, the other side by Robert Greenberger, brings the Gateways saga to a spectacular conclusion. Picard had stepped through the Iconian gateway, found aboard the flagship Petra vessel, and now he emerged into a forest that sang with bird calls and sworn with large insects. A short distance from his position, he saw a large gleaming dome building. Up closer, he saw red and orange filigree, snake from the dome's base, upward the top. The oval dome itself was a cobalt blue, shining wetly in what he presumed to be the late afternoon sun. Sweat had already begun to trickle down his neck, and he realized how warm it was. Too warm to be pleasant, and humid enough to indicate it had recently rained. He opened his tricorder. With some alarm, he found the instrument dead. His right hand reached for his phaser and saw that it too registered no power. With greater caution, Picard began walking around the dome. There was little doubt he needed to get inside and speak with the people. The ones he hoped were the one true Iconian people. No one had seen them in over 200 millennia. His boots beat down wildflowers, thick roby grass strands, and even fallen twigs. The rain helped moisten everything so it kept his movements quiet. To his practiced eye, Picard noted that everything outside the dome's structure was left to its natural state. The air seemed pure, so the dome gave off no harmful emissions. It also made no sound. There was not even a hint of a power current. After 20 minutes, Picard estimated he'd managed his way around a third of the dome. Nothing had changed, although the sun had dried up more of the surroundings. Captain Picard, welcome to our world. He whirled about and looked up. For the figure measured at least seven and a half feet tall. She was a willowy figure, not much in the way of musculature. She wore a dark marooned dress that reached the tops of her covered feet. Picard studied her with a trying to seem rude about it. Do you know why I've come? Of course. We have been studying your activity. Can you help me? Without answering, she turned and raised her left arm, revealing a plate of metal covering her forearm. A panel set within the base of the structure opened. The woman turned and began walking with a steady gate inside, and he presumed he was to follow. The moment Picard passed the threshold, the door began to seal itself, and he felt the modulated cooler air for which he was thankful. The corridor was devoid of decoration and was mostly silver and metallic. She finally turned left, going down a similar corridor, but after less than a minute, extended her left arm once more. The room he found himself in was immense, the gigantic view screen directly before him. On the screen was the gateway he'd found on the Petra ship. To his left were long benches, and seated on them were five others, two more women, and three men, all in similar maroon clothing. A woman on the bench turned to him. Captain Picard, you have arrived here when we sought to stay apart from galactic society. If you are truly the Iconians, then you know it is your technology we seek to control, to stop where others have begun. What has gone wrong? The gateway's function? Picard cleared his throat, and succinctly explained how the Petra found the technology and sought to sell it to further their personal goal of extending their empire. They knew enough to turn on the entire network, but not how to shut it down or even program direction. As a result, the unchecked access had resulted in wide spread trouble, even loss of life. You have a bright people, Captain. We have studied you since the first gateway was activated in many hundreds of years. Your response has been in the past to blow up our technology. The captain inwardly winced at the realization. The first gateway that had been discovered on a Kallanden outpost a century ago was destroyed by Spock on the Enterprise. Other gateways had all been destroyed as well by Starfleet captains. You could see the point. If you have studied us, then you know such destruction is a last choice. We would much rather simply turn them off, preserving your legacy. One of the men addressed Picard. Yes, we have seen that. The woman spoke again. When the first gateway was used by these Petra, it activated an alarm here. We had no idea what it meant. It has been so long since the last such alert, but we finally figured out that it meant our equipment was in use. Our leader at the time had to consult the computer records to find out what the alarm signified and what we were to do. Another man on the bench stood and gestured to the other five iconions in the room. We were formed. We other centuries gathered when our equipment is in use. Our laws say we are to monitor the use, record the species that implore the gateways, and watch for incursion. We left your space to be on our own, to pursue new interests and not to be bothered. Picard frowned at the answer. The Iconians built their empire, invented technology far beyond their peers, and just walked away from it all. What could they be building now? Captain Picard, the use of the entire network was something none of us had witnessed before. We were intrigued to see what would happen. All you people flitting here and there like insects drawn to nectar. Picard found an anger building within him. He wanted to avoid. You've just watched people steal, people die? Our laws say we are to watch, remain vigilant in case we are threatened. Picard approached them, and no one moved. I'm sworn to protect my people and I need your help to do that. I need to know how to shut down the entire network. The laws are vague about helping other species. Picard had expected something different from these people and wanted to keep his disappointment private. If I shut down the gateways, won't that enable you to return to your studies? Yes, it would. Then help me, please. The woman walked over to the console of controls. After she flipped four cobalt blue buttons, information streamed across a panel. Captain, the computer records show we do not have the control mechanism here. It seems our ancestors left the controlling device on the last world we visited before settling here. The records refer to a master resonator, but I can access no details. We can send you to that world to seek the device. The captain absorbed the disheartening news. He'd come a great way to seek these people and they seemed far from enlightened. Maybe they were closer to the title, Demons of Air and Darkness, than he ever wanted to admit. The records say what I am to do with the device. She shook her head, but one of the other women spoke up. The gateways are attuned to one another, so I have believed that the resonator can be inserted into any control panel and close down the entire system. And once I find the master resonator, how do I return to my ship? Through a gateway, of course. Why did you leave our region? Our presence threatened to tamper with the natural order on too many worlds. We migrated across space until we reached here. Since then, we have abandoned contact with other people. Concentrating on studying realms, our gateways could not reach. Picard looked at them and realized that however great the Iconians were 200,000 years in the past, these people were far removed from them. Whatever realities they studied kept them from the one they lived in, and they were clueless how to act. His anger dissipated and all he felt was pity. I cannot waste time if I am to seek this master resonator and send me. One of the men rose and walked the console. He labored over the controls. I have found the world. Captain, I am not sure I speak for all, but for myself. I wish you luck. I too do not want to see these gateways destroyed. It might be nice to visit new found friends. A gateway formed in the room. Nearly a rip in reality. Large enough for one man to enter. There was one location in sight, a lush green world, not dissimilar from the one they stood on. At a backward glance, Picard once more stepped into the gateway. Deanna Troy, carefully cupping her mug of hot chocolate, curled her feet underneath her legs and stared at the view screen in the captain's quarters. She disliked the decor and would have preferred to let the Marco Polo's real captain keep his eyes, but he was far from his starship and she was in temporary command. Any change will. Will Reicher, who was on the view screen, shook his head. He was in his personal quarters on the Enterprise, just a few hundred kilometers away. Nothing at all, Deanna. The captain's been gone for six hours without a word. She sipped at her chocolate before asking about the detained petrol leader. And Doral? Doral sitting in his guest quarters, looking at images of his remaining ships. They're down to 48 and it's getting a little cramp for them. The odds improved, don't they Will? Our 16 ships against their 48 is still three to one odds. Just talking to a maid Deanna feel better and kept the harsh reality of their situation just a little further away. Will, what's to become of the Petra? Their drive to expand their reach means getting them home during their lifetime is impossible. Doral can't even say for certain if the Petra MPa or even exists anymore. They remain close to the Galactic Center, way beyond any portion of space any of us ever have explored. Troy sipped her hot chocolate in silence for a moment. Wondering what progress was being made by their captain, who stepped through the Iconian Gateway found aboard Doral's lead Petra vessel. Six hours without knowing what he found on the other side, his orders have been strict. No one was to follow him through. After Picard stepped through the gateway to the other side, the good news was there was no dampening field on the verdant planet. The bad news was nothing technological was showing up on the Trichorda's screen. There were plenty of life signs. The planet was teeming with humanoid life, birds, animals and insects. But there was nothing to imply anything more than primitive development. As a result, Picard was faced with the full impact of non-interference directives. He had to somehow locate the master resonator in a manner that prevented altering the culture he was sure to find. He noticed the faint aroma of cooking meat. First, it told him there were intelligent people nearby. Second, it provided a direction. A well-worn path from the trees indicated that people used this area. It made sense that there was likely to be an encampment of some sort nearby. His trail led him to the forest's edge, which opened up to a small village. Before entering, he stopped to study the people. Like the Iconians, they were tall, thin folk. The skin was copper colored, darkened by the sun. Each war would appear to be cured animal skins for clothing and all carried walking sticks topped with ornate carvings. The Trichorda also told him one important detail. The food being cooked was safe for a human to eat. One of the men caught a glimpse of Picard. With long strides, a group of men hurried toward the captain. None may threaten moves, which pleased him. Picard addressed them. Hello. They all stared back at him. After a moment, the men tried to repeat the word. Hello. Picard pointed to himself and set his last name. Picard. The men pointed to themselves and repeated the word. Heh, heh. They seemed remarkably pleased with their progress. Picard made minute steps toward them, trying to make certain the translator picked up the words to begin processing. The leader gestured toward the village. On his way toward the center of the settlement, Picard took time to notice the decorations on the buildings, and he came to realize each home had some piece of sophisticated technology as door hangings, more decorative than anything else. Clearly there had been a superior civilization on this planet, but something had happened, and darkly he fretted over the Iconians' role in the planet's past. Finally, the translator began working. The captain smiled. Greetings. I am Picard, and I have come from a long way away. The man he presumed to be the village leader came toward him, a huge grin on his face. Picard, we welcome you. I am Hamish, elder of the village. Hamish, I have come from far away seeking a special item, a very old item. A woman spoke up. Why do you seek this object? I have many people in trouble at home, and ones wiser than I tell me it will help. It is the way of my people to ask for help when we must. We in turn offer help to those who ask. Hamish smiled. Picard, are you from the west? Truthfully his path led west, but he was not of the west. My travels have taken me in all directions. As I expected, young gods on their ordeal must have travelled the world to gain their granita. Picard couldn't even begin to imagine what a granita implied, but being called a young god set off internal warning bells. He'd been mistaken for a god once before by a low-tech culture, and it was not an experience he was eager to relive. Several other old men approached Hamish, and they clustered whispering back and forth. And Hamish spoke. Picard, we think you must travel to the city. It is but three days walk from here. It is filled with many unknown things, and it may hold your heart's desire. Poetic, he mused, but accurate. There was nothing he wanted more than to find the resonator and return to the enterprise. He sniffed and then realized there was one more thing he desired, dinner. Very well. I shall start at sunrise, if you would be so kind as to provide me with directions. After he ate and then slept, Picard was considerably more comfortable when he woke the following morning. An hour later, he was on a worn path leading away from the village, heading in a southeastern direction. Hamish had insisted on giving him two skins of water and some dried meats. Later, as he scurted the edge of a forest, he could hear a stream or river. This pleasant world was well on its way to full recovery from whatever the Iconians left behind. The sun was not too hot compared to yesterday, and Picard hoped he would see the city before nightfall. Within time, Picard noticed tracks in the path, parallel ruts that indicated some form of wheeled vehicle had been by. Less than an hour later, he heard the sounds of concerned voices. He quickened his pace and hurried forward. Within a few minutes, the road rounded a band and he saw the remains of a wagon teetering over a huge rock and pinning a man underneath. Watching in fear were women and children dressed differently than in the village Picard had visited. Picard saw they were paralyzed the point of inaction, so he stepped forward and approached the wagon. Don't be scared, help has arrived. All he needed to do was lift up an edge of the wagon so the man could be freed. He took several deep breaths, focusing his energies, then placing his back to the wagon. He firmly gripped the corner, planted his feet far apart and began exerting his strength. Finally, he felt the wagon rise. Quickly, come clear him away. When the man was dry clear, Picard let the heavy woods foot from his finger. Picard then slowly walked over to check on the injured person, one of the women bowed to him. You saved him, thank you young God. Picard turned towards the path, but a young girl stepped forward. Why leave us so quickly young God? At least let us feed you supper. Picard glanced at the sky and noticed it growing deeper in color. He had hoped to even glimpse the city today, but it seemed not to be. So he smiled at her and accepted the invitation. As the villagers set up cab, he sat back and spoke quietly with the children. They told him of their village, which was beyond the city, and how they loved traveling. One young boy seemed quite taken with Picard's actions, but didn't act like Picard was a god which the captain found refreshing. Instead, the boy asked questions about lifting the wagon. How his muscles felt. His name was Chonic. I've been to the city once. It's like no place you've ever seen. Tall huts, mostly broken, with weird looking vines connecting some of them together. The animals all avoided so it's a good place to hide. Picard tried to imagine the place and wondered how much of it still function. He smiled at Chonic. I'll find out for myself soon, won't I? Chonic smiled back. And I'm going to show you. Picard was alarmed by the pronouncement. He'd already learned Chonic had attached himself to this traveling party and was from one of the villages nearby. The last thing he needed was to be responsible for someone's life while he was rushing to save countless others. I can't do that. I must move quickly and I won't be able to properly look after you. Oh, I'll be looking after you, young god Picard. After all, I know how to get in there and you don't. The next morning Picard checked to make sure his equipment was still where he had secured it the night before. The captain had decided to use the phaser in tricorder as little as possible, refusing to raise the notion that a god, young or otherwise, might need such devices. After breakfast, the card and Chonic were ready to depart. Chonic, how far to the city? We could see it just after midday. Excellent. Then let's begin. The trail skirted the forest, but within two hours it had thinned and ended. Growing up to wide fields that seemed full of grains growing tall in the sun. After another hour or so, Chonic excitedly pointed out the first glimpse of the city's silhouette. Sure enough, spires and skyscraping buildings were topping the horizon. The captain estimated the city to be perhaps half a kilometer in width and another hour or two away. What it makes Picard the most was the utter silence as they got closer to the city. But after time, they heard angry voices. Chonic shrugged to say he didn't know who the people were. The nearest village has to be at least at days walked to the east. When Picard heard a baby's cry, he decided it was time for action. Breaking into his sprint, the captain soon left Chonic behind. In less than a minute, he spotted a cluster of people forming a loose circle. The circle was an infant, crying pitifully, naked and unattended. As he approached, the circle broke open and the captain could see a woman. Her ruffs spun clothes and tatters, lying on the ground. Standing over, yelling epithets without stop was an older man. Each person was holding something hard in the talic that was oval and shaped at one hand and spiky at the other. What is going on? Why is this baby being ignored? The baby is a sin. What should have been mine is not. I was not home the eight turns ago when this would have started. Picard looked down at the woman, who was quietly sniffling into her one in tax leave. And you will do what? The man looked at Picard as if he too were a newborn. I brought her here for the testing. She will live or die. If she survives, then her innocence is clear and she can bring the baby home. Picard disliked this notion of justice and felt he needed to act. Has she spoken for herself? Her been dassed. Picard reacted with instinct, not thought, and rushed the man, not in the dirt. The weapons wait in his hands forced him to tumble backwards to the ground. Now it was Picard who loomed over the man. Where's the justice in using something so sharp? You want the truth? Ask her. If she betrayed you, then let justice be done. With that, Picard walked over to the infant, whose cries had grown intermittent. He scooped it up and instantly the baby grew silent. Gently, he checked for bruises, saw none, and walked back to the woman. She was sitting up now and gingerly, he handed over the child. Tell the truth. One of the women turned to him. What are you? Mr. Traveler, and I'm on my way. He shot a glance at Chonik, giving him a warning look that said speak nothing of Godhood. Chonik looked up at Picard as they moved away. She might have deserved something. Yes, Chonik, a fair hearing. The accused must have a chance to speak in the defense. Where I come from, we have a very complicated set of laws so the innocent are protected and the guilt he have found out with facts, not guesses. Wow, that's very involved. How do you keep all those things straight? Protecting our laws is a trade given much importance in my land. All those laws and rules and things could make my head hurt. Picard smiled. Or give you a reason to live. Still, you're too young to worry about a trade. First, we must complete this adventure. The city was close now, and what Picard wanted to do was arrive and begin his hunt. From his tricorder, he'd already learned that the city had no electronic defenses. At least none he could detect. Weeds, plants, even the occasional tree had taken root in the outskirts of the city, choking the streets. Thick ivy-like vines practically enveloped the smaller buildings. The youth led the Captain to a wild, untamed section filled with tall bushes. Finally, he ran towards a structure that seemed indistinguishable to Picard from the others. This is it. I cut my way through here the last time I came to the city. Sure enough, Picard could see some of the thick ivy cut away, revealing hand and footholds that allowed one to reach an open second story window. Within minutes, the two climbed up and stood in a small room. The contents of the room were shattered, splintered plastic, metal, and other materials. With his tricorder, Picard took readings and pictures. What is that, Picard? You keep pulling it out. I call this a tricorder, and it lets me take recordings or pictures, among other things. It's a very powerful and useful tool to help me explore. Chonic merely shrugged and walked to the doorway, leading to the rest of the building. Picard followed, trying to imagine how he would ever find the master resonator in a city this size. When they were well into the city, night fell. With what light remained, they made camp and eight. Picard, how do we know what to look? But Chonic is an excellent question. The question was on his mind long before the boy asked. Aimless wandering would mean the resonator might be days away from discovery. He was looking for some kind of clue, maybe something in the placement of the device, or the architecture or ornamentation. John's light woke Picard, and he marveled at the beauty of unfettered nature replacing what had been a superior technology. He had to find the master resonator today and return home. Picard took a sip from a water skin and noted the intricate swirling pattern that had been etched onto one side. Staring at it, he let his mind wander for a moment, and he thought about the odd pointed end of the device, nearly used on the accused woman the day before. His oval nature was similar to the pattern on the skin, and it occurred to Picard that the dome structure on the new Iconian world was more oval than circular. Could the oval shape be significant? Chonic was still asleep, and Picard turned on his tricorder to study the exterior of the domed home of the Iconians. There was filigree work over the dome that he merely glanced at. That is, until his mind wandered for a second, and his eyes lost their sharp focus and suddenly all he saw were the spikes in different places of the filigree's design. Picard hastily grabbed a stick and sketched on the ground. He drew in the spikes as if the filigree were on a grid, similar to the grid of city streets through which he was searching. A picture emerged, with the spikes pointing like arrows to a specific section of the grid. Could they be pointing to the location of the city's gateway? In the memory, Picard estimated where he and Chonic entered the city and their approximate location. With the silent curse, he realized they would be far from the specified location, but at least he had an idea of which direction to walk. Gently he woke Chonic, and soon they were moving again, this time in a direction that Picard hoped would bring a resolution to the problem. They arrived at the targeted building, as the sun was already starting towards the horizon. The building would be dark within a few hours. Compared to the rest of the city, the building was nondescript. If it truly housed a gateway, one could not tell by design or ornamentation. The outside was reds and oranges with two windows missing. The first floor was filled with pillars supporting the entire building, but also had a series of rooms that seemed uniform in size and shape. There's a very wide staircase spiraling down below ground level. Chonic, we need to build torches so we can explore below. Can you find two very sturdy, heavy wood poles, branches or sticks? Despite being tired from all the walking, Chonic sprinted from the building out to the streets in search of supplies. He soon came back, dragging two branches. In five minutes, the torches were cut to size and ignited. The boy marveled when Picard used his phaser to light the torches. It only served to reinforce for Chonic the notion of Picard being a god. To the captain, it was mild contamination since Chonic could tell what he saw and not be believed. As they descended the stairs with the torches, Picard saw that the basement extended some thirty meters down. At the bottom of the stairs, he saw illustrations of landscapes that were unfamiliar, snowscapes, oceans, mountain views and cities. Colored circles in the walls seemed to form directional patterns, most leading to his left. The colored circles converged down one hallway and Picard chose to follow them. He was rewarded with a hall opening up to a large chamber. In the center was a familiar control panel, one he first saw on a world countless light years away. This was the gateway control room. Chonic looked up at Picard. What does that do? When it works, Chonic, it could help people find their way to other locations. It's very old equipment and I doubt it functions anymore. In reality, he knew it would have to work to send him home and there was little doubt that the equipment still functioned. He studied the chamber carefully, looking for someplace the master resonator might be housed. The walls seemed smooth and in the console itself he found no hidden panels or hatches. It grew frustrating as Picard knew he had found his goal, but the ultimate object eluded his grasp. Chonic growing bored and standing in the same place had been wandering in and out of the chamber using the hallways and place to run. At one point Picard watched him with a sad smile. So full of energy and eager to help, but everything was beyond his grasp. However, Picard watched a little more and saw something catch the youth's eye. Chonic walked along the hallway with his torch and looked closely at a section just before the hall opened into the chamber. He placed his tiny hand on a section of wall and pushed, revealing a doorway mostly hidden in the shadows. Picard quickly stepped over to him, their torches dancing together above them and peered into the newly discovered room. The air was stale and musty to Picard, but that wasn't important. What was vital was the rack set against the far wall. On it was the master resonator. He was sure of it. What confused him at first though was that there were fourteen of them identical to one another in size and shape. The resonator was larger than Picard's fists together, but flat and copper-colored. On top were four keys, two amber, one brown, and one a deeper shade of brown. He stepped towards them and touched one, feeling the cool metal. Taking it up it felt light, and as he turned it over he saw indentations that had first puzzled him. Is this it Picard? Yes, I think so, Chonic. I just didn't expect to find so many. To date, he'd never encountered spare parts of any sort. The Iconians built things to last, which meant all fourteen resonators were meant to be used. As Will Rikers sat forward in the command share on the bridge of the Enterprise, he shook his head in frustration and turned to data. The captain has been gone days, and despite the fact we have the Petrosh ships in a dampening field, they've managed to blow up one of our vessels. The android turned to Riker. Commander, how much longer will you give Captain Picard? Riker settled back in the command share, not at all comfortable. Just a little bit more. Without him and the solution, we might have to destroy all the gateways. That sir would be a loss to the Quadrant. I see if not lost your sense of understatement, Mr. Data. Yet from reports Riker had read a little while earlier, two planets were already critically crippled by the Iconian technology, adapting native energy to keep the gateways powered. A small war had broken out in an unaligned star system, and raids by Cardassian pirates were reported along the Klingon border. Riker considered the chronometer and mentally decided on six more hours, short enough so he could act before too many more lives might be lost. Picard walked back to the console, hefting one of the resonators, holding it above the control panels. Gently, he lowered the device, which fits snugly atop a cluster of amber and blue keys to the console's right. The entire resonator began to glow, startling Chonak, who backed away several feet. A small ball of light began to form above the resonator, and one of the amber keys began to blink. The light grew in size and began to alter shape, forming a sphere that swelled to engulf the top of the control panel. Within this sphere, smaller swirls began forming, and Picard realized that it resembled a model of the Big Bang Theory. As the seconds passed, the stars began twinkling, and the image altered slowly as galaxies formed. The familiar spiral shape of the Milky Way filled the light bubble, and then one at a time, purple lights began to show themselves in a concentration of Picard recognized as the Alpha Quadrant. In all, there were thirteen purple lights. His fingers brushed the amber blinking light. The Chonak stated the obvious. It didn't like you touching it. Picard frowned, and considered the likely options. After a minute or more, he realized he had no choice. He needed to return with the thirteen keys, then get them to the highlighted gateways. He suspected all thirteen consoles would not do anything useful unless they were all touched at once. Fourteen pieces to a single key, and somehow the Iconians, whom he met on the other planet, didn't know that. Using his tricorder, he recorded the light patterns on the console and the purple markers in the image. The Enterprise computers would be able to match this map against their own star charts, and adjusting for the time difference since these maps were first recorded, figure out where the resonators needed to go. Picard strode to the Antichamber and emptied his small bag of dried provisions. He then began filling it with the thirteen resonators. What troubled him was the fourteenth key. Someone might need to activate it from this planet. Chonak would have to get involved, but that raised concerns over tampering with the culture, but what harm could there be in asking a boy to press a button? Chonak, I need to return to my people with these. All of them must be fit onto similar machines, and then all of us might need to press the blinking button. How will I know, Picard? I'm not sure, to be honest, that it will be necessary. I think the machine will do something to indicate it is ready for you to do your part, but the result must be that it will turn itself off. Chonak smiled and nodded a few times. It will be safe, right? Then I will have helped a young god. The Captain broke into a happy grin. Yes, but once this is over, it will be our secret. He returned to the console and studied it. His right hand began flipping switches, as he recalled doing on Doral's battered petra ship. A gateway sprang to life near the far wall. Chonak began to walk toward it, but Picard called him back. But what is it Picard? It's called a gateway. Picard continued to fiddle with the controls, hoping he could at least find a starship's bridge. There, he spotted the forge walking across the rear of the bridge. It was time. Turning, he saw Chonak watch the gateway intently. They dressed like you. Is that where the young gods live? They are my companions, and we try and do the right thing much like you. However, it is time I go home myself. I need to step through the gateway and leave you to wait. I can't tell you how long it will be. Definitely more than a day. Okay Picard, you can count on me. Thank you Chonak. With that, the captain straightened his uniform, and at the right moment leapt into the gateway. Jordi LaForge was crossing the Enterprise Bridge, a pad in his hand, and Riker knew it was coming time to make a decision. He didn't want to make it. He didn't necessarily feel as if he was the right officer to decide the fate of the Iconian Legacy. Liker studied the engineer's recommendations as he strolled toward the ready room. He was so absorbed with the information, he did not notice the crewman coming his way, and they collided. Once on a carpeted floor, Riker looked up and saw Picard's smiling face. Sir, at ease will. Both men scrambled to their feet and with a center of attention. Is everything all right, Captain? Did you find the answer? Picard patted the bag full of resonators that remained at his side. Yes, I believe so will. Quickly, Riker updated the captain on what had transpired and in turn Picard explained his planet jumping and searched for the resonators. He handed the tricorder to data and asked him to begin the required analysis. A few hours later, a refresh Picard sat at the conference table with his crew. He had asked Captain Troy to patch in from her post on the Marco Polo to get her input. Data was standing by the monitor screen that showed his stellar map with the 13 purple sites highlighted. The pattern of dispersal does not as yet make sense. All are located on planets and fortunately all 13 planets still exist. All are within Klingon, Romulan, Ferengi or Federation space, aside from two that are within the former Thelonian Empire. Picard frowned briefly, but nodded. How do we get the 13 resonators into position? I have endeavored to work out a travel plan. It will require relaying the resonators to fast ships from here. My initial plan indicates it will take some 28.5 hours if every ship makes it schedule rendezvous. This will require the Enterprise and other ships to leave the area, spreading the resonators to others. Picard nodded. Go to work data. Troy spoke from the adjacent view screen. Captain, what about the p-traw? I have not come up with a satisfying answer as yet. As we leave to deliver the resonators, I will need the carb and glory to take charge of the p-traw ships until we return. Le Fords spoke up. The p-traw cannot be trusted, Captain, and I recommend we disable as many of the ships as possible. Prepare your plans, Jody. We'll contact the vessels we'll be meeting with. Deanna, relay the word to other captains in the area. Let's try to leave within the hour. Dismissed. Quickly, inefficiently, the crew stood and went about their business, and Picard was left alone in the observation lounge. What had felt good to be home, he disliked waiting more than a day to conclude the business at hand. And he kept thinking back to the world and little chonic, faithfully waiting for the signal that would help protect a galaxy from chaos. For ten hours since they left the p-traw ships, the Enterprise had been cruising along at warp nine with no incidents. It was carrying three of the resonators. At the same time, there was the specter of ongoing chaos represented by the still functioning gateways. Wars had broken out, natural disasters were occurring more frequently as the ancient technology began to harm the worlds they once serviced. If Picard was right, the fourteen resonators would make it possible to close down the gateways. Soon, the Enterprise transported two of the resonators to other fast ships, and with one left headed to its final destination. The planet was barren and desolate, so small and unimportant the stellar cartographers never bothered to give it a name. Starfleet's records indicated no one had ever been there. The cart stared at the viewscreen, down below was a gateway. The forge looked up from his console. The gateways functioning like all the others and seems to have huge energy reserves. Jody, transport down with me in case there's something unusual with the technology. With that, Picard stood and strode off the bridge, heading straight down to the planet. Finally, down on the lifeless planet and before the gateway, Picard placed the resonator on the console. At the same time, he knew that other Starfleet captains were placing resonators on the consoles on the other 12 planets. After the map of the Alpha Quadrant was displayed with the fourteen purple markers, the purple lights began to wink off. Picard wondered if it meant the link was being broken, that the gateway network was shutting down. Picard's eyebrows rose in surprise as the lights shifted, pulsating a bit, and then a face greeted him. The features matched the aconions he met only days ago. It was a placid female countenance. It spoke, but in a language Picard had never heard before. After a sentence, it seemed to wait for a reply. Then it tried again, this time with another language. Again, the silent wait, and again another language. Finally the words were in French, his native tongue. How may I help you, Captain Picard? How do I disengage the gateways? Our controls work both verbally and manually. Please, shut down the gateway network. Don't figure the relays. The lights on the console went dim. Networks closed down. Relays disconnected. Do you require anything further? Computer, could the system have been deactivated by any of the fourteen stations? No, the master resonator works off the biosignature of the one to make first contact. That would be you, Captain Picard. Picard stared at the system with more than a little disbelief. He literally had the power of the gateways in his hands, and no one else in the galaxy could take control. But it was over. The galaxy could go about its business without threat of further interference. Picard signaled his ship and was transported home. Chonic had waited in the chamber for more than a day when a glowing face formed and began speaking in gibberish. Chonic could tell it was speaking to someone. Young God Picard he assumed. He waited to see if he should do anything, but then the control before him began changing. Chonic thought it might be dying. Finally, the lights on the control went dim. The lessons he learned from Picard had filled his mind in all the hours he waited for the machine to perform its magic. Things were not always what they appeared, and that justice could take many forms. The lessons were good ones, and maybe when he was a little older he could teach them to others. Teaching sounded like a good thing to do, he considered chewing on the last strip of meat. But first, there was more for him to learn. He turned to walk out of the cavern, ready to leave the city behind him, and start something new. With the Enterprise en route back to the Petra fleet, the captain stood before Dural, the Petra leader. It's over Dural. We shut down the gateways. Your ploy to activate the gateways caused immense loss of life and great destruction. What you did, you did from some biological imperative, but I cannot forget that there were alternatives to the approach you took. I could leave you to the mercy of a coalition court, but that would detain you when that is clearly not of use to anyone. Dural looked up with a questioning expression, his Picard continued, you are explorers by nature, and there is much of the galaxy left to visit. I believe Mr. Dated can provide you with a course that will allow you to fulfill your imperative while keeping you from interacting with any of the races you tried to dupe. Finally, Dural spoke. We're banished? No. The universe is teeming with life, and we're letting you go out and find it before any of us gets the chance. Turn it to your advantage and open your minds to the possibilities. Dural nodded, taking in the words, obviously surprised that the course of action did not involve trial or death. Hours later, after the Enterprise had returned to the Petra fleet and transported Dural to his ship, Picard sat in his ready room, looking at the tricorder images taken on the world in which he found Chonic and the master resonators. He'd missed the youth and knew he had the power to go back and visit, but also recognized that he would never do so. The captain could never imagine an instance when circumstances would force him to use the gateways. It was a power he would hide. A secret he would no doubt take to his deathbed. Instead, he would prepare a report to Starfleet Command, complete with recommendations for reparations and commendations for selected staff, starting with Troy. The Petra ships had started forming as data directed, and they would be gone shortly. Once they were off long-range sensors, Picard knew he would return to Earth and accept his next assignment. As with most his missions, whatever they gave him, it would never quite turn out as the mission specks spelled out, and he wouldn't have it any other way. description: In "094 - Star Trek Audiobook: Gateways What Lay Beyond" episode 4, Captain Jean-Luc Picard revisits the Iconian Gateway from the previous three chapters of the saga. As he steps through the gateway, he finds himself in a lush forest and eventually discovers a large building with red and orange filigree design and a gleaming blue dome inside, hinting at an ancient civilization that has been missing for centuries. The episode concludes with Picard's encounter with the Iconian people who have been studying his presence on Earth, leading to a dramatic revelation about their origins and purpose.

transcript: The meeting room was where a particular brutal battle had been fought when the Rebel Army took over the Capitol building. Kira looked around at the assorted happy, but tired-looking faces and wasn't entirely sure what she was doing here. At best, she was a soldier, hardly what anyone would consider important. And she didn't want to become important. She'd done enough time traveling, both voluntary and involuntary, to know the risks. Flexing her arm, Kira went slightly. A wound she'd received was proving maddeningly slow to heal. Unfortunately, the space station Deep Space Nine and Dr. Julian Bashirius infirmary wouldn't be built for many millennia, leaving Kira to heal naturally. A tiny short-haired woman entered the meeting room last, not Laura Rislin. I hereby call to order the first meeting of the Government of the Perician Republic. Kira now knew the Pericia Remaro had first agitated for independence against the oppressive Laird regime years earlier. The nation of Laird had ruled the peninsula with an iron fist and a hefty tax burden. And though she was not the first to desire the removal of their yoke, she was the first to say so publicly. Ricky had died soon after she began that agitating, hung by Laird authorities. Her cause had lived on and was now finally victorious. As Natlar went into the details of what needed to be done next, Kira found herself tuning out. She'd been to plenty of meetings just like this. Hell, she'd led meetings just like this. But those meetings were thousands of years in the future and, paradoxically, in her own subjective past. She saw no reason to involve herself now. She stared out the window. At the large port beyond the city were docked several warships that carried the flag of the Nation of End Tree. Kira turned back to the table just as Natlar was addressing a short stout woman with salt and pepper hair. Admiral Ina, once again we thank you for all you've done for us. In a mirant nodded. We of End Tree simply followed the road the prophets laid out for us. Kira's eyes automatically went to the admiral's right ear which was presently adorned with an earring. Though nowhere near as elaborate as those worn in Kira's time, Kira knew that it symbolized devotion to the prophets. The admiral's comment elicited a snort from Torna. I doubt that the prophets were the ones who put those cannons on your ship's admiral. Natlar spoke before Ina could reply. Be that as it may, Jan will Torna. I would rather Admiral Ina did not return home just yet. We are still vulnerable at sea. If Admiral Ina leaves, Lared will return and take us back with little difficulty. I therefore would like to request that End Tree leave a delegation of five ships behind to protect the port. Torna's eyes widened in protest. Prefect, no. We'd be exchanging one oppressor for another. Admiral Ina looked at Torna sharply. My people do not oppress, General. The prophets... I am fully aware of your people's religious beliefs, Admiral. They don't change the fact that... General Torna, you will serve as liaison to Admiral Ina. Before Torna could argue further, a young girl came in. Excuse me, but three men are here claiming to represent the Vijora. Natlar barely hesitated. Send them in. To Kira's ear, well used to the nuances of politicians, the prefect sounded relieved that her argument with Torna had been interrupted. For his part, the General sat back down, but gloured at the prefect. Kira knew Torna well enough to be sure that he would pick up this argument sooner rather than later. The three men who entered war-red robes, they also wore earrings in their right ears. The oldest of the three spoke to Natlar. Greetings to you from the Vijora. We come prepared to offer you entry into the Vijora to add this region to the glory of the prophets. Torna raised his voice. The prophets? You wish to make us part of your theocracy? We are not a theocracy, General. The Vijora is a democratic government of the people of this world. Our goal is to unite the planet once and for all, so we will all be free to follow our paw without worrying about who rules us or who we will fight tomorrow. The envoy went on for quite some time, outlining in more detail what joining the Vijora would involve. Finally, Natlar spoke. You have given us much to think about. Torna was furious. We'd be trading one oppressor for another. I will abide by whatever you decide in this room, prefect, but I will not sit here and listen to any more foolish ramblings. Just remember this. Heriki Ramaro did not die so we could become part of the Vijora, or part of entry. She died so we could be free. And with that, he left. Two hours later, Kira found Torna in his quarters. You want the good news or the bad news? Torna didn't even look at her. I find it impossible to believe that there is good news. Well, there is. Natlar rejected the Vijora and offer. But now the bad news. The prefect wants you to relocate to the port and set up your office there to serve as liaison to Admiral Ina and the entry fleet. After your performance today, I think she wants to keep you far away from the capital building. Torna nodded bitterly. Yes, to keep my voice from being heard. Kira smiled. Tell us so. Even from the port, your voice is going to be heard. If I'm to be exiled, Ashla, I want you by my side. To guard my back and to keep me from making a complete ass of myself. Kira hesitated. Can I think about it? Of course. Let me know tomorrow. It will take me that long to pack up my own belongings and inform Lyra and the boys that will be moving. Kira and Norese lay on a bunk in the barracks that she shared with a dozen other soldiers. She once again cast her mind back to see how she should proceed forward. The last thing she remembered with any clarity was that heir a desert planet in the Delta Quadrant. She'd gone there and abandoned her runabout in order to block a gateway, a portal in space through which deadly theta radiation was flowing into orbit around the inhabited planet of Europa Nova. Her actions have prevented one lethal piece of radioactive waste from going through the gateway, thus saving the lives of the Oropani, as well as the task force she herself had assembled to evacuate the planet. After that, she couldn't recall what happened. She knew that she found a gateway on the planet where there had been none before. She knew that the theta radiation on the planet had grown to fatal levels, and she knew that she was now many thousands of years in the past on her home planet of Vajor, fighting in a rebellion that the history of her time had long forgotten. All she was sure of was that she no longer had the radiation sickness she'd been afflicted with, and the prophets had something to do with her sojourn to the past. Maybe. The gateways weren't built by the prophets after all, but the Iconians. In fact, there weren't any gateways within ten light-years of the celestial temple. Based on the report she read on wrote to Europa Nova, the gateways had not only come in all shapes and sizes, but all types. Some even seemed to work interdimensionally, so it was quite possible that the Iconians could move through time as well. She lay awake on her palate, listening to the sounds of the other slumbering soldiers. If the prophets did send her here, and she felt at the core of her paw that they were involved somehow, then they did so for a reason. She resolved to accept Torna's offer, first thing in the morning. Here a lost track of how long she'd been serving as Torna's adjutant at the port, but she'd been enjoying it immensely. Particularly now that the weather was warmer, the sun was shining, the core of the elotion was a clear dream. She nodded to the assorted dock workers who passed her by. One of them cried out, look! Here a world around. The Perician peninsula jutted out into the core of the elotion along the southern end of the coast of the continent. Any ship that came down the coastline from the west would have to, in essence, come around a corner. Right now, one of the largest and most impressive ships that could be found on the planet was coming into view around that bend. The green and black flag of End Tree whipped in the breeze from a mast with a second flag under the flag of the Perician Republic. Within half an hour, Admiral Inamurint and General Torna amiably came down the gangplants. Torna walked with Kira back toward their office in the rear of the marina. We found the pirates and took care of them in fairly short order. They didn't have anything to match Vera's cabin. Kira turned to Torna. It wasn't that long ago that the only way you referred to her was as the Admiral or that damned woman. To Kira's shock, Torna actually bliced. I suppose so. But she was efficient yet merciful with the pirates. She was very effective in questioning the pirate leader without being unnecessarily brutal, and she agreed to fly the Perician flag. The entered Torna's tiny office and Kira asked what the pirates had said. Actually, the most interesting intelligence we received wasn't from the pirates but from their slaves. Many of the most recent conscriptions they picked up were refugees from a disaster in the firecaves. Some of the slaves claimed there was some kind of blue fire when the caves collapsed, but I don't put much stock in that. Kira now knew exactly what had happened and precisely when she was. Some 30,000 years before she was born, the prophets banished the parades to the firecaves, sealing them in there forever. Many a few months ago, or rather 30,000 years from now, the emissary of the prophets, Captain Benjamin Sisko, went to the firecaves to prevent the parades from being freed and was never seen again, leaving Kira in charge of Deep Space Nine. Torna continued speaking. With the pirates gone, we'll need to work on expanding the marina to be able to accommodate more ships. Kira frowned. We're going to need more ships to hold off the pirates and the Lared Navy. Torna snorted. Ha, the Lared Navy's barely worth giving a title. Kira shook her head. Don't be so sure of that. We just got another report from Moliki. Moliki was one of the spies that the Parigian Free Army had observing the guns on in Lared, but Torna ignored her and went on at some length, describing how Ina had stopped the pirates. Kira was just glad that Torna and Ina were getting along. She had a feeling that that would be vital in the long run. The worst thing about the dungeon was the smell of dried blood, infected wounds, and the feces of assorted vermin. Kira looked over at Torna, sitting in the corner of the cell. The wound on his left arm was growing worse. If it wasn't treated soon, the gangrene would probably kill him. Kira had no idea how long the war with Lared had been going on. At this point, she couldn't even say for sure how long it had taken their retreating troops to bring Kira and Torna to Lared's capital city and the dungeon where they'd been languishing. Kira had been fearing this very thing since the collapse of the firecaves made more business for the port, which had indeed thrived. What she had not expected was the sheer strength of the Lared Army. The same army that Kira had helped repel had doubled its numbers and was much better armed. When the doors of the dungeon opened, a lary guard entered with a very short man dressed in a white jacket and white pants. Kira recognized in the mccoins that sometimes changed hands on the docks. This was Prince Siba Aftra of Lared. Aftra walked over to Torna. You will rise in the presence of royalty, General. Torna looked up at Aftra with the one eye that wasn't swollen shut. As soon as I'm in the presence of some, I'll consider it. Aftra gave the guard a glance, and the guard kicked the General in the stomach. With over in pain, Torna eventually managed to smile. I've been waiting for you to come and gloat over our capture. It is, after all, the only true victory you have won in this war. I can see by the look on your face that you appreciate the position you're in, General. Because of our alliance with the Bajora, we will destroy entry and put down your upstart band of rebels and finally control the entire southern coast. Torna realized with a shock that the Lared was so well armed because of the Bajora. The prince looked down on the General's dirty, bruised, swollen face with a sneer. I just wanted to see the infamous General Torna for myself. You will be publicly executed at dawn tomorrow. Aftra finally turned Akira. As for you, I suppose we should let Torna have one final night of companionship before we take you to the front lines. You'll make fine aero fodder. With that, I have to turn and laugh. Torna staggered to his feet. Damn those foul Bajora. I hope those prophets of theirs strike them down with lightning. The prophets don't look like that, Kira thought, but refrain from saying it aloud. Bachela, we've got to find some way out of here. If we can get back, tell them about this. We can change our strategy, try to hit the supply lines the Bajora are using. Suddenly the door opened again. A guard, a different one, came in, reached into his cloak, and pulled out a set of keys. Come on, come on. We haven't got much time. Torna's eyes went wide. Moliki, we had assumed you were dead. After this dent, they'll use my guts for building material. A spike can no longer make anything like an honest living in this environment. Moliki gave Kira the set of keys and again reached into his cloak. In any case, here's a map that'll show you how to get out of here once I bring you to the surface, as well as a map that shows the supply lines the Bajora are using. He put his hand on Torna's shoulder. Let me make something abundantly clear, General. Deviate even slightly from the route I've mapped out, and you're guaranteed to be captured. Moliki unsheath the sword he had in a belt sheath. You'll need this more than I will. Kira took it, and hefted it. It was a pretty standard design. Average balance, nothing's pertacular. But it beat being unarmed. Moliki spread out the map. Now come. Let us go over this map quickly before someone decides to check up on us. In over 33 years of life, Kira and Nerese have been sure many times that she was going to die. She'd been glad to have been wrong each time, but now she was starting to wish she would die. First, it spent two days navigating through a swamp. Then they'd gotten to the mountains. Torna had been fading in and out for quite some time. When he collapsed on the snow-covered ground, he clenched his jaw. Ugh. Keep forgetting that the arm doesn't really work. Ashla, I need you to cut the damn thing off. Look, Torna, I'm not a surgeon. And if I cut your arm off now, you'll bleed to death. The general smiled grimly. I suppose this means I'll just have to make it back to Parigia then. If we do not, Parigia will be lost. But half an hour later, Kira collapsed face first into the snow. The Suddenly, Kira's eyes fluttered awake. Where? Where am I? You're in the infirmary, Fort Tendro. Fort Tendro was practically on the front lines, Kira thought. That's where Torna and I were headed. She looked up to see a pleasant round face. I'm Dr. Maldic. Kira tried to rise from her cot. What about Torna? We were in the mountains and... Maldic smiled. Yes, you two almost died there. General Torna has already gone back to the capital. You and he had been declared dead by the Lared, you see. They claimed to have executed you. It therefore came as something of a surprise to see him stumbling into the fort, carrying you on his right shoulder. In any case, he left immediately to pass on some news or other about the Lared. And also to let his wife and children know he was alive. Kira spent what felt like an eternity on that cot. As time went on, news came from the front lines and from the capital. With the help of entry, the Perikians won, and soon she found herself transported by ship back to the Perikian port. Kira had never traveled much by sea. Her initial assumption that it would be much like flying in an atmospheric craft turned out to be optimistic. She managed not to throw up, but that, only through a supreme effort of will. When they came around the bend into sight of the port, she had other reasons for being ill. The port was on fire. There were no obvious peers available for docking. Half of them were damaged beyond youthfulness, and the rest were occupied. The marina itself was a massive chaotic activity, with small fires being put out and people coughing from a smoke. Someone noticed them eventually though, as a small rowboat approached the spot. Kira recognized its occupant as the assistant darkmaster, Kiran. As he pulled up alongside the ship, he sighted Kira. Good to have you back, ma'am. You should know that General Torna's in his office. You might want to see him. Kira accompanied him back on the rowboat to the marina. Kiran, what happened here? Hiran shook his head with bitterness. Lared's last stand, you could say ma'am. On his way back from Fort Tendro, General Torna pretty much beat the Lared on the land. Meantime, Admiral Ina came back here when she found out that the Lared Navy was going to throw their whole Amata out of it. Kira looked at the smoky, ruined port. Looks like they did. Oh, the Admiral. She threw back pretty good too. Cost her life, ma'am. It is dead? Eran nodded. I guess you didn't hear that Prefect Nautler was killed too. See, same time the Lared Navy did their last stand here. The Lared Army did likewise in the capital. We beat him back, mighty good. Truth be told, but not without a cost, if you know what I mean. When Kira entered Torna's tiny office, she saw that the General looked like a zombie. His eyes stared unblinking straight ahead. He smelled strongly of alcohol. Ashla, they're dead. I know, General. Heron told me about the Prefect and Admiral Ina. Torna swept the empty bottles from his desk and looked at Kira in despair. No, that's not who I mean. Lyra, my wife, she's dead here. Dead. And the children, all of them dead. I never got to tell them I was alive. Listen to me, Antoso, you can't just give up. Why not? Heaven I had done enough. No, you haven't. Farikia needs you. They need the man who beat back the Lared Army. Snarling, Kira got up and went to the other side of the desk. She grabbed Torna by the shirt. Get up! She led him, muttering and stumbling the entire way outside. She propped him up on one of the wooden railings that separated the small office building area from the main marina and pointed. You see that? I don't see anything but... Losing all patience, Kira screamed at him. The bodies! Look at the bodies! Those people died fighting for Perikia. So did Natlar, so did Ina, and so did your wife Lyra. You have no right to give up now because if you do, Lared has won. Without you, Lared or the Bajora will be able to come right in and take over. Torna stared straight ahead for several minutes. Then he turned back to Kira. His eyes were filled with sadness. I'm sorry. As she stared at the pathetic drunken figure of Torna and Toso, standing in the midst of the wreckage of the port, Kira at once realized that she made the right and the wrong choice in stepping through the gateway when she did. Whether or not Torna decides to drink himself into oblivion or takes charge of the Perikian government doesn't matter. Kira walked away then. Away from Torna and Toso. Away from the port. Away from the Corveil Ocean. Away from the Perikian Peninsula. Or, more accurately, she went under it to the fire caves. She had no idea why she went down there. Yet she was never more sure of anything in her life. Despite the fact that the Denorio's belt tacky on Eddies prevented any gateways from being constructed within 10 light-years of Bajor, Kira was not surprised by the fact that an active gateway was present to the caves. She felt supremely confident as she stepped through it, ready to face what lay beyond. Kira Nurese stared at the galaxy. She had seen computer models of what the galaxy would look like from outside it, but it did not prepare for the site before now. The entire galaxy was laid out before her. She stood in a small chamber about 8 meters in diameter. In the center of the room was a console with a design that looked iconic. But that wasn't what really interested her about the chamber. Except for one small portion that contained an entryway. The great dome that rose up from the floor was completely transparent and looked out onto space. Specifically, with a spectacular view of Kira's home galaxy, what humans referred to as the Milky Way, an Appalachian Kira was only just now starting to appreciate. Apparently this outpost was located somewhere in the great expanse between galaxies. Ah, there you are. She found herself transfixed. All her life, the stars as they were seen from a planet or a ship, were how she viewed the universe. But this was the first time on the outside looking in. Suddenly, Kira Nurese felt very, very small. A finger seemed to appear from nowhere and pointed a spot in the lower left quadrant of the vista spread out before Kira. The planet you come from is here. I believe you referred to it as Bejor. Kira tore her gaze away from a view and foughtled the finger back up the hand and arm it was connected to and finally to the body. The figure was huge though humanoid and wore a maroon cloak with a hood that obscured his features. Who are you? The figure hesitated. You might say I'm an emissary of the people who built this outpost, but that might have unfortunate connotations for you. Suffice it to say that I am the custodian of this place. You're an Iconian? The movement inside the cloak could have been an affirmative nod. You'll be happy to know that I was able to cure you of that unfortunate energy. It took Kira a moment to realize that he was referring to the Theta radiation poisoning. She had been on that erid desert of a planet in the Delta Quadrant. Theta radiation eating away at her when the gateway beckoned. Her tricorder had told her that the radiation levels were fatal. Of course, the Rashma part of her brain said as she looked down and saw that she was back in her uniform. Maybe it was some kind of dream or vision that would certainly explain. She cut the thought short and she felt a mild stiffness in her left arm. Looking down, she saw a badly healed wound she'd received the day they drove the Lared Army out of the capital city. She pointed to the wound. How did out of this get here? Presumably you received it at an earlier date. You're a big help. I assume that you wish to take the gift that has been given to you and then go home. Actually, I need to return to Europa Nova. I made a promise to the leader there that I would do everything I could. The custodian drifted over to the center console. I see. One of our haslat gateways is an orbit of that planet. Kira also approached the console. Haslat? Many different types of gateways were constructed over time. Some large and inelegant, some small and functional. Others that could be held in a palm of one's hand. The haslats were among the first and also among the largest. The custodian seemed to be just staring at the display, so Kira helped him along. Someone decided to dump theta radiation into that that haslat of yours. We had to evacuate everyone from the planet on the other side before the radiation levels became fatal. Yes. Yes. I see that now. But there is something blocking part of the gateway. Yes, that's one of our vessels. That's how we traveled by ship and I used mine to block the radiation from coming through and I understand Colonel. I observe your ships traversing the galaxy all the time from here. It is not a pastime shared by all my people. Then there are more of you? Yes. Some of them are dealing with this crisis now. I have faith in the centuries. Kira had no idea what that meant, but she didn't want to get off topic. What about Europa Nova? I can reprogram this particular haslat gateway to transport the matter that is emitting the energy on both sides into the star in System 022-Sci-T. The star there will render the energy inert. I will also remove the object blocking the gateway. To which system would you like it moved? Kira pointed to the Europa Nova star system. That one. The custodian made some adjustments on the panel. I assume by the state you arrived in that your species is vulnerable to this type of energy. Assuming that he meant theta radiation, Kira nodded. Yes. Very vulnerable. In that case, you must be careful. The gateway can remove the matter, but some of the energy will remain around that planet you were concerned with. You say it was evacuated? Kira nodded. The custodian touched a series of triangular panels. Repopulating it will be a challenge. Like I said, I made a promise. Then it is time for you to leave. A blue life shot out from the model of the galaxy and a gateway opened in the chamber with Kira and the custodian stood. Through it, Kira could see the bustle of ops on Deep Space 9. Before stepping into the gateway, she took one last look outside of the expense of the galaxy before her. She once again found the spot where the custodian had indicated that Bajor was. The custodian waited patiently while she stargazed, but eventually she turned away from a spectacular view. Enough self-indulgence. It's past time I went back to work. As she approached the gateway, the custodian turned to her. One of the things that doomed the Iconian Empire kernel was that the gateway technology meant that we could no longer travel. We lost sight of the journey in our desire to achieve our destination. Do not make that mistake. Kira smiled at the cloak figure. I won't. And thank you. Then she stepped through the gateway, knowing full well what lay beyond. Kira knew that Esri Dax had centuries of life experience, thanks to the Dax symbiote. And she knew that among her nine lifetimes, she had probably seen everything. So when Kira walked into ops, she found it a fairly amusing sight to see Dax jump up, scream, and drop the pad she was holding. As usual with the gateways, it was as if ops had been the next room over from the extra galactic outpost. The only change was that the outpost gravity was a bit lighter than that of Deep Space 9, so Kira stumbled a bit upon her arrival. As we Dax blinked several times. Colonel? Yes, Lieutenant, it's me. Fill me in on what has happened. Europa Nova has been completely evacuated. Most of the refugees are on Bajor. The stations filled almost to capacity. Kira smiled as she also heard the news that her crewmate, Tarana Atar, and even Quark had returned safely from their missions. But her joy was tempered, as she learned how many others were still on dangerous assignments to deal with the chaos the gateways were causing. Then she relayed her own astounding news. There won't be any more antimatter waste in orbit of Europa Nova. A full sensor sweep can determine how much contamination is still there. If we're lucky, it's little enough that we can work on repopulating sooner rather than later. Dax started to move toward a console, but she stopped and smiled. It's good to have you back there, Reese. I don't think this place could have taken losing another commanding officer. Kira nodded. Good to be back, Esri. And don't worry, I'm not going anywhere. I've still got too much work to do. Some time later, after Kira had taken care of a variety of administrative duties, not to mention assuring everyone that she was, in fact, alive, contrary to reports. She sat in her office, looking over the historical records she had been able to scare up from the Perician region. There was distressingly little from as long as 30,000 years ago. She had found no record whatsoever of the Lared, aside from some archaeological indications of some kind of empire from that time period that looked Lared like to Kira. The name of Torna and Toso did come up in several texts, as did that of others with that family name. Historians had debated just who and Toso was and what form his apparently tremendous influence had been in the peninsula. But given the number of landmarks and streets and such that had been named for him or other members of the Torna family, it was obvious to Kira that he had taken her advice. Assuming I was ever really there, she thought, as she rubbed her left arm, which still had the scar. Shutting down the computer terminal, Kira stared straight ahead for a moment, then picked up the baseball. Benjamin Sisco, the emissary, had always kept that baseball on his desk. The central element of a human sport that he had been inordinately fond of. The white spheroid with red stitching was a symbol of Sisco's presence. Even though the station was now hers to command, Kira had not been able to bring herself to remove the baseball. She wasn't sure why she had left it there. Now I know why. I kept thinking the back of my head that the emissary was going to return, hoping that he'd return and take the burden off of me, that he'd take the station back and everything would be back to normal. But that's not going to happen. This station is mine now. I've got responsibilities just like Torna did. And damn it, I'm going to live up to them. She opened a drawer and the desk and placed the baseball in it. I'll hold it for you Benjamin, for when you come back. But I need this to be my office now. She got up and went back into ops to continue down the road the profits had laid out for her.
description: In this episode of "Star Trek Audiobook," Kira leads a meeting in the capital city to discuss plans for independence from the oppressive Laird regime and calls for help from other nations. While she initially wants to remain out of the way, she eventually decides to involve herself after seeing no reason not to. The episode explores themes of sacrifice, resistance, and the challenges of creating change in a corrupt society.
