transcript: Simon and Schuster Audio presents Star Trek, Gateways, What Lay Beyond. Read by David Kay. Scattered throughout the galaxy are gateways capable of transporting matter and energy across unfathomable distances. Left behind by a long, vanished civilization, these mysterious portals offer a means of exploration or conquest many times faster than war travel. A reactivated gateway has hurled Captain Kirk and his Starship Enterprise nearly a thousand light years through space from an artificial planetoid on which is an old outpost once occupied by the Colandans, a people thought to be wiped out centuries ago by a viral plague. Kirk and his crew are under Starfleet orders to discover the secret of the ancient interstellar transporter and prevent it from falling into the hands of the enemies of the Federation. Unfortunately, the reactivated gateway has attracted the attention of two mysterious females, Commander Tasm and her officer, Luz, who claim to be none other than from the enigmatic Colandans. When Luz steals a key component of the miraculous technology and uses a gateway to escape, Commander Tasm pursues her. Understanding the threat to the Federation if he loses this component, Kirk now risks all to follow Luz and Tasm and leaps through the gateway. And now, the exciting continuation of the gateway saga, Star Trek, one giant leap by Susan Wright. Captain Kirk was suspended in the gateway, floating between the countless dimensions. The interstellar transport lasted for only a few seconds, but the flashing light seemed to freeze every thought and feeling he had. Then he was falling out the other side, rolling to his feet and unsteady in the soft surface. He was standing on the edge of a small platform, suspended near the top of a giant ship. The sheer parallel cliffs extended for miles to either side. Backing away from the edge, Kirk looked around and saw the two Colandans. Tasm, stop! Commander Tasm was on the other side of the platform, trying to rest away the large cylindrical unit from her errand officer, Luz. The blue neutronium cylinder was the key component of the gateway, and they were waving it around between them at the edge of an abyss. Kirk ran forward and jerked the cylinder away from Luz, pulled his phaser from his belt, and trained it on them both. Then he quickly assessed the situation. They were standing on a platform, hardly six meters square, but what he had mistaken was soft sand, was really some kind of plush, rubbery material that coated the rock. He took a few steps inside a tunnel that led from the platform into the cliffs, getting a better look at the thick beige stuff. It ran up the sides of the tunnel, covering them completely. Further in, the tunnel ended. When he poked at the stuff, it felt like a dense block of suede. Back outside, Kirk looked at both the retchions up and down the crevice. He had seen two metal plated buildings on top of the cliffs before jumping through the gateway. Now, he had to strain to see them. They were much further up on the opposite side. The sun in the orange sky was so bright, it made it hard to focus on the dull metal. He jerked his phaser at Luz. You brought us here. What is this place? Luz's lips drew back from her teeth. This is our birthing world. You want Calandans? We are Petra. You're such trusting fools. Tasm glared at her officer. Silence, Luz. You betrayed your pod. Luz rushed at Tasm. I saved the interstellar transporter. With surprise on her side, Luz managed to shove Tasm towards the edge. Kirk dropped the cylinder to go to Tasm's defense, but he wasn't exactly willing to risk his own life for hers. Aiming his phaser, he hesitated. Before he could fire, he was surrounded by people, hands grabbed his arms and took away his phaser. He counted eight humanoids, crowded onto the platform, dressed alike in whitish transparent bags, complete with enclosed hands and feet. The Luz hoods over their heads slid forward. The humanoids separated Tasm and Luz, and one took the cylinder. Kirk saw the humanoid's face was like melted wax with his nose, eyes and chin softened and flattened. Kirk pointed to the cylinder. I'm James T. Kirk of the Starship Enterprise, and believe that belongs to me. The androgynous Petra held up the cylinder. This is for the matriarchs to deal with. Kirk nodded. Lead the way. He was more than ready to talk to someone in charge. Kirk commanded Tasm had clearly lied to him about everything. Tasm and Luz were herded into the tunnel behind him. It had somehow become unclogged and continued much deeper inside the cliff. There was no obvious light source, but the pliable material covering the wall seemed to glow like amber under a light. It wasn't long before the tunnel ended in a slightly more bulbous section. Straight ahead were six hexagonal openings stacked three across and two high. Each opening was about a meter wide. The Petra holding the cylinder gestured to the first hexagonal opening on the bottom. In there. Kirk peered in, but he couldn't see out the other side. This is the way to the matriarchs? Without hesitation, the Petra guard seized his legs and arms, and before he knew it, they were tossing him into a hexagonal cell. They slapped something on the end. The seal was hard and peach colored, almost opaque. He could see the shadows of the Petra outside. Even as he kicked hard against it with both feet, he couldn't budge the seal. After a while, it was pitch dark inside. He was trapped. It was a tiny, claustrophobic place. A sarcophagus buried in the rock. Too bad his phaser was gone, but they hadn't taken his communicator. This is Captain James T. Kirk, the Starship Enterprise. Can anyone read me? I'm being held prisoner. This is Captain James T. Kirk, the Starship Enterprise. A different cause of action was required. Kirk strained with both hands to twist the communicator cover out of its hinge. It broke free and left a jagged edge. He dug the broken cover into the seal on the end of the cell. The jagged edge left a small slice in the flexible polymer-like material. It took a while for him to break through, only to find himself trapped again. Kirk carefully retraced his steps and found the tunnel's opening to the platform clogged with a dense mass of tan polymer. But now he knew that somehow the tunnel could be opened. He returned to the six hexagonal cells and searched the walls, pushing and poking, trying to find a place where the polymer would open up. Right next to the cells, his hands sank into the wall. He leaned in, pushing his arms into the center. The barrier irised into an open, tall enough for him to step inside another tunnel. Light slanted out of a doorway ahead. Edging closer, he could see a brightly lit cavernous space filled with various large pieces of equipment. His luck had changed. The chamber held the factory where the Petron made their garments. Inside the door were racks of drying coveralls, shining and smelling strongly like a brand new spacesuit. They were translucent and wet, drying to nearly a solid white. They were designed exactly the same, bags with legs ending in booties, and arms ending in four-fingered glows. A hood was attached to the neck. Kirk found one his size and pulled it on. With a hood up, no one would notice him in the darkness. Finally, feeling free to roam, Kirk slipped out of the garment factory and began briskly walking down the center of the tunnel. No one paid any attention to him, even when several Petron passed nearby. With their melted faces, he couldn't tell any of them apart. It took hours before he found what he was looking for, a docking bay for spaceships. Finally, he found a small shuttlecraft-type ship that appeared fully operational. He entered it, slid into the pilot seat, and examined the controls. They were like nothing he had ever seen. Uh-oh, maybe not so simple. I might need a native guide. Not that lose or tasm seemed predisposed to help him. Working at a panel, Kirk managed to call up the navigational chart. The pattern of a galactic star map was clear in any language. A red stationary indicator was near the center of the galaxy, in a spiral arm at the base of the beta quadrant. Kirk froze. If that red indicator meant what he thought it meant, he was 40,000 light-years away from Federation territory. Days, he tried to do the math. I think you'll take the grass between your little stubby toes down there. She smiled, but he'd awaken to cautious streak. Does color hurt? Braxton, color is one of the best things. Hunt, the hunt. The hunt. The hunt. The hunt. Local heralds were running through the streets, summoning all those qualified to hunt. Keller's side. What a shame. A free dancer had just landed here, but all its energy was lost. Hundreds of people would soon die. A horrific electrical death to tamp down more free dancers in a controlled environment, so one could be killed and its energy taken into storage. The hunt plane was nothing more than miles of ferrous flats brushed to a dull sheen by storms. The biohays, a shroud of primordial life surviving in the atmosphere, flickered and swam and tumbled. There were 20,000 people or so on this planet by Keller's best reckoning. The low number was a sad clue. According to the old records, there'd once been upwards of 100,000, all descendants of the crews and passengers. Of those first ships to pass through the gateway. Nature was intolerant here. The planet couldn't support a population. The living were more devolving than evolving. They survived, but didn't thrive. Starvation, competition, failure. The metal planet would never let them flourish. So they clung to a legend about going home. They wanted to go. They planned to go, unless they were chosen in the forest. They were chosen in the hunt of a freedancer or anointed, killed by accident or illness, and preserved to act as a high energy storage unit. They worked toward the goal of eventually leaving. The plan's most recent leg had been a monumental one. To take thousands of anointed through the gateway, then send a signal for the rest of the people to follow. That signal had never come. Instead, quite another signal had been sent. The anointed had been summoned down from their pedestal as all at once, not by destiny, but by Nick Keller in his determination to keep the gateway open. Taking the unexpected destruction of the anointed as a message, the living had hunkered down once more to the business of collecting energy from the freedancers, but this time with the idea of another 10,000 years of work before trying again. They'd used up almost all their stored energy to open the gateway and hold it open. Then power the small spinner fleet they'd launched. They had to hustle now, hunt more and more often, to gather enough energy to go on surviving. But Keller had come. He wanted them to use their new power stores in a different way, to go through the gateway en masse as they had originally planned. He was the only one who knew the clock was taking to a much nearer alarm. Challenger and the ship carrying the anointed could only hold the gateway open a few hours on their side, more than a year on this side. A year sounded long, but wasn't. The living had been waiting years on this side for the elders, Ryuda and Lunti, to send a summons that instead received a cutoff. They supposed the anointed had met with tragedy in space. After hundreds of generations, nothing had come of this. They had accepted two new elders, along with the one left behind, and they'd begun again. But Keller clung to his belief that the gateway was still open. He clamped his lips on his thoughts as he and Braxton worked side by side, along with hundreds of hunters from all the settlements, to fit woven gum segments into place and seal the seams. The mats protected the free dancers from the planet, but didn't protect the living from the free dancers. The living had learned long ago that they had to let the free dancers, well, there was no nice way to say it, let them feed. Rather quickly, the mats were pieced together into a gigantic circle of a size perfect for its task, big enough that the free dancers would be able to sense the living crowded upon it, but not so big that the living couldn't race for the edges when the time was right. Hundreds of healthy, innocent men and women would strip down to their birthday suits and plunge out onto the plane, then wait for the free dancer heard to see them, whatever that meant, and come to the trough. Against all instinct, the living had learned to simply stand there and be chosen in an electrical feeding frenzy that defied description. The people would stand with their faces up, fear clearly shown as the monsters came down, and wait for the elders to decide the free dancers had eaten enough that they would return the next time. Finally, the scramble back to the perimeter while the slaughter went on. Desperate hunters would pull on their silky chainmail tunics so they would be protected from the pyrotechnics, snatch up their arksbikes, pulpers, clamps, nets, and race back to harvest one free dancer for the reservoir of energy and the gizzard full of candleflies it provided. Courageous people would be dying soon and horribly, but not him and not Braggson. He needed to live, and he needed her to live. One of the hunters pointed at the sky. Look, a spinner! Keller raised his hand to shield his face from the ice particles and scanned the ugly sky. Beside him, Braggson hunched her shoulders and turned her unprotected face upward. It was a bug-shaped metallic vessel with forward mandibles and a bulb asternet, a spinner from the fleet on the other side of the gateway. And quite literally, the last thing Keller expected to see. Keller recognized the man who stepped from the spinner as the elder named Luntie. Braggson put her hand on Keller's arm. This will put to rest the idea that you may not have been honest with us. There were rumors that Ryuda and Luntie had died on the other side. Keller pushed his way through the crowd of hunters to face Luntie. Lunties spoke angrily to Keller. You don't belong here. We don't belong outside. We should never have gone. Keller held himself in check and went for information. What's the status on the other side? They think you're dead. Almost all the anointed are gone. Time is running out. Luntie, we've been getting ready. We've been storing energy to power the transport ships. All the living will be able to go through the gateway. Braggson appeared beside Keller and spoke softly to him. The plan is troubled now. Luntie's returned to us and he's an elder. There can only be three elders. Luntie's voice will now be heard with my voice and the voice of Camellus. Luntie spoke up again. We will not go through. We will destroy all the transporting vessels and we'll live here as we are meant. Keller couldn't believe his ears. MENT? Nobody's meant to live on this pie plate? There's no natural life here at all. He turned to the crowd and implored them. The gateway's still open. That's a clear message. My friends and Ryuda are holding it open. They're still waiting for us. Luntie held up his hand and pointed to the skies. The gateway remains open because Keller's friends are forcing Ryuda to push anointed after anointed into the processor. Wasted. Take the spinner, Keller. Go away and leave us alone. That's exactly what you'll be, Luntie. Alone. The crowd was nervous, doubtful, and suddenly scared. Luntie continued. If we go to space and the gateway closes before we go through, then we all die. All our energy will be used up. We'll freeze and starve by thousands. We have a fresh store of energy to be used in powerful vessels to go through the gateway to that place of horror. Or to be used to make life better here. More heat, more building, new way to hunt. Braxton interrupted. Keller, there are three elders. Since Luntie is back, he claims his place. If Camellus decides to stay or go, we do that. Luntie spoke boldly to the gathering of hunters. The elders speak with separate voices. Random order will declare which voice shall be final. There must be a hunt decision. When the first freedancer descends, all hunters will retreat except for the two challenges. One will be chosen. The other, the voice left behind, is meant to be heard. Since all the hunters were gathered anyway, and there were freedancers in the sky, the hunt decision would happen here and now. The judge would be Cyclops, Camellus, the impartial elder, impartial, vacillating really. Camellus was also dangerously superstitious. She was waiting for a sign that this was the right time to abandon the ridiculous planet. Keller turned to Camellus. What if both die? If both are chosen, Camellus step forward. They're neither is meant to be heard. There will be two new elders. Wait, what do you mean by two new elders? If I'm chosen, Braxton still will be... Camellus shook her head. You will not be on the hunt plane. Braxton is the dissenting elder. A hunt decision is made with elders. Keller appealed to Camellus. There's got to be something better. Camellus's remaining eye shifted back and forth as if scanning the old records and laws and rules and their details. Braxton can select a surrogate. Braxton gazed at it with miserable adoration. If you were chosen, Keller, there will be no one strong to speak for going. I will stand on the plane. A devious light came on in Luntie's eyes. Very well, Keller. You'll be on the hunt plane as my surrogate. Braxton will represent the voice to go. You will represent me and the voice to stay. Random order will decide which voice remains to be heard as it has for 500 generations. Keller fought his own inner arguments and tried to add up the situation. If Braxton lived, her voice remained and the ideal of going through the gateway would prevail. But Luntie could easily muddy the waters, play on Camellus's doubts and make the clock run out. He could stall enough to let the last anointed go into the processor and... gateway to finally close, locking the living to their fate on this side. Braxton wasn't the type to fight him hard enough. In fact, Luntie had Keller better than even Luntie realized. Keller had only his one ace, his big secret. He could arrange for one or the other to survive on the feast grid. He could do it artificially. Now what? Admit to these brave hunters that he'd been hedging his bets, immunizing himself and Braxton with tricorder scans. Tell them how different the energy acted on either side of the gateway. Giant shadows moved across the grid mats. Right, Luntie. But all I have to do is throw myself before the free dancer, and Braxton's voice remains. And I swear to do that, Luntie, I won't let your voice be heard. Around him, Luntie, Braxton and Camellus, a sea of hunters rounded their shoulders against the bitter wind. Their soft link sure to blaze with reflected lights from overhead. So, the free dancers would decide. Except that the tricorder would have more influence. He'd already scanned and immunized Braxton from being selected by the free dancers. Yet Keller hadn't immunized himself. And now he wouldn't. Braxton had to live. We have to send. Descending. Descending. Descending. Descending. Overhead, the first free dancer released his heat and floated down toward the grid to take its meal. Keller moved away from Braxton. When the free dancer came for him, he didn't want to be anywhere near her. He closed his eyes and stripped the tricorder strap off his shoulder. Suddenly, he was pushed forward and stumbled to one knee. His tricorder flew from his hand. Over him, Luntie was aiming the tricorder directly at him. Keller knew he would never be chosen. He would give the free dancers a burning mouth. Luntie, how could you possibly know? I have lived here a lifetime. Energy is aratonic. Now I've been to the outside and I know all things behave and strange dances. Luntie dumped the tricorder on the mats and raced away from the center of the feast grid. He didn't realize Braxton was already immunized. But now Keller was immunized too. If the free dancer chose neither of them, time would run out before another decision could be hammered into place. Luntie would still be able to keep his people here. The free dancers were getting closer. Keller called out to Kamelis. Wait! This decision's too important. Luntie must stand on the plane with Braxton and me. All three of us must take our chances. Luntie glared at Keller. Why should this be? Luntie has already been established. If your voice remains, Luntie, there won't be any doubts. Braxton will do what you want. I will too. That's my promise to the living. Luntie turned to Kamelis. I reject this. He uses our rules against us. Keller pointed out to Kamelis. Luntie's afraid of true random order. Kamelis fixed her single eye on Luntie. If you're afraid, Luntie, then I side with Braxton and we will go tomorrow. Brain began to pummel the confused crowd. The hunters were nervous, glancing up. Palettes of ice were melting in the heat of the first few free dancers as they came down directly over the hunt plane. Long strands of electrical floss, snapping like a woman's hair in the wind. All the hunters were on the plane with Keller, Braxton and Luntie at dead center. They left their non-conducting mail shirts behind, and thus would be unprotected from the savage tendrils of floss. Kamelis turned to the hunters. Clear the plane. Clear the plane. Her shot was carried dutifully through the throng, and the hunters raced for the perimeter to pull their mail shirts back on. There to stand and watch, as a great decision occurred on the grid. For a woman who had trouble making a decision, she was done with this one. With Luntie still standing on the plane, Braxton didn't understand the change and called to Keller. What happened? Keller called back to her. Stay there. It's the three of us now. Just stay put. Luntie had no choice but to stand his own ground as the first free dancer came down and the hunters flooded off the grid. As far as anyone else knew, this was a fair fight. Only Keller and Luntie knew otherwise. The shock floss moved toward Braxton, a maneuver which Keller had to battle in his own heart. He wanted to run a protector, but he'd already done all he could with his tricorder. Luntie never bothered to look at Braxton. Of course, he must assume Keller would already have immunized her. The tendrils snapped around Braxton, but quickly retracted at the taste of her. Luntie knew for sure now that he was the only vulnerable person here. I thought you were not so brutal, Keller. You know who was chosen now. Just between the two of them, Keller offered a nod of understanding. Yes, but it's your life against all these others. One person's life, one selfish person, against a whole community of Las Soles. Then you sentenced me, Keller. One more death in this place? I'm sorry for it. The free dancer came down. Luntie squinted and raised his arms to shield his face, but he was doomed. Floss snapped and sizzled around her. Keller knew his only duty was to move away from Luntie and let fate take its course. He had to take these people home. Luntie closed his eyes, gritted his teeth, and prepared to lose. But he never ran. Never even attempted to protect himself or change what had been choreographed, either by random order or by Keller's manipulation. Keller ducked the tendrils and watched Luntie a couple more seconds before he finally snapped. Braxton, get off the grid. Run! He shouted to the crowd. Art Spike! Someone seized a near Spike and heaved it. The 15-foot spear flew poorly, but enough to sail over Luntie's head toward Keller. Keller bunched up his body and propelled himself into the air. With his high hand, he knocked the Spike out of its path. A cartwheeled once and thumped to the mat's 10 feet from her. He rolled until his hands made contact with the Spike. The long device leaped into his grip. He rolled again, turned the spear end upward and gave a mighty shove. He kept the grip on the end of the Spike and plunged at Luntie. Once on top of him, Keller dug his fingers into a scene between the gum mats until his fingernails scraped metal, the planet's surface. With all the strength in his lean and muscled arm, he hauled back on the woven gum. With the other hand, he grounded the arc Spike's blunt end into the now-beared spot of surface metal and rolled for his life. The gum mats coiled around him and Luntie. Keller kept rolling until the mats were tight around them both in a rubber coffin. The free dancer was grounded. Luntie's body jolted against him. They were frying. Indescribable heat soon filled up his brain and broiled away his thoughts. Time lost meaning. He was aware only of a terrible hammering from outside as if the rubber wool was instead the head of a mallet. The planet surged up under the great electrical bladder and sucked back what had once given in some weird ancient trade. When the last crackle sounded, Nick Keller had stopped trying to handle the moment and simply allowed himself to be slaughtered, all the more surprised when he found himself alive. Keller forced himself and Luntie to roll free from the coiled mats. Around them and rising several stories on one side was the cooked mess that once been the free dancer that nearly killed them, now a mountain of black and flakes. Luntie was choking. Why would you save me? Possessed with sudden ferocity, Keller grinned and snarled at the same time. Because I don't have to accept the verdict of random order. Those aren't gods in the sky, they're animals. The free dancer chose you to die, but I choose for you to live. Luntie stared up at him. Behind the frothing hiss of the barbecued free dancer, they heard the cheer and rave of the hot air. The cheer and rave of the hunters were just now coming to understand what had just happened. Braxton came behind him. Her narrow face crumpled with fear. Next was Camilla's and her family. And two by two, three by three, the rest of the hunters pushed through the mountain of ash and fibrous smoldering flesh until there were hundreds crowded on the melted segment. Shaking with aftershock and satisfaction, Keller managed to stand up and glared down at Luntie. Random order is finished here. I'm in charge now. We don't belong here and we're not staying. Finally, blessedly, we're going to settle up and leave this moodless world. The On the other side of the gateway, from the science deck of the Starship Challenger, savanna ring maintained constant contact with Ryota on the grave ship, monitoring the energy output to the gateway. We're down to the last chamber of zombies. Any one of those corpses could nourish a power system on our side for months. But to keep that gateway open, we're pouring them in like penny candy. The Challenger Bridge crew were silent and close to despair. Suddenly, the navigator popped a renewed life. Sir, I'm reading metallic objects. Could it be ships? No one else spoke as they watched the gateways inside smolder, brightened like a spotlight behind smoke, and ultimately spew a single bulb-shaped ship made entirely of brass. The new ship was alone for only seconds before four more ships came behind it, then four more and more, and even more after those, until the swarm of brass-y ships crowded space around the frigate. The crew rose to stare with hopeful anticipation at the oncoming ships. A dot of light appeared on the port side. A micro gate spun itself into existence. A hand appeared on the edge of the micro gate. A moment later, Nick Keller himself appeared, or a frazzled version of Nick Keller. His hair, once sandy brown and casually tidy, now was beaten to a crispy shag about his shoulders, blackened at the ends as if burned. His friendly face was leathery from exposure, his clothing of perfect nightmare. He wore his regular trousers and burgundy cruiswetter, but they were gaudily patched with interwoven segments and chain mail. Keller stepped onto the bridge. Tell Ryota to stop powering the gateway. There's nobody left on the other side. We'll need the grave ship system to move these fraders. There's no more power coming from the other side. Just let the Dan Hole close up for good. He looked around and reveled in what he saw. The quarter-foil cut sparked shield on the side deck. The cobalt obsidian dome overhead. The multitude of flickering data screens, the carpet, the rail. This bridge is beautiful. Now he turned his fatigued gaze to his crew. He hadn't seen them in more than a year. He found his way to the command chair and ran his hand along the studded forest green leather, which looked to him as if it actually glowed. The redened skin on his cheeks and around his eyes crinkled into patterns as he smiled. The bridge winked and murmured its faint electrical song around him, so different from the disorderly crackle of the metal world.
description: In this episode of "Star Trek" audiobook, Captain James Kirk is transported through a mysterious ancient gateway by Commander Tasm and her officer Luz from an extinct civilization known as Colandans. This reactivated gateway allows for instantaneous travel across vast distances within the galaxy, offering a swift route to explore or conquer new territories. As they continue their journey, the characters face threats from these strange females who possess a crucial component of this technology. The narrative builds suspense and explores the implications of such advanced interstellar transportation methods in our timeline.

transcript: Awakened once more, the ancient Iconian gateways are rewriting the map of the galaxy, and nowhere more than in the new frontier. A century ago, the Imperial Thelonians separated two feuding alien races, the Aerons and the Marcanians, depositing each of them on a new world safely distant from that of their ancestral enemies. Now, the gateways have made it possible for the long, dormant blood feud to begin anew. Aided by two mysterious aliens, each with a gateway device, the two enemies battle of the planet Cinque. Captain Mackenzie Calhoun of the USS Excalibur and his wife, Captain Elizabeth Shelby of the USS Triton, find themselves fighting a losing battle to keep the horrific violence from escalating. And they're suddenly transported by an energy field to a planet of ice with a face certain death. The only thing that might save them is that there is a gateway on the frozen planet. And now, the continuation of the gateway saga, Star Trek New Frontier, Death After Life, by Peter David. And Kenzie Calhoun, Captain of the Excalibur, was so cold that it took his body long minutes to realize that he was once again in warmth. Calhoun had practically forgotten what it was like to breathe without a thousand needles jabbing in his chest. He was so dazed, so confounded that he had to make the effort to reorder events in his mind so that he could recall how he'd come to this pass. The cold had been so overwhelming that for what seemed an endless period of time, he couldn't think of anything beyond that. There had been cold and blistering winds that would have fled the skin from his body if he had been out there much longer. Cold and bodies. Two bodies. Yes, the aliens, both dead, lying there, face up in the snow, mere feet away from the great gateway. They had caused trouble, so much trouble for two races, for himself, for Shelby. Now Calhoun lay there, flat on his back, arms and legs played, trying to put together the pieces of his body and the pieces of his life. The ground hard and gritty beneath him. The heat of an unknown sun pounding down upon him. His extremities starting to tingle with the resurgence of blood circulating to them, and that was when he remembered Shelby. His wife, Elizabeth Paula Shelby, captain of the Good Ship Triton, had been swept away along with them to the frozen world that had, for a time at least, promised to be their final resting place. She'd been there with another man. Yes, yes, it was starting to come back to him. A man named Ibose, leader of a people called, called, what? The, the Marcanians. Yes, that was right. Ibose of the Marcanians, he'd wound up on the wasted frozen world along with Shelby. Then they'd fallen into a crevasse, and Shelby survived, but Ibose didn't. Simple as that. Shelby had been unconscious in his arms. He had cradled her, like a groom, delicately transporting his bride over the threshold on their wedding night. But there'd been nothing remotely romantic about it. She'd been unconscious, freezing in his arms, injured from her fall in the frostbite, and he held her as if he could will his own body heat into her in order to save her. It hadn't worked. Calhoun had spat out curse after curse, cried out against the unfairness of their circumstances, and simply refused to believe that it was going to end there on some nameless ice world who knew where. Then he heard a voice from nearby, rough and hard and disinterested in hearing any sort of griping of any sort. Life isn't fair. Deal with it. At first he didn't recognize it, and then it came to him. Roar toward him with the ferocity of a star exploding and firing Nova. Father? The shock was too much, because Mackenzie Calhoun realized that he was dead. That was all just dead, because his murdered father was speaking to him, and he'd never really made it through the planet of ice at all. It had all been some sort of cruel joke, and at that moment he and Elizabeth were lying on the planet's surface, becoming crusted over with sleet and snow. Even as he was half sitting up, Calhoun fell back without ever having opened his eyes. He struck his head hard on the barren and crusty ground beneath him, but never felt it. And so died Mackenzie Calhoun, without ever having a chance to see the sunset. But Kenzie Calhoun, captain of the Excalibur, was so cold that it took his body long minutes to realize that he was once again in warmth. As he lay there, flat on his back, trying to put together the pieces of his body and the pieces of his life, he remembered Shelby. Eppie. Eppie. Eppie. For a moment, he wanted to surrender to despair, to dwell upon how unfair all of this was, but whoever claimed life was fair in the first place. Certainly not Calhoun. Certainly not his father, the man from whom he'd learned so much. The man who had died, broken in body, but not in spirit, by soldiers representing an oppressive race whom the young Calhoun had eventually driven off his world. If he were here right now, Calhoun realized he'd be telling his son to stop lying about and dwelling upon his unfair lot in life. He was still alive, after all, and that was all that was important. Get up. Your wife needs you. On your feet, damn you, if you be a man. Why was he thinking about his father? The air of his surroundings was warm in his chest as he drew in great lungs full of it. Slowly, he sat up. He opened his eyes and immediately squinted against the brightness of the sun, and there was a few feet away from him on the parched ground. She'd probably never looked quite as awful in her entire life, and she'd never looked quite as good to Calhoun as she did at that moment. Hey, Mac. Calhoun wasn't looking at her. He was looking through her, around her, astoundingly all the pain, all the hurt, all the stress that his body had been through, was instantly forgotten. His legs were strong and firm again, blood pumping through them as if they were the legs of a 20-year-old. It only made sense, Calhoun realized. She had not, after all, been conscious when they went through the gateway. The last thing she had known was that they were upon a nameless ice world with death imminent. Shelby staggered to her feet. Mac, where are we? Well, seems familiar, but I'm not sure. You've been here, but you haven't been here. Neither have I. Calhoun studied the castle-like structures that dotted the horizon. The towers were tall, powerfully built. They had been carved right out of the cliffs of solid rock. Calhoun had looked upon similar structures in his youth, called Keeps, but they had always been silent and empty. A mute testimony to more ancient times when such fortresses provided great measures of security, along the bottom ridge of the fortress, was an array of tents. Mac, where are we? Xanax. He couldn't quite believe it until he actually said it. She shook her head in bewilderment. Your homeworld? Xanax? He nodded. Yeah, I think so. Yes. Mac, how the hell did we get to Xanax? A gateway. There was a huge one on the ice world. Much bigger than either of those transportable devices that the aliens had. It was activated, and I took us through there to here. He was so focused on his environment that he started slightly when Shelby stepped right in front of him. Mac, there's more going on here than that. It's as if you're in full battle mode like you're detecting an immediate threat. What's going on? I have a right to know, a right to be as prepared as you. He drew in a deep breath of air to confirm that which he'd already surmised. There's been fighting. I can smell it. There's blood in the air. Blood and death. Mac, really? And what does that smell like? Smells like chicken. What do you think it smells like? I don't know, Mac. I never noticed blood having a particular scent, and death is more concept to me than something definable by one's nose. He took a step toward her, looking down at her, and he felt a looming darkness behind his eyes. That epi is because you've never been up to your elbows in it. Screw you, Calhoun. Maybe I wasn't a teenage warlord hacking my way through corpse to stack five feet high, but I had a starship and crew dying around me when I fought the Borg. So don't tell me what I know and don't know, alright? Fair enough. But come on. Where? He pointed to the fortress in the distance. There. The Keep. They started walking. Somewhere along the way, Calhoun reached over and took Shelby's hand. It felt warm and comforting, and not only that, but he couldn't believe how quickly and thoroughly he'd recovered from near death. Even more remarkable was Shelby's recovery. They crossed the plane, approaching the mountainous area where the Keep was ensconced. Little clouds of dust were kicked up under their feet. He abruptly turned to her, the sun setting. She blinked. So, sons do that, at least once a day as I recall. But Calhoun shook his head, racking his brain, trying to remember. There's more to it though. I remember the sun starting to set. I think I didn't see it through though. I don't know why I'd get where it would drop us on Zenix. I don't know why I'm feeling so completely recovered in such a short period of time. But what I do know is that together we can handle just about anything. A sudden explosion froze Shelby and Calhoun in their tracks, and they looked ahead to the Keep. One of the lower sections erupted in flame. Another section of the Keep exploded, and people fell off the parapets. Calhoun was pinwilling as if they were hoping they could grab handholds from the very air. Calhoun yanked on Shelby's hand. Come on. She stayed where she was, looking at him incredulously. You want to head towards that? You're crazy. We're not budging. Calhoun heard it, smelled it before he actually saw it. A giant, flaming mass of burning slag, descending from overhead. A misfire from a catapult that was falling well short of its target, namely the Keep. It was, however, descending right toward the two Starfleet officers. Even as Calhoun pulled Shelby with him to try and get clear of it, he knew in his heart it was too late. The slag crushed their bodies and obliterated them. And so died Mackenzie Calhoun and Elizabeth Shelby, without ever having a chance to see the sun set. Together we can handle just about anything. A sudden explosion froze Shelby and Calhoun in their tracks, and they looked ahead to the Keep. One of the lower sections erupted in flame. Another section of the Keep exploded, and people fell off the parapets, arms pinwheeling as if they were hoping they could grab hand holds from the very air. Calhoun yanked on Shelby's hand. Come on. She stayed where she was, looking at him incredulously. You want to head towards that? You're crazy. We're not budging. But Calhoun hauled her forward. She was knocked off her feet by the impact of some sort of flaming massive. She had no idea what. All she did know was that it had crashed to the ground right where they had been standing. Mack, Mack, that was a close call. I was thinking the same thing, Eppy. Come on. They pounded across the plains toward the battle. Mack, why we running toward the site of the battle? Because it's better than being out in the open, and the Keep is returning fire. See? He was right. From the upper reaches a catapult-like device had appeared, and they were dispatching giant flaming wads of whatever at their still unseen aggressors. There ran toward the Keep, and although a couple of the flaming masses of whatever the hell they were landed near them, nothing came as close as that earlier one had. They were drawing within close range of the defenders in the upper reaches of the Keep, and the defenders were pointing at them now. For an instant Shelby was extremely concerned. What if these people took Calhoun to be an enemy and opened fire on him? And Calhoun was slowing down, looking at the defenders in wonderment. It can't be. Mack and Shelby spun just in time to see a horde of zenexions pouring over a ridge, charging full bore toward the Keep. Shelby remembered that Calhoun had once told her throughout the course of his world, there had never been any sort of civil war amongst his people. But what else could one possibly call this? Mack! Mack, we've got to get out of here! But even as she said it, she realized there was nowhere to go. The two sides were converging, with Shelby and Calhoun right in the middle, and there was no escape. Calhoun charged the men coming in behind them. Calhoun grabbed the head of one man with both hands, twisted once, and snacked his neck. Calhoun screamed at her. Get behind me! It was nothing short of butchery as Calhoun hacked and slashed like a bladed windmill. At the last second, she saw that someone had worked their way behind Calhoun and was coming at them. Suddenly the tip of a blade brushed against her back, causing her to jump away. That was when she realized, with a deep horror, that the blade had actually come right through Calhoun's body, driven through from the other side. She whirled just as Calhoun fell against her, coughing up blood. She sank to her knees, cradling him. She felt a pinch at her back, a pain, and suddenly she saw a blade protruding from between her breasts. Just missed the heart. That was lucky, she thought. Amazingly loosing even as her upper body jerked when the blade was yank clear, Calhoun finally managed to get out the strangest words. You're all dead. How can you be here when you're all dead? And that was certainly enough to confuse the hell out of her. Then the crowd of warriors seemed to separate, making way for someone. He was a burly man with a strong chin evident even though he had a beard and wild black hair tinged with gray. Shelby's chest was on fire. You, you murdering bastards. Why? The burly man pointed a sword at Calhoun. He knows why, don't you, son? Calhoun managed to nod, but Shelby didn't understand at all. All she knew at that moment was that her one wish was not to die in ignorance. Calhoun's father spoke to her. Welcome to Cazahera. And Shelby didn't get her wish. The last thing she saw just before she died was the sun setting. It was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen. And she hoped that Calhoun at least had a chance to see it as well. Calhoun awoke in a tent a sunlight on his face. The tent flaps had been pushed aside and his father's frame filled the door. Calhoun stood slowly, unsteady on his legs. Father? Grazie of Calhoun, father of Mahak-Endze of Calhoun, sized up his son. It did not seem to be especially approving of what he saw. He squeezed Calhoun's biceps and shook his head. By this age, your muscles should be hard as rock by now. Too busy surrounding yourself with weapons and security men to stay as fit as you should be. Well, what do you have to say for yourself? I...I'm sorry, sir. Grazie's face broke in a wide smile. Well, it will have to do then. You did last long enough to see a sunset. And that as you know, entitles you to an eternity of sunrises. Suddenly, overwhelmed by emotion, Calhoun took a step toward Grazie, his arms wide. But immediately his father retreated, his face darkening. Are you insane? About to embrace me? Me? Has this federation of yours made you softer than I thought? No, sir. Good, because this is cause of her, my son. Such delicate emotions are inappropriate here. For that matter, I'm concerned about the female you came with. Shelly? If that is her name, I. The simple fact is that she may not fit in here, Mahak-Endze. She may not fit in here at all. Immediately Calhoun pushed past his father into the sun and skidded to a halt. Elizabeth Shelby was lying flat. Her arms and legs flopped about like a stringless puppet. There was a sword lying near her, having just slipped out of her lifeless hand. Standing over, it was a burly, masterate arms, gripping a sword, still dripping with blood. He turned to Calhoun. Slow learner, but she'll get the hang of it. Calhoun did not hesitate. He simply picked up her fallen sword, turned it around, and ran himself through with it. This is Kazahara, my son. Such delicate emotions are inappropriate here. For that matter, I'm concerned about the female you came with. Shelby? If that is her name, I. The simple fact is that she may not fit in here, Mahak-Endze. She may not fit in here at all. Calhoun suddenly knew, beyond any question, as sure as he had ever known anything, that Shelby was in mortal danger. He dashed outside and skidded to a halt. Shelby was standing there with a bloody sword clenched in her hands and a look of pure fury on her face. Facing her was the masterate arms, minus one of those arms. Calhoun's father looked at her, prudently. Then again, son, perhaps you'll fit right in? Shelby gasped, unsure of what to say or do, at which point Calhoun walked her quickly and pulled her away. Shelby's face was turning the color of paste. Mack, Mack, what's happening? What's- we're in Kazahara. She whirled and gripped him by the shoulders. Where the hell is Kazahara? He let out a slow breath and tried to figure out the best way to explain what was essentially inexplicable. Does the name Valhalla mean anything to you? She frowned, racking her brain. It's, um, that place, Norse mythology, where the warrior women lived, the- the Valkyries, and they'd come and bring fallen warriors to this place, this hall of dead heroes, and that was Valhalla. She looked around at the foreboding landscape, cutting him off before he could continue. Are you telling me we're in the Zenexian version of Valhalla? More or less, yes. The big guy who came out of the tent I was in. That's my father. She was silent for a moment when he told her that. Mack, I know losing your father at a young age was traumatic for you, but- but what? Who are you implying? That I'm imagining it? Eppie. Kazahara is where Zenexian heroes cut down in battle go to die. When you first arrive, you have to survive to see your first sunset. If you don't, you keep going back to the point where you left off, and once you've done that, you awaken every morning to a day of warfare and battle, and it doesn't matter if you get hurt or if you die, because come the sunset the day ends and the next morning you wake up and it's a new day. She smiled in a way that looked to Calhoun like it was just shy of patronizing. I see, Mack, and why, just out of curiosity, did all those men attack you? I mean, you were their warlord once upon a time, right? Calhoun scratched his chin. Taking a guess, they're probably carrying grudges. I mean, yes, I led Zenex to freedom ultimately, but I also let a lot of them to their deaths. She shook her head with amusement. Mack, it's ridiculous. We can't be someplace that's not real. And what's next, Mack? Maybe we'll find our way back to the gateway, jump through and find ourselves in heaven, face to face with God. Is that what this is about, Eppie? You have trouble believing in higher powers, and as a consequence, all this is too much for you to cope with. I cope with being your wife, Calhoun. That's enough coping for one lifetime. He stepped in close to her. How about an eternity of lifetimes, Eppie? Because that's what we've got here. And finally, he stomped away, incensed over Shelby's refusal to accept what he was telling her. He didn't notice the freshly dug ambush pit until it was a millisecond too late. As he plunged with the jagged sharpened stones rushing to meet him, he cursed Eppie with his dying breath and wondered how many times he'd made that curse. How about an eternity of lifetimes, Eppie? Because that's what we've got here. And finally, he stomped away, incensed over Shelby's refusal to accept what he was telling her. At that moment, Shelby felt a sudden warning in her head. It was enough to make her cry out as if his life depended on it. Mac! He stopped, but remained with his back to her. She walked quickly to him. What's going on here, Mac? In the distance, she saw the Zinexians going through training maneuvers. For all she knew, another wave of opponents would come charging him across the way at any time. And why not? That's what it was all about, after all, wasn't it? Endless strife, endless battle. Mac, I think you want to stay. I think it's damn attractive to you. No rules, because they don't matter. There's nothing that says the gateways can actually take us to otherworldly spheres. We're trapped in some sort of other dimensional limbo, perhaps. It's a spatial equivalent of a holodeck. Calhoun began getting really angry at her. Why is it so damned impossible for you to believe? I've been hearing stories of Kazahira, believed in it, since as early as I can remember. And I heard about the Hundred Acre Woods, Mac, but I'm not going in search of Winnie the Pooh. This, all of this, it's not real. We have to leave. He looked at her defiantly. If this is being formed by our mutual delusion, why is it only someplace that I am familiar with? Because, Mac, I believe in you, more than I believe in anything in this world, or the next. Think about where we just came from, how we got here. He was looking at her blankly, and she thought, oh my god, he really doesn't remember. He's got amnesia or something. Mac, two races, the Aerons and the Marcanians, who were engaged in a centuries-long battle, battling over their own version of Paradise, a planet called Cinque, and their Battle of Mutual extermination was aided by two aliens, each with their own gateway devices. We all wound up on Cinque, only to discover the planet was a desolate wasteland, thanks to generations of fighting that had gone on previously. Calhoun nodded briskly and continued for her. Yes, and then both aliens turned on their gateways and it created some sort of force whirlpool that sucked us into the ice planet, where the gigantic gateway was waiting for us. And why are you telling me all this when I already know it? She stepped away from him and looked around at the vast plain instead. Rocks and craggy areas nearby them, and the endless vista of... of nothingness. Maybe you're right, Mac. Maybe I'm afraid to believe in the reality of this place, because then it implies that other things, things I'm not comfortable with, might also be real. He looked at it with confusion. Why not comfortable? Because Mac, things like heaven or angels or God, these are things that are, by definition, unknowable. I don't accept the concept of unknowable. If mankind can't discover it, learn from it. What's the point of it? To her surprise, he laughed gently, and she took his hands in hers. Mac, before, I was trying to make you realize that endless fighting is a useless way to spend one's life. It doesn't matter whether you're Marcanian or Zinexian. Do you get what I'm saying? Because whether you get it or not, I'm leaving. Leaving? Even if we manage to retrace our steps, all the gateway we'll do is put us right back out onto the ice world. Maybe we'll be rescued. Not a lot of time to be rescued in EPI. More likely we'll die. She shrugged. Well, then, maybe I'll get to explore the whole heaven thing after all. She stood on her toes, kissed him lightly on the cheek, and turned and started to walk away. He called out to her. EPI, you're asking me to give up everything I believe in, in order to be with you. And if we go back and we die together, I'd likely wind up back here, and you would be...wherever. She stopped, turned, and smiled. I guess that's what till death through his part is all about, isn't it, Mac? Calhoun let out a heavy sigh, and began walking toward her. Till death through his part, EPI. And with a cry of joy that was slightly choked, Shelby ran to him and threw herself into his arms. But from behind them came the gruff voice of Mac's father. Is this what you've come to then? They turned, and Groazzi was standing there. The mustache under his nose, bristling, his purple eyes, dark and furious as the sea. His hand was twitching near the great sword that hung from his hip. He spoke angrily to his son. A chance to be with me, to be with your own kind, and you throw it all away to run off with her. You would place love above the glory of battle. Have you no priorities? I have mine, Father, and you have yours. His father turned angrily away. You're no son of mine. No son of yours? Everything I did on Zenyx, I did in your memory. She's santered bastard, I cut down with my sword. I did so avenging your death. I freed a planet on your behalf, and if that isn't good enough to earn your approval in the afterlife, then to hell with you. Groazzi froze for a long moment, and then turned without another word, and strode away. Shelby placed a featherlight hand on his arm. Mac, are you okay? I'm fine. Let's get out of here. They moved quickly across the plains. No words exchanged between them. Calhoun led the way, scanning the ground. I'm reasonably certain that if we follow this path, Shelby interrupted, or we could just head for the gateway. She pointed ahead of them, and there, sure enough, was a glowing in the air. It was a distance away, but it was unmistakable. The gateway. Suddenly, the ground below them began to rumble. They looked behind themselves to see a horde of angry warriors coming after them, shouting Calhoun's name. And the gateway. The gateway was fading, about to cycle shut. They'd be trapped in Kazahira forever. They tried to run, but within moments, they were cut to pieces, and the ground ran red with their blood. And the gateway. The gateway was fading, about to cycle shut. They'd be trapped in Kazahira forever. They tried to run, but within moments, they were cut to pieces, and the ground ran red with their blood. And the gateway. The gateway was fading, about to cycle shut. They'd be trapped in Kazahira forever. They tried to run, but within moments, they were surrounded. Unstoppable, Grazi cut a path to Calhoun and Shelby, and the others fell back, confused and angry. Calhoun looked up at the dark face of his father. I thought you said I wasn't a son of yours. Yes, well, I realized that sometimes you're more your mother's son, and I loved her dearly. But she was no warrior. I miss her terribly. As much as I'll miss you. Go, damn you. He shoved Calhoun as hard as he could. Shelby caught him, and they ran. Grazi was everywhere, as was his sword, and no man passed as Calhoun and Shelby sprinted the remaining distance. Calhoun gripped Shelby's hand as tightly as he could, and together, they leaped through the gateway. Calhoun heard his father cry out. This has been a good day. And the sunset on Kazahira. One moment they were bathed and warmth, and the next, the wind and ice, was hammering them with a force of a thousand males. Calhoun went down, Shelby tumbling on top of him. He clutched her to him, and when he looked at her, his heart sank in dismay. While in Kazahira he had healed, but here, back in this marvelous real world to which she'd been so anxious to return, she was as banged up and bruised as before. After they'd gone through the gateway, what kind of miracle was it when all it did was spare them a quick death in exchange for a slower and more agonizing one? Then he looked at Shelby, who was gazing up at him, unable to move, barely able to speak, and he understood. It was a miracle because it was giving them a few last moments together, and any time that they were together was miraculous. They kissed passionately, holding each other close, icing over. The gateway saw it behind them. And then in his near-death delirium, Calhoun wondered whether Valkyries were descending from Valhalla. He managed to barely roll over, and saw with distant astonishment that a long-range shuttle craft was approaching. Before he passed out, Calhoun wondered, what do Valkyries need with a shuttle craft? When Shelby opened her eyes, she saw Calhoun smiling down at her, felt the distinctly unglacial warmth around her, and for just a moment she thought, you basted, you brought us back through the gateway, we're back in your idea of paradise. Here we go again. And then she heard a familiar voice, brisk with efficiency. Step aside please, Captain. Calhoun did so, and then Dr. Sellar was standing over her, guiding a medical tricoder along her, and nodding approvingly. Full circulation has been restored. Shelby immediately sat up. An instant later, the world spun around her and she flopped back. The only thing that prevented her from cracking her head badly was Calhoun's arm, catching her as she fell. It was at that point that Shelby realized they were in a shuttle craft. She looked up at Calhoun in confusion, her face a question. Easily reading her mind, Calhoun took her hand. Back on Cinque, our respective science officers managed to recreate the energy field that hauled us through to the ice world. Once they did that, they sent a shuttle craft through after us. Shelby looked concerned. But how will we get back from here, back through the energy field? Calhoun smiled. No need to worry. We're only three days out of the Lonian space. Dr. Sellar nodded. You were very fortunate. And with that the Vulcan headed toward the front of the craft, leaving Shelby and Calhoun alone in the rear section. Shelby squeezed Calhoun's hand tightly. Any regrets, Mac? He smiled. I'll tell you after I'm dead. And for a moment, just a brief moment, she thought that she saw pain and a longing for something he now knew he could never have or never be happy with. But then, just like that, it was gone.
description: In this episode of Star Trek New Frontier, Captain Mackenzie Calhoun and his wife, Elizabeth Shelby, find themselves transported to a planet of ice after battling an ancient Iconian gateway device with two mysterious aliens from the Aerons and Marcanians. As they try to survive on the frozen world, Calhoun recalls their encounter with Ibose, the leader of the Marcanians who survived falling into a crevasse but not his wife Elizabeth Shelby. The pair must navigate through treacherous terrain while battling an ongoing blood feud between two alien races and the remnants of their previous war.
