transcript: Simon and Schuster Audio presents Star Trek New Frontier Excalibur Restoration by Peter David Read by Joe Martin She knew he was coming before she even saw him. It wasn't unusual for her to feel that he was approaching. Truth be known, most days she would get a cold feeling in the base of her spine. At those times, wherever she was, whether it be doing chores in her rundown of bode or standing on the cracked and arid plane that constituted what she laughingly referred to as her property, she would stop what she was doing and wait to see if some sign of him appeared on the horizon. Most times, he did not. On such occasions, the feeling would naturally pass and she would return to whatever it was she had been doing. In short order, she would forget that she had felt any sense of dread at all. This time, however, when she did see him making his approach, naturally all those false alarms were forgotten. Instead, all Rila could think was, I knew it. I can always tell when he's coming. A gentle breeze was wafting across the plane, which was an unusual enough event in and of itself. She straightened the strands of green hair that were blowing in her face and turned back to the house. It was not much more than a hut, although it was built of sturdy enough materials that managed to keep the interior remarkably cool despite the crushing heat. Just to provide a bit of style, she had even constructed a small porch in the front of the hut. She now sat on the edge of the porch, arranging her hands neatly in her lap and staring out of the emptiness of her land. She had a sense of which direction he was going to come from and she stared off that way in contemplation. Every so often, she would glance down at her hands, turning them over and studying them as if she was looking at someone else's hands. There were leathery and weather-beaten. And she had been a little girl. Her skin had been so fair, so pale. But now it was such dark brown that it seemed as if the sun had baked her as thoroughly as it had the land around her. It was amazing, though, that the vegetation, her crops, was still fighting resiliently for life. They poked up through the cracks, green and brown cacti-like plants. They were going to need water, though, and very soon. It wasn't just her crops, either. She had been hearing as much from other homesteaders as well. They spoke to her, as always, with that telltale look of annoyance and resentment, even as they talked wistfully of the rain that was needed in order to salvage their crops. She looked to the sky, trying to feel the moisture in the air in her bones. Nothing was forthcoming. But she could have sworn that the intensity of the heat was growing, rolling in waves off the land. Not for the first time she felt a sense of vague despair. She didn't simply reside on the world of Yacaba. She fought it. She struggled with it every single day. Although she continued to sit on the porch, she still shielded her eyes with one leathery hand while studying the horizon line. Ironically, she knew what she was going to see before she actually saw it. Sure enough, there he was. To Pinsa. To Pinsa's skin was not a golden bronze color due to the sun. Instead, much of the paleness that was typical for those of the Yacaba race was still present. Not unusual, then, that to Pinsa was clad appropriately with a wide-brimmed hat and long coat that flapped in the steady breeze as he sped toward Rila's hut. He was clutching onto the rigging of his customized sail skipper, guiding it with an expert hand. Rila had to give him that much when he came to sail skippers in similar desert transportation to Pinsa with second to none. A smaller form was clutching onto the main mast of the sail skipper. Moak. She had been absolutely positive that her son had been indoors napping, but it was unquestionably Moak clutching onto the sail skipper. Moak. Look, Moa. For a moment, Rila was convinced that the sail skipper was going to crash into the side of the house, and then to Pinsa whipped it around. Moak jumped off the sail skipper and ran excitedly to his mother. You write it, Moa. Master Dependsa said he would take you. Dependsa smiled. Titles are never necessary among friends, Moak. A simple to Pinsa will do. Yet his gaze was not upon the son, but upon the mother. Rila returned his gaze. Quite expertly guided, Master Dependsa. However, considering I was under the impression that my son was indoors, I am most curious as to what he was doing sailing around the desert with you. Dependsa bowed deeply. You're asking the wrong person, Rila. I happened upon young Master Moak, wandering about on his own. Rila shifted her gaze to her son. Moak? What were you doing out? It's the hottest part of the day. Moak shrugged. Rila took him firmly by the shoulders. Why were you out? Moak took a deep breath. Looking for Dad, I didn't find him, did I? Because I thought maybe Master Dependsa... No, Master Dependsa is not Daddy. Are you sure, Ma? Terela surprised Dependsa stepped in. If I was your father, Moak, I would never have left. Much Terela's relief, the response seemed to satisfy the boy. Rila ruffled the hair on his head. Go in now. You're overheated. As Moak darted inside, Dependsas smiled. My home is considerably cooler. Yes, I am well aware of that, Master. Dependsa didn't seem to be showing any intention of departing. She caught one eyebrow in curiosity. Something else, Master? The child should be entitled to know who his father is. Does he? Her temper flared. That is between Moak and me. And me, Rila. The people of Nairun are likewise curious. People fear that which they do not know. Maester, what do you want of me? You know what I want, Rila. You provide a service. A service for which you charge nothing. That is foolishness. Rila was only half listening to him now. Instead, she was starting to detect the first bits of moisture. She looked her dry lips and looked to the skies, reaching out, gathering strength, as Dependsa continued speaking. Rila, the average person in Nairun does not understand your altruism. Rila nodded. But you, Maester, are not an average person. You are the most successful businessman in Nairun province, possibly in all Yakaba. So you would be far more likely to understand it. Yes? Oh, yes, but that does not mean that I endorse it. When you treat people with such compassion, they are reminded of their own shortcomings. Now, commerce, trade, self-benefit, these are the things which they can appreciate. If you charge them, they would come to love you. She took a deep breath to steady herself. Small dust devils were wearing across the plane. Dependsa didn't seem to be paying attention. Rila, it saddens me to see you so stubborn. I can provide you with a better home, better opportunities for yourself, for moke. You have no reason not to take advantage of that which I'm offering you. No reason except that I do not trust you and therefore would not join you in business. And I do not love you and therefore would not join you in bed. Startled, Dependsa noticed the darkening of the skies for the first time. The wind was coming up even more fiercely than before. Sudden gusts caught up the sails of his vehicle. He bolted for it as large droplets of water began to fall from the sky. The sail vessel was not designed to handle easily in such fearsome winds. All Dependsa could do at that point was hang on for the ride. And Rila for the first time in quite a while felt the urge to laugh without question or restraint. The rain came down even harder and still she remained outside allowing it to soak her through. Moke, moke bolted off the edge of the porch, ran to her clasping her hands at his small ones and they danced with one another in delirious circles of joy. In the city of Nairin, the rain was coming down just as fiercely and Maestra's co-feel was not impressed. She watched through her window with disgust. People were running about as quickly as they could, turning and somersaulting. Many had already stripped down to their undergarments and were dancing about like mindless heathens. In the meantime, the water collectors were doing their job. All of them fed into the underground reservoir from which the residents of Nairin were doing their job. The reservoir had, in recent years, dropped lower and lower. But then had come Rila and everything had been different. Maestra's co-feel bolted out the front door and into the street. Her feet sunk part way into the mud. The revelers did not see her at first, but then someone noticed them very quickly. The rain had been very quiet. The rain had been very quiet. The revelers did not see her at first, but then someone noticed them very quickly, who would spread. Maestra's co-feel was not one to mindlessly join in the celebrations of others. The Maestra's was said to be older than dirt, and considering the amount of dirt they had in Nairin, that was pretty damned old. Look at yourselves, gallivanting around like imbeciles. Prayster Milos, an older gentleman and the town's political leader, stepped forward. Maestra's celebration is good for the soul, is it not? Not when the celebration stems from obvious efforts to corrupt morality, and we all know of the immorality that poisons the woman known as Rila. You should be ashamed. I am a Maestra's by birthright, by training, by tradition. Am I to stand by and watch you make fools of yourselves in celebration of a woman who is not entitled to such worship? Her powers can only come from darkness. A voice came from the crowd. How do we know? The Maestra's could scarcely believe the question, since the answer was so obvious. How do we know her powers come from darkness? Isn't it obvious? We are all of us in this town, co-curfuring good people. If beings such as us were meant to have such powers, why wouldn't right-thinking, upstanding, morally straight people be giving them? Why not me, or the Prayster, with whom I may have my share of disagreements, but still seems to me a good and right-thinking man when all is said and done? Milos bowed deeply. I praise indeed Maestra's. Water dripped off the top of his head when he bowed, and self-consciously he brushed it away as she continued. Isn't it obvious that the very fact that she has this ability, and we do not, means that it is inherently evil? Do not let yourselves be caught up in her obvious chicanery. I know how difficult it is. I know how tempting it is to embrace the convenient. My lips know the same thirst, my throat the same part sensation as your own. If we suffer, we suffer together, but we should not allow the temptations of one woman sway us into thinking even for a moment that Kolkar above would support such abominations. And have you not considered the fact that since Rila came here, the rainfall has been even less than usual? Who was to say that she herself is not causing the extreme conditions? Her eyes swept the crowd. If she is capable of bringing us rain, why is it so difficult to believe that she can also deprive us of it? Go to your homes, get cleaned up, go about your business. The people of Nairen headed for their homes. The Maestris did not move, but instead simply stood there and watched them go. She knew them. She knew them all too well. They would make noises of repentance and claim that they felt badly for what had transpired. But the truth was that they were willing to tolerate Rila, and the Maestris knew that the time would come when she would have to do something about it. And when she did, that would definitely be the last anyone heard of the weather witch who called herself Rila. Captain Elizabeth Paula Shelby, newly installed commander of the Exeter, looked up at the woman seated across the desk from her. Commander Alexandra Garbick had come extremely, highly recommended. Slim, bordering on diminutive, she nevertheless possessed an air of quiet authority. Garbick leaned forward. Captain Shelby, what was he really like? Mackenzie Calhoun. Shelby had been studying Garbick's file on the computer screen, but now she turned and looked squarely at the woman she was interviewing. Tell me, Commander Garbick, do you think my views on Mackenzie Calhoun are remotely relevant to your interview? Look at it this way, Captain. If I am indeed made your first officer as I am hoping will be the case, I wish to learn more about Captain Calhoun, and in particular, the circumstances involving the destruction of the Excalibur. I've read the transcripts of the hearings, the discussions, but there seem to be things missing. If something occurred that was preventable, I want to know how to prevent it so that my ship and crew does not fall victim to the same fate. Shelby nodded. Are you familiar with the file known as the Double Helix Incident? Of course, Captain. A techno-virus designed to essentially collapse every computer base in the entire Federation, sending it spiraling into chaos. Shelby allowed a small smile. A very decorative way of putting it, Commander. The Excalibur, as it so happens, was squarely in the middle of it. Unfortunately, we didn't realize that there was a secondary virus also implanted within the ship's computer. The virus created a sort of internal null field around itself, so any attempts to spot it resulted in those attempts reflecting back upon themselves. Once the virus had, over time, thoroughly ingrained itself into every aspect of the Excalibur's system, it triggered a self-destruct sequence, setting the warp core to overload. Garbek's eyes widened. It was obvious that Garbek was wondering how Shelby could have survived. Then Garbek's eyebrows puckered slightly in thought. The life pods. But let me guess. The auto-eject sequences on the life pods were also shut down, which would have meant that the only way to do it would be to employ the extreme option of individual manual override on each of the pods. Shelby nodded. Right. We started loading crewmen into the life pods and ejecting them as fast as we could. The problem is, the manual ejection of the life pods has to be done from within the ship itself at the life pod stations. In any event, the crew acted smoothly together, helping each other into the pods, ejecting them from the ship to a safe distance. Eventually, though, it came down to Captain Calhoun and I. Naturally, he... Alexander Garbek didn't say anything at first. I'm sorry for your loss, Captain Shelby. However, the standard period of time between the realization of a warp core breach and the subsequent detonation of the ship is, at most, five minutes, eleven seconds. Five minutes to get the crew, the entire crew, into life pods? To eject them? Shelby shrugged. You would be amazed, Commander, how fear of imminent death can lend wings to one's feet. Now then, enough of me, let's talk about you. Fast track for promotion, double major death at the academy in both science and tactics. You're too perfect. What's wrong with you, Garbek? Nothing, Captain. It's a curse I've learned to live with it. She'll be laughed. She found herself liking Garbek, who then told her, a Captain, it's very simple. I come from a long line of Starfleet officers. That is my true home and that's where I'm supposed to be. I know every regulation backwards and forward. I know the case history of every major first encounter situation that every Starfleet Captain has ever had. She'll be nodded. I've prided myself on that for a very long time, Commander. Familiarity with rules, regulations. Garbek looked questioningly at Shelby. But Captain Calhoun didn't. Well, I have no wish to speak ill of the dead. No need to speak ill, Commander, if what you're saying is the truth. Captain Calhoun had only passing interest in regs, as if he took pride in finding ways around them. Shelby was surprised to herself speak in a tone of such gentle amusement. When Calhoun had been around and she had served under him, she'd found his attitude to be nothing less than relentlessly aggravating. If I may ask, Captain, considering your record of adherence to regs and the fact that your personal relationship with Mackenzie Calhoun ended badly, why did he make me his number one? I think it came down to the concept that he needed someone whom he could tolerate and who could in turn tolerate him. So, tell you what, Garbek. Congratulations. Welcome aboard the Exeter as First Officer. That night, Shelby lay on her bed and told herself, I'm not going to do it tonight. And yet, no matter how many times she thought about it, she kept wondering, what if there had been something she'd overlooked? What if there had been a way to save the ship, to save him? All the life paths were launched but two. One for the second in command, one for the Captain. Except someone needed to stay behind and provide the manual launch. I knew he was never going to allow it. Mack, I'm not leaving. Now, Eppie, that's an order. The Captain goes down with his ship. There's no up or down in Space, Mack. And suddenly, just like that, he was kissing me. He lifted me up in his arms, and the son of a bitch threw me into the space pod. As I landed, he lobbed something gently in my direction. It clattered on the floor and I looked down and realized that it was his shortsword. He'd been carrying it with him the entire time. It represented a direct link to his youth on Zenix. And he wasn't about to let it go up or down with the ship. It was as if it was the only tangible aspect of him that was of any importance. And if it managed to outlast him, then in some way, he would live on. The last view I had of him just before the door closed was Mack's mouthing words to me. The impact of a shockwave from the Excalibur's warp core explosion sent my pod tumbling end over end. At that moment, though, I didn't care whether I survived. But floating there in the escape pod, waiting for the rescue, I came to a self-realization. I loved him. Not much time passed, and Starfleet sent a ship to retrieve us from the depths of space. And who should it be but naturally, the Enterprise? When I briefed Captain Picard on what had happened, I could tell that he was upset. And why shouldn't he have been? After all, he was the one who first discovered a young warrior named Ma'aka Enzi of Khaldhoon and convinced him that he had a place in Starfleet. I mentioned to Picard that Mack had mouled something to me just before the door closed. Picard asked me about it. I told him, Mack said to me, I love you. Picard nevertheless smiled slightly at that. Indeed, that's typical for Mack, isn't it? Master of the well-timed Bon Maugh. I nodded. I suppose he didn't want to risk hearing my not saying it back. Picard considered that a moment. Or else Commander Shelby, who wanted to give himself incentive to come back and hear you say it. Shelby reached under her bunk and pulled out the shortsword that was the last remaining artifact, aside from her heart, that marked the passage through the world of one Khaldhoon. Damn you. It wasn't clear, even to herself, who she was cursing. Her self, or the deceased captain known as Mackenzie Khaldhoon. Moak was feeling rather proud of himself. He had managed to slip out of the house yet again, without his mother noticing, and he was feeling utterly at ease in the infernally dry and overheated afternoon. A few days ago, he'd been watching his mother speaking with the sail-skeeper man, Depenza. He seemed nice enough, but Moak's mother didn't seem to like him. Was Depenza his father? Moak didn't think so. Moak had reoccurring dreams about having a father. In those dreams, his dad was always tall and straight and proud, and he had eyes like storms and a smile as gleaming as the morning's son. There was an oasis nearby, although from an actual water point of view, it wasn't much of an oasis. Most of the plant life was brown and unappealing. However, there were a few rock formations that Moak enjoyed climbing, so it was one of his favorite places to go. One of his secret places, which he never even told his mother about because a boy is entitled to keep some things private. He got to the oasis end, even as he started to clamor up one of the rock formations, he wondered why it was that people always seemed to be muttering about his mother and him. What had they ever done to anybody? Why, his mom made water for them, or at least she encouraged it to rain and the clouds seemed to listen for the most part, although sometimes she was luckier than other times. The problem was that she usually could only make it rain for a short while, and the effort cost her mightily. She would take long naps, although she showed an almost supernatural ability to rouse herself to wakefulness anytime that Moak made the slightest attempt to depart the domicile. But this most recent endeavor appeared to have taken more out of her than usual, perhaps because there had been so little raw weather material to work with. Because she had been sleeping so soundly, Moak had been able to follow his own instincts and set off on his own little adventure. He had toyed with the notion of going into town and asking people directly why they had a problem with his mom and him. Suddenly a firm hand had grabbed him by the back of his shirt. Moak's feet pinwheeled in mid-air and then he was whirled around. He let out a choked sob and looked into a twisted and furious face. The man had a scar that ran down the right side of his face. His face was dark skinned, blistered, and red and bruised. Where am I? What planet is this? The man's question made no sense to Moak at all. The man was like no one else Moak had ever seen in this world. Was it possible? Dad? The man froze. His face right up against Moak's. Zion? You're alive? The man thought Moak was someone else. His son, presumably, who had apparently perished. Besides, who knew? Maybe the man was right. Maybe Moak really was his son. The only one who would know for sure was his mother. Let me take you home to mom. She'll want to see you. The man gaped at him. Your... your mother's here too? Am I dead? That's it, isn't it? I'm dead. Moak took the man's hand. You're not dead, you're just confused. Let me take you home. Do you have a subspace transmitter or beacon at home? Moak thought about the large illuminating lamp that his mother kept in one of the kitchen cupboards for emergencies. She referred to that as a beacon. Yeah, we do. Whatever men as there had been about the man was gone now. The man steadied himself by putting a hand on Moak's shoulder, and they started to move across the plains. It took a horrifically long time. The man would mutter things that Moak couldn't follow, stuff about the ship and blowing up and pods and epi. None of it made the least bit of sense. Moak wondered what his mother would say. For a little while at least Moak would fantasize what it would be like to be with his dad. And that was the greatest adventure of all. Moak brought the man to the small shed where they kept an assortment of their supplies, including the lukeb, a large hairy four-legged thing with rock-like skin and a large tusk that was handy for a rider to hold onto. Moak eased the man into the coolness of the shed. I'll get Mom. Moak shut the door behind him and raced toward his house. He bolted into the house, looked around frantically for some sign of his mother, and didn't see any. It was at that point that he hurt his mother's scream. Rila had been frantic with Worry, looking for Moak. She had started walking east but turned up nothing, and so she decided to head back the way she'd come. It was starting to get cooler, which meant that the lukeb would be far more willing to come out of its nice, cool shed and provide her with a means of locomotion. On her return she went straight to the shed and threw open the door. A man was lying on the floor. Slowly he sat up. His skin color, his hair, were both wrong. He had to be some sort of genetic freak capable of who knew what. There was a crazed look in his eyes, feral and ugly. She tried to gather her wits. Now, just, just stay where you are. Dan, Terry, slime, you killed my father! Suddenly he leaped right for her. For one crazed moment she thought he was going to rape her, and then when his hands clamped down on her throat she realized that he meant nothing less than to kill her. Dan, Terry, he kept raging about Dan, Terry, and she had no idea what in the world he could possibly be talking about. Moak was right there, shoving at the man, trying to get him off her. The crazy man swung his arm around, knocking Moak off his feet. Real his world started to grey out around her. The lukeb was suddenly heading away from the scene at a fairly brisk gallop, and attached to the creature's tusks was one end of a rope. The other end was secured around the man's ankle, and he was howling and furious the creature pulled him around. Moak ran to her, and his words were tumbling out so fast that Real had trouble understanding everything that he was saying. She could make out a couple of things like, I'm sorry, and the man wasn't so bad when he wasn't trying to kill you, Ma. That was when the lukeb trotted up to them. The man, clearly unconscious. His clothes were now shredded, his face and upper body bruised. Moak, we have to get the magister. The magister? But, Mom, he'll put him in jail. Real had pointed out her throat. He belongs in jail, Moak. If you hadn't thought so fast, tied him to the lukeb, I'd be dead by now. As soon as the man was tied up, Real had dragged him over into the shed, secured the door, and locked it for good measure. Then she and Moak mounted up on the lukeb and headed toward town as fast as they could. And as they did so, the man with the purple eyes and fearsome scar, dreamed of exploding ships. She'll be could scarcely believe it. She sat in her command chair and the Exeter, the steady flow of activity all around her, and she was reveling in it. And it was so quiet. It had seemed, back on the bridge of the Excalibur, that there was always someone chattering or going on about something that had nothing to do with anything. There would be Leffler reciting one of her many laws about something or other, or McHenry snoring, snoring at his post. But here, on the Exeter, it was so very, very, very quiet. The crew, handpicked by Shelby, went about its business with calm, certain deficiency. Everything her crew said or did directly related either to the current state of the Exeter, or updates on the ship's position while the powerful vessel continued en route to the planet, Marcus. At the Science Station, Lieutenant Commander Chris Tully turned to her from his post. A captain, atmosphere survey complete, Marcus's air is a bit thinner than Earth's standard, but should not present a problem. Garbeck turned in his seat to face Shelby. Will you be handling the away team yourself, Captain? I had intended to. Does that pose a problem for you, number one? Shelby had decided she liked that term. The car had referred to Riker in that way, and it had a good sound to it. No problem, Captain. This does not seem to have a good deal of potential for personal danger, so I don't see the harm. Marcus. Shelby was going to Marcus. It wasn't what she had been planning. Somehow, Shelby had just assumed that, with the loss of the Excalibur, she would be assigned back into Section 221G, formerly known as Thelonian Space. She had raised a mild protest with Admiral Jellica, who had told her that Starfleet was not going to reconfigure an assignment list just to accommodate a single officer. He had told her that they were likely going to be christening a new vessel as Excalibur that would probably go back into Thelonian Space. So far, during her first command on the Exeter, things had gone fairly smoothly, and Shelby was certainly hoping that the planet Marcus would fall into that same category. Marcus was a world on the outer edge of Sector 47B, and was now felt that the people of Marcus had advanced to a sufficient degree that they were ready to be given the opportunity to join the Federation. It was an exciting prospect for Shelby, being sent to handle the invitation personally. If her invitation got Marcus to join the United Federation of Plattents, who knew where the world might end up in terms of its involvement with and relation to other worlds, and their success would be in some small measure, Shelby's success. In the city of Nairin, Magister Ferrax had been in charge of enforcing the law for three years, nine months, and one day. For the most part, he found the residents' provincial, quick to anger, quick to judge, and slow to extend compassion. The only one he found particularly tolerable was that woman, Rila, the one who had a little place by the outskirts. Rila, the Rainmaker. She had brought rain cascading down in torrents for the benefit of the people, and in return, they had given her suspicion and scowls. He had once asked her why she did it. Rila, if you're packed up and left tomorrow, these folks wouldn't be the least bit sorry to see you gone. That's as it may be, Magister, but they would miss the water I bring them, so in that way they'd miss me. Since that time, he had made it his particular province to keep a special eye out for her, since she struck him as a special kind of woman. So when she had contacted Magister Ferrax about the strange man whom Moak had taken it upon himself to bring home, naturally, the Magister attended to it as quickly as humanly possible. In no time at all, he had written out to Rila's homestead and rustled up the mysterious stranger who was unconscious and tied up in her shed. Ferrax needed to take no more than a single look at the man to know that he was not, to put it mildly, from around there. His skin, his hair, everything was simply wrong. He did not dwell on it though, that was not his job. Nor did he worry too much about the fact that the man, at least that was what he appeared to be, was clearly ill, for that was also not his job. His job was to protect, and the best way to protect others from this newcomer was to make certain that he was put where he could do no harm to anyone. That of course meant jail, which was exactly where he put him. The newcomer made no protest, offered no resistance on the trip back into town. He simply lay slumped over the Magister's own lukeab, a larger, heartier version of the one who resided in Rila's shed, for the length of the journey. At most offering some muttered comments along the way that resulted more from matters flittering through his dreams, instead of anything having to do with the real world. Once he got the man back to the jailhouse, which was also where the Magister had his office, the Magister tossed him into a cell and slammed the door. From that point on, the Magister simply waited for the newcomer to die. He was not a Medman, and the Medman was not due back in the area for some weeks yet, so the newcomer at lay unattended and feverish, still tossing about in the narrow platform that served as a bed in the cell. After a short time, the Magister became accustomed to the moaning that arose from the cell. Unfortunately, Cusac, who was in the cell near to the newcomer, was having a bit more difficulty than the Magister when it came to ignoring him. Cusac made it quite clear to the Magister that he was not appreciating the new setup one bit. The Magister had put Cusac in jail when Cusac had been foolish enough to kill a man named Turkin over a game of cards while in the Magister's presence. Pharax had simply no choice but to arrest the stupid sod. Cusac's beefy hands were each wrapped around one of the bars on the cell door. How am I supposed to sleep, Magister? I shouldn't be here in the first place. When my brothers catch wind of this... When your brothers do, they'd be best advised to leave bad enough alone and not make it worse. Late one evening, not long after Pharax had incarcerated the newcomer, he was sitting in his office minding his own business when he heard a slamming against the cell door from inside. Pulling his place here from its holster, he rose and stepped through the door to the adjacent area where the cells were. There he saw the newcomer, his eyes wide and wild, clutching the door bars and looking around as if he was some sort of caged animal. The pods are all gone, crew is in them, all of them had to be done manually. Shuttle Bay, only hope? Cusac moaned from the celled next door. Dear, Gulker, shut him up, Magister. You shut up, Cusac. Pharax found what the newcomers sent extremely fascinating. He spoke to the sick man. You're in the shuttle bay. Are you leaving the ship? The newcomer shook his head fiercely. Trapped, bay doors are not responding. Make it work. Got to. Blow it open. The Scar faced man through himself against the jail door. Again and again. Shield's gone. Navigation out. Calm out. Barely holding it together. Force of explosion. Propelled. No idea where. No idea. Lost. Can't get my bearings. Planet ahead. Don't know it. Trying to hold it together. Fighting to get retros online. Slow it down. I'll burn up. Burn up if I don't slow down. Got it. Like flying a brick. Hitting atmosphere on fire. And that was when something jogged in the Magister's memory. A few days ago he'd been sitting out at sunset looking at the night sky and seen something that bore resemblance to a shooting star. Was this man some sort of outer space creature? As quickly as the thought crossed the Magister's mind, he shook it off. He was simply not given to flights of fancy. Then the newcomer toppled over. Q-Sack looked at the Magister. Is he dead? The Magister shook his head. Nope. Don't appear to be. What if he dies? Then we bury him and move on. He did not, however, die. The next morning, not only did the Magister see his strange prisoner alive, but awake and sitting up and, other than his odd coloring, looking fairly normal. The first thing that struck the Magister was how the gaze of the Purple Eye seemed to pierce him. How are you feeling? The Purple Eye'd man blinked very slowly. Damp, I appeared to have sweated through everything I have on. The man glanced around. Where am I? You're on the planet Yacaba, in the city of Naren, in my jail. The man's fists gripped the bars, testing their strength. Which would seem to indicate in your eyes that I am a criminal, Magister Notted. In respect, you attacked a woman, tried to kill her. That seemed to startle him. That is unfortunate. I was not myself. Really? And may I ask who you yourself are? Calhoun. Mackenzie. Calhoun. Just passing through, are you? In a manner of speaking? Yes? The Magister leaned back in his chair. Well, Mackenzie Calhoun, it would seem that you're not going to be passing through quickly. I'm not a threat to anyone. Thing is, Mackenzie Calhoun, that's not up to either you or me. You're guilty of trespass and assault. Only the Circuit Judiciary can set the charges aside. I was injured, feverish, possibly even concussed. Have something to do with your crash and shuttle? That obviously caught him off guard. Calhoun looked at the Magister with surprise and even a bit of respect. When can we talk to this Circuit Judiciary? When he comes through this way on a Circuit? About five months. Calhoun simply processed the information and announced, so you're saying that I have no choice but to wait? The Magister smiled. Yes, as a matter of fact, Calhoun shook his head. That is unfortunate for you. You seem a decent enough man. I would not like things to end badly for you. The Magister smiled evaporated, and he didn't look directly at Calhoun for the rest of the day.
description: In this episode of "Star Trek New Frontier Excalibur Restoration", Simon and Schuster Audio presents Peter David's audiobook read by Joe Martin. The narrator discusses a moment of intense dread followed by a feeling of certainty that she knows someone is coming, despite the absence of any physical signs. As she waits for her visitor, she reflects on how long it has been since she felt such an overwhelming sense of fear.

transcript: The next morning, the Magister had a feeling that the day wasn't going to be going well when he emerged from his simple bunk in the back room to discover the frosty visage of Maestris Cofield waiting for him. Even worse, the rest of her was attached to the visage. Her gaze traveled over to Calhoun. So this individual is the creature that assaulted Rila. She approached the cell just within range of Calhoun. But the Magister was slightly saddened to see that Calhoun made no move against her. Cofield announced after a time, he's very odd looking, even somewhat ugly. But then again, what would one expect from someone who would consort with Rila? Ferex sat behind his desk. I would know Maestris. Is there something I can help you with? Uh, yes. You can tell me why you would give so much priority to a woman like that, and displace a little respect for a woman such as I. description: In this episode of "Star Trek Audiobook: Imzadi 1 of 2," Captain Spock's crew reluctantly evacuates from an ominous city they've been tasked to protect, sensing something significant has changed in their captain. The bond between the crew and their commanding officer is strained as they realize the immense sacrifices he's made and the loss he's endured since his last battle. Mary Mac, a Project Administrator on Forever World, arrives at Data's compound seeking guidance but finds herself more confused than ever before. This episode explores the emotional journey of Spock, the complexities in their relationship, and Mary Mac's quest to understand the mysteries of forever.

transcript: Maror didn't know what he was running from, or running to, but there was one thing that he was certain of. He was going to kill that damn betazoid woman before this jungle adventure was over. She sat on a rock nearby, and to his frustration she looked exactly as she had the day before, and the day before that. Even though her clothes were ripped and dirty, her face filthy, her hair hanging and stringing ringlets that had lost all their bounce in the moisture of the jungle. Even with her shoes gone, her prospects slim. Still she had her composure. Maror sneered at her. Are you wondering why I haven't killed you yet? You hope that I will serve some purpose in the near future. Her calm was infuriating. He walked over to her and yanked her rudely to her feet. I still can't believe that you survived the crash and others of my men didn't. I was not tense. I had relaxed myself. Your men were tense. The stiffness resulted in the internal injuries that killed them. Thank you for your diagnosis. He led her through the jungle, watching carefully all about him for any sign of pursuit. Eventually, the vegetation around them thinned out. Ahead of them was a cleared area, a watering hole. He turned to her. You first, if it doesn't make you sick, then I'll drink some. She knelt down in front of the water, cupped her hands and brought it to her lips. She sipped gingerly. You realize, Maror, that you have nowhere to run to. You're just marking time. I've never been caught. I take tremendous pride in that. Besides, maybe they'll eventually conclude we fell into one of those, what do you call them, mud pits. You sound very confident. A few days ago, I wouldn't have been able to tell otherwise. But from the time I've spent with you, I can tell you're afraid, terrified of captivity. It's not pride. It's fear of being caught. That's enough water for you. Move my turn. You know, I was just tired of you before, but now I'm really, really sick of you. Your use as a hostage is being outweighed by the fact that I really just want to kill you and get you out of my... Oh! Diana, having seized the opportunity to shove him into the water, now turned and ran like hell. As she dashed, pail-mailed through the jungle, she heard him crashing behind her. She had seized the moment to try and escape because her empathy had convinced her that Maror was quite serious. He was about to kill her. She might not have any future opportunities to escape her. She dodged to the right and stumbled on an outstretched roof. She fell and her right hand closed on a small pointed rock. She scrambled to her feet and kept going. A blaster roared behind her and she could feel the heat. For one insane moment, she envisioned Will Riker coming to her rescue. She had been such an idiot to waste the time that she had with him. Her own fears had held her back. Now she would never have the opportunity to act on the impulses that she had denied. Abruptly, the ground in front of her angled sharply upward. Just as she started to climb up the slope, a hand wrapped around her foot. Got you, you betazoid bitch! She tried to get away, but Maror pushed her down to the ground, pressing his blaster against her stomach. Well he won't. Very slow and painful way to die. It's what you deserve. You've ruined everything. Let her go. Maror looked up, his already pale face going one shade later. Riker was standing about ten feet higher on the slope. He held a phaser aimed squarely at Maror. Now Federation man, you put your phaser down or I'll kill her. I swear. Alright, just don't hurt her. Let her go. And I'll take her place. Riker tossed his phaser to one side. At that moment, Deanna jabbed a sharp stone into Maror's hand, drawing blood. He let out a howl. It was all the distraction Riker needed. He leaped and plowed into Maror, pushing Deanna clear. The two men went down, rolling and shoving, each of them trying to get leverage. With a quick twist of his hip, Riker slammed Maror up against the tree with a bone jarring jolt. Maror lost his grip on the blaster and Riker made a grab for it. Maror's foot lashed out, kicking the blaster away into the underbrush. And then the cinderene drove his foot up into Riker's face. By the following morning, there had been one change of security guards since the captain had ordered a watch put on Deanna Troy. Wolf however had remained the entire time. As Riker approached, Wolf turned to him with a fierce protective scowl. No one has seen or spoken to Councillor Troy, except for a carefully supervised visit by Dr. Crusher. Excellent, Mr. Wolf. Riker to Councillor Troy, are you awake, Deanna? Yes, Commander. Awake and ready to go. Moments later Deanna, Wolf, Riker, and the guards were heading down the hallway. They attracted curious glances as others walked past them. Deanna leaned over to Riker. Do I really require an entire entourage? Just until we get to the conference room. Once you're there, you'll be safe. And Wolf and the others can return to their duties. In the quarters of Commander Riker, Admiral William Riker crouched in a corner and pulled at the heel of his boot. He kept twisting it until it came clean off. Then he emptied its contents into his palm. Before leaving the admiral sequestered in the cabin, Commander Riker had removed several weapons from his older self. But there was no way he could have noticed the ultra-miniature phaser that the admiral had hidden in his boot heel. The admiral prayed he had done the right thing holding back information. He knew his job wasn't finished. If it were, if Deanna were out of danger, then the guardian would have pulled him back to his own time. But that hadn't happened, which meant Deanna still wasn't in the clear. He had to get out. He went to the far wall. He knew that the officer in the adjoining cabin had already gone off to his morning duties. So this was definitely the preferred exit route. He held the phaser close to the wall, set it for a low and quiet setting and fired. A pencil-thin beam of light emerged from the miniature phaser. The ship's security system did not recognize the futuristic phaser. Instead, it identified the weapon as the closest analog, namely a hand-held arc welder. This was hardly a weapon, and therefore no security alert was required. Riker continued his work undisturbed. The two security guards outside Commander Riker's quarters took no notice from the door to the adjoining quarters' fist open. As a result, they never had a chance to react before the phaser beam now set to stun, cut loose from the miniature weapon in the hand of Admiral Riker. Instantly, they both fell to the ground, unconscious. Admiral Riker grabbed them each by one wrist, backed up and dragged them into the cabin from which he just exited. Inside the cabin there was a large hole that Riker had cut through with the phaser. He left them lying on the floor. When the Admiral re-emerged from the cabin, he was wearing the uniform of one of the guards. Although there was nothing he could do about his obvious resemblance to the Enterprise's second-in-command, at least he could make himself a bit less noticeable as he moved through the corridors. As he tried to determine his next move, he muttered to himself, All right, Data, if you are here, where would you be? What would you be up to? Would you really be so cold-hearted as to kill Diana? And if so, how would you go about it? At the conference room, the Cinderean ambassadors Nitzi and Asa finally entered. Nitzi bowed slightly to the assemblage. Our apologies! We were unaware that the switch had been made to this conference room. Asa was staring at Diana Troy with a most peculiar expression on his face, and Diana started to feel the first tickle to her mind of something. Something that she was starting to place, the vague feeling that she had encountered once before when she had been capted years ago of a Cinderean Raider. In the corridor, Admiral Riker suddenly skidded to a halt. Of course, that's what he'd do. He turned and barreled down the corridor. Minutes later he was entering Data's quarters. Riker moaned softly. Data was lying, unmoving, on the bed. It was clear he'd been shut off and tossed there like a sack of wheat. To make matters worse, his head was gone. Riker allotted 60 seconds to locate the head before he went after the future Data himself. It would have been nice to have the strength of the present Data as backup, but he would make do if he had to. He always had in the past, or future, or whatever. The door to the conference room hissed open and Data stepped in. Picard looked up as the android approached him. A private matter, Captain, for Councillor Troy. Data proceeded to move over to the Councillor and Riker. I have some rather distressing news. Admiral Riker, your future self, Commander, seems to have suffered some sort of massive heart attack. Dr. Crusher says he's barely stabilized, and he's calling for you, Councillor. I don't feel him in that sort of distress. He's barely conscious, Councillor. Perhaps that affects your empathic abilities. I took the liberty of coming in person, Commander Riker, rather than using communicators, in the event that unauthorized individuals are somehow tapping into our comm systems. Good thinking, Mr. Data. Will. I'd better go to him. I'll go to. Are you certain you wish to do that, Commander? Watching yourself die, I'd think it would be difficult for you. He's right, Will. Please. I don't want to put you through that. Date is with me. I'll be fine, honestly. If you ask me, I think you're being overly concerned. The danger is probably over. Data nodded in agreement. With three seconds to spare and his self-imposed countdown, Admiral Reicher found Data's head. It had been wrapped carefully in a sheet and shoved into the back of the closet. He activated it as soon as he pulled it from the cloth. Data blinked and looked around, then he stared up into the face of his liberator. I assume you are not the person who put me into this predicament. You appear to be Commander Reicher, but considerably aged. Come on, Data. We're going. Can you operate your body from here? With a cybernetic impulse from Data's positronic brain, his body lurched off the bed like something from an old horror film. Sir, be careful to face me forward so that I can see where I am going. Reicher bolted into the corridor and started down the hallway. Data's head tucked under one arm. Would you care to apprise me, sir, of what is occurring? Reicher proceeded to lie through his teeth. I am an older version of your Commander Reicher, as you must have surmised. But I'm from another dimension. I'm pursuing lore, your twin, who killed Deanna in my dimension and now has come here to perform the same murderous act. His motives are a complete mystery to me. Reicher knew if he told Data the truth, or even part of it, he might have a bigger problem than when he started. If this data decided that the future data's mission was a sound one, then Reicher might very well have two Androids trying to kill Deanna. Data accepted the lie without question. The Admiral realized it made as much sense, if not more sense, than the truth. Commander Reicher sat down again as Data and Troy walked out of the conference room. He turned to Picard. My future self is very ill. Data says he's calling for Deanna. She's going to him. Picard studied Reicher to make sure that his second in command was dealing with this news. But Reicher's face was inscrutable. In fact, he seemed lost in thought. Deanna Troy looked worriedly at Data as he stepped to one side when they emerged from the conference room. He gestured for her to go first. They started down the hallway. Data studied her long neck, trying to decide what would be the most painless method of disposing of her. For some reason, now that the moment would shortly be at hand, he felt reluctant. But his duty was clear. In the conference room Reicher suddenly jumped as if someone had jammed a rod into his back. Picard looked at him in surprise. Captain, Data said he's calling for her. I know, number one. You told me that you don't understand Captain. That's exactly what Data said he's calling he's. Not he is. And he said it several times. He used contractions. But Data doesn't use. Immediately both officers were on their feet. But Reicher was near the exit. The ambassadors were babbling at utter confusion as Reicher bolted out the door. He saw them just turning the corner of the corridor. As if from a separation of years he shouted after them. Deanna! It's a trap! Deanna spun around as Reicher's words and his mind reached out to her and warned her. Data, aware that he had been found out, drew back his fist. And Deanna saw it just as she turned. He stepped forward and drove his fist straight toward her face. With a cry of alarm Deanna dropped back. Data's fist whistled barely inches from her face and smashed into a wall, going in with such force that it penetrated up to his elbow. The card came from nowhere, hurtling through the air and grabbing Data from behind. Data lifted Picard completely off his feet and was about to hurl him when Commander Reicher plowed into the android, tackling him around the legs. It knocked the android off balance and he lost his grip on Picard who tumbled down on top of him. The ambassadors who had come running from the conference room were all shouting at once. Data was turning his attention to Deanna. Reicher, indomitable, was grabbing at Data's leg trying to slow him down. Picard, using the wall for support, was pulling himself to his feet. Everywhere there was confusion, chaos, raw emotions running rampant. And that was when Deanna pointed at the cinderene delegation. They've been deceiving us. Time froze. Then with amazing calm, Nitzi spoke. This is a lie. No, no, it's not a lie. Aza looked to Nitzi. Shut her up. Make her shut up. But Deanna continued. I sense that you want Data to succeed. You did not come here in good faith. I sense duplicity, lies, cheats, anything to stall for time for the cinderene. You hope to use these peace talks as stalling tactics to forestall your empire's collapse. And once you've received the Federation's help, you'll resume your thieving war-like ways. This is madness. But Deanna ignored Nitzi's protest and instead whirled toward Aza. And you. You especially wanted me dead. You'd do anything to see me dead. You. You tried, didn't you? You tried to kill me. But something in my drink at the reception. I sense your emotions. Homicidal. Murderous. It took me time to punch through the cinderene resistance. And you tried to get rid of me before I could. The air around them seemed to be shifting. Coming to life somehow. There was a crackling of energy that seemed to come from nowhere. Aza howled. You went past the... Bitchew ruined everything. From his sleeve, Aza produced a small phaser, smaller than almost anyone had seen. He had a clear shot at Deanna. He wasn't going to miss. And suddenly, arcing through the air over Deanna's head was a tumbling golden object. It struck Aza squarely in the chest, knocking him backwards. The phaser shot went wide. The golden object skidred across the floor and rolled up to Deanna's feet. We looked down in astonishment at Deanna's face. I suggest, counselor, that you duck. Deanna stood there, looking down in confusion. A second later, Deanna's body slammed into her from behind, knocking her to the floor next to Deanna's profusely apologizing head. His apologies were drowned out by the phaser beam that crackled over them. It envelopes a staggering him, and he screeched in protest. Admiral William T. Riker advanced on him slowly and exterably the power blasting from his favor. You're from my time, aren't you? That's the only place you could have gotten that weapon. You're from the time stream that had been and will be again. A time stream in which the Cynderene's duplicity was revealed by Deanna, and their piece initiative turned down. It was the downfall of your race, so you decided to come back and change your race's history to your liking. Kill the woman who blew the whistle on them. And in one reality, you've got away with it, but not in my reality, you murderer. Not in mine, because you picked the wrong focal point. Around them the scream of the phaser merged with the howling of the air, and Azer was knocked completely off his feet and sagged to the floor, unconscious and helpless. Then the air around them was roaring, roaring with far off winds that seemed to call from another time and place, from an infinity of maidens. A coruscant and sparkling whirlpool of color and life. Azer started to dematerialize his very molecules being drawn into the vortex around him. Commander Riker lost his grip on David who was also starting to fade. Deanna whirled to face the admiral. He too was being drawn off. The color seemed to be fading from him. He reached out to her. Deanna! Heedless of the danger to herself, Deanna Troy stretched out her hand to the man who had crossed decades, remodeled the universe all for her. Her hand passed right through him as if he were a ghost. The ghost of things yet to come. She cried out to him. I'm sorry. I tried to touch you one last time. He smiled. His body disappearing like the Cheshire cats. His voice sounded distant. Don't be sorry, Deanna. Maybe it won't be the last time. Besides, who really cares about all this physical touching, not young Deanna truly? He's the spiritual that's important. That's forever. And then, with the final roar and burst of wind that swept over everyone in the corridor, he was gone. And her riker entered Deanna's quarters, his hands behind his back. We okay, Deanna? She shut off the computer screen she was studying and folded her hands. Why shouldn't I be okay? Well, you went through a lot yesterday. We both did, but that was twenty-four hours ago. I bounced back quickly, given time. She walked slowly toward her. I thought you'd be interested. The Cameloid disappeared about the same time as the others. Oh, and the Cinderene ambassador has been sent packing. The peace initiative has fallen apart, and the experts predict that it's just a matter of time now before the entire Cinderene civilization collapses, which is apparently what was supposed to happen the first time. The data has his head together, so to speak. Apparently, I, the Admiral, that is, told data that this other data, the one trying to kill you, was actually lore. And was it? Riker paused and thought about it. I don't know. I know Deanna believes it to be. I think he's far more satisfied with the notion that it was lore than he would be with the concept that there would be a circumstance in which he'd try to murder you. Of course, we have no idea what influences will shape data over the next forty years. He might very well decide that, given the life of one woman versus the reality that he knows, the woman is dispensable, even if that woman is you. That's a hell of a thing for him to have to live with. So maybe it would be better if Deanna finished the thought for him. If we kept it between ourselves, consider it kept. So did you come here to discuss everything except what you really want to discuss? Namely us? Riker let out a slow breath. She waited for him to speak. Deanna, I don't know what's going to happen with us. I saw what I developed into without you. Can't say I liked it. But that was when you had been pulled from my life prematurely and completely. We could continue in the way that we are now and as long as you're there to be friend, confidant, soulmate. Things could work out well for both of us. I see what you're saying. Of course, on the other hand, if we become or go back to being lovers, things could work out even better for us. Or worse, he shook his head. I feel so ridiculous. We really have to wait 40 years until we're ready to take a chance on the two of us. No, Will. We just have to wait until we're ready. It might take 40 years or who knows? It might take 40 days. We have to wait and see. But at least we have a chance. It's up to us how we use it. That's true. Oh, by the way, Deanna, I made something for you. It's only an approximation, of course, based on my memories, memories which were filled at the time with the sight of a particularly new bile, young maid of honor and her lovely figure. He brought his hand from behind his back, and it was a thin white gauze headband. That's like the one Chandra wore. Ah, so I did make it close enough so that it's recognizable. Deanna, if you wouldn't mind, turning your head. She angled her head around and he looped it around and back, pulling her hair through. She stood and presented herself for inspection. How does it look? As beautiful as the woman wearing it. She felt her emotions turning to melted butter and she went to him. He enveloped her in his arms and their lips came together. And for a long moment, all the confusion and complexity of their lives fell away. And they were once again the young man and woman, hungering for each other. The couple shyly learning about one another and exploring the things that each of them lacked and each of them provided. The new lovers in the jungle intoxicated with their environment and each other. She was the woman whose life he'd saved and he was the man whose life she had made. And they had all the time in the universe. Mary Mac watched in astonishment as four people emerged from the swirling vortex of the Guardian of Forever. Admiral Reicher, Commodore Data, Lieutenant Blair, and one more form that tumbled forward clearly unconscious. She went to them and rolled the body over to get a better look and confirm what she thought. This is Marlach, the scientist I told you about, the one who vanished. We just thought he left the planet. Reicher prodded Marlach's unconscious body with his toe. Oh, he left all right. But he left through the Guardian. All handedly he created a universe in which his people's plans succeeded and they grew once more into a strong marauding race, but not anymore. And then the Guardian spoke. All is as it was. Data turned to face the Guardian. You mean that Admiral Reicher did indeed restore the timeline to its original form? That his actions were, in fact, correct. All is as it was. And now Blair stepped forward his long fur swirling. For crying out loud. If you knew that time had been tampered with in the first place and that the Admiral was doing the right thing, why in hell didn't you tell us that? You did not ask. There was a long silence except for the winds howling. Blair took a step closer to the Guardian. We didn't ask. Reicher started to laugh. We didn't ask. You mean everything we went through? All the difficult decisions we had to make, all the...we didn't ask. Blair stood in quiet amazement. It's true. We didn't. How very foolish of me. In my determination to uphold the Starfleet imperative of non-interference in time, I overlooked the obvious. You forgot Mr. Data. The first duty of Starfleet, which I thought about while I was with Captain Crusher. The duty that supersedes all imperatives and directives. That we must always seek the truth. Moments later, Mary Mac had enlisted Blair's aid in dragging the unconscious Marlach away. Data and Reicher stood before the Guardian. I want you to understand, Admiral, that I am truly sorry for my actions. It's all right, Data. On the face of it, what you did or tried to do was correct. It's curious, Admiral. In my efforts to kill Deanna Troy, I made several clumsy mistakes. I did not intend to, but I did. Perhaps you did intend to, Data? Perhaps you wanted to be stopped. One of the key things about being human is that you don't always know why you do the things you do. The important thing is that it's all worked out for the best. Has it, Admiral? Consider, while we are on this planet, we are untouched by whatever changes might have been made by our reparations. In Marlach altered time, we and our memories simply altered with it. Now, however, we are at the center of the change. When we leave this world, there is no certainty as to what will happen to us. Our memories may shift to accommodate the new time stream. Or we may retain our memories, but be in a strange new environment. There is even a remote possibility that we may blink out of existence if we do not exist as entities in this time stream. I don't think that's going to happen, Data. And you know why? Because I think that this thing, the Guardian, is God's window on the universe. And I don't think God would have let us in through his window if he didn't intend for us to live in his house. That's very spiritual, Admiral. It didn't used to be spiritual, but I had a good teacher. I don't know what else there is to say, Data, except... Data put up a hand momentarily silencing Riker and paused to get the correct inflection of his next words. Let's get the hell out of here. Riker nodded. I think that probably covers it. Riker gazed up at the swirling skies, the vast colored streaks and my asthma of temporal rifts that formed the heavens above the forever world. And he realized that in the skies swirling and whirlpool's shape, he saw a painting he'd seen a lifetime ago. There were reds and purples, and then in the midst of this vast mixture of cosmic existence, he saw an image. We're going to face a new and different universe, Admiral. Are you not at all afraid? No, Data, I'm not afraid at all. I think it's going to work out just fine. And he called out as he had called out in hopelessness and despair for year upon year of desolation. And the answer came. Whether it was from within him or whether it came from somewhere out there in the galaxy, from someone who was the better part of all that he was, he couldn't be sure. But it was there just the same. Tears came to his eyes as he heard in his head the words that he'd waited half a lifetime to hear. Sweet and musical, and a voice filled with promise. Welcome home, anxiety. transcript: Music Simon and Schuster Audio presents Star Trek, The Next Generation, I, Q, by John Delancy and Peter David Read by John Delancy with Marnie Mosaman There seem to be no reason to go on The planet, the planets that held fascination for her, once She had contemplated those miracles of natural construction Moving in the relaxed elliptical paths around their respective suns They seemed of infinite variety, some huge, some small, some with rings glittering in the rays of starlight that managed to illuminate them Some freezing cold, others seething with molten activity But, but, but, she was tired of looking Big worlds, little worlds, inhabitable, uninhabitable, what difference did it make? Nothing of any consequence would ever truly occur again because the multiverse had become absolutely, screamingly dull and boring It was all an abysmal failure Oh yes, life had held fascination for her, once In one galaxy there was a race that was so old it had forgotten it was even alive In another, a race of beings lived as pure thought In yet another, there was a group that assumed it was a preeminent force, not realizing that others far more advanced Orby and microscopic lived out their lives as undetectable entities within the minds of the superior race Manipulating everything they did But, it was getting to be so, so damn noisy When the multiverse began it wasn't teeming with life It was gloriously stupendously quiet It was possible to think, to contemplate and truly appreciate the multiverse for what it was Unfortunately, it had been impossible to leave well enough alone Now the multiverse was a cacophony of voices, it was distracting and annoying And made her nostalgic for the way it had been in the beginning She now stood upon the beach and contemplated an end to it all She liked the beach, she liked that the water lapped the shore caressing the sand like a lover She liked the horizon, the horizon with the pink sky at the ocean The sky was now in dark blue, perhaps mirroring her increasing despair She wore no clothing, it was an unnecessary affectation The breeze caressed her long hair and tickled her shoulders, but she needed more time So she knelt down and built a sand castle It was a rather impressive construction, she meticulously designed the turret, even created a courtyard and a moat And she sat back and stared at it, the water level began to rise, filling the moat Eventually the foundation gave way, as all things eventually give way She watched this little drama, seated several yards back with her knees drawn up and her arms wrapped around her leg Before too long the castle collapsed completely, and still she walked The darksome waters lapped at her toes, but came no closer Finally the tide began to recede, there was now only a sinkhole where the castle had once been, with little bits of flotsam and jetsam swirling about It was an image that pleased her, and pleasing images were few and far between Flotsam and jetsam indeed, all of it, all of it was going down the drain Yes, she was sure, that was how it was going to end It was time, she rose and took a step toward the ocean It appeared to move toward her, as if begging her to join it Come to me, it seemed to say, come to me and put an end to it all A third step, a fourth, a limb She stepped on something, it was partially buried in the sand, it appeared to be glass A bottle, she said aloud, which was the first word she had uttered in quite some time She knelt down and picked it up, there was something inside the bottle, a message She felt a rush of curiosity, where was this message from, who had sent it, and what possible significance could it have? The core commit, a most satisfying, popping sound, when it was finally yanked free Extricating the manuscript was a deliriously prolonged ordeal She could see that it was a narrative, yes, a narrative, and what a truly remarkable narrative it was There was much within it, she already knew, and yet so much that she didn't To actually discover something outside her knowledge was indeed amazing It was accelerating She stopped for a moment to gather herself In her nonlinear existence, everything happened at once She couldn't discover the end of the story while reading the beginning, but she resisted the impulse Instead, she sat down on the sand, stacking the pages neatly on her bare thighs Although the printing was small, there were a number of pages Apparently the author had quite a bit to say She slit her hands along the manuscript's edge to make sure that the pages were just so And then she began to read, while the rest of the universe waited The narrative began thus I Q My instinct is to start with me It's a natural instinct, I suppose, since I was there at the beginning I've been around for as long as I can remember, and until this day, presuming one can call this a day I had always made the assumption I would be here forever Forever is a very, very long time One doesn't tend to dwell on the end, because such an event is naturally unthinkable even to one such as me And if the end ever did come, I always assumed that I and my equally powerful fellows would be able to mount a defense against it Each of us, even as a lone individual, can do anything, so when you have an entire continuum of infinitely powerful fellows It would seem only logical to assume that there is nothing that can possibly stand against our collective will Except a two-year-old who's teething, but that's a nightmare all its own Allow me to introduce myself, I am Q Known to my friends, relatives, and associates as, the wonderful, the magnificent, the living end I come from the Q continuum, a place that has existed since before time was time It was our lot to push, to prod, to experiment, to see the picture within the great tapestry that is the universe In other words, to boldly go where no one has gone before At least, that was our mandate when we first started It has changed somewhat, and now my fellow Q specializes in sitting about on the rocking chair of life, watching the universe pass them by Another point of useful information, I am omnipotent Some think this is a bad thing, I of course do not It is the state to which I am most accustomed I am able to accomplish whatever I desire simply by willing it to be so There are some who try to moralize about my activities to act as if what I do is right or wrong I don't share that point of view, right, wrong? Only thinking makes it so My actions are my own, and I am answerable only to myself In that respect, I can almost be considered a force of nature One doesn't question the ethics of a hurricane, quake, or ion storm, these things simply exist I am the same, I am above good and evil I cannot be measured, I cannot be judged, or poked, or prodded I am not the sort that you would choose to cross, in other words Don't tread on me I travel, I test, and with any luck I am able to raise some species a bit higher than they were before making my acquaintance To that end, there is a particular individual to whom I find myself drawn His name is Jean-Luc Picard He is a middle-aged bald, oddly accented man who oversees the activities aboard the Starship Enterprise The Starship belongs to an organization called Starfleet It is the flagship of the fleet, which makes it the most advanced ant on the Ant Hill When I first met Picard, I thought him an insufferably pretentious man who hardly deserved to be taken down a few pegs Arrogantly sure of himself confident in his ability to see all sides of a situation and arrive at a solution best for all concerned Picard epitomized to meet everything that is wrong with the human race Although these aforementioned traits may also be apparent in me, they are also well justified in me There is nothing more galling than some little pipsqueak strutting as stuff, but that's a discussion for another time Well, now that I've waxed on, built up ahead of steam, I suppose we must reluctantly start with Picard It makes sense from a narrative point of view and besides, one should work from the lesser to the greater And so in that spirit, we will begin with Picard and work up to me Now of course, you may be wondering how I know what Picard was up to on that morning, that fateful morning that began the last of all days It's because I'm omniscient I'm omniscient in real life, and I'm omniscient as a narrator How's that for consistency? So, to get back to my story, Picard and Data were fishing Ah, I suppose I should speak for just a bit about Data, Mr. Calculatorman Data is conceivably the most pitiable being in all creation He is a gold-skinned android who should have the word wistful tattooed on his forehead If humans are a laughably pretentious species, what could be worse than a creature whose highest aspiration is to be a human? How inconceivably sad In terms of intellect, he is light-years beyond even the most brilliant human mind Yet he still considers himself inferior He wishes to be one of them To put it delicately, his desire is short-sighted To put it indelicately, it's bone-stupid He would truthfully be better served if he got as far away from humans as possible Cozing up to an old Volvo, or maybe a pencil sharpener, would do him a world of good But I know that's not going to happen anytime soon The card and Data on this particular morning were on the holodeck of the Enterprise They spent a lot of time together those two, a boy in his computer The holodeck is, in many ways, the ultimate fantasy fulfillment An outgrowth of an ancient form of entertainment called the movies It gives humans the opportunity to control their environment and their fantasies With a few words, they can shape the holodeck into whatever reality they desire The fact that this reality is unreal doesn't matter a wit when you get right down to it As long as they can strap on a feedback of buttered popcorn and guzzle a gallon of sugar water All's right with the world So back to the holodeck Our dynamic duo is relaxing on a small yacht called the Hornblower The sea was calm because Picard, master of all his surveys, wanted it that way He's also a control freak The sky was a rich blue, the sea gulls circled overhead Picard was seated in a comfortable chair which was bolted to the deck of the ship His rod and reel locked in position was easily removable Should he manage to snare the big one Picard couldn't help but notice the intensity with which data was regarding the fishing pole Data, he said, this is supposed to be a relaxing experience Relax Oh Data ran this casual instruction through his positronic brain But the simple order to relax had him somewhat befuddled Is this sufficiently relaxed, captain? While Data was attending to business, Picard asked, Q, can you move? Oh, sure, Picard. I'm just practicing to be a mime. Better yet, I've decided birds need more statues to poop on. Do you seriously think I'd be posed like this? How am I posed anyway? Your arms are outstretched, your right leg is forward of your left, and slightly bent. Wonderful! I look like an Irish step-dancer. May we assume, ask Data, that you have been frozen in place by your fellow Q, so that you cannot in any way interfere with the end of the universe? That is a safe assumption, yes? Well then, he continued, even in the face of oblivion, your fellow Q retain a sense of irony. They can retain this! I said, and I tried to make a lewd gesture, but I was unsuccessful. It's just like that time with the fire, I sighed. Picard looked up at me, fire? What are you talking about? You know the Greek legend about Prometheus? Yes, of course, Epicard. He brought fire to mankind. And for his transgression, the gods chained him to a rock and left him there for the birds to eat his innards. Why'd you bring this out? Well, if you must know, I was Prometheus. But I'd stare at me. What do you mean you were Prometheus? How could there be... I assume you've heard of racial memory, events so cataclysmic, so monumental that they inform us as to who and what we are? Go on, you said. It was a long time ago. There was a group of you humans sitting about and staring for Lornley at the forest primeval. You seemed ready for a little pick-me-up, so I gave you fire. I wanted to see what you'd do with it. Not surprisingly, the first human thought it was something to put on his head. It was hilarious to watch. Of course, the other cues weren't happy with me. I was supposed to have observed your race from a purely scientific point of view, and they felt I had gone too far. It was their belief that humans would have died off without interference, and that planet Earth would have had cockroaches as its dominant species. They were very disappointed with me. So they chained me to the side of a mountain, and assorted beasts of the wild came along and chewed on my liver. Q, do you really expect me to believe your outlandish tale? You know, Picard, it doesn't really matter whether you believe me or not. Data had been watching the entire exchange with Naira Flicker of Cognizance when, all of a sudden, he came out of sleep mode. Let us assume for a moment that your description of history has some measure of truth to it, he said. Oh, yes, let's, I said. It is clear that you are not presently still chained to a rock. Obviously, you were released. Was that a collective decision of the Q continuum to release you? I cast my memory back to a time long ago. No, I said finally. It was the actions of one Q who unilaterally decided he did not wish to see me suffer. Picard began to look hopeful. Which Q, do you remember? We already found him, I replied. He was driving the cab and... My voice trailed off. On a hunch I reached out, metaphorically, of course. There he was, observing. He knew I had found him. He was hiding behind a big chestnut tree. What Picard and Data saw was a pigeon who had treated me in such a disgraceful manner. Fluttered down from overhead and settled on my shoulder. Do I have to talk to a bird, I said? The pigeon vanished in the burst of light to be replaced by a smirking Q, still in his cabbie outfit. You look quite statuesque, you said. Get me off this thing, I screamed. Q, he said, since virtually the beginning of time you have screwed up one thing or the other, including entire civilizations. I'm probably not in my right mind, but... he passed his hand in front of me and I stumbled off the pedestal. He then took a step towards me and continued his rang. In the past, he said, your misjudgments have had negative consequences for you or the poor unsuspecting species with whom you've meddled. But so helped me, Q, if you botched this up. You're what? Kill me, I asked, rubbing the back of my neck. He shook his head and smiled sadly. No. Suddenly there was a massive thunderbolt from on high. Q had just enough time to let out a shriek and then he was blown from existence. It was nothing left but a pile of ashes. I couldn't believe what I just seen and obviously neither could data or Picard. I guess the Q on high were upset. I had the feeling more thunderbolts were on their way. Now, said Picard with characteristic understatement as he looked at the sky, would be a superb time to be situated elsewhere. I agreed. A wiggle of my nose and we were gone. Last thing I heard was the roar of our leader, the great and all powerful Q, raging, you can't stop the end, Q. Nothing can. He'll get over it, I thought. As for me, I wasn't going down without a fight.
description: In this episode, "NA - Star Trek Audiobook: I.Q. part 1 of 3," Simon and Schuster Audio presents the captivating story of a woman who longs to return to her favorite planet from the vast multiverse of science fiction, but now finds it all too boring and noisy. The podcast delves into her reflections on life's fleeting moments and the desire for peace in a world filled with endless possibilities.
