transcript: As I'm sure you've surmised by now, all of this was relevant because I had intuited that a representative of the M continuum was lurking in one of the nearby buildings. I didn't know which of the M was behind all this, but I was hoping it wasn't M. Anyone, but M. I could sense a steady flow of power emanating from the building. I found it tremendously annoying that someone from the M continuum was functioning at normal strength. Something was seriously out of joint, and it wasn't just my nose. I heard shouts of anger coming from within the building. Then abruptly the shouting ceased, and there was another voice, a female voice, and one that I knew all too well. It was M. I sighed softly, just my luck, of all the people in all the crazy gin joints, it had to be her. I squared my shoulders, ignored the guards, and walked into the lobby. Cue! I've been waiting for you. Yes, I'm sure you have, I said. The guards stepped aside, and I entered a large auditorium off the lobby, with a proscenium stage flanked by columns that rose to a glittering domed ceiling. M was seated on the stage in one of the most lavish chairs I'd ever seen. She was not especially tall, but she had an annoyingly regal bearing with close cropped red hair and a steely glimmer in her eyes. She was swathed in a great purple robe, and she wore her arrogance like a low-cut negligible. Supplicants lay at her feet, attending to her every wish. Greetings, Cue. It's been too long. Not long enough, M. My eyes narrowed. Why do you need guards, old powerful one? Those? Therefore display, nothing more. What are you doing here, M? I'm the adjudicator. Surely you must have determined that for yourself? All around us is chaos, a frenzy of fire and destruction. It is my job to bring order to disorder. Is it now I fold in my arms? And how did you get this job? Did you answer a help-wanted ad? It is my place within the grand order of things. Oh, how very humble of you, M. It's quite unlike you to know your place. I am but a player, Cue, content with my part. Who is behind this, M? She shrugged. I do not know nor do I care. I sense the end of the universe, and I'm satisfied that I've done right by that universe. My conscience is clear. My business in order. How is your conscience, Cue? I'm not concerned about my conscience just now. What I'm worried about are my wife and my son. Where are they? How would I know? And why would I care? I suspect you do know. If members of your pathetic continuum had arrived, don't you think I would have brought them here? I believe you. Do you? How kind of you? And since you have no clear idea of what's going on, M, I'll take my leave. Immediately two of the guards stood in my path. It's not that easy, Cue, said M. I've waited forever for this moment. You who sat in judgment on so many others, you are now going to leave. I'm going to have others sit in judgment upon you. There was a flash of light, and I found myself standing in a docket. A huge clamp was wrapped around my mouth. I pulled at it with all my might, but I was unable to yank it free. M snarled. I'm tired of listening to you. This is my trial, and you have no say in the matter. She waved her arm, and Picard and Data were escorted into the auditorium. They looked filthy, but otherwise seemed none the worse for wear. It was not until I saw them that I realized I had actually missed them. Picard, for his part, took one look at my trust up mouth and smiled. That figured. We found these two wandering about, M said, sounding almost conversational, as if she expected me somehow to be able to reply. Who are you, to man to Picard? You may call me M. I am the one who holds your existence in my hand, little man. So I'd be circumspect if I were you. Sit down over there and be quiet. You, and she pointed to Data, shall serve and accuse Defense. In what way does Q require defending, asked Data? He needs all the defending he can get, and make it amusing. Since I have been put in the position of defending Q, may I ask what the charges are against him? Of course. M snapped her fingers, and a lengthy list appeared in her hands. Q is charged with not knowing his place. Excessive arrogance, interfering in the lives of other beings, but most of all Q is responsible for the end of the universe. I would have laughed out loud had I been able to. Obviously, Data said smoothly. All other considerations are insignificant compared to your final charge. What proof do you have? What proof do I need? I say it, therefore it is true. You are serving as both prosecutor and judge, Data pointed out. That is not reasonable. My function is as I desire it to be, not what you desire it to be. That matter makes no sense. You are allowing your anger to cloud your judgment. My judgment is quite clear. Thank you for your concern. She rose from her chair. Let me put things into perspective. The Q continuum, as well as the M continuum, is one of the keystones of the universe. We hold everything together. That is our purpose, our reason for being, our place within the universe. And while the M continuum has continued its responsibilities, the Q continuum has not. The Q simply sit about, consumed by boredom, caring for nothing least of all their obligation for keeping the great universal machine running smoothly. And because of that, like a mechanism devoid of lubricant, the universe has broken down. And this Q is the worst of a bad lot. He has upset the universal balance. The universal balance, ask Data? I'm afraid that such a notion is not codified by any law that exists on any planet. You cannot try him upon a law that is being fabricated on the spot. Of course I can. It's his fault. His fault. His fault. I feel the need to Data began, but he was drowned out. The audience was picking up the chant. His fault. His fault. His fault. His fault. His fault. Your honor, it appears that Data tried again to get a sentence out, but the rising din made it impossible. And then, not only to my surprise, but to the surprise of Picard as well, Data shouted. This was no ordinary shout, mind you. Data was a machine, remember, and he came with a volume control, ten being loudest, except I'm sure he cranked it up to an eleven. What are you people? Stupid? His amplified voice bounded and rebounded off the upper reaches of the dome. This is absurd. You are letting your emotions carry you away. What she is saying makes no sense. She is playing upon your anger. You're overwhelming need to tear down what you don't understand. He now turned to M and addressed her face to face. Why are you doing this? The entire building began to shake. She is causing all of this. She is seeking a scapegoat for her actions. She is the one. She is the reason for the end of everything. Are you going to stand by and let her get away with this? Are you? Are you? Are you going to spend your last hours of life in fear? Or are you going to take matters into your own hands and make a difference? Well, are you? The crowd went berserk. What a performance. The restraint on my mouth suddenly gave way and fell to the floor. There was a stampede to the stage. M was attacked from all sides. She fought viciously but the mob swallowed her out. How dare you stay away from me or all? Oh. But they didn't heed her warnings. The dome started the shake and huge chunks of stone fell to the floor. Cracks in the foundation opened beneath my feet. I glimpsed them trying to tear herself free. Her clothes were ripped, her hair disheveled and there was fire in her eyes. I do not mean that metaphorically. I mean there was actual fire in her eyes. Whereas before she had managed to contain her anger this time it consumed her. Her entire body erupted in flames. What a sight it was. To this day I shall never forget her screams. Where are we, Father? l had absolutely no idea. l looked around. l said, l once had been a jungle, but the trees had been cut down. l now there was nothing but mud. Did you hear that? Data said, peering off into the distance. lt was a loaning sound. Father, little Q said slowly, I don't think I want to be here. Your mother's here, I said. And little Q nodded slowly. I know. No one can help her. He whispered. And he was trembling. And I don't want to see her like that. Of course we can help her. By just being here we can help her, I said firmly. Are you sure she's here? Aspikard. I nodded. And so we set out to find her. After a short while we saw a cluster of huts just ahead of us. They were small and wretched. People were scattered about on the ground. They looked desperately ill. Every last one of them was emaciated. Their eyes were sunken. Their skin's yellow. They were all moaning. Picard was trying to keep his composure. Data began the sob. There were no tears, but the emotions were there. We've hit bottom. It was Picard. And I knew he was right. He couldn't get any worse. I picked a man at random who was just sitting there. How long have you been here? How did you get here? I said. He fell over. He wasn't dead. He just fell over. He was as if he had run out of whatever meager energy was required to keep him upright. And then the ground turned liquid beneath him like quicksand. And he began the sink. He offered no protest. Gave no struggle to free himself. He just sank. Madness, I whispered. Madness. Q, we have to leave this place because said urgently. And go where? You said it yourself, Picard. We've hit bottom. There's nowhere else to go. Father? My son had spotted something. I looked. It was the Lady Q. Looking as forsaken as the others. And her eyes. They had crystallized. She was blind. Look away. I whispered a little Q. But he didn't. He stared. Transfixed. My God. Set Picard. I turned and glared at him. Your God? Your God? Don't talk to me about your God, Picard. Because if he should happen to show his face, we're gonna have words. Mother? Little Q called to her. There was no response. Mother? He said again. Nothing. Stay here. I cautioned him. I knew he was terrified. I couldn't blame him. So was I. I knelt down next to her. Q, I said. To my surprise, there was the faintest hint of a smile. Tell me. I'm not dreaming. She said. You're not dreaming. It's me. No. It can't be true. We're dead. You can't be here. I am. And I moved to take her hands in mine. But she remained out of reach. I moved closer. And still she seemed out of reach. I am dead. We are all dead. She continued. It's over. It doesn't matter. Come back to me, I said. Come back to us. Our son is here. I found him. I've been searching for him just as I've been searching for you. This isn't what you think. It's a challenge of wheels. But you can overcome it. You can. The lady Q pitched forward. And the ground began to swallow her up. Don't you do it, I howled. Don't you give up? Nothing. I have nothing to live for. Nothing. Q, I love you. I do come back to me, I said. The back of her head had already sunk out of sight. Only her face was visible. Her face. And the hair that framed it. She stared at nothing. And then let out that terrible, rattling moan. It was gone. I had lost her. My son looked up at me and began to weep. We stood there deep in our thoughts until Picard broke the silence. That night over there, I see it, I said. Perhaps it watched only. Perhaps it leads to somewhere else. Somewhere we can feel more helpless and watch more people die. Do you have a better idea? He said. No. No, I suppose I don't have a better idea. And I certainly don't want to stay here any longer. We walked in the direction of the light. I see it, data said. What do you see? A house kept. A small house with a white picket fence. I see it as well, said Picard, as he squinted into the light. I could see the house, too. A charming little house with a white picket fence. And a brick path that led to the front door. And standing in the front door was the lady Q. Wave him. Do you see her? I whispered a little Q. Yes, he said a naze. She's very pretty. Who is she? Who? Why? That's your mother. No, it's not mother, said little Q, shaking his head. It's someone else. A pretty lady with long black hair. She's smiling at me. Picard, I said, do you see her? Vash murmured Picard. What? I turned to him. What do you mean? Where? There, right there. Picard pointed at the house. Vash, he said, I'm so sorry. I'm sorry I wasn't here for you. Do you see her Q? No, I don't. But let's see this farce through to the end, shall we? Let's go into the house. We walked up the brick pathway leading to the front door. When I placed my hand on the door knob, I paused and wondered what new trap we were walking into. And whether I even cared. We entered. It was one room, and it was empty, except for four chairs. There was another door on the opposite wall, and it was locked. Data, Picard said, and he pointed to the front door. Data crossed quickly, but not fast enough. The front door slammed shut. It's locked, Captain. And I can't budge it, he said. Very well, said Picard. Now what, asked little Q? I looked around the room and said, it doesn't matter, and I sat down in one of the chairs. I had no strength left. We need to find out who's behind all this. Picard, one of two things is happening. Either the universe is ending through entropy, or it's ending at the behest of some being or force. In either case, I accept it. All right? I accept it. I refuse to keep going around like a rat in a maze, and I'm just not going to do it. Q? What? You are in the depths of despair, Picard said, with that annoying degree of authority he always seemed to carry. If there is another level, it may well be acceptance. If that is the case, Picard, I don't care. I just don't care. And then I stop talking. That's when Data spoke up. What he said, however, was not designed to improve the situation. The far wall is 32.343 centimeters closer than it was before. The three of us looked. Data was right. The wall was getting closer. That's not good, said Picard. Picard put his hands up against the wall and began to push. Data did the same. If I hadn't held their efforts in such contempt, I might have joined them. Q, damn you, get over here, shouted Picard. My son looked at me. Clearly, he was waiting for me to take the initiative. With a sigh, I stepped to the center of the wall and little Q immediately followed. Don't give up, shouted Picard. We braced our backs against the one wall and brought our feet up against the other in a last, pointless effort to stop the wall from moving. Despite our struggles, it didn't take long before we were being crushed to death. I took little Q in my arms, kissed him, closed my arms, and surrendered to my feet. And that's when the back door sprung open. We tumbled through little Q and I, even as I heard the horrific slam of the two walls and a nauseating crunch of flesh and bones. We fell into a puddle. A puddle, actually, and all around us were shouts and cheers and the deafening sound of people counting ten, nine, eight. There was the honking of horns and a general air of celebration. I looked around at confusion. We were back in Times Square, back in the Q continuum, back where we had started. And Q, the blonde Q, who had helped in my escape, the one who had been blown out of existence, drove up in his taxi in green, plopsidedly. Nice to see you finally accepted the inevitable Q. You're just in time for the finale. And he pointed at the huge black ball at the top of the building. I understood. I understood everything now. You let me go, I said, to the blonde Q, to keep me busy. You were the ones who created the rift and everything in it, just to occupy me so I wouldn't be able to get in the way. You'd get in the way of the end, right? The countdown was on. Seven, six. Perhaps, he said. Or perhaps you're giving us too much credit. Perhaps we're really as much in the dark as you are. Perhaps in the final analysis, there are some things we are simply not meant to understand. We learned long ago to accept that fact, Q. You never did. But perhaps now, finally at the end, you have. He shook his head, and there was a hint of sadness in his face. Except you, as we have. She would have wanted you to be an example to your son. Show him. Show him that a truly omniscient being knows where he stands in the universe. It may be the single greatest gift you can give him. It will most certainly be the last. Four, three. The ball, which was really a black hole, was descending. Unstoppable. Is it time, Father? Has little Q. I looked around at the joyous faces of the other Q. Individuals I had known for eternity. They were at peace, and I envied them. I looked back at little Q. I think so, son. Yes. Two, one. Happy endings. Everyone screamed. There was a flash, and all of reality began to twist and distort. Through the explosion, I could see something at the center of the fireball. It was... it was... the crevasse, the pit, the hole, the void, the drain, the giant drain that the universe was flushing down. Everything was now turning faster and faster. The Q continuum began to split apart, and it wasn't just us. It was everything, everywhere, in every corner of the universe. Those who understood what was happening, and those who didn't. Those who were tuned to the cosmos, and those who were simply going about their business, all were swept away. It was the end. No mistaking at this time. The end of everything. We watched the buildings of Times Square dissolve and swirl onto the drain. I saw members of the continuum happily hurled themselves into oblivion. Everything around us was being torn, sonder, but still we held our ground. It was as if we were being saved for last. My son looked up at me. Father, he said, Father, I am very afraid. I do not want to accept, but if you say I should, if you say it's alright, then I will. Tell me what to do, Father. I need to know. I looked into his eyes, and I could see the reflections of reality itself. From every edge of the universe begins to swirl away. You see, I have no recollections of my own beginning, not really. However, when I stared into my son's face, I saw myself as if for the first time. I felt a beginning, a first. A personal me start to emerge. This was my universe too. I helped create it. And this was not the way I wanted it to end. Whatever was doing this for whatever reason, I wanted to make sure at least someone objected. That someone stood up proud and said, no, no, no, no. No to the great world pool, no to the abyss, no to the capriciousness of it all. This had to be the work of some great mad being. I will never accept I held into the storm. I will rage against the coming of the end. I will spit into the face of the void, with the last bit of strength I have. I held my son close to my chest. You want me? Come and get me. I will never give up. Never. From the pit of oblivion, I will rise up and strike at you. I will never accept. I am Q. I am forever. I stretched out my hand and a bottle appeared. A bottle with this manuscript tucked inside. A testimony to all I had been through and what we had suffered. These, these are my terms. Read them and weep and know that I, Q, and the trickster, the Lord of Chaos and the one liner, thank you very much. I Q defy you to the last. And if you think you can stop me by ending the universe, then I am here to tell you you are going to have to do better than that. And I threw my arm back and hurled the bottle with all my strength into the mouth of the abyss. That second my son was torn from my arms and the bottle tumbled end over end into the heart of the maelstrom. It was good. It was good to laugh. It made her forget herself for a moment. It made her feel light and fun and attractive. I should have known. She said, I should have known if anyone could moon me to laughter, it would be you, trickster. She rose from the beach where the waters left against her legs and she stretched. In one hand she held the bottle and the other the maelstrom. She started to walk and sure enough after a time she found him there, the boy laying on the beach, washed ashore like a piece of trip. He was unconscious. She clothed herself in sea foam because it pleased her. She had been naked for so long, but she felt it somehow suited the woman. She knelt down next to the boy and shook him. He coughed several times, opened his eyes and looked up weirdly. You, he managed to say, I saw you outside the little house. You smiled at me. Yes, she said. Why were you there? It pleased me to be there. You're very pretty. You have very nice eyes. They're very blue. Thank you. She tilted her head and looked at him thoughtfully. You have much of your father about you. Some of your mother too, but most play your father. You know my parents, my father? Oh yes, I've had my eye on your father for quite some time now. We met once face to face, although he didn't understand the significance of the meeting. He didn't know who I was. He thinks he knows so much. He knows so little. He knows everything the boy said, challenging her to refute him. I believe you. She smiled. They sat silently for a time. Now what said the boy? Do you know, she told him, after giving a matter some thought, that if only one decent man had been found, saw him. And Gamora would have been saved. Who were they? They were cities. Oh, he eyed her curiously. Are you saying my father is a decent man? Why am I? You are quick, aren't you? What a clever boy. She ruffled his hair affectionately. Then she said, it's not quite that simple. Decent perhaps, but also stubborn and irritating. And what pride? Fighting to the last. And in the end, he even prayed after a fashion. A rather belligerent prayer, I'll grant you that. But a prayer on the left. That wasn't easy for him. And he made me laugh. I had forgotten what that felt like. I think I have forgotten a great many things, more than I would have thought possible. I think I shall live for another day. I don't understand. Good lad. Remarkable lad. Only those who know they don't know can truly know. I still don't think I understand. That's all right. Neither do I. And I've been at it longer than you. She took the last page of the manuscript, produced a pen, and wrote four words on the back of the page. Then she rolled it up and put it back into the bottle, sealing it in with the cork. My father made that, he said. He threw it, I know. And I'm throwing it back. And you too, memory. She then scooped up some sand and fashioned a small boat the size of the boy. Remarkably, it floated. She then handed the bottle to the boy and said, here, get in, take this, and be off with you. But no but. And she kissed him lightly on the forehead and helped him onto the boat. Tell your father. And she stopped to think. The boat was already drifting up to sea. Tell him what called the boy. But he was beginning to feel sleepy, although he had no idea why. What should I tell him? Tell him that Melanie says hello. And she blew him a kiss. He fell asleep immediately, and she watched him until he was gone. And she laughed once more, and enjoyed the sound of herself, laughing. Enjoyed herself. She thought it extremely ironic and amusing that her prayers had been answered, especially when she didn't even know that she'd been praying. She laughed once more, allowed her dressed to dissolve back into sea foam, and then vanish into the universe. The deck of the horn blower bobbed up and down slowly as Picard raised his head and looked round in confusion. The sea was as smooth and blue as it had been at the beginning of their fishing trip. The sky was cloudless. Nothing seemed amiss. He looked down at himself. His skin was clean. No cuts. No bruises. He was as far as he could tell. Perfectly fine. Data. Data. I'm down here, Captain. Data's voice came from below decks. I think you should see this, sir. Picard rose on shaky legs and made his way below. There sprawled on the deck was me and the lady Q. For a moment Picard thought we were dead. Then again until moments ago he thought himself dead as well. Q, he said? Yes. We said in unison? Where are we? On the holodeck of the Enterprise, at least I believe so, Picard said. Where's my son? Said Lady Q. I've not seen him, Picard said, but I've not searched the entirety of suddenly Data cried out, pointing out to sea. There. Out there. Everyone looked, and sure enough, floating on the water was a small boat. And on it was the little Q. He was asleep on his back, and he was clutching something to his chest. Data. Hard to port. Bring us around. Oh, no. Be hell with it. End program. This time the holodeck obediently disengaged. The water, the boat, all of it vanished, leaving me, the lady Q, Picard and Data on the glowing holodeck floor. And little Q was there as well. But incredibly, he was still in the little boat, and the bottle was still in his hands. Oh. Picard could not even hazard a guess. The bottle dropped to the floor with a thud, but did not break. Lady Q and I ran over to the boy and scooped him up in our arms. What happened, Father? What did it all mean? I don't know, I said. And I don't know if we'll ever know. I then picked up the bottle and stared at it. There's a piece of paper in this bottle. It's a note. The lady wrote a note. Lady? What lady I said? She said she knew you. Her name is Melanie. I was stunned. Do you know her, said Picard? Um, from centuries ago, Times Square, but she... I stared at the bottle once more, and then turned to Picard here. You open it, Picard. Why me? Picard, I said slowly. I've spent my entire existence looking for answers. I think there's an answer in this bottle, and I'm not certain I'm ready to receive it. Picard didn't pretend to understand. Instead, he uncorped the bottle and pulled out the paper. He unrolled it and saw what was written on it. Four words, just four little words. Picard smiled. Actually, Q, he said gently. I think you should read it. It may be the only answer you'll ever get. He handed me the note. I took it and read the message. Let there be light. description: In this episode of "NA - Star Trek Audiobook", the narrator is frustratedly investigating a building where they suspect there's a M continuum representative operating under normal strength. They overhear M addressing an audience, discussing her work as the adjudicator for bringing order to chaos. The scene transitions into a courtroom setting, and we learn that M has been appointed to rule over others who are "sitting in judgment." Despite being instructed to leave, she insists on staying behind, revealing that her wife and son have gone missing, causing concern within the audience.

transcript: We went everywhere at once. Humans can do that as well except they do it on a much lower and more simplified level. They call it dreaming. All one has to do in order to go everywhere at once is to turn one's mind inside out and step through. So I went everywhere. Considered all the possibilities and tried to determine just where we should go next. I had to do it on the QT because other Q were close on my heels. We needed a safe place and I found it. Poised on the edge of the great abyss. Why the world? Picard managed to get out. Why have we returned here? Picard I said to find out what's happening we need to literally get to the bottom of this. That is where we will find the answer. And and with that I stepped boldly towards the crevasse. It was big. Grand Canyon big and I wanted to observe it before jumping in. So how do we get down as Picard? It would seem climbing is the only option unless you can simply materialize us down there. That in fact is my intention I told him. And with a non-essential flourish I caused us to disappear in a burst of life. Our next stop? The bottom of the abyss. Managing my surprise when we found ourselves still at the top. It would appear we have not moved. Data said thank you thank you for that brilliant evaluation data I shot back. What happened to you? I don't know what happened Picard. Is something defying your abilities? Why don't you go and say it louder data why don't you just go around with a billboard to make a big fat announcement. Calm down Q I know it's a bitter pill to swallow but data was just asking a question. One question too many. And while we're at it let's get something straight I'm still Q an infinity of options minus one is still an infinity of options. There was a sudden flash and three pairs of anti-gravity boots materialized on our feet. I smiled smugly and walked straight towards the crevasse. You see Picard I said we shall float down as gently as hair follicles deserting your scalp. I walked confidently over the edge, hovered there for a moment. The gravity boots working as expected. Then the only thing that prevented me from plunging straight into the void was that I reached out and snagged a rock. Your powers don't seem to function within the proximity of the crevasse Picard said. I believe I can be of service in this matter said data. He walked straight to the edge of the abyss swung his legs over the side and dropped out of sight. What are you doing cold Picard? We heard the sound of chiseling creating hand holds sir. Shall I continue captain? By all means Mr. Data Picard answered back good thinking. I waited a few moments to give Data and Picard a head start and then followed. It was a long way down and after a few steps I began to wish I could pray. We too don't pray you see we never have. A prayer is after all an appeal to a higher authority than ourselves. That authority is usually created and deified by lesser beings. Beings who attempt to put a label on that which they don't understand in hopes of grasping it. The simple fact is there is no such thing as God. I know I know there's more in heaven and earth than has dreamt of in any philosophy but the concept of one single supreme being now now it's too nonsensical even to contemplate. Of course there are things that one doesn't understand and that's perfectly acceptable. There are things even I don't understand. The human fascination with the accordion for instance and coconut oil incomprehensible. Oh and baseball it makes me sad to think that the great Colosseum's of old with all the pomp and circumstance and the eating of Christians would be turned over to a sport as banal as baseball. Just goes to show certain things don't get better. But to return to the concept of God I have been worshiped as a God so I know the mindset that brings about these attitudes. It's all hogwash and nonsense. God exists for three reasons to explain that which cannot be understood to fulfill a spiritual longing and to have someone to whine to about the unfairness of life when things go wrong. Obviously none of the above applied to me. The thought of breaking down and begging for help from some supreme all seeing all knowing deity is nothing but absurd. After all if you follow the logic the alleged being allowed the predicament to occur in the first place and it is from this same being you're asking for salvation. I just don't get it. No no prayers for me. So I lowered myself down into the crevasse all by myself. I heard data as he punched each new handhold and as I'd listened I began to realize what the problem was. It was the big picture. Omnitions enables you to see the big picture in ways that no one else can but even if one is omniscient you still have to squint to see the individual dots that make up the picture the same as everyone else. Think of point-alism. I spend my days studying dots and so in examining the minutiae I find ways to spend eternity without going mad. Remember the big picture is routinely open and clear to me but not this time. This time I couldn't see the picture for the dots. I was exploring completely uncharted territory with no clue as to where I was going or what was going to occur. In a way I sorely envied Picard. This was something to which he was quite accustomed. He runs headlong into things all the time without the slightest clue as to how it's going to turn out. Perhaps that was the reason he was along. I needed someone who had no trouble with Boldly going where no one in his right mind had gone before and of course data would tag along for comic relief. Data came to God's voice distracting me from my reverie. Data? It was an urgency in his tone. Immediately I realized why. The sound of data's chipping away at the rock face had stopped without warning. Picard what's going on with data I called. Can you see him? No Picard shouted back up to me. Any thoughts as to our next move Mon Capita I asked? Silence. Picard you're not remotely amusing. Still silence. What a fine pickle this has turned out to be I muttered. That's when I heard the scream. It was long. I pitched and distinctly female and for a moment just a moment I was absolutely positive that it was my mate. I called out to her then suddenly the toe holes weren't there and I plunged into the depths. The scream was ear splitting. After what seemed an awfully long time I began to realize it was not the shriek of a woman. It took me a moment to identify the sound as something I hadn't heard in ages. A train whistle? Yes. A train whistle. I was standing on the platform of an old train station. The wooden planks were rotted and covered with grime. There was a train in the station and it let out another whistle. It sounded for long like a child crying for its mother. It now occurred to me that I was also hearing over the shrieking of the train whistle voices crying, pleading, shouting, begging, a cacophony of misery. One sentiment was loudest of all expressed over and over again. This can't be happening. This isn't happening. This isn't real. We're all going to be fine. Yes, sir. Re-bop. Regardless of the fact that they were all being pushed and crowded like cattle, they held on to that sentiment like a drowning man holds on to a life preserver. There are a lot of people on that platform and they were crowding in on me. You have to understand I am Q. I know I've said that before but it's comforting to repeat it. When people see me approach they tend to keep their distance. Masses people part by great waves when I arrive. I'm quite accustomed, thank you very much, to having a sphere of untouchability around me. I like it that way, who wouldn't. It serves to remind others of who they are and who I am and the great gulf between us. Do not begrudge me this and certainly do not think me unique. After all, every God demands worshipers. No God is an island. Beings who are supposedly all seeing, all knowing, all powerful, nonetheless have an insatiable need to have worshipers reiterate their status every day and twice on Sundays. Now me, I am no God and I happen to know that no such thing exists. But even I like to have my fancy tickled every now and then. Hear me, fear me, steer clear of me, for I am Q, the beginning and the end, the Alpha and the Omega. It has a certain ring to it, a certain je ne sais quoi. Suddenly the crowd parted. I saw data coming towards me. He was pushing people aside in a fairly studied rhythm. Shove, push, apologize, shove, push, apologize, all the way from one side of the platform to the other. Since he was doing such a good job of it, I decided to stay in place and have a look around the station to arrive. The train was interesting, very interesting. A powerful steam locomotive with quite a number of cars attached. They were not what would normally be considered passenger cars. They were cattle cars designed for carrying animals, absentia and beings. People were being herded into these box cars by overseers who clearly were enjoying their job. I was not surprised to see that these overseers were from the more aggressive races. The Gem-Hadar, the Cardassians, the Crill, etc. etc. They all had whips, bludgens, cattle prads, the typical devices of torment that one associates with these events, and they use them with all the relish the average sadis typically employs. Data arrived. Are you all right, he inquired? Well, my powers aren't functioning, I'm surrounded by zombies other than that I'm fine. These people do not seem to be thinking clearly. I have been listening to their conversations, and they appear to believe that none of this is actually occurring. It would seem, he then heard a familiar voice behind us, the voice of Picard. Why are you standing there, he said? Data reacted with as close to astonishment as he ever came. I turned to see what he was gaping at, unsure as to why the android would be so stunned at the sight of his commanding officer. Immediately I understood. It was Picard, in a manner of speaking. He was clothed entirely in black. His left hand had been replaced by a blaster. His face was deadly pale, and half of it was obscured by an elaborate visual mechanism which doubled as a means of tracking and regulating his every thought. We stand here, I said, because we do not wish to surrender to the herd instinct. Your wishes, said the being known as luchutus of Borg, are irrelevant. You will enter the car. It is our desire, began Data, to prevent the end of the universe. We are attempting. Your attempts are irrelevant. Your desires are irrelevant. You are irrelevant. Enter the train now, or you will be permanently irrelevant. Luchutus held up his weapon arm. I made a move to walk past him and he struck me squarely across the face. Q, perhaps we should cooperate, Data said, after considering the situation a moment. I didn't move except to touch my bleeding mouth. My thoughts were dark, very dark, but without my powers. Data said softly, if you are dead, you will not be able to help your family. Are you saying that resistance is futile? I'm afraid so, yes. We made our way to the waiting boxcars. Luchutus took up a position atop the train. Smoke was billowing from the smokestack, obscuring him from time to time before the wind carried it away. I next heard Picard shout, Data, but this time it was coming from a different direction. No talking. Talking is irrelevant. Picard's head snapped around when he heard the voice. He couldn't believe what he was seeing, but within moments we were unceremoniously shoved into the boxcar, and a massive door slammed shut. Things looked bleak. Once inside the boxcar Picard made his way to my side. He looked stunned. Did you see him? Yes, Picard. We saw him. At that moment the whistle screeched, and the train lurched forward. Picard spotted a Vulcan standing stoically in the corner. If one is looking for sound, logical thinking a Vulcan is a good individual to go to. Excuse me, sir, Picard said, do you know where we are and where we are going? The Vulcan looked at the card with quiet assessment and said, we are not going anywhere. I beg your pardon, said Began? These beings regarded us with a sort of distant and contemptuous attitude that we were quite accustomed to. In other words, they behaved like us. They also looked like us. That was really off-budding. Alien races slogging in out with one another such as the Klingons and the Romulans are all well and good, but the true measure of a first-class entity is when those who hate each other are indistinguishable from one another. That makes it all the more pointless, and the pointlessness is in and of itself the point. So they sized us up, and we sized them up. Hello, they said. We are of the M Continuum. Indeed we replied. And where and what might the M Continuum be? The M Continuum is where we live, came the reply. It was like talking to a Mobius Strip. And we, since you have asked, are your enemies? Enemies really. Why? Because, they said, there is something about you that really pisses us off. And there it was, boiled down to the essentials with all the trimmings neatly shunted aside. Ah-ha! So, you're here because of the universal constant, we said. They considered that for a moment, and then said, uh, why, yes, yes, it would appear so. Another pause, and then we said, so we understand one another. Yes, it would appear so. But you still piss us off, and we want to kill you. Interesting, we said. But wouldn't it be best to develop a more eloquent reason? There was an awkward silence, and then one of them said, that is always to be preferred. They then went into a huddle. There was a lot of gesticulation and low mumbling that none of us Q could make out. Finally, one of the M's was picked to deliver the new, enhanced reason. He said, you are aware, no doubt, that we pre-exist you. No, we weren't aware, we said, and we all looked at each other somewhat bewildered. They continued. You are merely a copy of us. Really? And since we pre-exist you, and since you are merely a copy of us, we've crossed dimensions of space and time to annihilate you. Well, Greece, my monkey said one of the Q, but no one on either side seemed really upset. He just wasn't working. The reasons weren't pointless enough. Then very much as an afterthought, one of the M blurted out. Your mother wears, well, that did it. That was all that was required. And in salt, like that, was beyond the pale, and so we went to war. It's all in the QM, chronicles. Read them and weep.
description: In this episode of "Star Trek Audiobook: I.Q.", the narrator embarks on a journey through various dimensions, using his Q powers to travel to different locations. After finding a safe place and answering some questions from Captain Picard, he steps into the bottom of the Grand Canyon and disappears as Data materializes them down. They then head towards a crevasse where they encounter anti-gravity boots and data's help in making hand holds for their descent. The episode concludes with the group crossing the Grand Canyon and praying for their safety as they continue on their journey.

transcript: Pro-consul Arasian, with several of his personal escort and tow, negotiated a corridor on his way to the Federation prisoners' cell. He might have interrogated them sooner of course, but one of the cardinal rules of interrogation was to allow a prisoner time beforehand. This is Arasian. Your evidence? This is Commander Hijak. We've received a message from Romulus. I believe it is the one you were waiting for. Arasian thought for a moment. Relay it to the terminal in Barnock's office. I'll view it there. Arasian out. It didn't take long for Arasian to make his way to the office or to close the door so he could be alone. And it took even less time for him to activate the terminal. Then it was just a matter of accessing the message, which had already been downloaded from the vengeance. Actually the Pro-consul mused, it wasn't a message at all but a packet of information. On one side of the monitor screen there was an image of the human who had perished in the transport ship. On the other side there was a block of data. Arasian leaned forward to read the small-faced characters. Interestingly thought, after just a few moments, very interesting indeed. There was a file on the human as long as his arm and then some. The man's name was Scott. Montgumery Scott. Born. The Pro-consul blinked. Then leaned closer to the screen. That date was wrong he told himself it had to be. If this was the same Montgumery Scott and the homeworld computers had indicated there was no other. The man would have to have been 150 years old. For a Vulcanoid that was merely middle aged but for a human. Apparently Scott had served on an earlier version of the Enterprise under a Captain James Kirk. It seemed almost impossible that it could be the same man. He would have been too elderly to participate in such an escapade. Too frail. And yet in a way it made sense. The Montgumery Scott in the file was an engineer of considerable acumen. And the prisoner would have to have been in command of such expertise. Or he could not have set up a call for help in the form of an engine pulse. Or taken charge of the transport that eventually proved his undoing. Arasian scowled. Too bad the human had decided to take his own life. Or he would have gotten to the bottom of this mystery a long time ago. In fact, wait, he thought. The color draining from his face. The Enterprise. Excitedly, Arasian stored the Scott file and called up another. A detailed report on the Enterprise of a hundred years earlier. Scrolling quickly, he found the personnel section which described those crew members for which biographical information was available. Using his finger, he went down the list until he came to the name of the vessel's first officer. There. Slowly a smile spread across Arasian's face. Montgumery Scott had served alongside the reputed leader of the Unificationist Movement on Romulus, the Vulcan named Spock. And was it not a strange coincidence that Scott should appear in the Empire just now, when a contingent of the rebels had been captured on Constanthes? A very strange coincidence. Unless the great Vulcan diplomat was one of those who had been captured. And he had been in their hands all along. Proconsul's smile brought in as he pondered the possibilities. And then instantly faded. After all, it wasn't the forces of the home world who had discovered Spock. It was Thorus. Arasian's hands became fists. Did the governor know what a valuable prize was in his possession? Or was there still time to rest the Vulcan from him? Deactivating the monitor, he rose from his chair. As he headed for the door, he realized he would need to obtain additional ships. His overriding concern was to obtain Spock before Thorus could make a hero of himself. And that might require some firepower. The day of the trial had come. The Unificationists would be judged in an enclosed amphitheater located in the Command Center. As they entered, Spock noted the rows of seats that rose all around them filled with Constantherine citizens. He placed their number at a thousand, conservatively. Directly in front of the Unificationists on a raised podium, sat Governor Thorus. As soon as the rebels were all present in the central pit, Thorus stood up behind his judicial desk and addressed his fellow citizens. We are here to carry out the justice of the Romulan Empire. And beyond the Vulcan mused, since the cameras posted at Interfals suggested the event was being broadcast over subspace channels. The governor went on. In these proceedings, we will consider those who would destroy all we have achieved as a people. We will judge them. And then we will devise their punishment in the process, reaffirming the glory and might of the Empire. The crowd roared at the approval, pausing to let the applause die down. Thorus turned a scornful eye on Surak's followers. Thousands of years ago, the seeds of the Romulan Empire were grown on the planet Vulcan among a powerful race of conquerors. However, before the mightiest on that world could unite it in a common purpose, a plague was visited on Vulcan. A philosophy of weakness overcame the population. The strong on Vulcan were faced with a choice. Rule over a race of passive cowards or strike out into the reaches of space and found an empire. Before which the galaxy would one day shut her. This became our empire. The governor pointed to the unificationists. These traitors who stand before you would destroy that strength. They studied the teachings of the very weaklings on whom the Empire turned its back. They seek to spread that philosophy among us and reunite us with Vulcan under a tyranny of cowardice. Thorus lowered both his accusing finger and his voice, forcing the crowd to listen carefully. But this traitorous plot ends here, and it ends now. Our operatives have apprehended the traitors you see before you, and collected incontrovertible proof of their guilt. Thanks to these efforts, the Empire will survive. It will endure. When the governor paused this time, a tremendous din of approval rang through the crowd, even greater than before, he nodded, approving them. We are not here to determine the guilt or innocence of those you see before you, for their guilt is certain. We are here to see justice done. Thorus turned again to the students of Sorok. Do any of you traitors wish to confess your crime and pledge your allegiance to the Empire before your sentences pronounced? His followers would remain true to the movement even now. Despite the re-emergence of their Romulan emotions. If that were possible, perhaps there was yet hope for reunification. Finally, the Tan, the youngest of the prisoners, stepped forward and broke the silence. We choose the right of statement. Inwardly, the Vulcan smiled at his friend's optimism. I would not be so foolish as to accept that waiter, Mr. Scott. Spock looked out on the 40 or so Romulans standing amid a sea of industrial cargo containers in a vast storage chamber. After their faces were unfamiliar to it, still they were fellow unificationists. Until now, Spock and his followers had restricted their activities to Romulans. Now on this outer world known as Constantus, it was spread the word of Sirok further than it has ever been spread before. As one, every Romulan in the room lifted his or her hand into Vulcan greeting. Spock returned to Jephthur. With long and prosper, followers of Sirok. The one called Balan, to whom this building belonged, responded in the prescribed manner. Peace and long life to you, teacher. We are in a safe place and may speak freely here. Spock nodded and began the speech he had prepared. Followers of Sirok, you honor me with your presence. You show great courage in attempting to bridge the gap between our two people, so our one in blood. In the months to come, I shall endeavor to share with you what I have learned from the teachings of Sirok. Since ancient times, when we were one people, the relationship between student and teacher has been a sacred one. The Vulcan paused for a moment, but before he could continue one of Balan's people rushed into the room, the man made no effort to curb his emotions. Someone here is using a transmitter, Balan. To his credit, Balan retained his control as he turned to the Vulcan. Teacher, we have been betrayed. A moment later, the first Romulan soldiers burst into the room, disruptors in hand. For a brief moment, the unificationist struggled with him, but the struggle was short. It ended with several of Spock's comrades falling and agony to the soldiers' crackling blue disruptor. The Vulcan himself did not resist. What's more, he encouraged the others not to resist either. Resistance was not logical in this case. Clearly, there would be no escape. Finally, order was established. A stillness settled over the room as the Empire's newest prisoners conceded their fate. A few moments earlier, Spock had seen hope in the faces of the Constantherians. After all, they were greeting a teacher who would take them down Sirok's path. Now those same faces were full of despair. This was just the sort of meeting that put Leonard McCoy to sleep. In fact, he'd nearly dozed off twice already. At the moment, he was listening to the Starfleet cultural anthropologist who sat across the table from him in the Zapata's conference room. The man's name was Gibbs. In many ways, the stogara people of contradictions. They showed openness when they invited Starfleet to visit their world 75 years ago, leading to Admiral McCoy's first contact encounter with them. On the other hand, they have asked all Federation personnel to leave their world on four previous occasions, never extending an explanation. Drake, the tall red-haired captain of the Zapata, nodded sagely. Of course, none of the other periods of isolation lasted more than a standard month until now. Carmen, a thin, dark-haired woman who'd made a career out of conflict mediation, leaned forward. That's true, Captain. There is no precedent for an isolationist period of this duration in our experience with the Stug. McCoy sighed. In his day, he had watched Starship captain size up a problem in an instant. He would not let this charade go on another minute. Why don't we just go to the Stug Capital, beam down and ask them why they cut off relations with us. An embarrassed silence descended over the room. When Drake broke it, he spoke to McCoy patronizingly. An interesting idea, Admiral. Has your experience with the Stug provided any insight into why that might be successful? The Admiral made no effort to match the captain's soft, polite tone. My experience as a Starfleet officer for over 100 years has been that one should never overlook the obvious. Captain, there's a priority one. What's the message for Admiral McCoy from Starfleet Command? McCoy felt a chill. Someone's died, he thought. Drake touched him on the shoulder. You can take it in my ready room, Admiral. McCoy nodded, exiting the conference room. He couldn't shake his sense of dread. At 145, his main regret was that he'd lived to see so many friends kick the bucket. Entering the captain's ready room, he allowed himself to be guided around Drake's desk. Captain offered him a seat, but he waved it away, preferring to stand. He watched Drake exit, then turned his attention to the desktop monitor. Computer, relay message for McCoy, Leonard H. Admiral, to this station. Without delay, the small screen in front of him produced an image of Admiral Keaton. Keaton was highly placed in Starfleet security. Whatever this was about, it was important. Admiral McCoy, I'll get right to the point. I have bad news. It appears your former colleague and friend, Ambassador Spock. McCoy finished the sentence for her. Has been killed, how did it happen? The Admiral shot him a quizzical look before she spoke again. No, Admiral McCoy, you misunderstand. To the best of our knowledge, Ambassador Spock is still alive. That in fact is the problem. McCoy felt a tide of relief wash over him. What do you mean that's the problem? Ambassador Spock has been on the planet Romulus for a while now. He's working with a small group of Romulan insurgents called Unificationists, who are seeking a reconciliation with the planet Vulcan. However, he and several other Unificationists were taken prisoner recently on one of the Romulan outworlds, a place called Constanthus. Taken prisoner, right? Do the Romulans know who they've got? Apparently not. However, if they find out, we're facing a security breach that could be of most serious threat to the Federation. The implications of Spock's capture were quite clear to McCoy. As an Admiral, he'd learned more about Federation security than he'd ever wanted to know. What's the plan to get him out? We're dispatching a Galaxy-class vessel to the Romulan neutral zone, Admiral. So what's the name of this Galaxy-class ship? Keaton paused for a moment as if she were delivering important news. It's the Enterprise. Montgomery Scott was sleeping when the computer woke him. Rising, he saw that it had picked up a priority one communication heavily encrypted, and it had contained one of the subjects he'd programmed the computer to flag. The engineer waited to see if the Goddard would be able to decode it, with the help of the circuits he'd added for just that purpose. After all, Starfleet didn't fool around when it came to security. After a long moment, the message came through. At first, it brought a smile to Scotty's face to see McCoy again on his monitor, but the feeling faded quickly when he heard the news from Admiral Keaton. Spock was in danger, grave danger. Even if the Romulans never found out the Vulcan's identity, Romulan's justice was swift and sure, and in the Empire, there was only one punishment for treason. What's more, the Federation was in a difficult position. It couldn't launch a full-scale attack to retrieve one man. A smaller-scale rescue would have a better chance, but not much. And when the Romulans discovered it, they'd be merciless. In the old days, Scotty had believed that anything was possible. But he was alone now, in a solitary shuttle with none of the backup he'd enjoyed in his miracle worker days. This time, there was no hope, none at all, unless... Checking the navigational computer, he saw that he could cover the distance in a reasonable time, possibly even quickly enough to save Spock. But there were too many variables, too many things Scotty didn't know and couldn't plan for. He quit that line of thinking, deeming it unproductive, then he reset his shuttle's course. Starbase 178 and what he needed were 12 hours away, but he had a lot of work to do before he arrived. Captain Jean-Luc Picard shifted uncomfortably in his ready-room seat. Better than anyone could possibly guess Picard mused. Edrich seemed happy that he didn't have to go into a long briefing on McCoy. Then our business has finished, Captain. The American Empire The American Empire The American Empire The American Empire The American Empire Scottie had barely landed the Goddard at Starbase 178 when he found himself rushing to catch the Starship tour. Thank you for your interest and enjoy your Starship adventure on the USS Yorktown. Scottie nodded, so far so good. Computer, is the unit operational? Has it been modified in any way? A ship like this stole that cloak from the Romulans, you know? The Starship got chased by three Romulan battle cruisers when it tried to get away. Man, that must have been something. After a couple of minutes, he caught sight of the youngster in front of a turbo lift and commanded him to halt. Reluctantly, the boy obeyed. But Scottie wasn't angry, not in the least. For the simple matter to halt the engine over mode and to lock out the shuttle bay, so the doors wouldn't open when the maintenance crew arrived. They knew it would be a simple matter for the star-based crew to recalibrate sensors and penetrate the obsolete cloaking system. But in those few minutes, the York town would make it well out of their range. He'd done it. Governor Tharis of Constanthes leaned back in his chair and eyed his ship. He was his chief of security. Tharis wondered if they knew how short their future would be. After all, he prided himself on meeting out swift and sure justice. At his approach, the traitors' heads turned.
