Nor when it's door opened, did he look back. He simply stepped inside, let the doors whisper closed again. For the first time in years, someone else was in charge of the Enterprise. McCoy tapped his communicator badge. Admiral McCoy to shuttle bay one. Is Commander Riker still there? Commander Riker is gone, sir. He and Commander Data and Commander LaForge have left in the adjustment. Is there anything I can help you with, sir? I guess not, Lieutenant. I just wanted to let them know that Captain Picard is no longer in charge here, but then they'll find that out soon enough. McCoy out. Sitting down in the Captain's chair, McCoy could feel Councillor Troy's scrutiny and her confusion. He turned to her. You're surprised, Councillor, don't be. Captain Picard and I had a little disagreement. That's all. I'll be running things till we've pried Spock loose from that den of vipers. Tapping his communicator again, McCoy looked up at the intercom, create hidden in the ceiling. This is Admiral McCoy. Until further notice, I'll be replacing Captain Picard as Commander of this vessel. I expect you to respond to my orders as you'd respond to his. That'll be all. Troy looked at him. Admiral, I know you are within your rights to assume command. However, it has been a long time since you've had occasion to deal with alien races. Stop right there, Councillor. I'm all too familiar with the Romulans. And they've got my friend. I'll be drawn and corded before I let... ...Warf cut him off before he could finish. Admiral McCoy, I have obtained the communications link with Constanthus. You will be speaking with Governor Farris. A moment later, the Governor's image filled the view screen. As far as McCoy could tell, Farris was a typical Romulan administrator, B.D.I.D., Wary, and not half as smart as he thought he was. Greetings, my name's McCoy, Leonard McCoy. I am Farris, Governor of Constanthus. And the reason for your communication? The Admiral shrugged. I wanted to see if we can't work something out with regard to those unificationists you're sitting on. Is it not customary to conduct negotiations with the homeworlds? Actually, we tried that. A fellow named Ereji and said he'd think about it. You know what that means, don't you? I'm no spring chicken, Governor. I don't have time for a runaround. Now, the way I see it, you're the one who captured the rebels. It makes sense to me that you'd be the one who decided their fates. The Admiral leaned forward in a conspiratorial kind of way. Governor, I'm presenting you with an opportunity. A chance for you to improve your position in the Empire without making martyrs out of those rebels. Farris seemed interested. Inwardly, McCoy congratulated himself. He had the Romulan right where he wanted him. The Admiral described the offer Picard had tendered Ereji and, however, in this version of the transaction, Farris would get credit for extracting the Empire from its pickle. And Ereji and, by contrast, would be made to look like a fool. The idea seemed to please the Governor. So, have we got a deal? I will consider it and return your communication when I have an answer for you. The Governor's image vanished from the view screen, replaced by the star field that had preceded it. Turning in his seat, the Admiral noticed that Counselor Troy was looking at him again. If anything, she seemed more concerned than before. Don't have a canary, Counselor. When it comes to Romulan's, the direct approach is the best approach. Trust me on this. But far from giving him her trust, Troy got up and left the command center. McCoy could feel the tension the Counselor had left in her wake, the chill. He ignored it. After all, as Picard himself had pointed out, people's lives depended on what they did here. And McCoy wasn't going to let anyone deter him from doing what he had to do. The General's At the helm of the Justman, Riker scanned his monitors as he approached the Romulan outpost at three quarters in Paul's speed. Their strategy was a simple one. They would pass by the outpost, locate Captain Scott, and beam him up. If all went well, they'd be heading for the neutral zone before Scott's captors at any notion he was gone. Data, who was sitting beside Riker, spoke up. Sensors show an orbiting vessel that could be the Yorktown. This would seem to confirm a conclusion that Captain Scott, stopping in mid-sentence the android, frowned ever so slightly. Commander, there is also a Romulan warbird in order. Riker heard a curse from the rear of the shuttle where Jordi was manning the Justman's transporter unit. Data turned to the first officer. I do not believe they have spotted us yet, Commander. They must be operating on passive sensors only. Still, I estimate they will detect us in no more than four and a half minutes. Riker thought for a moment. Data, can you tell me where the warbird's positioned with regard to the outpost? The android is second or two to assimilate the information on its monitors. The warbird appears to be on the opposite side of the planetoid from the ground installation. From our angle of approach, it is located just over the northern horizon. The first officer nodded. Good. Then with a small adjustment, we can place the planetoid between us and the warbird and still have line of sight access to the installation. If we're careful, we may be able to use the planetoid itself for cover and get close to the outpost without the warbird's knowing about it. Jordi sighed. But getting in is only half the problem, Commander. Even if we can do that and sneak Scott out, they're eventually going to realize he's gone and when they do, they'll have a warbird to stick on us. Riker looked at him. In that case, we'll have to find another way to elude it, or hope that one presents itself. He made the course adjustment. It took them out of their way and delayed their arrival at the planetoid. But it was necessary if they were going to keep the warbird in the dark. By the time they crept within transporter range, the first officer could see the planetoid through the observation port. It was a dead-grade rock devoid of even an atmosphere, featureless, except for the Romulan installation that clung to it like some kind of artificial octopus. Riker pointed to the spot on his monitor. There it is. Fortunately, a place that old isn't likely to have the sensor capacity to detect us at this range. Scan it for human life science data. The android complied. Unfortunately, it seemed they'd hit another snag. There appears to be some sort of magnetic shield around the central portion of the installation, Commander. No doubt, a measure designed to prevent just the sort of rescue we had in mind. Jordi chimed in from the rear of the shuttle. We can use the remote control bands to beam down and penetrate the shield on foot. Since the outer limits of the place are unshielded, all I need to do is find a blind spot in their sensor net. Riker nodded. Get to it, Jordi. Don't spare the horses. Riker looked around at his new surroundings. A moment ago, he'd been standing on the shuttle, waiting for Jordi to complete the transporter protocols. Now he was in a narrow, poorly lit corridor somewhere in an outer arm of the sprawling Romulan installation just outside the magnetic shield. Data and Jordi were right beside him. Like the first officer they were armed with phasers and trike orders and each of the more remote transporter control band. Together they scanned for approaching Romulans, the word heading within 100 meters. Riker considered the stretch of corridor that led toward the center of the installation, where they would undoubtedly find Captain Scott. They wouldn't have made any sense to erect a shield around part of the outpost and then hold him somewhere else. Silently, he took the lead. They passed through the shield without incident. Then for several long, tense minutes, they continued along one corridor after the next, deftly approaching the center of the place by the most obscure route possible. When their trike orders picked up a couple of guards cutting across their path, they retreated to the closest intersection and concealed themselves until the Romulans had gone by. Then they resumed their journey. A short time later, they entered what looked like a detention area, though the cells they could see were quite empty. The first officer checked his trike order for human life signs. Strangely, he couldn't find any. He shook his head. How could that be? Looking up, he saw the Jordi and Data were just as puzzled as he was, wherein blazes was Captain Scott. Suddenly, the android's head snapped about. He gestured to indicate something up ahead of him. Most likely the first officer thought another couple of guards passing by. Then Data's head snapped around again, this time in the opposite direction, and again in the third direction. By then, Riker knew there was something going on. He brushed past the others and stuck his head out into the corridor. The next thing he knew there was a blinding flash of sapphire energy, a flash that might have caught him square between the eyes of Data had and hauled him back. Jordi shook his head. We're surrounded, aren't we? Data nodded. Yes, we are. All avenues of egress are blocked. The engineer turned to Riker. Your call, Commander! The first officer tightened his grasp on his phaser. If the Romulans were onto them, there wasn't much chance of their getting away. On the other hand, he didn't love the idea of being taken prisoner. Follow me, gentlemen. This is called making a break for it. Diving out into the corridor, Riker rolled and came up, firing. He didn't have to look behind him to know that Data and Jordi were right behind him, giving the Romulans all they could handle. Then he heard the sound of footfalls behind him. Glancing over his shoulder, he saw that another pack of Romulans had caught up with, cursing he turned to fire back and back. But this time he wasn't so lucky. It has rubbed her beam, caught him in the shoulder, and spun him around. A second one swept his leg out from under him. The last thing he recalled was twisting awkwardly in the air, and wondering how much it would hurt when he landed. Proconsularegians stood with his hands clasped behind his back and surveyed the bridge of the Federation Starship. The registry on the exterior of the hall suggested this was the York town, the Starship employed more than a century ago. But it had a Romulan cloaking device. One of the original modules developed on the home world, long before cloaking technology was perfected. Of course the device had since been upgraded and by someone who knew what he was doing. But its rudimentary construction was still eminently recognizable. How had the Federation gotten its hands on it? None of the records he could find gave him any answer, but then even a proconsul couldn't access quite everything in the Imperial databanks. Now there was a bigger question. Why had this vessel crossed the Federation neutral zone? Commander Grandjock had called its pilot a madman, and yet a madman with a talent to run a starship on his own. A raging approached the red orange railing that encircled the command center and ran his fingertips along its surface. A middle-aged human on an antiquated vessel. A mission that defied all logic. The proconsul sighed. It was something missing here. Some bit of information he lacked. But what could it be? Proconsul. A raging turned and saw one of his aides approaching. Data pad in hand. The man's name was Tiroc. Your Eminence. There is an energy leak in the vessel's warp engine. A raging looked at him. An energy leak is a dangerous? No proconsul. What's more, it does not appear to be accidental. A raging regarded Tiroc. Not accidental are you saying the human sabotaged this ship? Not sabotaged your Eminence simply created a condition which would direct a pulse out into space. I believe it may be an attempt to communicate with the Federation. Certainly that theory would be supported by the direction in which the energy is leaking. Though it would require a more thorough examination to determine if there is a code involved. The proconsul didn't need to conduct an investigation. He could feel the truth of the matter in his bones. More than likely, Tiroc was right. The energy leak was a means of sending a message to the Federation, a call for help perhaps. He clapped Tiroc on the shoulder. You've done well, Tiroc. Now do something more. See to it that the human's activities are curtailed until I transport to the surface, which will be in a matter of myths. Of course, your Eminence. As Tiroc made contact with the ground installation, the proconsul seethed. Clearly this madman wasn't mad at all. It was one thing to commandeer an ancient starship and try to take it behind Romulan lines. But to devise such a clever way of calling for assistance. Proconsul, Herragion turned, surprised at the alarm in Tiroc's voice. The man looked ill. What is it, Tiroc? The... the human, your Eminence. He's gone. His anger mounting even higher, Herragion whipped out his own communicator and made contact with the base. He would soon straighten this out. Commander Barnock. A moment later, the base commander responded to his voice tremulous. I don't know what to say, your Eminence. The human was under the watch of... Herragion interrupted the conversation. Your Eminence senses show that one of our transport vessels has broken orbit without authorization and is leaving at maximum speed. Herragion couldn't believe it. He terminated the communication and initiated another one. This time with the commander of the vengeance. This is the proconsul. Bring me aboard. Now! In seconds, he found himself on the Warbirds Bridge. He turned to Commander Hayjack. There's a transport vessel that's just broken orbit, Hayjack. I want it pursued. Hayjack barked some orders. Immediately the bridge through sets of works. By the time the proconsul took up a position in front of the viewscreen, it had obtained an image of the departing transport. The vengeance was a good deal faster, Herragion assured himself. The human would not get away, despite everything. I want the pilot of that vessel taken alive. Hayjack, he owes me an explanation and a great deal more. Hayjack turned to his weapons officer. Car get the transport's warp drive. Warp drive targeted, Commander. Photon torpedo is ready. Hayjack's eyes narrowed. He gave the order to fire. As Heragion watched the viewscreen, he saw the transport racked by a barrage of photon torpedo. All of them focused on the portion of the vessel where the warp drive was most vulnerable. He smiled as the transport dropped out of war. Then, before his startled eyes, the transport blew out. The shards of its hole went careening in all directions, including light and the viewscreen. The proconsul realized that his mouth was hanging open. He shut it, then cast a glance over his shoulder at Hayjack. I said I wanted him alive, Hayjack. Hayjack shook his head, disbelieving. I don't understand your MS. Those torpedoes shouldn't have caused an explosion. They should have disabled the warp drive, nothing more. The Heragion turned back to the viewscreen, where the fragments of the transport were still tumbling through space. Perhaps the Commander was correct. Perhaps the human had seen that he would be caught and interrogated, and escaped the only way he could by destroying himself. But this wasn't over yet, Heragion resolved. Clearly, they knew what the human looked like, and he'd shown up in a Starfleet uniform. That meant there was a good chance of their matching him with a Starfleet personnel file. Open a secure channel for the home world, Hayjack. As the Commander moved to it to comply, Heragion promised himself he would get to the bottom of this, one way or another. Spock surveyed his followers' faces. At the start of their captivity, they had been willing to learn. In some cases, even eager. But as the day of their trial came closer, their tempers had flared. There had been disagreements, bitter words. Some arguments had nearly come to blows. He'd had to concede finally that these were Romulans, not Volcanals. No amount of education would change that, even if they were to live many years instead of the single day left of it. Yet they were here now, looking to him for a palliative that would relieve them of the pain they were in. And as their teacher, he would do his best to ease their passage. Above all, the universe is ordered by logic, in both the realm of normal space that we inhabit, and the other dimensions we have observed. Even in the chaos of subspace mechanics, we can see the elegant symmetry of the universe. For the moment his students seemed to forget their plight, caught up in the hopefulness of his lesson, encouraged, he went on. Sirak tells us to find order in chaos. When asked about the possibility of life after death, he said, it would be illogical for the universe to create complex, reasoning beings only to dispose of their minds when their bodies no longer functioned. That principle was the basis of the Vulcan practice of preserving the katra, the sentient soul of the dying in the hall of thought. Unfortunately, none of his students would have their minds saved that way, but he didn't dwell on that fact. We will live on in one manner or another. When the tyranny of the empire is but a distant memory, what we do here and now will be remembered. For a moment there was silence. Then one by one, his students raised their hands in the Vulcan salute. It was the equivalent of applause, and it swept through their ranks as a wind sweeps through the desert. Scraces was the last to respond, but in the end he raised his hand as well. The Vulcan felt a rush of pride, a natural response, which it would have been illogical to deny. He had reached all of those before him, even the difficult Scraces. It was a satisfying moment, and it was made more precious because he would enjoy so few of them before the Romulan sentence was carried out. Nodding almost imperceptibly to his students, Spock raised his hand to return the salute. Arraging regarded the three Starfleet officers crumbled on the floor of the corridor, surrounded by Commander Barnock and a dozen of his guards. One of the intruders was clearly human, the other two he wasn't so sure about. After all, one had a mechanism that halfway encircled his head, some device which the Pro-Consul had never seen before, and the third seemed too pallid to be a human. Arraging stroked his chin, and they were trying to free the other prisoner you say, the one who took his own life just a little while ago. Barnock was eager to be of service. Yes, your Eminence, we can think of no other reason for their being here. Bring them all to the nearest cell, Commander. I want to interrogate them at my leisure. And Barnock, don't let these slip away as the last one did. I will double the watch, Pro-Consul. Barnock gestured to his waiting subordinates. Immediately, his men bent to the task of lifting and transporting the prisoners. Arraging considered what their presence here meant. Both the original prisoner and his mission were important to Starfleet, or they wouldn't have sent a team here in an attempt to retrieve him. Now, Arraging was more eager than ever to identify the mysterious individual who had destroyed himself trying to escape from the outpost, and to determine why the man had crossed the neutral zone in the first place. Of course, with his new group of prisoners in hand, he was that much closer to finding out. The The Alone in his quarters, Picard stared at his personal terminal and re-ran the log of McCoy's conversation with Governor Thoris. It was all he could do to restrain himself. Somewhere across the imaginary border of the neutral zone, three of his people were risking their lives to rescue one of the greatest figures in the history of the Federation. If their mission had been fraught with danger before, it was now doubly so. He thought about asking Dr. Crusher to judge McCoy incompetent to run the ship. That was her prerogative as chief medical officer. But she wouldn't do it unless the admiral really was incompetent. And as much as the captain disagreed with McCoy's practices, he couldn't say for certain that the man was unfit. Come. The door slid aside, revealing his Klingon tactical officer. Warf peered at the captain. Sir, I have accumulated additional data on Romulan ship deployments. The gleam in the Klingon's eyes told Picard there was something interesting about the information Warf had gathered. However, the captain reflected, he was no longer in command. The Klingon seemed to see that in his expression. I told the admiral I had this information, sir. However, he did not seem very interested. I was advised to... ...file it. Picard gestured to a chair. In that case, Lieutenant? Have a seat. The Klingon moved to a chair on the other side of the room. Apparently, sir, the sector of space to which the Romulan ships have been sent is bounded by the border opposite the neutral zone. They share this border with a race called the Stug, which cut off relations with the Federation recently for no apparent reason. The Stug are a formidable people, according to all records of our dealings with them. However, they have never succeeded in unifying themselves sufficiently to pose a threat, either to the Federation or anyone else. Picard frowned. So, why would the Romulans have committed so many of their vessels to Stug space? It was clear from the Klingon's expression that he didn't know. Picard sighed. Continue to keep an eye on the situation as a wolf. Perhaps the Romulans, or even the Stug, will do something that will illuminate their motives for us. The tactical officer inclined his head. Aye, sir. Without further ado, he rose and made his exit. The captain watched the door slide closed behind war. Like the Klingon, he wished he knew more about what was going on out there. But as long as the Enterprise was someone else's to command, he could only watch and wait.
description: In this episode of "Star Trek Audiobook - Crossover: Episode 1", Jonathan Frakes narrates Michael Jan Friedman's adaptation of Choose 2 Audio. Spock meets Balan and his followers in the storage chamber on Constantus, where they're trying to unify with Romulans after an encounter that leaves them confused about Sirok teachings. The meeting ends in chaos when a Romulan soldier disruptor attack results in several unificationists' deaths. Despite hope initially shown by the Constantherians, their faces now reflect despair as they accept their fate under Imperial control. This episode delves into themes of cultural unity and human sacrifice amidst political tensions within the Star Trek universe.

Keerin of the House of Mistral led at a slow breath as his heart slammed against his chest. He ignored the stars that hung in space around his high-powered fighter-shuttlecraft. Instead, his full concentration was on the great mothership of the Gratsy-Mills. It loomed in front of Keerin, dark blue and oblong, with towers jutting out at odd angles. Swarming about it, insect might were a variety of single and double-pilot ships. They were small, maneuverables, and deadly. Never in Keerin's 18 years have you been disnervous. He made his final weapons check. He was ready. And then a call came from one of the Gratsy-Unis patrol ships demanding that he stayed his business. This is Keerin of the House of Mistral. I go where I wish, I do what I wish, and I take what I wish. Keerin took one more look at the battle lane, belted himself in, and slammed into overdrive. His craft shot forward, dipping just under the two fighter ships that were trying to intercept him. He dropped like a stone, then leveled off. The fighters banked around, came after him, weapons blasting. Keerin slammed into reverse. The fighters shot cast him, leaping straight into his computer-conscious sights. Keerin opened fire. The twin guns of his shuttled blasting. He clipped the wings of both fighters, sending them into a spiral. Momentarily clear, he dove towards the mother ship. He could see the landing bay was directly ahead of him. Suddenly he was hit. He lurched wildly, trying to get the shuttle under control. It hurtled into the docking wall. The walls tried past him the blur. The bottom of the shuttle sparked and squealed. It spun about, half turned. The rear ends slammed into the wall. Keerin was forced back against his seat, gasping and dizzy. His head was still ringing from the ears splitting howl of metal on metal. He could see men of the Gratcyonas running towards him, shouting and pointing. He leapt from his crippled ship, knocked beside the nearest guard, and charged into the main section of the mother ship. The corridors were large, with elaborate swirls of blue and orange. Keerin began to run. A right turn, another right, a left hand. He skidded to a halt. Keerin was standing in the open doorway of the Grand Court of Gratcyonas. The court was crowded with friends and family, and everyone was staring at Keerin as if he had been... expected. The head of the house of Gratcyonas took a step forward. He was massive, with a shock of red hair swept back over his gleaming blue face. He was known simply as Gratcyonas, which was the hereditary title. Sarah, his daughter, stood next to him. She was watching Keerin's every move, hungrily. Gratcyonas walked to within a few paces of Keerin, and then stopped. His arms folded. Yes. Keerin's mouth moved, but nothing came out. Then he saw Sarah mouthing words. The words tradition dictated, he should say. I, Keerin, heir to the house of Mistral, come to thee as a supplicant, and as one who demands the hand of thy most honorable daughter in marriage. And if I do not grant it, then I shall fight thee for her. Keerin drove as hard a punch as he could at Gratcyonas' face. Gratcyonas caught the boy's fist effortlessly. He had a grip like steel, and to Keerin's astonishment, he laughed loudly. Thou as shown, spirit, son of Mistral. If she will have thee, then the hand of my only daughter is yours. Keerin crossed quickly to Sarah. You'll have me? Of course. Keerin's voice dropped to all his spurt. How did I do, Sarah? Of fine, Keerin. You did just fine. In the conference lounge of the Enterprise, Captain Picard smiled at his officers whom he had called together. Picard seemed in particularly good humor. Gentlemen and ladies, Starfleet has chosen us to act as hosts to a wedding for a very important group of people, the Tzarin. Not an unusual occasion in and of itself, of course, but this is a cross-marriage between the houses of Nostral and Gratcyonas. Data, if you wouldn't mind. Yes, Captain. The Tzarin are a space-going race of merchants, somewhat similar to the Earth peoples known as Chipses. The Tzarin usually travel in groups of two or more houses for mutual protection. The Nostral and Gratcyonas are two of the oldest and most influential houses. There has been a rivalry between the two for many years, but solid business dealings have prevented it from developing into hostilities. Picard nodded approvingly and turned to his officers. It has, in fact, developed into something far better. The son of the head of the Nostral family is marrying the daughter of the head of the Gratcyonas family. Doctor Crusher could not contain her enthusiasm. Oh, how sweet! Like Romeo and Juliet! Yes, Doctor. The play by your William Shakespeare, a treat is on parental neglect and teen suicide. It's a bit more than that data. That play contains some of the most famous and moving romantic passages in history. By in my youth, I was in a production of Romeo and Juliet. I didn't know that, Captain. Did you play Romeo? Ah, Mercutio. Prior Lawrence. No, Doctor. The point is that... Captain, whom did you play? I played Juliet's nurse. It's a superb heart. Oh, yes, Captain. I'm sure you were adorable. The point I'm trying to make is that in this case the houses are not feuding. It's been very civilized. They have specific courting customs which the young man, Kieran, accomplish with flying colors. So you see, Mr. Data, there will be no teen suicides. Now, Tazarin Protocol, in this case, requires that a third party perform the wedding ceremony. Naturally, I shall do the honors. We will rendezvous with the Tazarin in 72 hours. In addition, several races who are principal customers of the Tazarin will be sending delegates as well. I will need a detailed list of all representatives as well as profiles on any security risks. Wharf's scowl seemed even darker than usual. Is there another problem, Mr. Wharf? Is it necessary to turn the Enterprise into a catering hall? The mission is to promote interstellar harmony and goodwill. I can assure you, Mr. Wharf, we are not a catering hall. Picard here. Captain, this is Guynan. I have that assortment of hors d'oeuvres you asked me to put together. Picard felt the uncomfortable glare of the Klingon security officer upon him, while Beverly Crusher and Deanna Troy discussed the advantages of hot dogs and buns over miniature quiche lorains. Picard cleared his throat. Guynan, we'll get back to you on that. Much later. Guynan stared out of the viewports of the Ten-Ford Lounge. She was smiling, and then suddenly her eyes narrowed. Something was wrong. But what? At that moment, Captain Picard entered the Ten-Ford Lounge, accompanied by the fathers of the bride and groom. They were there to inspect the Ten-Ford Lounge, since it would be used to host one of the many intended receptions. Guynan immediately composed herself. Guynan was struck by the difference in the fathers. Gratzionis being loud and boisterous, while Nestrao was soft-spoken and somewhat adenoidal. This, gentlemen, is our Ten-Ford Lounge, one of the places that you will be invited to use in planning the festivities. How long do you anticipate requiring the Enterprise facilities? Oh, I thought you knew, Captain. A week. A week. A week? Nestrao, are you serious? An entire week? Of course he's serious, Picard. It's customary. Are you saying our children are not worth it? Of course not, Gratzionis. But we have a level of discipline and order that must be maintained. I cannot tolerate the disruption of my ship or her crew. We are all quite clear on this point. Good. Now, you wanted to see the bridge. Picard always took pride in the ship, but rarely more so than when truly knowledgeable people looked the Enterprise over with nods of approval. There were murmurs of most impressive and then abruptly, warred interrupted. Incoming transmission from another arriving wedding guest. It's someone who has been here before. On Audio-Lutenant? Enterprise, this is the Ambassador shuttle from Beta-Z, prepared to transport over the Delicate from Beta-Z. A daughter of the Fifth House. A daughter of the Fifth House. A holder of the Sacred Chalice of Rakes. A holder of the Sacred Chalice of Rakes. Transporter room, transport over the representative from Beta-Z. Oh, her retainer, Mr. Hulme, is undoubtedly with her. Aire to the Holy Rings of Beta-Z. Aire to the Holy Rings of Enterprise. She's gone. Good riddance. Was there difficulty, pilot? Oh, that's the last time I transport that woman. I sympathize about her being in mourning, but she never shut up the whole trip. Diana Troy's dark eyes white men's astonishment, but that was nothing compared to her amazement when the shuttle pilot informed her that Bloxana Troy was in mourning for her daughter. Diana barely waited until Riker Picard and Data had left her mother's quarters before she turned to Bloxana, her slim body shaking with barely contained fury. Mr. Hulme was unpacking Bloxana's wardrobe, and virtually every dress was the black of a woman in mourning. Mother, do you realize how embarrassing it is for me to explain to the others that you are acting as if I'm dead just because of some archaic Beta-Z tradition called the Abrax? They're not dead in the physical sense, little one. Just dead in the hope that you'll ever find a mate to share the rest of your life. Perhaps others could ignore the Abrax, but being a daughter of the Fifth House requires that I uphold all Beta-Z traditions. Mother, the Abrax was from a time when life was charter, and a woman's role was to be wife and mother. So if you weren't married by a certain age, the family would go into mourning very loudly. That way they could attract someone who needed a good wife in the same way he needed a good farm animal, and he knew the family would not be too fussy. But life is different now, mother. description: In this episode of Star Trek: Q In-law 1 of 2 from Simon & Schuster Audio Works, Major Barrett and John Delances present the story of Keerin of the House of Mistral as he makes his way through the bustling Grand Court of Gratcyonas during an audience with his family. The journey is fraught with tension, as Keerin tries to navigate the expectations and scrutiny of his noble lineage while dodging the hostile Gratsy-Unis ships that are following him. As Keerin's head begins to ring from a metal-on-metal collision in his shuttlecraft, he finds himself standing before a massive red-haired man known simply as Gratcyonas. The air is thick with tension, and it becomes clear that Keerin has been expecting something different from this meeting with the family of the High Queen of Gratsy-Mills.

description: In this episode of the Q In-law podcast, Sarah discovers she is a wizard with the power to see into the minds of mortals and understand their deepest desires. She soon realizes Kieran loves her more than anyone else but also reveals his past relationship with an astral body and his feelings for her. The Q then appears in two couples' dreams and hearts, showing them that humans are not always warlike but can create as well.

transcript: A few minutes later, the card found data waiting for him. Mr. Data, how long until we've completed the Tachyon Scan? Data hardly found it necessarily to think about it. Approximately one hour or forty-five minutes, sir. Good. Once that's done, I want you to analyze the information, find a way to shut the anomaly down, but I don't want to do anything that will exacerbate the problem. Data nodded. I could prepare a risk analysis on whatever solution I devise. Good idea, Mr. Data. Without any further ado, Data made his exit, intent on the task ahead of him. The captain watched him go, then picked up the pad and walked over to the observation portal. It was just starting to feel that they might have a fighting chance against the anomaly when everything changed. The card found himself on a craggy ledge. Looking down, he saw that he was perched high above a vast, chaotic soup. A miasma of steaming lava and bubbling gases. It was hot here, so impressively hot that he already found himself perspiring. And the air was full of fine black flax. Cue, standing beside him. Welcome home, captain. The card wiped the sweat from his forehead. He honestly didn't know what Cue was talking about. Think back, Picard. Don't you recognize your old stomping grounds? This is Earth. France, in fact. About oh, three and a half billion years ago. Give or take any on us, though. Smells awful, doesn't it? All that sulfur and volcanic ash. I really must speak to the maid. His eyes stinging from the debris in the atmosphere. The card turned to Cue. Is there a point to all this? Or are we just on another of your merry travel logs? Cue looked a scance. Travel logs, you wound me, John Luke. All I'm doing is trying to further your miserable education. Indeed, Cue. And exactly what am I to learn in this place? How to asphyxiate myself? Cue smiled knowingly and pointed to the sky. Look, pretty impressive, wouldn't you say? As Picard followed Cue's gesture, his mouth went even drier. All he could see from horizon to horizon, filling the heavens with its ominous brilliance, with the spatial anomaly that they'd located in the defrancest. But here, it was even bigger. The anomaly is here. And Earth? Cue impatiently explained. At this point in history, the anomaly is everywhere. It has filled the entire quadrant of your galaxy. Picard's eyes were watering from the ashes in the air. He tried to make sense of the fact that the further back in time he went, the anomaly grew larger. A abruptly Cue took off along the length of the ledge. John Luke, quickly, there's something over here I want you to see. Cue knelt by a small muddy pond at one end of the ledge. The captain went over to see what Cue was looking at. Together, they peered down into the murky water. Finally, Picard asked the inevitable question. Cue, what am I looking at? Why, I'm all in Capitan. This is you. And may I say, you've never looked better. Picard found himself becoming annoyed. Cue was toying with him. Me, Cue. I'm serious, John Luke. Well, in a manner of speaking, you see, right here, life is about to form on this planet for the very first time. Two proteins are about to combine and form the first amino acid. One of the building blocks of what you laughingly call life. Despite himself, Picard was intrigued. Impossible as it was to see anything. He couldn't help but lean closer to the surface of the pond. Suddenly, Cue recoiled, disappointment etched into his features. Oh, no, why? Nothing happened. Nothing at all. Picard stared at him through eyes rubbed raw by primordial pollution. What do you mean nothing happened? Don't tell me you stopped it. Cue looked at him and wagged his finger. Now, John Luke, we've talked at length about your incessant need to blame me for all your problems. You did this all by your lonesome, I assure you. The Captain frowned. I did nothing, Cue. Cue stood and pointed to the sky. Oh, contrary, you did that. And that disrupted the beginning of life. Picard looked down again at the murky waters and then looked up, intending to question Cue further. Picard shifted in time and was looking at Deanna Troy instead. By her uniform and her hairstyle, he could tell he was back in the past. Troy spoke as if he were answering a question that he had just posed to her. Dr. Salard had reported that 23 children on board had contracted some kind of illness. She said their tissues appear to be reverting to some earlier state of development. She thinks it's been caused by the anomaly, sir. Picard nodded and turned to Tasha. Lieutenant informed Starfleet command that we believe the anomaly has toxic effects. I already have, sir. They've ordered us to withdraw from the neutral zone and to escort the Pilgrim's ships back to Federation territory. The Captain considered the order grimly. Tell Starfleet what remaining here. However, we'll tell the Pilgrim's ships to withdraw. Tasha's eyes flashed in cool anger. I'm afraid I can't let you do that, sir. We've received direct orders to leave the neutral zone, sir. There are children dying, children we may be able to save if we act now. At our presence here is in direct violation of the Treaty of Algernon. Picard remained calm, despite the stakes they were playing for. Are you questioning my orders, Lieutenant? Tasha took a breath to steady herself. Yes, sir. I am. And unless you take this ship back to Federation territory, I'm prepared to relieve you and take command of this vessel. Picard hadn't been prepared for that. He looked around and saw the rest of the bridge crew was watching the confrontation. Picard eyed Tasha. He wanted to tell her that they would grow to know and trust one another. He wanted to say that one day she would be willing to lay down her life for him. For now, all he could do was appeal to his officers' pride and integrity. Lieutenant, you are coming close to Mutiny. Worf stepped forward. It would not be Mutiny if the ship's counselor certified you unfit to command. All eyes fell on Troy. She frowned as she felt the burden of her task. She looked at Picard, seeking information not only with her eyes, but with her betazoid talents. Captain, do you intend to obey the order from Starfleet? There were a number of ways he could have handled the situation, a number of ways he could have answered her, but the counselor would detect any attempt at subterfuge. He opted for the simple truth. No, I do not. And I'm sure that you all want an explanation, and I could give you one. I could tell you that an omnipotent being from another space-time continuum has been shifting me through three time periods. That he has threatened the destruction of mankind, and that it has upped me to save humanity. But you would probably call me insane. He turned to Troy. It all falls on your shoulders, counselor. Have I really demonstrated a lack of mental competence or evil intent? What am I simply following my own conscience, trying to do what I believe is best for the ship and for the Federation? He waited while she probed and reprobed his consciousness, scanning for signs of malice or duplicity. A moment later, she announced her verdict. You're right, Captain. I don't sense any mental instability or malicious intent. Therefore, I can see no grounds to find you unfit for command. Picard turned to Tasha. You can still attempt to relieve me if you wish. Tasha shook her head. No, sir. I may be many things, but I'm not a mutineer. If Troy says you're fit for command, then I'll do my duty. Very well then, Lieutenant. Contact the lead to Relian ship. Tell them we'll be evacuating all civilians and nonessential personnel from the Enterprise to their vessels. Once we've completed the evacuation, they are to leave the neutral zone. Turning to data and O'Brien, he told them to follow him. A few minutes later, they were down in engineering and checking the monitors. Data seemed just the slightest bit frustrated. Captain, I do not see any way to dissipate the anomaly. O'Brien swore softly. Sir, the anomalies output is greater than the combined energy of our entire fleet. It's just too big for us to handle. Picard thought for a moment. Let's concentrate on how this anomaly was initially formed. Speculation. Data was the first to respond. Temporal ruptures in the space-time continuum are rarely a naturally occurring phenomenon. It is therefore most likely that this anomaly was caused by an outside catalyst. Our tachyon pulse has been unable to completely penetrate the anomaly. If we had information about the center of the phenomenon, we might have a basis for speculation. Mr. Data, can you find a way to scan the interior? In theory, Captain, a tomographic imaging scanner capable of multi-phasic resolution would be able to penetrate this much interference. But such a device is still only theoretical. Abruptly, Picard realized that he'd shifted again. He was no longer in the past, in engineering, now he was back in the present. At the aft station on the Enterprise's bridge, Data was still with him. More importantly, there was an opportunity here. In the past, they'd recognized a need for more information about the anomaly's internal workings. Mr. Data, do we have a tomographic imaging scanner on board? Yes, sir. Can you use to scan the center of the anomaly? Data began to scan. Sir, there is a great deal of interference. But I am getting some unusual readings. And the captain's head was suddenly full of images and concepts he couldn't begin to comprehend. It was stag, overwhelming. Q went on. His voice, a distant drone. The real voyage of exploration has yet to begin, Jean-Luc. Avoid vastly unlike any other in your experience. But it has nothing to do with mapping, scar systems and charting nebulae. This time his memories were clear and complete. He remembered all that had happened. Because of that, the vents could not help but pursue a different course. Troy put her hand on his arm. Is something wrong, sir? The card shook his head. Not at all. In fact, I think I'll go back to bed. I could really do with some sleep. description: In this episode titled "All Good Things - Side 4," Captain Picard finds himself on Earth billions of years ago in the midst of a powerful spatial anomaly, and Cue, the card's friend, guides him through their chaotic environment with humor. The two navigate challenges such as intense heat and toxic gases while searching for a way to shut down the anomaly. Despite Cue's teasing, Picard becomes increasingly annoyed by his antics.

Once more, for old times, he grinned, knowing exactly where she meant. As he had a thousand times on the Enterprise, he held up his hand in that old familiar way. Engage. The card looked around and saw that he was no longer aboard the past year. He was back on the Enterprise in the past. O'Brien cast a quarulous look at him. Engaged to wear, sir. Taking a deep breath to steady himself, Picard studied the view screen. It showed him the sun and several planets that constituted the Chavez system. But that was no longer his objective. Mr. O'Brien said course for the Devron system and engage at Wharf 9. Troy looked at him, concerned evident in her dark eyes. Sir, the Devron system is inside the neutral zone. Tasha chimed in as well from her position at tactical. We've received no orders to enter the zone, sir. The captain cast a withering glance at her. I'm aware of that, Lieutenant. Carry out my orders, chief. Picard could tell that worried looks were being exchanged behind his back. He did his best to ignore them. Lieutenant Yarr, contact Farpoint Station. I want to speak with Commander Riker. In a few moments, the image of young, beardless Will Riker sprang into view. Commander Riker, I just wanted to let you know we won't be picking you up at Farpoint Station as scheduled. Riker seemed mildly disturbed. I see. May I ask why? Not at this time. His exec showed a little surprise, but he didn't act on it. And how long do you expect to be delayed, sir? Picard shook his head. I'm not sure at the moment, however, I'll keep you updated. Please inform Dr. Crusher and Lieutenant LaFarge about delay as well. Understood, sir. After Picard brought the transmission to an end, he glanced up at the view screen once again to see the stars. And he felt time shift again. The image of a Romulan commander filled with the view screen. He was back in the present. The Romulan was Tomalock. Picard had run into this craggy-faced Romulan before, and he looked every bit as formidable as on those previous occasions. So, Captain, how long shall we stare at each other across the neutral zone? That is another alternative, you know. And what is that? It's obvious that we're both here for the same reason, to find out more about the anomaly in the Devaron system. We could each send one ship into the neutral zone with the sole purpose of investigating the anomaly. Picard could see the Romulan silently weighing the details of the proposition. At last, Tomalock nodded. It is a great one ship from each side, but I warn you, if another Federation starship tries to enter the zone, you needn't make threats. I think we're all aware of the consequences. Very well. See you in the Devaron system, Captain. A moment later, the Romulan was gone, replaced by a static starfield full of neutral zone constellations. Picard had turned to the officer who was sitting at Khan. Set calls for the Devaron system, Ensign, warp 5. Engage? It didn't take long to reach the Devaron system and discover that something there was well worth the trip. Data swiveled in his chair. According to our sensors, we have located the anomaly. Geordi whistled from his engineering station. I've never seen anything like that. On the screen, the anomaly was a riotous blaze of color. He just threw with shafts of silver light. It was both spectacular and frightened. Picard had turned to Data who was sitting at ops. Full scan, Mr. Data. Captain watched Data's fingers fly over his controls. Suddenly, Picard had the strangest feeling that he had made another time shift. A quick look around confirmed it. Tasha was a tactical. He was back in the past. Data turned to glance back over his shoulder at Picard. We are approaching the Devaron system, Captain. Sensors are picking up a large subspace anomaly directly ahead. All stop, on screen. As before, the view screen showed him the conflagration of temporal energies that comprise the spatial anomaly. This time, however, it took up a good deal more of the screen, who's bigger than in the present. Full scan, Mr. Data. Taking a couple of steps forward, the Captain appeared at the screen. Again, he felt himself shift in time. The anomaly was gone from the view screen, which now displayed a single yellow sun and three lifeless nondescript planets. His thoughts were so muddled, his brain so unresponsive, that he knew he was in the future again. Data was at an aft console, working with Leforge as war flocked on. I made a complete scan of the Devaron system. Sensors showed nothing out of the ordinary. Picard walked over to the aft console. His heart was thudding against his ribs. Surely they had made some mistake. But I've already seen it in the other two, the other two time periods. There should be a huge spatial anomaly here. Leforge looked up. I'm sorry, sir, but I've conducted a full sensor sweep out to one light year from the past year. No temporal anomalies or anything even resembling one. Beverly walked over to join Picard and the others at the science station. It wasn't the result she had hoped for. Her heart went out to Jean-Luc. However, the evidence was undeniable. There was nothing to be seen here, nothing at all. But Picard was insistent. Have you scanned the subspace bandwidth? Geordi nodded. Yes, sir, the subspace barrier is a little thin in this region of space, but that's not unusual. In other words, we still haven't got anything to hang our hat on. The older Picard was bewildered. I don't understand. I've already seen it in the other two. The other two time periods. Why isn't it here? Warf, who had been working on a neighboring console, suddenly looked up with concern and addressed Beverly. Captain, I have been monitoring Klingon communication channels and several warships have been dispatched to this sector. They are searching for a renegade Federation vessel. Picard tugged at Beverly's sleeve. You're not thinking about leaving, are you? Jean-Luc, there's nothing here. There should be. There has to be. Turning to data, he leaned over and grabbed him by the shoulders. There must be some other way to scan for temporal disturbances, something that is not covered in a normal sense of sweep. Data considered the suggestion. There are several methods of detecting temporal disturbances, but we are limited by the range of equipment on the past year. This ship is designed primarily for medical emergencies, not a scientific research. Beverly interposed herself between the two of them. Jean-Luc, we've done all we can. We have to head back to Federation territory. Data went on, unperturbed. However, it may be possible to modify the warp deflector to emit an inverse tachyon pulse, which could scan beyond the subspace barrier. That slim hope changed Picard's demeanor again. All of a sudden, he was shaking his fists in the air in front of him. Very good, make it so. Beverly turned to data. Wait a minute, data, how long would this take? To make the modifications and search the entire Devron system will take approximately 14 hours. Wharf side. Those Klingon warships are anywhere from 8 to 11 hours away. Beverly knew she'd have to be crazy to pursue this thing any further, even if Data did give Jean-Luc's theory some credence. But then, she'd done crazy things before. Alright Data, begin modifying the tachyon pulse. Ensign Chilton lay in a course back to the Federation. If we haven't found anything in 6 hours, we're heading back at maximum warp. Picard protested. 6 hours aren't enough, Beverly. We have to stay here until we find it no matter how long it takes. Beverly felt something boil up inside her. Ensign Chilton, carry out my orders. Jean-Luc, may I see you for a moment. Without another word, she led him into her radio. As the doors closed behind them, she whirled on him, her face flushed with anger. Don't you ever question my orders on the bridge of my ship again. You would never have tell her that kind of behavior back in the Enterprise, and I won't hear. He had to concede that she had a point. You're right. I was out of line, it won't happen again. But you have to understand, the stakes here are enormous. You have assured me that all of humanity will be destroyed. I know Jean-Luc, and that's why I'm willing to stay here a little while longer and keep looking. But I also want you to consider the possibility that none of what you're saying is real. It was like a slap in the face. He took a step backwards. What are you saying? Beverly moved toward him. She took his hands and hers. Jean-Luc, I care for you too much not to tell you the truth. You have advanced eeromotic syndrome. I have to weigh the possibility that all of this, anomaly, the threat to mankind, everything, is in your mind. I'll stay here for another six hours. And that's it. Then we're heading home. And I want you to remember something. If it were anyone but you, anyone at all, I wouldn't have come here in the first place. I wouldn't even have considered her. Releasing his hands, she returned to her bridge and left him in the room to Simmerdah. Alone, Picard mauled the whole thing over. He had pushed her, pushed all of his old friends about as far as he could. But he could push them no farther. Suddenly he got the sense that he was no longer by himself. There was someone in back of him. Whirling, he saw what looked like a parody of an elderly man. Someone with bags under his eyes, a mop of scraggly gray hair and baggy ill-fitting clothes. The grizzled old fellow was leaning on a cane and holding a hearing trumpet to one ear. And of course, it wasn't just any old buzzard who had materialized uninvited on the past year. It was cute. What was that she said, Sonny? I couldn't quite hear. Picard scowled, what's going on here, Q? What have you done with the blasted anomaly? The old crow leaned closer to him, as if to hear better. What's that? Where's your mommy? I don't know, Sonny. Where did you leave her? The captain's anger rose hot and red. Stop this foolishness and answer me. Q wagged a spindly, arthritic finger at him. You young, whippa-snappers are so impatient, always wanting answers. Why don't you just slow down, smell the roses, learn to appreciate the finer things in life. Picard took an angry step toward his nemesis, who, with a quickness that belied his elderly condition, raised his cane and planted the tip of it in the center of Picard's chest. Now, don't get carried away, my ancient friend. You'll give yourself a heart attack, and I wouldn't want you to shuffle off before your time, which should be very soon, in any case. The entity peered into Picard's left eye. Eh, is that a blood clot in there, or are you just glad to see me? Captain fought down his fury. Just tell me one thing, alright? This anomaly we're looking for. Is this what destroys humanity? Q smiled, a hideously wrinkled smile. You're forgetting Jean-Luc. I said, you destroyed humanity. By doing what? That's for me to know, and you to find out. I thought I made that clear already. But when will this take place? In a flash, Q vanished. Suddenly Picard realized he was no longer on the past year, but back in the present, on the bridge of the Enterprise. The anomaly was on the view screen. Picard walked forward to ops. Report, Mr. Data. Data consulted the monitors on his console. The anomaly is 200 million kilometers in diameter, sir. It is a highly focused temporal energy source which is emitting approximately the same energy output as 10 G-type stars. Picard considered the information. And what is the source of that energy? I am uncertain, sir. Sensors have been unable to penetrate the anomaly. Picard thought for a moment. In the future time frame, Data had made a suggestion. Data. What if we modified the warp deflector to emit an inverse tachyon pulse? That might scan beyond the subspace barrier and give us an idea what the interior of this thing looks like. Data seemed a little surprised, but he considered it. That is a most intriguing idea. I do not believe a tachyon beam has ever been put to such use. What is more, I had no idea you were so versed in the intricacies of temporal theory. The captain smiled at the irony. I am not, but I have some friends who are. Make it so, Mr. Data. Data stood up from his place at ops. I believe we can make the necessary modifications in main engineering. As Data headed for the turbolift, Picard turned back to the view screen. The anomaly roiled on, a symbol of annihilation that he did not yet understand. However, it was determined that he would. In main engineering, Data worked alongside LaForge making the adjustments the captain had called for. Data I had no idea that Captain Picard had such a handle on temporal theory. Using the beam to scan past the subspace barrier, that is pretty innovative. If it works, Data pointed to one of the monitors they were working with. We can get more power if we reroute the circuit to the deflector array, than Data initiated the tachyon pulse. On another monitor, LaForge could see a thin oscillating beam emerge from the deflector addition begin scanning the anomaly. When LaForge made an instrument check, he smiled. The boss is holding steady, we're starting to receive data from the scan. Before LaForge could finish his thought, he felt a sudden stab of pain in both his eyes. He brought his hands to his face. Damn. It's like somebody put an ace pick through my temples. And my visor is picking up all kinds of spectra-manic distortions. LaForge stood up, staggered, lost his balance, and felt Data catch him before he could fall. The next thing he knew, his friend was speaking to the intercom system. Data to sickbay, medical emergency, and main engineering. Picard shook his head. He had his hands full, wrestling with Q, his time shifts, and humanity's survival. Now something else seemed to be rearing its ugly head. The engineer was sitting on a biobed with his visor off. As he looked on, Dr. Crusher pointed to LaForge's eyes. Look at them, you can see the difference yourself. It was true, whereas LaForge's eyes had previously been perfectly colorless. They now showed signs of having irises. The signs were faint, but they were there. Picking up a scanning device, Crusher used it to perform a quick examination and announced the results. Nothing short of amazing. The DNA in his optic nerves is being regenerated. I'm starting to see the formation of a retina. This is if he were growing brand new eyes. LaForge swore beneath his breath. That's why I started to feel pain. My optical cortex was falling out of alignment with my visor. Picard didn't understand. How is that possible? Beverly turned to him. It shouldn't be possible at all. There's no medical explanation for a spontaneous regeneration of dead tissue. As they pondered her remark, nurse Agao approached them. She held out a pad to Beverly. Dr. We've just gotten reports from two crew members who say they have old injuries that are healing themselves. I'm not sure what to make of it. From a terminal off to the side where he had been working, data approached them. I believe that I may have a partial explanation for what is happening to Commander LaForge and to the others as well. I have completed my analysis of the anomaly. It appears to be a multi-phasic temporal convergence in the space time continuum. It is, in essence, an eruption of anti-time. The captain looked puzzled. Anti-time. Yes, sir. It is a relatively new concept in temporal mechanics. The relationship of anti-time to normal time is analogous to the relationship of anti-matter to normal matter. Anti-time would possess the exact opposite characteristics of normal time, operating in some kind of temporal reversion we do not fully understand. The card was beginning to catch on. You're saying that the anomaly is the result of time and anti-time coming together in the same place. That is correct, sir. Something has ruptured the barrier between time and anti-time in the Devron system. I believe this rupture is sending out waves of temporal energy which are disrupting the normal flow of time. Data turned to gaze at LaForge. It is possible that the DNA molecules in Jordy's optic nerves are not regenerating themselves, but simply reverting to their original state. You mean his eyes are getting younger? Data nodded. For all intents and purposes, yes. The card considered the implications. So the temporal anomaly has certain rejuvenating effects. Certainly doesn't sound like the destruction of humanity. Mr. Data, any idea what could have caused the rupture between time and anti-time? Data looked confused. Anti-time, sir. Abruptly, Picard realized that data was sitting at ops, not at a terminal in sickbay. He gathered that he had returned to the past. Moving quickly to Data's console, he began entering information as quickly as he could. The others, Tasha, Wharf, O'Brien, and Troy, were no doubt watching from their stations wondering what in blazes he was up to. I believe Mr. Data, that if we modify the deflector to send out an inverse tachyon pulse, you'll find that the anomaly is a rupture between time and anti-time. That is a fascinating hypothesis, sir. Where did you encounter it? It would take too long to explain. In the modifications, send out the pulse. Once you've done that, start working on a theory as to what could have caused the rupture. As Data began to comply with his orders, Picard took in the image of the anomaly on the view screen. Mr. O'Brien, how big is the anomaly? Approximately 400 million kilometers in diameter, sir. Picard shook his head, wishing he had a better grasp of what was going on. I still don't understand why it's larger here. Brian shot him a puzzled look, but before he could ask a question, Wharf addressed the captain from the aft console. There are five Turellian transport ships holding position in the Devron system, sir. We're being hailed by the lead ship. Their pilot's name is Androna. On screen, Mr. Wharf. In the next instant, the view screen filled with the image of a smiling Turellian. Enterprise, you are a welcome sight. We've been receiving threats from the Romulan Empire ever since we entered the neutral zone. I'm glad to see you're here to protect us. Picard frowned. Why have you come here? Androna's expression became even brighter. Once we heard about the light, about the power it had to heal illness to rejuvenate the elderly, we had to come here. The captain sighed. Judging by the looks on his officers' faces, they were rather confused. None of them had seemed had heard anything about this. Of course, they hadn't just leaped through time. They hadn't been sitting there in Beverly Crusher's sick bay where a man's eyes were growing younger, listening to reports of injuries that had healed themselves. We can't really be certain that the light has this power, and there may be dangers side effects we're not aware of. The Turellian wasn't moved. I have five ships full of sick and dying people, Captain. If there's even a chance it's true, I can't turn back now. Picard was frustrated with his response. Unfortunately, he didn't have the authority to order them away. I warn you that if the Romulans should decide to intervene, I may not be able to protect you. I understand. We'll take that risk. Good luck, Captain, to both of us. A moment later, and Drona's image was gone. Picard mauled the situation over for a moment, then headed for his ready room. As the doors parted for him, Picard felt everything shift. He was in Beverly's ready room on the past Ture, and it sounded like they were under attack. As he moved toward the door, the deck suddenly bucked under his feet, nearly throwing him down. He made use of whatever handholds he could find and ventured uncertainly onto the bridge. Beverly was sitting in the center seat, giving orders. What's going on, Beverly? Wharf looked up from the console, he'd commandeered. The D-cling on attack cruises have de-cloked to port and starboard. We are surrounded. Ensign Chilton called out. Shield strength down to 52%. Minor damage to the port nacelle. Beverly looked to Chilton. Warp speed, Ensign. Get us out of here. Chilton worked at her con board. I can't comply. Warp power off line, sir. Another volley hit the pasture. At the time, Beverly was nearly thrown from her chair. Bring us about. Course, 148. Mark 215. Full impulse. The ship came about, but it didn't do them much good. The Klingon attack cruises were right on their tail. Yet again, they were raked by enemy fire. On the bridge, they felt the impact of the series of vicious jolks. Ensign Chilton announced from her station. Power fluctuating, shields down to 30%. Beverly bit her lip. Behind her, she heard Picard make himself heard over the melee. Weapons status, Mr. Wharf. For that one moment, Picard almost looked and sounded like his old self. The answer he demanded from Wharf wasn't long and coming. Our phasers are no match for their shields, sir. Our only hope is to escape. Consumed with anger, Beverly World. I thought you said I had eight hours, Wharf. What the hell are they doing here now? Wharf looked resigned. These must be ships from some other sector. Beverly turned to the forge. We need warp power. Now! The former chief engineer worked at his console, but it didn't look good. Finally, he raised his head. Sorry, Captain. They're just too much for us. I can't keep the phase-inducers online. Shields down to 9%. One more hit, no collapse entirely. Beverly cursed under breath. There was only one option left. Wharf, open and channel, signal our surrender. Thirty years ago, the Klingon would have protested. Older and wiser now, he simply complied. A moment later, he looked up. They will not accept our surrender. They intended to complete what they began. Before she could assimilate the information, the ship lurched again under the Klingon's garage, throwing her clear of the captain's chair. Before she hit the deck, she saw Chilton's console explode in a geyser of sparks, catching the ends and falling the face. Picard came to the woman's aid as quickly as he could, but Beverly could see that it was too late. Renzen was dead. In the meantime, Wharf had taken over Chilton's duties from his aft console. Our shields have collapsed. We are defenseless against them. Returning to her captain's chair, Beverly ignored her bruises and fixed her attention on the viewscreen. It was only a matter of time now, seeing that their prey had nothing left, the Klingons would apply to deathstroke. The data suddenly announced. Then there's another ship de-cloaking, bearing 215, Mark 310. It's the Enterprise. Beverly's heart leapt at the mere mention of their old ship. Returning her attention to the viewscreen, she watched as the galaxy class vessel de-cloaked behind and above in an unsuspecting Klingon cruiser. Suddenly, the Enterprise had let loose with a furious volley of phasers and photon torpedoes. Hammer beyond its capacity to defend itself. The attack cruiser shot apart and a cloud of blue plasma. Before anyone on the pasture could celebrate, the medical ship hitched again. Blaforge shouted above the north. Direct hit to the warp core, heavy damage. Cards face went white with dread. Wharf core can't let that happen. We have to stabilize it. As the Klingon ships were disengaging, the pasture was rocked yet again. Blaforge was frantically working the console. Captain, I can't stabilize the core. It's going critical. Broccoli, the voice came through over their intercom grid. Enterprise the pasture. Our sensors show your ship as a warp core breach in progress. Prepare for emergency beam out. Card looked up in wonder. It was Riker. Many of them could speculate why he had decided to help. They found themselves transported to the bridge of the Enterprise. The officer at Tactical announced, the pasture crew was safely bored Admiral. The Klingons are still moving officer. Have a light year distant. Satisfied that the battle was over, Riker turned to the new arrivals and favored them with a smile. Well, isn't somebody going to say thank you? Wharf took a step toward the Admiral. His face was racked with barely restrained fury. There is nothing to thank you for. If you had not turned the captain down and he came to you for help, none of this would have happened. Riker's smile disappeared. What about you, Wharf? I can't believe you let a defenseless ship cross into hostile territory without an escort. The cards stepped between them before the confrontation could escalate. We don't have time for this will. You have to shut down the warp core breach on the pasture. The subspace barrier in this region is very thin. If that ship explodes, it could rupture the barrier. Flood this whole area with anti-time. Don't you see this could be the very thing that destroys humanity? Riker looked at Picard as if he had gone completely mad. Then number one turned to Data, to Jory, and finally to Beverly. What the hell is he talking about? She shook her head. Frankly I'm not sure anymore. Jean-Luc grew wild. He grasped Data by the arm. Data? Tell them. Tell them. Yes sir. The subspace barrier in this area is quite thin. Though not unusually so. Picard pointed to the view screen where the pasture hung, crippled in space. It's hull charred by disruptor fire. If that ship explodes, it could destroy everything. Suddenly with shocking finality the ship vanished and burst of blue-white energy. That stared at the screen in horror. What was it? Was this the doom Q it foretold? The one he had failed to avoid despite his advanced knowledge of it? Riker turned to his tactical officer. Full scan Mr. Gaines. Any sign of a subspace rupture? The man worked for a moment. Picard dreaded what he would hear. But when Gaines looked up, he was hardly perturbed. No sir. The subspace barrier is intact. Everyone seemed to relax. Everyone that is except Picard himself. He didn't understand it and he said so. But Riker didn't seem to feel compelled to give him an explanation. Alright. Let's get out of here. Engage Cloak. Gaines looked up. Cloak is not functioning. We took a direct hit to the starboard, plasma coil, engineering reports, seven hours until we can cloak again. Riker frowned. Then we'll do this the old fashioned way. Lay in a course back to the Federation. Maximum Warp? Picard took hold of Riker's tunic. No. We can't leave. We have to stay here to find the cause of the temporal anomaly. I caused it, dammit. Though I don't know how. Riker pulled Picard's hand away. Captain Picard, there could be other attack cruisers on the way. We're getting out of here while we still can. We can't will, please. Everything depends on this. Please listen to me. Too late. Picard caught sight of the hypo spray in Beverly's hand. He started to turn to fend it off, but he was too slow. He heard a hiss as she released the spray's contents into his bloodstream. Fighting the instantaneous effects. He lurched forward. Picard nearly bumped into a crewman as he came around to bend in the corridor. The man, an officer in engineering, apologized. Judging by the man's uniform and his own. Picard realized he was back in the present. But where is he going? He thought for a moment. Sick Bay. Of course. Beverly had asked him to come down there. He said she wanted to speak with him. Was it Jordy? Had something changed with regard to his condition? The doors parted as he came near. He saw that Beverly wasn't that the engineers bet at all. She was at another one, tending to Alyssa Ogawa. Seeing Picard enter and satisfy that a gawa would be all right for the moment, Crusher took the captain aside. Alyssa lost her baby. I think it's the same thing that happened to Jordy. Somehow, the temporal energy from the anomaly caused the fetal tissue to revert to an earlier stage of development. It was as if the unborn child began to grow younger and younger still, until finally, the DNA itself began to break down. The captain tilted his head to indicate the nurse. How is nurse a gawa? Beverly shrugged. Physically, she's fine, at least for now. But if this temporal reversion continues, I don't think any of us are going to be fine for much longer. Our cellular structures are changing. Instead of dividing, our cells are coming together, reverting to earlier cellular structures. This could kill us all. Cards lips pressed together as he contemplated it. It was a horrible prospect. He took another look at a gawa. Could this be the catastrophe Q had warned him of? Is humanity going to devolve into the single-celled creatures that had been its primeval forebears? Looking up, he called over the intercom to tell data to meet him in the observation lounge.
description: The episode "All Good Things - Side 3" explores the complex and chaotic situation facing Captain Picard and his crew in a universe where they find themselves repeatedly jumping through time with no clear explanation of their purpose or destination. Despite their best efforts to avoid destroying humanity, they encounter unexpected events such as spatial anomalies and the appearance of an unknown entity called Q. The episode delves into philosophical questions about free will versus determinism and the nature of reality itself. As Picard grapples with these challenges, he realizes that there may be a deeper connection between his own time shifts and the cosmic forces at play. The episode culminates in a surprising revelation about Q's intentions and motives, adding an element of mystery to their already uncertain existence in this alternate timeline.
