transcript: Her jaw clenched in rage, Marla Karu leaned over the shoulder of her assistant, Komplem, who was manning the sign station on the bridge of the Darsor. She watched the curious sensor readings from Aluna scroll across the screen. What in the divine are those crazy Klingons doing down there? Captain Uzel stepped to her side. They must be fighting something on the planet. What's the creatures they've been telling us about? Marla turned to the captain in confusion. Creatures? The only ones down there are... she stopped, because she was about to say that curate Molofson and his followers were already living on Aluna, but that was a secret she had vowed to keep. Captain Uzel eyed his leader with mild disapproval. Haven't you been reading the dispatches from Starfleet? These Genesis planets are dangerous places. Marla scowled. That's our home you're talking about. But we've got so much left to do. Not only do we have to stabilize those satellites and get them back into orbit, but we've got to get the replicators on every ship making parts for the transporter booths. Have you seen the prototype? Uzel shook his head. That's one thing I haven't had time for. But Regent, I urge you to read the dispatches from Starfleet. For one thing, they're sending us an expert on Genesis planets. Marla Karu furrowed all six of her eyebrows. Oh, now they send us experts. First the wave and then someone to explain it? After our eight million survivors are safe, I'll listen to their experts and their excuses. Marla headed for the doorway at the rear of the bridge and Captain Uzel called after her. Where are you going Regent? Down to the planet to see what the Klingons are doing. Regent Karu. The Klingons said that everyone going to the planet must wear an environmental suit. Marla sniffed with disdain. They don't sound as brave as they're made out to be. Halfway to the transporter room, Sirus' gentle set stepped from a doorway and moved in front of Marla. Regent Karu, may I have a word with you? Marla tried to slip past her. I'm very busy. The Seerus mustard her considerable charm. The overseer is not well, and I'm worried about him. You know, if he dies, one of my other husbands will become overseer and they could rescind the decree making you Regent. Surely, you can spare a few moments for your benefactor's wife, for your lover's wife. Marla tried to keep a composed expression on her face, but she must have failed because the Seerus smiled in triumph. Oh, you didn't think I knew about that. I did. I chose not to bring it up at your heresy trial because we had so much other evidence against you. Marla glanced around to see if anyone had overheard, then she pointed down the corridor. I'm headed to the transporter room. We'll ask the operator to leave. Then we can talk there. A few moments later they entered the transporter room, and Marla dismissed the transport operator. As the door whooshed shut, Seerus' genocide turned to the Regent and crossed her arms. First of all, what has happened to us is bad enough without completely overturning the order of our society as well. What we need is to get back to normal as soon as we can. Normal Seerus? You haven't been down to Illuna to see what it's like, have you? Marla Karoo moved toward the transporter console and pointed to the platform. Go stand over there. You're going down to the planet to see what our Klingon friends have been doing. Geneset looked at her in horror, tugging at her elegant scarlet gown. I'm not dressed for it. Marla smiled. You will be an inspiration to the Klingon warriors. Go ahead. Get on the platform. Hesitantly, Seerus' genocide stepped onto the transporter pad, and Marla Karoo fought the temptation to scatter her molecules into the stratosphere. She entered the coordinates and strode over to the platform and took her place beside the Seerus, who was trembling. Freezing foul-smelling wind assaulted them as they materialized on the planet's surface in the middle of a snowy blizzard with immense trees shaking all around them. Within seconds, they were surrounded by towering figures, armored from head to toe and carrying disruptor rifles. Who goes there? Marla drew herself up and pereously to answer. The rulers of this planet. Is Ambassador Worf here? You must wear headgear and environmental suits, or we will transport you to the dog-jay and put you in quarantine in our brick. There is a dangerous fungus on this planet which can affect your mind. I want to see Ambassador Worf. I am Worf. Worf's underling returned with suits and headgear and handed them to the women. Unless she was cold, Marla didn't argue anymore as she pulled on the overly large protective gear. Her teeth chattering, Geneset was even quicker to obey their orders. Worf was still furious at them. Haven't you read our dispatches? The Genesys wave also brought invaders to this planet. They killed seven of our officers and wounded fifteen others. Worf picked up a handful of moss from the ground and held it out to the women. They can take on the form of persons known to you, which is why they are so dangerous. Marla waved off his explanation. Our main concern are the people stored in our transporter satellites. We have to start setting up transporter stations and beaming them down immediately. Worf held his ground. That is impossible. We have no idea how many of these creatures there are. There may be millions of them. I can't guarantee your people's safety. Neither can I, Ambassador, but down here they've got a fighting chance. Up there, they've got no chance at all if the computers fail. The big Klingon considered her request for a moment, then nodded. Very well. We will speed up our timetable. We'll start erecting shelters and you can erect the transporter platforms you need. By daylight we should be ready. But don't leave this clearing. Worf motioned to his comrades and the Klingons dispersed, going back to their grim business. Marla turned to look at Sirus Geneset, whose stunned face was barely visible behind the visor in her helmet. Marla wasn't sure but she thought she saw tears in the pale eyes of the Sirus. Rest assured Sirus, we'll change Aluna back to the paradise it was. Let's go back to the ship. Overseer Tejaret tossed fitfully in his sleep in the royal state room aboard the Darsor. By leaving all the decisions up to Marla Karu, he had turned his back on countless millions of lives because he was too cowardly to make the tough choices himself. Shivering with the sweat of guilt and remorse, Tejaret reached across his bed for Geneset, but his wife was no longer there. He knew he could get out of bed and roam the corridors of the ship like a ghost but what good would that do? Who wanted to see him, the ghost of a former ruler? They didn't need him anymore. Suddenly, he heard a soft, feminine voice coming from the calm panel outside his door. Open your door and turn out the lights. He reached to touch the panel on the table at his bedside. A curvaceous figure shrouded in flowing silk padded into the room. He recognized the perfume as Genesets and he breathed a sigh of relief. My darling, I need you so badly. Her barely clad figure slithered into his arms. I know. Kiss me, my overseer. Eagerly seeking a measure of forgetfulness, Tejaret touched her supple lips with his own. She tasted oddly bitter, not like before, but he momentarily lost himself in their mutual passion. Then his chest began to constrict, as if he had been running too fast, too far. As he began to cough and gag, his lover pulled away from him and left him grasping for both her body and the air. Tejaret, then he seemed to hear a babble of voices from all those millions of subjects he had abandoned to their fate. And they welcomed him to the grip of the divine hand. As the door of his steak-room wooshed open and a shadow slipped out, the vaunted overseer of a luna, who had ruled for three generations of peace and prosperity, collapsed in his bed and died. Alexander cringed when he saw his brother Jeremy, lying in a sick bay bed aboard the Dog J. The burns on his face and body were very serious, although no longer like threatening. Jeremy looked up at his brother and tried to smile. They burned off all my nice blonde hair. Girls back home are going to be disappointed. I heard you're going to see home very soon. The young human grunted. I don't want to. But a Starfleet run about is dumping someone off here and taking me back. Come on, Jeremy. You know you'll get better treatment at Starfleet Medical. Nobody ever accused Klingons of being great healers. Ah, yeah, I know, I know. They keep asking me why I don't have two or three of every organ like you do. Alexander laughed and chained the subject. Well, we now have reinforcements on the planet. So Dad sent a big force to march from base two to base one. Now that we're using just bladed weapons, we've had a lot fewer casualties. We need to establish a bigger perimeter and enlarge the two camps because the illunions want to start bringing their people down. Jeremy mustered a pain smile. Is he... is Dad coming to visit me? He's meeting the specialist Starfleet ascending us, so he'll be there to see you off. Alexander stepped away from the bed and wound his way through the crowded sick bay and into the corridor, where he was met by a shuttlecraft pilot. Alexander Rosenko? You ought to report to the illunions vessel Darsor. They have requested a Klingon representative, and you're the closest and most able according to Ambassador Worf. Alexander suppressed a smile, amused that his father considered him so capable. Fifteen minutes later, a Klingon shuttlecraft slid into the shuttle bay at the Darsor, and as Alexander disembarked, he was met by the two strong-willed women he had seen the night before. The older, scholarly regent, Marla Karu, and the regal beauty, Sirus Geneset. Marla scowled at him. And you are? Duty chief Alexander Rosenko of the Yavang, son of Worf, House of Martok. And your father couldn't come? My father is busy securing the planet for your people. What is the emergency? Sirus Geneset sniffed back a sob, and he noticed that her eyes were red. My husband, overseer to Jareb is dead. We fear he's been murdered. The young Klingon frowned at this revelation, wondering what he could do, when the two women immediately pointed at one another and spoke in unison. She did it! Alexander held up his hands. Ladies, what do you want me to do? I can explain. Alexander turned to see a handsome allunen of middle age and fine clothing come striding toward him. Excuse me for being late. I had some urgent documents to sign. I am overseer Padrin. I have succeeded overseer to Jareb. Padrin gazed pointedly at Marla Karu. And I have relieved Professor Karu of the title of regent and assumed her duties and powers. Marla's hands bald into fists. You can't do this now? You've got to let me finish my work. You're condemning eight million people to death. Padrin glared at the former regent. I am doing no such thing. You can proceed with all the tasks you have to do. But you are a suspect in the overseer's death. Padrin looked fondly at Sirus Geneset. You are also a suspect, my dear. I'm sorry, but you must be confined to quarters until the inquiry is complete. He turned again to Alexander. This death puts what's left of our government into chaos. I welcome any help you can give us. Alexander's mind worked furiously about what to do. Can I see the body and the evidence? To understand why you think one of these esteemed ladies murdered overseer to Jareb? Absolutely. Padrin turned to the cadre of uniformed officers behind him and gave them orders. You two constables accompany the seerus to her quarters and make sure she stays there. You two accompany Professor Karu to the laboratory and make sure she stays there to do her work. The two women and their escorts left the shuttle bay. Remaining behind were Alexander, overseer Padrin, and a young lad who had accompanied the group. Alexander pointed to the boy. Who is this? Padrin explained. This is Farlow, the seerus's third husband. It is typical for our well-bred females to have three husbands, and he and Geneset wed on the day we left Aluna. The toe-headed lad smiled at Alexander. I'm pleased to meet you. I'm just as confused as you are, but I'll help you any way I can. The Klingon smiled back, liking the lad immediately. Are you the next in line to be overseer? Farlow shrugged. I guess so, but it doesn't look like it's a healthy job to have. It only took a few minutes for them to walk down the main corridor to the state room where the overseer laid dead in his bed. Alexander was struck by the luxury of the furnishings and also the odor of a very opulent perfume. If he wasn't mistaken, it was the same scent that seerus Geneset had been wearing in the shuttle bay. An older doctor was near the bedside. Padrin approached him. Dr. Geddon, this is Alexander Regenko, a representative of the Klingon Empire. He is in charge of our inquiry. Please tell him what you told me. The medical man took a deep breath and consulted a handheld device before answering. Tijaret was poisoned. There are traces on his lips of illsoden, a very fast-acting nerve agent which is often used in large-sized pest eradication. What I couldn't tell from my examination is whether he was poisoned or whether he committed suicide. But there's no trace of illsoden in this room. If he administered it himself, what did he do with it? Plus, he had a visitor late last night. Alexander raised an eyebrow. A visitor? Who? Overseer Padrin answered. We don't know, but she was female. One of the ship's passengers saw her in the corridor. The lights were dimmed and the witness couldn't give us a description except to say it was a female wearing night clothes. We know that the overseer and the seerus came back here alone for one unit of time after dinner, and then the seerus and the regent went down to Aluna. Later, the seerus returned to the ship, apparently was alone for some time, then spent the rest of the night with me. Dr. Geddon added an important observation. The time of death coincides with the sighting of the woman who was seen coming out of here. She could not have entered unless he opened the door for her, so it must have been somebody he knew. Alexander took a deep breath while he collected his thoughts. I know very little about your society, but in Klingon society there is an old tradition of claiming power by murder and violent duels to the death. Padrin looked aghast at the idea. We have a very orderly transition of power based on bloodlines in DNA. Nobody has to commit murder to claim power. Besides, who would want to be in charge during these troubled times? You benefited overseer Padrin, and Regent Karu suffered. Why would you suspect her of murder when she was the first to suffer from his death? Padrin pursed his lips as if he were hesitant to answer. Regent Karu and overseer Tijaret were lovers, and she and seerus genocet were enemies. Owing to that and many philosophical matters. She and genocet were seen arguing last night, and the question of returning power to our family was bound to be a problem no matter what else happened. I thought it was best to remove that friction from the equation. If she really wants to do her work, she can help the lunens without being Regent. Alexander nodded. So you and genocet got your way. Padrin shook his head. Not my way. I was happy being the seerus consort. I never wanted this job. Alexander rubbed his eyes, feeling way over his head. He would rather be down on the planet's surface battling those fiendish moss creatures. That thought brought him to a disturbing conclusion. He turned to the white-suited figure of Dr. Gerten. Dr. you need to make sure that no one on this vessel or any of your ships has been infected by the fungus we encountered down on the planet. You must test everyone on this ship. It might explain what happened to the overseer. In the laboratory on the Darsor, Marla Karu tried to forget her anger and grief, long enough to concentrate on monitoring the progress of the work crews, rushing to put the satellites back into orbit at the same time that they attempted to stabilize the bio-neuro networks. She also had to oversee the manufacture of several thousand compact solar-powered transporter booths to be transported to the planet as soon as the Klingon secured a large enough area. Fortunately, slaving at her side was Vilo Garlet, who must have been sent by the divine because he was able to fulfill all the development work on the transporters, especially their secret purpose to re-terraform Aluna. At first Marla was a bit annoyed to see Kandra, the young friend of the new seerus consort, working alongside Vilo Garlet, but her colleague trusted the young lady, having saved her life. As the units of time passed, Kandra became more and more of a fixture in the laboratory. Still, Marla made certain never to discuss her secret plans with anyone but Vilo Garlet. She approached Vilo during one break when they were alone. How was the programming going on the Chromosynthesis box? Garlet nodded weirdly. Our flora and fauna will be layered on top of the existing Genesis growth, with results that I can't entirely predict. My main concern is the coverage. We've got to make sure to get one of these transporter boxes at every hundred measures for it to be successful. Since a transporter component is solar-powered and unidirectional, tell the Klingons that we must have complete coverage in order to keep them working around the clock. The next two days would be crucial, Marla decided, because they would either prepare the planet to receive the eight million survivors, or they would lose them all. She glanced at her timepiece and frowned. Star Fleet's expert is due to arrive soon. Four stood in the cavernous shuttle bay of the Dogjay, with both of his sons at his side, waiting for the arrival of a Star Fleet runabout. Jeremy lay on an antigrav gurney that floated at waist level. He was miserable at the prospect of returning home wounded. Standing at the ambassador's other side, Alexander was preoccupied with his new assignment among the Illunans. While they waited for the arrival of the runabout, Worf and Jeremy listened to Alexander's account of the overseer's suspected murder. Worf could offer little advice. For a Klingon, the murder of a weak, ineffectual leader sounded like the normal course of events. Out of the hatch of the runabout, an attractive woman stepped forward to meet them. It had been many years since Worf had seen Dr. Lea Brahms, and she looked somewhat older and thinner. She greeted Worf and his sons, holding out her hand to engage in the human custom of the handshake. Please to meet you. I've been reading about what you've been going through. But Regent Karu could not be here? Alexander spoke first. I'm afraid not. She's in confinement on an Illunan ship because she's suspected of committing a crime. The shuttle craft dropped in altitude and swept over majestic trees on the edge of a muddy stream that was trickling through the bottom of the wash. It was silt-ridden now, but the more it rained, the clearer it would flow. In space, the rarefied atmosphere blazed with a light that was almost crystal in its fragility and purity. The great Klingon warships soared swiftly over the string of satellites, expelling bursts of plasma that had built up through countless Wharf excursions. The Enterprise also followed a row of satellites, venting as much plasma as she had, considering her Wharf Corps was gone. Captain Picard still had a skeleton crew because he was also in a recharging and refitting mode. Almost all the shuttle craft had launched to aid in the rescue effort, but he didn't want to risk using transporters. The majority of the crew were safer on the ground, although there were disturbing reports of evacuees encountering large, predatory beasts on the new Illuna. The forge announced from his engineering station on the bridge. Forty-five minutes left, they are cutting it close. From her co-pilot's seat on the shuttle craft, Marla turned to data. We barely have enough time to let everyone out of the buffers. We can't wait any longer. At the controls, Regimal cut the thrusters and let the shuttle craft drift toward a metal flower suspended in space. And a Lunan transporter satellite in very good condition. Data looked up at Marla Karu and Lea Brahms. You have been discussing what to do, so I presume you can do it without our help. Marla jumped to her feet. Yes, we can. I'm going to transport into the satellite, while Dr. Brahms sends the repeat command. Data gave a placid smile of understanding. There is no need to explain. I have very good hearing. Give me a moment to alert the ships and the ground teams. Marla bounded onto the small transporter pad in the rear of the cabinet. Crossed from the lavatory and waited for data's command. You are cleared to transport. However, your assistant compum may be angry because you are technically still his property. Marla managed to smile. Give him my regrets. Energize. As Marla's body swirled into a tubular rainbow, at the same instant the satellite blinked on, and several of their sensors kicked into high gear spewing readouts onto all their screens. Lea Brahms thrust her fist upward. It's working. Have we gotten the whole chain working? Regime all relayed the good news. On either side of us we have got machines coming on. We are sending something to the planet. You'll just have to hope the cargo is in good condition. Gorth held his breath as the transporter booth closest to camp, the one in which curate Molov-Zahn's body had been discovered, blinked on. Riker, Alexander and overseer Farlow also stepped to his side and stared at the wearing blue box. A dazed child about ten years old stepped out, followed by an aluminum woman who gripped the child protectively. All right! Yeah! Farlow and Alexander rushed forward to lead the small family away from the booth so more survivors could exit. All over the planet, dazed survivors were stepping out of transporter booths and meeting welcoming parties who tried to explain the strange sights and smells. Dr. Crusher and other medical teams were standing by, but the vast majority of evacuees suffered more from shock, grief and denial for which there was no medical cure. Although they were alive after having survived a power loss, a fungus and other dangers, for them it was but an instant since they boarded the transporters in their cities and towns. All those places were gone. In return, they had inherited a bizarre wilderness, which only accentuated their loss. Still, there was great joy among all those Alunans who had come days earlier, either by ship or by the first transporter release. There were also wonders to be seen in this strange world. Amazing growth and destruction, incredible animal life and lush forests bordered by great plains which were already growing grass. Apparently this grass was a wild grain which the Alunans knew how to cultivate and harvest. Wharf and the Klingons maintained a watch for the moss creatures, but they were never seen again on Aluna. In his hospital bed at Starfleet Medical Center in San Francisco, Wharf's adopted son Jeremy sat up as he continued to learn about Aluna's fate from his father. No more moss creatures at all? What did you call them? Alexander sat with a grin on the side of Jeremy's bed and repeated the name. Pock-lod! And those big slugs we called them Nuzh-Garg were very good eating. The Klingons ate so many that they were going extinct even before the anti-genesis thing went off. Wharf shook his head with disapproval. Our crew was getting quite addicted to them. Don't tell Starfleet, but some Klingons are planning a hunt for Nuzh-Garg on one of the other Genesis planets. Rare, dangerous to catch and quite tasty. They might become a Klingon delicacy. Alexander continued their report to Jeremy. And the Alunans seemed to like their new overseer too. He's got a good head on his shoulders and he wants to do well. There's a lot of raw materials to rebuild and food is growing and the Federation will continue to assist. Wharf nodded his head solemnly. We freed 90% of the people trapped in their satellites, which is an extraordinary achievement. I wish the person who made it possible could have seen it. Jeremy understood that his father was referring to the former regent, Marla Karu. But he had another question for his father. And the Enterprise? Wharf grunted with amusement. They are still in orbit around Aluna, waiting for Starfleet to bring a new warp core. Alexander laughed and shook his head. But I don't think they mind. It's almost like shore leave at this point, with lots of romantic, isolated places to visit. Jordy LaForage and Leah Brahms looked very happy and so did Commander Riker and Counselor Troy. Wharf took a step closer to the bed and patted Jeremy gently on his shoulder. Now, son, you must rest so the doctors will release you on schedule. You can rejoin the Officer Exchange Program next week, and I'll do what I can to get you back on the dog J. Jeremy held out his fist to the two Klingons. Kapla. The family joined fists and echoed the sentiment. Kapla! Star Trek, the next generation. Genesis Force was written by John Vornholt and read by Tim Russ. It was abridged for audio by George Truett. It was recorded at Mark Graule recording in Los Angeles, with editing by Rick Bradley and Dan Maccassie. Post-production and sound design by Gary Fink. Music composed by Richard Emmett, Carl Schurts, Carl Schurief, Sam McCally and Rick Bradley. The associate producer was Kelly Gilday. The director was Bob Walter. Star Trek, the next generation. Genesis Force was produced by Karen Perlman. This has been a presentation of Simon & Schuster Audio. Also available from Simon & Schuster Audio. Star Trek, the next generation. The Genesis Wave Books 1-3, written by John Vornholt and read by Tim Russ. Star Trek, the next generation. Genesis Force is available in hardcover from Pocket Books.
description: In this episode, Marla Karu is upset about strange sensor readings on Aluna indicating Klingons might be fighting something there. Despite a warning from Captain Uzel that it could be dangerous, she insists they must go to see what the Klingons are doing. Her husband Sirus offers to talk to her about it while he's not busy with his current concerns, but Marla refuses and heads to the transporter room to speak with Regent Karu, who wants to know more about why the Klingons were ordered to wear environmental suits on the planet.

title: The Valiant
file_path: media/StarTrek TNG/The Valiant.mp4
transcript: Simon & Schuster Audio presents Star Trek, The Next Generation, The Valiant, by Michael Jan Friedman, read by Anthony Stewart-Head. Captain Carlos Terrasco, the SS Valiant, stood in front of his captain's chair and eyed the phenomenon pictured on his viewscreen. It stretched across space without boundaries or limits, a blazing vermillionabis without beginning or end. Their optical scanners registered what looked like the universe's biggest light-share, but there was nothing there as far as their other instruments were concerned. Terrasco and his crew of 88 had set out from Earth years earlier, aiming to chart a stretch of space from their home system to the farthest reaches of the Milky Way galaxy, part of a sector that Terran astronomers had labelled the Alpha Quadrant. They had almost completed their assignment when they encountered an unexpectedly powerful magnetic storm that flung them light years off course, well past what Terrasco's cartography team reckoned was the outer edge of the galaxy. The storm had wrecked both their warp and nuclear impulse engines. Finally, after weeks of languishing under the glare of alien stars, Terrasco and his people got underway again, glad to be heading home. And all had gone well, until now. One thing was for sure, they weren't going to get back to Earth without passing through this thing. Summers, the curly hare brunette at the helm controls cast a glance back at the captain. You still want to go through it sir? Do we have a choice? Let's do it. Terrasco looked back and saw that Commander Rash out, his first officer had joined them. I hope I'm not too late sir. Not at all, the show's just starting. The closer they got, the more tumultuous the phenomenon appeared. The ruby light within it began to ry than shimmer, giving birth to monstrous caverns and towering eruptions. All available powered with the shields. Suddenly the ship jerked hard to starboard. Terrasco turned to Gardenhire as operations officer who reported. We're all right, shields are holding fine sir. Terrasco turned back to the view screen. They seemed to be entering a deep red-vained chasm. The lights on the bridge began to fling. Abruptly the deck lurched beneath them, as if they were riding the crest of a gigantic wave, sending Hollandsworth the science officer flying backwards out of his seat. Rash out began to move to Hollandsworth's side. Stick bay, we need someone up here on the double. Then Rash out seemed to light up from within. His bodies have fused with a smoldering red glow. He fell to his knees beside the unconscious Hollandsworth. Terrasco glared the view screen. All right, get us out of here. Wrestling ship hard to starboard, some has aimed for a patch of open space, and the valiant climbed out of the starboard abyss. Terrasco had never been so glad to see the stars in his life. Trying not to breathe in the black fumes from the science console, he made his way to his science officer. Before he could try to help, the lift doors parted and a couple of medics emerged. We'll take it from here, sir. Terrasco backed off and let the medical personnel do their jobs. Then he did his. Damage report, Garden Hire. Shields down, sir. Scanners, communications, lasers, all offline. Summers looked up from a console. The main engines are shot. Every last circuit is burned out. Terrasco turned back to Rashad, who was now stretched out on his back, eyes staring at the ceiling. A medic was trying to breathe air into his lungs. The medic looked at the captain. Let's get them to Sick Bay. The captain took hold of Rashad under his arms, though he knew his chief medical officer wouldn't be able to help the map. On the other hand, Hollandsworth still had a chance to pull through. The medics lifted up Hollandsworth, then they squeezed into the still open lift compartment. In less than a minute, they reached the Sick Bay. Its doors were wide open, giving them an unobstructed view of the facility's eight intensive care beds. Three of the beds were occupied, though metallic silver blankets had been pulled up ominously over the patient's faces. The captain felt his heart sinking. He had assumed the only casualties were those suffered on the bridge. Gourvoi, the valiant's florid-faced chief medical officer, looked grim. Put them down here and get up to deck sent. There are two more in engineering. The medics did as they were told and took off, leaving Gourvoi to examine Hollandsworth with a hand held by a scanner. He glanced at the captain. He will heal. I wish I could say that for the others. Do me a favor and cover Rashad, will you? Tarrasco gazed at his first officer, then he took a blanket and draped it over Rashad. Gourvoi glanced at the captain. The others lit up like lightning bugs. He needed two, right? Tarrasco nodded and considered the man-sized shapes beneath the metallic blankets. But why them are not anyone else? Well, that's the question, all right. The captain started to leave sickbay when the medics came huffing in from the corridor. They were carrying yet another victim, a baby-faced engineer named Davidov. Then chief engineer McMillan came shuffling in with one of his men leaning on him for support. Tarrasco recognized the injured man as Agnason, McMillan's first assistant. Agnason was a big man, tall and broad-shouldered, with a strong jaw and a fierce blonde moustache. The chief engineer cursed beneath his breath. He started to glow. He and Davidov both. It was the damnedest thing. The captain looked at Agnason. He was glowing and he's still alive. Agnason rubbed the back of his neck. I'm fine, just a little lightheaded is all. Then the big man picked up his head and Tarrasco's jaw fell. Agnason's eyes, normally a very ordinary shade of blue, were glowing with a luxuriant silver light. Captain's Log, December 30, 2069. Tomorrow will be New Year's Eve. With six of our comrades dead, no one feels much like celebrating. So instead of toasting 2070, we're trying to expedite the process of bringing basic systems back online. Chief McMillan says the war drive may be beyond repair, and if we are restricted to impulse power, none of us will live long enough to see Earth again. Jack Gourvoi completed the last of his autopsy reports, sat back in his chair and heaved a sigh. Six casualties the doctor reflected and each one showed the same characteristics. Severe damage to the victim's nervous systems. Cerebral cortices burned out as if someone had plunged live wires into them. He glanced in the direction of the intensive care unit, only a small slice of which was visible from his office. He could see Agnason, the only patient left to him now that the science officer Hollands worth was well enough to return to his quarters. The engineer was sitting up in his bed, glancing at a printout of his DNA analysis. Unlike the others who had burned with that strange light, Agnason didn't appear to have suffered any ill effects. Though his eyes had changed color, his vision was still perfect. In fact, the man claimed he felt better than ever before. Under normal circumstances, Gourvoi would probably have discharged him and pronounced him fit for duty. But he couldn't. Not when the engineer was their best shot at obtaining an understanding of their comrades' deaths and by extension, the forces that comprised the space phenomenon. Abruptly the medical officer realized that Agnason was returning his scrutiny. Gourvoi pretended to be busy with something else for a moment. When he looked up, his patient was gazing at the analyses again. As Captain Tarrasco entered Gourvoi's office, he could see the doctor appearing at his monitor screen. You called? The medical officer didn't look up. I did indeed. McMillan says we'll be lucky to get the warp drive up and running this century. That estimate may be a little pessimistic. The doctor swiveled his monitor round. It showed Tarrasco a collection of bright green circles, some empty and some filled in. I give up, Doctor. What is it? It's a DNA analysis. Those circles are traits. Sexual orientation, height, eye color and so on. Agnason created it from memory. About an hour ago he told me he was bored with lying in bed while I ran tests on him, so I gave him something to look at. His DNA analysis. He decided to play a game with himself to see how much of it he could memorize. The Captain absorbed the information. Obviously this has something to do with his eyes. I'd like to see him. Speak with him. The Captain left the doctor's office and entered the intensive care unit. Agnason's eyes were closed. For a moment, Tarrasco considered whether he should speak with the engineer at a later time. Then Agnason spoke like a man still wrapped in sleep. There's no time like the present. He turned to the Captain and opened his eyes, fixing Tarrasco with his strange silver stare. He smiled as he propped himself up on one elbow. The Captain felt a chill climb the rungs of his spine. The doctor told me you developed a knack for memorizing things. You mean the DNA analysis? To tell you the truth it wasn't that hard. I just gazed at it for a while and suddenly it was the most familiar thing in the world to me. That's pretty amazing, Agnason. The engineer shrugged. I suppose you could say that. But you know what's really amazing. Tarrasco shook his head. What? Agnason pointed past him. That. The Captain felt a whisper of air on the back of his neck. Welling in response he saw something silvery sweeping towards him and put his arms up to protect himself from it. Too late he realized what it was. A metallic blanket from one of the other beds. As it sank to the floor the engineer laughed. Tarrasco turned to Agnason, uncertain how the man had done it. That wasn't funny. The engineer bit his lip to keep from laughing some more. Sorry sir, I just thought. It seemed to make sense at the time. Tarrasco tried to affect a facade of confidence and calm, but he didn't feel as qualities on the inside. He left Agnason lying there and left the intensive care unit. He felt an urgent need to talk with his officers. Captain Tarrasco regarded the handful of staff officers he had summoned to the Valiance observation land. I think you all know why we're here. You've heard the rumors. Pelletier the perpetually grim faced head of security spoke up. I'd like to hear some facts. The Captain nodded. Here's what we know. During our attempt to get through the phenomenon Agnason lit up and collapsed. But unlike the Sikhs who shared his experience, he survived. Govoy picked up the thread. He more than survived. He became a superman. Without even trying Agnason can absorb information at astounding rates of speed. Pluck thoughts out of people's minds even move objects through the air without touching them. Nourasco continued. According to Lieutenant Summers, Agnason manipulated her helm controls from his bed in sick bay and to add insult to injury he projected his face onto her monitor. There was silence in the room for a moment. Then Pelletier spoke up. He won a recommendation. Place Agnason in the brig and put a 24 hour watch on him, and if he tries anything like tugging on the helm again, you have him sedated. We don't have the luxury of waiting until Agnason becomes a problem. We have to act now. Hollensworth cut in. We're all assuming that Agnason is going to use his abilities to hurt us to work against us. I'm here to suggest that he may decide to help us. When I was lying in intensive care recovering from my burns, I felt as if there was someone there with me, encouraging me, helping me to heal. I think it was Agnason. The captain looked to Govoy. Is that possible? Govoy shrugged. Who knows? The man can read minds and move objects around. Maybe he can help people heal as well. Chief Engineer Macmillan dismissed the idea with a wave of his hand. He's just like you and me. Security Chief Pelletier chuckled bitterly. Except he can steer the ship just by thinking about it. We're just talking about restraining him. Pelletier turned to Tiresco, his eyes as hard as stone. What are you going to do, sir? The captain frowned as he thought about it. Macmillan had been one of them, right from the get-go. He'd risked as much as anyone to carry out the Valleons mission to the stars. The man had rights. For the time being, I'm just going to talk to Agnason and let him know he's treading on thin ice. Pelletier didn't look happy. And if he starts throwing people around instead of blankets? The captain looked him in the eye. I guess we'll cross that bridge when we come to it. Captain's Log's supplemental. I've had another conversation with Agnason. This time I made it clear to him that I wouldn't tolerate his tampering with any of my ship's systems, or for that matter, frightening any of my crew. I also told him that he was to cooperate fully with Dr. Corvoi in his efforts to explore his condition. Agnason seemed to understand the consequences of diverging from my orders and promise to follow them. Jack Corvoi was studying his monitor screen in his office when Agnason showed up at his door. I've had enough of this intensive care. I'm tired of listening to you calling the shots. You and the captain. Suddenly Corvoi realized the extent of the transformation that had taken place. It wasn't just the engineer's nervous system that was changing. It was his personality as well. The doctor would be damned if he would let such a thing walk the valley and unchecked. Out of my way, Dr. Agnason, we can help you. You just have to go back to intensive care. The engineer lifted his chin in indignation. You like it there so much, why don't you go there? Before the doctor could do anything to stop him, Agnason grabbed him out of front of his uniform and sent him hurtling headlong toward intensive care. The last thing Corvoi saw was the engineer's blanket drape bed as it rushed up to meet him. And, mercifully, he lost consciousness. Dan Pelatea hefted the laser in his hand as he made his way toward engineering and hoped that he'd guessed correctly. He had discovered Dr. Corvoi slumped to the base of a bio-bed, bleeding freely from his nose and mouth. At that point, Agnason had gone from being a misguided fellow crewman to a dangerous and potentially deadly fugitive. And where was he most likely to go? Other than a place where the slightest manipulation could place the ship in mortal jeopardy, especially when that place was where he'd spent most of his waking hours over the last few years. Pelatea glanced at the too many taken with him. Remember, fire only on my command. We don't want to blow the warp core with a stray shot. The doors to the engine room were open. All the security chief saw were the surprised faces of Macmillan and his engineers. Agnason it seemed wasn't there. Carlos Terrasco paced the bridge, wondering if Pelatea and his people had caught up with Agnason yet. If the man's powers kept growing, if he became too big a threat, they might have to consider even stronger measures. Is that how you treat a man who followed you out into space? The Captain World and saw a strapping blonde figure standing at the threshold of the open turbolift. Agnason stepped out onto the bridge. Pelatea's security teams were looking for me everywhere else. This was the only place I could go. Knowing that the engineer could read his mind, Terrasco tried not to think how his bridge officers would be slipping the pistols from their belts to use them. But Agnason must have caught the captain's thought. He whirled to send a laser flying out of the navigator's grasp. Agnason lifted his hand to strike the crewman. A beam from the barrel of Terrasco's pistol caught Agnason in the chest, knocking the wind out of him. Agnason slumped to the deck, looking woozy and deflated. Before Terrasco could even think about squeezing off another shot, he saw something happen to the engineers eyes. Miraculously, the silver glow in them faded. They became the blue of summer skies, the very human blue that Agnason had likely been born with. But a moment later the light in Agnason's eyes returned, and with it came a restoration of his incredible strength. The bridge officers fired at the same time, knocking Agnason senseless. And when he crumpled this time, Terrasco was ready. Take him to the break. Jack Govoy hadn't previously spent any time in one of his beds in Sigbei, and now that he had spent some time there, he didn't like it. The doctor could still feel a dull ache where he'd hit his head. Responding to his request, Captain Terrasco had come to Sigbei. He told the captain that he'd figured out why Agnason and the others were affected by the phenomenon. So what did he come up with, Doctor? Govoy friend. Extra sensory perception. Terrasco looked at him. That's it? That's it. Mind you, not all of our seven casualties were tested for it, but three were. Agnason, David Offen, Kolodny. David Offen, Kolodny scored pretty high, but Agnason, he was off the charts. So it makes sense that someone with Agnason's predisposition toward mental abilities would develop this brand of powers. The captain shook his head. What about the rest of the crew? Are we going to have any delayed cases? I don't think so. Of the 38 whose records show they were tested, none showed any particular talent for ESP. Well, thank heavens for that at least. So now that we know about Agnason's ESP, is there a chance that we can use that knowledge to change him back? Govoy shook his head. I don't think so. The captain sighed. Then you don't want to know what happens now. Security Chief Pelletier saw the engineer stare on the other side of the barrier. He glanced over his shoulder at one of his security guards. Contact the captain. Let him know that Agnason's coming too. Pelletier turned back and saw that the prisoners' eyes were open. You're a fool if you think you can hold me. That I'm a fool, Agnason. But if you were in my place, you'd be doing the same thing. That made the engineer smile. No, Pelletier. That's not true at all. If I were in your place, I would have killed me some time ago. While I still had the chance, I'm getting stronger all the time. And as if to prove his point, Agnason extended his hand into the vertical plane of the electromagnetic field. Sparks sputtered around Agnason's wrist, making him grimace with pain. But he didn't pull his hand back right away. He left it there, enduring what no mere human could have endured. You know it's only a matter of time. It was then that Pelletier noticed the patches of white at Agnason's temples. The man's appearance was changing again. He hoped the captain would hurry. They might not have much time. Captain's Log supplemental. I'm sending out this message boy despite my hope that we of the Valiant will still make it back to Earth. The boy contains all our computer data from the past several days which will explain how we wound up in these unfortunate straits and why I've opted for such a drastic response to them. Glancing at Garden Hire, Tarrasco nodded to show his ops officer that he'd finished. Garden Hire manipulated the controls on his panel. Releasing the boy captain. On the bridge's forward view screen, Tarrasco saw a small grey object go spinning off into the void like a child's top. Chief Pelletier to Captain Tarrasco. Agnason is having another go at the force field. He's been in contact with it for nearly a minute and he doesn't seem to have reached his limit yet. The captain could hear the urgency in Pelletier's voice. It was becoming increasingly obvious that he had to act. Agnason was a deadly threat to the life of every man and woman on the Valiant. And ultimately, Earth. He had to put his dread aside and do something about it. Tarrasco followed the bend of the passageway reluctantly. The brig was just down the hall. He could have ordered one of his crewmen to destroy the prisoner for him, but Tarrasco wasn't the type to put that kind of burden on one of his people. He was less than 20 metres from the brig when he realised that something was wrong. It was too quiet. Drawing his laser pistol from its place in his belt, Tarrasco held it before him and advanced more wearily. After a few seconds, Pelletier's muscular body came into view. The security chief was sprawled across the floor, his neck bent at an impossible angle. At any moment he thought Agnason might reach out with his mind and strangle him to death. But it didn't happen. The captain reached the brig unscathed. The two security guards who'd been helping to guard Agnason were laid out on the deck. Their necks broken as badly as Pelletier's had been. Tarrasco pressed the intercompad next to the brig. Agnason has escaped the brig. He's already killed three security officers. He is extremely dangerous and to be avoided at all costs. Repeat. Your next Tarrasco. After all. What do I need with the canton? Or a crew for that matter? The words echoed ominously in Tarrasco's brain. He scanned the corridor in other direction, but there was no one there. In the confines of his mind, Tarrasco swallowed back his fear and asked the engineer. Where are you? Not so far away. I'm getting closer all the time. The captain spun and there was Agnason. His eyes ablaze with silver light, a cruel smile on his otherwise expressionless face. You can't kill me, Captain, but I can kill you. He lifted his hand to carry out his threat. Tarrasco struck first. The pale yellow laser beams slammed squarely into Agnason's chest, but little by little, the engineer began to make his way forward again. Nothing can stop me. Tarrasco didn't have time to duck the bolt of livid pink energy. The next thing the captain knew he was sitting with his back against the bulkhead, feeling as if he'd broken every bone in his body. The corridor erupted with a blinding yellow light. It caught Agnason by surprise and sent him staggering into the bulkhead. The captain knew that this might be his last chance. Looking around for his laser pistol, he found it lying on the deck less than a meter away. Putting aside the pain that squeezed him like a vice, he dragged himself over to the weapon and took hold of it. Skewered in the back by Tarrasco's beam, Agnason crumpled to his knees and fell forward, momentarily unconscious. The captain gave an order to the two security officers who came to help them up. We need to get Agnason to the weapons room. We have to get rid of him while we still can. Kneeling at Agnason's side, the captain felt the man's neck for a pulse. It was faint, but the engineer was clearly still alive. His eyes, or what the captain could see of them through the engineer's half-closed lids, they weren't glowing anymore. They had returned to normal again. The security guards grabbed Agnason and began moving in the direction of the Valiance weapons room. There were hatches that were closer to their location. Unfortunately, Tarrasco mused, shoving Agnason out into space might not be enough. If the engineer was able to survive in the vacuum, and he might be, it was also possible that he could work his way back inside. The weapons room was dominated by a pair of missile launchers, empty at the moment. The captain pointed to one of them, put him inside it. The security officers placed the unconscious engineer in the open launch slot. And they started to slide the missile door into place. That was when Agnason woke up. The engineer set up and slammed the missile door open. He released bolts of raw pink lightning at the two security guards, sending them flying across the room. He turned to Tarrasco. You can't stop me, captain. Not anymore than an amoeba can stop an affant. Tarrasco knew he should have done the heart thing, the heartless thing, and destroyed Agnason as soon as he tampered with a ship. Suddenly, it came to him. As the engineer raised his hand against the captain, the captain trained his beam on the deck below Agnason's feet. After all, this was the weapons room, and the valiant boasted two kinds of weapons. One was atomic. The other was a laser cannon system supplied with power by heavy duty conduits. As luck would have it, one of those conduits ran directly under the spot where Agnason was standing. It took a moment for Tarrasco's beam to punch through the deck, plating. A spout of blue-white electroplasma rose up and engulfed the engineer. His clothes burned off, his skin and hair blackened and oozed with blood. But his eyes still glowed with that eerie silver light. Tarrasco raced across the room to the intercom grid. This is Tarrasco, all hands abandoned ship immediately. Repeat, all hands abandoned ship. As Tarrasco looked at the engineer, Agnason's flesh began to repair itself. How many conduits can you open without destroying your ship? The captain didn't allow himself to think of the answer. Instead, he aimed his weapon at the deck below Agnason and fired again. As Agnason wimpered and clutched it himself with blackened claw-like hands, Tarrasco roused the two security guards, both of them still alive. Get out of here, grab the nearest escape pod and get off the ship. What about you, sir? I'll follow when I'm certain Agnason can't come after us. It was alive, of course. Tarrasco had no intention of following the security officers. When he turned back to the engineer, to his amazement, the man was almost healed again. What are you building? It's simple. Suddenly, Santana turned away from the tractor node and looked back over her shoulder at him. The expression on her face, one of anxiety, made the security officer wonder what the woman was up to. He heard her voice in his head. Park, something's wrong. We can send someone tampering with a command junction. Joseph looked at her, wary of a trick. Who's doing it? Santana didn't answer right away, and she made a single word materializing his brain. Jamar. The security officer walked over to the nearest console and tapped into the Stargazer's internal senseonet. However, there was no indication of any tampering, and Jamar, apparently, was in his quarters. He turned back to Santana, wondering what she was trying to pull this time. No one is anywhere near a command junction. She looked up at Joseph. Damn it, I can feel him. Reacting to the woman's display of emotion, he put his hand on the phasepestal dangling at his hip. I'll have someone check Jamar's quarters. Her dark eyes filled with dread. No, by then it'll be too late. The security officer drew his phaser, leery of what Santana could do with the doctor's neurotransmitter flowing in her veins. Move back. She looked at his weapon, then at him again. You don't understand. Then something happened. Joseph wasn't sure what. He seemed to lose control of his limbs, his body becoming a heavy and unresponsive mass of flesh. The phaser fell from his limp, paralyzed hand and hit the deck. And a moment later, the security officer joined it, his mind spiraling down into darkness. As Picard watched, Girda Asmon to manipulate her controls. A moment later, the viewscreen filled with the image he'd been waiting for. The depot looked more like a fortress than a supply facility. As prodigious as the enemy's fighting ships were, the depot was bigger and better armed by a factor of at least ten. It was perhaps the truest symbol of New Yard pride they had seen yet. Suddenly, an alert light on the captain's armrest began blinking red. Noticing it, Picard touched the pad beside it. Mr. Vigo. Hi sir. I've got a problem in the phaser line. Command Junction 28, accessible from deck 10. Picard straightened and glanced at Ben Zoma. Let's go. Together, they entered the turbo lift and punched in a destination. Then they removed the phasers they had hidden in their tunics. When the lift stopped at deck 10, they got out and ran down the corridor. Before long, they came to a ladder and a round door that would give them access to the network of Jefferies that permeated the ship. Picard went up the ladder first, pulled open the door and crawled into the tube. As Ben Zoma had promised, he wasn't far behind. After they came to the first intersection, they heard the clatter of a violent confrontation. They looked in every direction. Ben Zoma finally spotted it. There. Picard saw two combatants. One appeared to be Santana. The other was a dark, many tentacle thing that could only have been Jumaar in his natural state. The colonists was trying to hold the Calvin off with her arms the way any human might try to hold up something big and monstrous, and not having much luck. But to Picard surprised and dismay, she was also launching a series of tiny pink lightning bolts at her adversary. The Calvin recoiled wherever the tiny lightning struck, and the rest of him remained unaffected. Blinging one slimy limb after another at his target, he tried to impeller her to crush her in his powerful embrace. Ben Zoma swore beneath his breath. For her to take John, we've got to do something. Picard nodded. But to whom? Clearly one of the combatants was the saboteur they'd been looking for. But the other was an innocent bystander at worst, and at best a hero who would risk life and limb. The Calvin turned to him and underwent a transformation. He seemed to reshape himself before Picard's eyes, his tentacles shrinking and consolidating, giving way to arms and legs. In a matter of seconds, Jumaar had assumed his human form again. With an unconscious Santana in his arms, he approached the Starfleet officer. I have apprehended the saboteur. Picard didn't lower his weapon, and Jumaar stopped in his tracks. Is something wrong? Picard declined to answer the question. Put Santana down and back away. The Calvin notes placed the colonist on the curved surface of the tube and retreated. Picard pointed to Santana with his phaser. Benzoma makes sure she's still alive. Benzoma moved to the woman's side. She's still with us all right. Before he could get another word out, Jumaar began to change again. His human attributes melted away and a swarm of long dark tentacles took their place. But raised his phaser and aimed at the center of the monstrosity. But before he could press the trigger, he felt something clammy close around his hand and wrench his weapon out of his grasp. Benzoma wasn't quick enough either. Jumaar snatched the man's phaser away with one tentacle and lashed him across the face with another. Unable to escape, Picard watched helplessly as a swarm of tentacles slither towards his throat. The Calvin's grip tightened and Picard's breath was cut off. They saw darkness closing in on him. The Calvin seemed to stagger under the impact of a phaser's fire and lose his grip on Picard's wrist and ankle. Picard's instincts told him to run to get out of the range of the Calvin's deadly tentacles. But he resisted the impulse and did something else entirely. He sought out his captors face if he could indeed be called a face and drove his fist into it as hard as he could. The yellow eyes blinked and the pink more screamed at surprise. The Calvin collapsed, his long snake-like limbs flying in every direction. Picard kicked away a tentacle that lay across his foot and turned to his rescuer. It was Pug Joseph, staring wide-eyed at Jumaar with his weapon still in his hand. Mr. Joseph? The security officer looked as much in need of an explanation as Picard. Before Picard could clear up any of the confusion he had the Calvin's other victims to think about. Locating Ben Zoma, he saw that his friend was trying to sit up. A good sign indeed. Santana on the other hand was still stretched out on the bottom of the tube. Picard told Joseph, I believe she will be alright. But she wouldn't be participating in any battles anytime soon, he decided. And not just because of the beating she'd taken. Pecard had never demonstrated the ability to create pink lightning bolts before. But Gary Mitchell had. If the Magnion's new found ability was a side effect of the Doctor's Silasinine, Picard was going to shut the experiment down as soon as possible. Picard to security. I need all the officers you can spare on the double. I'm in a Jeffress tube accessible from deck 10. I have injured to get to sick bay. Ben Zoma was holding the side of his mottled swollen face as he stuck it to his feet. What happened? We found our saboteur. Jalad Ben Zoma sat on a bio bed in sick bay and allowed Greyhorse to inject him with a hyperspray full of penchillars. Picard who was watching asked Greyhorse. Then you agree? Greyhorse nodded. Absolutely. We can't let the Magnions direct our tractor beam if even one of them is exhibiting unexpected side effects. Ben Zoma looked across the triage area at Santana. She was awake, but dazed. The result of a severe concussion. Picard Joseph was standing beside her, theoretically to guard against her doing anything rash. But in truth, the security officer looked more concerned than watchful. As Ben Zoma understood it, Santana had knocked Joseph out in an effort to reach Jomar before he could carry out his latest act of sabotage. When she found herself unequal to the task, she roused the security officer telepathically, something she couldn't have done without the psilocynine amplifying her abilities, and summoned him to tip the balance. Ben Zoma was glad she had, and he wasn't the only one. Suddenly a handful of security officers escorted Jomar into sick bay. The Kelvin had assumed human form again, Ben Zoma noticed, and didn't appear to be offering the officers any resistance. The Grey Horse indicated an empty bio-bed. Bring him over here. Jomar protested. I am not in need of medical attention. I'll be the judge of that. As the Kelvin was brought to the bed, Ben Zoma looked at Picard. Are you all right? I'll live, if only long enough to find out our guests' motivation for sabotage. I'd be interested in that story myself, and now that we're not headed for the depot any longer, we'll have plenty of time to hear him tell it. We're not headed for the depot? Our secret weapon is put, remember? Without the magmians manning our attractive beam, we don't stand a chance. And with our saboteur out in the open, there's no reason to even pretend we're going. Gerta Asmon's voice interrupted over the intercom. Commander Picard, two of the Naiad ships have left the depot and are coming after us. The muscles in Picard's jaw rippled. Then again, perhaps we'll be having that battle after all. Ben Zoma sighed. Without the magmians, we'll be outgunned. They turned as they heard Juma's voice. We can still beat them. Picard looked into the Calvin's pale blue eyes. I beg your pardon. I said we can still beat them. That is, if you allow me to complete the work I did in an attempt to minimize the effects of your plasma flow regulator and distribution manifold on your phases' system. Ben Zoma understood. I get it now. You were trying to streamline our plasma delivery system and beef up our phaser power. That is correct. The incidents you no doubt attributed to sabotage were inadvertent and unfortunate. Picard regarded the Calvin with narrowed eyes. You were expressly forbidden to tamper with the phaser system. Juma looked unimpressed. The Nuyad must be stopped, Commander. But I had every confidence that the Stargazers plasma conduits could tolerate the modifications. Picard turned ruddy with anger. It wasn't your choice to make Jumaar. I stand corrected. However, you now have an option that you would not have had otherwise. Picard Nuyad was right. The alternative was to take a chance on making Gary Mitchell-style monsters out of St. Towners contingent. And that in the long run might be infinitely more dangerous. Say well Jumaar, how much time do you need? Not much. Twenty minutes perhaps. Picard nodded. You've got it. Second Officer's Log's supplemental. Rather than wait for the enemy vessels to come to us, I've decided to go on the offensive and meet them head on. I hope Jumaar's phaser enhancement is everything he claims it to be. In the dusky vermillion illumination of a red alert, Picard eyed the pair of Nuyad vessels on his viewscreen. Power of phasers and photon torpedoes raise shields. The enemy vessels peeled off in different directions, aiming to catch the Federation ship in a crossfire. Picard thought for a moment and turned to his helm officer. So after the one to starboard. Abruptly the Stargazer veered to the right, keeping one of the Nuyad ships in sight while momentarily ignoring the other. Lock on target. Fire. Twin phaser beams last through space and skewered the enemy ship. The Nuyad ships are come to a second explosion and then a third and finally came apart in a white-hot burst of debris. They had a reporter from our station. Enemy vessel to port. Bring us about. As they swung hard to port the viewscreen displayed their other antagonist. Target and fire. Again the enemy ship was ripped to shreds. Ben Zoma looked at Picard. Now what? Now we go after the depot. His colleague smiled a half-hearted smile. I was afraid you were going to say that. If you were in my place would you be turning back now? If I were in your place, Jarluk, I wouldn't have gone this far in the first place. By Picard's estimate they were still 250 billion kilometers from their target, more than 20 minutes travel at warp seven. With their pursuers out of the way, there was still plenty of time to change course and head for the barrier instead. But Picard had undertaken a mission and he was determined to see it through. The struggles would soon be over. One way or the other. Picard Joseph looked down at Serenity Santana whose dark eyes were closed in recuperative repose. She might have died in her fight with Jobah, he told himself. The Kelvin might have miscalculated and killed her. Then Joseph would never have had the chance to speak with Santana again and to tell her he was sorry. He had almost prevented her from going after Jomar. If he had been successful the Kelvin would have faced Picard and Ben Zoma alone without any help from Santana. There was no telling what would have happened to the officers then. Picard trusted her Joseph thought. Maybe I should have trusted her too. He resolved to tell her that when she woke. There's no need. You told me already. Santana opened her eyes and Joseph felt his face flush with embarrassment. You were reading my mind. Are you upset with me? Not anymore. Not after what you risked to stop Jomar. Santana smiled weirdly. I was afraid he would transform me into a tetrahedron the way he transformed Santana. That made me fight a little harder. I'm glad you're not angry at me. So was he. He said so. I'm so tired Lieutenant. Would you do me a favor and stand guard over me just for old times sake? He nodded. I'd be glad to. A moment later Santana was asleep. Twenty minutes later as the Stargazer reached the Nu Yard supply depot. Once again Stargazer's phaser beams punched through the shields of each of the guarding vessels and each Nu Yard ship met its demise in a ball of yellow white flame. That left only one target. The supply depot. Picard gave his order to Vigo. Aim for its center. Fire when ready Lieutenant. But the supply depot struck first. Seizing the captain's chair for support Picard rode out one bone jarring impact after the other. Vigo's voice was talked with urgency. Sir, faces are offline. Picard felt the blood rush from his face. Without the amplified phaser power, Jamai had given them they were all but toothless. And the supply depot's gunners were too accurate. Their weapons too powerful. Then Picard remembered something that one of his professors had taught him back at the academy. The larger and more complicated objects shaped, the more difficult it is to protect effectively. The depot was very large, very complicated. And Rama had to have some chinks in it. He had to find them. Mr Vigo analyzed the installation's shield structure, see if you can find a weak point. He peered over the pandalite shoulder as he called up a sensor-driven picture of the enemy's shields. Together they poured over it. Vigo pointed to a spot between two of the massive diamond shapes that encircled the depot. There's a lower gravitation concentration at each of these junctures. If we can get close enough, we might be able to penetrate one with a few well-placed photon torpedoes. Picard agreed. We will get close enough. His helm officer did as she was instructed. Like a hawk stooping to take a field mass, the Stargames are darted for the depot's weak spot. The new yard gunners must have seen them coming. Picard felt the bridge shiver. The view screen went dead for a second, then flickered back to life. Girder called out. It's down 90%. Picard shouted over the hiss of seething plasma. Now Mr. Vigo. A string of golden photon torpedoes went hurtling toward the depot. Vigo unleashed one torpedo assault after the other, pounding the installation in a half-dozen places, and everywhere the matter-hanty-matter packets landed, they blew something up. Finally, the last remaining section erupted in a fit of expanding energy, painting the void with its glory. Then it faded, leaving an empty space where a new yard presence had been. Second officer's log, supplemental. We have returned to Magnaier to drop off the colonists who aided us with our tactical enhancements. Fortunately, none of them have shown any lasting effects from their exposure to Silasinine. As for Jomar, I am grateful for his assistance in destroying the no yard depot, which proved critical to our efforts. However, his arrogance, penchant for violence, and insistence on implementing his plans over our objections, mark him as someone the Federation should avoid in the future. Picard gazed at Serenity's antenna, the son of her world sinking through tall trees behind her. Will you miss me, Commander? Torn between emotions, Picard shrugged. What can I say? I wish we had met under different circumstances. Then, you won't miss me. I didn't say that. It was Ben Zoma. We're ready to leave, sir. Give me a minute. Picard had. Santana smiled. You know, we magnions like our privacy. But if you ever get the urge to visit us, Picard nodded. I'll know where to find you. Then she and the mountain and the sunset were gone, and he found himself standing on a transporter pad, feeling empty and terribly alone. Carter Greyhorse was on his way to the mess hall to secure some lunch when he saw Gurda Asmond turn into the corridor up ahead of him. He would never have planned to confront Gurda with his feelings about her in a million years, but something about the moment seemed to wreak of opportunity. Miss Asmond, her expression wasn't an especially inviting one. What do you want? I'd like to talk with you sometime. He kept on going. Leave me alone. He grabbed her arm to hold her back. Please, I really need. Before he could finish what he was saying, Gurda lashed out at him with a heel of her boot. Without thinking, the doctor reacted and caught the navigator's foot in his hand. Suddenly, Gurda's attitude changed. She looked surprised at his quickness. Twisting out of his grip, she lashed out again, this time with her fist. It hit him hard in his solar plexus. As Greyhorse doubled over, she struck him in the chin with a heel of her hand. The blow drove his head up and back, sending him staggering into the bulkhead behind him. I didn't mean to antagonize you. Just let me. As before, she attacked him before he could speak. But suddenly, he slugged her. Either she hadn't expected Greyhorse to retaliate or he just got lucky, because the blow caught her sharply in the side of the head. He spoke up while he had the chance. You're all I can think of. I can't go on like this. Gurda's eyes narrowed. You fight like a child. Greyhorse drew a deep breath. That was it then. Gurda couldn't make it any planer than that. He turned and retreated down the corridor. But before the doctor could get very far, Gurda spoke again. Greyhorse, meet me in the gym tomorrow morning at eight. Perhaps I can teach you to fight like a warrior. The doctor had never been an emotional man, but he felt such joy then. Such a rush of heady optimism that he could barely find the voice to get out of a response. He promised her. I'll be there. As the star-gazer hung motionless in space, Picard gazed at the immense rose-colored expanse of the galactic barrier. He turned to the helm. Wop six. Then with the gesture that suggested forward motion, he added, engage. And they sailed into the scarlet abyss of the barrier to return to Federation space. description: In this episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation," Captain Carlos Terrasco and his crew aboard the SS Valiant venture into uncharted territory, encountering a mysterious red light that threatens their mission. After narrowly escaping an unexpected magnetic storm, they face a perilous journey through an immense void as they near Earth.

Security law started 4-4-3-6-1.3, Lieutenant Warnehope reporting. It now appears that I should have taken more interest in the Michael Contamination Project under the direction of Dr. Zemil and Len Costa. The main laboratory notes have been destroyed and vital information may be lost forever. The cost of superior, Dr. Khan Malu, has confirmed that Dr. Len Costa has erased wholesale banks of computer records. Given the esteemed reputation of the costas, this serious breach of security was totally unexpected. Among many other achievements, the costas perfected the biofilter, which identifies and removes contaminants during transporter operations. They are not just husband and wife, but science's most famous ongoing collaboration. In view of their many contributions to the Federation, we are proceeding cautiously in our investigations. According to Dr. Malu, Len Costa had recently exhibited other moments of irrational behavior, but nothing of this magnitude. Captain Picard has ordered Council of Troy to perform a thorough psychological examination of Dr. Len Costa. At this point, I am only certain of one thing. E-racer of the files was not a sudden impulse, but an act of premeditated sabotage. Len Costa looked more like a disheveled, hyperactive child than a woman during 80 years of age. Deanna Troy could hardly imagine that this was the person, along with her husband E. Miel, who had spearheaded the microcontamination project for so many years. Uncertainty, anger, confusion, pain. The salvo of emotions struck Deanna with such force that she nearly recoiled.
