Why don't you read my mind like Dr. Malu? I'm not a poor-blooded betasoid like Dr. Malu. And even he can't read minds. Only communicate telepathically. Who cares? A two-year-old could read my mind. I want off of this ship. I can't stand it here any longer. The other side, wondering how much more of this she could stand. Sit down, Dr. Costa, and be quiet. Miraculously, the scientist sunk into her chair and stared at the younger woman. Her disjointed stare lasted only seconds before she buried her face within trembling hands and sobbed. He's leaving me. Who's leaving you? Emile. Instinctively, the counselor reached out for the distraught researcher and caught her in her arms. Deanna was not a large person, but Lynn Costa felt as small and helpless as a wounded sparrow in her embrace. There, there. You are among friends. It's always been, Verg. Not friends. I'd galaxy full of microcontaminates to categorize, isolate, and learn to avoid. I'd start coming to the enterprise with the crowning achievement of our careers. But instead, it has been our downfall with rape-like hands Dr. Costa gripped Deanna's tunic and held on desperately. But ever it takes, counselor, you must get us off this ship before—before what? What are you afraid of? As if she had said too much, Lynn Costa suddenly pulled away from the counselor and backed toward the door. Can the finish tomorrow comes in there? Deanna sighed. It was almost midnight, and the counselor thought they might both do better with some sleep. Certainly, Dr. Costa. But first thing tomorrow. The wild-eyed and wild-haired image of Lynn Costa didn't go away easily. But at last Deanna welcomed to sleep. She was troubled by a disturbing yet fascinating dream in which she was completely enclosed in a white suit and white helmet. Her labored breathing echoed in her ears, and the stale scent of reconstituted air assaulted her nostrils. Sweat beaded upon her brow and the back of her neck, and she fought off feelings of claustrophobia. She was in a sterile white room with a row of oblong pods, each just barely large enough to seal a human within. Through gray-tenant glass, she could see a mass of miniaturized equipment within each pod. Beakers, tubes, and sensors. The pods were familiar. It also vaguely threatening. She was drawn to the closest pod. She knew instinctively something was wrong with it. As she peered into the smoky glass, a stream of yellow gas seeped from a valve on the outside of the pod. The stream became a flood, and noxious fumes invaded her eyes, nose, and mouth. Gellicott membranes burned with searing pain as she gagged uncontrollably. The seat was never intended to keep surrounding air out, and the yellow gas poured in. She struggled to stay on her feet, but the battle was already over. She was dying. Deanna bolted upright in her bed, panting for breath. Her hair clung to her sweat-drenched neck and shoulders. She swept her hand over the panel beside her bed, and the lights came on full. She staggered out of bed and rushed to the food slot, where she punched up a large glass of water. She gilted ravenously, trying to erase the dry burning in her throat. Pressure to Troy. Are you awake, Deanna? Troy here. Yes, Beverly, I'm very much awake. I'm sorry to interrupt you during your sleep period, but it's about Dr. Lynn Costa. Profound dreaded well within Deanna's soul. What about Dr. Costa? Did you read my log? Can you please come to sit there? Lynn Costa is dead. Security Log, 3844261.8, Lieutenant-Warf reporting. At approximately 0-2-15 hours, the body of Dr. Lynn Costa was discovered in the laboratory of the Microcontamination Project on Deck 31. Dr. Crusher estimates that Lynn Costa died almost immediately from an unexpected discharge of toxic gas. The gas is of an unknown content, but according to Dr. Grassdow, Lynn Costa was working on a highly theoretical experiment in reactive purification, that is the conversion of solid contaminants to a gaseous state for easier removal. She conducted her experiment alone during off hours in a class zero pod because she knew it could be dangerous. We suspect there was a rupture in a valve or seal. Dr. Costa was wearing a standard clean room suit and helmet, which only filter air flowing out, not in. Due to negative pressure, the class 1 clean room where the accident occurred is self-sealing. Ships monitors indicate full containment of the gas and no danger to any other member of the crew. The filtration system is currently purging the clean room of the gas. According to Councillor Troy, Lynn Costa was depressed and distraught over a failing marriage, and we cannot rule out the possibility of suicide. To my thinking, the only possible reason for suicide would be cowardice in battle, but then I am not human. Captain Picard and Councillor Troy went to inform Emil Costa of his wife's death and found him mildly intoxicated. Apparently, against ship's regulations, he had been drinking laboratory-grade alcohol. These events are sufficiently troubling to Captain Picard that he has asked Councillor Troy and myself to investigate. Deck 5. Councillor, are humans really so susceptible to depression that they would take their own lives? I am afraid so, Worf. They have a long history of obsession with death. I believe it stems from the early religions in which the afterlife is portrayed as being preferable to real life. The perble if deposited Deanna and Worf on Deck 5, where they were to conduct the first interview of the day with Khan Malu, the cost of superior. They strode out to find a thin-mail Vulcan waiting for them. I am Sadek. I work on the micro-contamination project and I will show you where Dr. Costa's body was found, but first Dr. Malu would like to speak briefly with you. Worf liked dealing with Vulcans. You could speak frankly to them and not waste time being tackled, as you had to with humans. They followed the point-a-year humanoid to a rather sumptuous office by enterprise standards. The Captain's ready room paled by comparison. The walls were festooned with sculpted glass cases which contain mounted insects from all over the galaxy. Each case was a hand-crafted work of art on its own merit. The various preserved creatures ranged from Earth scorpions, curled to strike, to centurion water beetles with multiple webbed heads. Dominating the cabin was a massive amber desk, a hunk of petrified resin in which thousands of beta-zoidin grubs were forever frozen. At first glance the noted entomologist and administrator, Khan Malu, was less pre-possessing than his office. He was short, squat, and possessed of dense eyebrows which curled back into a kinky mass of gray hair. Welcome, counselor. Lieutenant, I wish your visit here could be under more pleasant circumstances. Worf nodded. Nice office. Deanna leaned forward expectantly. Dr. Malu, what do you think happened to Len Costa? I have no idea. I was as surprised as anyone. I have always given the Costa's complete autonomy on their projects, and they certainly don't need my guidance. I can't imagine what happened down there. Deanna looked puzzled. But, Dr. Malu, you were the one who alerted me to Len Costa's mental condition. True counselor, but I was following Starfleet regulations. Nothing more. Willful destruction of official records is a serious breach of security. We never got a good explanation out of her. Worf looked frustrated. Who might know something, doctor? Khan Malu motioned to the quiet floken. Dr. Sadic has been with a microcontamination project longer than anyone, except the casters. You should also talk to the junior assistants, grass-style, and the Earth Girl, Shana Russell. Those are the only people who came into contact with the casters on a regular basis. Of course, you will want to talk to Emile. Worf nodded. First, we want to see the clean room. Working on Deck 31 bestowed a certain mystique among the scientific community. It and its residential decks, 32 and 33, were sandwiched between deuterium reactors above and a mass of environmental support equipment below. This restricted location made Deck 31 highly secure, and the logical choice for any sort of experiments that were dangerous or classified. Sadic led Diana and Worf into a circular room with racks of quite clean room garments. The floor under their feet became a silver grating through which air flowed easily. The Vulcan noticed they're discomfort. Your first air shower. There will be others as well as an ultraviolet bath. The suits are light, and you may wear them over your clothing. Diana Troy selected a garment from the racks. Are all these rooms negative pressurized? It depends. Biomedical labs are usually negative pressurized so that airborne particles cannot escape. On the other hand, the transition rooms are positive pressurized so that dirtier air cannot come in. Water pressure is our greatest ally in keeping the environment clean. Even through the suit and helmet, Diana felt the rapid rush of air over her body as they entered the triple work. Courts tubes throbbed over her head and under the white booties coming on her feet. They entered a vast room with smaller self enclosed clean rooms dotting its surface, like igloos on an Antarctic plane. Diana moved to the large window overlooking the Class 1 clean room. It was exactly as she had remembered it from her dream. The white sterility, the role of ominous gray tinted pods, and the miniature lab equipment and sensors within each pod. Suddenly, the sense of deja vu overwhelmed her and she gripped the window ledge for support. Warf rushed to her side. Gausleur, are you all right? Yes, I'm fine. Dr. Santek, is it safe for us to enter? Yes, levels are normal. Particle count is .62, lethal gas analysis is negative. Relative pressure is at a negative 12% and pod number one has been deactivated. The white room was featureless except for the window and the pods. Diana counted 8 of them, all identical except for the identification screens built into their heavily sealed hatches. Some of the screens were dark, but others bore electronic descriptions like Beetlejuice 3, ionized atmosphere, eudrexal compound process reclimant, and space vacuum, hold for grass-dow. The approached pod number one. Its screen was dark. Warf studied the enclosure for a moment, then turned on a dust-free tricorder satik had furnished him. Warf moved the instrument along the smooth shell. Dr. Santek, please help me check the integrity of the seals. I shall. The regulator valve appears intact. Reluctantly, Diana edged closer to the gray enclosure. The ductus satik can the pressure flow both ways through the valve. Could the gas have escaped from there? The Vulcan shook his head. Highly unlikely, experiments with any sort of risk factor are automatically conducted under negative pressure. They passed a century and Warp ushered the wise and scientist into one of the comfortably appointed cells. Now Dr. Costa, did you kill Car and Maloo? No. I told you. When I left him he was alive. Why did you shoot me with a phaser weapon set to stun? I don't know what you are talking about. Go away. The frail white-haired old man curled up in the bunk sobbing pathetically. He didn't seem at all like the kind of desperate lunatic who would willfully murder two people or betray the Federation. At least, thought Warp, they had a strong witness in Ensign Crusher. Ensign Maloo had been hounding Len and Emil for details of a discovery they were keeping secret against Starfleet regulations. Emil could hardly deny complicity in that crime. Len's destruction of the computer records now made perfect sense, and he couldn't forget Shana Russell's testimony that she had heard Khan Maloo threaten Len's life. At least the web of secrecy, deceit, and violence was beginning to make some sense. In the wrong hands, an undetectable and indestructible sub-microbe would be the perfect weapon for sabotage and biological warfare. The death of Len Costa will not be pursued at this inquiry. There is still some doubt that she was murdered or who the perpetrator might be, but there can be no doubt that Khan Maloo was murdered at close range by a phaser weapon set to full. Emil Costa had the weapon, the motive, and the opportunity. I can foresee no other verdict, but guilty. However, there is the troubling aspect of why a man who had committed cold-blooded murder would reset his phaser to stun me. Why did he spare my life, and why did he alert Sadic to check on the experiment in the pod room, in effect saving Wesley Crusher's life? Perhaps this further proves that Khan Maloo was murdered for revenge, or perhaps it only shows that Emil Costa was far from rational. Since learning of the full involvement of Khan Maloo in these matters, I have asked Councillor Troy to investigate his personal records and effects. The habits of beta-zoids can be somewhat eccentric, and she is more likely than anyone else to uncover more evidence. Deanna Troy felt like it should be over. The agonized death of Len Costa, the brutal murder of Khan Maloo. The attacks on Worf and Wesley, and now the imprisonment of Emil Costa. It all sounded like a climax to a Victorian play, with the villain safely behind bars. Then why did she still feel an overpowering sense of dread? Somewhere, she sensed the desire for revenge lurking beneath the veneer of everyday life aboard the Enterprise. She rounded the corridor, leading to Khan Maloo's office and bumped headlong into a figure hurrying in the opposite direction. Shanna Russell recoiled from her in shock. I just heard Councillor. I was working in the clean rooms, and the inner Khan in my helmet must not have been working. This is horrible. How can Dr. Maloo be dead? Come yourself, Shanna. This has been a shock to all of us. Did you think by going to Khan Maloo's office you would find him? I don't know what I thought. I'm just so confused about everything. What is happening to us? Deanna put her arm around the girl's shoulder and comforted her. You must be brave. Emil Costa is standing trial for the murder of Khan Maloo, and you will probably be called to testify, as I will. But I don't know anything. What will I tell them? Just answer their questions truthfully. Thank you, Councillor. I think I will see who's in the 10-forward room. I don't feel like being alone. I would join you, but I have work to do here. Leaving Shanna Russell, Councillor LaTroy walked down a corridor that was totally deserted. She wondered if Khan Maloo's door would be locked. A bigger problem would likely be the volume of data he would have. Beta's always were in federate record keepers, and they enjoyed the more arcane aspects of the practice. They seldom kept records only one way. His door whooshed open at her approach, meaning it had been left unlocked or set to open automatically for anyone who approached. Deanna stopped abruptly. Maloo's computer screen was on. Of course, thought Deanna. He may have gone off and left it that way. But Khan Maloo didn't seem to be the careless type. Would he go off to a secretive meeting and leave his screen on and his door unlocked? She glanced back toward the door, a fleeting impression of Shanna Russell in her mind. The computer was already open to Khan Maloo's file area. Deanna worked long into the night shift. The administrator's files on the people under his direction were complete, but oddly dry and impersonal. No where was the opinionated flair of the man himself. The Beta'soid pushed herself away from the immense desk. She stood and glanced about the room. Not that she expected to find a sheaf of yellowing papers lying on the floor, but it was not uncommon for a Beta'soid to keep a secret diary or notebook. With the walls literally crawling with bugs, it wasn't an easy office to search. Deanna found herself distracted at every instant by a regular mantis or an endorian soapworm. He tried to LaForge. Are you busy, Jordy? No, particularly, Deanna. I just finished up an experiment for Wharf. What did you have in mind? Can you come up to Khan Maloo's office on deck five? I need a fresh pair of eyes. Commander Jordy LaForge scanned the room with the visor apparatus that augmented his sightless eyes. Did bugs don't give off electromagnetic impulses, do they? Not that I know of, Jordy. Jordy stopped before a dark wooden case that contained a dozen phosphorescent centipedes and carefully pried it open. As Deanna moved closer, his fingers reached hesitantly toward one particularly large and ugly specimen. The chief engineer wasn't careful enough, and the exotic insect crumbled to dust beneath his fingers. But underneath it, mounted to the board, was an isolenear optical chip. Bingo! Thank you, Jordy. Let's see what's on it. Within seconds, Jordy had plugged the chip into a slot on Khan Maloo's console, and Deanna was trying to access it from his keyboard. Their excited expressions turned to alarm as gibberish scrolled across the screen. I'm sorry, Deanna. Something must have damaged the contents. No, it's not that. I've heard of this, but I have never seen it. It's a subliminal code. Code was how the computer analyzed it. You don't understand, Jordy. This isn't a code based on some mathematical or relational equation. It's distinctly betasoid, and it depends on subliminal thought patterns. Khan Maloo himself did not know the code when he wrote it. Come again? It's like making a coded imprint of the contents of your subconscious. He wrote it while in a trance, knowing it would look like gibberish to him, too. But he knew he could read it in the future, if he concentrated. Hmm. I think I know what you mean. On ancient Earth, people from certain religions used to speak in tongues and write in unknown languages, but they had no way to interpret what they had done. What do you want me to do with this chip? I'm going to go back to my courtism and think about it, Jordy. This place is making me jumpy. In the sanctity of her darkened room, Deanna Troi drifted in and out of sleep. Her dreams were filled with the spirit of Khan Maloo. His image, his face, his voice, his thoughts, and his coded writings fought for her subconscious. The code appeared to her like love letters. Heart-filled attempts to communicate his secrets. Of course, they were love letters to himself, and she told herself she shouldn't read them. But she knew he wanted her to read them. She willed herself fully awake. Her closest comrades were on K-Ron Rock at the hearing. It was up to her to find more evidence to support Worf's case. What she needed was a beverage containing a stimulant. She picked up the isylinear optical chip just because it felt comforting to hold it and patted over to the food slot. Computer, I'd like a small pot of English tea. After several seconds, there was no synthesized voice response, and nothing happened at the delivery tray. Computer, may I have a glass of water? The complex mechanism hung in the wall like a shiny crater. It was dead. Alright, I'll go down to ten-forward and get a pot of tea. And I hurriedly dressed and took only one thing with her. Karn-moulous secret isylinear chip. It was one of those overcast days, ruled by a good stiff breeze. The kind of day Deanna remembered so well from her youth. The metal was a light with orange coal blossoms. Little more than a few centimeters tall. The giant miller reads whipped in the breeze. The blue tassels hurling winged to seeds into the wind. And the moss squished pleasantly under her boots. A drizzle struck her in the face, and she thankfully turned her face forward to lick the rain with her tongue. She hugged her old shawl tighter around her shoulders and recalled how it had been knitted by a friend of her mothers. She wanted to feel like a child again, to rediscover the primitive emotions of childhood. Poetry, frivolity, the joy in taking a walk these were the triggers that allowed a betazoy to access parts of the mind shut off to most species. She continued her stroll marveling at the authenticity of the holodeck setting and wondering what was over the next hill. She offers her carol to cancel with Troy. The intrusion broke her mood, but only slightly. Troy here. An environmental technician is requesting entrance to your quarters to fix your food slot. My food slot. I didn't even report it. Please let him in and thank him for his prompt attention. The appointment can wait until you are present. Donate for that. I may be here on the holodeck for some time. Out. One word Deanna told herself that she ran down a floured hill, the wind slicking back her here. One word. One name in Carn-Moulou's subliminal code might lead to others. Lynne Costa, she thought. The person who had started it all. She would look for Lynne Costa's name and she would know it when she saw it. Deanna twirled for a moment. Her scarf billowing behind her as she chanted the nonsense words of a nursery song remembered from long ago. A glow with exertion and the warmth of fond memories, she stopped spinning and stood perfectly still. End the program. The room returned to a black sick minute enclosure. Deanna tolled off and went back to her quarters, feeling refreshed and renewed. She knew she had the key. Deanna returned to her quarters and plugged the optical chip into her computer console. An odd melange of characters and symbols apparently typed at random, crawled across the screen. She lightly perused the strange formations waiting for something, anything, to jump out at her. Suddenly small clumps of the alphabet soup made sense. Names and simple words leapt out at her. Excitedly, she paged through more screens, finding more names, all of them from the microcontamination project. Lynne. She repeated aloud as she typed, is the queen hag. Emile is a naughty jester. Sadic is the heir apparent. Grass-dow is a footman. Shanna is Jasmine. She stopped abruptly and peered again at the jumbled letters on the screen, and the words she had typed beside them. What did terms like footman, Jasmine and Jester mean? Was there another code underneath? She couldn't report to Worf, because he was on the starbase, enmeshed in the hearing. The computer would only allow an emergency message to reach him. Her head hurt, and she thought about getting some tea. Had Deanna not imagined a brimming cup of tea at that moment, she never would have seen the slight trail of steam spewing from the flute slot. Damn, she muttered to herself. I thought they fixed that thing. She took a single step toward it and felt her legs buckle. Then every muscle deserted her, and she crumbled to the floor, gasping for breath. Blackness engulfed her senses, but she clung to consciousness for the split second it took to grip her and sick me a bit. Troy to sick bay. Emergency. Emergency. Emergency. Worf was surprised when Judge Watanabe put Emil Costo on the stand before the defense had presented its case. But he didn't object. He understood the judge's desire to comprehend the secret dealings between the deceased and the accused. With very little prodding, Emil Costo was eager to tell his story. It was Vegratu. That's the planet where I found the sub-microbe. I trapped it myself while we were in orbit and did all the preliminary tests myself. We knew it was special right away. Len and I immediately transferred the test data to our private file and started making only oblique references to it. All we knew was that we wanted to control the discovery until we had a clear goal for it. I ejected the only sample that we had into space. No one but Len and I knew where to get more. We went to car in Malou for advice and that was our biggest mistake. Crusher to Worf, emergency override. Worf motion to the judge. Excuse me, your honor. Worf here. What is it, doctor? Report to sick bay at once. A few minutes ago, Deanna Troy nearly died. I want her to rest, but she insists on speaking to you. Worf questioned Dr. Brevley Crusher at the sick bay entrance. Who brought her in? She called sick bay herself. The computer analyzed her voice patterns and deemed them sufficiently traumatized to initiate a direct beaming. Or else we'd be attending another funeral. The Klingon snarled low in his throat and the hair on the back of his neck tingled with anger. He followed Dr. Crusher into the intensive care unit. Deanna lay propped up in bed, not looking to ill except for her pale complexion and the one smile she tried to give Worf. He'd noticed she was lying perfectly still, as if the slightest motion was too much of an ordeal at the moment. I am sorry, Deanna. I put you in danger. Nonsense. We are getting close now, and the guilty one is getting desperate. It's not Emile. In coded records, Khan Meluh wrote, Lin is the queen hag. Emile is a naughty jester. Sadik is the heir apparent. Grassdowl is a foot man. And Shana is Jasmine. That's just one entry in his notes. In my quarters there is an isolinear chip. We must have it. Rest. You have done enough. Worf to security. Send the four men detailed to Deanna Troy's quarters at once. A wait my arrival. Acknowledged. Worf to the forage. Jordi here. How is Deanna? As well as can be expected. Can you meet me at her quarters? I sure can. Bring a tricorder, Jordi. Out. Jordi and Worf rounded a bulkhead to see this security detail standing outside the open doorway of Deanna Troy's cabin. Lieutenant Worf? The door was open when we got here. Addis, Ensign. Remain on guard. Jordi turned on his tricorder. Worf I can find traces of toxic chemicals, but not in a quantity to be dangerous. Black streaks stretched like the fingers of a star from the gaping hole. Jordi kept his distance from the charred wires and steaming green goop. Direct shot. When they didn't find Deanna's body, they made a quick decision to destroy the evidence of their murder attempt. Commander, if you will handle the investigation from this inn, there is something I must do. My all-means were, leave this mess to me. Worf strode angrily down the corridor away from Deanna Troi's cabin. Again, the murderer had anticipated their actions and beaten them. Deanna Troi had found something, the first piece of evidence that hadn't been planted for them to find, like the blue vial. While he had been playing courtroom on K-ran Rock, Deanna Troi had been doing his job. As he charged angrily down the corridor, he nearly knocked over the Vulcan, Sadak. Pardon me, Dr. Sadak. I was preoccupied. I heard about what happened to Councillor La Troi. I thought I might be of some assistance. Do these impressions mean anything to you? Lin is the queen hag. Emile is a naughty jester. Sadak is the heir apparent. Grassdow is a footman and Shanna is Jasmine. Sadak blinked and furrowed his eyebrows slightly. In a monarchy, Lin would certainly be considered the queen. Emile was more capable of laughter and the human trait of joking than the rest of us. And one could say he has been naughty. I am the heir apparent to the microcontamination project. As I understand the term footman, it could mean a servant. I leave it to you to say whether Grassdow qualifies. As for Shanna being Jasmine, I did hear Dr. Maloo call her that once. What? You say Jasmine is a name? He used it as such. I only heard him call her that once though. Warf rushed back to his command post and his computer console. Computer, what is Shanna Russell's full background? Shanna Russell, born Jasmine Terri on Earth, City of Calcutta. Age 25 standard years, received Bachelor of Science degree. Wait. When did she change her name? 8.5 months ago. Horulate the name Terri with the records of Lin and Emile Costa. Searching? One match found. Meghan Terri was a co-worker with Acosta's approximately 26 years ago in the Dayton bio-filter experiments. She sued them for scientific plagiarism over bio-filter version 897-G, which was eventually accepted as the Federation standard. Corlate Meghan Terri and Jasmine Terri. Mother and daughter. You heard a rustling behind him in the direction of the laboratory and turned to see Shanna Russell aiming a phaser directly at his head. That's enough of that. Raise your hands. This time my phaser is not set to stun. Why didn't you kill me when you had the chance? I liked you. Even I make mistakes. Now stand up slowly, keeping your hands up and back away from that console. Worf did exactly as he was told. He had dealt with dangerous creatures from all over the galaxy, but none of them were any more cold-heartedly ruthless than the small human female. For a mother, she was the one who really perfected the bio-filter. Shanna's pretty face clotted with anger so ugly, imported on dementia. It was worse than that. All three of them were equals in the project, but Emil was having an affair with my mother. He promised to leave his wife if she would turn over the results of her work to him. Like a fool, she believed him. They stole her work and got her reassigned while they soared to a claim. On top of that, my mother was pregnant. Emil is my father. Worf could envision a sad little girl who must have been haranged constantly about how the costas had ruined her mother's life. As a Klingon orphan by the ravages of war, he understood the lore of revenge. He also understood its destructiveness. You succeeded in destroying them. Yes I did. Killing Lin was satisfying because of the complexity involved. But watching Emil suffer was so fulfilling. He had no idea who I was or what was happening to him. But Khan Malu knew who you were. Of course, he knew my mother and her whole history with the costas. When he wanted someone to spy on him over this business with the sub-microbe, he came to my school to find me. We decided to change my name to hide my identity, and he spent his sabbatical teaching me betazoid mine techniques to fool Deanna Troy. I've always been a good student. Why did you kill him? He was the only one who knew who I was. Plus killing him resulted in even more suffering for Emil. How could I resist? I'm sorry about Councillor Troy. But if she had died as planned, you wouldn't have known about the Isolinear chip, and we wouldn't be having this conversation. Let's go to the shuttle bay. So intent was Shana's gaze on the tall Klingon, that she didn't see the slim Vulcan standing just outside the doorway. Sadik gripped her neck for only a second, but it was enough to render her unconscious for several minutes. Warth led out of sigh. Thank you again, Sadik. I did not do it for your benefit, Lieutenant. We are terribly behind in the micro-contamination project, and we need to give doctors Costa and Grasta back to work. Security Log. Supplemental. Lieutenant Warth reporting. Security charges against Emil Costa were dropped after Shana Russell's apprehension. Conspiracy charges could be leveled against the doctor, but that seems unlikely given his long record of service to the Federation. Both Dr. Costa and Grasta have been remanded to Starfleet for counseling. If all goals well, they should be released in a few months. The same cannot be said for Shana Russell. Her psychoanalysis and treatment will probably take many years. The micro-contamination project has been disbanded. Sadik has been assigned to other duties, namely heading a team dispatch to Vega II in order to study the sub-micro-first hand. Councilor Troy is almost fully recovered, and she's been talking about cooking her own meals instead of using the food slot. It is alarming to think what might have happened to her. I remain deeply disturbed by these events. Like Shana Russell, I have experienced the madness of revenge. Like the Costals, my own people practiced secrecy and deception until it nearly destroyed them. I can understand the motives of personal gain and ambition all too well. That is why the Federation is a free and open society. There will be no more secrecy about the sub-microb discovery. Sadik and his team will study it openly and share their knowledge. As the Costals learn to their regret, a terrible secret cannot be kept.
description: In "Contamination," Star Trek's The Next Generation brings us a tense episode where Dr. Len Costa has been accused of sabotaging records during the Michael Contamination Project. Despite initial disbelief from Deanna Troy, who is skeptical of his rational behavior and recent outbursts, they must confront the reality that their collaboration with him could be put at risk. The situation escalates into an emotional breakdown as both argue for leniency in Costa's actions, revealing a complex relationship fraught with trust issues and deep-seated resentment.

description: In this episode, Captain Mackenzie Talhoo reflects on her return to the fleet after five years away, focusing on her interactions with new crew members and her experiences adapting to their roles. She discusses her relationships with chief engineer Burgon, science officer Solita, and security chief Zack Kebran, as well as her approach to dealing with her own scars from a previous encounter. Talhoo is searching for the right candidate for first officer, hoping to find someone she can trust and respect.

Suddenly there was a cut on his arm and then a slash across his chest, and he wasn't even fully aware of how they had gotten there. The son was faster than the father, or else Calhoun was slower. The area around Fallon was crowned with vessels of all sizes and shapes trying to put as much distance between themselves and the shattering planet as possible. Status on the current population. Most of them have managed to clear out in private vessels, sir. We've evacuated over a thousand people onto the Excalibur. Calhoun noticed Siquan standing off to the side very quiet. Are you all right, Ambassador? Of course not. On the screen, Fallon continued to shudder. Its entire surface ribbed with cracks. And then, suddenly, something thrust up from within. It was a claw. A single giant flaming claw, miles wide, smashing up through what was once a polar ice cap. Then another flaming claw, several hundred miles away. And then a third and a fourth, but these at the opposite ends of the planet, and they seemed even larger. Then the planet broke apart in a stunning display of manner and energy. Fallon erupted from the inside out. And there was a creature unlike anything that Calhoun had ever seen. It seemed vaguely avian in appearance, with feathers made of roaring flame and energy crackling around it. Its talons of flame flexed outward, and its massive wings unfurled. Its beak was long and wide, and it opened its mouth in a screen that could be heard in the depths of space. Incredibly, stars were visible through the creature. It was as if it was a creature that was both there and not there. What the hell is it? The gong stood in slow astonishment. Oh my god, it can't be. Don't you get it? It's the Great Bird of the Galaxy. Shall we look at the scans of the gong? Oh, come on, that's a myth. The Great Bird, in the airlessness of space, continued to move its wings. It crackled with power, extending its jaws. It gobbled up floating chunks left over from Fallon. And then it seemed to turn its attention to the starship Excalibur. Calhoun shook his head. I do not like the looks of this. Aren't baby birds hungry first thing after they're born? The creature moved towards them. OK, McHenry, move us out at warp factor one. Let's draw it away from the area and give everyone a chance to clear out. K-bron looked up from tactical. Incoming message from one of the vessels, sir. Save it, Lieutenant. Mr. McHenry, get us out of here. The Excalibur went into reverse thrust, pivoted, and moved away from the shattered remains of Fallon, with the Great Bird of the Galaxy in hot pursuit. For going turned to Calhoun. According to the legend, there can only be one Great Bird at a time. And when its senses its end is near, the Great Bird imparts its essence into a world gestates over centuries and is then reborn. I guess that's why it was mythological. Take centuries for the egg, if you will, to hatch. But you told me, May the Great Bird of the Galaxy roost on your planet was a blessing. Obviously, it was. Look at the prosperity that Fallon saw during the time of the roosting. But when it hatches, the planet is destroyed. Letler interrupted. Sir, it's catching up. And then, with a twist of its powerful wings, the Great Bird seemed to warp through the very fabric of space. It disappeared without a trace. Shelby looked at the view screen of stars. Where do you think it went? McHenry shook his head in amazement. Anywhere it wanted to. Shelby looked at Calhoun, still bloody and bruised from his fight with Rajan. Captain, I suggest you get yourself down to sick pay. Good advice, Commander. Would you mind escorting me down there? As they headed to the Turbullet, Calhoun paused and turned to Kebran. Oh, we had an incoming message. What was that about? Kebran tapped his combo and a voice instantly recognizable as Zorran's, filled the bridge. Zorran's chilling laughter continued in Siquan's memory long after the message had ended. In his ready room, Calhoun had just finished mounting the sword back onto the wall. Shelby entered and stood just inside the door. I was wondering. I was about to head down to the team room and have a drink. Thought, you might like to come along. That sounds great. He regarded the sword for a moment. You know what was interesting. When I tried to save Rajan, I did so without even thinking about it. It was instinctive. I always felt my instincts were based in pure savagery, but now, Shelby smiled. Your survival instincts were, sure, because they're what you needed in order to get through your life. But being a Starship Commander isn't just about survival. There's much, much more to it than that. And I suppose that you're prepared to tell me what that is. Of course, chapter and verse. Well, epic. Maybe, just maybe now. I'm prepared to listen. And I'm prepared to tell you, if you just stop calling me by that stupid nickname. As they headed for the door, she paused. One quick question. You told me that you had a vision of me long ago. Just out of morbid curiosity. Was I wearing any clothes in that vision? Nope. Stark. Make it. She sighed. Yeah, well, it's comforting to know that some instincts never change. I guess. And they headed to the team room for a drink. Star Trek. New Frontier was written by Peter David and read by Joe Morton. description: In Book 4 Endgame of New Frontier, a crisis unfolds as refugees from Nelkar are subjected to an unusual power play by their hosts, leading Mackenzie Calhoun to confront them directly. The episode explores the morally complex situation and highlights the consequences of turning a blind eye to the well-being of innocent people.

transcript: Simon & Schuster Audio presents Star Trek, the Next Generation, Relics by Michael Jan Friedman, based on the television episode story and teleplay by Ronald D. Moore, read by James Doen, with an introduction and conclusion by Le Bar Burton. It's easy to idealize the past. Take sailing ships, for instance. Not the big, hard-hulled vessels we use today to travel through subspace from one star system to another. No, I'm talking about the clumsy, little wooden canvas jobs men used in the old days to navigate their planet's oceans. When I was young, I liked to imagine myself at the helm of one of those ships, the wind singing in my ears, the taste of salt spray on my lips. I like to pretend that I was on some long, secret voyage sent off by a beautiful queen. There was always a beautiful queen it seemed, braving impossible dangers to explore lands no one had ever seen before. It was all stirring, very romantic. Of course, if my dreams had been a little more historically accurate, I probably wouldn't have come back alive from any of those voyages. In those days, sailors often didn't. If the scurvy didn't get them, there was a host of other diseases waiting in the wings, not to mention starvation, dehydration, and the occasional hurricane. Then I got older and my dreams came to revolve around more recent times. I imagined myself on board some early starship back in the days when everything was theoretical and experimental, and nobody was quite sure their shiny new machines would work the way they were supposed to. But I didn't dream that I was at the helm any longer, or even in charge. In those old or more mature dreams, I was the ship's engineer. The guy everyone turned to when things started to fall apart. The guy who could always figure out a way to do what needed to be done. Of course, it wasn't all romance and adventure in those days either, but the casualties were a lot fewer and the problems were a good deal more interesting. And so, when I took the entrance exams for Starfleet Academy, I wasn't aspiring to be Jory LaForge Captain. All I wanted was to be Jory LaForge Chief Engineer. Then I could be one of those guys who put everything back together when it began to fall apart, just like in the good old days when they were still just feeling their way through the galaxy. Yeah, it's easy to idealize the past until you smack into it at warp 9.95. Captain Picard? Jean-Luc Picard was in his ready room, studying a monograph on the formation of accretion bridges in binary star pairs. Yes, Mr. Data? Sir, there is something here that you should see. I'm on my way. Rising? The Captain rounded his desk and headed for the exit. Mr. Data would not have summoned him unless this were a matter of some urgency. As the ready room door slid aside, he noted that Will Riker, his first officer, was already hovering over Data's position at the aft science station. A moment later, he joined them. What is it, Data? A subspace radio wave, sir. I have identified the signal. The transmission appears to be a Starfleet code used between 50 and 80 years ago. Code 1, Alpha 0. Ship in distress. Riker was in tweet. Computer, are there any Starfleet vessels reported missing in the sector? Negative. It was a Captain's turn to pose a question. Computer, expand parameters to include radiation sectors? A list of ships came up in one of the monitors. Transport ship SS Genolan, NC567, was reported missing on start 87893.1 while en route to Norpin 5. Riker exchanged glances with the Captain. 75 years ago, sir. I'd say we found the Genolan. But we're a long way from Norpin 5. They must have gone pretty far off course. Indeed, number one. Picard turned to Tina Riker. The petite black woman sitting at the Khan Station. Ensign, establish coordinates for the source of the signal and plot a course for them. Walt Factor 8. I, sir. Walt Factor 8, Captain. Why the Haracer? The Captain frowned. His first officer had a point. If the Genolan had waited for 75 years, it could wait a little longer and yet... Call it intuition, number one. The Captain's secret. The Captain's secret. The Captain's secret. The Captain's secret. The Captain's secret. Will Riker drummed his fingers on the armrest of his seat in the command center? For four days, they'd been riding through subspace, heading for a rendezvous with what was left of the Genolan. Captain? It was Worf. Turning away from the science console, Picard answered him. Yes, Lieutenant? We are approaching the coordinates of the distress signal. The card turned to Ensign Riker. Bring us out of Worf, Ensign. I, sir. Riker stood. He got antsy whenever the ship was about to close in on its objective, particularly one it had been pursuing as long as this one. Unfortunately, the main view screen showed nothing except an unfamiliar star field. They were still millions of kilometers short of the signal source, which they would now approach on impulse power. Suddenly, the Enterprise was rocked as if a giant hand had grasped it and was shaking it like a tambourine. Riker grasped at the back of Riker's chair to keep from being catapulted across the deck. Then, as abruptly as it started, the shaking stopped. But that was no guarantee that they wouldn't be treated to a repeat performance. Yellow alert. As Riker headed back to his place on the command center, Descartes and Data were barely a step behind him. The Captain glanced at Worf. Report, Lieutenant. We have entered a massive gravitational field, sir. Descartes frowned, and he wasn't the only one. After all, there was nothing on the screen close enough to possess a gravitational field, much less one as powerful as the thing they'd run into. Riker turned to the Android second officer, hoping for more information. Data was bent over the op station, having replaced the crewmen who had been sitting there before. Mr. Data? Commander, there are no stellar bodies listed at these coordinates in our charts. However, sensor readings indicate the presence of an extremely strong gravitational source in this vicinity. It is directly ahead. It didn't make sense, Riker thought, unless the object creating the field was cloaked somehow. Picard must have had the same idea. Mr. Worf? Can you localise the source of the gravity field? Yes, sir. On screen? The star field on the view screen changed, reflecting another view, and if one looked closely, there was a small dark ball at its center. The captain turned to Worf again. Magnify, Lieutenant? The image increased several orders of magnitude, until it could be seen more easily. It now appeared as round and smooth as a billiard ball, but because it was so dark, it was hard for Riker to discern anything else about it. Sensors? Data swiveled in his chair. I am having difficulty scanning the object. However, it would appear to be at least 200 million kilometres in diameter. Riker looked to Picard. The captain's surprise mirrored his own. Sir? That's almost the size of Earth's orbit around the Sun. Indeed, number one. Why didn't we detect it before now? Any idea, Data? Captain? The object's enormous mass is causing a great deal of gravimetric subspace interference. That interference might have prevented our sensors from detecting the object before we dropped out of warp. Picard's brow wrinkled as he gazed at the view screen. Mr. Data? Could this be a Dyson sphere? There is no comparative data, Captain. However, this object does fit the general parameters of Dyson's theory. Riker looked from one to the other. A Dyson sphere? It's a very old theory, number one. I'm not surprised that you haven't heard of it. A 20th century physicist Freeman Dyson postulated that an enormous hollow sphere could be constructed around the star. This would have the advantage of harnessing all the radiant energy of the star, not just a fraction of it. The population living on the interior surface would therefore have a virtually inexhaustible source of power. Are you saying there might be people living in there? The answer was supplied by Data. Possibly a great number of people, Commander. The interior surface area of a sphere this size would be equivalent to that of more than two hundred. Fifty million-class M planets. Wolf looked up from his tactical console. Sir, I have located the distress signal. It is coming from a point on the northern hemisphere. Absorbing the information, Picard turned to Riker. Take us into synchronous orbit above that point. Hi, sir. They still had to answer the 75-year-old distress call Riker mused. But their interest in the Genolan had already paled beside their interest in the sphere. Gradually, they pulled closer to it until they at last achieved the synchronous orbit that Picard desired. The monstrous object looked like a giant wall in space, stretching in every direction as far as the eye could see. Where before the sphere had appeared perfectly smooth, it was now possible to discern intricate patterns on the surface. We are holding position at 30,000 kilometers above the surface, Captain. Thank you, Ensign. Sir, yes, Mr. Data? The distress signal is coming from a federation ship which has impacted on the surface of the sphere. It is the transport ship, Genolan. Riker nodded. Any life signs? Our sensors show none, sir. However, there are several small power emanations, and life support is still functioning at minimum levels. Out of the corner of his eye, Riker noticed Picard looking at him. Knowing exactly what the captain wanted, the first officer tapped his communicator. Bridge to engineering. Jordy? Meet me in transport of room three? Then he turned to the Klingon security chief. Mr. Woff, you're with me as well. As Jordy materialized on the Genolan with Riker and Woff on either side of him, he scanned their surroundings. Huh? A bit cramped, isn't it? Riker took out his tricorder. Come on, let's have a look at it. The lights were dim. One or two of the consuls were damaged or burnt out. There were piles of ash on the floor, and in several spots the bulkhead was caved in. Jordy shook his head as he took it all in. This ship really went through the ringer even before it crashed. Wonder what happened to it? Sniffing the air, Riker turned to the Klingon. Pretty stale in here. See if you can increase the oxygen level, lieutenant? Nodding. Woff moved over to one of the consuls. Meanwhile, Jordy's tricorder led him to the transporter controls, not that he expected to find anything of interest there, but he had to cover all the bases. A moment later, he was glad he had. Commander? What is it, Jordy? This transporter is still online. It's been fed power from the auxiliary systems. Riker bent over the transporter controls to do some checking of his own. How about that? The materialization subroutine has been disabled. And that's not all. The auxiliary phase and users have been connected to the emitter array. The override is completely gone, and the pattern buffer has been locked into a continuous diagnostic cycle. That doesn't make any sense? Locking the unit in a diagnostic mode just sends inert matter flowing through the pattern buffer? Suddenly, Jordy saw something on the console. Something he hadn't noticed before. Damn. Someone's pattern is still in the buffer. Riker's eyes narrowed as he followed Jordy's pointing finger. You're right. It's completely intact. Less than 0.003 signaled degradation. But how is that possible? Jordy shrugged. I don't know. I've never seen a transporter system Jordy rigged like this. Riker frowned. Jordy? Could someone survive in a transporter buffer for 75 years? The chief engineer bit his lip. It had never been attempted not to his knowledge anyway. But... I know a way to find out, Commander. Ever so carefully, Jordy worked the controls of the transporter unit. Then taking a deep breath, he touched one final command area and looked to the tiny platform in front of him. In the next instant, he saw a figure taking shape. It wavered in the beam, acquiring a density and a snail's face. And then, with a last surge of energy, solidified. Riker shook his head in admiration. My god, Jordy, you did it! And so he had. For what stood before them was a living, breathing, and a fire. A denison of the 23rd century. And except for the arm he held in a sling. He was hardly the worst for wear. For a moment, Montgomery Scott was overcome by a wave of vertigo. He didn't know who he was. Much less where he was. Then it all came flooding back to him. He was in the Genon, in the Ops Center. They crashed. Only he and Ensign Franklin had survived. And with a dearth of supplies staring them in the face, their only hope had been... He looked around. There were two men standing in front of the transporter platform, staring at him. One of them, the shorter of the two, wore a strange, high-tech band around his eyes. Both sported uniforms that he had never seen before, but they rescued him from the transporter loop, so they probably weren't hostile. The transporter loop, he thought. Franklin! Where was Franklin? Shaking off his wooziness, Scott came down off the platform and headed south to the ship. He was straight for the transporter console. Seemingly fascinated by him, the two men stepped aside to let him bustle by. No sooner had Scott reached the console than he began checking out its monitors, verifying his readings. We've got to get Franklin out of there. One of the men spoke up. Someone else's pattern is still in the buffer? I? Matt Franklin and I went in together? Almost done, he told himself. Another couple of levels to examine. Here. And here. And then he... Wait a minute. Scott stared at the last monitor, the one that covered the enducers. He didn't like this. Something's wrong. One of the enducers has failed. Turning to the man in the band, he bocked an order. Boosted again on the matter stream. Moving to a nearby console, the man complied. description: In this episode of Star Trek: The Next Generation, Michael Jan Friedman reads from a novelization of "Relics," which focuses on Captain Picard and his crew navigating a binary star system for scientific research. Data points out an urgent subspace radio message indicating a potential danger in the vicinity. This excerpt highlights the tension and urgency felt by the characters in exploring previously uncharted territories, emphasizing their sense of duty to complete their mission despite the challenges they face.

transcript: The end of everything Harold did itself as a metallic hum near Montoya's left ear. No need to turn around and look. The hum had to come from a one eye, a lead colored object about the size of a human torso with a single staring camera eye and a bristling spiky penumbra of antenna that was gliding behind Montoya's head, intercepting and reading his thoughts. Montoya knew his only chance for survival was to keep from thinking about the small case that rested lightly in his hand. He ignored it, shut his eyes to it, hummed a tuneless tune to forget about it. What the case held was of no monetary work, yet was valuable beyond reckoning. To possess it here on the planet of Rampart was a crime punishable by death. In spite of his efforts, fugitive thoughts that lurked in the shadows of his mind came to him. He heard the one eye come closer. Two broad-shouldered figures, their white uniforms bearing the blue cephalic security logo confronted Montoya. One of the CS men pulled at the case in Montoya's hand. Montoya let it slip out. They guided him along the wall to a cage-like elevator. He started to weep. The lift emerged onto the roof. Montoya let the sobs shudder through him, tears streaming down his face. The CS men led him within a few meters of the roof's edge as they approached the door of the hovercraft. Suddenly Montoya flailed out with his cuffed hands, causing the surprised CS man to lose his grip, but all his strength Montoya grabbed at his case, ripping it right out of the other CS man's hands. With a triumphant yell, he flung the case outwards. The case opened as it fell toward the ground far below. Yellowed old pages fluttered free and scattered in whitening gyres on the wind. He smiled to himself, his trick, his sadness, and worked, a stop for the one eye so the device wouldn't guess at his spontaneous last act and kill him to prevent it. He kept his eyes on the pages as they grew smaller and smaller. A hundred CS officers and special agents converged on the area where the pages had fallen. They all wore protective helmets with electronic visors that turned printed words into gibberish for their eyes. A hundred CS officers quickly set up roadblocks and evacuated residents, then set to work finding the scattered pages and burning them in portable mini incinerators. One page had floated far. It alone had escaped the CS and their incinerators. It lay negatively on a small patch of grass behind an elementary school. At noon recess, a red haired girl from the third grade class chased a ball and came upon the page. She had never seen such an old and discolored piece of paper. She picked it up and with big green and quisitive eyes looked at an illustration on the page. It appeared to be of a man tied onto a kind of sled and surrounded by a busy swarm of people no bigger than his finger. She read the words on the page. About four hours after we began our journey, I awake by a very ridiculous accident. For the carriage being stopped a while to adjust something that was out of order, two or three of the young natives had the curiosity to see how I looked when I was asleep. They climbed up into the engine and advancing very softly to my face. One of them, an officer in the guards, put the sharp end of his half-pike a good way up into my left nostril, which tickled my nose like a straw and made me sneeze violently. The green-eyed girl laughed. She looked at the top of the page and saw a title line. Gulliver's travels are voyage to lilyput. She sensed that the page was something forbidden, something the grown-ups told you to never ever touch or look at or you'd get a disease. But her fascination with the page overcame her caution. She hid the page in her dress, hoping to take it home that day. Counselor Deanna Troy sat in her cabin on the Enterprise. She was about to fulfill, in her own way, the primary mission of the USS Enterprise, exploration of new worlds and discovery of alien life. To begin observations, all she had to do was utter a single word to the computer. She sounded it in her mind. She began to feel vertigo. The feeling intensified as if she were spinning faster and faster. She couldn't focus her eyes. The walls of the cabin were disintegrating. She felt herself thrown out of her chair, tumbling through space. Then she hit the ground, face down. She lay still for several moments, regaining her equilibrium. Then she realized the ground was hot enough to burn her skin. She quickly got to her feet and with a devastating shock, saw that she was in the middle of a wasteland. Desert. I wasn't alone in that desert, a great matriarch, as big as the planet itself was there too. Troy stopped for a moment and Captain Jean-Luc Picard watched her with concern. She lived in the ground and I never saw her, but she gave me water and kept me alive. There were dangers she couldn't protect me from. There was a predator that looked half like a lioness and half like a human. I escaped from it, but in the night I was confronted by another danger, a giant man whose skin was like a mirror, in which I saw images of war and apocalypse. Somehow I woke myself up. I'd been in front of my computer all along and yet I had been to another world as well. They're real Captain and they're close to the ship. I feel them as other worlders. Picard questioned her gently, then told her he was going to scan the area around the ship and try to discover who the alien beings were. He assured her the ship's computer would keep track of her vital signs. After she left, Picard wondered if he'd been too distant with her. She often reminded him that he needed to show more emotion. They even had a meeting on the subject scheduled for today, a meeting that had been postponed many times and would have to be postponed once again. Wesley and Data sat at their consoles on the Enterprise Bridge waiting for the ship's sensors to scan the surrounding space. Data touched his keypad to reset the external sensor for new frequencies. There, we must now wait for this sequence to compute. Perhaps, Wesley, this is a good opportunity for me to present you with my gift. Data assumed a heraldic pose. The teachings of Macaroon, Erotica, doing a little thing we call three-toed minty fresh logo tissue. Quest for the Golden Aphids, where they call the wind, Mr. Conceited Begone. I walked down spanked Mandrel Strassa with gently yielding fun bladder under warranty. Prometheus, indicator light blinking through the hydrogen eternity. Boo! Boo! Data looked at Wesley. The answer was laughing. A puzzled, almost sad look crossed Data's face. That was not the reaction I had anticipated or hoped for. I thought I had composed my first artistic poem. Suddenly Data looked down at his console. The indices were changing rapidly. We have found something. The recorder marker from the Huxley was not what we were looking for. But it's a major find, nonetheless. The others in the conference room, Data, Troy, and first officer Riker listened rapidly to Picard. The Huxleys, Captain Bowles, had been one of the fleet's great explorers, and the fate of his ship was a major unsolved puzzle in Starfleet's history. The marker has yielded few facts, but it seems the Huxley was attacked by other ships in the Roofiyuki Nebula. Starfleet has asked us to enter the nebula and check a certain planet for survivors. Number one, you and I will meet later to plan the particulars of this mission. That's all. Troy looked out the port of the dense blue veil of the Roofiyuki Nebula. More than ever, she felt the hidden presence of the other worlders, and she began to shiver. Seated at the captain's left, Troy watched the planet grow larger on the bridge of U-Screen. Picard rose slowly from his command chair. Censored information, Mr. Data. Coming in range now, sir, I'm picking up electromagnetic transmissions from the surface band. Put it on screen if you can. This is Jean-Luc Picard, captain of the USS Enterprise, from the United Federation of Planets. The bridge screen filled with the face of a human male in his mid-30s. He wore a military-type uniform. I am Major Faris. We know you come from Earth. You have entered the sovereign space of Rampart. We want nothing to do with you. That is why our ancestors left Earth 200 years ago. I assure you, Major, as Commander of the Enterprise, the Federation does not wish to interfere with your Fairs. We are here merely to investigate the disappearance of the USS Huxley. Faris' back was now to the view screen. He seemed to be getting advice from some other authority. Another man about 20 years older took his place. I am Kriton, Director of Sepholic Security. Your investigation would be a waste. There are no lies on this world. Your story of the Huxley is a deliberately concocted fiction I suggest you take your ship and leave. Picard looked at Deanna Troy. What do you feel about Kriton? The counselor replied without hesitation. He's telling the truth as he sees it. I am sure he has never heard of the Huxley. Picard's voice tightened. Do you, Kriton, know anything about the disappearance of the USS Huxley? Absolutely nothing, Captain Picard. Then Kriton looked down and pressed a button on his desk. Picard stared at the view screen. Kriton, your weapons are no match for my ship. You're going to limit both our options if you fire on us. And even if you did destroy us, other Federation ships would come one way or another. The Federation will have its answer. I'm not firing, Captain. It would be the deterrent or destroy your Federation. I will allow your investigation, but I will tolerate no interference in our affairs. We have an epidemic going on here and a violent insurgency. If your people help them, they will be criminals as well. Your search can begin now. All you have to do is allow us to inspect your ship to assure us you carried no infections or forbidden materials. As Troy walked down the Enterprise corridor with a visiting party, she was aware of a metal box floating along behind her. Its lens zoomed in and out and its antennai beatled at her, then at Picard. Kriton and Ferris called it a one eye. They had brought several one eyes onto the ship for the detection of contraband or disease. The search went on for hours. Kriton had just stopped the tour near the holodeck when Picard lost his patience. Since you haven't found any diseases or contraband here, Kriton interrupted. We have found it in abundance, Captain, the disease of imagination, fiction, myth, blasphemy, religious heresy, the many forms of the all-pox. Your story of the Huxley is a fiction. You spread the filth of imagination wherever you go. It is in your schools, your speech, your actions, and your minds. Your children are brought up in a madhouse taught by lunatics and devils. Oh, I see, said Picard. It's a good thing for you that your people left Earth centuries ago. Your kind has phased itself out, thankfully, on that planet. Let me make this even simpler for you. In our computer, we have a copy of every notable piece of literature, art, and music ever produced by humankind, from the first Paleolithic cave paintings right up to the present. Everything, no matter who banned it in whatever country, for whatever reason, got it. Kriton backed away. He exchanged a glance with Ferris, then looked at the One Eye. In response, the One Eye's surface sprouted a gun. The two security men with the group drew their faces, but the One Eye, reading brainwaves, had already intercepted their thoughts. It felt both men with a deadly stream of radiation before they could fire. Ferris knocked Picard out with a blow to the head. Riker moved to help his captain, but the One Eye was in his way. It was going to fire at him, and he had no weapon. He grabbed Troy and they ran until they found refuge in an empty hollevent group. Riker hit his communicator. Riker to Wharf. Wharf here. Wharf, the One Eyes are weapons. Put the ship on alert, the captain has been taken hostage. We are tracking him, sir. They gained entrance to the transporter room. Riker managed to make it to the bridge just as the transporter room came on the view screen. Chief O'Brien lay unconscious on the platform. Ferris and Kriton entered with Picard, a One Eye hovered over the unconscious chief. Can you tell me what that device is doing to O'Brien? Some kind of scanning, sir. Possibly reading memory information encoded in O'Brien's brain tissue. Possibly it is capable of reading thoughts of active brain waves as well. Riker pondered the remark. On screen, Kriton held Picard's communicator. Yes, thought Riker. Ferris and Kriton would know all about our communicators if their One Eyes had been reading minds. And that is why they were able to outwit and outshoot the crew. Kriton held the communicator to his lips. Riker, we are going to transport to the surface of Rampard with your captain. We'll return him when I am convinced that you'll leave my world alone. Believe me, said Riker, I want nothing to do with your world. I'm willing to call off the search, at least for now, if you surrender the captain. No, I'm not about the risk my planet's safety based on your word. Commander, was Petroy. Could you ask about the other worlders? The doubt was plain on Riker's face, but Troy continued. I've had time to observe him. I now suspect he is hiding something. It feels like the other worlders. I want to be sure. Riker turned back to the view screen and described Troy's encounter with the other worlders. Another fiction, science fiction, the worst of all. Your every bit as sick as the criminals on Rampard, the dissenters. I think you planned to help their insurgency. That's really why you came here. As Troy watched Kriton's blanching, mask-like face, she sensed that he had indeed experienced the other worlders or aliens of some similar kind. It was something he could never admit to. Something that terrified him. As the crew watched, Ferris and Kriton set controls on the transporter, Riker searched for a way to free the captain. But the one eyes could counter any move he made. In the end, he could do nothing but watch as the men from Rampard beamed off the ship with Picard. Riker sat in the command chair. Data? Can you put the beam down point on screen? Yes, sir. An aerial view of a sprawling concrete complex came on the screen. In large lettering, Cef-com was written on the side of the building. Data studied the sensor information. Sir, this is security force headquarters, highest density of surveillance gear and weaponry. Riker looked at the screen. This is probably where they'll hold the captain, not a place we can beam right into. Data cycled the screen through different wavelengths. There, Riker strode closer to the screen.
