Now, without them, he couldn't sustain the Odysseus character. She would need his help getting into Seftcom. Her best chance to complete her mission was if Odysseus completed his. She had to help him or lose this chance to get into Seftcom. She tried to talk him out of his depression, but he insisted that he couldn't do the impossible deeds of Homer's Odysseus, and thus could never actually be that character. Who are you to say what's possible, demand Detroit? Who gave you the authority? The people on the other side of that wall think they have it, and look what it's done to them. Odysseus stared at the river. Troy had an idea. She concentrated with all her empathic ability. You're remembering someone you loved, she said. You're a little boy, writhing on your shoulders, laughing. He turned to her in astonishment. Now you know for sure that I'm a seer, she said. I really do come from another world. If that's possible, then it's also possible that you can be Odysseus. Troy felt a change taking place within him. He walked to the river's edge and scooped up dirt and started rubbing it into his clothes. Troy was baffled, but then remembered that when Odysseus returned to Ithaca, he disguised himself as a beggar. Odysseus joined the other dissenters. Troy could feel them tuning like an orchestra. Two dozen people at many races and cultures merging into one chord. Then Nikitushka Lomoth rolled a boulder off a cliff smashing the wall. The break-in had begun. Kiyote and Guna Bibi sat in a stolen van sabotaging military communications. Guna Bibi played her dicery dew into a microphone. At her song of fertility, the helixing all noted DNA itself, calmed over headsets and radios throughout sefta. Kiyote peered out of the van. Outside, confused soldiers scurried about. A few fell to the ground or covered their eyes or cried out in terror. They were having seizures in their white temporal lobes. The creative image and music parts of their brains had been starved for so long that Guna Bibi's song had triggered wild hallucinations. As Odysseus drove his stolen truck along a service road that ringed the seftkom complex, Troy watched the disruption through the truck's window. Guna Bibi's deejure do hum from the radio. When the song finished, Kiyote's voice replaced it. I'm going to tell a story that Glingit Indians tell about the statue that came to life. Ama? Kiyote's voice was cut off. Troy heard a muffled sound and then the voice of a CS officer. Odysseus sped up the truck. We'll still make it and we'll free the others too if we can make it to that bridge. Odysseus grabbed Troy's arm and pulled her out of the truck toward the bridge. In front of him, Odysseus could make out the form of a CS officer at the bridge, gun drawn. The officer started running towards them and suddenly in mid-stride pulled off his helmet and cast it aside. Odysseus froze when he saw the man's face. Ferris, he said, in astonishment. The two men were now almost face to face. Powell, I've been waiting for this for ten years. A payback for all the men I've lost to your dissenters. Troy sensed something snap inside of Ferris. The controlled mean of the CS military officer gave way to a need for consummation. Ferris thumbed a button on his weapon. She sensed his grim animal satisfaction as he fired. The radiation-patterned hit of Dizzy's square in the chest. The bearded man yelled something unintelligible. Then collapsed. One eyes and soldiers arrived and surrounded the scene. Ferris once again became the operational military man. He was going to follow procedure to the letter. He unclipped a small case from his belt and squirted CS truth serum up Odysseus' nostrils. Stay with me, Powell, Ferris said. I need the names of other insurgents. Odysseus mumbled. Hurry, said Ferris. Yarmios. Yarmios who? Yarmios. Pig farmer. Ferris parked orders to his soldiers. Relay these into the computer. First one is Yarmios, a pig farmer. Odysseus seemed to regain the strength in his voice. Euryclia, my nurse. Adaltolechus. And Polypsies. Ferris tried to repeat the names to his soldiers. Then stopped as the one eyes grew up around him in attack formation. And a soldier's reflex, Ferris, grouped for his own gun. The one eye killed him. Instant. As Troy stared at Odysseus, perceiving he was now dead, she heard snatches of conversation between the soldiers. Looks like Ferris tried to report fiction. But Ferris used the truth drug on that guy's own. How could he give Ferris fiction to report? I don't know. Maybe to him it was truth. The CS soldiers began to pull Troy away. She looked one last time at Odysseus. His open eyes reflected the thunder-headed cumulus clouds. The clouds of Zeus, Alastor. Zeus, the Avenger. Troy was led into Creighton's office. She sensed the inner terror welling up in him, his terror of the other worlders, of imagination itself. You're useless to me, he snapped at Troy. You're captain, your first officer, and your android are no longer necessary either. I've already defeated your ship, you can't touch me now. An image appeared on Creighton's monitor. The Enterprise was plunging downwards, the dull red heat of atmospheric entry already showing on its shields. Troy strained not to panic, to focus on something else. She found herself looking at his hands. They were unscared and looked like they belonged to someone else, and artists' hands. They fidgeted it compulsively. Now he stood and spoke. For the high crime specified in the Code of Counsel of Truth, Deanna Troy is sentenced to bodily destruction by injection. No, wait, cried Troy. I know what you're hiding. I've had those mythical creatures invading my mind too I could help you. Creighton glared at her. A fabulous to the end. The execution detail arrived at Creighton's office in minutes. Creighton accompanied the CS security men as they led Troy up to the bridge where guards stood in formation around Descartes, Riker, and Data. They had barely restored Picard's memory when CS men crashed into the lab and took them prisoner. As Troy saw her crewmates, she felt suddenly weak. For a moment, she blacked out. The guards kept her from hitting the ground and the whole group paused. When she was able to walk again, the group moved on. Troy and her shipmates were led to a small, stark room. Here they were strapped into chairs on a table behind them. Four syringes waited. Troy's heart was pounding so hard she began to think the earth was throbbing. And suddenly, the earth really was throbbing. The nurse, confused by the noise, dropped a syringe. Creighton screamed at her, inject them! The vibration emanating from the ground reached a peak. Suddenly the roof caved in and a giant human hand moved in through the hole. It grabbed Creighton and lifted him out of the building. The owner of the hand was a hundred feet tall and dressed like an 18th century seafarer. Cords dangled from his arms at legs as though he had been tied up. Troy realized she had seen him before on a page from Gulliver's travels. This giant was Gulliver in the flesh. Nearby, Creighton barked orders at the crew of a radiation cannon. The cannon fired a great blast at Gulliver. Gulliver swayed and reached for the cannon. It fired again, and he collapsed. C.S. troops hurried onto the square, and for a moment, Troy thought they were going to re-arrest her and her shipmates. But in the next moment, pandemonium broke loose. A huge crowd of beings swarmed onto the square. A vast invasion by characters from myth, metaphor, fiction, all forms of human imagination. The charge was led by Sechmet the lioness, Egyptian goddess of the desert sun. The head of an ass protruded from the hair above her eyes, and over the ass was a blinding, solar disk. Troy saw dissenters helping the myth beings. She saw Rihanna, now a beautiful grown woman in queenly dress, riding a magnificent leaping horse. She saw Gunabibi dancing in the middle of the square, spreading her nature, fertility. Vines grew with time-lapse speed from the concrete at her feet, and twining guns and jeeps in a green arabesque. Creighton frantically tried to rally his C.S., but they seemed to be losing their weapons ineffective, confusion supreme. Some had abandoned the fight and looked around in pure bewilderment, others were laughing hysterically. Then the colossal Aztec figure of Tezcatlipoca, the mirror man, thundered onto the square. Creighton's mask-like face cracked into a bitter smile as he slammed the firing button. The great sound erupted from the radiation tank. The radiation flash reflected off the mirrored surface of Tezcatlipoca's chest, and returned straight at Creighton. Creighton disappeared in a cloud of vapor. All around Troy, the myth beings began to rise from the wreckage and walk about. Troy's aunt couldn't move. She looked down at her hand. It had the appearance of marble. At that moment, Troy realized that she had become a statue. Her body and her emotions themselves were now stoned. Odysseus came out of the crowd and stood looking at her. I know you, do I not? From some other place or time? He began to pull the debris off of her. It's all right. I know how to awaken the woman trapped as a statue. Pygmalion, the sculpture, did it once. He touched her wrist. Her hand tingled and came alive. He squeezed her shoulder, and it became soft under his touch. The warmth spread. He stroked her cheek and her hair, and she felt her entire body reawakening. She breathed and moved her limbs. Emotions came back in a rush. She was supremely, innately happy. Some inner source had been tapped. Some inner conflict released. She opened her eyes. She was alone, lying on her back, staring at a night sky. Then she turned her head and saw that she was surrounded by soldiers. Creighton stood near her. The card, Data and Riker were nearby, still handcuffed. She was still on the seph-com bridge near the actual spot where Odysseus had died. She had passed out. Then suddenly, Troy felt the unmistakable body-dissolving rush of the Enterprise transporter. In the next moment, she found herself standing in the Enterprise transporter room with her shipmates. The ship was safe, thanks in large part to Geordi and Chops. The engines had been repaired and the one eyes destroyed. Picard, Riker, Troy and Data headed for the conference room to debrief one another. Troy still didn't know how the beam-up had been accomplished. Picard glanced at Data. We have the illustrious Data to thank for that, unbeknownst to all of us, Data caught and disassembled a one eye and fashioned its antenna into a communicator. When all of us were in the same spot, he signaled the Enterprise. He had to keep this device hidden, even from us, otherwise the one eye would have read our brain waves and sabotaged the rescue. Troy beamed at Data. Well, I understand that one eye couldn't read your brain, but how did you disable one in the first place? Data gestured to his shipmates. I will refrain from taxing you with an exhibition, as I have observed a peculiar human reaction to it, however. My poetry apparently stymied the one eye's. Troy heard the conference room doors swish open. Two diminutive people entered. Troy remembered Olaf and Una. They came directly over to Troy. Una looked at her gravely. May we discuss a professional matter with you that seems to have involved your crewmates as well as you? Troy nodded. Olaf took over. We visited Earth not long ago. As ethnographers, we traveled the planet, recording all forms of creative imagination. We used our favorite medium, akin to your holography, which plays directly into the viewer's brain. Virtual reality. Well, as a counselor, you wanted to view our ethnographic movie. We told you that sometimes, though rarely, a life form has trouble with the medium after experiencing it. You insisted on watching all four hours anyway. As they spoke, Troy's memories of the meeting began to rise to her conscious mind. I must have blocked it out as a way of trying to suppress the trauma, I suppose. Was there something in your movie about a statue that comes to life? Oh, many things, said Una. There was the Winter's Tale, Pygmalion, a Tlingit Indian story, and others as well. Did you ever show Criton your movie, asks Troy? Olaf and Una looked blankly at each other. They hadn't. That meant Troy still had no solution to the puzzle of Criton. The car took his seat on the bridge. Nothing more from Starfleet Wharf? The earlier orders stand, sir. We are to leave and let Starfleet handle the matter. The bridge crew waited for Picard to tell them to warp out of orbit. But as he prepared to speak, his communicator came to life. Troy to Captain Picard. Picard here. I think I've found the missing piece to the puzzle. As soon as the Grey Drizzly Dawn came, Criton led a troop of CS men to the dissenters' prison quarters. One by one they were taken from their cells and inducted into the death march. Criton kept the execution march going, but he felt as though he'd just been pushed into a mental abyss of imagination, of insane fictions. He'd been having the visions for days, and now they were going to overwhelm him. The worst part of it was that he himself appeared in these visions. The stories full of the all-pocks were always about him. As the execution march reached the bridge, Criton took a last look at the sky. She saw vast grey and white clouds moving in stately unison, high up in a faraway gap of blue, a flock of birds circled. The birds circled slowly. The island froze in her tracks. There were no birds on Rampart. But there were, Aguya. Now Criton and the soldiers stopped and looked up as well. The Haguya pulled into a formation and began to dive. They were diving at the bridge. As they became more visible and more undeniably alien, the other person inside Criton awoke from his ten-year sleep. He was Captain Alfred Bolz. He recognized that the stories trying to take over his mind were not fictions at all. They had all really happened to him. The strange vessel that had dominated his psychosis was in truth, his very own ship. It was the USS Huxley. Criton's personality and artificial construct folded itself into a corner like a piece of furniture. Bolz was now in control. His Starfleet training told him what to do. Everybody, hold your fire and lower your weapons. One of the Haguya glided down and landed. Riannon ran up to the creature, her friend, and spoke to it softer, then leapt to its back. And was born into the air. One by one, the other Haguya landed and then took the dissenters up to safety among the clouds. Aboard the Enterprise Picard watched the view screen. Data tapped his panel, choosing different views of the CS man, and the man Troy suggested was Captain Bolz of the USS Huxley. Picard peered at his view screen, intently. Mr. Data, let's track our man. Data tapped his keypad. On screen, Bolz turned and hurried into the sephcom building. Bolz sat at a terminal, his fingers stumbling over the keys. Bolz watched his life as a starship captain unfold on the monitor. He replied the last images of the Huxley and the CS man pulling him out. Only him. Bolz looked away from the screen. Had he heard somebody? There was no more time. He left the terminal and ran to the repository. A startled CS officer complied with the director's demand for an Enterprise communicator. Picard sat in his command chair and waited as his crew tried to contact Bolz. Troy was becoming nervous. Her hypothesis that Crichton was Bolz could be wrong. She might be endangering the ship for nothing. She was about to express this concern to the captain when the bridge speakers started to vibrate roughly. Come in Enterprise. Picard stood up. This is Captain Picard. To whom am I speaking? To Captain Alfred C. Bolz, permission to beam aboard your ship captain. Picard turned to Wharf. Have the man beamed up. Troy Picard and Riker spent a long time talking with Bolz. Large areas of his memory were missing. He still had the knowledge he'd learned that the Academy, but couldn't remember being there. You were torn between two pursuits, Cepicard. Star Fleet and holography. You were a holograph artist. I expect when you get back you'll be able to visit galleries and see plenty of your work. Bolz was stunned. That could explain why I, or rather, why Crichton had a special aptitude for video images, why he rose through the ranks. Yes, said Troy. I eventually remembered that you had been an artist. Everything fell into place then. How I first felt Crichton was secretly remembering aliens. Then how I felt he was hallucinating fictions. In fact, he was remembering aliens. Those he'd seen in Star Fleet, but he mistakenly believed them to be fictions. The conversation turned to the future of Rampart. All agreed that the revelation of alien life, of science fiction becoming real, would eventually topple the CS and change life on the surface of the planet. Bolz said his thanks, but before he left, he asked Troy one favor. Please don't tell me too much about my past. I'm in an enviable position actually because I get to do that all over again. As he departed, the doors switched behind him. Cepicard turned to Riker. Why don't you take the bridge for a moment, number one? I need to speak to the counselor. When Riker had gone, Picard turned to Troy. Still having regrets about your choice, Counselor? Your risk in the interest of discovery? My choice to watch Olaf and Una's movie? No. I learned something. I had an anxiety I wasn't even aware of. You remember I had been telling you lately that you were concealing too many emotions? Yes, we still have a meeting pending on that. Troy smiled slightly. Well, I didn't know it, but I was actually afraid that I was burying my own feelings. That's why in my other world or dreams, I kept seeing myself turn into a statue. It was my own fear of turning into a cold, unfeeling person. And will you continue your research on the movie? Picard asked. Troy felt herself tense up. I want to, but the flesh is weak. That research was what started my chances and amnesia. Counselor, I'm not suggesting you should do anything you don't want to or anything dangerous. I just hope you'll one day continue with the research. That's all. Troy could feel the wheels turning at Picard's mind. Diana, do you remember that big number you once told me about? You're talking about the number based on average synapse count of possible states of one human brain. The number of possible thoughts and feelings one person is capable of. I think that's it, said Picard. How big did you say it was? Two raised to the power of ten trillion. Yes, and that's more than all the grains of sand on all the planets in the universe. More in fact than the total number of atoms in the entire known universe. Troy looked Picard square in the eye. I know what you're telling me. I won't give this up. The captain was right, thought Troy. She sat down to her computer. If you start backing away from knowledge, there's no end to it. Computer, I wish to commence with some research. It was a crucial moment. She was going to speak the title of Olaf and Una's movie, the word that had started the whole thing last time. She gripped her chair until her fingers hurt. Tell me about the Tukirpa, she said. What does the word mean? She held her breath and waited for the room to begin spinning, for her world to start disintegrating. Working? Tukirpa. A word used by several Aboriginal peoples of Australia. It refers to the eternal ones of the dream, the beings of myth or the myth world itself. The eternal dream time. Do you wish further information? She let herself breathe again. Nothing terrible had happened. She was still in her chair, in her cabin, on the Enterprise. Her anxiety seemed to have evaporated. In its place, she felt relief and the exhilaration of embarkation. Yes, she said. Gulliver's Fugitives was written and adapted for audio by Keith Shuri. It was read by Jonathan Frakes. Post-production was by Gary Fink and Karen Perlman. Original music by Sam McCallie, Carl Schurts and Richard Emmett. The director was Jesse Boggs.
description: The podcast episode "Star Trek: The Next Generation - Gulliver's Fugitives" focuses on Captain Picard solving a case involving a metal humming device and a fugitive named Montoya, leading to an unexpected twist where Montoya escapes with the help of his wits. In another subplot, it details the aftermath of the incident, including how CS agents deal with the scattered pages and the girl who finds one escaping from their incinerators. The episode explores the characters' backgrounds and how their pasts shape them in the present situation.

transcript: Simon & Schuster Audio Works presents Star Trek, Deep Space Nine, Emissary, novelization by J.M. Diller, based on the teleplay by Michael Pillar. Bury by Rick Berman and Michael Pillar, performed by non-visitor. Ben Sisko's first encounter with Jean-Luc Picard shattered his life forever. On Star Date 4-4-0-0-2.3, a fleet of 40 Federation Starships received orders to proceed to Wolf 359 to intercept a Borg vessel on its way to Earth. The Saratoga was the first to arrive. Lieutenant Commander Benjamin Sisko served as a Saratoga's first officer. Like the rest of the crew, Sisko had never seen a Borg, and knew little of the race saved that Starfleet Command deemed them a grave threat. He knew that most who engaged them perished. Sisko was not afraid. He had absolute faith in himself, his captain, his ship, the fleet. But he had not been prepared for the size of the thing. On Saratoga's main bridge view screen, the Borg's ship hung grey and motionless against a backdrop of stars, dwarfing the Federation vessel with its vastness. It was a huge, ungainly cube of space-borne metal with thousands of tiny compartments, like a gigantic metal hive built by insects. Captain Storle leaned forward in his chair and frowned, a small, faint crease appearing between his dark, up-swept brows. Sisko took note of the gesture. For the captain, it was the equivalent of a muttered curse. Storle was a Vulcan, dedicated to the repression of feeling in the pursuit of pure reason. The screen flickered and went dark. In place of the Borg's ship, a face appeared. A human face. Jean-Luc Picard, the famous captain of the Enterprise, stood on the bridge of the Borg vessel. And yet, it was not Picard. Not human. Not machine. But a monstrous marriage of metal and flesh. One of Picard's arms had been extended with an intricate, mechanical prosthesis. His eyes augmented with a sensor scope protruding from one temple. His pale face was frighteningly blank. His dignity, his warmth, were gone. If any part of Jean-Luc Picard remained, the man-machine hybrid gave no sign. The sensor scope flashed red, word softly and angled forward, studying the humans with an intelligence's empty and cold space. I am locutus. You will be assimilated. Resistance is futile. You will disarm all weapons and escort us to sector 001. Sisko's lips parted half an astonishment, half an outrage. Like hell, we will. 001 was earth. Captain Storl's gaze serenely affirmed Sisko's sentiment. Sisko stared down at his viewer and saw a schematic display of three starships gliding silently into formation around the Seratoga. The gauge, the Q-Shoo, and the Melbourne. Captain Storl then gave a serious order. Move us to position Alpha Ensign. Load all torpedo bays, ready phasers. The card's image disappeared abruptly and was replaced once more by the Borg ship. Rannock, the Bully and tactical officer, moved pale blue hands over his console. The Borg ship is attempting to lock onto the Melbourne with its tractor beam. Captain Storl's attention did not waver from the screen. Target the origin point of that beam, Lieutenant Fire, when ready. Sisko watched the screen as Saratoga's phasers and torpedoes straight through the void, flared briefly against the leaden surface of the Borg ship. Then dimmed. Simultaneously, the Borg ship fired a bright searing beam, striking the Melbourne. For an instant, the Melbourne Trimmed, illumined against the blackness by a deadly corona flight. Sisko squinted against the painful brightness on the screen, forced himself not to look away as the Melbourne's hope exploded into scorched hurtling fragments. Forced himself not to think of those dead and dying on a bridge, very like the one he was on. A part of his mind screamed that they were all certainly about to die, that he should leave his post, find his wife and son, spend his last few seconds with them. But the rational part knew that Jennifer and Jake's best chance laying his ability to perform his duty. The deck lurched. Sisko staggered, regained his footing as Lieutenant ran up, called out from his console. The Borg are attempting to lock onto us. Captain Storl clutched the arms of his chair for balance. Evasive maneuvers, Delta pattern, at the navigation console, Encentama Mota glanced down at a readout. Captain were not moving, they've locked on. Sisko watched the screen as the gauge and the key was to open fire on the Borg vessel, trying in vain to save the Saratoga. Just as Saratoga had done for the Melbourne. Vevorishly, Rannock worked his console to maintain the Saratoga's shield, but with no effect. Shields are going. The bridge went down. And with a roar, erupted in flame. Sisko was slammed to the deck. When Saratoga rided herself, he drew in a lung full of smoke, coughed, and pushed himself to his knees. The bridge laid dark and smoldering, illumined only by the sparks raining from damaged consoles. Sisko strained to hear his captain's calm voice. Being a Vulcan and stronger than most of his crew, Storl would be the first to recover, if he was alive. Damage report! No one answered. The emergency lights flickered once, then came on. Sisko pushed himself insteadly to his feet. Damage report! In the dim light, Rannock wounded, bleeding, pulled himself up on his console, while Sisko moved quickly from body to warm body, feeling for pulses. Finding none. Captain Storl's unseen eyes were staring, serenely, through the haze. Sisko drew his hand away from the Vulcan and rose slowly to face Lieutenant Rannock, who hunched over his console in obvious pain. Direct hit. Decks. One through four. Sisko knew that his wife, Jennifer, and son, Jake were there. He touched his common sigma. Engineering. Your status. There was no reply. Sisko and Rannock exchanged grim looks. Suddenly, the computer's loud overriding voice echoed on the silent Haysfield bridge. Warning! Damage to war core. Containment failure in four minutes. Sisko hid his insignia again, all hands prepared to abandon ship. As he moved toward the lift, he kept thinking about Jennifer and Jake. Then he turned back. Rannock was still huddled over the console. Lieutenant. Let's get the civilians to the escape pods. Rannock nodded and followed. When the turbo lift doors opened, Sisko felt heat on his face. He and Rannock stepped onto the deck and staggered to the left. The deck was tilting, stabilizers were failing. Life support would be next. Sisko calmly reasoned that he would be able to make it to his quarters to see if Jennifer... Fire leapt at them from a side corridor, cinging the shoulder of Sisko's uniform. He grabbed Rannock's arm and together they fought their way past the flames toward a frantic group of civilians struggling with arm loads of personal possessions. Sisko shouted over the roar of flames. Leave everything. Go to your assigned evacuation area now. Sisko continued on, passing other civilians, searching for two faces. Warning! Damage to warp core. Containment failure in three minutes. When he arrived at his quarters, the door was jammed open. Thick, dark, small bill about. Sisko stepped into it without hesitation. An explosion had ripped a large hole in the deck, allowing fire to leap up from the level below. His quarters, a lifetime of accumulated possessions, were destroyed. He pushed his way through scorched debris. Jennifer! He pushed aside smoldering fragments of furniture and twisted metal bulkhead, searching. At the edge of the largest pile of collapsed bulkhead in wreckage, he uncovered her hand, limp and smudged with soot from the smoke. He set to work with the strength and intensity that bordered on insanity. The edge of the bulkhead was jagged, sharp. His hands became bloody and blistered by the heated metal. Within seconds, he had uncovered Jennifer's twisted upper torso and discovered Jake's small dark body beside her. She had shielded the child with her body and taken the brunt of the blow. He could see no blood, but in the darkness and the smoke was difficult to be sure. It's gonna be okay. I'll get you out of there. You're gonna be okay. He's strained, letting the sharp, hot, metal cut into his palms. But he could not lift the wreckage that crushed his wife's lower body. In desperation, he circled, cleared away more debris, found a way to reach underneath the wreckage and pull Jake free. The boy was unconscious and badly bruised, but breathing. The boy moved slightly in his grasp. Okay, Jake. We'll just get your mom now and get out of here. But Jennifer was pinned too tightly. Sisko was struggling to lift the wreckage again when Rannock's silhouette appeared in the doorway. Commander, sir, we have to get to the escape pods. Sisko stopped pushing against the bulkhead and met the boe in startled gaze that focused on his charred, bloodied hands. Sisko stared down at them numbly. The only thing that mattered was Jennifer. Rannock, just help me get her free. That's an order. The boe in stared at him in mute horror. He reached down and scooped Jake up in his strong arms. She's gone, Commander. There's nothing we can do. Warning, damage to warp core. Containment failure in two minutes. Sisko shook his head. He knelt beside Jennifer and took her cool limp hand in his bloody one. If she had to die, then he could not leave her to do so alone. You go ahead, Lieutenant. Take the boy. The security officer appeared in the doorway, and Rannock handed the boy off to him. Then grasped, Sisko's arm and yanked him to his feet. Now, sir. No. I can't leave without her. Rannock pulled with all his might. Powerless against the boe's greater strength, Sisko was propelled toward the door. Damn it. We can't leave her here. Rannock replied by pushing him out the door. Sisko did not remember running through the burning corridors. Did not remember joining the dozen others in the cramped escape pod. Sisko remembered only two things. The sight of Jake, still unconscious in the security officer's arms. And the sight of the dying Saratoga as other tiny pod sailed free. Sisko made his way to the port hole and stared at the receding wreckage. Space was lit up like a summer sky with heat lightning. The Kyushu was gone now, and the gauge would be next. The Borg were right. Resistance was futile. All was destroyed. In his mind, he laid dead beside Jennifer. Their bodies consumed by flame. He watched as Saratoga exploded like a small sun and let himself be blinded by the light. Three years after the incident at Wolf 359, Commander Benjamin Sisko stood in a soft grass, fondly watching his 12-year-old son. Under the shade of a large old oak, Jake sat fishing on a large rock. Trousers rolled up to the knees, bare feet dangling in the water. Hey there, son. Jake turned at the sound of his father's voice, lips stretched in a reluctant grin. A shaft of sunlight pierced the branches and gleaned in his dark, curly hair. The smile so increased his resemblance to Jennifer that Sisko drew in a silent, painful breath as he crossed over and perched beside his son on the rock. Time had not dulled the memories of his wife. Sisko returned to the horrors of the Saratoga each night in dreams. At least, Jake was there each day to remind him of the good things that might otherwise be forgotten. Jennifer's same shy crooked grin. Jennifer's gestures. Jennifer's good nature and complete inability to stay angry about anything for more than a full minute at a time. Jake was angry now, and like his mother, doing a miserable job of hiding it. How they biting? Jake shrugged and turned his attention to the red and white bobbing cork. Small fry, thrown back. Wanna go for a swim? Don't have time, son. We gotta get ready. A sullen look came over the boy's face, and Sisko experienced a pang of guilt. It won't be so bad, Jake. And I've never figured out how to live without her. The Jennifer alien won't beside him, so you choose to live here. It is not linear. A wave of emotion swept over him, and it last broke. No, it's not linear. Cisco knelt in the wreckage and wept amid the flames. The alien stood quietly as he grieved. There were no more questions left, no longer any need for words. The Jake alien graced him with a faint smile. And a look of compassionate understanding. Cisco wiped the tears from his cheeks, and returned the smile with gratitude. We only have six photons major. Kira kept her gaze fastened on the screen. We're not going to win this battle with Torpedo Zensen. Kira watched with anxious exhilaration as a torpedo streaked through the starlet blackness and exploded in dazzling bursts just off the lead warship starboard bow. Kira's stance was defined as she placed upon firmly on the situation table beside her. You don't think Starfleet took command of this space station without the ability to defend it, do you? His full lips twisted into a sneer. Your space station could not defend itself against one Cardassian warship. She drew herself to her full height and took a menacing step toward the screen. You're probably right, Jusad. And if you were dealing with a Starfleet officer, they'd probably admit we have a hopeless cause here. But I am just a bajouren who's been fighting a hopeless cause against Cardassians all her life. So if you want a war, I'll give you one. She drew back her chest heaving with honest rage. The Cardassian shook his head, speechless at her impudence. The screen darkened abruptly and Jusad's image was replaced by that of stars and ships. Bored the bridge of the Cardassian warship, Jusad stared at the space station on his view screen. He had no idea what to make of the bajouren major's threat. How could he be sure such threats were idle, now that Starfleet had command of the base? His first officer gave a slight bow from the shoulders and waited for Jusad to signal with a nod before beginning to speak. They were using a Thoron field to block out Sensors' gull, but we were able to penetrate it. Jusad ran a finger across his lips to his chin. What are their defenses? According to our scans, an estimated 5,000 photons integrated phaser banks on all levels. Jusad frowned in amazement. When did they transport all these armaments? How did they install them without our knowledge? Somehow, they've created a massive illusion of Duranium's shadows. His officer leaned toward him. Why risk a confrontation goal? The fourth order can be here in a day. Jusad sighed in utter frustration. And so can Starfleet. On Deep Space Nine, Bashir turned toward Dax as if to clasp her in joy. They went for it. We've done it! Frowning faintly at her console, Dax addressed Kira. Major, the lead ship is sending out a subspace message asking for reinforcements. Kira stared at the screen. She had dealt too long with Cardassians to trust them. Too soon for a victory celebration, doctor. Mr. O'Brien. The Ensign checked his readouts, recalling slightly at what he saw. The ships are being deployed into a standard attack formation, sir. Bashir fell silent. Kira exchanged grim glances with O'Brien and Dax. She felt sorry that they would have to die. Battle stations. The obstacles shuttered beneath the heels of Kira's boots. She shifted her weight, managing to keep her balance. Not a direct hit, thank the prophets. As the station rocked under the impact O'Brien called her. They may just be testing us. I could run a pulse compression way through the phaser bags, put out a blast that'll make them think twice. Kira clutched the console with one hand as the deck shook again. Do it. She watched along with the others as the phaser blasts streaked toward the Cardassian warship and made contact with the vessel. But the Cardassian's fire showed no sign of easing. Kira held on with both hands as the station rocked. Damage report. Direct hit. Level 14. Empty storage bays no casualties. The sense of relief was short-lived. Dax called to her. She'll turn down to 27%. Just then. Kira's world heaved to one side with a deafening roar slamming her face down onto the deck. O'Brien reached for his console and pulled himself back to his feet. Dax called out over the chaos. The fuel conduit has ruptured on the promenade. Major Kira addressed O'Brien. Can you divert the main power flow? His fingers began working his panel before she could get the words out, but the result made him grimace in frustration. Controls are locked. A voice emanated from the comrade. Oto-to-ops. I've got wounded people down here. Have you seen that doctor of yours anywhere? Kira turned toward Bashir but he was already moving for the turbo lift. For the first time, the major was honestly glad to have the young doctor on the station. Brian wondered if it mattered that much. They were all dying now. It was just a matter of time before the Cardassians managed to rupture another fuel line and another and another until the station went up in a blaze that would light up the pejorn sky like a small sun. The turbo lift had just descended out of sight and the station reeled again and again. Dax called to the officers. Shields at 18% and falling. Kira dragged her fingers across the console edges as if to dig them into the metal, staring at the warships with a bitter sense of failure and depthless rage at herself for trusting the profits and her own foolish dreams. Her whole life had been one protracted struggle against this enemy and now she had lost. Just as her people, her planet, would ultimately lose. A Brian must have sensed her desperation. I might still be able to give you one more round, Major. Kira pulled her hand away from the console and stood without support. No. Signo the lead Cardassianship that we will proceed with the Dax interrupted. Her normally even toned filled with an excitement that made Kira turn her head to stare at her. Major, I'm reading a neutrino disturbance. 15 kilometers off the forward docking ring. It's the wormhole. On screen, the wormhole exploded into view, shattering the darkness with the shimmering rainbow blaze of light, looking to Kira like the Celestial Temple. It was the most beautiful sight she had ever seen. In the mouth of the wormhole, the tiny runabout appeared, followed by a gigantic Cardassian warship some 50 times its size. Cisco's voice loud and triumphant came over the calm. Cisco to DS9. Kira could not quite keep herself from grinning like a fool at the sight of Cisco on screen perfectly unharmed and grinning like a bit of a fool himself. Sorry to be so late. I didn't know we were having company. Clear me for docking, Mr. O'Brien. I, sir. Cleared for Padsy. Kira laughed as, for the first time. She realized the firing had stopped. When Cisco stepped through the airlock onto the promenade, he was feeling like a man reborn. For the first time in three years, he felt freed of his grief, freed of the past, able to look at the future. The clouds of guilt and self-pity had lifted, leaving him with clear vision. He knew what he wanted. He wanted to remain on DS9, wanted to continue to help the bejorns. But turning down the position at Visteris University was not a decision he could make alone. He would have to talk about it with Jake. The boy's feelings had to be considered. Cisco's attention drifted to the promenade. One of the shop fronts had been heavily damaged, and he could see where one of the buried fuel lines had erupted scorching the deck. Odo and Beshear were crouched over a wounded bejorn, and talking in such a decidedly amicable fashion, Cisco did a mild double take. Jake ran out of the crowd and threw himself into his father's arms. Cisco hugged the boy with a surge of love so fierce he blinked back to yours. Dad, I was so scared you, you wouldn't come back. Cisco patted his son's back as he would an infants. It's okay. I'm home. Hey, you smell like smoke. You okay? Yeah, there was a fire, but it got put out. You should have seen it, Dad. It was real scary for a while. The Cardassians were firing on us and the whole promenade was shaking, and even after Odo said the runabout had disappeared in the wormhole, I knew you'd come back. Jake stopped and blinked as though the thought had finally occurred to him. Are you okay, Dad? What happened out there? I've never been better. I'll tell you all about it when we get back to our quarters. He slipped an arm around the boy's shoulders and together they walked over to Odo and Beshear. The bejorn woman they were tending smiled in faint recognition up at him. Cisco asked about casualties. Beshear looked up at him. 13 injured commander, none seriously. Cisco nodded and moved with Jake toward a turbo lift. There's something I need to talk to you about tonight. A decision I need you to help me make. I got a job offer earlier today as a professor at a university. University? You mean you'd be a teacher? Jake wrinkled his nose at the thought. Well, is that really what you want to do, Dad? It doesn't sound very exciting. It's at Visteros University, Jake, on Earth. He braced himself for an excited outburst, for Jake to fling himself into his father's arms again, but instead, the boy frowned. I thought you'd be happy, Jake. Well, I guess I'm happy if you're happy. I just don't care anymore, Dad. I want you to do what you want to do. And I'd have to leave Nog. I mean, I hardly had any time to get to know him. A slow smile spread over Cisco's face. You patted the boy's shoulder gently. I think we can manage to give you that time, Jake. Before he could say more, the lift came to a stop at ops, as the two of them stepped out. Dax called to him. The Cardassians are waiting to speak to you, Benjamin. The images of Gulch's side in Dukat appeared before him on the view screen. Cisco graced them with a tight little smile. Welcome back, Gulch. Dukat revealed a white sliver of teeth. Commander, I'm pleased that we were able to escort you safely home. Cisco exchanged a faintly amused look with Kira. Gentlemen, I've made contact with the life forms that created this wormhole. Just sawed straightened and gave a threatening look. Then I must state our position that this phenomenon is clearly in territory that has been controlled by the Cardassian Empire for six decades and as such. Cisco cut him off. I have made an agreement with these beings on behalf of the planet Beijor that allows for safe passage through the wormhole. Those who violate that agreement will find themselves lost between here and the Gamma Quadrant. If you care to challenge what I am saying, I suggest you fly back into the wormhole and see for yourselves. A long silence passed as the Cardassian scalded him and then Dukat addressed him with no small amount of bitterness. Just who are these beings? Cisco opened his mouth to begin a long explanation. Then stopped and smiled faintly as a simpler, truer answer occurred to him. The prophets of the Celestial Temple. He turned to find Kira gazing at him with unmasked wonder. The following day, the Enterprise returned and Jean-Luc Picard requested permission to board the space station and hear firsthand from Cisco what had happened. When Cisco glanced up from his monitor in his office and saw Picard lingering in the doorway, he rose and extended his hand. This time, Cisco smelled no smoke, heard no wailing, saw no red flash of a sensor's scope, no monstrous hybrid of metal and skin. This time, he saw only a man. A very human man built of flesh and blood would have been deeply scarred by the Borg. Cisco forgot his own pain and considered Picard's and felt ashamed of his earlier behavior. He clasped Picard's hand firmly and was relieved when the pressure was returned. Picard narrowed his eyes slightly. Curious that this sudden warmth, Cisco wanted to say forgive me, but the words died in his throat. Instead, he smiled in apology. Picard caught the smile and returned it. Cisco released Picard's hand and motioned for the captain to sit. Picard spoke first. So, Commander, apparently your transfer to DS9 has already borne fruit. I'm most curious to hear how you would manage to locate the wormhole. Cisco grinned and told him, explaining everything. Picard listened with great interest, nodding with approval at Cisco's praise for his officers, and at his optimistic outlook on the effect the wormhole would have on the bajorn economy. It seems you've put Beijor on the map, Commander. This should become a leading center of commerce and scientific exploration. And for Starfleet, one of our most important ports, Cisco hesitated and then looked at Picard. Captain, regarding our conversation about someone to replace me, Picard's expression grew opaque, unreadable. I'm sorry, I haven't had the time to communicate it to command. Cisco relaxed in relief. I would prefer you ignore it, sir. I'm not sure I can, Commander. Are you certain this is what you want? Because we can't afford to have someone in command here who... I'm certain, sir. Picard regarded him in silence for some time, and then he stood and stretched his open hand across the commander's desk. Good luck, Cisco. Good luck to you, sir. And Cisco had no doubt that the captain understood perfectly well what was meant. Cisco transported Planet's side alone, save for a very special burden, carefully hidden from sight in its receptacle. This time, as he walked down Beijor's streets, his attention was drawn not to the destroyed buildings, but to the signs of rebuilding, of new life. Shopkeepers had set up an open air market in the square near the temple, and the air was filled with the voices of haggling merchants and buyers. In the distance, the aubergine mountains stood, serene and breathtakingly beautiful. Cisco came to the entrance of the Great Stone Temple and paused before stepping from the bright sunlight into the cool shadows. A young monk appeared almost immediately and bowed from the shoulders. Commander, welcome. Cisco smiled, returned the bow. The monk turned and strode briskly through the great echoing chamber. Cisco followed. The exterior walls had been patched, and monks now worked on restoring the interior ones. Kyo Paka stepped forward out of the darkness. Her smile was as radiant as Cisco's own. Commander Cisco, I see you have brought us yet another gift. Cisco laughed aloud. No, Opaka, just returning one, you gave me. He followed her to the reflecting pool holograph, and together they went downstairs into the secret chamber. Opaka gently took the arc from him and placed it on the shelf. Cisco smiled faintly. Fourteen planets have already contacted us about opening trade routes through bajorn space. Opaka nodded as she turned to him. The prophets have been generous. He moved toward her, eager to tell of the amazing, timeless beings within the warm hole. I have a lot to tell you about your prophets, Opaka. She silenced him with a wave. Does it surprise you that I do not wish to hear? He drew back, disappointed at not being able to share all that he had learned, but then he considered her point of view and gave her a small understanding smile. She returned it with relief. Perhaps that is why a disbeliever was destined to seek them. One should never look into the eyes of her own gods. Cisco nodded inside of the memory. It was quite a journey. She took a step toward him and reached for his jaw with gentle fingers, tracing her way up to his ear. This time he relaxed and did not recoil from her touch and felt no pain. Interesting Commander. This is only the beginning of your journey. Star Trek Deep Space 9, MSRI, was performed by Nana Visitor. The novelization was by J.M. Dillard, based on the Teleplay by Michael Pillar. Story by Rick Berman and Michael Pillar. It was a bridge for audio by George Truitt and directed by Bob Walter. Post Production by Stephen Erickson. description: Benjamin Sisko first encounters Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: Deep Space Nine as a Saratoga crew member tasked with intercepting a Borg vessel en route to Earth. Despite his faith in himself and the crew, he is overwhelmed by the sheer size of the Borg ship and Picard's monstrous hybrid form. This encounter leaves Sisko with a strong sense of determination to fight against the threat posed by the invading aliens.

transcript: in verbal rationalization. Why do I need a personal log to justify executing my law enforcement duties on Deep Space Nine? Either I maintain order in this maelstrom of immorality, in which case what do my methods matter? Or else I fail, and I should be discharged. But the chattering class of Federation officers has dictated that every action be thoroughly justified before, during, and after the fact. Thus I bow to the inevitable. This particular incident began when a rattle-trapler nation freighter that looked like something the pharengi dragged in limped through the wormhole from the gamma quadrant. The owner, a Captain Square Deal John Reel, assuming that isn't an alias, rushed straight to Quark, our own public enemy number one, owner of the source of the maelstrom of immorality, Quark's place. There, they concluded a transaction for a sealed Cardassian lockbox. The deal was typically pharengi. Captain John Reel demanded hard latinum up front, but Quark managed to talk the dim-witted lonation into selling the box on consignment, splitting the proceeds. I'm not making this up. Sixty, sixty. As I said, lonations are not known for their blinding intelligence. I was quite worried about the box's contents. I decided to investigate. Odo, the shape-shifting constable of Deep Space Nine, suddenly loomed behind Quark, causing the startled pharengi to leap to his feet. You damn spy! What were you this time? A chair? A waste-disposal unit? What was I? Why I was your conscience, Quark. No wonder you didn't notice me. What do you want now? Constable Odo put his hand firmly on the Cardassian box. This will be scammed by Chief O'Brien before anybody opens it. What if there's a bomb inside? Quark tried to snatch the box from Odo's grip. He argued and weadled, then grudgingly, conceded, primarily because he was unable to budge Odo's hand from the box. All right, all right. But it's mine! All mine! And I don't want O'Brien opening it, just scanning. After an interminable search, they managed to track down Master Chief Miles O'Brien, the station's chief engineer. Busy as he was, he grudgingly made time when Odo told him the box was from the Gamma Quadrant. An often dangerous, three-inert objects, a Cardassian disruptor, a disruptor, discharged, also some unknown device. What does it do? Well, not enough power to do anything much. Quark plucked the box from Odo's frustrated grasp and stormed back to his own office. But the constable stuck like gum to the Ferengi's heels. After futilely trying to shoe Odo away, Quark set the box on his desk and began to gently pick the lock. Inside were three squatty statues each more grotesque than the last. The depleted Cardassian disruptor, absolutely valueless, and the unknown device whose only value lay in its mystery. The device was shaped like a dark grey belt buckle, larger than a phaser, but smaller than a tricorder. Tiny sucker pads made it stick to the box, to Quark's hand, to the table when he yanked his paw away. There was no physical button, but Quark's sensitive ear hairs told him it had a microwave switch. He picked up his ear pricker, a Ferengi tool for manipulating frequency locks and other electromagnetic buttons, and gently probed the device. Odo glared suspiciously at Quark. Where did you get that burglar's lock pick, Quark? It's perfectly legal too. Definitely a microwave vortex switch. So, what does this thing do? I haven't the slightest idea that I have no more time to waste on you. I have a station full of less successful criminals than you to jail. Hand it over. It's mine, you can't have it. Hand it over for testing. O'Brien will thoroughly test this item before you get it back. I'm sure he'll be able to get around to it in a few days. But what if the oafax that accidentally destroys it while testing it? Then you can pay that pirate captain 60% of the nothing you'll get for it. You were spying on me. Furious, Quark leaped up, the alien device in one hand, ear pricker in the other, poised dramatically. If there's any testing to do, I'll do it myself. Stand by to be dazzled. No, put that down. I will not allow you to jeopardize this station by activating some unknown gamma-quandrant device. Quark pressed the ear pricker contact button, probing the force vortex. The ear pricker matched frequencies immediately. Deep Space Nine lurched beneath Ferengi's feet. The lights vanished into a soupy blackness. Squealing like a stuck Greek up pup. He dropped both ear pricker and alien device, feeling his body rolled flat like cookie dough. He awoke on the deck in eerie silence. The dim blue glow of emergency lighting lit the office. Quark climbed shakily to his knees, rubbing his aching ears. A puddle quivered on the floor. It drew into itself, formed up into a column of constable odo. Odo gloured as if to say, I meant to do that. Something was terribly wrong, but for a moment Quark could not identify the problem. Then he noticed his sensitive ears were sending an urgent message. Silence. Silence. Silence. No customers. No howls from the dabble players. Quark heard nothing but the steady hum of his antique Klingon clock. What? What happened to the rest of the station? Maybe your new toy made them all go away. Shaking, Quark stooped, picked up the alien device instead of his beloved ear pricker. He could not have said why. As he stood, he felt a metal band clamp around his biceps. It was Odo's hand, which he had shifted into a mannequil. The constable touched his comb badge. Odo to ops. Odo to ops. Major Kira, are you available? Anybody? Ops? Engineering? Security? A Chief O'Brien, can you get the lights on in Quark's place? Where is everybody? Alright Quark, let's take a little stroll. Odo propelled Quark out the office door and down the stair onto the main floor of Quark's place. It was dark. All the lights off, as in the office. There were no customers. Something was on the floor, a bundle. Odo knelt, examined it. I think you'd better have a look at this. Reluctantly Quark crouched, stared at the bundle. It was a man, a pharengi. It was wrong. He was covered with dried blood from a dozen wounds. Quark backpedaled from his brother's body. I had nothing to do with this. You're my witness, Odo. I didn't see a thing Quark. I was a puddle of liquid, remember? Rom had been slain by a dozen puncture wounds, each made with considerable force. Odo made a pair of long fingers, inserted them into one hole, and plucked out a flattened cylinder of soft metal, approximately ten millimeters in diameter. Do you recognize this Quark? It's not mine. I mean you, villain. Do you recognize what kind of weapon this is? Quark peaked between his fingers. Chemically propelled rifle bullet. Now, why would someone use it on a shopkeeper? Quark, I think I see more bodies. They found four other corpses, all customers shot by the same sort of chemically propelled bullets. Odo sought for a motive. Is there anything missing, Quark? Missing? Taken. Was anything taken by the killers? Taken? You mean stolen? Reminded of pharengi priorities, Quark ran to the safe. Inside were six bars of gold pressed latinum, untouched, and thousands of dabbo chips. Not a single item of value was taken. You mean, you mean they did all this for some reason, other than loot? Odo ignored the pharengi's question. I don't like this. Firearms allowed. Somebody should have heard the weapons discharge. Where is everybody? Odo dragged Quark out of the door into the promenade, then stopped in confusion. Dozens of dead bodies were piled in heaps along the bulkheads. Even manacled by Odo's fist, Quark managed to cringe, a remarkable display of contortionism. It's not my fault. I didn't do it. It's you. You did it. Silence, Quark. Do you have a chronometer that isn't tied to the station computer? I have an antique Klingon clock in my office, battery powered. Why? I need a time check for the investigation. I have a terrible feeling. I know what's happened. What investigation? Even if we're the only people left alive on this station, I am still the constable and I will conduct an investigation. Any questions? No, no questions. Klingon clock. I have a terrible feeling I know what's happened. Odo took the stairs forward at a time, dragging Quark. In the Ferengi's office the constable studied the clock. Quark, what time do you see on this clock? Quark glanced at the clock, then did a double take. Wait! That can't be right. The batteries must be low. What does it show? It says 1035, started 4-7-2-3-7-point-8, but that's wrong. That's three days from now. Besides, my pocket watch shows it's 12-38 already. Odo stared at the clock. When he spoke, his voice was thick with emotion. No, Quark, it's not wrong. Your blasted gamma quadrant device seems to have locked us into a static time bubble for three days. And somehow, during that time, something or someone attacked and destroyed Deep Space Nine. And if no one has come to be told by now, after all this time, then I suspect they aren't coming at all. Major Kiranuri's first officer of Deep Space Nine had the calm. She finally asked the question that had puzzled her all day. Has anybody seen Odo or Quark for the last 26 hours? She was not particularly concerned about the latter, but it was odd that both Constable and Public Enemy Number One should disappear simultaneously. Lieutenant Jadzia Dax, the Trill Science Officer, checked her console. Ship coming through the wormhole? No, I haven't seen them, Kiran. What is that? It doesn't match any ship designs I've ever seen, and there's something else weird. Yes? Well, it reached the wormhole so it has warp speed capability, but there is no antimatter on that ship. Kiran, these guys are visitors from the gamma quadrant. They have to be. Commander Monitor Three, Dax thinks the ship is from the gamma quadrant. The voice of Benjamin Sisko Commander of Deep Space Nine floated over the communications link from his office. I'll be right down. High above them, Sisko popped out of his office. Kiran wondered, not for the first time, how he managed to always have a uniform so crisp you could cut bread with the creases and boots so shiny you could bounce a laser off them. Sisko approached the ops table. Hail them. The alien voice echoed eerily through ops. You will surrender your prisoner or be destroyed. Kiran responded instantly. Shields up. Lieutenant Dax huddled over her science console, pre- to naturally calm. They're speaking in Cardassian, but they're not Cardassians. Open a channel, and this is Commander Sisko of Bajoran and Federation Station Deep Space Nine. We are holding no prisoners from the gamma quadrant. Prepare to be boarded. Dax get us some help. Kira futilely tried to raise the constable. Odo, Odo answer me. Security, anybody, priority one. Nobody responded to either Dax's subspace message or Kira's emergency call. Chief O'Brien responded from the engineer in well. They put a shield around the station. It's stopping all subspace communications. Can you break through it, Chief? No, Lieutenant. Sisko interrupted with a more urgent question. Chief, are our own shields holding? So far, sir, but we can't break out. Sisko nodded, decided to escalate the situation. Kira fire phasers, but just burn their noses a bit, nothing too serious. Kira's fingers ripped across her console almost too fast to see. Damn it, I can't walk on them. Firing by visual. She fired two short phasers bursts, one of each propulsion part of the alien ship. The blue phasers' stream struck their targets. Incredibly, the phaser blasts reflected like lasers of a mirror. Astonished, she fired a barrage along the alien hull. Wherever the phasers struck, they were affected. Incoming, large metallic, missile of some sort. Kira tried to lock onto the missile to shoot it down, but was as unsuccessful as before. I can't lock on the damn thing. Chief O'Brien remained unruffled. Don't worry, sir, the shields are holding. But the missile passed through the shields as it would a pane of colored glass. Everyone froze. Only Sisko moved to the tractor beam console. Batter up! The commander activated the tractor beam, swept it like a baseball bat, and sent the missile spinning off above the station. Blast, foul ball. O'Brien was stunned. What he had just seen was impossible by every rule of physics he knew. Commander, it went right through the shields like they weren't there. A white light flayed on the screen. At the same time, every electronic display in ops blinked off, then flickered back on again. Security here, Major Kira, are you all right? Find Odo immediately, urgent, incoming number two. Kira followed Sisko's lead, using the tractor bat to knock the next missile far away before it exploded. Chief, I want to know how a torpedo could slide through our shields like butter. Sir, I think we have a worse problem to worry about. What problem is that, O'Brien? Sir, when that thing exploded, it knocked our shields down for a half second. During that moment, I think they beamed some people aboard. Where? Promenade. Incoming three. Kira was kept busy for several minutes as the alien ship fired missile after missile. Somebody has to go hunt them down. Where the hell is Odo? Gone, since yesterday, I got security out looking. Just then, the station rocked as another missile exploded. O'Brien, you know this station better than anyone, beamed directly to the security office and find those invaders. Sisko to Bashir. The eager voice of Julian Bashir, the station's medical officer, answered immediately. Bashir here, sir. Where under attack, casualties might be coming your way. It could get heavy, Doctor. We've been boarded by what might be a strike team. They're on the promenade. I understand, sir. I'll prepare. Kira, patch me station wide. This is Commander Sisko. I regret to inform you that Deep Space Nine has been invaded by a hostile force. There are invaders inside the station. Everybody must evacuate the promenade immediately. Return to the habitation ring. That is the direct order. Sisko out. Major, get me a continuous feed from O'Brien. I want to know everything that happens before it happens. Miles O'Brien materialized in the security office. A platoon was just preparing to confront the invaders. I hate to say this, but you'd better take me along. The platoon crept along the promenade following Chifo Brian's tricorder readings. The chief held up his hand and they all halted. Just around the curve, fifteen are bunched up in the middle of the deck, twenty meters ahead. Lieutenant Moru, Odo's second in command, nodded and put her finger to her lips. She gestured and the platoon swept forward slowly. There was no mistaking the invaders. They looked like they stepped out of a hollow play about extra galactic stormtroopers, grey and black armored suits, shiny black bubble helmets and a strange looking weapon O'Brien had never seen before. Lieutenant Moru spoke through a universal translator PA system in her helmet. Nobody move. The aliens did not bother responding verbally. They leveled their own guns. Moru's security platoon fired first. Cold blue phaser beams glanced out and every shot hit its target. But the beams reflected in a kaleidoscopic swirl of high intensity energy bursts that burned holes through the surrounding bulkheads. description: The protagonist is investigating a Cardassian lockbox containing three statues that turn out to be strange Belt Buckles used by Ferengi for their rituals. The device in the middle resembles an ancient belt buckle and sticks firmly to anything it touches, including Quark's hand. Despite being curious about its contents, Odo insists on keeping an eye on Quark, leading to a thrilling episode of Deep Space Nine where we learn more about Ferengi customs, interstellar politics, and even the history behind Belt Buckles.

description: The introduction to Quark's "Legends of the Ferengi" podcast episode discusses the origins and philosophy behind the Ferengi characters in Star Trek's Deep Space Nine. It details how these space-faring people from the planet Ferenginar were formed based on 285 guiding principles, with a focus on honesty and fair business practices. The introduction is delivered by Quark himself, sharing that while he got paid for writing this episode, his publisher did not contribute financially to its creation. The episode then delves into a fictional story about an eccentric shopkeeper named Old from the village of Noy who sells Beatlesnuff and Latinum in exchange for lobes as proof of purchase, highlighting the Ferengi's business philosophy.

description: "The Fall of Terok Nor" is a podcast episode narrated by Joe Morton that tells the story of the 12-year-old Cisco and his mother Sara during their journey on Deep Space Nine. Through flashbacks, they relive moments where they witness the endgame of a war being played out in an endless regression. The episode explores themes of faith, destiny, and the power of perspective as they finally understand why they're here - to teach Picard about the importance of knowing that "each heartbeat is another time."
