Janeway whirled and found Carrie's horrified eyes through the fading silhouette of another engineer. The boy stared in amazement as his atoms dispersed into nothing. Initiated emergency? Without further warning, the alien transporter beam caught Janeway, choked off her breath, spirited away her words. She could only rage in silence as the engine room around her dimmed, faded, and then was gone. The moon was so beautiful. Sunlight sparkled off the surface of a small pond, reflecting back a summer sky as blue as a china bowl. On the big white house, the shutters and porch rail were painted the same color. It was a pretty effect, Paris decided. Even if it had no place 70,000 light years from the Terran Midwest, it so chillingly resembled. Paris jerked around, startled by the unfamiliar voice, and nearly ran into Harry Kim behind him. There was crew all around them, scattered as far away as the barn in the tree line, but all apparently unhurt. At the foot of the house's wraparound porch, Janeway in a group of engineers milled in a small knot while a smiling, gray-haired woman waved to them from the top of the stairs. I've got a picture of lemonade and some sugar cookies. Paris and Kim jogged forward to join up with Janeway's small band. Captain, Paris was uncertain. Janeway cut him off with the frown. Don't believe your eyes, Mr. Paris. She studied the reading on her tricorder as the old woman on the porch continued to smile. We've only been transported 100 kilometers. We're inside the array. Beside her, Kim waved his own tricorder over the setting. There's no indication of stable matter. All this must be some kind of holographic rejection. Janeway nodded and slipped her tricorder back onto her belt. Above them, the old woman clucked her tongue at them as she poured some colored liquid from a picture. You poor things. You must be worn out. Sit down and rest a while. Janeway lifted both hands to politely refuse. No, thank you. My name is Katherine Janeway, Captain of the Federation Starship Voyager. Still smiling, the old woman pushed the glass into the hands of one of the silent engineers, then wiped her fingers on the bib of her apron. Just make yourself right at home. The neighbor should be here any minute. Something seemed to catch her attention behind them and her smile widened. Why here they are now. A swarm of chattering people swept over them without warning, clasping hands kissing cheeks. It felt like some sort of ludicrous family reunion. Paris found himself pinned between Kim and a young woman in blue and white calico. The young woman smiled shyly. We're glad you dropped by. The old woman clapped her hands. Now we can get started. You're all invited to the welcoming bee. A bent, gapped-tooth-old man with nothing but a wisp of frail white hair picked up a banjo. Let's have a little music. Propping one foot up on the wooden steps, the old man stomped out a four-bit with his heel, then launched in with a banjo until it sang like a living thing. Standing shoulder to shoulder with Janeway and Kim, Paris watched the country folk dance and clap and laugh without feeling any urge to join in their festivities. Later, Janeway sat on the wide porch steps and watched their hosts spread a patchwork quilt of colored blankets out on the impossibly perfect lawn. Now they wandered placidly among the crew with bowls and platters of food balanced on their hands, inviting everyone to join them as if they were old friends. Paris and Kim rejoined Janeway at the foot of the stairs after completing a tour of the surrounding area. Paris gave their report. The crew scattered around this farm captain, but they're all accounted for. Janeway nodded and glanced around to take a quick count of who was in sight. Move around, scan the area, see if you can find anything that might be a holographic projector. The farm girl was waiting for Paris and Kim around the corner of the house, along with a big fluffy dog. She pointed toward what looked like a slanted box made of two wooden doors on the ground a few meters away. Their root cellar shot over there. It's real private. The girl smiled up at Paris, real his life, and he had to admit that the spurt of hormones leaping through his system in response to her attentions felt equally heady and real. Kim sighed and turned a shoulder to them both. Paris, she's only a hologram. Paris shrugged, ignoring the blush he felt creeping into his cheeks. No reason to be rude. Kim barked in surprise, distracting Paris from his fantasies. Spore Assistant life signs. Kim pointed at the sagging barn near the back of the property. He turned to the girl as he started forward. What's in the barn? Nothing. Just a big old pile of hay. Come on. Let's go see the duck pond. Why bother? The duck pond wouldn't be any more real than the barn or the dog or the girl. Paris moved up alongside Kim as they approached the looming structure. The girl called from behind them. There's nothing in there. It's just a dark, smelly barn. But a barn that smelled more like ozone than animals and whose wide open doors seem to suck down light like a ravening black hole. Even as Paris watched, the lines of the building hardened and pulled in on themselves, sharpening the image into a knot of menace that only hid in the shape of a barn. The level's on Kim's equipment shot skyward. It felt colder inside somehow. And as dark as a grave. Paris felt Kim move unconsciously closer and squinted at the ensigns tricorder as the girl tugged at his sleeve from behind. See? Nothing but hay. Paris didn't answer. Beside him, Kim lifted the tricorder and cocked his head with a frown. There's a life form here. Just one. Where? Kim turned slowly. His eyes locked on the readout as he swept the small sensor unit across the farm girl. The hay mound, the walls. It's everywhere. The tricorder sang as he aimed it beyond the pile of hay. I'm also reading some kind of matrix processing device. It may be the holographic generator. Paris! Kim spun, waving the tricorder toward the barn's rear wall. Humanoid life signs. Over there. A bolt of lightning seemed to explode through the building, smashing back the shadows. Paris ducked, shielding his arms with the crook of his arm. On the tail of the blaze, a presence as heavy as thundercloud swelled into being in front of them. Paris pushed Kim behind it and squeded up the farm girl as she materialized in her path. Eyes of flame, her voice changed. I'm not ready for you yet. From behind, the farm dog growled in Kim. Paris slapped his combat urgently. Paris to Janeway. He didn't feel the blow that sent him flying. Only heard the explosion inside his skull when the farm girl's fist made contact and saw the wave of darkness that crashed up to meet him as he fell. When Janeway and the engineers first rushed into the barn's dank interior, her eyes at first refused to adjust to the new dark. She glimpsed Kim back against a stall with the dog's teeth latched in his sleeve. And Paris crumpled at the farm girl's feet. Janeway swallowed bitter frustration when she realized that they were all weaponless, powerless, captured. The sound of the barn door slamming behind them made her jump. Very well, since no one seems to care for any corn. The voice belonged to the aging banjo man, but it was the woman from the house who flashed into existence barely inches from Janeway's face. Behind her, around her, everywhere the rest of the farm folk appeared in the same eye blink. We'll have to proceed ahead of schedule. Janeway opened her mouth to protest and found her voice frozen in her throat. Behind the ring of farmers, the barn's rear wall dissolved. Janeway could only stare at the horror beyond. A room longer than Voyager's longest corridor extended past the back of the barn and into an unseen distance. Slabs hovered in neat rows along either wall, each holding a naked humanoid body. Tubes and wires and probes descended from the ceiling to pierce the bodies in more places than Janeway could count. Light, as white and hurtful as a sun, blasted outward from the holographic farm folk. They shattered into nothingness, engulfing all sight and sound, eradicating the barn and everything in it until Janeway felt herself suspended, frozen, falling, and then jerking to awareness on her back. In the chamber, staring upward at an array of probes and needles, Janeway tried to struggle as the first of the implements slithered down toward her naked body. Somewhere to her left, Kim screamed. No, her mind railed. I won't allow this. They can't do this to my crew. Then the probe made its inexorable contact, cold metal against warm flesh, and pushed its way inside her chest. Her mind crashed down into silence, even as her soul still cursed their tormentor in every way it knew how. Janeway came awake without fanfare. Pushing up to her knees, she lifted her head and looked around. She was in engineering. Carrie and the rest of his team lay scattered around the bay. Some of them already sitting up, others just crawling stiffly upright. Beside Janeway, the core seal enveloping the warp drive hummed and glowed in placid oblivion, just like they hadn't left. But Janeway knew that couldn't be true. Climbing to her feet, she slapped at her combag. Janeway to bridge. Anybody there? Yes, Captain. Rollins here. How long were we over there? Almost three days. There was a delay during which Janeway assumed he checked his station's readout. Ma'am, then the key ship is powering up its engines. Tractor them. Janeway headed for the turbo lift as she signaled to every combatch throughout the ship. All senior officers report to the bridge immediately. Paris recognized the sick bay the moment he opened his eyes. Crew members staggered to their feet from beside workstations under examining beds. The medical drapes that had covered the dead doctor and nurse were neatly folded on a counter. But the bodies themselves were gone. The holographic doctor he realized. The only one left behind when the alien array evacuated Voyager. Turning, Paris scanned the crowded room for Kim as the doctor shifted its attention from a patient to Paris. Could you explain what has transpired? Ignoring the doctor Paris addressed the nearest computer. Computer, locate Ensign Kim. Ensign Kim is not on board. Paris tapped his combatch with a growing sense of panic. Paris to Captain Janeway, Kim didn't come back with us. He must still be over there. Acknowledged. Computer, how many crewmen are unaccounted for? One. Paris had already darted out the sick bay doors on his way to the bridge when the computer elaborated. Ensign Harry Kim. On the bridge Janeway commanded. Hail the Maki. Janeway tried not to fidget as Rollins fought with Voyager's damaged systems to bring the comm unit online. The image of a big Native American appeared on the screen. Commander Chikote, I'm Commander Catherine Janeway. How do you know my name? Behind him, his own bridge was in shambles. One wall of consoles dead and burned as black as space. We were on a mission to find you when we were brought here by the array. One of our crewmen is missing. Was he transported back to your ship by accident? No. Something very much like suspicion warred with uncertainty on the Maki commander's face. A member of our crew is missing too. Belana Torres, my engineer. Janeway tried to imagine what a young Starfleet Ensign and a Maki engineer could have in common that an alien might want, but failed. Commander, you and I have the same problem. I think it makes sense to try and solve it together, don't you? How can we? I'm fully aware that your crew is wanted for crimes committed in the Demilitarized Zone, but Chikote, the Demilitarized Zone is thousands of light years away. I don't think that means much right now, do you? He stared at her for a long moment, then nodded shortly. Three of us will transport to your ship. Before Janeway could object, he cut the transmission. She moved away from the center of the bridge, sparing only a quick nod toward Paris as he hurried out of the turbolift to join her beside the operations console. Rollins reported. They're powering down their engines, dropping their shields. The tingle of a transporter beam diffused through the bridge. The Maki solidified into three separate figures to Kote in the middle, each facing outward with his phaser drawn. The Vulcan member of the trio lowered his weapon the instant the transporter beam released him, but Janeway still heard half a dozen members of Voyager's crew push away from their stations to bring their own phasers to bear. She spun on them before they could fire. Put down your weapons. They hesitated, but slowly obeyed and slipped their phasers back onto their belts. You won't need those here. She waved the Chikote's phaser, then waited. It raised her opinion of Chikote when after a moment of studying her and the crew, he slowly holstered his phaser and motioned to his companions to do the same. And it made it even harder to smile a welcome to the Vulcan without feeling like she was ruining what little ground she'd gained with the Maki leader. It's good to have you back to Valk. Chikote jerked as though stabbed, lacing his hands behind his back, Tuvok turned politely to his Maki captain. I must inform you that I was assigned to infiltrate your crew, sir. I am Captain Janeway's chief of security. Chikote looked as though he couldn't decide whether to be angry at the Vulcan or at himself. Were you going to deliver us into their waiting hands, Vulcan? My mission was to accumulate information on the key activities, and then deliver you into their waiting hands. Chikote clenched his jaw and his fists, and turned away from Tuvok. His dark eyes settled on Paris, and the anger in his face gave way to cold hatred. I see you had help. Paris retorted, it's good to see you too, Chikote. The maki almost spat his response. At least the Vulcan was doing his duty as a Starfleet officer. But you? You betrayed us for what? Freedom from prison? Latinum? What was your price this time, Puka? Stepping purposefully in front of the other commander, Janeway planted a hand on his chest. You're speaking to a member of my crew. I expect you to treat him with the same respect you would have me treat a member of yours. When Chikote took a grudging step backward, she lowered her arm. He didn't seem quite able to take his gaze off Paris though, and the pure hatred Janeway saw in his eyes was disturbing. Janeway broke the silence. Now, we have a lot to accomplish, and I suggest we all concentrate on finding our people and getting ourselves back home. Tuvok made his allegiance official by moving away from Chikote to stand at Janeway's elbow. Based on my initial reconnaissance captain, I am convinced we are dealing with her single entity in the array. I would suggest that he scanned our computers in order to select a comfortable holographic environment. In effect, awaiting room to pacify us prior to biometric assessment. Paris frowned. An examination? Tuvok dipped a single nod. It is the most logical explanation. Why else would we have been released unharmed? Paris gave a little snort. And all of us were. Janeway turned to Tuvok. Break out the compression phaser rifles. Meet us in transporter room two, we're going back. We'll divide into two teams, Mr. Tuvok. While Chikote and I look for Kim and Torres, your job is to find out as much about this array as you can. She aimed a frowning glance at the alien structure dominating the view screen. It brought us here. We have to assume it can send us home. As Tuvok led Chikote and the other Maki toward the turbolift, Janeway turned to Rollins. Mr. Rollins maintained red alert. Keep us on constant transporter locks. Paris interjected softly. Captain, I'd like to go with you. The simple bravery on the young man's face caught Janeway by surprise. If this has something to do with what Chikote said, it doesn't. I just, I hate to see anything happen to Harry. Janeway clapped him on the shoulder, nodding him toward the door as she sprang into motion again. Come on. Ducks still drifted placidly on the mirror-bright surface of the holographic lake. Willows shushed beside the blue and white farmhouse. Everything was just as they'd left it, only without the dog or the farmfolk. After the banjo playing farmer remained, perched on the porches' steps with his eyes closed as he plucked something eerily wistful out of the banjo's strings. Tuvok opened his tricorder. There are no humanoid lifeforms indicated, Captain. Human torres are not within tricorder range. They may not be on the array. Chikote motioned at the banjo player. He can tell us where they are. Waving her own rifle to her left hand, Janeway tapped the Mackey standing next to her and motioned him to join Tuvok. Maintain your calm link. I don't want to lose anyone else. Tuvok nodded, then moved away. Waving Paris and Chikote had a flanker, Janeway started toward the house. The hologram on the steps kept on playing, eyes closed. Why have you come back? You don't have what I need. Janeway swallowed and urged to slap the banjo out of the hologram's hands. I don't know what you need. And frankly, I don't care. I just want our people back and I want us all to be sent home. The hologram silenced its banjo and blinked at her with an old man's patronizing smile. Well now, aren't you contentious for a minor bipedal species? This minor bipedal species doesn't take kindly to being abducted. It was necessary. Janeway felt Chikote start to move and stopped the Indians forward lunge with her elbow. He spoke, eyes intent on the hologram. Where are our people? The hologram shrugged. They're no longer here. Janeway pressed. What have you done to them? You don't have what I need. They might. You'll have to leave them. Chikote shook his head. We won't do that. We are their commanding officers. We are entrusted with their safety. They are our responsibility that may be a concept you don't understand. The hologram's eyes turned upward at Janeway, looking completely alive. No, I do understand. But I have no choice. There's so little time left. Janeway frowned. Left for what? I must honor the debt that can never be repaid. It looked off into the distance. Its expression bleak. But my search has not gone well. Janeway glanced back at Paris and Chikote, but saw only the same confusion in their eyes. Tell us what you're looking for. Maybe we can help you find it. The hologram sniffed in amused derision. You. I've searched the galaxy with methods beyond your comprehension. There is nothing you can do. You're free to go. If it's ever possible to return your people, I promise you I will. Chikote growled. That's not good enough. Janeway's frustration mounted. You've taken us 70,000 light years from our home. We have no way back unless you send us and we won't leave without the others. The hologram stood and stared off toward the duck pond. Sending you back is terribly complicated. Don't you understand? I don't have time. Enough time. Then somehow, before Janeway had fully registered the fading of the light or the disintegration of the landscape, brightness took over where the artificial world no longer stood. And she was back on board the bridge of Voyager, facing the other four members of her landing party with no idea what to say to them. No idea what had brought them here. Jan didn't hear their voices, so much as feel them. He's regaining consciousness. Then the light flared painfully bright in front of his eyes and the brilliance burned past pain and seared the back of his skull. Kim wanted to tell them to move the light away but couldn't force more than a horse moan past his lips. Still, the brightness receded on the heels of his thought and the pain washed aside as he blinked his vision clear. A face swam into focus above him. A warm face belonging to a man he didn't know. He smiled at Kim and asked gently, how do you feel? Terrible, Kim thought. I can't even see your lips move. But he made himself take an unsteady breath. What am I doing here? Where am I? Something very much like unhappiness flashed across the man's face and he turned to look towards someone on his right. A young woman took the man's shoulders and steered him away as she moved to stand beside Kim's bed. Please, don't try to move yet. You are very ill. Kim pushed up onto his elbows and tried to kick himself free of the sheets, tangling him to the bed. Ew, there's a mistake, I'm not. Then he saw the thick knots of flesh distorting his hand and arm and his voice constricted into a tiny cry. What's wrong with me? Kim had never seen such grotesque masses on anything still purported to be alive. He jerked open the neck of his gown, found even more thick swellings there, and had to blink hard against the swirling darkness of shock when it pressed the edges of his vision. Someone else screamed from the other side of the ward. Kim jerked toward the cry just as one of the medical attendants crashed into a table filled with equipment and shattered it to the ground. A boil of movement exploded from where the attendant had been, and a powerful figure leapt free with no more effort than Kim would have expended in swatting a fly. The female patient whirled as if sensing Kim and their eyes locked for just a moment. I know you. Kim thought in stark surprise. He remembered her face, dark and brooding, on one of the slabs in the back of the holographic barn. He must be one of the mikki. Orderlies were suddenly filling the room, and the mikki female nearly killed two of them fighting her way toward the door. The attendant who had first smiled down at Kim, wormed his way into the struggling knot of bodies with some unrecognizable device clutched in his hand. Hold her still. She howled like an animal, bucking underneath the combined weight of so many enemies. When the attendant reached past the wall of orderlies, and Kim heard the unmistakable hiss of a hypo-sprease, just before the mikki fell still and silent at the bottom of the bundle. The attendant gave a relieved sigh. Bring her over here. Kim hugged the sheets against him as he watched the orderlies gather the unconscious woman with a gentleness that was almost bizarre. The coarse, ropy growths, discoloring the mikki's arms and neck, trapped his attention. He wondered if whatever was wrong with him and this mikki was what happened to the rest of the crew. Was this illness why they were now alone? And what did that say about their chances of survival? Kim wished their captors had left him something more to wear than this gown and thin blanket. Thinking of death with no one else here beside him, Kim suddenly found the dull alien hospital. Unbearably cold. Janeway sat alone in a ready room. Impulse and decisions arrayed like an army across the table in front of her. Captain's log starred a 483-15.6. We've traced the energy pulses from the array to the fifth planet of the neighboring system, and believe they may have been used in some fashion to transport Kim and Torres to the planet's surface. Come in. Tuvok paused a painfully proper four steps into the room, his hands laced behind his back. Captain, I have observed something peculiar about the pulses. They are getting faster. She sat a little straighter. Faster. Tuvok dipped a single nod. The interval between each pulse has decreased by .47 seconds since we arrived. I can offer no explanation. She laughed a little, a dark, frustrated laugh that she didn't like the sound of much, and waved him forward to join her. It's only one of the mysteries we're dealing with, Mr. Tuvok. Look at this. Turning her monitor to include them both, she leaned discreetly to one side so that Tuvok could see the planetary diagram. It's virtually a desert, the whole planet. Not one ocean, not one river. It has all the basic characteristics of an M-class planet, except there are no nucleogenic particles in the atmosphere. Tuvok lands down at her, one eyebrow arched. It would mean the planet is incapable of producing clouds and rain. Janeway nodded. I've studied thousands of M-class planets I've never seen in atmosphere without nucleogenics. There must have been some kind of extraordinary environmental disaster. A yawn captured her suddenly, and she hid it behind a vigorous face scrubbing. As soon as repairs are complete, we'll set a course for the fifth planet. Captain, you require sleep. She reached for her waiting data pad with a sigh. Kim's mother called me just after he left Earth, the lightful woman, her only son. He'd left his clarinet behind and she wanted to know if she had time to send it. I had to tell her no. She glanced up at Tuvok without meaning to. Did you know he played clarinet in the Juilliard youth symphony? Tuvok hesitated. I did not have the opportunity to meet Mr. Kim. It sounded so final when he said it that way, as though he knew he'd never have the chance now. I barely knew him either. I never seemed to have the chance to get to know any of them. I have to take more time for that. It's a fine crew. I've got to get them home. The crew will not benefit from the leadership of an exhausted captain. Janeway couldn't help but smile. You're right. As usual. I've missed your counsel, Tuvok. He inclined his head in acknowledgement. I am gratified that you came after me, so I can offer it once again. I spoke to your family before I left. Are they well? Well. But worried about you. One of many Vulcan non-expressions ghosted across Tuvok's face. That would not be an accurate perception, Captain. Vulcans do not worry. Or feel gratitude, she thought. They miss you. That seemed to suit him better. As I do then. I'll get you back to them. That's a promise, Tuvok. He accepted it as stoically as he would any other truth. Janeway smiled wierly and watched as the Vulcan nodded his goodnight and retreated through the ready room door. Now, if only she could believe herself so easily. Five hours later, Janeway's combat chirped and interrupted a non-sleep characterized by endless worry and angry frustration. Bridge to Captain Janeway. Go ahead, Tuvok. We've encountered a vessel within a debris field. We're showing a humanoid life form on board. On my way. She rolled to her feet and slipped through the door to the bridge. Hail them. On the view screen, a vast scattering of ships glittered and tumbled among what could only be satellite debris and the remnants of wrecked probes. Then the screen brightened and a small, dome-headed alien appeared. Whoever you are, I found this waste zone first. Janeway allowed herself a slight smile. We're not interested in this debris, mister. Neelix. And since you aren't interested in my debris, I am delighted to meet you. An enthusiastic smile split his curious features. Janeway smiled in return. I'm Captain Catherine Janeway of the Federation starship Voyager. Neelix granted her a courtly nod. I have no idea what it means, but it sounds impressive. Do you know this area of space well, mister Neelix? I am famous for knowing it well. How may I be of service? She avoided extending a specific request for the moment. Do you know anything about the array that sending energy pulses to the fifth planet? I know enough to stay as far away from it as possible. Wait. Let me guess. You were whisked away from somewhere else in the galaxy and brought here against your will. Janeway felt a strange stirring of dread. It sounds as though you've heard this story before. Sadly, yes. Thousands of times. Well, hundreds. Maybe 50 times. His preoccupation with accuracy scattered with the wave of his hand. The caretaker has been bringing ships here for months now. Janeway frowned. The caretaker? That's what the Ocampa call him. They live on the fifth planet. Did he kidnap members of your crew? As a matter of fact, he did. It's not the first time. Do you know where he might have taken them? I've heard they're sent to the Ocampa. Nothing more. It was more than she'd known before. We appreciate any help you could give us in finding these Ocampa. I wish I could help. But as you can see, there is so much debris to investigate today. You'd be surprised that things of value some people abandon. Of course, we'd want to compensate you for your trouble. There's very little you could offer me. Unless? Yes. His dark eyes brightened eagerly. Unless? Of course you had...water? Janeway knew the surprise showed on her face. If you help us find our missing crew members, you can have all the water you want. Neelix dropped his jaw in dumb amazement. That sounds like a...reasonable arrangement. More than reasonable. And Janeway had the advantage of knowing it. Good. We'll beam you over and tow your ship into our shuttle bay. Mr. Tuvak, go to Transporter Room 2 and meet our guest. Neelix shifted uncertain eyes between Janeway and the Vulcans retreating back, as Tuvak headed for the turbo lift. Beam. Janeway lifted an eyebrow. So, Transporter technology wasn't the norm among space-faring worlds on this side of the pond. That was something worth keeping in mind. We have a technology which can take you instantly from your ship to ours. It's quite harmless. May we? He lifted his arms in acceptance. Marvelous wonder still lingering on his face as the Transporter reduced him to sparkling atoms and ghosted him away.
description: Simon & Schuster Audio presents "Star Trek Voyager: Caretaker" novelization by LA Graf, based on a teleplay by Michael Pillar and Jerry Taylor. Captain Catherine Janeway is at Auckland control when the Federation Penal Settlement requests assistance for a detainee named Thomas Parris who was previously convicted of cybercrime but found suitable for rehabilitation. Upon arriving, Janeway learns that Parris is already employed with the Federation and offers him a position, initially seeking his commitment or intelligence on behalf of the Commission to discuss further.

transcript: The silence of the dim alien infirmary only exacerbated the sick weakness in Kim's stomach. Sitting up, he tried to adopt an heir of professional calm as he tugged wide the collar of his gown, and peeped down it to inspect the knobby growths he'd already examined some five or six other times. A shaky little sigh escaped him. A groggy snarl from the other side of the infirmary snagged his attention and Kim glanced nervously toward the sound. He listened intensely for a moment, then recognized the voice as coming from the swarthy maki who had tried so desperately to escape the night before. Swinging his legs over the edge of the bed, Kim tossed a quick glance toward the closed infirmary door before padding barefoot across the cold floor to the only other occupied bed in the room. Kim studied her dark face and ridged brow, and wondered what bloodlines had carved such permanent fury into her face, painted such a dark luster through her raven black hair. It's okay, it's okay. Then the key jerked upright with a horrified gasp. Kim jumped back, suddenly glad he hadn't tried to touch her, and found himself meeting her accusing glare with what he was sure was a look of stunned innocence. Who are you? What is this place? The growths on her arm and neck were more livid and extensive than his own. Kim shrugged, and offered what he hoped was a reassuring smile. My name is Kim, Harry Kim. I'm an ensign on the starship Voyager. I was kidnapped from the array just like you. I don't know where we are. She surged out of the bed and set out across the room. What was Starfleet doing at the array? We were looking for you, actually. Kim watched her prowl from bed to table, table to wall, and realized that what he'd taken for direction was nothing more than frustration screaming for a way to get out. One minute we were in the Badlands the next. He threw his arms wide for lack of any better way to express their predicament. You mean you were trying to capture us. Yeah, consider yourself captured. He made a show of padding around at his skimpy gown. I know I have a phaser in here somewhere. The McKee glared at him before belining for the only door. I don't find this at all amusing Starfleet. He had a feeling she didn't find much amusing. She started tugging at the door handle. There's no point, it's locked. I've already tried it twice. She pushed him aside when he tried to move in front of her, and Kim could tell by the bunching of the muscles in her jaw that she had no intention of letting something like a locked door or some strange tumors keep her in confinement. He caught at her wrist as she pounded the door with increasing violence. Hey, hey, what's that going to accomplish? She was stronger than he expected, and nearly slammed him to the ground when he suspected all she meant to do was shrug him away. Her hands clenched into white knuckled fists to shower the door with a thunder of blows. What are they doing to us? What are these things growing on us? Kim stayed very still. Janeway out. The last thing she heard before reaching up to tap off her calm badge was Paris' shout of breathless relief. I see them. Paris hadn't expected them to look so awful. He touched the young Anson's face and forced a wan smile when Kim's eyes fluttered open. It took you long enough. How could I let down the only friend I've got? Paris flicked a glance at the female on the stairs above Kim. She must be Chikote's missing Maki crewman. He clapped his calm badge. Paris to Janeway. We found them, Captain. Good work. Don't wait for us. Get them to safety. It was always easy to obey commands that asked you to do what you already wanted to. You've been to pick up Kim. Paris nodded at Neelix to help Kim's friend. We gotta get out of here. Cass trotted up the stairs. This way. I know where we can get through the barrier. Hefting Kim more securely across his shoulder. Paris followed her as quickly as he could. The barrier filled the end of the passage, like a spider's web spun from light. When he eased Kim to the ground near a spot on the web that had unraveled away from the floor. Cass got down on her knees beside the breach. Whatever you do, don't touch it. We've been told it'll burn your skin off. Neelix stumbled in with the Maki woman clinging to his arm. You crawl through a hole that small? It was the only way out. And as if to demonstrate, Cass slipped her legs through the darkness and slithered nimbly under. Neelix almost melted with appreciation. Isn't she remarkable? On the other side of the barrier, Cass took Kim's hands to help him through. Guiding the Maki woman through behind Kim, Paris stepped aside to motion Neelix forward. Neelix scrambled under the damaged barrier without having to be encouraged. As Neelix was through, Paris went to his knees and slid his phaser under the breach. The motion to the bare rock wall still standing between them and freedom. I've got it set. Just point and fire. Neelix obeyed without question. The phasers buzzed in counterpoint to the falling force field. And hot stones splattered the floor as Paris pulled himself through the hole. The wall Neelix burned through was barely three meters thick. Outside, smoke rose in columns all the way to the distant horizon, flagging other tunnels already sealed shut by the array. Paris slapped his combatch. Paris Devoyager, can you lock onto us now? Rollins' voice barely sounded above the roaring wind. Affirmative. But I'm only reading five signals. The others are... A burning flash of light tore past directly overhead, thundering his last words as it struck the ground somewhere below the horizon. The ground lurched like a mad animal beneath him, and Paris heard the terrifying crack of rock on far away. Shoving came into the dirt, Paris threw himself across the underman and waited, with his face buried against Kim's back into the rumble of falling stone died away. When he rolled to look behind, the mouth of their exit belched dust from a cave in too deep to see. He fumbled for his combatch. Paris to Janeway. No answer. Chicote. Tufa. Do you read? Pulling Kim to his feet, Paris switched comb channels. Voyager, prepare to transport everyone in this group except me. Nelix angled a disbelieving stare up at Paris as Paris passed Kim into his arms. You're not thinking of going back in there. Paris didn't take time to answer. As he prepared to head back for the tunnel, Nelix sighed and bobbed forward to touch his nose briefly to Kess'es. The fool needs company. Take care of them, dearest. I'll see you later. She nodded mutly, gathering Kim and the McKee close against her as Nelix gently fixed his own combatch to her shift. Smiling, Paris tapped open a channel to the starship. Voyager, make that three to beam up. Lock onto the other combatch and energize. The warbling tremolo of the transporter tingled the air around them and Nelix danced away from it to join Paris. Then, impatient to be on his way, Paris clapped Nelix once on the arm as a signal to follow, and ducked back into the cave. Paris heard the sounds of movement just before rounding the corner to find Janeway and the others. Chevak was unconscious, green blood flowing from a gas in his head, and Chikote was missing. Dragging the Vulcan toward the surface, Janeway pointed behind her and gasped. Chikote's back there. His legs broken. While Nelix stayed with the captain, Paris dashed into the darkness in search of the McKee. He saw that the stairs were collapsed and sagging, even before a new tremor crashed through the tunnel like a tsunami. When Paris grabbed blindly at the stair railing, the ancient metal crumbled like sandstone at his touch. He tightened his grip on the rail, sliding onto his bottom in search of traction on the damp cave floor, and just as abruptly, the shaking stopped. Climbing to his knees on the lip of the overhang, Paris looked downward toward where he knew the stairs ought to be. Assuming the stairs were still there at all, the steps had sagged a good two feet. The rest of the railing was torn out of the wall, leaving only the weakest of supports still holding the stairs from falling. His face creased with pain. Chikote scowled up at Paris from several steps down. Get out of here, Paris, before the whole thing comes down. It was only a two-foot step, not even a hop, onto the swaying length of the stair. I intend to, as soon as I get you up. Chikote stiffened at Paris' first step. They'll collapse, we'll both die. Every inch of Paris' insides quivered as he shifted his weight forward. On the other hand, if I save your butt, your life will belong to me. Isn't that some Indian custom? The pain in his expression only made Chikote's glower more fierce. Wrong tribe. Paris placed his second foot on the stair. I don't believe you. I think you'd rather die than let me be the one to rescue you. Just then the stairs dropped, the bottom of the shaft. Fine. Be a fool. If I have to die, at least I'll have the pleasure of watching you go with me. Paris planted his feet as firmly as he could on the rocking structure, and hauled Chikote onto his shoulders. Isn't there some Indian trick where you can turn yourself into a bird and fly? Why us out of you? You're too heavy. Paris tried not to pay attention to the long, empty depth, stretching into infinity just a misstep to his right. When he drew near the top, Janeway leaned down to pull him across the dizzying gap. He heard the staircase crash into wreckage behind him, but was too frightened to look back. Janeway kept her hand locked on his elbow all the way up to the surface. Paris almost thought it was possessive relief he read in her determined features. But maybe that was just his imagination. Janeway had never been so grateful for the efficiency of modern medicine. Janeway and Torres were quickly healed, and even Chikote's leg and two-vox head injury were nothing more than memories by the time Rollins called down to sickbay to tell Janeway that two Kason ships were making a run for the array. Sending Neelix and Kest to their quarters, where she hoped they'd be safe for a time, Janeway let Chikote and Torres return to their ship as she took the rest of her crew with her to the bridge. She wasted no time when the Turbulift released them into the bridge's busy clamor. Tearing the weapon systems online, Red Alert. Chikote and the McKee were ahead of them, already trying to get in front of the lead Kason ship as the array loomed large and dark ahead of them. The caretaker still spat fat gobs of white light toward the planet's surface. Tuvak glanced up from his panel. The lead Kason ship is hailing a scat. Onscreen. Jabin's cracked, dust-stained face rippled into being on the viewscreen. Have you come to investigate the entity's strange behavior too, Captain? All we care about is getting home, Jabin. We're about to transport over to the array to see if we can arrange it. The Kason leader cracked a harsh laugh. I'm afraid I can't permit you to do that. We have no dispute with you. We have a dispute with anyone who would challenge us. This is ridiculous. We have no intention of challenging you. But Jabin already signaled angrily to someone offscreen. And I have no intention of letting anyone with your technological knowledge board the array. Jabin, we can discuss this like two civilized... Be cut off communications with a snarl. And Jain Wei saw the flash of the Kason ship's weapons fire just before the energy packets detonated against their screens. Fire phasers, evasive pattern Delta IV. They made a clean hit, raking the Kason ship from stem to stern. As the McKee ship's single phaser bang slashed at the second Kason's exposed underside, Jain Wei slapped open the comm channel. Jain Wei to Chikote. Tuvak and I are beaming to the array. Can you hold off the Kason? I think so, Captain. Good. She left him to his fight. Standing. Mr. Paris, you have the comm. He hesitated a mere second, as though not sure she'd actually spoken to him. Then he darted for the helm before she could change her mind. Yes, ma'am. She joined Tuvak at the Turbulift. Ensign Rollins maintained transporter locks, emergency beam out status. Then she let the doors close and whisk them to the transporter room. The holographic barn on the array seemed darker somehow. From somewhere nearby in the darkness, a lonely banjo played. Tuvak's tricorder sank counterpoint to the disintegrating melody. He gestured farther back into the barn without looking up from his sensors. The data processing system is behind this wall, Captain. You know what to do. As Tuvak moved away, Jain Wei stepped gingerly into the deeper darkness. She didn't see the old man so much as sense him, huddled in a corner. The banjo on his lap drifted mistily between his hands, as uncertain and ephemeral as its music. He looked up at Jain Wei with a melancholy smile. You are nothing, if not persistent. She paused to kneel a half meter from him. We need you to send us back where we came from. That isn't possible. The hologram faded back into the shadows, then swelled towards solidity again, this time without the banjo. I have barely enough strength to complete my work. You're sealing the conduits before you die. If I don't, the Kazon will steal the water. But in a few years, when the Ocampa's energy runs out, it won't be. It won't matter. They'll be forced to come to the surface, and they won't be able to survive. Without me, they're helpless. I've failed them. He turned to her with eyes impossibly dark. You once spoke to me of your responsibility for your crew. The Ocampa were my responsibility. When you did turn their planet into a desert, didn't it? Jain Wei thought she saw a very human surprise flutter across the holograms' features. We know there was an environmental disaster about the time you arrived. That was the debt that could never be repaid, wasn't it? We're explorers from another galaxy. We had no idea our technology would be so destructive to their atmosphere. Two of us were chosen to stay behind, to care for them. There's another like you here? The entity shook its head. Not anymore. She went off to look for more interesting places. She never understood why the Ocampa needed so much care. They didn't realize how vulnerable they were. Why were you bringing ships here, infecting people with a fatal illness? Its face folded into an expression of dismay and distress. I never meant any harm. They didn't die from illness. because they were incompatible. Incompatible? Don't you understand? I have been searching the galaxy for a compatible biomolecular pattern. In some individuals I found cellular structures that were similar, but... Janeway could only stare. You've been trying to procreate? I needed someone to replace me, someone who would understand the enormous responsibility of caring for the Ocampa. Only my offspring could do that. Did you ever consider allowing the Ocampa to care for themselves? It seemed horrified of the suggestion. There. Children. Janeway reached out to touch its arm. Children have to grow up. We're explorers too. Most of the species we've encountered have overcome all kinds of adversity without a caretaker. It's the challenge of surviving on their own that helps them to evolve. Maybe your children will do better than you think. They are ignorant, dependent, bipeds. Then educate them before you die, give them the knowledge they need to survive. It shook its head. Would you put your most dangerous technology in the hands of your children? I would be sending them the means to destroy themselves. You said yourself that in a few years they'd be doomed anyway. We have another saying. If you give a man a fish, he will eat for a day. If you teach a man to fish, he will eat for a lifetime. Voyager to Janeway. We've got problems here. Behind Kim's voice, the crash and wail of ship's sirens wove a horrible reinforcement to his words. The Kazon just got some backup. The Kazon's sensors put the newly arrived Kazon cruiser at a good 80 times the size and mass of the little fighters they'd already been fighting. Power and engine output flashed right off the screens, and Chikote didn't see any reason to waste the time recalibrating sensors just so he could get an exact greeting. On screen, the monster ship had already carved half way through Voyager's forward hull, and was dogging it like a terrier on a bone. Chikote commented needlessly to Tori's. They're in trouble. I'm setting a collision course, but the guidance system is disabled. I'll have to pilot the ship manually. Get the crew ready to beam to Voyager. As Tori's ran off to prepare the crew to evacuate, Chikote opened a subspace channel. Paris, my crew's coming over. Tell one of your crackerjack starfully transported chiefs to keep a lock on me. I'm gonna try to take some heat off your tail. Acknowledged, but don't even think for a second this gets us even. Your life is still mine, Puka. Paris out. Chikote gritted his teeth as the huge alien cruiser began its lumbering turn to face him. As his ship tore past Voyager and honed in on the Kazon monster, Chikote saw the Kazon loose a ball of burning plasma that slammed into him like a fist. Paris's voice came back at him through the wailing of alarms. I'm getting you out of there, Chikote. The next blast from the Kazon exploded a panel at the back of the bridge. Not yet. You're breaking up. Stand by to transport. If Voyager transported now, the Kazon would dust this little ship like so much space debris, and all they'd have for Chikote's efforts was one less target to draw the enemy's fire. Wait! Pumping the last of his ship's power into a leap he knew would probably rip its loyal engines apart. Chikote spiraled toward the cruiser and waited until nothing but starship filled his view screen. Now! The brilliance of destruction overwhelmed him, and spangles of light closed around him and lifted him away to nothing. A peel of what might have been summer thunder trembled through the darkened barn. The holographic projection lifted its eyes to a point beyond Janeway's shoulder. Twisting around, she saw Tuvak approaching through the darkness. I can access the system to send us back to Federation's face, but it will take several hours to activate. Janeway turned back to the entity. Unless you help us. The hologram looked away. I wish I could, but I have very little time left. Lip's moving, it stared blindly outward for several seconds before its voice abruptly returned. I am taking your advice. I've begun to transmit the contents of my databanks to the Okampa. I have also initiated a self-destruct program. Janeway's heart leapt into her throat. If you destroy the array, we'll have no way to get home. The Okampa's enemies cannot be allowed to control this installation. In minutes, it will be destroyed. You have to go now. She thought at first that the entity had physically banished them, thrown them somewhere far from the array, with the same powerful abruptness with which it had seized their ships and stolen their bodies. Then the darkness of the barn leapt back into existence, flicked away, and dashed back again. Cloudy, smoke-filled light suddenly became the final reality, and she recognized the huge open room now around them, as the same chamber Kim and Paris had discovered on their first visit to the array. Whatever had happened, it had eradicated whatever maintained the holographic projection system. She signaled the ship. Voyager, report! Paris's voice crackled across the open channel. A Kazon ship has just collided with the array, Captain. Are you alright? Affirmative. Stand by. Where the entity's holographic projection had huddled only moments before, a huge, vaporous creature now heaved and groaned. The termination program has been damaged. The Kazon must not gain control of this installation. Then the creature folded down with a heavy sigh, until the last glimmer of its physical form missed it completely away. At Jainway's feet, a misshapen lump of what looked like some alien ore twinkled weakly before slipping into total darkness. Tuvak moved up alongside her. Shall I activate the program to get us back? And what happens to the Ocampa after we're gone? Captain, any action we take to protect the Ocampa would affect the balance of power in this system. The Prime Directive would seem to apply. Would it? If he were human, Jainway would have suspected him of invoking the Prime Directive in an effort to manipulate her. We never asked to be involved, Tuvak. But we are. She smiled sadly in unspoken apology. I'm afraid your family will have to wait a little longer for you. Tuvak nodded, and Jainway tapped her combat. Away team to Voyager, two to transport. Voyager Bridge was positively crowded by the time Jainway and Tuvak arrived. Torrez and Chikote looked up. Chikote smelled like the burned remains of a fuel depository. The captain trotted down the steps to her command chair. Mr. Tuvak, ready a tri-cobalt device. Mr. Kim, open a channel to the Kazon. The view screen rippled and reformed, replacing the image of a damaged array with Jainway's weather-beaten face. Be advised, Captain. I have called for additional ships. I'm calling to warn you to move your vessels to a safe distance. I intend to destroy the array. Jainway's face went still with shock. You can't do that. I can. And I will. She tossed a nod at Kim. End transmission. Almost immediately, the ship rocked beneath a new torpedo strike. Kim looked at his console. They're increasing fire, Captain. Chills are holding. Move us to 400 kilometers from the array, Mr. Paris. Torrez lunged across the railing almost into Jainway's lap. What are you doing? That array is the only way we have to get back home. I'm aware everyone has families and loved ones at home they want to get back to. So do I. But I'm not willing to trade the lives of the Ocampa for our... convenience. We'll have to find another way home. Torrez barked, angry laughter. What other way home is there? Chikote grabbed her when she would have surged forward, and Torrez whirled on him. Who is she to be making these decisions for all of us? She's the captain. You must have been a fine commander when Starfleet had him. Jainway thought. That was the Federation's loss. Tuvok looked up from his tactical station. The Tricoble device is ready. Paris sang out from the con. In position. Taking a deep breath, Jainway nodded stiffly. Fire. Voyager shuttered only faintly when the Tricoble device was released. A spinning glimmer of energy flashing like a brilliant diamond, arced out from under the nose of the starship, speeding through the glowing sea of battle debris on its way toward the array. As the deadly packet disappeared into the tangled strutwork of the array, a great blossom of destruction boiled outward. It was over. No one spoke for a very long time. Then Kim broke the silence. The lead Kason ship is hailing us. On screen. The hatred blazing in the Kason leader's eyes nearly drilled a hole through the starship's heart. You have made an enemy day. Then he cut the channel without giving Jainway a chance to reply. Not that she had anything to say. Tuvok glanced up from his console. They are withdrawing, captain. On the view screen, an ever expanding plasma cloud that used to be the array swelled outward until it filled the night. Obscuring, at least for the moment, all thought of life beyond itself, all hope of anything but the salvation. It no longer offered. The Stepping into the captain's ready room, Paris wasn't sure what to expect. Jainway turned away from the observation window as the door whispered shut behind him. You asked to see me, captain? She nodded, folding her hands. Mr. Paris, you have a problem. I've invited Chikote and the other Mackie to become part of this crew. It seemed the only reasonable thing to do under the circumstances. Paris swallowed an insane urge to giggle. Will you provide a bodyguard for me, captain? Jainway smiled oddly. It seems you already have one. Mr. Chikote said something about his life belonging to you. He'll be taking responsibility for your safety. Paris allowed himself a thoroughly evil grin. I think I'm going to enjoy this. Jainway cocked her head in speculation. Don't be so sure. He's also going to be my first officer. Everyone aboard the ship will report to him, including the lieutenant assigned to the calm. At first he was going to ask what the hell this had to do with him. Then something in his throat nodded before any sound came out, and his brain caught up an instant later. Me? I've entered into the ship's log on the state that I'm granting a field commission of lieutenant to Thomas, Eugene, Paris. She leaned across the table to offer him her hand and a welcoming smile. Congratulations. Paris wrapped her hand in both of his. For the first time in my life, I don't know what to say. You've earned this, Tom. I'm only sorry your father won't know. He'll know when we get back. Because if he could be standing here with a renewed commission, he had to believe that anything was possible. Never! It's just you, Tom. You don't have to answer anything. You don't have to say anything. You don't have to say anything. Nelix's voice warbled through the open ready room doors just as Janeway was preparing to leave. Ah, Captain! We were just coming to see you. Janeway greeted Neelix and Kes with a smile. We've supplied your ship with water, Neelix. It's ready to go. Neelix bobbed his head nervously. Well, you see, that's what we wanted to discuss. We'd like to go with you. Janeway blinked at him. I'm sorry, this isn't a passenger ship. Kes jumped in. Of course not, we won't be passengers. Neelix finished for her. We'll be valuable colleagues. Whatever you need is what I have to offer. You need a guide? I'm your guide. You need supplies. I know where to procure them. I have friends among races you don't even know exist. You need a cook. You haven't lived until you've tasted my angla busk. It will be my job to anticipate your needs before you know you have them. A puckish twinkle lit in his eye. And I anticipate your first need will be... me. Neelix pulled Kes into a possessive embrace. And where I go, she goes. In my own way, I'm an explorer, Captain. On my world, exploration meant defying the caretaker just to walk on the surface. I took that chance because I had to. My father taught me that the greatest thing an ocapa can do is to open her mind to all the experiences and challenges that life has to offer. I can't begin to imagine where this ship might take us. I know I'll never see my home world again. But I want very much to be part of your journey. Janeway studied her in gentle amazement. Sying, Neelix hugged Kes to him even tighter. Ah, isn't she remarkable? Yes, Janeway thought and wonder. Aren't we all? The bridge was still crowded, but most of the debris had been removed since the K-Zon battle. On the view screen, Kes's home world drifted lazily, an unchanging marble of Dusty Amber. Chikote waited at the first officer station, wearing his new Starfleet uniform as though he'd never taken it off. At engineering, Torrey's looked only a little uncomfortable in her corresponding golden black. Stepping down to her command share, Janeway tried to touch each expected look with a reassuring nod. We're alone in an uncharted part of the galaxy. We've already made some friends here, and some enemies. We have no idea of the dangers we're going to face. But one thing is clear. Both crews are going to have to work together if we are to survive. That's why Commander Chikote and I have agreed that this should be one crew, a Starfleet crew. And as the only Starfleet vessel assigned to the Delta Quadrant will continue to follow our directive to seek out new worlds and explore space. Our primary goal is clear. Even at maximum speeds, it would take 75 years to reach the Federation. I'm not willing to settle for that. There's another entity like the caretaker out there somewhere who has the ability to get us there a lot faster. We'll be looking for her. And we'll be looking for wormholes, spatial rifts or new technologies to help us. Somewhere along this journey, we'll find a way back. Turning, she rested her hands on the back of Paris's chair and looked beyond his head at the eternal possibilities waiting for them behind every planet, every star. Mr. Paris, set a course. We're home. The Earth is the most powerful star in the world. The Earth is the most powerful star in the world. The Earth is the most powerful star in the world. The Earth is the most powerful star in the world. Star Trek Voyager, Caretaker, was read by Robert Piccardo. It was adapted for audio by L.A. Graff from her novelization, based on the Teleplay, by Martin. The Teleplay, by Michael Pillar and Jerry Taylor. Story by Rick Berman and Michael Pillar and Jerry Taylor. The director was Jill Dembe Guest. The recording engineer was Rick Dasher at Mok Grau recording services, with tape editing by Stephen Strassman. Post-production and sound design by Gary Fink. Post-production supervisor was Linda Walman. Original music was composed by Sam McCallay, Carl Shurps, Richard Haman, Eve Big Larian, and Richard Emmett. Pea music from the Star Trek television series was composed by Alexander Courage and Gene Roddenberry, and used courtesy of brewing music. The associate producer was Florence Barrow Adams. description: In this episode, "089 - Star Trek Voyager Audiobook: Caretaker 2 of 2," starfleet officer Harry Kim, captured and held in an alien infirmary by a maki named Rina after the end of "Caretaker 1 of 2," tries to negotiate his way out while explaining he was on the USS Voyager when they were kidnapped. Despite being interrogated repeatedly about their location and purpose, Kim maintains his innocence and insists on his right to freedom.

transcript: Star Trek Voyager Full Circle by Kirsten Byer or W. Fred Byer If you enjoy this and the other audiobooks on my channel, please like and subscribe. Part 1, What Fates Impose, June 2380 Prolog Then this was everything Chakote imagined it would be, perhaps more. Though the simulated version created by Tom Paris on Voyager's Holodec many years earlier had its charms. It bore the same relation to the real thing as replicated eggplant parmesan did to, well, food. If one could be struck by serenity, such was the cumulative effect of the water of the Grand Canal lapping gently beneath the ponted liscalzi, the faintly pungent yet sweet taste of the air, the dim luminescence of the crescent moon hanging above. Complemented by its dimmer counterparts in the small vote of candles sitting atop the cafe's scattered outdoor tables and the light blanket of damp warmth that nature had tossed over the city on this summer night. La Zuca, the 15th restaurant to bear the name on the site since its establishment in the mid-19th century, was close enough to the most heavily trafficked of Santa Clausi streets that it should have been buzzing with life on a night such as this. The closest public transport station was two blocks away, having long ago replaced the ancient Santa Lucia railway station. The bridge of bare feet, arched over the canal less than a hundred metres in the distance. And by all reports, the food was authentic Northern Italian and absolutely delicious. Still, the cafe was all but deserted, and Chacote honestly wouldn't have wanted it any other way. It stood to reason that only days after an attack by a monstrous Borg cube, residents might still be skittish about returning to their normal lives or venturing too far from home. But having faced the Borg down more than once, Chacote could not share their pessimism. At least, La Zuca had been open, unlike many other local businesses. If Catherine didn't arrive soon, he might have to go ahead and at least sample the cuisine without her. He'd already opened the first of what he hoped would be at least a couple of bottles of red wine. There would be no scent the whole on the menu this evening. He didn't think she'd mind if he started them off with a small anti-pastel appetizer from the menu he'd already had time to memorise. With luck, if he ordered it now, it would arrive at the same time as the Admiral. Admiral Janeway. Chacote had to smile to himself. It wasn't that Catherine didn't deserve to be a vice-admiral. She'd been a Starfleet captain for years before taking command of Voyager and bringing her safely through the Delta Quadrant. Her record was unassailable. What Chacote still found hard to believe, even two and a half years since Voyager's return from its seven-year journey, was that Catherine had so readily accepted the promotion upon their return to Earth. Of course, it would have been bad for him to turn down the offer from Starfleet Command. And if the history of this timeline bore any resemblance to that of the Admiral Janeway, who had assisted her younger counterpart in bringing Voyager home, it did suggest that Catherine would continue to climb steadily through the ranks. But she had been his captain when they met, and for the first seven years of their life together. Though technically also a captain in his own right, Chacote had chosen to accept the position of her first officer when his Machuise vessel was sacrificed to save Voyager in their first battle with the Kazone. He still vividly remembered the sight of Catherine. Standing on Voyager's bridge with her chin held high, but her heart clearly torn as she struggled briefly with her decision to destroy the array that had brought them to the Delta Quadrant, and was their best chance for a timely return home. When she had finally given the order to end some Kim to fire tricobolt payloads at the array, Belana Torres had demanded furiously to know what gave her the right to make that decision for all of them. Even Chacote had been surprised at the time by how quickly a response had formed on his lips. She's the captain, he had said, settling the matter once and for all. Even now it was hard not to see Catherine in the light of her most compelling and inspiring role, the center seat of a Starfleet vessel. As his captain, she had earned his respect and loyalty. Harder to pinpoint was the exact moment along the way when she had also won his heart. Still, the damage was done. In nearly ten years of discovery and exploration, success and bitter loss on the field of battle, and ultimately, the tedious demands of Judy, he had never wavered in his commitment to her. Finally the time had come to make that commitment more real and permanent than fate had allowed until this night. In the past he might have felt a certain amount of anxiety at the prospect, but now the idea that he and Catherine would move side by side into their future brought only a sense of peace and relief. It was simple. It was right. It felt like destiny. The only thing troubling him even slightly was the fact that Catherine was now over a full hour late. Most likely, Chacotei assured himself, she and the rest of the admiralty were still working long hours in the aftermath of the attack. He hadn't spoken to her, as he'd hoped to, when Voyager was finally allowed to enter the soul system, following their deep space mission to the Yaris Nebula. The area had been restricted after the appearance of what, by the brief reports he'd heard, had been a massive cube, and traffic in and around Earth was only now returning to normal. They had agreed to meet for this dinner almost a year earlier. Only three weeks ago, Catherine had reminded him of their date, as if he needed a reminder, and half teasingly described the cruel fate that would befall him should he stand her up. He knew that in the interim, she had undertaken a classified mission, but surely she was backed by now. Chacotei refused to doubt that wherever she was at this moment, it was here, with him, that she wanted to be and would be as soon as possible. Opposite him at her empty place was a gift he had long wished to return to her.
